remark: 1. A village in Galilee where Jesus performed a miracle.
introduce: Cana is a village in the region of Galilee that appears in the New Testament; it is a place name presumed to refer to a site north or northeast of Nazareth. According to the Gospel accounts, it is described as the place where Jesus' early ministry and miraculous acts took place.
biblecontents: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus' mother was there (John 2:1). Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him. (John 2:11). Jesus came again to Cana of Galilee, where He had made the water into wine (John 4:46). The sons of Zebedee and two other disciples were together, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee was with them (John 21:2).
geography: Scholars hold differing opinions about the exact location of Cana. The most likely candidates are Kafr Kanna, about 8 km north of Nazareth, and Khirbet Qana, about 13 km to the northwest. These sites lie near the ancient route linking the Sea of Galilee and Nazareth, and at that time they took the form of agriculture-based settlements.
history: Under Roman rule, the region of Galilee was a mixture of Jewish tradition and Hellenistic culture. At that time Cana was a typical small village of Palestine, and its economy depended mainly on farming and the cultivation of grapes. The wedding customs described in the Gospel of John reflect the communal rites and everyday life of Jewish society of that day.

remark: 2. A brook forming the boundary between the descendants of Ephraim and the descendants of Manasseh.
introduce: Kanah is a place name mentioned in the Book of Joshua in the description of the boundaries and territories of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh; it refers to a brook or hill country in the central region of the ancient land of Canaan.
biblecontents: Kanah was the point joining Tappuah, on the western boundary of the tribe of Ephraim, with the brook of Kanah, and the land west of that brook was the boundary assigned to the tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 16:8). In connection with the boundary of the tribe of Manasseh, this place name also shows that the brook of Kanah served as a boundary line separating the towns of Manasseh from the towns of Ephraim that lay among them (Joshua 17:9).
geography: Geographically, Kanah is presumed to be the region of Wadi Qana, which flows from the central mountain range of Palestine westward to the Mediterranean coastal plain. This stream is called Nahal Kanah today, and it forms a natural boundary line dividing the hill country of Ephraim from the hill country of Manasseh.
history: In the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, this region was used as a buffer zone between the Canaanite city-states and the tribes of Israel, and as a natural landmark marking territorial boundaries. Kanah has historical significance as a topographical reference point for making clear the allotment of land and jurisdiction in the process of the tribes' settlement.

remark: 3. A town of the tribe of Asher near Hammon and Rehob.
introduce: Kanah is a place name that appears in Joshua 19:28; it is mentioned as one of the border areas allotted to the tribe of Asher in the distribution of land among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: It is a place included in the boundary area allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, and it is recorded as part of the region that runs through Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah as far as Greater Sidon (Joshua 19:28).
geography: Kanah is presumed to be at the same location as present-day Qana in southern Lebanon, and it lies inland to the southeast of Tyre. This area has the topographical feature of being where the coastal plain that the tribe of Asher occupied meets the mountainous region.

remark: 2. The name of Palestine west of the Jordan River.
introduce: Canaan refers to a land located in the Fertile Crescent between the eastern coast of the Mediterranean and the Jordan River in the ancient Near East; in the Bible it is a geographical name frequently mentioned in connection with Abraham's route of travel and as the object of the covenant.
biblecontents: The boundary of Canaan extended from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, and on to Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim (Genesis 10:19). Terah took Abram, Lot, and Sarai out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan, but they stayed in Haran (Genesis 11:31). Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions they had gathered in Haran, and went to the land of Canaan, and there they arrived (Genesis 12:5). When Abram came to the oak of Moreh at Shechem, the Canaanites were living in the land at that time (Genesis 12:6). Because the Canaanites and the Perizzites were living in the land at that time, a quarrel arose between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot (Genesis 13:7). Abram lived in the land of Canaan, while Lot stayed in the cities of the plain and moved his tent as far as Sodom (Genesis 13:12). God promised Abram the land of the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites (Genesis 15:21). After Abram's wife Sarai had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, she gave her servant Hagar to Abram (Genesis 16:3). God made a covenant with Abram and his descendants to give them all the land of Canaan, where he was a sojourner, as an everlasting possession (Genesis 17:8). Sarah died in Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan (Genesis 23:2).
geography: Canaan is a region bordered on the west by the Mediterranean Sea, on the east by the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, on the north by the Lebanon mountain range, and on the south by the Negev desert. It has diverse topographical features, being divided into the coastal plain, the central hill country, and the Jordan Rift Valley, and from ancient times it was a strategic crossroads through which the trade routes of the Way of the Sea and the King's Highway passed.
history: In the Bronze Age, Canaan was run under a system of independent city-states, and it was subject to political and economic influence between the civilizations of Egypt and Mesopotamia. After the middle of the second millennium BC it took the form of a vassal state under Egyptian rule, and various Semitic tribes migrated there and settled, forming a mixed culture.

remark: 「Enclosing the city」 1. It was a chief city of Perea.
introduce: Gadara was one of the cities belonging to the ancient Decapolis league, a strategic stronghold located southeast of the Sea of Galilee. In the New Testament it is mentioned as the place where the event of the healing of demon-possessed men occurred.
biblecontents: When Jesus came to the region of the Gadarenes on the other side, two demon-possessed men came out from among the tombs and met Jesus (Matthew 8:28).
geography: Gadara is located about 10 km southeast of the Sea of Galilee and is identified with the area of Umm Qais in present-day northern Jordan. It sits on high ground overlooking the Yarmuk River and the Jordan River valley, and so its terrain includes rugged slopes.
history: In the Hellenistic period Gadara was an important center of culture and learning, and in the Roman period it exercised self-government as a member of the Decapolis league of cities. At that time this region was strongly influenced by Greek culture, and traces of a typical Roman city remain, such as a Roman theater, a colonnaded street, and public baths.

remark: 「Holy place」 1. A place in the wilderness of Zin.
introduce: Kadesh is an important oasis of the ancient Near East and a strategic stronghold located between the Negev desert and the wilderness of Zin. In the Bible it appears mainly under the name Kadesh-barnea, and it served as a long-term stopping place and administrative center on the route of Israel's exodus.
biblecontents: Kadesh is recorded as a region through which the allied forces of Chedorlaomer passed when they conquered the Amalekites (Genesis 14:7). In the time of Abraham it is mentioned as a region lying between Kadesh and Shur, and it is also the place where Hagar met the angel of the LORD beside a spring (Genesis 16:14). Afterward it also appears as a region where Abraham lived (Genesis 20:1). In the Book of Numbers, after the Exodus, it is the place where the people of Israel sent out spies and received their report (Numbers 13:26), and the place where Moses' sister Miriam died and was buried (Numbers 20:1). It is also the place where Moses sent messengers to the king of Edom to request passage (Numbers 20:14, 20:16), and the point where they stayed before moving on to Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22). It is also the scene of the event in which Moses failed to uphold God as holy at the waters of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin (Numbers 27:14). Israel also camped at Kadesh after passing through the wilderness of Zin (Numbers 33:36).
geography: Kadesh is presumed to be present-day Tell el-Qudeirat, and it is located at the boundary between the northeastern Sinai Peninsula and the Negev plateau. Because there is a perennial oasis here, it has the geographical advantage of securing a water supply that allowed a large number of people to stay in the arid desert environment. To the south the wilderness of Zin stretches out, and to the north it serves as the gateway to the passage leading to the southern hill country of Canaan.
history: From the Bronze Age this region was used as a major stopping place for caravans crossing the desert. Kadesh lay at a crossing of the trade route linking the Arabian region with Canaan and had high political and military value. According to the biblical record, this region bordered on Edom, and it became a geographical variable that created diplomatic tension with Edom when Israel's route of travel was being determined.

remark: 「Sanctuary of Barnea」 1. The oasis in the wilderness where Israel, who left Egypt under the leadership of Moses, stayed the longest.
introduce: Kadesh-barnea is the principal base and center of wilderness life where the people of Israel stayed on their journey toward Canaan after leaving Egypt, according to the Bible. Geographically it lies on the southern boundary of Judah, at the entrance by which one enters Canaan from Egypt.
biblecontents: Kadesh-barnea was the reference point that determined the southern boundary of Canaan (Numbers 34:4). Joshua conquered the region from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza (Joshua 10:41). Caleb stated that when he was forty years old, at the time of the conquest of Hebron, he had been sent by Moses from Kadesh-barnea as a spy (Joshua 14:6, Joshua 14:7). It is recorded as one of the points through which the southern boundary line of the tribe of Judah passed (Joshua 15:3). From Mount Horeb by way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea was an eleven-day journey (Deuteronomy 1:2). The people of Israel left Mount Horeb and came to Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:19). The time it took from Israel's leaving Kadesh-barnea until crossing the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years (Deuteronomy 2:14). When the people of Israel were commanded at Kadesh-barnea to go into the land of Canaan, they grumbled against the LORD and did not believe Him (Deuteronomy 9:23). Moses recalled the past event in which Israel had sent spies from Kadesh-barnea and pointed out their unbelief (Numbers 32:8).
geography: Kadesh-barnea is presumed to be the area of Ain el-Qudeirat, and it lies between the northeastern Negev desert and the boundary of the Sinai Peninsula. Although it is a desert environment, an oasis with abundant groundwater has formed here, so it has an environment suitable for a large population to live or stay. It is a strategic stronghold for entering southern Canaan, and it is situated at a point where several ancient trade routes cross.
history: During the Bronze and Iron Ages, Kadesh-barnea went through a history of repeated occupation and settlement because of its geopolitical importance. In Israel's exodus journey it served as an important center where the people camped and stayed for a long time. Archaeological excavations have confirmed that a large fortress was built in this region in the period of the kingdom of Judah, which is related to the statecraft of the kings of Judah, who sought to defend the southern boundary and control the trade routes.

remark: 「Winepress」 1. One of the five great cities of the Philistines.
introduce: Gath is one of the five principal city-states of the Philistines, an ancient city that served as a political and military center in the Levant region in the early Iron Age.
biblecontents: Gath was a region where the descendants of Anak lived, and some of them remained there even after Joshua's wars of conquest (Joshua 11:22). It is mentioned as one of the principal cities ruled by the five rulers of the Philistines (Joshua 13:3). When the Philistines moved the ark of God to Gath, calamity broke out in that region (1 Samuel 5:8). As a guilt offering, the Philistines presented a gold tumor for the Gath region (1 Samuel 6:17). Israel recovered from the Philistines the territory from Ekron to Gath (1 Samuel 7:14). Goliath of Gath confronted the army of Israel in the Valley of Elah (1 Samuel 17:4). Every morning and evening Goliath came out before the camp of Israel and defied them (1 Samuel 17:23). The army of Israel pursued the Philistines as far as the gates of Gath and Ekron (1 Samuel 17:52). David fled from Saul to Achish, king of Gath of the Philistines (1 Samuel 21:10). In Gath, David feared for his own safety and escaped the danger by pretending to be insane (1 Samuel 21:12).
geography: Gath is presumed to be present-day Tell es-Safi, in the plain of Israel, and it is located at a strategic point linking the hill country of Judah with the Mediterranean coastal plain.
history: From the Late Bronze Age through the Iron Age, Gath functioned as a core stronghold of Philistine civilization, and until it was destroyed around the ninth century BC by an attack of King Hazael, it interacted with the surrounding great powers as a city-state with strong walls.

remark: 1. A town of the tribe of Dan.
introduce: Gath-rimmon was located within the territory of the tribe of Dan in ancient Israel, and it is one of the Levitical towns allotted to the Kohathites, a Levitical clan.
biblecontents: Gath-rimmon was one of the towns included in the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:45). Afterward this town was given as a dwelling place to the family of the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:24).
geography: Gath-rimmon is presumed to be located near the Shephelah, a coastal plain region, and present-day geographers identify this place with Tel Gerisa or its vicinity.

remark: 2. A town of the Levitical clan in the tribe of Manasseh, east of the Jordan River.
introduce: Gath-rimmon was a town allotted to the Kohathites among the descendants of the tribe of Levi in ancient Israel, and it was a city located within the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: The half-tribe of Manasseh gave Gath-rimmon and its pasturelands from the place where they lived to the Levites, the Kohathites (Joshua 21:25).
geography: The exact location of Gath-rimmon is sometimes presumed in modern archaeological surveys to be Tell es-Safi near the hill country of Ephraim, or a plain area similar to it, but it remains a place about which scholarly debate still exists. This town had the regional characteristic of lying adjacent to the territorial boundary of the tribe of Manasseh.

remark: 「Winepress of the dug well」 1. A town of Zebulun
introduce: Gath-hepher is an ancient town recorded in Joshua 19 in the Old Testament, a border town on the east allotted to the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the distribution of territory among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: When Joshua distributed land for the tribe of the descendants of Zebulun, the boundary reached Gath-hepher and Eth-kazin and extended as far as Rimmon (Joshua 19:13).
geography: Gath-hepher is identified with Khirbet ez-Zurra (Tell Gath-hepher), near present-day El-Meshhed, about 4 km northeast of Nazareth in Lower Galilee. It is situated in a hilly area linking the fertile Plain of Esdraelon with the hill country of Galilee.
history: It developed as a settlement in northern Canaan in the Iron Age and functioned as a major eastern defensive stronghold of the tribe of Zebulun. Archaeological excavation has confirmed the remains of fortified walls and dwellings from the Iron Age II period.

remark: 2. The birthplace of the prophet Jonah
introduce: Gath-hepher was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in northern Israel in Old Testament times. This place is known as the hometown of the prophet Jonah.
biblecontents: Just as the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, spoke through His servant Jonah the prophet, son of Amittai of Gath-hepher, Jeroboam restored the territory of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kings 14:25)
geography: Gath-hepher is presumed to be Khirbet ez-Zurra, located in the area northeast of present-day Nazareth in Israel. It was situated on high ground belonging to the border area of the tribe of Zebulun at that time.
history: This region is recorded as the base where the prophet Jonah was active around the eighth century BC, during the reign of Jeroboam II of the northern kingdom of Israel. At that time northern Israel was expanding its territory and prospering economically, taking advantage of the weakening of Aramean power.

introduce: Gath-rimmon is a place mentioned in the Old Testament as one of the towns allotted to the descendants of the tribe of Levi. It was located within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim, and it forms part of the system of cities of refuge and surrounding towns that were provided to the Levites as dwelling places.
biblecontents: Aijalon and its pasturelands, within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim, were given to the Kohathites of the tribe of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:69). Joshua 21:24 refers to the same place as Gath-rimmon and specifies it, together with Aijalon, as a Levitical town of the Kohathites (Joshua 21:24).
geography: Gath-rimmon is presumed to be located near the Plain of Sharon, a plain region of present-day Israel. In archaeological surveys, sites such as Tel Jerishe or Tell el-Mukhmar are sometimes discussed as likely candidates, but disagreement still exists among scholars about the exact archaeological identification.
history: Gath-rimmon is highly likely to have functioned as a strategic stronghold because it lay near the Way of the Sea, the international trunk road linking Egypt and Mesopotamia in the ancient Near East. Although this region is recorded as an allotment of the tribe of Ephraim in the period of the kingdom of Israel, it has the character of a border zone where shifts of power between the native Canaanite forces and Israel occurred frequently.

remark: 「Possession of Gath」 1. A town in the Shephelah; it received this name because it was near Gath.
introduce: A town located in the Shephelah, the plain region of the kingdom of Judah, it is presumed to be a place closely related to Moresheth, the hometown of the prophet Micah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in a prophecy of judgment that, because the kings of Judah caused Israel and Judah to sin, the people of Moresheth-gath would have to say farewell (Micah 1:14).
geography: It is located in the Shephelah of ancient Palestine and is presumed to be present-day Tell Goded or its vicinity, but its exact location is a matter of archaeological debate. Being geographically adjacent to Gath, the center of the Philistines, it was a region that shared the cultural and political influences of both sides.
history: When Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah around the eighth century BC, the towns of the Shephelah suffered great damage as strategic strongholds, and Moresheth-gath too is analyzed to have been within the sphere of influence of this military clash. It served as the southwestern defensive line and a trade route of the kingdom of Judah.

introduce: Gath-hepher was a town belonging to the tribe of Zebulun in northern Israel in Old Testament times, a place known as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah.
biblecontents: Jeroboam II, king of Israel, restored the territory of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, and this was fulfilled just as the word had been spoken through the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai of Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25).
geography: Gath-hepher is presumed to be Khirbet ez-Zurra, a present-day place name, or nearby Tell Gath, and it lies within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, near Nazareth in the region of Galilee.

introduce: Iscariot is a name referring to the region from which Judas Iscariot came in the New Testament, and it is known to be a transliteration of the Hebrew Ish Kerioth. It carries the meaning "a man from Kerioth."
biblecontents: The New Testament repeatedly mentions, in introducing Judas Iscariot, that he was from Iscariot. Judas Iscariot was one of Jesus' twelve disciples (Matthew 10:4, Mark 3:19, Luke 6:16), and he plotted to hand Jesus over to the chief priests (Matthew 26:14, Mark 14:10, Luke 22:3). The Gospel of John states explicitly that he was Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon (John 6:71, John 13:26), and it records that he conceived the idea of betraying Jesus and actually carried it out (John 12:4, John 13:2).
geography: Iscariot is generally identified with Kerioth in southern Judea. Among the list of towns of the tribe of Judah in Joshua 15:25, which includes Hezron, that is, Hazor, and Amam, Kerioth-hezron is presumed to be that very location. This is a settlement located south of Hebron, in the southwestern part of the Dead Sea region, and scholars generally regard it as the site of Khirbet el-Qaryatein.
history: Among the group of Jesus' disciples, in which Galileans were predominant under Roman rule in Judea at that time, the fact that he alone came from Iscariot in southern Judea creates a meaningful distinction in the social and geographical background of the day. From the perspective of first-century Judean geography, Kerioth is regarded as one of the place names symbolizing the traditional boundaries of the Judean heartland.

introduce: Kartah is a town recorded in Joshua 21 in the Old Testament, one of the Levitical towns within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun that were allotted to the Merarite descendants of the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: What was given to the families of the Merarites, the rest of the descendants of the Levites, was, from the tribe of Zebulun, Jokneam and its pasturelands, and Kartah and its pasturelands (Joshua 21:34).
geography: Kartah was located within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee, and it is presumed to have been situated near the route leading to the Jezreel Valley and the foot of Mount Carmel. Archaeologically, Khirbet Qattina or Tell el-Far, near Jokneam, are discussed as likely candidates, but opinions among scholars are divided on the exact identification of the location.
history: In the period of Israel's settlement and the early monarchy, the tribe of Levi was not allotted an independent territory but lived scattered among the principal towns of each tribe and performed religious and judicial functions. As a base allotted to the Merarite clan within the tribe of Zebulun, Kartah was an administrative center showing the social relations between the agricultural settlers of the northern Galilee region and the Levitical community.

introduce: Kartan is a town that appears in Joshua 21 in the Old Testament, one of the Levitical towns within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in northern Galilee that were allotted to the Gershonite descendants of the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: From the tribe of Naphtali, they were given Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge for the manslayer, together with its pasturelands, and Hammoth-dor and its pasturelands, and Kartan and its pasturelands, three towns in all (Joshua 21:32).
geography: Kartan is presumed to have been located in the Naphtali plateau region north of the Sea of Galilee or near the Huleh Basin. Archaeologists propose Khirbet Qaryun or Tell Katanah on the northeastern side of the Sea of Galilee as candidate sites, and it is identified with the same place as Kiriathaim, which appears in the parallel text of 1 Chronicles 6:76.
history: Kartan lay in the mountains of Galilee, rich in the water resources and routes of northern ancient Canaan, and in the process of the settlement of the tribes of Israel in the Iron Age it functioned as a dwelling place for Gershonite Levites. Linked with the neighboring city of refuge Kedesh and with Hammoth-dor, it served as a center for maintaining defense and administrative order in the northern border zone of the tribe of Naphtali.

introduce: Carites is a designation that appears in 2 Kings 11; it refers to Caria, an ancient place name in southwestern Asia Minor, and to the place of origin of the elite mercenary guard that protected the royal palace and the Jerusalem temple in the period of the southern kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds of the Carites and of the guards and brought them into the house of the LORD; after making a covenant and having them swear an oath, he showed them the king's son Joash (2 Kings 11:4). The commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards, and all the people led the king down from the temple, and by way of the Gate of the Guards they reached the royal palace and seated Joash on the throne (2 Kings 11:19).
geography: Geographically, Carites corresponds to ancient Caria, the southwestern coastal region of Asia Minor (Anatolia) bordering the southeastern Aegean Sea. Some scholars also regard it as synonymous with the Cherethites from the island of Crete, and it is connected with the eastern Mediterranean coastal region, where maritime trade and military activity were vigorous.
history: Around the ninth century BC, the states of the ancient Near East and the Mediterranean coast employed professional foreign mercenaries, free from ties of blood and place, in order to secure the safety of the royal house and prevent palace coups. Like the Cherethites and Pelethites of David's time, the Carites served as a bodyguard directly attached to the royal house of Judah, and in the process of religious and political reform that ended Athaliah's usurpation of the throne and restored Joash, they exercised decisive military force.

introduce: Kamon is a place name mentioned in Judges 10, an ancient town east of the Jordan where Jair, a judge from Gilead, was buried after his death.
biblecontents: When the judge Jair died, he was buried in Kamon (Judges 10:5).
geography: Kamon is located in the northern highlands of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and it is identified with Qum (or Qumeim), west of Irbid in present-day northern Jordan, or with Tell Qamun near Taiyiba. Lying between the Yarmuk River and the Jabbok River, it forms hill country favorable for farming and livestock raising.
history: In the early Iron Age, in the period of the judges, Jair, who was a leader of the Gileadite clan, had thirty sons and administered thirty towns in the land of Gilead called Havvoth-jair. Kamon served as one of the political and administrative centers of the house of Jair, and it was an old and strategic stronghold east of the Jordan, so much so that it appears again in the record of the Hellenistic historian Polybius as the fortress town of Kamous, which Antiochus III captured in 218 BC.

introduce: Garmite is a place name or tribal name recorded in 1 Chronicles 4; it is the name of a regional clan that appears joined with Keilah, a town in the Shephelah within the territory of Judah.
biblecontents: The sons of the sister of Naham, the wife of Hodiah, were the father of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite (1 Chronicles 4:19).
geography: Garmite is presumed to be located in the area around the town of Keilah (Khirbet Qila), in the Shephelah (the lowlands of Judah), a buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain. It is hill country about 13 km northwest of Hebron, and with a fertile valley plain alongside it, it has had a location suited to farming and fortification since ancient times.
history: The text of Chronicles, which arranged the genealogies of the Judean community after the return from exile, has the character of reaffirming the ancient settlements and land ownership of the clans of the tribe of Judah. Garmite refers to a prominent local clan, or a settled village, within the tribe of Judah that settled around the Keilah region, and it reflects the historical traces of a local community that prospered under the administrative jurisdiction of Keilah, a military stronghold.

introduce: Gabbatha is a name that appears in John 19:13; it is a Hebrew place name designating the place where the judgment seat on which Pilate sat to interrogate Jesus was located. In Greek it is called Lithostrotos, which means "stone pavement."
biblecontents: Pilate, having heard Jesus' words, brought Jesus outside and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha (John 19:13).
geography: Gabbatha was probably located inside the Fortress of Antonia, northwest of the temple in Jerusalem. This was the place the Roman governor used as his residence when he visited Jerusalem, and its courtyard was paved with stone slabs.
history: According to Roman administrative custom, a governor set up a judgment seat at a particular location when conducting an official trial. The name Gabbatha reflects the linguistic situation of Jerusalem at that time, and shows the architectural style of Roman public buildings and the way the local people gave place names in response to it. Before the First Jewish-Roman War, the Fortress of Antonia, which was the command post of the Roman army, was one of the main points where such judicial authority was exercised.

introduce: Cappadocia is an ancient place name designating the highland region of central Anatolia, and in the Bible it is recorded as one of the places of origin of the Jews who gathered in Jerusalem at the event of Pentecost.
biblecontents: When the devout Jews who visited Jerusalem at Pentecost each heard in their own dialect according to their region of origin, those who came from Cappadocia were also included (Acts 2:9).
geography: It corresponds to the highland region of the Anatolian plateau in present-day central-eastern Turkey, an inland region bordering Pontus on the north, the Taurus Mountains on the south, the Euphrates River on the east, and Lycaonia on the west. A distinctive tuff terrain formed by volcanic activity is characteristic of it.
history: Around the sixth century BC it was a dependency of the Persian Empire, and after the death of Alexander the Great it maintained an independent kingdom, until in AD 17, in the time of the Roman emperor Tiberius, it was incorporated as a province of the Roman Empire. In the period of the spread of Christianity, several cities developed under the rule of the Roman Empire, and because it lay on the route of the Silk Road, it was a strategic stronghold where the cultures and commerce of East and West crossed.

introduce: Capernaum is an ancient city located on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, and in the Roman period it functioned as a center of fishing and trade. In Hebrew it means "village of Nahum," and it is frequently mentioned in the New Testament as a main site of Jesus' ministry.
biblecontents: Jesus left Nazareth and went to live in Capernaum, by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:13). Here Jesus entered the synagogue and taught (Mark 1:21), and the people were amazed at His teaching (Luke 4:31). It is also the place where a centurion came to Jesus to have his servant healed (Matthew 8:5, Luke 7:1). In Capernaum Jesus stayed at Peter's house and healed a paralytic (Mark 2:1), and He also talked with Peter about the matter of paying the temple tax (Matthew 17:24). There is a record that He pronounced judgment on Capernaum, which did not repent although it had seen much of Jesus' teaching and miracles (Matthew 11:23, Luke 4:23). Also, the disciples stayed in a house in Capernaum and argued on the road about who was the greatest (Mark 9:33).
geography: It sits on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and is adjacent to the Way of the Sea, the main commercial road connecting Damascus and Egypt at that time. With fertile plains and the lake alongside, it had the ideal environment for fishing and agriculture to flourish.
history: Capernaum, located within the territory of Herod Antipas, was a strategic point where a customs post was set up and taxes were collected. It is presumed that there was a stationing place for the Roman army, and as a result of excavations, the site of a first-century synagogue and remains presumed to be Peter's house have been found, which have great archaeological value.

remark: 1. A town located on the border of Asher in the northeast of Canaan.
introduce: Cabul was a town located in the northern region of ancient Palestine, a place connected with the boundaries of the territories of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a border area of the tribe of Asher, and is described as a point where the boundary goes eastward past Beth-emek and Neiel, advances to the left of Cabul, and reaches the valley of Zebulun (Joshua 19:27).
geography: It is a place identified with the village of Kabul in the Galilee region of present-day northern Israel, and it lies in the hill country east of the Plain of Acre.
history: It is also mentioned as one of the twenty towns in the region of Zebulun that King Solomon gave to Hiram, king of Tyre, as compensation, but there is a record that Hiram did not consider this region satisfactory and called it the land of Cabul.

remark: 2. The name that Hiram, king of Tyre, gave, being displeased that Solomon gave him twenty towns of Galilee in return for helping with the construction of the temple and the royal palace.
introduce: Cabul is a place name designating the towns of the Galilee region that were mentioned in the period of the reign of King Solomon of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: When King Solomon gave King Hiram of Tyre twenty towns in the land of Galilee, Hiram looked at those towns and was not pleased with them, and he called that place the land of Cabul (1 Kings 9:13).
geography: Cabul is presumed to be located in the region of Galilee in present-day northern Israel, and archaeologically it is identified with the area of Tell Kabul, southeast of present-day Acre.
history: It contains the historical circumstances in which Solomon provided Hiram with towns in Galilee in return for receiving the materials needed for the construction of the temple and the royal palace, but Hiram was dissatisfied because the soil of that region was poor or its economic value was low. The name Cabul carries the meaning in Hebrew of "not bound" or "worthless."

introduce: Gaza is a strategic stronghold located on the coastal plain in the southwest of Palestine in the ancient Near East, and one of the principal city-states of the Philistine confederation.
biblecontents: It was mentioned as a boundary point of Canaan (Genesis 10:19), and the place where the Avvim lived was conquered and inhabited by the Caphtorites who came out of Caphtor (Deuteronomy 2:23). It is recorded as a region conquered, from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, at the time of Joshua's wars of conquest (Joshua 10:41), but it was one of the strongholds where the Anakim remained even after the conquest (Joshua 11:22). It was included in the territory of the five rulers of the Philistines (Joshua 13:3), and it was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:47), but in the period of the judges the tribe of Judah also captured it temporarily (Judges 1:18). When the Midianites invaded Israel, they advanced as far as near Gaza and laid waste the produce of the land (Judges 6:4). Samson went down to Gaza and met a prostitute (Judges 16:1), and the people of Gaza guarded the city gate and lay in ambush in order to seize Samson (Judges 16:2).
geography: It is located on the coastal plain along the Mediterranean coast, at a key point on the Way of the Sea, the international trunk road leading from Egypt through the Levant to Mesopotamia. It served as a passage linking the arid desert region with the fertile coastal region.
history: It was a city continuously inhabited from the Bronze Age, and in the period of the Egyptian New Kingdom it was under Egyptian influence. Around the twelfth century BC the Philistines, a branch of the Sea Peoples, settled there and it became their principal city, and throughout the Iron Age afterward it had a relationship of political and military conflict with Israel and the kingdom of Judah.

introduce: Casiphia is the place to which Ezra sent a delegation in order to recruit servants for the temple among the Judeans returning after the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: Ezra sent to Iddo, the leader who was staying at a place called Casiphia, and to his brothers, requesting that they bring Levites to serve for the temple of God (Ezra 8:17).
history: It is presumed to be a place name under the Persian Empire after the Babylonian exile, but its exact location and concrete topographical information have not been clearly established archaeologically. It is analyzed, however, to have been one of the particular settlements within Babylon where the Judeans lived at that time.

introduce: Gaash is a place mentioned in the Bible, used mainly to indicate the burial place of Joshua and the hometown of one of David's mighty men.
biblecontents: After Joshua, who led the people of Israel, died, he was buried north of Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 24:30). The Book of Judges also repeatedly mentions that Joshua was buried north of Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim (Judges 2:9). Also, Hiddai, one of David's thirty mighty men, is recorded as a person born at the brooks of Gaash (2 Samuel 23:30, 1 Chronicles 11:32).
geography: Gaash is described as a region located in the hill country of Ephraim. Mount Gaash is presumed to be near Timnath-serah, and its specific present-day location has not been clearly identified archaeologically. The brook of Gaash mentioned in connection with Hiddai is interpreted as a wadi region near Mount Gaash.

introduce: Cauda is an island located in the Mediterranean Sea, a point the apostle Paul passed when he encountered the violent storm called Euraquilo while being taken as a prisoner to Rome. It is identified with the present-day island of Gavdos.
biblecontents: When the ship Paul was on passed under the small island called Cauda, they barely managed, having narrowly escaped the fierce storm, to secure the lifeboat (Acts 27:16).
geography: Cauda is a small island located about 45 kilometers south of the island of Crete. It lies on a main sea route of the Mediterranean, and it has the topographical feature of temporarily shielding ships from the storms of the sea.
history: In the Roman period this island was used by sailing ships as a temporary anchorage for avoiding bad weather, or as a landmark on the sea route. The sailors of that time used the terrain of this island to reduce the effect of the wind, and carried out work such as recovering the damaged lifeboat or reinforcing the ship's equipment.

introduce: Gai is used in biblical place names as a noun designating a particular area, but rather than being fixed as a proper noun, it is a place interpreted from the context as meaning a landmark on the road leading to Ekron or a part of a town.
biblecontents: The men of Israel and Judah rose up with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai and the gates of Ekron, and the wounded Philistines fell along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron. (1 Samuel 17:52)
geography: It lies on the route through which the Philistine army passed when it retreated from the Valley of Elah. Its geographical location has not been precisely determined, but it is presumed to be in the plain region between Shaaraim and Ekron, or near a Philistine defensive stronghold.

introduce: Caesarea is an ancient port city located on the Mediterranean coast, and in New Testament times it functioned as the administrative center of the Roman province of Judea and as a strategic stronghold.
biblecontents: Jesus and His disciples went out to the villages of the region of Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27). Philip appeared at Azotus, passed through many towns preaching the gospel, and came to Caesarea (Acts 8:40). The brothers took Saul down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus (Acts 9:30). In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of the troop called the Italian Regiment (Acts 10:1). The next day Peter entered Caesarea, and Cornelius was waiting, having called together his relatives and close friends (Acts 10:24). Just then three men were standing at the house where we were staying, men who had been sent to me from Caesarea (Acts 11:11). Herod went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there (Acts 12:19). Paul disembarked, went up to Jerusalem and greeted the church, then went down to Antioch, and he arrived at Caesarea (Acts 18:22). The next day they left and came to Caesarea, and they entered the house of Philip, one of the seven deacons, and stayed there (Acts 21:8). Some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, and they took with them Mnason, a Cypriot, at whose house we were to stay (Acts 21:16).
geography: It was a port city located on the Mediterranean coastal plain, and it served as the western gateway of the region of Palestine. It lies north of Joppa and south of Mount Carmel, and it is a strategic geographical point where Roman maritime traffic and the movement of goods were frequent at that time.
history: It was a city whose construction Herod the Great began around 22 BC and completed over about twelve years, and it was named Caesarea, after the name of the Roman emperor Augustus Caesar, in order to dedicate it to him. The residence of the Roman governor was located here, so it became the political and military center of the region of Judea, and with an artificial harbor built, it was a city equipped with modern infrastructure at which large ships could anchor.

introduce: Caesarea Philippi is an ancient city located at the foot of Mount Hermon in northern Palestine, and its original name was Paneas. This region was expanded and remodeled in the Roman period by Philip the tetrarch, and it was named Caesarea Philippi after the name of the Roman emperor Caesar and Philip's own name.
biblecontents: When Jesus and His disciples came to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked His disciples who people said the Son of Man was (Matthew 16:13).
geography: It is located near Banias Falls, one of the main sources of the Jordan River, and it is a region with fertile soil and abundant water resources. Situated on the southern slope of Mount Hermon, it lies on strategically important traffic routes, and it has the topographical features of well-developed limestone cliffs and caves.
history: It was originally a place where the goat-footed god Pan of Greek mythology was worshiped, and was called Paneas. In 20 BC the emperor Augustus granted this region to Herod the Great, and Herod built a temple there for the emperor. Afterward his son Philip greatly expanded the city and made it his capital, and combining his own name with the name of the emperor, he called it Caesarea Philippi.

introduce: Canneh is an ancient city that appears in Ezekiel 27:23, mentioned as one of the surrounding regions that had trade relations with Tyre.
biblecontents: The merchants of Haran, Canneh, Eden, Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad were your merchants; they brought beautiful things in chests, with purple garments, embroidered work, and bright fabrics, and traded in exchange for your goods (Ezekiel 27:23).
geography: It is presumed to be a city located near Haran, in northern Mesopotamia or in the upper region of the Euphrates River.
history: Judging from its being mentioned together with Haran and Eden, place names cited in the period of the expansion of the Assyrian Empire, it is regarded as a city that was included in the economic trade network of the Mesopotamian region at that time.

introduce: Karka is a place name mentioned in the course of describing the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, and it appears as part of the geographical coordinates connected with the setting of the territory of southern Judah.
biblecontents: In Joshua 15:3, Karka is described as a point on a route that starts from the Ascent of Akrabbim, the starting point of the southern boundary line, reaches Zin, passes south of Kadesh-barnea, goes by way of Hezron, passes Addar, and turns around to reach Karka (Joshua 15:3).
geography: It is a place located on the southern boundary of the ancient tribe of Judah, and it lies on the route leading from the southwest of the Dead Sea to the Negev desert. The exact archaeological identification is under dispute, but geographers generally presume this region to be near present-day Wadi el-Qarrah or the dry-stream region around it.

remark: A town of Gad east of the Jordan River.
introduce: Calcol is presumed to be a person, or a place name, connected with the family line of Ethan the Ezrahite and his brothers, who are mentioned as men of wisdom in the time of Solomon. It appears as a proper noun in the biblical record, but several theories exist about its actual identity.
biblecontents: In the context explaining that Solomon's wisdom surpassed all the wisdom of the people of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt, persons named Heman the son of Mahol, Calcol, and Darda are mentioned (1 Kings 4:31). It is also mentioned as one of the sons of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, and they are recorded as wise men (1 Chronicles 2:6).

introduce: Carchemish was a strategic stronghold of the ancient Near East and a major town on the bank of the Euphrates River, and it appears as a key place in the struggle for supremacy among Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt.
biblecontents: King Josiah was killed in battle when he tried to stop Neco, king of Egypt, who was going out to the battle of Carchemish (2 Chronicles 35:20); in the expansion policy of Assyria it is mentioned as a conquered place compared with Calno and Arpad (Isaiah 10:9); and afterward it is recorded as the place where King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated the army of Egypt (Jeremiah 46:2).
geography: It is located on the western bank of the upper Euphrates River, and it is presumed to be the area of Jerablus on the present-day border region between Turkey and Syria. It sits at a crossing of the major trade route and military route of movement linking Mesopotamia with the Mediterranean coast.
history: Around the eighth century BC it was occupied by the Assyrian Empire and became an important administrative base, and in 605 BC the battle of Carchemish was fought, in which Nebuchadnezzar II of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and Neco II of Egypt clashed. Babylon's victory in this battle became the decisive turning point at which supremacy in the Near East passed from Assyria and Egypt to Babylon.

remark: The region south of Babylon.
introduce: Chaldea is a name designating the southern region of ancient Mesopotamia; in the Bible it is mentioned mainly as the center of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and as the agent that destroyed the kingdom of Judah. This region includes the fertile alluvial plain of the lower Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, and it was a core political and military stronghold of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: The LORD sent the Chaldean forces, the Aramean forces, the Moabite forces, and the forces of the sons of Ammon against Judah to destroy it (2 Kings 24:2). When the wall of Jerusalem was breached, the king and all the soldiers fled by night, but because the Chaldean army had surrounded the city, they went by the way of the Arabah, were pursued by the Chaldean army, and were captured in the plains of Jericho (2 Kings 25:4, 5). Nebuzaradan, the commander of the Chaldean army, tore down the wall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:10), and the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands of the temple and carried the bronze to Chaldea (2 Kings 25:13). Gedaliah, the governor appointed by the king of Babylon, was betrayed by the Chaldeans and killed (2 Kings 25:24, 25), and because of this the remnant of Judah and the army commanders were afraid and left the Chaldeans and fled to Egypt (2 Kings 25:26). The king of the Chaldeans killed the young men of Judah with the sword in the temple and plundered the articles of the temple (2 Chronicles 36:17).
geography: Chaldea means the region of the lower basin of the Euphrates and Tigris Rivers north of the Persian Gulf, that is, the southern area of present-day Iraq. Geographically it is an alluvial plain with well-developed waterways and marshes, and ancient cities such as Ur and Eridu are distributed around Babylon. Because this region has abundant water resources, it functioned from ancient times as a center of agriculture and trade.
history: From the early first millennium BC the Chaldeans settled in the southern region of Babylonia and expanded their influence. In particular, when Nabopolassar founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire, the Chaldean dynasty took hold of supremacy in the ancient Near East. By the time of Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylonia, which had become a military power, invaded the kingdom of Judah and captured Jerusalem; as a result the governing system of Judah collapsed, and a history unfolded in which a considerable part of the population was forcibly relocated to Babylon.

introduce: Babylon of Chaldea designates the southern region of ancient Mesopotamia; in the Bible it is described mainly as the center of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and as the core seat of the power that destroyed the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: Ezekiel describes the dress of the Chaldeans as that of men with splendid belts around their waists and multicolored turbans on their heads, and records that they were people born in the land of the Chaldeans in Babylon (Ezekiel 23:15).
geography: Chaldea lies in southern Babylonia, the alluvial plain region of the lower Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, and in ancient times it consisted of marshlands adjacent to the Persian Gulf and fertile farmland.
history: Chaldea originated from tribal groups of Semitic stock that lived in this region from the early first millennium BC, and when Nabopolassar founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire, they took hold of royal power and rose to become the dominant power of the Near East in the early sixth century BC.

introduce: Ur of the Chaldeans is a city-state located in the southern region of ancient Mesopotamia, recorded as the birthplace of Abraham and the place where his family lived before moving to Canaan.
biblecontents: Haran died in his native land, Ur of the Chaldeans, before his father Terah (Genesis 11:28). Terah took Abram, Lot, and Sarai and left Ur of the Chaldeans, wishing to go to the land of Canaan (Genesis 11:31). God brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldeans and promised to give him the land of Canaan (Genesis 15:7). God chose Abram, led him out of Ur of the Chaldeans, and changed his name to Abraham (Nehemiah 9:7).
geography: It is identified with the area of Tell el-Muqayyar in southern present-day Iraq. In the past it was located on the fertile alluvial plain of the lower Euphrates River, and because of changes in the course of the river, it now lies at a point quite far inland from the coastline.
history: As one of the centers of Sumerian civilization, it was a powerful city-state whose dynasties flourished from the third millennium BC. It possessed a strongly centralized system and the building technology of the ziggurat, and the society of that time had a systematic administrative system with highly developed commerce and the recording of documents.

introduce: It is one of the ancient cities that Nimrod built in the region of Asshur after going out from the land of Shinar. It is a major town mentioned together with Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Resen.
biblecontents: From that land he went out to Asshur and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah (Genesis 10:11), and Resen between Nineveh and Calah, which is the great city (Genesis 10:12).
geography: It is identified with the area of Nimrud, southeast of Mosul in present-day northern Iraq. It lies on a fertile plain near the point where the Tigris River and the Great Zab River meet.
history: Around the ninth century BC it was rebuilt as the capital of the empire by Ashurnasirpal II of the Assyrian Empire and flourished. It was a political and military stronghold where the great palaces and temples of the Assyrian kings were built, but its status as a center weakened when the capital was moved to Dur-Sharrukin in the time of Sargon II.

remark: A city in the center of Asia Minor under Roman rule.
introduce: Galatia is a region located in the central part of ancient Asia Minor; in the Bible it appears as a place of Paul's missionary journeys and the destination of his letter, and it is a region mentioned as one of the recipients of 1 Peter.
biblecontents: Paul and Silas passed through the land of Phrygia and Galatia and preached the gospel (Acts 16:6). Paul went through the region of Galatia in order, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:23). Paul gave instructions to the churches of Galatia about the collection (1 Corinthians 16:1). Paul wrote a letter to the churches in Galatia (Galatians 1:2). Paul called the Galatians foolish and said that Jesus Christ had been clearly portrayed as crucified before their eyes (Galatians 3:1). Crescens, a fellow worker of Paul, went to Galatia (2 Timothy 4:10). Peter sent a letter to the sojourners scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1).
geography: Ancient Galatia designates the central highland region of Asia Minor, and it borders Bithynia and Pontus on the north, Asia and Phrygia on the west, Pisidia and Lycaonia on the south, and Cappadocia on the east. This region includes a central inland plain made up of rugged mountainous areas and pastureland.
history: The name Galatia derives from the Gallic tribes of Europe, who migrated and settled there around the third century BC. When the Roman Empire annexed this region in 25 BC it became a Roman province, and administratively it was reorganized as the province of Galatia, which included a wider area. In the apostolic age Galatia was under Roman political control, and it was a region where diverse Greek culture and local culture coexisted.

introduce: Calneh is a city of the ancient Near East; in the Old Testament it is mentioned as one of the cities of the land of Shinar and as a major stronghold under the influence of the Assyrian Empire. In scholarly terms it is identified with the same region as Calah or Nimrud in present-day northern Iraq.
biblecontents: The beginning of Nimrod's kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:10). The prophet Amos, comparing it with the great powers of that time, said to visit Calneh and see whether it was better than Hamath (Amos 6:2).
geography: Calneh is located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River, about 30 km southeast of Mosul in present-day Iraq. This region has high agricultural productivity on the basis of fertile alluvial soil, and it is a strategic stronghold connected through the ancient canal network with Nineveh, the center of the Assyrian Empire.
history: Calneh was rebuilt as the capital of the empire around the ninth century BC by Ashurnasirpal II, king of Assyria, and afterward it prospered as the political and military center of the Assyrian Empire. Archaeologically, large royal palaces and temples and stone tablets containing imperial records have been excavated, and it is regarded as an important site that proves the royal power and administrative system of that time.

introduce: This is a region mentioned as the place where, after Hezron died, Caleb went in to Ephrath and lay with her, and she bore Ashhur.
biblecontents: After Hezron died, Caleb went in to Ephrath, and Abijah, the wife of Hezron, bore Ashhur to him by this, and Ashhur was the father of Tekoa (1 Chronicles 2:24).
history: It has the character of a background account describing the relationships among persons who appear in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, where Caleb, a descendant of Hezron, appears in combination with the place name Ephrath.

introduce: Calno is one of the city-states of the ancient Near East, a place mentioned as a region conquered in the period of the expansion of the Assyrian Empire.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the king of Assyria conquered Calno just as he did Carchemish, conquered Hamath just as he did Arpad, and conquered Samaria just as he did Damascus (Isaiah 10:9).
geography: It is presumed to have been located in northern present-day Syria or near the basin of the Euphrates River, but several hypotheses exist among scholars about the specific site, and there is no fixed location.
history: It is a place name that shows a historical example of one of the many city-states conquered as the kings of Assyria expanded their territory westward around the eighth century BC, and which in the course of the Assyrian invasion was destroyed or became a vassal state paying tribute.

introduce: Galeed is a Hebrew place name designating the heap of stones that Jacob and Laban set up as they covenanted not to cross each other's boundary. It means "heap of witness," and it has the same meaning as the Aramaic name Jegar-sahadutha (Genesis 31:47).
biblecontents: Laban called the heap of stones Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed (Genesis 31:47). Laban declared that this heap of stones was a witness between himself and Jacob, and for this reason the name Galeed was given (Genesis 31:48).
geography: Galeed is presumed to be in the mountainous region of Gilead east of the Jordan River. It is difficult to pinpoint its exact location archaeologically, but it is generally regarded as a border area near Mahanaim.
history: It is the site of a kind of border treaty concluded in order to resolve the dispute between Jacob, who was returning home from Paddan-aram, and Laban, who pursued him. This is in line with the Mesopotamian custom of setting up a heap of stones to commemorate a covenant, and it has as its background a historical event in which the two men ended their conflict at the point where their spheres of influence overlapped and promised mutual non-aggression.

introduce: Galilee is a place name designating the northern region of Palestine, and it is derived from the Hebrew galil, meaning "circle." This region includes the upper Jordan River and the Sea of Galilee, and it is located in the northern frontier zone of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee (1 Kings 9:11). Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali of Israel, took the people captive, and carried them off to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Among the towns allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee and its pasturelands are mentioned (1 Chronicles 6:76). Isaiah prophesied that the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, which had formerly been in distress, would glorify the Way of the Sea and Galilee of the nations beyond the Jordan (Isaiah 9:1). Having heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he departed for the region of Galilee and went to live in a town called Nazareth (Matthew 2:22). Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan and was baptized by John (Matthew 3:13). When Jesus heard that John had been arrested, He withdrew to Galilee (Matthew 4:12). The land of Zebulun, the land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea beyond the Jordan, and Galilee of the nations were mentioned (Matthew 4:15). Walking by the Sea of Galilee, He saw Peter and Andrew (Matthew 4:18). Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues (Matthew 4:23).
geography: Galilee is divided into Upper Galilee and Lower Galilee. Upper Galilee in the north is rugged mountainous country, whereas Lower Galilee in the south is made up of comparatively low hills and fertile plains, and it has an environment favorable for farming and livestock raising. To the west it borders the Mediterranean coastal plain, and to the east it faces the Jordan Rift Valley and the Sea of Galilee, so it is rich in water resources.
history: After part of the region was ceded to Hiram, king of Tyre, in the time of Solomon, it was frequently invaded by neighboring great powers such as Assyria because of its geographical position. In particular, under Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria, as large-scale population movements took place together with intermixture with foreign peoples, it also came to be perceived by the Judeans of the south as a region lacking legitimacy. In the Roman period it was under the rule of the house of Herod, and at the time of Jesus' activity it bore a distinctive cultural and religious coloring that set it apart from Jerusalem, the center of Judaism.

introduce: Kedesh in Galilee is a town that was allotted to the tribe of Naphtali at the time of the conquest of Canaan, and it is an important base city located in the hill country of Galilee west of the Jordan River. This region was designated a city of refuge, and it was also used as a Levitical town.
biblecontents: The Israelites set apart Kedesh in Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali, as a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7). Also, Kedesh in Galilee, a town of the tribe of Naphtali, together with its pasturelands, was given to the Levites who were descendants of Gershon (Joshua 21:32).
geography: This region, presumed to be present-day Tell Kedesh, lies on the high ground west of the Huleh Basin and is a strategic stronghold in the northern hill country of Galilee. The surrounding area has the topographical features of fertile farmland and abundant water resources.
history: Kedesh was a native town that existed from the early Canaanite period, and after Joshua's wars of conquest it was incorporated into Israelite territory. In later periods it functioned as one of the administrative and religious centers of the tribe of Naphtali.

introduce: Nazareth is a small village located in the southern hill country of Galilee, and according to the biblical record it is the place that formed the background of Jesus' childhood and upbringing.
biblecontents: The crowds replied, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.” (Matthew 21:11)
geography: Nazareth is a village in the form of a basin located in hill country at an elevation of about 350 meters. It sits at an inland point about 25 kilometers west of the Sea of Galilee and about 30 kilometers east of the Mediterranean Sea. It is surrounded by limestone hills and lies adjacent to ancient thoroughfares linking the plains with the highlands.
history: In the Second Temple period, Nazareth was a farming village so small in population and so slight in economic influence that it is hardly mentioned in outside literature. According to archaeological surveys, Nazareth in the early Roman period was an agriculture-based community, a settlement in a relatively isolated form compared with the nearby large city of Sepphoris. Compared with Jerusalem, the heart of the province of Judea, it is classified as a frontier region far from the historical and political centers.

introduce: Gallim is a place name that was located within the territory of ancient Israel, a place whose existence is confirmed through the biblical record. This place name is mentioned in the context of explaining events connected with persons of the house of Saul and the route of Assyria's invasion.
biblecontents: King Saul gave his daughter Michal to Palti, and Palti's hometown was Gallim (1 Samuel 25:44). Also, the prophet Isaiah, describing the route by which the Assyrian army advanced toward Jerusalem, prophesied that the daughters of Gallim would cry aloud (Isaiah 10:30).
geography: Gallim is generally presumed to have been within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. It appears to be a region geographically adjacent to Anathoth, Laishah, and Anathoth, which are mentioned in Isaiah 10:30, and it is analyzed to have been a village located on the strategic route toward Jerusalem.

remark: 1. A mountain jutting out in the land of Canaan.
introduce: In Hebrew, Carmel means "orchard" or "fertile land," and it designates a strategic stronghold and topographically distinct region in the ancient Palestinian area. In the Bible it is used mainly as a place name referring to the mountain range along the Mediterranean coast and a particular region of the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: Among the kings of Canaan whom Joshua conquered, the king of Carmel is included (Joshua 12:22). Also, the Carmel region is mentioned in the course of describing the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:26).
geography: Carmel is roughly divided into two regions. One is Mount Carmel, the coastal mountain range that extends southeast from the Mediterranean coast, and the other is the highland region of the hill country of Judah located south of Hebron. The Carmel mentioned in Joshua 12:22 is presumed to be a region within the territory of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua 19:26 means the Carmel region facing the Mediterranean in connection with the boundary of the tribe of Asher.
history: From the Bronze Age, Mount Carmel was a strategic base through which the Way of the Sea, an international trade route, passed. The king of Carmel who appears in Joshua 12:22 is recorded as one of the local rulers who confronted the army of Israel at the time of the wars of the conquest of Canaan. The Carmel of Judah is the place where King Saul set up a monument of victory, and it is a place where traces remain of an ancient city known as the dwelling place of Nabal and Abigail.

remark: 2. A village in the hill country of Judah.
introduce: Carmel is an ancient town located in the hill country of Judah, designating a place about 11 kilometers southeast of Hebron. It is identified with the area of Khirbet el-Karmil today, and in the history of ancient Israel it is recorded as one of the territories of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:55). It is the place where, after King Saul won the war against Amalek, he set up a monument to commemorate himself (1 Samuel 15:12). It was the place where a rich man named Nabal tended livestock, and David asked for help there on the day of the shearing of Nabal's sheep (1 Samuel 25:2, 1 Samuel 25:3, 1 Samuel 25:5, 1 Samuel 25:7). It is also the place where, after David married Abigail, who had been Nabal's wife, Abigail followed David together with her maidservants (1 Samuel 25:40). It is mentioned as one of the strongholds within the territory of Judah where David stayed before taking refuge among the Philistines to escape Saul (1 Samuel 27:3).
geography: It lies on high ground south of Hebron, adjacent to the border of the Judean wilderness. Topographically, it is formed along the ridge of the hill country of Judah, and together with nearby Maon and Ziph it forms a principal settlement of southern Judah. The surrounding area has a dry climate and infertile soil, but in the past it was used as pasture for grazing flocks of sheep or as a town for the management of livestock.
history: From the early Iron Age it performed its function as a settlement of the tribe of Judah. In the time of David it was a strategic point where the political and economic interests of southern Judah were intertwined, and in particular, before royal authority was established, it became an important strategic base during the process in which David was gathering power and associating with neighboring tribes. In later periods too it is presumed to have served as the southern defensive line of the kingdom of Judah and to have been gradually fortified.

introduce: The Mount of Olives is a mountain located east of Jerusalem, a region that is mentioned throughout the Bible as a boundary facing the temple of Jerusalem and as an important route of travel.
biblecontents: David, fleeing Absalom's rebellion, went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives weeping (2 Samuel 15:30). It was prophesied that on that day the feet of the LORD would stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:4). Jesus and His disciples came near Jerusalem, to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 21:1, Mark 11:1). On the Mount of Olives Jesus gave His disciples teaching about the end times (Matthew 24:3, Mark 13:3). After the Last Supper, Jesus went out to the Mount of Olives singing a hymn (Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26). The disciples praised God with a loud voice on the descent from the Mount of Olives (Luke 19:37). Jesus taught in the temple by day, and at night He rested on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37).
geography: It is a mountain ridge that rises across the Kidron Valley east of the old city of Jerusalem, and the name of the mountain derives from the fact that many olive trees grow wild there. To the west one can look out over the Temple Mount of Jerusalem, and to the east it has the topographical character of leading on toward the Judean wilderness and the Dead Sea.
history: It is a place that forms the eastern boundary as seen from the walls of Jerusalem, and in ancient Judaism it was also anticipated as the place where the Messiah would appear. Because of its geographical position, it served as the eastern gateway for entering and leaving Jerusalem, and it has been recorded as a strategic point through which people passed in times of war or major movements from the time of King David.

introduce: The Mount of Olives is a mountainous area located east of Jerusalem, and in the Bible it is known as a region where many olive trees grow wild. In Hebrew it is also called by the name Gethsemane, and it has the topographical character of facing the temple of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: When Jesus and His disciples drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage and Bethany, at the place called the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples, instructing them to go to the village opposite and untie a colt and bring it (Luke 19:29).
geography: It is a mountain ridge situated across the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, with an elevation of about 800 meters. To the west one can look out over the temple precinct of Jerusalem, and to the east it forms a slope leading on toward the Judean wilderness and the Dead Sea.
history: It was used as a principal burial ground of the Jews from before the Second Temple period, and by religious custom it was one of the main routes for entering Jerusalem. Even in the period of Roman rule, it had a regional value as a place where the movement of people and goods entering and leaving Jerusalem was active.

introduce: Caphtor is an ancient place name recorded in the Bible, known as a region closely connected with the origin of the Philistines. In ancient Near Eastern scholarship, this region is generally identified with the island of Crete in the Mediterranean Sea.
biblecontents: The Caphtorites who came out of Caphtor destroyed the Avvim who lived in the villages as far as Gaza and settled in their place (Deuteronomy 2:23). For the day is coming when the LORD will destroy the Philistines and cut off those who remain on the island of Caphtor (Jeremiah 47:4). "Are you not like the Cushites to Me, O children of Israel?" declares the LORD. "Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?" (Amos 9:7).
geography: Caphtor is geographically connected with Crete, an island in the Mediterranean Sea. In ancient Egyptian records it appears under the name Keftiu, which has the geographical character of a center of Aegean maritime trade.
history: Historically, Caphtor is the region where the Minoan civilization arose and flourished. The theory that the Philistines, presumed to be a branch of the Sea Peoples, moved from Caphtor around the twelfth century BC and migrated to the southwestern coast of Canaan is supported with archaeological evidence.

introduce: Cappadocia is a region located in the central highland area of Asia Minor; in ancient times it was an independent kingdom, and in the Roman period it was administered as one of the principal provinces.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the destinations of the apostle Peter's letter, sent to the sojourners scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1).
geography: It is a highland region in the interior of the Asia Minor peninsula, bordering the Euphrates River on the east, the Lycus Valley on the west, and the Black Sea coast on the north. A tuff terrain formed by volcanic activity is characteristic of it, and it has a dry climate at high elevation.
history: Around the sixth century BC it was ruled by the Persian Empire, and afterward, passing through the Hellenistic kingdoms, it was incorporated into a Roman province in AD 17 by the Roman emperor Tiberius. As a strategic stronghold, a major trade route that was part of the Silk Road passed through it, and it was a region where various peoples and cultures crossed.

introduce: Cabbon is one of the towns that was located within the allotted territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: In the list of towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, it is mentioned between Eglon and Lahmas (Joshua 15:40).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the Shephelah of the tribe of Judah, that is, in the hill country between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country of Judah, but its exact archaeological identification has not been determined to this day.

introduce: Kabzeel is recorded as a town located on the southern boundary of the territory of the ancient tribe of Judah, and it is a place name known as the hometown of Benaiah, one of David's mighty men.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a region close to the border of Edom at the extreme south among the towns that the descendants of the tribe of Judah received as an inheritance (Joshua 15:21). Also, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, one of David's mighty men, is recorded as being from Kabzeel, and he is described as a man who carried out the valiant deeds of Kabzeel (2 Samuel 23:20, 1 Chronicles 11:22).
geography: The exact location of Kabzeel has not been clearly established archaeologically at present, but it is presumed to have been located near Arad in the Negev region of southern Judah, or in the border zone with Edom.

introduce: Kattath is a place name that appears in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a place mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Zebulun.
biblecontents: Kattath is included among the towns obtained by lot by the tribe of the descendants of Zebulun, and it is recorded as one of the twelve towns and their villages, together with Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem (Joshua 19:15).
geography: The exact location of Kattath has not been clearly established by modern archaeology, but it is generally presumed to have been located in the vicinity of the Jezreel Valley, the plain region of southwestern Galilee allotted to the tribe of Zebulun, or in the hill country north of it.

introduce: Kadmonites is a name designating the Kadmonites, one of the native tribes of the land of Canaan, and in Genesis 15:19 it is listed as one of the tribes that lived in the land of the covenant promised to Abraham.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the tribes that lived in the land that God promised to give to Abraham when He made a covenant with him (Genesis 15:19).
history: It is classified as a tribal group of the Near East in the Bronze Age, and it is a tribe whose clear identity has not been established archaeologically or historically. There is a theory that the name Kenizzites is connected with Kenaz, the ancestor of the Edomite tribe, but scholarly opinion is not unanimous on whether the Kenizzite tribe mentioned in Genesis 15, from this period, is the same group as the Edomite-line Kenizzites that appear later in the Bible.

introduce: Gerasenes is a place name that appears in the New Testament, designating a city located in the region of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee. Within scholarship, a view that identifies it with Jerash in present-day Jordan and a view that regards it as Tel Gergesa on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee stand in opposition.
biblecontents: Jesus and His disciples arrived in the region of the Gerasenes on the other side of the sea (Mark 5:1). When Jesus came to the land of the Gerasenes and stepped out of the boat, a demon-possessed man met Him (Luke 8:26). All the people around the land of the Gerasenes were seized with great fear and asked Jesus to depart from them (Luke 8:37).
geography: Gerasenes is a region located southeast of the Sea of Galilee, and in the Bible it is described as the region of the Gerasenes. Topographically there is a steep slope adjoining the lake, and attempts continue to find a geographical connection with the biblical record that the herd of pigs rushed into the sea. Since present-day Jerash is more than about 50 km from the lake, the theory that the place name in the Bible is likely to refer to Gergesa, a small village near the lake, is the dominant one.
history: Gerasenes was one of the principal cities of the Decapolis, where the influence of ancient Rome was strong. In the Roman period, as a strategic stronghold, it took the form of a city-state in which Hellenistic culture and the Roman administrative system were combined. This was regarded as a Gentile region, and rather than persons of Jewish background living there, it was a place where pagan culture and ways of life predominated.

introduce: Chezib is a place name that appears in Genesis, recorded as the place where Judah's son Shelah was born.
biblecontents: Judah fathered Shelah at Chezib, and when Shelah was born, Judah was at Chezib (Genesis 38:5).

introduce: Gennesaret is a place name designating a fertile plain region on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and the village of the same name. The Greek Gennesaret derives from the Hebrew Chinnereth, and this region has been famous since ancient times for its high agricultural productivity.
biblecontents: Jesus and His disciples crossed over by boat and arrived at the land of Gennesaret (Matthew 14:34). When they had crossed over and moored the boat at the land of Gennesaret, the people immediately recognized that it was Jesus, went around that whole region, and came bringing the sick on their beds (Mark 6:53-54). As the crowd pressed in to hear the word of God, Jesus stood by the lake of Gennesaret and saw two boats at the edge of the lake (Luke 5:1-2).
geography: It refers to an alluvial plain about 5 km long on the northwest of the Sea of Galilee, between Capernaum and Magdala.
