Thanks to the water coming down from Mount Arbel and its abundant springs, the soil here is very fertile, and the climate is mild, so it is a region where a variety of fruits and vegetables grow well.
history: According to the account of Josephus, Gennesaret is described as the most fertile place in the region of Galilee. It was a center of agriculture where for ten months of the year a variety of crops such as walnuts, palm trees, figs, and olives were produced. It was regarded as one of the economically prosperous regions of Jewish society at that time, and it was linked to the ancient road network, so the distribution of goods was brisk.

introduce: Geruth Chimham is a place name that appears in the Book of Jeremiah in the Old Testament, a place located on the route by which refugees went down to Egypt after Babylon's invasion of Judah.
biblecontents: After Gedaliah, the governor of Judah appointed by King Nebuchadnezzar, was assassinated, the remnant of the people of Judah and the army commanders, fearing Babylonian retaliation, stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem while fleeing to Egypt (Jeremiah 41:17).
geography: It is known to have been located near Bethlehem, and it is presumed to have been a region lying on the main southern route from Judah to Egypt at that time (Jeremiah 41:17).
history: After Babylon captured Jerusalem it appointed Gedaliah as governor, but an incident occurred in which Ishmael assassinated Gedaliah. It served as a temporary base where the remnant of the people of Judah assembled before fleeing to Egypt in order to escape Babylon's retaliation for this (Jeremiah 41:17).

introduce: Gebim is a place name presumed to have been a town located near the north of Jerusalem in the kingdom of Judah of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a place name lying on the route by which the Assyrian army advanced toward Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:31).
geography: It is often suggested that it was probably the area of present-day Hizma, about 10 km north of Jerusalem. This region belongs to the territory of the tribe of Benjamin and is one of the strategic points of entry into Jerusalem.
history: When Sennacherib, king of Assyria, invaded Judah around the eighth century BC, it is mentioned as one of the places that lay on the Assyrian army's line of advance and were threatened. At that time the Assyrian army came down, passing in order through the towns of the region of Benjamin from the north, in order to besiege Jerusalem.

introduce: Gezer is a strategic stronghold of ancient Canaan, a town located on the route linking the coastal plain with the hill country. Archaeologically it is known as Tel Gezer, and from early biblical times it was a place where disputes over possession between Israel and the surrounding powers were frequent.
biblecontents: Horam, king of Gezer, came to help Lachish but was defeated by Joshua (Joshua 10:33). The king of Gezer is mentioned as one of the thirty-one kings Joshua conquered (Joshua 12:12). It was included in the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim (Joshua 16:3), but the Canaanites lived there and the tribe of Ephraim did not drive them out (Joshua 16:10, Judges 1:29). Afterward it became a town allotted to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:21). King David struck down the Philistines from Gibeon as far as Gezer (2 Samuel 5:25). King Solomon rebuilt Gezer and fortified it (1 Kings 9:15), and Solomon rebuilt Gezer, which Pharaoh king of Egypt had conquered and given as a gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife (1 Kings 9:16, 9:17).
geography: Gezer is located in the area of Tel Gezer in present-day central Israel. Because it sits on a hill at the mouth of the Valley of Aijalon, which links Jerusalem and Joppa, it is a strategic stronghold connecting the coastal road, the international trade route, with the hill country. Because of this geographical advantage, it occupied a position of great military and economic importance.
history: Traces of human habitation are found from the Bronze Age, and it was a principal town of Canaan, so much so that it appears often in ancient Near Eastern records such as those of the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III and the Amarna letters. According to the biblical record, it was strengthened with Egyptian support in the time of Solomon, and archaeological excavations have confirmed a city gate structure and defensive facilities of the Solomonic type. It has a history of coming under the influence of surrounding great powers afterward as well, including the Assyrian invasion.

introduce: Kenite refers to a nomadic people who lived in southern Canaan and near the wilderness of Judah, or to their settlements. They were not entirely identical with the people of Israel in blood or religion, but they maintained friendly relations and interacted closely with them historically.
biblecontents: In Genesis, in connection with the covenant made with Abraham, they are mentioned as one of the tribes living in the land that God would give to Abraham (Genesis 15:19). The Kenites, descendants of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, lived with the descendants of Judah in the wilderness of Judah south of Arad (Judges 1:16). Heber the Kenite left his camp and pitched his tent beside the oak of Zaanannim, near Kedesh (Judges 4:11), and his wife Jael killed Sisera and contributed to Israel's victory (Judges 4:17, Judges 5:24). Before striking Amalek, Saul warned the Kenites, who lived mixed among them, to leave so that they would not be destroyed together with Amalek (1 Samuel 15:6). When David raided the southern region of Judah, he deceived Achish and reported that he had raided the region of the Kenites (1 Samuel 27:10), and afterward, when he sent portions of the spoil taken from Amalek, he sent gifts also to the towns of the Kenites (1 Samuel 30:29). In Chronicles, the genealogy of the Kenite clans, which forms the root of the clans of scribes living at Jabez, is recorded (1 Chronicles 2:55).
geography: Their main dwelling places were the Negev desert in southern Judah and the wasteland region near Arad. They had a nomadic character rather than a settled one, and as time went on they appear to have moved and settled as far as the vicinity of Jabez, north of the hill country of Judah.
history: The Kenite clan is presumed to be a group closely connected with Midian. From the record in which Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, is regarded as a Kenite, it can be seen that they entered into an alliance with Israel from the early period of the exodus. Afterward, in the process of Israel's settlement in Canaan, they existed either absorbed into the territory of the tribe of Judah or as an independent group living in symbiosis with them. Until the time of Saul and David they maintained military and economic relations as political partners of Israel.

introduce: Cenchrea was a port city of the Achaia region of ancient Greece, located on the Saronic Gulf east of the city of Corinth. This city was one of the core bases of maritime trade linking the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf.
biblecontents: Paul had his hair cut at Cenchrea because of a vow he had made (Acts 18:18). Paul recommended Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, and urged the church at Rome to welcome her (Romans 16:1).
geography: Cenchrea is a port located on the coast of the Saronic Gulf about 11 kilometers east of Corinth. Situated at the eastern end of the Isthmus of Corinth, it served as an important gateway for trading with the East through the Aegean Sea.
history: In the Roman period Corinth operated two ports: Lechaeum in the west handled Italy and the western Mediterranean, and Cenchrea in the east was devoted to trade with Asia Minor and the Eastern regions. It was an international port city where commercial activity was brisk and where diverse cultures and religions flowed in.

introduce: Gethsemane is a place located east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley, on the western slope of the Mount of Olives, and according to the biblical record it is a place that Jesus and His disciples frequently visited.
biblecontents: Jesus came with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane and ordered the disciples to stay there while He prayed (Matthew 26:36). Also, when Jesus and His disciples came to a place called Gethsemane, Jesus told His disciples to sit while He prayed (Mark 14:32).
geography: Located on the middle slope of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron Valley, east of the wall of Jerusalem, it is archaeologically a sloping terrain suited to the presence of olive-pressing facilities.
history: The name Gethsemane derives from the Hebrew Gat Shemanim, which means "olive oil press," suggesting that this area was olive farmland at that time.

introduce: Chorazin is an ancient village located on a hill northwest of the Sea of Galilee, and in the Gospels of the New Testament it is mentioned as one of the main bases of the region of Galilee where Jesus' ministry was concentrated.
biblecontents: Jesus performed many mighty works in Chorazin, but He rebuked the people there for not repenting, and said that if those mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth (Matthew 11:21). Also, in sending out His disciples, He declared woe to the region of Chorazin, which rejects the gospel (Luke 10:13).
geography: Chorazin is located in hill country about 3.2 km north of Capernaum, and it is a strategic stronghold from which one can look out over the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee.
history: According to archaeological excavations, the remains of a synagogue with a basalt foundation, presumed to have been built between the second and fourth centuries, have been found here, and traces have been confirmed of a village that served as a residence of Jews at that time, where agriculture-centered economic activity took place.

introduce: Habor of Gozan designates the region to which the people of Israel, taken captive after the Assyrian Empire destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel around the eighth century BC, were forcibly relocated.
biblecontents: The king of Assyria captured Samaria, took the people of Israel captive, and placed them by the Habor River in the region of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6). Also, the king of Assyria took the people of Israel captive, led them away to Assyria, and placed them by the Habor River in the region of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 18:11).
geography: Gozan is presumed to be the northern region of the Assyrian Empire, that is, present-day northern Mesopotamia and eastern Turkey. The Habor River means the Khabur River, one of the main tributaries of the Euphrates River, and this region lay within the sphere of rule of ancient Assyria and was a strategic stronghold convenient for settling and managing forcibly relocated people.
history: The Assyrian Empire carried out a policy of forcibly relocating conquered peoples throughout the empire in order to prevent rebellion in the conquered lands and to secure labor. After the northern kingdom of Israel fell around 722 BC, the rulers of Assyria, including Sargon II, scattered the main tribes and leadership of Samaria to the region of the Habor River and the land of Media, seeking to weaken their ethnic identity and raise productivity within the empire.

introduce: This is a name presumed to be a personal name or a place name connected with the descendants of Shelah of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Cozeba is mentioned together with Jokim, the men of Cozeba, and Joash and Saraph, who ruled in Moab, and these are connected with the families that ruled in Moab and then returned to Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 4:22).
history: In the text, the possibility that Cozeba is a personal name and the possibility that it is a particular place name are raised at the same time, but in the context of population movements in the ancient Near East and a settled society centered on clans, it is also interpreted as designating a particular region or settlement where a branch of the tribe of Judah lived.

remark: 1. A region of Egypt where Jacob lived.
introduce: Goshen is a name designating the eastern region of the Nile Delta in ancient Egypt, recorded in the Bible as the pastureland to which Jacob's family migrated and where they settled.
biblecontents: Joseph proposed to his father Jacob and his family, who were living in Canaan, that they live in the land of Goshen (Genesis 45:10). Jacob sent Judah ahead to meet Joseph and to lead the way to the land of Goshen (Genesis 46:28), and Joseph went to Goshen and met his father Jacob (Genesis 46:29). Joseph instructed his family to settle in the land of Goshen so as not to give offense to the Egyptians as herdsmen (Genesis 46:34). Joseph reported to Pharaoh that his brothers wished to live in the land of Goshen (Genesis 47:1), and they asked to stay in the land of Goshen in order to sojourn there (Genesis 47:4). Pharaoh gave them the land of Goshen to live in (Genesis 47:6). The people of Israel settled in the land of Goshen, were fruitful, and multiplied (Genesis 47:27). Not only Jacob's family but also their flocks, herds, and all their possessions remained in the land of Goshen (Genesis 50:8). Among the plagues that struck Egypt, at the time of the plague of flies, Pharaoh set apart the land of Goshen alone, where the people of Israel lived, so that there was no plague there (Exodus 8:22).
geography: Goshen is presumed to be the eastern Nile Delta region (near the Wadi Tumilat), and with its fertile soil and abundant water resources it offered an environment suited to livestock raising and farming. This region is connected with the floodplain of the Nile, and since it lies at the eastern gateway for entering Egypt from Canaan, it was geographically a strategic stronghold.
history: The Goshen region is known to have been a place where Asiatic immigrants settled in large numbers during the Middle Kingdom of ancient Egypt and the Second Intermediate Period. In particular, in the time of the Hyksos dynasty this region was a place where trade and population movement between Egypt and the Levant were frequent, and it has regional characteristics in which the background of the settlement of the people of Israel as shown in the Bible and the historical circumstances coincide.

remark: 2. The southern region of Canaan between Gaza and Gibeon.
introduce: Goshen is a region in southern Canaan that appears in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a fertile territory between the southern hill country of Palestine and the Negev, distinct from the Goshen of the Nile Delta of Egypt.
biblecontents: Joshua conquered the region from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza and the whole land of Goshen as far as Gibeon (Joshua 10:41). Joshua took the whole land of Canaan, that is, the hill country, the Negev, the whole land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel (Joshua 11:16).
geography: This Goshen is a buffer zone where the hill country of Judah in southern Canaan meets the Negev desert, a hilly plain region that spreads out between Gaza in the west and Gibeon in the north. A Mediterranean climate and a desert climate cross here, forming an environment suited to grazing and farming.
history: At the time of Joshua's wars of conquest, in the transition from the Late Bronze Age to the Iron Age, it was a strategic rear area controlled by an allied force of minor cities of southern Canaan. By occupying this region through the southern campaign, the army of Israel prepared a bridgehead for taking control of central and southern Canaan.

remark: 3. A town in the hill country of Judah.
introduce: Goshen is an ancient town located in the southern hill country of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua 15 in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Among the list of towns of the hill country obtained by the tribe of the descendants of Judah, eleven towns with their villages, including Goshen, Holon, and Giloh, are recorded (Joshua 15:51).
geography: It is identified with a hilly area in the southern hill country of Judah, about 18 km southwest of Hebron. Present-day ed-Dahariyah or nearby Khirbet Tatrit is proposed as a likely candidate.
history: In the Iron Age it was part of a network of mountain towns formed as the tribe of Judah settled in the central hill country. It was a settlement that defended the central hill country of Judah from the Negev wilderness to the south and carried on mountain farming of grapes, olives, and the like.

introduce: Gur-baal is a place name mentioned in Chronicles in the Old Testament, recorded as a region that God struck in the time of Uzziah, king of Judah.
biblecontents: God helped Uzziah against the Philistines and against the Arabs living in Gur-baal and the Meunites (2 Chronicles 26:7).
geography: Gur-baal is generally presumed to be near the region of Edom or northern Arabia, but its exact location has not been clearly established archaeologically.
history: During the reign of King Uzziah, Judah strengthened its influence over its southern territory and the surrounding peoples, and Gur-baal appears as a region associated with Arab forces in connection with Judah's military expansion at that time.

remark: 1. The region and people of Ethiopia and Abyssinia where the descendants of Cush lived.
introduce: In the ancient Hebrew Bible, Cush is a term designating the region of Nubia, which corresponds to present-day southern Egypt and northern Sudan. In ancient Near Eastern texts it is called Kush, and it signifies a powerful kingdom formed around the upper Nile River.
biblecontents: The event is recorded in which Moses took a Cushite woman as his wife, and Miriam and Aaron criticized him (Numbers 12:1). When David's son Absalom died, a Cushite appears as the messenger who carried the news to David (2 Samuel 18:21, 18:22, 18:23, 18:31, 18:32). There is a mention that when Sennacherib, king of Assyria, attacked Judah, Tirhakah, king of Cush, tried to fight against him (2 Kings 19:9). In the time of Rehoboam, Zerah the Cushite invaded Judah leading an enormous army (2 Chronicles 12:3, 14:9).
geography: Cush designates the territory south of the first cataract of Egypt that embraces the middle and upper Nile River. It includes the area of present-day Republic of the Sudan and part of Ethiopia, and geographically it developed around the fertile Nile valley lying between the east of the Sahara Desert and the Red Sea.
history: From around the eighth century BC until the middle of the seventh century BC, Cush formed a powerful kingdom centered on Napata, conquered Egypt, and established the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. It maintained close political and military relations with Egypt at that time, and it came to appear in the biblical record in the process of engaging in international struggles for power with great powers such as Assyria.

remark: 2. The region south of Ethiopia.
introduce: Cush is a place name designating the Ethiopia of the upper Nile River in ancient Africa and the southern region of Nubia, and in the prophetic books of the Bible it is mentioned as a distant people of the south and as part of the domain of God's rule.
biblecontents: The prophet proclaimed, "Woe to the land of whirring wings beyond the rivers of Cush" (Isaiah 18:1). It was declared that My worshipers, the daughter of My scattered ones, will come from beyond the rivers of Cush bringing offerings to Me (Zephaniah 3:10).
geography: It is an inland region of northeastern Africa that includes the Nubian plateau south of the first cataract of the Nile, southern Sudan, and the Ethiopian highlands. It is a vast tropical highland region through which flow the tributaries of the Nile, the Blue Nile and the White Nile, and the Atbara River.
history: In the first millennium BC it developed into the Kingdom of Kush (the Napatan and Meroitic civilizations), and it took control of trade routes in abundant gold, ivory, ebony, and the like. In the ancient Near Eastern world it was known as a military power possessing powerful chariot corps and archer corps.

remark: 3. A plateau surrounded by the Nile River and the Atbara River.
introduce: Cush is a biblical place name designating the ancient Near East and the African region, and it is generally used in the Hebrew Bible as a term meaning Ethiopia or the region of the upper Nile River. Genesis 2:13 mentions it as the land that the Gihon River, one of the four rivers that flowed out of the Garden of Eden, winds through.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the name of the second river is Gihon, and that it winds through the whole land of Cush (Genesis 2:13).
geography: Geographically, Cush designates a broad area that includes Nubia, in the middle and upper Nile region, and present-day Ethiopia. In the context of Genesis 2:13 it is mentioned in connection with the location of Eden, but scholars are divided over pinpointing its location in modern geography and the identity of the Gihon River.
history: Historically, the Kingdom of Cush flourished around the Nile valley around the eighth century BC, and it formed the Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt and even ruled Egypt. Throughout the biblical record, Cush frequently appears as a powerful state south of Egypt and a political force in close relationship with Egypt.

remark: 4. A region in Susiana and Media.
introduce: Cush is the Asiatic Cush that appears in Genesis in the Bible, and it designates the region inhabited by the Elamites, Susiana, and the Kassite people in eastern Mesopotamia, distinguished from the Cush of Africa.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the name of the second river is Gihon, and that it winds through the whole land of Cush (Genesis 2:13). Cush also fathered Nimrod, who was the first mighty man on the earth (Genesis 10:8).
geography: It corresponds to Susiana (the plain of Elam), where the foothills of the Zagros Mountains east of the Tigris River meet the Mesopotamian plain, and to the southwestern part of Media. It is the ancient civilizational sphere of southeastern Mesopotamia through which the Karun River and the Karkheh River flow.
history: It is the place of origin of the people called Kashshu (Kassite) in ancient cuneiform inscriptions. As the home territory of the Kassite dynasty that ruled Babylonia from the sixteenth century BC to the twelfth century BC, it was deeply involved in the formation of ancient Mesopotamian civilization.

introduce: Kenaz is a name designating a branch of the Edomite people, and it is a term that means the head of a tribe living in the land of Edom or the region where they lived.
biblecontents: Kenaz is mentioned as one of the chiefs of Edom among the descendants of Esau, and they are included in the genealogy of chiefs of the land of Edom (Genesis 36:15). Also, Chief Kenaz is listed in the list of the chiefs of Edom together with Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar, and others (Genesis 36:42). In Numbers, this name is cited when Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite is mentioned (Numbers 32:12). In Chronicles, too, the genealogy of the chiefs of Edom, including Chief Kenaz, as descendants of Esau is reaffirmed (1 Chronicles 1:53).
geography: The Edom region where the Kenaz tribe lived is a terrain formed around the Seir mountain country southeast of the Dead Sea, a rugged mountainous area extending to Moab on the north and to the Gulf of Aqaba on the south. This region was rich in copper mines and was a crossroads of transport through which caravan trade routes passed, but there is a lack of archaeological basis for clearly identifying the name Kenaz itself with a particular city or an independent territory.
history: Kenaz is a name representing a tribal unit of early Edomite society, and it is presumed to be a group that shared kinship or geographical proximity with the tribes of Israel at the time of the conquest of Canaan. In particular, judging from the fact that Caleb is classified as a Kenizzite, it can be called a historical trace showing the possibility that members of the Edomite tribes were incorporated into, or mixed with, the tribal society of Israel.

remark: 1. A city in the hill country of Judah, in the direction north of Hebron.
introduce: Gedor is one of the towns located in the hill country allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Gedor is included in the list of towns of the inheritance that the descendants of the tribe of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:58).
geography: It is a region located near the north of Hebron, and it is identified with the area of Khirbet Jedur in the present-day West Bank. Since it sits on the highland plateau of the hill country of Judah, it is topographically located on high ground.

remark: 2. The hometown of Jeroham of the tribe of Benjamin.
introduce: Gedor, which appears in 1 Chronicles 12:7, is a noun designating the region where the sons of Jeroham, one of the families of the tribe of Benjamin, lived, or the family from that region.
biblecontents: Joelah and Zebadiah, sons of Jeroham from Gedor, who joined David's mighty men, are mentioned (1 Chronicles 12:7).
geography: In Hebrew, Gedor means a fence or a fortified place, and it is known as a town in the hill country of Judah. Its present-day location is identified with the area of Khirbet Jedur, about 15 km southwest of Bethlehem.

remark: 3. A place near the south of Judah, where the tribe of Simeon lived.
introduce: Gedor is a place name that appears in 1 Chronicles 4:39, a place mentioned in the course of the descendants of the tribe of Simeon moving in search of pasture.
biblecontents: The descendants of the tribe of Simeon went from the east side of the valley to the entrance of Gedor and sought pasture for their flocks (1 Chronicles 4:39).
geography: The possibility has been raised that the Hebrew Gedor is confused with the region of Gerar, but geographically it is presumed to be located near the Negev in southern Palestine, or near the entrance of the valley of Gerar.

introduce: Kerioth-hezron is a place name that appears in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a place mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Kerioth-hezron is Hazor, and it is one of the towns included in the list of the southern inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:25).
geography: It is presumed to be located near the Negev desert in the southern region of the tribe of Judah, and it is regarded as the same place as Hazor or as an adjacent area. The exact modern location is disputed archaeologically, but it is generally identified as a southern settlement within the boundary range of the tribe of Judah.

introduce: Chephar-ammoni is a place recorded in the Book of Joshua in the Bible as one of the towns of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: Among the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin received according to their families, twelve towns with their villages, including Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba, are mentioned (Joshua 18:24).
geography: It is classified as a town located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, but its exact location today has not been clearly identified archaeologically. From the ending -ammoni in the name, the possibility is raised that it reflects a place name connected with the Ammonites or the character of a border region adjacent to them.

introduce: Chesulloth is one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Issachar at the time of the conquest of Canaan in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Chesulloth was included in the boundary of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar, together with Shunem (Joshua 19:18).
geography: Chesulloth is presumed to be located near the northeast of the Jezreel Valley and is identified as being near the southwestern foot of Mount Tabor. By its present-day place name it is often identified with the area of Iksal.

introduce: Kehelathah is one of the stopping places where the people of Israel stayed on their journey after leaving Egypt toward Canaan.
biblecontents: The people of Israel left Rissah and camped at Kehelathah, and they left Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher (Numbers 33:22-23).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is presumed to have been located in the Negev desert, the northeastern region of the Sinai Peninsula, or in its vicinity.

introduce: Geliloth is a place name that appears in the Bible in describing the northern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin, a region presumed to derive from a root meaning "circle" or "cycle" in Arabic.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the boundary of the inheritance of the descendants of Benjamin proceeded northward from En-shemesh and reached Geliloth (Joshua 18:17). This point is described as being located opposite the slope of Adummim (Joshua 18:17).
geography: Geliloth is presumed to be near the slope of Adummim near Jericho, and this is a place with the topographical feature of lying on the route going up from the Jordan Valley to Jerusalem.

introduce: Kinah is a town located near the southern boundary of the land allotted to the ancient tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Kinah is mentioned as one of the towns of the southern region allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:22).
geography: Kinah is presumed to be located in the southern zone where the hill country of Judah meets the Negev desert, but the specific archaeological site and the place with which it has been identified are unclear.

introduce: Gidom is a place name that appears in the Book of Judges in the Old Testament, the place mentioned last as the inhabitants of Gibeah of the tribe of Benjamin were fleeing from the allied army of Israel.
biblecontents: The Benjamites turned toward the wilderness and reached the rock of Rimmon at Gidom, and Israel followed them closely along the main road as though gleaning, as far as Gidom, and killed two thousand men (Judges 20:45).
geography: The exact location of Gidom has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is presumed to be east of the hill country of Benjamin, that is, the Jordan Valley or the wilderness region northwest of the Dead Sea. It is regarded as a place with the topographical feature of lying adjacent to the rock of Rimmon.

introduce: Kidron is a place name designating the valley located between the eastern wall of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. It formed the eastern boundary of ancient Jerusalem and functioned as an important geographical stronghold related to the defense and drainage of the city of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: The tribe of Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron and lived among them (Judges 1:30). David crossed the Kidron brook and headed for the wilderness to escape Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:23). Solomon commanded Shimei not to cross the Kidron brook (1 Kings 2:37). King Asa cut down the Asherah pole that his mother Maacah had made and burned it at the Kidron brook (1 Kings 15:13, 2 Chronicles 15:16). King Josiah burned in the fields of Kidron all the articles made for Baal and Asherah and carried their ashes to Bethel (2 Kings 23:4), and he took the Asherah image brought out of the temple to the Kidron brook, burned it, and ground it to powder (2 Kings 23:6). Also Josiah tore down the altars that Ahaz and Manasseh had made and threw their dust into the Kidron brook (2 Kings 23:12). In the time of Hezekiah the priests brought out the unclean things from the temple and carried them to the Kidron brook (2 Chronicles 29:16). The people of Judah removed all the altars and incense altars in Jerusalem and threw them into the Kidron brook (2 Chronicles 30:14).
geography: It is a deep valley located east of Jerusalem, running from north to south. To the west lie the Temple Mount and the city of Jerusalem, and to the east it abuts the Mount of Olives. It has the topography of a wadi in which no water flows except in the rainy season, and it served as the natural eastern line of defense of the ancient city of Jerusalem.
history: As the eastern boundary of Jerusalem, it was used as a place for disposing of various kinds of refuse arising from the temple and of unclean objects connected with idol worship. In particular, it can be confirmed that Asa and Josiah, the reforming kings of Judah, used this point as a symbolic place for waste disposal and judgment in the course of destroying idols. Topographically adjacent to the wall, it frequently appears in historical records as a route of military movement and a strategic stronghold.

introduce: Chitlish is a place name mentioned in Joshua 15:40 in the Bible as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Among the list of towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, Gad, Chitlish, and Eglon are mentioned side by side (Joshua 15:40).
geography: Chitlish is presumed to be located in the Shephelah within the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, that is, in the low hill country between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain, but the specific modern archaeological site has not been clearly determined.

remark: 1. A town of the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan River.
introduce: Kiriathaim is a town in the Moabite region east of the Jordan recorded in the Bible, regarded as an ancient settlement located in the area of present-day Jordan. The Hebrew name means "two towns," and it is mentioned as one of the areas that the tribe of Reuben built or rebuilt and occupied in the past.
biblecontents: The descendants of Reuben built Kiriathaim, together with Heshbon and Elealeh (Numbers 32:37). In the time of Joshua it is recorded as one of the areas allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:19). The prophet Jeremiah proclaimed a message of judgment concerning Kiriathaim, that it would be put to shame and destroyed (Jeremiah 48:1, Jeremiah 48:23). The prophet Ezekiel also spoke of the opening up of Kiriathaim, the glory of Moab (Ezekiel 25:9).
geography: Kiriathaim is presumed to be a region located in the plain northeast of the Dead Sea, east of the Jordan River. Archaeologically, Khirbet el-Qureiyat, near Madaba, is discussed as a likely candidate. Since it sits in a fertile highland region, it had an environment suited to farming and livestock raising.
history: It was originally Moabite territory, but in the course of Israel's conquest east of the Jordan it became the possession of the tribe of Reuben. Afterward, however, depending on Israel's political circumstances, it passed again under Moabite control or became the object of territorial disputes, and in the later Old Testament it came to be regarded again as one of the principal cities of Moab. Moab's claim to rule over this region is also confirmed in ancient inscription materials such as the Mesha Stele.

remark: 2. A Levitical town in Naphtali.
introduce: Kiriathaim is a Levitical town in northern Galilee recorded in 1 Chronicles 6 in the Old Testament, a town within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, the same as Kartan, which appears in Joshua 21.
biblecontents: Kedesh in Galilee and its pasturelands, Hammon and its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim and its pasturelands, of the tribe of Naphtali, were given to the descendants of Gershon (1 Chronicles 6:76).
geography: It was located in the highland region of Upper Galilee, north of the Sea of Galilee or west of the Huleh Basin. As a parallel place name to Kartan in Joshua 21:32, it is identified with the remains of Tell Katanah or Khirbet Qaryun.
history: It was a dwelling place of Gershonite Levites who settled within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in northern Israel in the Iron Age. It served as a religious base that monitored the traffic routes of the northern border zone and maintained observance of the law and the order of the community.

introduce: Kiriath is a place name mentioned in Joshua 18:28, a region classified as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: Kiriath is specified as one of the towns obtained by lot by the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28).
geography: It is highly likely that Kiriath is an abbreviation of Kiriath-jearim in the Bible, and it is presumed to be a town in a mountainous area located in the border region of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28).

introduce: Kiriath-baal is a town located near the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, mentioned in the Bible as an old name or another name of Kiriath-jearim.
biblecontents: Kiriath-baal is one of the two towns also called Kiriath-jearim, and it is recorded as one of the places in the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:60). This town is also mentioned as the same place as Kiriath-jearim in the description of the border of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:14).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Abu Ghosh or nearby Tell al-Azhar, and is located in the hill country of Judea about 15 km west of Jerusalem. It is a strategic stronghold situated on the main route going up from the Philistine plain to Jerusalem.
history: It is conjectured to have been originally a place name connected with the Canaanite worship of Baal, but in the time of Joshua it was incorporated into the territory of the tribes of Israel. Afterward it was called Kiriath-jearim, and it is known as the place where the ark of the covenant stayed for a considerable period until David moved it to Jerusalem.

introduce: Kiriath-sannah was a town located in the hill country of Judah in the south of ancient Canaan, a place name better known by the name Debir.
biblecontents: Kiriath-sannah is also called Debir, and it is recorded as one of the list of hill-country towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:49).
geography: It is a region presumed to be present-day Tell Beit Mirsim, located in the hill country of Judah southwest of Hebron. The surrounding area consists of barren mountainous terrain.
history: It was originally a stronghold where the descendants of Anak lived, but it is an area that was conquered in the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan. Afterward, according to the record of the Book of Judges, this town is also closely connected with the conquest activities of Othniel.

introduce: Kiriath-sepher is an ancient town located in the hill country of Judah in southern Canaan, a name that carries the meaning "city of books." It is a place that later came to be called by the name Debir.
biblecontents: Kiriath-sepher was originally called Debir, and Caleb offered to give his daughter Acsah as a wife to the one who conquered it (Joshua 15:15-16). Othniel captured it and took Caleb's daughter as his wife (Judges 1:11-12).
geography: It is a town of a mountain region located within the territory of the tribe of Judah. Archaeologically, the view that it is Tell Beit Mirsim, southwest of Hebron, is dominant, but some scholars identify it with Tell Rabud.
history: The name Kiriath-sepher is sometimes interpreted as suggesting that it was a Canaanite archive or a center of scribes. As a strategic stronghold in southern Canaan, this town was one of the first objects of conquest in the early period of Israel's settlement.

introduce: Kiriath-arba is an ancient city located in the hill country of Judah in southern Canaan, a place that later came to be better known by the name Hebron. Arba was called the greatest man among the descendants of Anak.
biblecontents: The name Kiriath-arba was given after the name of Arba, who was the greatest man among the Anakim (Joshua 14:15). When Joshua gave a portion to the descendants of Judah, he gave Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, to Caleb according to the command of God (Joshua 15:13). This place is recorded as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:54). Afterward it was designated as one of the cities of refuge assigned to the descendants of Levi (Joshua 20:7), and was given as a town of the Kohathite clan, descendants of Aaron (Joshua 21:11). The descendants of Judah struck down the Canaanites who lived in Kiriath-arba and captured it (Judges 1:10).
geography: Kiriath-arba, identified with Hebron, is a strategic stronghold located in the hill country of Judah at an elevation of about 900 meters above sea level. Because its ground is higher than its surroundings, it is advantageous for defense, and being about 30 kilometers south of Jerusalem, it served as the center of the southern region.
history: Kiriath-arba is an ancient city that has existed since the Bronze Age, and in the Bible it is described as one of the strongholds of the descendants of Anak, a race of giants. According to Egyptian place-name lists and archaeological surveys, this area already had the form of a city-state with strong walls from the early Iron Age of Canaan, and it held historical importance even before the settlement of the tribe of Judah.

introduce: Kiriath-arba is a place name mentioned as one of the areas where the tribe of Judah settled after the return from exile, and it is generally known as the old name of Hebron.
biblecontents: Among the villages where the descendants of Judah who had returned from exile lived, Kiriath-arba and its surrounding villages are included (Nehemiah 11:25).
geography: It is identified with the Hebron region and is the central city of the hill country of Judea, about 30 km south of Jerusalem.
history: It is a place named after the name of Arba, a giant of the descendants of Anak, and it had existed as a major stronghold of the ancient Near East since before the conquest of Canaan.

introduce: Kiriath-jearim was an ancient Canaanite town located near the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. This area is recorded as an important place where the ark of the covenant was temporarily enshrined in early Israelite history.
biblecontents: Kiriath-jearim is mentioned as a border area stretching from the spring of Nephtoah to Mount Ephron (Joshua 15:9). It is listed among the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, and at that time it comprised two towns and their villages (Joshua 15:60). It appears again when the western border is described (Joshua 18:14), and it is stated that the border of the inheritance of the descendants of Benjamin begins at Kiriath-baal, that is, Kiriath-jearim, and reaches the western end (Joshua 18:15).
geography: It is presumed to be modern Abu Ghosh or nearby Tell el-Azhar. Located west-northwest of Jerusalem, it is a strategic stronghold connecting the central mountain range of the hill country of Judah with the coastal plain. Owing to the nature of the mountainous terrain, it was a town formed on high ground that was easy to defend.
history: It was originally one of the towns of the Gibeonites, and there is a record that in the time of Joshua they made peace with Israel. Afterward, after the ark of the covenant at Shiloh was captured in the war with the Philistines and then returned, it has historical importance as the place where it was kept for a long time in the house of Abinadab until David moved it to Jerusalem.

introduce: Kiriath-arba is a town of the ancient Canaan region, a place that later came to be better known by the name Hebron. It is a long-established settlement that existed even before the time of Abraham, and it is regarded as the same place as Hebron.
biblecontents: Sarah, the wife of Abraham, died in Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan, and Abraham mourned and wept (Genesis 23:2). Also, Jacob went to Mamre of Kiriath-arba and came to his father Isaac, and this is the place where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned (Genesis 35:27).
geography: Kiriath-arba is located in the central part of the hill country of Judah, situated on high ground at an elevation of about 900 meters or more above sea level. Because its ground is higher than the surrounding area, it is advantageous for defense, and with fertile soil and abundant water sources, it has had an environment suited to settlement since ancient times.
history: The place name Kiriath-arba is interpreted as derived from the name of Arba, a giant and the ancestor of the descendants of Anak. It was a fortress where ancient tribes such as the Amorites and the descendants of Anak lived from before the time of Abraham, and afterward, in the course of the conquest of Canaan by the tribes of Israel, it was allotted to Caleb and became his inheritance.

remark: A town of Judah on the border of the tribe of Benjamin.
introduce: Kiriath-jearim is a town of important significance from the standpoint of the history and religion of ancient Israel, a place name that appears in the records from the time of Joshua to the time of Nehemiah. It was one of the towns of the Gibeonites, and is known as the place where the ark of the covenant was kept for a long time.
biblecontents: After making peace with the Gibeonites, Joshua arrived at Kiriath-jearim, one of their towns (Joshua 9:17). The place called Mahaneh-dan, named because the descendants of Dan camped there, is located behind Kiriath-jearim (Judges 18:12). The people of Beth-shemesh sent the ark of the covenant to the people of Kiriath-jearim to keep it (1 Samuel 6:21), and the people of Kiriath-jearim moved the ark and put it in the house of Abinadab on the hill, and consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark (1 Samuel 7:1). For the twenty years that the ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim, all the house of Israel longed for the LORD (1 Samuel 7:2). The clans of Kiriath-jearim are divided into the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites (1 Chronicles 2:53). David assembled all the congregation of Israel and wanted to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 13:5). David and all Israel went up to Kiriath-jearim and brought the ark of God (1 Chronicles 13:6). David had already brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim and placed it in the tent he had pitched in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 1:4). After the return from the Babylonian exile, 743 descendants of Kiriath-jearim returned to Jerusalem and Judah (Nehemiah 7:29).
geography: It is located about 15 km west of Jerusalem and is identified with the area of present-day Tell Azhar or Deir el-Azhar. It is located near the border of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and is characterized by hilly mountainous terrain. Located near the valley of Sorek, it sits on a strategic route of movement.
history: It was originally a town of the Hivites who were living among the Gibeonites, but it was annexed to Israel in the time of Joshua. Since the ark of the covenant was enshrined here for about 20 years (or more) from its return from the Philistines until it was moved to Jerusalem, its religious importance was very great. Afterward, when King David moved the ark to Jerusalem, its role as a political and religious center changed. There are also records that after the exile the residents continued to live there and took part as members of the Judean community.

introduce: Kiriath-huzoth is a place name mentioned in the Book of Numbers in the Old Testament as the place to which Balak, king of Moab, went in order to receive Balaam.
biblecontents: Balak went with Balaam and they came to Kiriath-huzoth, and Balak slaughtered oxen and sheep and entertained Balaam and the officials who were with him (Numbers 22:39).
geography: Its exact location is disputed among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be a region within the plains of Moab or one of the towns north of the Arnon River. By its Hebrew etymology it has the meaning "city of markets (streets)," and it appears to have been one of the strategic strongholds of the Moabite kingdom at that time.
history: It is a place that appears in the course of Balak, king of Moab, who was wary of the advance of the people of Israel, summoning Balaam, the diviner of Mesopotamia. By hospitably receiving Balaam, Balak sought to achieve his political aim of having Israel cursed.

introduce: Kir is a place name of the ancient Near East, closely related to the origin of the Aramean people, and a region mentioned in the Bible mainly in the context of military alliances or movements.
biblecontents: It is recorded that Elam took up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield (Isaiah 22:6). Other passages of the Old Testament also mention that the Arameans came up from Kir (Amos 9:7).
geography: Its exact location is debated among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be a region in northern Mesopotamia or east of the Tigris River. The view that it is Kiru, which appears in ancient Assyrian records, or a nearby region, is dominant.
history: It is known as the homeland of the Arameans, and there is a record that around the 8th century BC, after Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria conquered Damascus, he forcibly resettled its inhabitants in the region of Kir (2 Kings 16:9). This was part of the large-scale population transfer policy of Assyria at that time.

introduce: The Girgashites were one of the ancient tribes that lived in the land of Canaan; the name refers to the area occupied by the Girgashite clan, who were sons of Canaan and descendants of Ham.
biblecontents: The Girgashites are mentioned as one of the sons of Canaan (Genesis 10:16, 1 Chronicles 1:14), and are included in the list of inhabitants of the land that God promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:21). Afterward, when the people of Israel entered Canaan, they were specified as one of the seven nations that had to be conquered (Deuteronomy 7:1, Joshua 3:10, Joshua 24:11). Also, in Nehemiah's prayer it is recalled that God gave their land to the people of the covenant (Nehemiah 9:8).

introduce: The Girzites were an ancient people of the ancient Near East, one of the groups that David raided while he was living in Ziklag.
biblecontents: David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites; for those nations had been the inhabitants of the land from of old, as one goes to Shur and to the land of Egypt (1 Samuel 27:8)
geography: It is presumed to be a region located near the wilderness of Shur and on the route toward Egypt, which is a nomadic zone near the Negev desert in southern Canaan.

introduce: Gibeah is one of the towns of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in Joshua 18:28 of the Old Testament, a region that shares an etymology with Gibeah, which in Hebrew means "hill."
biblecontents: In Joshua 18:28, Gibeah is recorded as one of the fourteen towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, together with Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), and Kiriath (Joshua 18:28).
geography: The territory of the tribe of Benjamin lay between the tribes of Ephraim and Judah, and Gibeah is presumed to have been situated in the highland mountain region north of Jerusalem.

introduce: Kibroth-hattaavah is a place named to commemorate an event that occurred during the Exodus journey of the people of Israel, and in Hebrew it has the meaning "graves of craving."
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the places where the people of Israel, by harboring craving in the wilderness, incurred the wrath of the LORD (Deuteronomy 9:22). Moses said that at Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah the people provoked the LORD to wrath (Deuteronomy 9:22).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is presumed to be on the route from Mount Sinai toward Kadesh-barnea. Considering the route of movement of the Israelite camp at that time, the view that it lay somewhere in the northeastern part of the Sinai Peninsula is dominant.
history: It was an event that occurred during the wilderness journey after the Exodus; because of the complaints of the people who wanted to eat meat, quail were supplied in great numbers, but in the process many were struck down and buried there. This event is described in detail in Numbers 11.

introduce: Kibroth-hattaavah is a place where the children of Israel stayed during the Exodus journey, and its name has the meaning "graves of craving."
biblecontents: When the people of Israel craved meat and complained, the LORD sent quail, but before they could even chew the meat He sent a plague, and many died (Numbers 11:33). For this reason that place was named Kibroth-hattaavah (Numbers 11:34). Afterward the people left Kibroth-hattaavah and reached Hazeroth (Numbers 11:35).
geography: It is presumed to be located on the wilderness route leaving Mount Sinai toward Kadesh-barnea. Its exact location has not been identified, but it is regarded as being near Taberah, in the northeastern region of the Sinai Peninsula.

introduce: Kibroth-hattaavah is a place the Israelites passed through after leaving the wilderness of Sinai on the way to Hazeroth, and is known as the region where the people, giving way to craving, suffered a plague.
biblecontents: The Israelites proceeded from Kibroth-hattaavah to Hazeroth (Numbers 33:16). Kibroth-hattaavah, also called Kibroth-hattaavah, is specified as a stage of the journey before Hazeroth (Numbers 33:17). This place has the meaning of the place where the people who had craved were buried (Numbers 11:34).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is generally presumed to be in a wilderness region north or northeast of Mount Sinai. It shares the topographic features of being adjacent to Hazeroth.

remark: One of the four towns that the Hivites built in Canaan.
introduce: Gibeon is a major town located in the central highlands of Canaan, the dwelling place of the Hivites, who made peace with Israel and formed an alliance during Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: The inhabitants of Gibeon deceived Joshua and made a treaty of peace (Joshua 9:3). Unlike the other towns of Canaan, they are described as a great town that made a treaty with Israel (Joshua 9:17). Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, learned that Gibeon had made peace with Israel and was afraid (Joshua 10:1). Gibeon was like a royal city and was greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty warriors (Joshua 10:2). So the five Amorite kings, including the king of Jerusalem, united and attacked Gibeon (Joshua 10:4, 10:5). The people of Gibeon urgently asked Joshua for help (Joshua 10:6), and Joshua defeated them in a great slaughter at Gibeon (Joshua 10:10). The event of the sun standing still over Gibeon forms the background of this battle (Joshua 10:12). Joshua conquered all the region from Kadesh-barnea to Gibeon (Joshua 10:41).
geography: Gibeon is presumed to be el-Jib, located about 8 to 10 km northwest of Jerusalem. It sits on high ground about 700 m above sea level in the central mountain region, and it is a strategic stronghold connected with the surrounding plains and a position able to control the road to Jerusalem.
history: In the Bronze and Iron Ages, because this area was a crossroads of traffic, a large settlement inhabited by a considerable population had formed. At the time of the conquest of Canaan, Gibeon had the form of an independent city-state with strong walls and skilled military strength, and it had a system by which it could make independent diplomatic decisions within the sphere of the neighboring Amorite powers.

introduce: The Kishon is a river that flows across the Valley of Jezreel, a geographical place that formed the background of important military clashes and religious events in biblical history.
biblecontents: God promised to give Israel victory by drawing Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, and his chariots to the River Kishon (Judges 4:7). Sisera gathered at the River Kishon with nine hundred chariots and all his troops (Judges 4:13). In the song of Deborah and Barak, the River Kishon is described as a torrent that swept away the enemies (Judges 5:21). After seizing the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, Elijah brought them down to the Kishon brook and put them to death (1 Kings 18:40). The sons of Hashem the Gizonite are mentioned in the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:34). The psalmist mentions the destruction that Sisera and Jabin suffered at the Kishon brook and sings of the defeat of foreign nations (Psalms 83:9).
geography: The Kishon River rises east of Mount Carmel, passes through the Valley of Jezreel, and flows into the Bay of Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. Its flow is small in ordinary times but turns into a torrent in the rainy season, and because of the low topography of the Valley of Jezreel in particular, it frequently floods, making it terrain that places great restrictions on military movement.
history: Because the Valley of Jezreel was a major trade route and military stronghold of the ancient Near East, the Kishon area became the battlefield of several wars. Besides the battle between the Canaanite army and Israel, the First Book of Kings records it as a place of religious purification where Elijah put the worshipers of Baal to death. This shows that the Kishon was a point where internal conflict of faith within Israel and struggle against external hostile forces coexisted.

introduce: Chisloth-tabor is an ancient place name located near northern Galilee in the Palestine region, a town that existed on the boundary line of the tribe of Zebulun.
biblecontents: Chisloth-tabor is located at the point where the border, turning from Sarid eastward toward the sunrise, goes to the border of Chisloth-tabor, goes out to Daberath, and goes up to Japhia (Joshua 19:12).
geography: Chisloth-tabor is presumed to be a name referring to the slope of Mount Tabor or the area around it, and it has the topographic feature of lying adjacent to the northeastern edge of the Valley of Jezreel. Modern geographers identify this area as near the village of Iksal at the southwestern foot of Mount Tabor.
history: It is a place mentioned in the course of describing the boundary divisions of the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun at the time of Israel's settlement. As a strategic stronghold linking the lower plain of Galilee with Mount Tabor, this area serves as a historical indicator showing the arrangement of the dwelling places of the early tribes of Israel and the system of territorial division.

introduce: Kishion was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar at the time of the distribution of the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Lots were drawn for the tribe of the descendants of Issachar according to their clans, and their inheritance included Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Joshua 19:20). It was one of the towns received from the tribe of Issachar and was given to the Levites, descendants of Gershon (Joshua 21:28).

introduce: Giah is a place name mentioned in 2 Samuel 2:24 of the Bible, a place located on the route of the battle in which David's army and the army of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, clashed.
biblecontents: Joab and Abishai pursued Abner, and at sunset they came to the hill of Giah, by the road in the wilderness of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:24)
geography: Giah is presumed to be a rugged hill country near Gibeon, and is known as a strategic point on the way east or southeast from Gibeon. At present its exact archaeological location is difficult to specify, but topographically it is understood to be a waypoint situated in a mountainous region.

introduce: Chios is a Greek island located in the eastern Aegean Sea. In ancient times it was a major member of the Ionian League, and it is recorded as one point on the route of the apostle Paul's third missionary journey.
biblecontents: There is a record that the apostle Paul, on his way to Miletus, sailed and arrived opposite Chios (Acts 20:15).
geography: Chios is an island situated in the sea near Ephesus in the region of Ionia, on the western coast of Asia Minor, and it lies on an important sea route connecting Samos and Miletus when sailing.
history: Ancient Chios prospered economically and culturally as a member of the Ionian League, and in the time of the Roman Empire it was a strategic stronghold adjacent to the province of Asia, a point where sailors frequently stopped.

remark: 1. The second river that rises in the Garden of Eden.
introduce: Gihon is a place name recorded as one of the four streams that flow from the Garden of Eden in Genesis.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the name of the second river is Gihon, and that it winds through the whole land of Cush (Genesis 2:13).
geography: From the geographical standpoint of the ancient Near East, the Gihon was described as a river flowing around the land of Cush; Cush is generally associated with Nubia or the Ethiopian region of the upper Nile, but within the geographical context of the Bible, it is difficult to specify an exact modern geographical location that connects it with the location of Eden.

remark: 2. A place near Jerusalem where Solomon was anointed and proclaimed king.
introduce: Gihon is an intermittent spring located in the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, the main source of drinking water for the city of Jerusalem and the center of the succession to the royal throne of ancient Israel and of the construction of waterways.
biblecontents: In order to set Solomon on the throne as king, King David instructed the priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan to bring him down to Gihon and anoint him king over Israel (1 Kings 1:33). So Zadok, Nathan, and the others set Solomon on a mule, went down to Gihon, anointed him, and installed him as king, and the people rejoiced and shouted (1 Kings 1:38). Afterward, the fact that the priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan had anointed Solomon king at Gihon became known in the royal palace (1 Kings 1:45). King Hezekiah, in preparation for the Assyrian invasion, blocked the water outlet of the spring of Gihon and brought it into the city (2 Chronicles 32:30), and King Manasseh built an outer wall in the valley west of Gihon, outside the City of David, and strengthened the defenses (2 Chronicles 33:14).
geography: Gihon is the only natural spring, located in the Kidron Valley below the eastern wall of Jerusalem. It has a structure in which water wells up from an underground aquifer, and owing to its topographical characteristics it supplied the water resource essential to the inhabitants of ancient Jerusalem.
history: From the Bronze Age, the area around the Gihon spring provided a core environment where people could live, and there is a record that when David conquered Jerusalem from the Jebusites he entered the city through a water channel. The Siloam Tunnel built in the time of Hezekiah is a product of ancient engineering that diverted the water of the Gihon spring into the city and made it possible to withstand an enemy siege.

introduce: Chinnereth is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, mainly meaning a border or town designating the region east of the Jordan River and the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. By its Hebrew etymology it is presumed to derive from the shape of the lake resembling a harp, and its name later changed to Gennesaret in the New Testament period.
biblecontents: Chinnereth appears as a point that sets the northern border of the promised land (Numbers 34:11). It is mentioned as a geographical reference forming the border of the Jordan Valley up to where the Jordan reaches the Sea of Chinnereth (Deuteronomy 3:17, Joshua 13:27). It is recorded as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Naphtali (Joshua 19:35). In the days of Baasha, king of northern Israel, it became the object of the historical event in which Ben-hadad of Aram conquered the whole land of Chinnereth together with Ijon, Dan, and Abel-beth-maacah (1 Kings 15:20).
geography: Chinnereth includes the Plain of Gennesaret, a fertile plain located northwest of the Sea of Galilee, or refers to a town nearby. Being adjacent to the point where the Jordan River flows into the Sea of Galilee, it has an environment with abundant water resources that is favorable for farming. This region shows the topographic feature in which the surrounding mountain regions and a low elevation below sea level coexist.
history: From the Bronze Age, this region functioned as a strategic stronghold connecting the Jordan Valley with the coastal road. In the period of Israel's settlement it was included in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, but because of its geographical importance it was frequently attacked by the neighboring great power, Aram-Damascus. After being destroyed by the Aramean army around the 9th century BC, it gradually disappears from the historical record, or reappears in the New Testament period under the name Gennesaret.

introduce: Chinnereth is the name designating a town located in the northern region of Canaan and the plain area around it, a place name associated with the western shore of the Sea of Chinnereth, later called the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: Chinnereth is mentioned as one of the spheres of influence when Jabin, king of Hazor, formed the northern Canaanite coalition (Joshua 11:2). It is also presumed to be the same as, or adjacent to, Hammoth-dor, a town allotted after Joshua's wars of conquest to the descendants of Gershon of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:32).
geography: Chinnereth includes the plain area located on the western shore of the present Sea of Galilee, and is a strategic crossroads connected to the Huleh Basin to the north and leading to the Jordan Valley to the south. On the basis of fertile soil and abundant water resources, it has had conditions suitable for the development of farming and fishing since ancient times.
history: According to archaeological surveys of the Bronze Age, Chinnereth was under the sphere of influence of the Canaanite city-states and was incorporated into the defense system of the northern Canaanite confederation centered on Hazor. Afterward, following the period of Israel's conquest, it was distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali, but until it was fully Israelized, political and military alliances with neighboring cities appear to have continued.

remark: The Assyrian region between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea.
introduce: Kir is a place name of the ancient Near East, a place mentioned in the Bible and in ancient Near Eastern inscriptions in connection with the origin of the Arameans. It is perceived as a region closely connected with the Aramean kingdom.
biblecontents: When Rezin, king of Aram, attacked Judah, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, conquered Damascus and carried its people captive to Kir (2 Kings 16:9). In the prophecy of judgment against Moab, it is mentioned that Kir of Moab, a major town of Moab, will be destroyed in a single night (Isaiah 15:1). A judgment was proclaimed that God would cause the people of Damascus to be carried captive to Kir (Amos 1:5). There is a statement that, just as God brought the children of Israel up out of Egypt, He also brought the Arameans up from Kir (Amos 9:7).
geography: Scholarly opinion is divided on the exact location of Kir. Some scholars presume this region to be northern Mesopotamia or the area near the Zagros Mountains east of Babylon. Ancient inscriptions and other sources describe this region as the home territory of the Arameans or as the place to which they were forcibly resettled.
history: Around the 8th century BC, the Assyrian Empire implemented a policy of forcibly resettling conquered peoples. After conquering Aramean Damascus, Tiglath-pileser III resettled its inhabitants in Kir, in the eastern frontier region. Kir is sometimes presumed to be a place connected with the place of origin of the Arameans, and it is a place that shows the geopolitical movement the Aramean people experienced under Assyria's expansionist policy.

remark: 1. A region west of the Jordan River near Jericho, where Israel spent its first night after crossing the Jordan River.
introduce: Gilgal was an important strategic base where the people of Israel stayed immediately after entering the land of Canaan in the time of Joshua, and it is the first camp established after they crossed from the east side of the Jordan River to the west.
biblecontents: On the tenth day of the first month the people of Israel went up from the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho (Joshua 4:19). Joshua set up at Gilgal the twelve stones he had taken from the Jordan (Joshua 4:20). Because the LORD rolled away the reproach of Egypt at Gilgal, that place has been called Gilgal to this day (Joshua 5:9). The Israelites camped at Gilgal, and on the evening of the fourteenth day of that month they kept the Passover on the plains of Jericho (Joshua 5:10). The Gibeonites came to the camp at Gilgal and asked Joshua for a treaty (Joshua 9:6). The Gibeonites sent word to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and asked for help (Joshua 10:6). Joshua went up from Gilgal with all his army and mighty men (Joshua 10:7). Joshua marched all night from Gilgal and came upon them suddenly (Joshua 10:9). Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal (Joshua 10:15).
geography: Gilgal is presumed to be a region located on the plain west of the Jordan River and east of Jericho. Located at the Jordan crossing point and on the route entering the interior of Canaan, it has flat terrain favorable for military movement and supply.
history: In the early stage of Israel's conquest of Canaan in the Late Bronze Age, Gilgal served as a military outpost and an administrative center where religious rites were carried out. This area functioned as headquarters while Israel assembled its army and carried out operations to attack the southern and central regions of Canaan.

remark: 2. A town between Dor and Tirzah.
introduce: Gilgal is a place name in central Canaan recorded in Deuteronomy 11; unlike the Gilgal near Jericho, it is a place located opposite Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal near Shechem.
biblecontents: These two mountains are recorded as being across the Jordan River, that is, along the road toward the setting of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah opposite Gilgal, beside the Oak of Moreh (Deuteronomy 11:30).
geography: It is located in the central hill country of Ephraim/Samaria, near Shechem, and is a hilly area from which the valley of Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal can be seen. It is presumed to be modern Jiljilia or Jaljulia in the Samaria plain.
history: Before Israel's entry, it was an important geographical landmark near the Oak of Moreh, where there was a sanctuary of the Canaanites. From the patriarchal period it functioned as a religious and geographical reference point of the Shechem region, connected with the deeds of Jacob and Abraham.

introduce: Giloh is a town located in the hill country of Judah in ancient Israel, a place name known as the hometown of Ahithophel, the counselor of King David.
biblecontents: Joshua recorded Giloh as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah after the wars of conquest (Joshua 15:51). Ahithophel, who was the royal counselor and strategist of David, is mentioned as being from Giloh, and when he betrayed David and joined Absalom's rebellion he was staying in his hometown of Giloh (2 Samuel 15:12). Also, Ahithophel, the father of Eliam, one of David's thirty-seven mighty men, is specified as a man of Giloh (2 Samuel 23:34).
geography: Giloh is a town located in the hill country of Judah, and the theory that identifies it with Khirbet Jala, located southwest of Hebron, is dominant as a modern place name. This is a region included within the administrative scope of the ancient kingdom of Judah.
history: Giloh was one of the important regional strongholds under the influence of the tribe of Judah in the early period of David. It was a region that produced a prominent figure such as Ahithophel, but no further historical sources have been found regarding what political role Giloh played after Absalom's rebellion.

remark: 1. A mountainous region east of the Jordan River belonging to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh.
introduce: Gilead is a mountainous region located east of the Jordan River, situated between Bashan in the north and the plain of Moab in the south. Because of its fertile soil and abundant pastureland, this region is known as a center of livestock raising and trade in the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: Jacob fled from Laban, crossed the river, and headed for Mount Gilead (Genesis 31:21). Laban pursued Jacob for seven days and overtook him in Mount Gilead (Genesis 31:23). He camped with his relatives in Mount Gilead (Genesis 31:25). In Gilead, Ishmaelite traders carrying spices, balm, and myrrh appeared, and Joseph was sold to them (Genesis 37:25). Manasseh begot Machir, and Machir begot Gilead (Numbers 26:29). The descendants of Reuben and the descendants of Gad saw the land of Gilead and considered it suitable for livestock (Numbers 32:1). Moses gave the land of Gilead to the tribes of Gad and Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32:26). He said that if they took part in the conquest of Canaan, they would obtain the land of Gilead as a possession (Numbers 32:29). The descendants of Machir son of Manasseh went to Gilead, captured it, and drove out the Amorites (Numbers 32:39). Moses gave Gilead to Machir son of Manasseh, and he settled there (Numbers 32:40).
geography: It is a term generally designating the mountainous region east of the Jordan River, and its range extends to the Yarmuk River in the north and the Arnon River in the south. Topographically a plateau region has formed, and when rain falls adequately it has an environment favorable to the development of agriculture and livestock raising.
history: At the time of Israel's wars of conquest of Canaan, the tribes of Gad and Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh valued this region highly and asked Moses to be allotted it as their inheritance. This region had been under the rule of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, but after Israel's occupation it became a major stronghold east of the Jordan.

remark: 2. A mountainous region west of the Jordan River near Jezreel.
introduce: Gilead is a mountain place name west of the Jordan that appears in Judges 7, a hill country near Mount Gilboa and the Valley of Jezreel, distinguished from the vast region of Gilead east of the Jordan.
biblecontents: "Whoever is fearful and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead," and the people who turned back were twenty-two thousand, and those who remained were ten thousand (Judges 7:3).
geography: It is located on the northern ridge or hilly area of Mount Gilboa, which overlooks the spring of Harod, southeast of the Valley of Jezreel west of the Jordan. It is rugged mountainous terrain opposite the hill of Moreh where the Midianite army had camped.
history: Around the 12th century BC, it was the military standoff point of the decisive confrontation where the judge Gideon, confronting the large nomadic invading army of Midian, summoned the army of the northern tribes and selected three hundred mighty men.

introduce: Ramoth-gilead is a strategic stronghold located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, a place recorded in biblical history as the key point of territorial dispute between Israel and the kingdom of Aram and as a city of refuge.
biblecontents: It was designated as one of the cities of refuge allotted to the descendants of Merari of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:38). In the time of King Solomon, as the district of Geber, he governed the villages in Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 4:13). King Ahab wanted to advance on Ramoth-gilead to recover this region from Aram (1 Kings 22:3), and asked King Jehoshaphat to accompany him (1 Kings 22:4). Before this battle four hundred prophets prophesied victory (1 Kings 22:6, 22:12), but the prophet Micaiah prophesied disaster (1 Kings 22:15, 22:20). In the end Ahab went into battle disguised, but he died at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:29). Afterward, in the time of King Joram as well, this place remained a battlefield between Israel and Aram (2 Kings 8:28).
geography: It is located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and is presumed to be Tell es-Zafat or Tell el-Husn in the area of present-day Jordan. Being adjacent to the King's Highway, it was a crossroads of very high economic and military value, and it has the topographic feature of making it easy to use the natural defenses of the surrounding mountain ranges.
history: Ramoth-gilead, located on the border zone between the northern kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Aram centered on Damascus, became the cause of continuing disputes. In particular, during the Omride dynasty running from King Ahab to Ahaziah and Joram, military conflicts over possession of this region occurred frequently. This goes beyond a mere matter of territorial expansion and has the character of a struggle for strategic supremacy to secure the trade routes and livestock resources east of the Jordan.

introduce: Mizpah of Gilead is a place name located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan, which appears in the Book of Judges as the place where Jephthah mustered his army and carried out operations before going to war with the Ammonites.
biblecontents: Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he advanced against the Ammonites (Judges 11:29)
geography: It is a town located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and there are several theories about its exact location. As the most likely candidate site, Tell edh-Dhib, located north of the Jabbok River, has also been pointed to, and since the place name Mizpah means a watchtower or high place, it was strategically situated in a mountainous area from which there was a view.
history: Mizpah of Gilead was used as a strategic stronghold in the course of territorial disputes between the tribes of Israel and surrounding peoples in the early period of the judges. In particular, as the place where Jephthah rallied the army of Israel before the war with the Ammonites, it shows the military tension between Israel and Ammon over control of the Gilead region at that time.

introduce: A region located east of the Jordan, a term designating the Gilead region that was historically the dwelling place of the Amorites.
biblecontents: That year they struck down and oppressed all the Israelites who were on the other side of the Jordan River in Gilead, in the land of the Amorites, and oppressed them for eighteen years (Judges 10:8)
geography: As a plateau region east of the Jordan River, it borders Bashan to the north and Moab to the south, and is divided north and south by the Jabbok River as a boundary. It has the regional characteristics of fertile soil and dense forests.
history: It was originally a region ruled by Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites, but after Israel defeated them and occupied it in the course of the conquest of Canaan, it was allotted as the inheritance of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Afterward, it is a strategic stronghold where territorial disputes frequently arose with surrounding peoples such as Ammon and Aram whenever Israel's power weakened.

introduce: Jabesh-gilead is a town located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, a strategic stronghold closely connected in biblical history with the royal house of Saul.
biblecontents: The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead took the bodies of Saul and his sons, whom the Philistines had beheaded, from the wall of Beth-shan and gave them burial (1 Samuel 31:11). David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh who had buried Saul, blessing their kindness and encouraging them (2 Samuel 2:4). David also highly valued the loving-kindness the men of Jabesh had shown to Saul and personally commended them (2 Samuel 2:5).
