Afterward, David took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the place of the men of Jabesh, who had stolen them from the Philistines and buried them, and laid them to rest in their burial chamber (2 Samuel 21:12).
geography: It is located in the Gilead region east of the Jordan River and is presumed to be in the area north of the Jabbok River. Situated on high ground from which the Jordan Valley can be overlooked, it has the topographic feature of being advantageous for observing and defending the surrounding plains and passes.
history: After the incident in which Saul rescued the people of Jabesh, who were being threatened by Nahash the Ammonite, the people of Jabesh maintained strong loyalty to the royal house of Saul. This relationship continued even after Saul's death, appearing in the act of recovering the bodies against the Philistines, and it persisted as political solidarity until the time of David.

introduce: Jazer in Gilead is a place name located in the land of Gilead, the region east of the Jordan, a place mentioned in the Chronicles as part of the administrative districts and management system.
biblecontents: In the time of King David, Jerijah of the descendants of Hebron was in charge of all the affairs of the land of Gilead, including Jazer in Gilead (1 Chronicles 26:31).
geography: It is located within the Gilead region, a plateau east of the Jordan River, and although its specific geographical boundaries have not been clearly established archaeologically, it is presumed to be one of the administrative strongholds of Gilead.
history: It shares the background of an era in which, in the process of the Davidic kingdom establishing a centralized system of rule, administrative districts for the region east of the Jordan were put in order and men of the house of Hebron were stationed to take charge of the census and regional management.

introduce: Ramoth in Gilead is a town located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan, a place mentioned in the Old Testament as a strategic stronghold and one of the cities of refuge.
biblecontents: It was chosen as one of the inheritances of the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, and it is a city of refuge allotted to the descendants of Merari of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 20:8). After the time of David it was a place where territorial disputes between Israel and the kingdom of Aram were frequent, and it is also the place where King Ahab died in battle with Aram (1 Kings 22:29-37). Jehu was also anointed here and proclaimed king of Israel (2 Kings 9:1-6).
geography: It is located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and Tell el-Husn in the northern part of present-day Jordan, or nearby Tell er-Rumeid, are mentioned as candidate sites. This region sits on high ground able to control the main road network of Gilead, so it has topographic features advantageous for military defense and transportation.
history: Ramoth in Gilead was a town located in the border zone between the kingdom of Israel and the Aramean kingdom of Damascus, where the struggle for dominion between the two nations was fierce. In the era of the divided kingdoms after King Solomon, the kingdom of Israel used this region as a frontline base for defense. Because of its strategic importance, frequent battles over it are recorded down to the time of Ben-hadad, king of Aram, and of Ahab and Joram, kings of Israel.

introduce: Jabesh-gilead is a town located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, a strategic stronghold closely connected in biblical history with the royal house of Saul.
biblecontents: When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard that Saul and his sons had been killed by the Philistines and hung on the wall of Beth-shan, their mighty men arose, took the bodies, brought them to Jabesh, and buried them (1 Chronicles 10:11-12). Earlier, when Nahash the Ammonite was about to attack Jabesh, Saul had gathered troops and rescued it (1 Samuel 11:1-11).
geography: It lies in the hill country of Gilead, the region north of the Jabbok River east of the Jordan River, and is presumed to be the area of present-day Wadi Yabis in Jordan. Owing to its topographic feature of overlooking the Jordan Valley, it served as a gateway for traffic and military movement.
history: At the end of the period of the judges, in connection with the problem of the survival of the tribe of Benjamin, it has a history of being punished for not taking part in the general assembly of Israel, and afterward, through the war with Ammon immediately after Saul took the throne as the first king of Israel, it provided the occasion for the establishment of Saul's kingship. The act of keeping faith with him after Saul's death and recovering his body is cited as an example showing the solidarity among the tribes in Israel at that time.

introduce: Cilicia is a region located on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, corresponding to the southern coastal plain area of present-day Turkey. It borders Pamphylia to the west, the Taurus Mountains to the north, and Syria to the east, and from ancient times it functioned as an important passage of Mediterranean trade and a political stronghold.
biblecontents: Among those who disputed with Stephen in Jerusalem were Jews from Cilicia (Acts 6:9). This region is mentioned in the letter sent after the Jerusalem council to the brothers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia (Acts 15:23). During his second missionary journey, Paul traveled through Syria and Cilicia and strengthened the churches (Acts 15:41). There is a scene in which Governor Felix confirmed that Paul was from Cilicia (Acts 23:34). In the course of being taken to Rome as a prisoner, Paul sailed across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5). Paul mentioned the fact that after his conversion he stayed in the regions of Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21).
geography: Topographically, Cilicia is divided into Cilicia Trachea, the rugged mountainous area of the Taurus Mountains, and Cilicia Pedias, a fertile plain area. This region has a strategic passage called the Cilician Gates, which crosses the Taurus Mountains and connects to the interior of Anatolia, and it played a key role in the logistics and military movement linking East and West.
history: In the Hellenistic period this region was ruled by the Seleucid dynasty, and later, at the end of the Roman Republic, it also became a base for pirates. After being conquered by the general Pompey in 64 BC, it was incorporated as a Roman province. In particular, Tarsus, the chief city of Cilicia, was an academic center where Stoic philosophy flourished at that time, and as a leading city inhabited by those who held Roman citizenship, it is recorded as the birthplace of Paul.

introduce: Tarsus in Cilicia is a city located on the Mediterranean coast, the birthplace of the apostle Paul and a region closely related to his early life.
biblecontents: Paul introduced himself as a citizen from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). Paul also states explicitly that he is a Jew born and raised in Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 22:3).
geography: Tarsus was located on the lower reaches of the Cydnus River and secured the sea route out to the Mediterranean, and it was a crossroads of traffic connected with the interior through the Cilician Gates of the Taurus Mountains.
history: Through the Greek and Roman periods it was a city where learning and commerce flourished as the capital of the Cilician province. In particular, in the early Roman Empire it enjoyed a reputation as a university city where high-level educational institutions were located, and it is presumed that Paul's family obtained Roman citizenship through residence here.

introduce: Chilmad is a place name mentioned as one of the cities that had trade relations with ancient Tyre. In the Hebrew Bible text it is recorded by the name Chilmad.
biblecontents: Among the regions that traded with Tyre, the merchants of Haran, Canneh, Eden, Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad traded with Tyre (Ezekiel 27:23).
geography: It is presumed to be one of the cities located in northern Mesopotamia or the upper Euphrates region, but its specific modern location is still disputed in scholarship. It appears to have been on a trade route mainly adjacent to the regions of Haran or Asshur.
history: In the early 6th century BC, Tyre had formed a vast trade network centered on the Mediterranean. Chilmad is analyzed as having taken part in the trade as one of the inland cities that supplied luxury goods such as dyes, spices, or textiles within Tyre's extensive international trade network.

introduce: Gilboa is a mountainous area located on the east side of the Valley of Jezreel, the place where a decisive battle between Israel and the Philistines took place in the time of King Saul.
biblecontents: The Philistine army camped at Gilboa, and in opposition Saul gathered his army and camped on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 28:4). In the battle with the Philistines the army of Israel was defeated and was killed and fell on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:1). The next day the Philistines found the bodies of Saul and his three sons on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:8). A young man testified that he had gone up on Mount Gilboa and seen that Saul was dead (2 Samuel 1:6). In his lament David prayed that no dew or rain would ever fall again on the mountains of Gilboa, and mentioned that it was the place where the shield of Saul and Jonathan had been cast away (2 Samuel 1:21). David gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the battlefield at Gilboa and buried them (2 Samuel 21:12). In the battle with the Philistines the men of Israel fell and died on Mount Gilboa (1 Chronicles 10:1). The Philistines found Saul and his sons who had died on Mount Gilboa (1 Chronicles 10:8).
geography: Mount Gilboa lies southeast of the Valley of Jezreel and is a ridge-shaped terrain overlooking the Jordan Valley. It is identified with the area of present-day Jebel Fuqu'a, and its height is about 500 meters above sea level. With the surrounding plain and high slopes, it is a strategic stronghold where, militarily, occupying the high ground and securing a line of retreat are important.
history: It is the region where the kingdom of Israel, ruled by King Saul around the 11th century BC, clashed with the Philistine coalition army equipped with strong military power. At that time the Philistines maneuvered along the plain of the Valley of Jezreel and pressed the defensive line of Israel. With the defeat in this battle the foundation of the rule of Saul's dynasty collapsed, and as a result it became the political turning point at which David built the united kingdom of Israel.

introduce: Kir-hareseth is a major town and fortress of the kingdom of Moab, a place name presumed to be Kerak in the area of present-day Jordan. It is also called Kir-heres, the capital of Moab, and is mentioned as a strategic stronghold.
biblecontents: When the allied army of Israel, Judah, and Edom attacked Moab, they destroyed the walls of the towns and threw stones, and surrounded and attacked Kir-hareseth (2 Kings 3:25). The prophet Isaiah, prophesying the fall of Moab, mentioned the people of Moab mourning for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth (Isaiah 16:7), and wrote that his heart moans like a harp and laments for Kir-hareseth (Isaiah 16:11).
geography: Kir-hareseth is a natural fortress located in the rugged mountainous area southeast of the Dead Sea. Surrounded by deep valleys, it has topographic conditions very advantageous for defense, and as the central stronghold of the kingdom of Moab it played the role of controlling the surrounding region.
history: Around the 9th century BC, it was the place that became the last battleground when Joram, king of Israel, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and the king of Edom united and attacked Mesha, king of Moab. Afterward, in addition to the biblical records, it is confirmed through the Mesha Stele that it occupied an important place in Moab's construction and system of rule.

introduce: Kir-heres is a place name that appears in the text of the Book of Jeremiah lamenting the destruction of Moab, and is traditionally regarded as the same place as Kir-heres, one of the major towns of Moab.
biblecontents: Jeremiah, proclaiming the destruction of Moab, wrote that the men of Kir-heres would mourn because of their ruin (Jeremiah 48:31). It is also described that his heart moans like a flute and laments for the men of Kir-heres (Jeremiah 48:36).
geography: Kir-heres is presumed to be a town located in the Moabite plateau region southeast of the Dead Sea. Ancient records such as Josephus and the majority opinion of scholarship equate this place name with Kir-hareseth, which appears in Isaiah 16:7 and 11, and it is generally identified with the area of Karak in present-day Jordan.
history: Moab was under the sphere of influence of Israel after the time of David and Solomon, but afterward it built up its power as an independent kingdom. Kir-heres is a core stronghold also mentioned in the inscription of Mesha, king of Moab, and as a strategically fortified town it served as the political and military center of Moab.

introduce: Gimzo is a place name mentioned in 2 Chronicles 28:18 of the Old Testament, recorded as one of the towns that the Philistines occupied in the time of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: The Philistines raided the cities of the plain and the south of Judah, and occupied Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco and its villages, Timnah and its villages, and Gimzo and its villages, and lived there (2 Chronicles 28:18).
geography: The exact location of Gimzo has not been clearly established by modern archaeology, but according to the biblical record it is presumed to be one of the towns located in or near the Shephelah, the lowlands of Judah.
history: In the time of King Ahaz, the Philistines took advantage of the turbulent period of the kingdom of Judah to occupy by force the main strongholds of the Shephelah region and to exert influence (2 Chronicles 28:18).

introduce: Gibbethon was a town allotted to the tribe of Dan in ancient Israel and also distributed to the Kohathite descendants of the tribe of Levi, and geographically it is a strategic stronghold adjacent to the Philistines.
biblecontents: Gibbethon is recorded as one of the towns that the tribe of Dan received as an inheritance (Joshua 19:44). Afterward this town was allotted as a dwelling place to the Kohathite descendants among the tribe of Levi, and although it was not one of the cities of refuge, it was set apart as a town of the Levites (Joshua 21:23). In the time of Baasha, king of Israel, Israel besieged Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and King Nadab was killed by Baasha while attacking this town (1 Kings 15:27). Afterward, in the time of King Omri as well, the army of Israel camped to attack Gibbethon again (1 Kings 16:15). In the end, it was Gibbethon that was the place where all the people in the camp heard the news that Zimri had rebelled against the king and become king (1 Kings 16:17).
geography: Gibbethon is presumed to be present-day Tell Malat, located in the northern part of the Shephelah, the plain region on the Mediterranean coast. This region is a buffer zone connecting the territory of the Philistines with the mountain region of Israel, and is situated on a flat passage easy for military movement.
history: From the early period of the kingdom of Israel, Gibbethon was a disputed area that was under the influence of the Philistines or lay on the border line with them. The repeated attempts of the kings of northern Israel to conquer Gibbethon show that this region was a military stronghold for checking the power of the Philistines and for expanding or defending territory. The fact that external military operations around this town continued even amid internal political instability such as the usurpation of the throne suggests the strategic importance of this region at that time.

introduce: Kibzaim was located within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim in the time of Joshua, and is one of the towns distributed to the Kohathite descendants of the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: Kibzaim is included in the list of towns allotted to the Kohathite descendants, the Levites, within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim (Joshua 21:22).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the hill country of Ephraim, but its exact present-day location has not been clearly established archaeologically. Some scholars also raise the possibility that Kibzaim is the same place as Geba, which appears in Joshua 18:24.

introduce: Gittaim is known as a town located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel, a place name mentioned twice in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as sojourners to this day (2 Samuel 4:3). There were descendants of Benjamin living in Hazor, Ramah, and Gittaim (Nehemiah 11:33).
geography: The exact location of Gittaim has not been established archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to have been located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, east of Joppa or near Lydda.
history: It is the place to which the inhabitants of Beeroth fled after Ish-bosheth, son of King Saul, was killed, and it is recorded as one of the towns where the community that returned from the Babylonian exile resettled.

remark: [Watch] A town in Galilee where Jesus grew up. Jesus tried to teach in the synagogue of his hometown Nazareth, but they did not accept him.
introduce: Nazareth is a small village located in the region of Galilee, a place described in the New Testament as the hometown of Jesus and the place where he grew up.
biblecontents: It is the place where the angel Gabriel announced to Mary that she would conceive Jesus (Luke 1:26), and the place where Joseph and Mary lived after returning from Bethlehem (Luke 2:4). Jesus grew up in Nazareth (Luke 2:4), and after reaching adulthood he left this place and moved his residence to Capernaum (Matthew 4:13). Jesus was called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23), and was referred to by people as Jesus of Nazareth (Mark 1:24, Mark 10:47, Mark 14:67, Matthew 26:71, Mark 16:6). There is a record that Jesus moved from Nazareth in Galilee to the Jordan River in order to be baptized (Mark 1:9).
geography: Nazareth is situated in the mountainous area of Lower Galilee, on high ground overlooking the Valley of Jezreel. Because of its isolated basin terrain, it lay far from the main road network of ancient times.
history: In the 1st century Nazareth was a very small agricultural community, a remote village without great political or economic influence within Jewish society. According to archaeological evidence, the residents at that time were mainly engaged in making farm tools from limestone or in simple farming, and it is presumed to have been an environment with limited interaction with the outside world.

introduce: Naaran is a town related to the distribution of inheritances among the tribes of ancient Israel, a settlement that was located on the border of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim or nearby.
biblecontents: Their settlements and lands were Bethel and its surrounding villages, and extended to Naaran on the east, and on the west to Gezer and its surrounding villages, and also to Shechem and its surrounding villages, as far as Ayyah and its surrounding villages (1 Chronicles 7:28).
geography: Naaran is presumed to be the same place name as Naarah, located on the west side of the Jordan Valley and north of Jericho, which corresponds to the eastern border area of the tribe of Ephraim.

introduce: Naioth is a place name that appears in 1 Samuel 19, a proper noun designating the dwelling place of a community of prophets located near Ramah. The Hebrew Naioth carries the meaning of a dwelling or lodging.
biblecontents: David fled from Saul's threats to Samuel at Ramah, and he and Samuel went to Naioth in Ramah and stayed (1 Samuel 19:18). Saul sent messengers to Naioth to seize David, but when they met the company of prophesying prophets there, they were unable to arrest David (1 Samuel 19:19).
geography: Naioth is presumed to be a district located within Ramah, and the present Ramah is identified with er-Ram, located about 8 km north of Jerusalem. The exact location of Naioth itself has not been clearly established archaeologically.
history: It is mentioned as a place from the period when the community of prophetic disciples led by Samuel was organized and operating. Amid the situation of political conflict caused by the kingship of Saul at that time, it seems to have served as a place where the people Samuel was protecting took refuge or trained.

introduce: Nain was a town located in the region of Galilee, a place recorded as the site of one of the events during the public ministry of Jesus Christ. As a present-day place name, it is identified with the village of Nain in Israel.
biblecontents: When Jesus went to a town called Nain, his disciples and a large crowd went with him, and as he drew near the gate of the town, he saw people carrying out a dead person (Luke 7:11).
geography: Nain lies on the northern slope of the hill of Moreh, located southeast of Galilee. It overlooks the Valley of Jezreel and is about 10 km southeast of Nazareth.
history: Detailed historical mentions of this town in ancient literature other than the biblical record are rare. It is presumed to have been one of the small farming communities in the Galilee region in the time of the Roman Empire, and at present it remains a small village inhabited by Arab residents.

introduce: The Nile River, as the lifeblood of ancient Egyptian civilization, appears in the Bible as a geographical element symbolizing the abundance and prosperity of Egypt, and in the prophecies of the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah it is described as Egypt's economic center and trade route.
biblecontents: The meadows by the Nile and all the fields along the Nile will dry up, blow away, and be no more (Isaiah 19:7), and those who fish in the Nile will lament, and those who cast their fishing line into the Nile will mourn (Isaiah 19:8). The grain of Shihor and the harvest of the Nile were great revenue, and it became the market of the nations (Isaiah 23:3). O daughter of Tarshish, overflow your land like the Nile (Isaiah 23:10). The Nile rises and surges like a river (Jeremiah 46:7). Egypt says it will rise like the Nile and cover the land like a river (Jeremiah 46:8). When God passes through the sea of distress and strikes the waves of the sea, the depths of the Nile will all dry up, the pride of Assyria will be brought down, and the scepter of Egypt will depart (Zechariah 10:11).
geography: The Nile River flows through the northeast of the African continent and is the longest river in the world; in Egypt, in its lower reaches, its annual flooding supplied fertile alluvial soil and played a role in maximizing agricultural productivity. The delta region of the Nile functioned as a granary from ancient times, and the river water was the core element of the Egyptian ecosystem, serving as a means of transport and providing drinking water and irrigation water.
history: Ancient Egypt predicted the flooding season of the Nile to decide sowing and harvesting, and on that basis formed a strong centralized state. In the period when the Bible was being written, Egypt carried on active trade with neighboring nations on the basis of the agricultural products produced through the Nile. The prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah are understood either as warning that this economic base of Egypt would collapse through war or environmental disaster, or as expressing the power of Egypt by comparing it to the flooding of the Nile.

introduce: Nahalal was a town allotted to the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the conquest of Canaan and also one of the towns assigned to the tribe of Levi; it was located in southern Galilee, near the Valley of Jezreel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns included within the boundary of the inheritance that the tribe of Zebulun received after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:15). Later, Nahalal is named in the list of towns that the tribe of Zebulun gave up to the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:35).
geography: Nahalal is often identified with Tel Nahalal, located on the western edge of the Jezreel Valley in what is now northern Israel, and in Judges 1:30 it also appears under the place name Nahalol. The area borders a fertile plain and so enjoys geographical advantages as a center of agriculture and as a crossroads of travel.
history: After the wars of conquest it was assigned as territory of the tribe of Zebulun, but according to the record in Judges, the tribe at first failed to drive out the native Canaanites completely, and there is a record that they continued to live there and were put to forced labor for the Canaanites. Later, when the town was handed over to the tribe of Levi, it served as a religious and administrative center.

introduce: Nahalol was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the conquest of Canaan in ancient Israel, but it was inhabited by the native Canaanites.
biblecontents: Because Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kidron or the inhabitants of Nahalol, they lived among the Canaanites and did forced labor (Judges 1:30).
geography: Nahalol is presumed to have been located at the northwestern edge of the Jezreel Plain, and is identified with modern Tel Nahor or the surrounding area. Topographically, it sits on a plain suited to agriculture and at a crossroads of travel.
history: It is an example showing that, even after the tribes of Israel received the land of Canaan, the native inhabitants offered strong resistance centered on fortified towns or maintained compromising relations. Nahalol is recorded as one of the towns that the tribe of Zebulun at that time could neither fully conquer nor drive out.

introduce: Nahaliel was one of the places where the Israelites stayed during the journey of the exodus, a point located along the route of moving on, past the Arnon valley, to the plain east of the Jordan.
biblecontents: The people of Israel left Mattanah and came to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel they reached Bamoth (Numbers 21:19).
geography: Interpreted from its Hebrew etymology, the name carries the meaning "valley of God" or "river of God," and it is generally presumed to be a wadi (valley) landform north of the Arnon River. Its exact location is difficult to determine, but it is known to refer to a stream basin running from the Moabite plateau toward the Jordan Valley.

remark: The descendants of Naphtali and the region of Galilee where they lived, east of Asher and north of Zebulun.
introduce: Naphtali was the fourth son of Jacob, born to Rachel's maidservant Bilhah, and the name also refers to one of the twelve tribes of Israel that took its name from him. He is mentioned as one of the sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:25, Genesis 46:24), and his name signifies that Rachel had prevailed in her rivalry with her sister Leah (Genesis 30:8).
biblecontents: Rachel, in her rivalry with her sister Leah, named him Naphtali, meaning that she had prevailed (Genesis 30:8). He is included in the list of the sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:25, Genesis 46:24), and when Jacob was dying he likened Naphtali to a doe let loose and prophesied that he would be one who gives beautiful words (Genesis 49:21). He was included in the list of Jacob's sons recorded at the time of the exodus (Exodus 1:4), and the census showed 53,400 men aged twenty and over able to go to war (Numbers 1:42). During the march through the wilderness he was stationed in the northern camp together with the tribes of Dan and Asher (Numbers 2:29, Numbers 10:27). At the dedication of the tabernacle, Ahira, the commander of the tribe, presented his offering (Numbers 7:78). In the census just before the conquest of Canaan it was recorded as 45,400 (Numbers 26:48).
geography: It was located in the northeast of the land of Canaan, bordering the Sea of Galilee and the upper Jordan River to the east and touching the Lebanon mountain range to the north. It included the fertile region of Upper Galilee and served as a strategically important gateway to the north.
history: After settling in Canaan, the tribe of Naphtali, because of the rugged terrain of the north, suffered foreign invasions more often than the other tribes, and during the kingdoms of David and Solomon it was used as an important military stronghold. Later it became part of the northern kingdom of Israel, and it is the region that experienced the early history of captivity resulting from the invasion of Assyria.

introduce: Kedesh in Naphtali was a town located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in northern ancient Israel; it was designated a city of refuge in the time of Joshua and was one of the principal strongholds of northern Canaan.
biblecontents: Barak, the son of Abinoam, was summoned from Kedesh in Naphtali, and Deborah commanded him to go to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men of the Israelites (Judges 4:6). Also, Joshua set apart Kedesh in the hill country of Naphtali as a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7).
geography: It is identified with present-day Tel Kedesh (Tel Kedesh) and is situated on the western highland of the Huleh Valley. Strategically located on the passage linking the fertile plains of northern Galilee with the hill country, it served from ancient times as a crossroads of traffic and a point of defense.
history: Originally a town of the Canaanite peoples, it was allotted to the tribe of Naphtali after Israel's wars of conquest and was used as a city of the Gershonite descendants of the tribe of Levi and as a city of refuge. When the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III invaded Israel around the eighth century BC, the inhabitants of this region were taken captive, and afterward, in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, it served as an administrative center.

introduce: Neapolis was a port city in the region of Macedonia, the first place where the apostle Paul set foot when he began his missionary journey into Europe.
biblecontents: Paul and his companions set sail from Troas, ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day came to Neapolis (Acts 16:11).
geography: It is located near present-day Kavala in Greece, on the coast about 15 km south of Philippi, a major city of Macedonia. As a natural harbor on the Aegean Sea, the city served as a gateway into Macedonia.
history: Neapolis was a strategic point as the place where the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road network, began. It was closely connected with Philippi, then a Roman colony, and functioned as a key port city through which military and commercial supplies moved within the province of Macedonia.

introduce: Nephtoah was a spring or place name that lay on the boundary line between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: The boundary reached to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah and went out to the cities of Mount Ephron, and then turned toward Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim (Joshua 15:9). The boundary reached from the sea, that is, from the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, to Mount Ephron, and went north to the northern end of the valley of the son of Hinnom in the Valley of Rephaim (Joshua 18:15).
geography: It is identified with the area of Lifta at the western entrance of present-day Jerusalem. Topographically it lies on the slope of the Jerusalem highlands and has a water source from which spring water wells up, so it was used as a geographical boundary point.

introduce: No was a major city of ancient Egypt, mentioned in the Bible in prophetic contexts concerning the judgment of Egypt. In present-day archaeology this place name is presumed to be Thebes, the capital of the Egyptian Old Kingdom period, or Memphis.
biblecontents: The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, says: Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt with her gods and her kings, even Pharaoh and those who trust in him (Jeremiah 46:25). I will also make Pathros desolate, set fire to Zoan, and execute judgments on Thebes (Ezekiel 30:14). And I will pour out my wrath on Sin, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the multitude of Thebes (Ezekiel 30:15). I will set fire to Egypt; Sin will be in great anguish, Thebes will be torn open, and Memphis will have enemies by day (Ezekiel 30:16).
geography: No was a city on the upper Nile in ancient Egypt, and in the biblical context the name was used to symbolize the heartland or a strategic center of Egypt. Biblical scholars often identify this place with Thebes on the upper Nile (present-day Luxor), while some point to a connection with Memphis.
history: No was the political and religious center of the New Kingdom period of ancient Egypt, and great temples serving the god Amon were concentrated there. Around the seventh century BC it suffered great damage from the Assyrian invasion, and this historical decline is often cited in several prophetic books of the ancient Near East as a symbol of the fall of Egypt.

remark: A town of Gilead, originally named Kenath.
introduce: Nobah (Nobah) is a place name of the ancient Near East that appears in Numbers and Judges and is a location connected with the conquest activity and military routes of the tribes of Israel. The name was used not only as a place name but also as a personal name; when Nobah, a member of the tribe of Manasseh, gave his own name to the village he had conquered, it became fixed as a place name.
biblecontents: After Heshbon was destroyed, a broad region reaching as far as Nobah became the object of conquest (Numbers 21:30). Nobah, a descendant of Manasseh, captured Kenath and its villages and called it Nobah after his own name (Numbers 32:42). In pursuing the men who dwelt in tents, Gideon attacked the enemy army near Nobah and Jogbehah (Judges 8:11).
geography: Scholarly opinion is divided over the exact location of Nobah, but it is generally presumed to have been in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River, or in the region of Bashan. Judging from the record of Judges 8:11, it was likely a strategic point in the desert region east of Gilead or near Hauran.

introduce: No-amon is the biblical name that refers to Thebes, which was the capital of ancient Egypt; it denotes a flourishing city that, situated on the upper Nile at that time, exercised powerful influence.
biblecontents: The prophet Nahum, prophesying the destruction of Nineveh, cited the case of Thebes, which lay among the rivers and used the waters as its rampart and which was brutally destroyed, and warned that Nineveh too would meet the same fate (Nahum 3:8).
geography: No-amon corresponds to the area of present-day Luxor in Egypt and is a region that spread widely along both the east and west banks of the Nile. The Nile was this city's main thoroughfare and the basis of its agricultural production, and at the same time it served as a natural fortress protecting the city from outside invasion.
history: No-amon was the political and religious center of the New Kingdom period of ancient Egypt, and temples serving the god Amon were concentrated there. In 663 BC it was captured and plundered by the army led by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, and this event is recorded as a historical event that gave a great shock to the ancient Near Eastern world of the time.

remark: 1. A Levitical town of Benjamin, two miles north of Jerusalem.
introduce: Nob was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin in Israel, a place that in the time of King Saul was the residence of priests and the site of a sanctuary.
biblecontents: It is the place where David, fleeing from King Saul, met the priest Ahimelech, obtained the consecrated bread, and received the sword of Goliath (1 Samuel 21:1). Doeg the Edomite informed Saul of the meeting between David and Ahimelech (1 Samuel 22:9). Saul summoned the priests of Nob and interrogated them (1 Samuel 22:11), and in the end he had Doeg kill the priests of Nob and the men, women, children, and livestock of that town (1 Samuel 22:19). After the return from captivity, it is mentioned as one of the towns in which the descendants of Benjamin lived (Nehemiah 11:32). It appears as a place name along the route by which the Assyrian king Sennacherib advanced to attack Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:32).
geography: Nob was a town of the tribe of Benjamin located north of Jerusalem. From the record of Isaiah 10:32, it is presumed to have been situated at a place with a view of Jerusalem or on the main route of approach for entering Jerusalem. Its exact archaeological location is disputed, but many hold the view that it should be identified with the area near Mount Scopus, north of Jerusalem.
history: Nob appears to have been the place where priests temporarily resided and carried out sanctuary functions in the course of the ark of the covenant being moved to Kiriath-jearim after the destruction of Shiloh. The massacre of the priests here by King Saul became a historical turning point in the downfall of the house of Saul and the strengthening of the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty.

remark: 2. A town of Egypt, west of the Nile and south of Cairo.
introduce: Noph was one of the major cities of ancient Egypt, and in the Bible it is mentioned as a place where the princes of Egypt and Jewish refugees lived. Scholars hold that the place name rendered Noph in the Hebrew Bible refers to Memphis, the capital of ancient Egypt.
biblecontents: The princes of Memphis have become fools; the princes of Memphis are deceived (Isaiah 19:13). The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have also broken the crown of your head (Jeremiah 2:16). The word concerning all the Judahites who live in the land of Egypt, those who live at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and in the land of Pathros (Jeremiah 44:1). Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes: Stand up and prepare yourself (Jeremiah 46:14).
geography: Noph refers to Memphis, an ancient city located at the point where the Nile Delta and Upper Egypt meet. It lies on the west bank of the Nile and, both strategically and geographically, served as a key point of Lower Egypt.
history: Memphis was the capital of Egypt in the Old Kingdom period and a political and religious center. In the biblical period it was the time when the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt was ruling, and the Jews who had gone down to Egypt to escape the Babylonian invasion settled and lived at Memphis together with Migdol and Tahpanhes. Memphis was at that time a powerful fortress and administrative center of Egypt, and one of the important places of refuge for the people of Judah.

introduce: A region described as lying east of Eden, the place where Cain settled after leaving the presence of God following his murder of Abel.
biblecontents: Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden (Genesis 4:16).
geography: Apart from the record that it lies in an easterly direction from Eden, there is no specific topographical information by which a particular point can be identified in terms of modern geography.

remark: A town of Judah south of Jerusalem.
introduce: Netophah is not a term directly mentioned as a place name or personal name within the biblical text, and the biblical passages presented likewise do not contain the name Netophah. Those passages mainly deal with David's mighty men, the lists of those who returned from captivity, and place names in the region of Judah.
biblecontents: 2 Samuel 23:28 mentions Zalmon the Ahohite, and 2 Samuel 23:29 mentions Maharai the Netophathite (2 Samuel 23:29). 2 Kings 25:23 mentions Jaazaniah, the son of a Netophathite (2 Kings 25:23). 1 Chronicles 2:54 mentions the clans of the Netophathites as descendants of Salma (1 Chronicles 2:54). 1 Chronicles 9:16 records the Levites who lived in the villages of the Netophathites (1 Chronicles 9:16). 1 Chronicles 11:30 mentions Maharai the Netophathite (1 Chronicles 11:30), and 1 Chronicles 27:13 and 27:15 mention Maharai the Netophathite and Heldai as the commanders of the tenth and twelfth divisions (1 Chronicles 27:13, 1 Chronicles 27:15). Ezra 2:22 and Nehemiah 7:26 record that men of Netophah were included in the lists of those who returned from captivity (Ezra 2:22, Nehemiah 7:26).
geography: Netophah is presumed to be a town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah. It was probably near Bethlehem, and geographically it is classified as part of the hill country of Judah. The location of the exact site is disputed archaeologically, but among scholars there is a view that identifies it with present-day Beit Fajjar or its vicinity.
history: Netophah played an important role in the time of King David as a military stronghold or as the residence of a particular clan. The fact that Maharai, one of David's mighty men, came from here shows that this town served to supply manpower within David's system of rule. Afterward, in the early period of the Babylonian exile, it is mentioned as one of the remnant communities of Judah, and after the return from captivity it is recorded as a member of the community that rebuilt Jerusalem and the region of Judah.

introduce: Neballat was one of the towns in which the descendants of the tribe of Benjamin lived in ancient Israel, a place mentioned in connection with the distribution of the population that settled in the area around Jerusalem after the return from captivity.
biblecontents: Neballat is recorded as one of the towns of the descendants of Benjamin who lived in Hadid, Zeboim, and Neballat (Nehemiah 11:34).
geography: From the standpoint of present-day geography, it is presumed to be a plain adjacent to the area of Hadid near Joppa (present-day el-Haditha), which lies on the border of the Plain of Sharon, northwest of Jerusalem.
history: When the Israelites who returned after the Babylonian exile were distributed among the towns together with the rebuilding of the wall, it was included in the list of towns where the tribe of Benjamin settled and formed part of an administrative division.

introduce: Nezib was a town located in the southern part of the ancient hill country of Judea, and it was one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Judah at the time of Joshua's conquest.
biblecontents: Nezib is mentioned as one of the towns in the list of towns in the southern highlands when Joshua divided the inheritance of the tribe of Judah by lot (Joshua 15:43).
geography: It is situated at the boundary point between the Shephelah plain, southwest of Hebron, and the hill country of Judea. Its present-day location is presumed to be Khirbet Beit Nasib, about 11 kilometers southwest of Hebron.

introduce: Neiel is a place name that appears in Joshua 19:27, one of the points located on the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher.
biblecontents: In the course of describing the northern boundary of the tribe of Asher, it is mentioned as one point on the route that starts from Beth-dagon, passes Zebulun, reaches the valley of Iphtah-el, and goes north through Cabul, Hebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah as far as Sidon (Joshua 19:27).
geography: Its present exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is presumed to be a point on the boundary line, taking into account the topographical features of northern Galilee or the vicinity of the Acco Plain.

introduce: Nehelam is a place name that appears in the Book of Jeremiah, a name designating a particular place of residence within the Jewish community taken captive to Babylon, or the place of origin of a person, Shemaiah.
biblecontents: Shemaiah the Nehelamite sent a letter to Jeremiah telling him not to prophesy falsely (Jeremiah 29:24), and in response God, through Jeremiah, criticized Shemaiah for having taught the people to prophesy falsely (Jeremiah 29:31). Moreover, in the context of prophesying that Shemaiah and his descendants would receive calamity from God and that his line would be cut off, it again states that he is a Nehelamite (Jeremiah 29:32).
history: During the Babylonian exile, the Jews who had been taken captive lived scattered in various parts of Babylon, and Nehelam is presumed to be a particular settlement or village within the Babylonian region where some of them lived together. At that time, among the Jews living in Babylon, there was conflict between Jeremiah in Jerusalem and the false prophets of Babylon itself.

introduce: Nicopolis was a city located in the region of Epirus in ancient Greece, a strategic point built in the Roman imperial period. It is known as the place where the apostle Paul urged Titus to come to meet him.
biblecontents: Paul instructed Titus to come to Nicopolis quickly when he sent Artemas or Tychicus, and he had determined to spend the winter there himself (Titus 3:12).
geography: Nicopolis lies on the Ionian Sea, the western coast of Greece, and is situated north of the entrance to the Gulf of Ambracia. Its present-day name is near Preveza, and thanks to its strategic position it served as an important hub for ancient sea traffic and overland movement.
history: This city is a city of victory built by Octavian to commemorate his victory in the Battle of Actium in 31 BC. In accordance with Roman city planning, a large theater, a stadium, public baths, and the like were constructed, and during the reign of the emperor Augustus it prospered as a center for extending Roman influence and administering the region.

introduce: Nineveh was the most important city, and one of the capitals, of the Assyrian Empire, located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River in northern ancient Mesopotamia. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly as the center of Assyria, and it appears as the main setting of the Book of Jonah.
biblecontents: Nineveh is mentioned as one of the cities that Asshur built (Genesis 10:11). Also, a great city was formed among Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen (Genesis 10:12). The Assyrian king Sennacherib, after attacking Jerusalem, withdrew and lived in Nineveh (2 Kings 19:36, Isaiah 37:37). God commanded Jonah to go to this great city of Nineveh and cry out against it because its wickedness had come up before him (Jonah 1:2, Jonah 3:2). Nineveh was so great a city that it required a three days' journey to cross it (Jonah 3:3), and Jonah entered the city and cried out for a day's journey, proclaiming that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 3:4). Thereupon the people of Nineveh believed God and proclaimed a fast, and from the greatest to the least they put on sackcloth (Jonah 3:5). When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he too rose from his throne, took off his royal robe, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes (Jonah 3:6).
geography: Nineveh corresponds to the area of Mosul in present-day Iraq and is situated along the eastern bank of the Tigris River. The present-day archaeological site, the mound of Kuyunjik, is understood to be its core location. The area is a strategic point linking the fertile plains of northern Mesopotamia with the main trade routes.
history: Nineveh reached its heyday when it was confirmed as the capital of the Assyrian Empire in the time of King Sennacherib in the seventh century BC. At that time it developed into one of the largest cities in the ancient Near East, with its walls greatly expanded and a water-supply system and palaces built. However, in 612 BC it fell to the allied forces of Neo-Babylonia and the Medes, bringing about the fall of the Assyrian Empire.

introduce: Cnidus was a port city in the region of Caria that held an important position in ancient Mediterranean trade and navigation, a place name mentioned as a stopover on the apostle Paul's journey to Rome.
biblecontents: The ship carrying Paul, after many days of barely making headway, arrived off Cnidus, but because the wind did not permit them to continue, they sailed along the coast of Crete, passing by Salmone (Acts 27:7)
geography: Cnidus is a port city at the tip of the Triopion peninsula of Caria in the far southwest of Asia Minor; situated between the island of Cos and the island of Rhodes, it is a strategic point linking the Aegean Sea and the Mediterranean Sea.
history: In the Hellenistic period Cnidus was a center of learning and the arts, and as a port with a temple famous for its statue of Aphrodite, it served as a hub of sea traffic and as a place of refueling and rest for ships.

introduce: Nimrah is a place name in the region east of the Jordan mentioned in Numbers 32:3, one of the lands that the descendants of Gad and the descendants of Reuben, judging after the conquest that it was suitable for raising livestock, asked Moses to give them as an inheritance.
biblecontents: “Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon, (Numbers 32:3)
geography: Nimrah is presumed to be a plain near the Abarim mountain range east of the Jordan River and is identified as the same place as the nearby place name Nimrim. It was fertile pastureland northeast of the Dead Sea and had an environment suitable for grazing livestock.
history: Originally this region was within the domain ruled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, but the Israelite army defeated Sihon and occupied it. Afterward, in the course of Israel's settlement, the tribe of Gad received this land as its allotment and rebuilt the town.

introduce: According to Genesis 10, Nimrod was a descendant of Ham and a son of Cush, and he is depicted as a man who ruled Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar and built a mighty kingdom. In Micah 5:6 it is mentioned together with the land of Assyria as his land, and it was used as a symbolic place name for a particular territory or dominion.
biblecontents: The prophet Micah prophesies that when the Assyrian enters this land, he will lay it waste with the sword, and he mentions that they will rule their land and the entrances of the land of Nimrod with the sword (Micah 5:6).
geography: The land of Nimrod refers to the plain of Shinar in ancient Mesopotamia, which means the lower basin of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in present-day southern Iraq. However, in the context of Micah 5:6 it is described as a region contrasted with, or adjacent to, Assyria, and so it is broadly interpreted as a domain of rule encompassing the whole of Mesopotamia.
history: The prevailing view is that Nimrod was not so much a historically real individual as a name symbolizing the rulers who unified the early city-states of Mesopotamian civilization. The expression in Micah that sets Assyria and the land of Nimrod side by side appears to have been used as a historical idiom referring to the regions under the influence of the Assyrian Empire, the hegemonic power of the ancient Near East at that time.

introduce: Nimrim was a place name located in the ancient land of Moab, a region well known for its abundant water resources and the pastures around it resulting from them. In the Bible it appears mainly as a place whose desolation is described in the midst of prophecies of judgment against Moab.
biblecontents: There is recorded a prophecy that the waters of Nimrim would dry up and the grass around them would wither and become parched (Isaiah 15:6). Also, in the proclamation of Moab's destruction, there is a description that the cry that began at Heshbon and Elealeh passes Jahaz and reaches as far as Zoar, to the waters of Nimrim (Jeremiah 48:34).
geography: Nimrim is generally identified with the area of Wadi Nimeira, southeast of the Dead Sea. This area has abundant springs that flow into the Dead Sea, so the surroundings had formed fertile pastureland. In ancient times it held important strategic value as a source of water supply for Moab.

introduce: Nibshan was a town located within the territory distributed to the tribe of Judah in ancient times, one of the settlements situated in the wilderness region on the western shore of the Dead Sea.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in Joshua 15:62 as one of the list of towns distributed to the tribe of Judah, and it is recorded that six towns, including Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En-gedi, belonged to the wilderness region (Joshua 15:62).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the wilderness zone near the western shore of the Dead Sea, and in present-day archaeological surveys the area near En-gedi in the southeastern Judean wilderness is sometimes proposed as a candidate site, but its exact location has not been determined.

introduce: Tahchemon is a place name mentioned as the place where Josheb-basshebeth the Eznite, one of David's mighty men, was active. However, its exact location has not been determined archaeologically to date.
biblecontents: These are the names of David's mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite, the Eznite (also called Adino), the chief of the captains, who at one time struck down and killed eight hundred men (2 Samuel 23:8)

introduce: Dan-jaan is a region that Joab and the commanders visited when David conducted a census; it is a rare place name for which, among biblical place names, no record is found other than this passage.
biblecontents: It is recorded that Joab and the army commanders, on David's orders, crossed the Jordan River, began at Aroer, that is, the town in the middle of the valley, passed through Jazer, and reached Gilead, the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and Dan-jaan (2 Samuel 24:6).
geography: The Hebrew text writes it as Dan-jaan, but among scholars there is much geographical debate over whether this means the region of Dan or a particular place name in the northern region. From the context it is presumed to be a place north of Gilead or near the northern border region (2 Samuel 24:6).

introduce: Tadmor was a town in the wilderness built during the reign of King Solomon, a place that shows Israel's territorial expansion at that time and its securing of strategic points.
biblecontents: Solomon built Tadmor, and it is one of the towns in the wilderness (1 Kings 9:18). Also, it is recorded that after Solomon attacked and captured Hamath-zobah, he built Tadmor in the wilderness (2 Chronicles 8:4).
geography: Tadmor lies in the desert region of Syria and is identified with the area of present-day Palmyra. It stands at an oasis between Damascus and the Euphrates River, and has the geographical advantage of serving as a key stopover on the caravan trade routes linking East and West.
history: Historically Tadmor was a region of very high economic value, connecting Mesopotamia with the Mediterranean coast. Solomon's purpose in building this town included a strategic intent that went beyond merely expanding territory: to control the trade routes passing through the region, manage the flow of goods, and consolidate the economic foundation of the kingdom.

introduce: Taralah is a place name mentioned as one of the towns of the tribe of Benjamin that appear in the Old Testament book of Joshua.
biblecontents: Among the list of towns of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, the name is listed together with Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus, and others (Joshua 18:27).

introduce: Damascus refers to Damascus, the capital of present-day Syria, and was an ancient city-state that in biblical history was the center of the kingdom of Aram and that had frequent conflict and exchange with Israel.
biblecontents: Abram pursued Chedorlaomer and his allies and won the victory, reaching Hobah, to the left of Damascus (Genesis 14:15). Abram mentioned Eliezer of Damascus as his heir (Genesis 15:2). David struck down the Arameans of Damascus, won a military victory, and made them his vassals (2 Samuel 8:5). In Solomon's time Rezon became king in Damascus and opposed Israel (1 Kings 11:24). King Asa sent a gift to Ben-hadad, the king of Aram who lived in Damascus, and asked him to break his alliance with northern Israel (1 Kings 15:18). God commanded Elijah to anoint Hazael to be king of Damascus (1 Kings 19:15). Ahab made a treaty with Ben-hadad, king of Aram, and obtained the right to establish streets in Damascus (1 Kings 20:34). The commander Naaman claimed that Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, were better than all the rivers of Israel (2 Kings 5:12). When Elisha visited Damascus, Ben-hadad, king of Aram, was sick and sent a man to him (2 Kings 8:7). Hazael took every good thing of Damascus to Elisha in order to inquire about the sickness of Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:9).
geography: Damascus is situated in a fertile oasis region east of the Anti-Lebanon mountains, and the Barada River flows through it, giving it optimal conditions for ancient agriculture and urban development. As a crossroads of the trade route linking the Mediterranean coast and Mesopotamia, it is a region of very great commercial importance.
history: Existing since the second millennium BC, Damascus rose to be the political capital of the kingdom of Aram after the Arameans occupied it. During the Iron Age, Damascus at times came under the dominion of the kingdoms of David and Solomon, but it gradually built up independent power and grew into a major power that applied direct military pressure on the surrounding situation of the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah.

introduce: Aram of Damascus was a state formed by the Arameans of the ancient Near East centered on Damascus, a region closely connected with Israel's expansionist policy in the period of David's monarchy.
biblecontents: When David struck the Arameans of Damascus, they became David's servants and brought tribute, and the LORD gave David victory wherever he went (2 Samuel 8:6). The Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, and David killed twenty-two thousand of the Arameans and placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became David's servants and brought tribute (1 Chronicles 18:5-6).
geography: Damascus is an oasis city located east of the Anti-Lebanon mountains and a crossroads of the trade route linking the Mediterranean coast and Mesopotamia. Based on the fertile land of the Barada River basin, it was a strategic stronghold in which the political and economic interests of the surrounding nations had been intertwined since ancient times.
history: Around the tenth century BC the Aramean forces rallied around Zobah, but after David's wars of conquest Damascus rose as the new center. David stationed military garrisons in this region and exercised influence over it, and thereafter, until the time of Solomon, it remained a vassal state paying tribute under Israel's hegemony.

introduce: Tahpanhes was a town located in the eastern part of the Nile Delta in ancient Egypt, and in the Old Testament Book of Jeremiah it appears as the place where the remnant of Judah lived when they fled to Egypt. In Hebrew it is called Tahpanhes, and in Greek it is known as Daphnae.
biblecontents: The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have also broken the crown of your head (Jeremiah 2:16). Johanan and all the commanders of the forces took the remnant of Judah and entered the land of Egypt and came to Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). At Tahpanhes the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, telling him to take large stones and hide them in the brickwork at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:8-9). The word came concerning all the Judahites who live in the land of Egypt, those who live at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and in the land of Pathros (Jeremiah 44:1). Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes: Stand up and make ready on every side (Jeremiah 46:14).
geography: Tahpanhes is a strategic point located at the northeastern edge of the Nile Delta. It served as Egypt's eastern gateway linking Egypt and Canaan, and, lying near the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, it was a meeting point of sea and overland trade.
history: Around the seventh century BC, Tahpanhes was greatly expanded as a military base by Psamtik I of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt. Greek mercenaries were stationed here, and it was the headquarters of the garrison defending Egypt's border. After the fall of Jerusalem, the nobles of Judah and the remnant, including Jeremiah, moved here as political exiles, and it has been archaeologically confirmed as a historical fact that the Pharaoh of Egypt at that time maintained a palace here.

introduce: Taberah was a place where the Israelites who came out of Egypt stayed during their journey in the wilderness, and its name means "burning" in Hebrew. This place takes its origin from the event in which the fire of God blazed among them because of the people's complaining.
biblecontents: When the people of Israel complained with evil words in the hearing of the LORD, the anger of the LORD kindled a fire that burned at the edge of the camp, and for this reason the place was named Taberah (Numbers 11:3). Also, Taberah is mentioned, together with Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah, as one of the places where the people of Israel provoked the LORD to wrath (Deuteronomy 9:22).
geography: The exact location of Taberah has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is presumed to be a wilderness area on the route leaving Mount Sinai and heading for Kadesh-barnea. In the biblical context, on the basis of the record that they left Taberah and moved on to Kibroth-hattaavah, it is regarded as being in that vicinity.

introduce: Daberath was a town located within the territory of a tribe of ancient Israel, a place mentioned in the Old Testament both as a Levite city and as a border area of the tribe of Issachar.
biblecontents: Daberath is mentioned as a place included within the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:12). Afterward, Daberath is recorded as a town assigned from the tribe of Issachar to the Gershonite clan, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:28, 1 Chronicles 6:72).
geography: Daberath is identified with the same area as the village of Daburiyya, located on the eastern side of the Jezreel Plain in present-day northern Israel. This spot lies at the southwestern foot of Mount Tabor and so occupies a strategic position topographically.

introduce: Tripolis is a name that designates a people or a group of persons from a region under the ancient Persian Empire, recorded in Ezra 4:9.
biblecontents: The people of Tripolis are included in the list of officials and peoples who sent a petition to King Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:9).
history: It is presumed to be one of the peoples who migrated from the region of Mesopotamia as a result of the forced resettlement policy carried out after Sargon II of Assyria conquered Samaria. Within the administrative system of the Persian Empire at that time, they are mentioned as members of the force that lived in the region of Samaria and hindered the Jews' rebuilding of the temple.

introduce: Tarsus is the central city of the Cilicia region in southeastern Asia Minor, the Tarsus area located in present-day Mersin Province, Turkey. It is known as a crossroads of learning and commerce in the ancient world.
biblecontents: In a vision God told Ananias to look for Saul of Tarsus (Acts 9:11). Saul was sent off to Tarsus with the help of the brothers in Jerusalem (Acts 9:30). Afterward Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul (Acts 11:25).
geography: Tarsus lies on the fertile plain south of the Taurus Mountains, and has the topographical advantage of the Cydnus River flowing through the city to the Mediterranean Sea. This geographical setting enabled it to serve as a key hub linking ancient sea and overland trade routes.
history: In the Hellenistic period Tarsus gained renown as a center of learning, and in the Roman period it had high political importance as the capital of the province of Cilicia. Many of its citizens held Roman citizenship, and the level of education was so high that it was known as the cradle of Stoic philosophy of the day. In particular, as the gateway to Cilicia, it was an economic center where the cultures and goods of East and West crossed.

remark: A trading port in Spain.
introduce: Tarshish refers to a major maritime trading base and port city located at the western end of the world as the biblical authors perceived it in the context of the ancient Near East and the Mediterranean world. It is described as a metal-producing region that carried on maritime trade in cooperation with Phoenician Tyre, mainly in the time of Solomon and the time of Jehoshaphat.
biblecontents: Solomon's ships of Tarshish, together with the ships of Hiram, brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks once every three years (1 Kings 10:22). Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber (1 Kings 22:48). Solomon's ships went to Tarshish and carried gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks (2 Chronicles 9:21). Jehoshaphat joined with Ahaziah to make ships to go to Tarshish, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber (2 Chronicles 20:36, 20:37). The psalmist likened the ships of Tarshish to something shattered by the east wind (Psalms 48:7), and mentioned that the kings of Tarshish would bring gifts (Psalms 72:10). Isaiah prophesied that the ships of Tarshish would be an object of judgment that humbles pride on the day of the LORD (Isaiah 2:16), and, in connection with the destruction of Tyre, proclaimed that the ships of Tarshish would wail (Isaiah 23:1, 23:6).
geography: Scholarly debate continues over the exact location of Tarshish, but the view that identifies it with the region of Tartessos in Spain, at the western end of the Mediterranean, is generally dominant. Ancient Greek and Roman geographical writings also mention southern Spain as a mining region producing abundant silver and gold and as a center of maritime trade. Some scholars also raise the possibility that Tarshish is not a proper noun designating a particular port city on the Mediterranean coast, but means the large ships themselves that carried on long-distance trade, or is a name embracing the Phoenicians' sailing bases within the Mediterranean.
history: Between the tenth and eighth centuries BC, the Phoenician city-state of Tyre held the lead in Mediterranean trade. To secure metal resources they opened sea routes as far as the Iberian Peninsula, and in this process Tarshish came to hold an important position as a supplier of metal raw materials, especially silver. King Solomon of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah gained access to the Tarshish trade route through their alliance with Tyre, which is regarded as a historical indicator that the economy of ancient Israel was closely connected with the Mediterranean maritime trade network. Afterward, with the expansion of Assyria and changes in the situation in the Mediterranean, the importance and character of the Tarshish trade underwent change.

introduce: Taanach was an important Canaanite town and strategic point located at the southwestern end of the Jezreel Valley in northern ancient Israel. It was one of the regions ruled by Canaanite kings at the time of the wars of conquest, and afterward came to lie within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: The king of Taanach is included in the list of Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:21). The tribe of Manasseh received as its inheritance Taanach and its villages, lying between the tribes of Issachar and Asher, but it did not completely drive out the Canaanites living there (Joshua 17:11, Judges 1:27, 1 Chronicles 7:29). Afterward Taanach became a town assigned to the Kohathite descendants of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:25). The battleground where Deborah and Barak fought against the army of Sisera was at the waters of Taanach (Judges 5:19). In Solomon's time, authority over the district of Taanach was entrusted to Baana (1 Kings 4:12).
geography: Taanach is identified with present-day Tell Taanach and is situated in a strategic position overlooking the Jezreel Valley. Located at the entrance to the Dothan Valley, it was adjacent to the Way of the Sea (Via Maris), the ancient international highway linking the coastal plain with the Jordan Valley. Set in a fertile plain, it had conditions suited to agriculture.
history: Taanach was a city continuously inhabited from the Bronze Age, and it was an influential town to the extent that it is mentioned in various documents of the ancient Near East, such as the record of Thutmose III of Egypt's battle of Megiddo (around the fifteenth century BC). Through archaeological excavation, cuneiform documents known as the Taanach tablets were discovered here, and these are an important source showing the political and economic situation of the region at that time. Even after the period of Israel's settlement, Taanach was a region frequently in dispute with neighboring great powers because of its strategic importance.

introduce: Taanath-shiloh was a town or place name located on the boundary line of the tribe of Ephraim in ancient Israel, and in biblical geographical studies it is mentioned as a marker for fixing the northern boundary of the territory distributed after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The western boundary turns north to Michmethath, and on the east it turns around to Taanath-shiloh and passes by it on the east of Janoah (Joshua 16:6).
geography: Its present location has not been determined precisely, but it is generally presumed to have been located in the area southeast of Shechem. Archaeologically, the theory identifying it with present-day Khirbet Tana is the strongest, and it has the topographical feature of lying between the eastern slope of the hill country of Samaria and the Jordan Valley.
history: In the process of Joshua fixing the boundary of the inheritance he allotted to the tribe of Ephraim after the wars of conquest of Canaan, Taanath-shiloh was used as a geographical reference point. Afterward, amid historical upheavals such as the period of the division of the kingdom of Israel, this region came to have significance as a strategic point, but cases in which a clear historical event is recorded in ancient literature outside the Bible are rare.

remark: 1. The northernmost town of Canaan.
introduce: Dan is a place name in northern ancient Israel and also the name of a tribe; it is the place that was renamed after the region originally called Laish was conquered.
biblecontents: When Abram heard that his nephew Lot had been taken captive, he led out his three hundred eighteen trained men born in his house and pursued the captors as far as Dan and defeated them (Genesis 14:14).
geography: Dan lies at the northern end of the Huleh Basin and is a fertile region through which flows spring water that rises from Mount Hermon. Containing the major sources of water of the upper Jordan River, it has an environment very favorable to farming and settlement.
history: Originally this region was a city-state named Laish that had exchanges with Sidon. After the time of Joshua, the tribe of Dan lost the land originally allotted to it, moved north, and conquered this place, and then called it Dan after the name of their ancestor. Afterward it became a symbolic point of Israel's northern boundary.

remark: 2. The tribe of Dan, or the region where they lived.
introduce: Dan was the fifth son of Jacob, born to Rachel's maidservant Bilhah, and is the ancestor of the tribe of Dan, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. In the Old Testament the tribe of Dan is mentioned in connection with producing skilled craftsmen for the building of the tabernacle, with the census, and with its position during the march through the wilderness.
biblecontents: God appointed Oholiab son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan as a craftsman to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:6). Oholiab, a man skilled in fine carving and embroidery, was employed in the design of the tabernacle (Exodus 35:34). He also contributed to making all the furnishings of the tabernacle (Exodus 38:23). The leader of the tribe of Dan was Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai (Numbers 1:12), and the census showed 62,700 men aged twenty and over (Numbers 1:39). During the march through the wilderness, the tribe of Dan was stationed on the north side of the camp (Numbers 2:25). They marched last of all the camps (Numbers 2:31, Numbers 10:25). There is a recorded case in which the son of a woman from the tribe of Dan blasphemed the name of the LORD and was punished (Leviticus 24:11).

introduce: Dannah was a town located in the hill country of Judah among the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is included in the list of towns belonging to the hill country of Judah among the towns that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:49).
geography: Archaeologists identify present-day Khirbet ed-Dina (Khirbet ed-Dina) as the location of Dannah. It is one of the ruins of an ancient settlement situated near the center of the hill country of Judah.

introduce: Dalmanutha is a place name that appears in the Gospel of Mark, a region on the shore of the Sea of Galilee mentioned as the place where Jesus' boat arrived.
biblecontents: Jesus got into the boat with his disciples, crossed the Sea of Galilee, and came to the district of Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10).
geography: It is presumed to be located on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, but its exact location has not been determined archaeologically. Matthew 15:39 refers to the same event and records that he came to the region of Magadan, so Dalmanutha and Magadan are sometimes interpreted as adjacent regions or as designating the same place.

introduce: Dalmatia is the name that designates the southern part of Illyricum, one of the provinces of the Roman Empire, located on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.
biblecontents: It is recorded that when the apostle Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Demas, who had been his fellow worker, loved the world, deserted Paul, and left for Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10).
geography: It corresponds to the coastal region of present-day Croatia, and has the topographical character of being bounded on the west by the Adriatic Sea and surrounded on the east by the Dinaric Alps.
history: Around the first century BC it came into conflict with the Roman Empire, and in the reign of the emperor Augustus it was completely conquered and incorporated as an administrative district of Rome. Afterward it developed into a major Roman military stronghold and commercial port, and served as a base for the spread of Roman culture in the western Balkan Peninsula.

introduce: Tabbath is a place name that appears in Judges 7:22, an area mentioned as one of the places where the battle took place between Gideon's three hundred men and the army of Midian.
biblecontents: It is recorded that when the Midianite army fell into confusion at the sound of Gideon's trumpets and fled, their line of flight reached Tabbath near Zererah, and extended to the border of Abel-meholah (Judges 7:22).
geography: It is presumed to be located near the Jordan Valley and is judged to be a point on the geographical route linking Zererah and Abel-meholah. Scholars disagree over its exact present-day location, and its connection with any particular archaeological site has not been clearly confirmed.

introduce: Dabbesheth is a place name that appears in the Old Testament book of Joshua, a name indicating a boundary point of a town distributed to the tribe of Zebulun among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: It is recorded as the point where, going up westward, the boundary reaches Maralah, meets Dabbesheth, and meets the brook that is east of Jokmeam (Joshua 19:11).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the western hills of the Galilee region or in the plain area nearby, but its exact present-day location has not been clearly determined archaeologically.

introduce: Tahtim-hodshi is a place name mentioned in the census carried out by King David, a place presumed to be located near the northern boundary of the region of Gilead. Its original Hebrew name is Tahtim Hodshi, and there are differences among ancient manuscripts concerning its meaning and its exact location.
biblecontents: There remains a record that, for the census, David crossed the Jordan River, passed Aroer and the town in the middle of the valley, went by way of Gad, and reached Tahtim-hodshi (2 Samuel 24:6).
geography: Tahtim-hodshi is presumed to be in the northern part of the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River, that is, near the region of Dana adjacent to Damascus. It serves as a geographical milestone showing how far north the extent of David's territorial expansion reached at that time. However, the exact archaeological identification of the place name itself has still not been clearly agreed upon.
history: It shows the boundaries of the administrative districts at the time of the census carried out in the latter part of King David's reign. This place name is recorded differently in some ancient manuscripts, including the Septuagint, and so the possibility of a copyist's error in the process of transmission of biblical place names, or the process of change in the place name, is also discussed in scholarship.

introduce: The Great Sea mentioned in the Bible is the name that refers to the Mediterranean Sea, which forms the western boundary of Israel. In the geographical context of the ancient Near East, it is an important reference point as the western boundary line of the territory to be occupied by the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: The western boundary shall be the Great Sea for your boundary; this shall be your western boundary (Numbers 34:6). Draw your northern boundary from the Great Sea to Mount Hor (Numbers 34:7). From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun, shall be your territory (Joshua 1:4). The western boundary is the Great Sea with its coastline; this is the boundary on all sides of the land that the descendants of Judah received according to their clans (Joshua 15:12). Ashdod, with its towns and villages, and Gaza, with its towns and villages, as far as the Brook of Egypt and the Great Sea (Joshua 15:47). See, I have allotted to you by lot, as an inheritance for your tribes, the remaining nations from the Jordan westward to the Great Sea, together with all the nations I have already destroyed (Joshua 23:4).
geography: The Great Sea means the present-day Mediterranean Sea, a sea stretching long along the western coast of the Levant. As seen in the records of Numbers 34 and Joshua 15, this sea is a geographical upper limit that served as Israel's western boundary, as a natural line of defense, and as a route of maritime trade.

introduce: Derbe was an ancient city located in the region of Lycaonia in southeastern Asia Minor, a place name for which there remain records of visits during the apostle Paul's first and second missionary journeys.
biblecontents: Paul and Barnabas fled from persecution in Lystra to Derbe, where they preached the gospel and made many disciples (Acts 14:6, 14:20). Later, during his second missionary journey, Paul visited Derbe again and met Timothy (Acts 16:1). Also, Gaius, who was from Derbe, accompanied Paul on his missionary journey (Acts 20:4).
geography: Derbe is presumed to be located near Karaman in present-day Türkiye, on the Lycaonian plain about 60 km east of Lystra. This city lay on the road leading to the Cilician Gates and served as a crossroads of traffic.
