history: In the Roman period Derbe was included in the province of Galatia, and around AD 41 it received the name Claudiopolis from the emperor Claudius and secured the status of a self-governing city. In its early period it was a border city of the Lycaonia region, but under the Hellenistic and Roman administrative systems it grew into a regional center city.

introduce: Decapolis means "ten cities" in Greek and designates a league of cities centered on Hellenistic culture formed east of the Jordan River and southeast of the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: Having heard of the fame of Jesus, large crowds from Galilee, the Decapolis, and other places followed him (Matthew 4:25). After the man who had been possessed by demons in the region of the Gerasenes was healed by Jesus, he proclaimed in the Decapolis what Jesus had done for him (Mark 5:20). There is a record that Jesus passed through Tyre and Sidon and went through the region of the Decapolis to reach the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7:31).
geography: The cities of the Decapolis were distributed mainly on the Transjordan plateau east of the Jordan River and on the fertile plain southeast of the Sea of Galilee. It is a broad region that includes present-day northern Jordan, southern Syria, and part of the Golan Heights of Israel. However, these cities did not form a single administrative district but took the form of a loose league of individual cities.
history: After the conquest of Alexander the Great in the fourth century BC, Hellenistic culture flowed in and cities were built; later the Roman Pompey conquered the region in 63 BC and granted it autonomy, and the league of ten cities was consolidated. These cities served as Roman administrative and military strongholds, and had a distinctive Hellenistic social structure and economic characteristics set apart from the Jewish cultural sphere.

remark: The 23rd place of encampment after leaving Egypt in the exodus, and the 12th place of encampment after leaving Mount Sinai.
introduce: Terah is one of the stages of the Israelites' wilderness journey that appear in Exodus and Numbers, an encampment passed through after setting out from Hazeroth and before crossing the Red Sea.
biblecontents: The people of Israel left Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah; they left Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez; they left Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah; they left Libnah and camped at Rissah; they left Rissah and camped at Kehelathah; they left Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher; they left Mount Shepher and camped at Haradah; they left Haradah and camped at Makheloth; they left Makheloth and camped at Tahath; they left Tahath and camped at Terah; they left Terah and camped at Mithkah (Numbers 33:27-28).
geography: Terah is presumed to be located in the northeast of the Sinai Peninsula or near the Arabah valley, but its specific geological location has not been clearly determined today. It is regarded as a particular stopping point on the route along which the people of Israel were moving at that time.

introduce: Thebez is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament book of Judges as the town Abimelech attacked just before he met his end.
biblecontents: Abimelech encamped against Thebez and captured the town, but while he was attacking the people who had fled to the tower inside the town, a woman threw an upper millstone that struck his head, and he was fatally wounded (Judges 9:50).
geography: Thebez is identified with the Tubas area in the present-day West Bank. This is a point about 20 kilometers northeast of Shechem, situated at a crossroads of traffic leading to the Jordan Valley.
history: In the period of the judges, Thebez took the form of an independent city-state, and it was attacked after resisting the expansion of Abimelech's power. Afterward, in the biblical record, Thebez no longer appears as the setting for any major historical event.

introduce: Thebez is a place presumed to have been a town located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River in the time of ancient Israel. Apart from the biblical record, it is an unknown place for which there is a lack of archaeological evidence by which its reality or location could be determined.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in the scene in which Joab, the commander of the army of David, king of Israel, cites the case of Abimelech to his men and asks in return who it was that struck down Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth at Thebez (2 Samuel 11:21).
geography: Thebez is generally confused with the Thebez known today as Tell el-Husn, but in view of the context of 2 Samuel 11:21 the possibility is raised that it was located near Gilead east of the Jordan. In terms of modern geography, the exact identification is unclear.

remark: A city in Macedonia.
introduce: Thessalonica was a major city of the region of Macedonia and a port city that served as a key base during the apostle Paul's missionary journeys. Located on the Via Egnatia, the principal Roman trunk road, it was regarded as a strategic point.
biblecontents: Paul, Silas, and Timothy passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia and arrived at Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). The people of Thessalonica were more noble-minded than those of Berea; they received the word with eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). When the Jews in Thessalonica heard that Paul was proclaiming the word of God, they came there too and stirred up the crowds (Acts 17:13). Aristarchus and Secundus, men of Thessalonica, traveled with Paul (Acts 20:4). When Paul was being taken to Rome, he boarded a ship of Adramyttium that was about to sail to the coast of Asia, and Aristarchus, a man of Thessalonica, was with him (Acts 27:2). Even while Paul was in Thessalonica, you sent aid for my needs, not once but twice (Philippians 4:16). Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy wrote a letter to the church of the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:1, 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Demas loved the world, deserted Paul, and went to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:10).
geography: Thessalonica is a port city located on the northern shore of the Thermaic Gulf in Macedonia. The Via Egnatia, the important east-west Roman road, passed through this city, and it served as a center of traffic and commerce. Thanks to the topographical feature of mountains and sea lying close together, it was a natural fortress and a base of maritime trade.
history: In 315 BC the Macedonian king Cassander founded it by uniting several existing settlements and named it after Thessalonike, his wife and the half-sister of Alexander the Great. After Rome incorporated Macedonia as a province, it became the capital of Macedonia, and having been granted the status of a free city by Rome, it was able to exercise autonomous administration and judicial authority.

introduce: Dehavites is a name designating a particular group that lived in the region of Aram in the period of the ancient Persian Empire, or the administrative district to which they belonged.
biblecontents: In the petition sent to King Artaxerxes, they are mentioned as one of the groups who accused the Jews (Ezra 4:9).
history: The Dehavites are presumed to have been a tribe or immigrant group of Aramean descent that appears in the petition sent by the officials of the region of Samaria to hinder the Jews' rebuilding of the temple during the reign of Artaxerxes I of the Persian Empire (Ezra 4:9). They appear to have been one of the forces that exercised administrative influence in alliance with the peoples who had been resettled in the region of Samaria by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon at that time (Ezra 4:9-10).

introduce: Tel-melah is one of the place names mentioned in the list of the Israelite community that returned after the Babylonian exile, a region recorded as the place where people whose identity was unclear lived.
biblecontents: There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not show whether they belonged to the descendants of Israel, nor establish their clans or genealogy (Ezra 2:59). There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove whether the house and genealogy of their ancestors belonged to Israel (Nehemiah 7:61).
history: It is presumed to be one of the Jewish settlements that formed within the region of Babylon after the Babylonian exile, and the prefix "Tel" means, in the ancient Near East, a mound built on the ruins of an ancient city. Judging from the difficulty of confirming their status in the course of the return, this region suggests that the Jews in Babylonian society led an independent communal life.

introduce: Tel-abib was one of the settlements where Judean captives lived during the Babylonian exile, a region located on the bank of the Kebar River.
biblecontents: Ezekiel came to Tel-abib on the bank of the Kebar River, where the captives lived, and stayed there among the captives for seven days, overwhelmed (Ezekiel 3:15).
geography: Tel-abib is presumed to be located in the basin of the Kebar River (canal) near Nippur, the heartland of the Babylonian Empire. It is known as a plain region through which flowed the Nar Kabari canal, an irrigation work of ancient Babylonia.
history: In the early sixth century BC, after Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylonia conquered the kingdom of Judah, he forcibly relocated the upper classes and craftsmen of Judah to Babylon. To support the Babylonian economy they were put to work on state projects such as reclaiming wasteland and digging canals, and Tel-abib was one of the administrative districts that served as a communal settlement for such captives and for managing their labor. The name of this region appears to derive from Til abubi, which means "mound of flood or destruction" in Babylonian, and this reflects topographical features connected with the maintenance of irrigation works at that time.

introduce: Tel-harsha is a region mentioned as the place where, among those who returned to Jerusalem from places such as Tel-melah and Tel-harsha in Babylon at the time of the return from the Babylonian captivity, those who could not prove their family or genealogy lived.
biblecontents: There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not show whether the house and genealogy of their ancestors belonged to Israel (Ezra 2:59). There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not offer proof whether the house and genealogy of their ancestors belonged to Israel (Nehemiah 7:61).
history: In the process of the Jews returning under the decree of Cyrus of Persia after the Babylonian exile, it was a period in which proving purity of descent was very important. Tel-harsha is one of the place names included in the list of returnees, and is presumed to have been one of the Jewish settlements or places of residence that existed within the region of Babylon at that time. According to the record, those from this region could not present any grounds for proving that they were members of the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Tochen is a place recorded as one of the towns where the descendants of the tribe of Judah lived.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns that the tribe of Simeon received as an inheritance within the share of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:32).
geography: Scholars disagree over its exact location, and it is generally presumed to be one of the towns located in the southern Negev region of the tribe of Judah. Since it appears in the same list as Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan mentioned in Joshua 19:7, it is closely related geographically to those towns.

introduce: Dothan is a strategic point located in the northern region of ancient Israel, a city near the Jezreel Valley about 15 km north of Samaria. The archaeological site known as Tell Dothan lies alongside a fertile plain and major trade routes, and from ancient times it served as a center of population settlement and traffic.
biblecontents: It is the place where Joseph's brothers, who were tending sheep at Shechem, plotted to kill him when Joseph arrived after them, and finally sold him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:17). Later it was the place where the prophet Elisha was surrounded by the army of the king of Aram, and at that time Elisha, seeing the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, demonstrated the protection of God (2 Kings 6:13).
geography: Dothan sits on a hill about 200 meters above sea level and lies in a fertile basin called the Valley of Dothan. This region was located at an important passage connecting the Way of the Sea, an ancient international trade route, with the Jezreel Valley, and so had very high economic and military value.
history: It was a city continuously inhabited through the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, and was used as a strategic stronghold in periods of political upheaval in the northern kingdom of Israel, such as the Assyrian invasion. Through archaeological excavation, city walls and defensive works from the Middle Bronze Age have been identified, and many remains that carried out administrative functions in the period of the northern kingdom of Israel have been discovered.

introduce: Tophel is a place name located in the Arabah wilderness east of the Jordan River, a place name mentioned at the beginning of Deuteronomy when describing the place where Moses proclaimed the law to the people of Israel.
biblecontents: These are the words that he proclaimed to them beside the sea beyond the Jordan, in the Arabah wilderness, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab (Deuteronomy 1:1)
geography: Its exact present-day location is difficult to determine archaeologically, but scholars presume it to be somewhere southeast of the Dead Sea or in the Arabah region of the Jordan Valley.

introduce: Topheth was a place located in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom outside the walls of Jerusalem, and it is recorded as the place where idolatrous practices such as human sacrifice were committed in the period of the kingdom of Judah in late ancient Israel. Afterward this place is mentioned as a place symbolizing the judgment and destruction of Judah.
biblecontents: King Josiah defiled Topheth in order to make it unclean, in order to prohibit the idolatry practiced there of making children pass through the fire (2 Kings 23:10). Isaiah, describing the judgment on Assyria, mentioned that Topheth had long been prepared for the king (Isaiah 30:33). Jeremiah accused the people of Judah of having built high places at Topheth and committed the abomination of burning their own children as offerings (Jeremiah 7:31). For this reason Jeremiah prophesied that the name of this place would come to be called the Valley of Slaughter, and that so many corpses would be piled up that there would be no place to bury them (Jeremiah 7:32, Jeremiah 19:6). It was also proclaimed that Topheth, as the place of Judah's judgment, would become a place of ruin that, like a broken earthen vessel, could never be restored, and that the houses of Jerusalem would become unclean like Topheth (Jeremiah 19:11, Jeremiah 19:12, Jeremiah 19:13, Jeremiah 19:14).
geography: Topheth was located inside the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, adjacent to the south or southwest of the walls of Jerusalem. Topographically it corresponds to a valley area suited for disposing of a city's refuse or burying corpses.
history: Topheth is known as the place where the rite of human sacrifice, offering children to the god Molech, was performed. In the course of King Josiah's religious reform in the late seventh century BC, such foreign religious rites were officially abolished. Afterward, from the archaeological standpoint, the Hinnom Valley continued to be used as a place for burning Jerusalem's refuse, and for this reason Topheth came to be a byword for destruction and unclean death after the fall of the kingdom of Judah.

introduce: Dor was a strategic point on the coastal plain of ancient Palestine and one of the major city-states of Canaan, a port city that served as a base of Mediterranean trade.
biblecontents: The king of Dor joined the northern Canaanite coalition and opposed Joshua (Joshua 11:2). The king of Dor is included in the list of Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:23). The tribe of Manasseh was allotted Dor and its villages, located on the boundary between the tribes of Issachar and Asher, but at first it could not completely drive out its inhabitants (Joshua 17:11, Judges 1:27). In Solomon's time Ben-abinadab was appointed as the district governor in charge of all of Dor (1 Kings 4:11). Dor is recorded as the portion of the descendants of Manasseh, within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 7:29).
geography: Dor is a port city on the Mediterranean coast at the southern foot of the Carmel range, identified with present-day Tel Dor. It lies adjacent to the fertile Plain of Sharon and has natural harbor conditions, giving it the topographical advantage of being favorable for sea traffic and trade.
history: Settled from the Bronze Age, Dor was strongly influenced by Phoenicia, and in the Late Bronze and Iron Ages it is known as the dwelling place of the Shekelesh, one of the Sea Peoples. Even after the period of Israel's settlement it maintained regional influence as a powerful fortress, and in the time of Solomon's reorganization of administrative districts it functioned as a key economic and administrative base. Afterward, in the period of the Assyrian Empire, it was also reorganized as a provincial administrative center of Assyria.

introduce: Tolad is a place name that appears in 1 Chronicles 4:29, one of the towns allotted as an inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the list of towns where the descendants of the tribe of Judah lived (1 Chronicles 4:29).
geography: It is presumed to be a town located near the Negev desert in the southern region of the tribe of Judah, and the prevailing view is that it is the same place as the Tolad mentioned in Joshua 19:4.

introduce: Ptolemais was a port city on the ancient Mediterranean coast, located in the area of present-day Acre in Israel. In the Acts of the New Testament it is mentioned as a place passed through on Paul's route of return from his third missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul left Tyre and continued his voyage and came to Ptolemais, where he greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day (Acts 21:7).
geography: Ptolemais is a strategic point on the plain along the northern Mediterranean coast of Palestine. It served as a passage leading from the Phoenician coast to the region of Galilee, and because it had a natural harbor it was used from ancient times as a base for sea trade.
history: Originally a Phoenician city, it was renamed Ptolemais by Ptolemy II Philadelphus in the Hellenistic period. Afterward, in the Roman imperial period, it held political and military importance as a major port city, and functioned as a center of traffic linking the region of Judea and Syria.

introduce: Tob is, according to the biblical record, a place name located in the Aramean region east of the Jordan; it is mentioned as the place where Jephthah fled and lived to escape the Ammonites, and as the place where the Aramean coalition assembled to wage war against David.
biblecontents: Jephthah fled from his half-brothers to the land of Tob and lived there, and worthless men gathered around him there (Judges 11:3). When the war with the Ammonites began, the elders of Gilead went to Jephthah in the land of Tob and asked him to become their commander (Judges 11:5). In the time of David, the Ammonites hired twenty thousand foot soldiers from the Arameans of Beth-rehob and Zobah, along with the king of Maacah with twelve thousand men, and had them assemble at Tob (2 Samuel 10:6). The Aramean coalition camped at Tob and prepared for war, facing David's army (2 Samuel 10:8).
geography: Tob is located in Transjordan, the region east of the Jordan River, and is presumed to correspond to the area of present-day southern Syria or northern Jordan. Lying adjacent to the major trade routes of the ancient Near East, it had the character of a military strongpoint.
history: At that time Tob appears to have been an Aramean-type city-state outside Israel's direct rule, or a region under its influence. From the case in the time of David in which the Ammonites gathered the troops of this region to use as a base against Israel, one can confirm the military alliance between the Aramean princes and Ammon at that time.

introduce: Dophkah is a place where the Israelites set up camp after leaving Alush during the route of the exodus.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Alush and camped at Dophkah (Numbers 33:13).
geography: The exact location of Dophkah has not been clearly determined archaeologically at present, but there is a theory that presumes it to be in the northwestern Sinai Peninsula or near the area of Wadi Feiran.

remark: A lecture hall (school). Connected with the apostle Paul. The place where Paul lectured for two years in Ephesus and spread the gospel.
introduce: Tyrannus is a place that appears in Acts 19:9, meaning a lecture hall or auditorium that the apostle Paul used as a base of ministry for spreading the gospel in Ephesus.
biblecontents: But when some became hardened and would not obey, slandering this Way before the crowd, Paul left them, set the disciples apart, and reasoned daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9)
geography: Tyrannus was located in Ephesus, then the capital of the province of Asia, and took the form of a public building or private lecture hall where rhetorical instruction and philosophical discussion of the ancient city were conducted.
history: According to ancient Western literature and some variant readings of the biblical manuscripts, Tyrannus is presumed to have been a lecture hall named after a man called Tyrannus, a rhetorician of that time. The intellectuals of Ephesus at that time held philosophical discussions and lectures in such places during the rest period from noon through the afternoon, and Paul made use of this custom to teach and lecture to the disciples during the hours other than the morning.

introduce: Tyre was a major port city located in the Phoenician region on the Mediterranean coast and was a center of maritime trade and timber export in the ancient Near East. It established a relationship of economic and technical cooperation with Israel and is known as the place that supplied materials and craftsmen for the building of Solomon's temple.
biblecontents: It is a fortified city mentioned as part of the boundary of the tribe of Asher in the time of Joshua (Joshua 19:29). In the time of King David, Hiram king of Tyre sent David cedar wood, carpenters, and stonemasons to build a palace (2 Samuel 5:11, 1 Chronicles 14:1). There is a record that at the time of David's census the survey team led by Joab visited the fortress of Tyre (2 Samuel 24:7). Solomon again cooperated with Hiram for building the temple, and Hiram floated cedar and cypress timber of Lebanon down the sea as far as Joppa (1 Kings 5:1, 1 Chronicles 22:4). Hiram of Tyre, a skilled craftsman in working bronze, made the furnishings of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:13, 1 Kings 7:14). As payment for the work, Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee, but Hiram did not like the land and called it the land of Cabul (1 Kings 9:11, 1 Kings 9:12).
geography: It is located on the southern coast of present-day Lebanon, and in ancient times it was a maritime city composed of an island area separated from the land and a coastal area opposite it. It possessed natural harbors and so had an environment favorable to sea trade and shipbuilding.
history: From the second millennium BC, Tyre flourished as a major Phoenician city-state. In particular, around the tenth century BC, in the reign of Hiram I, it took control of maritime trade and enjoyed its economic heyday. Amid the surrounding great powers it maintained its strength through diplomatic neutrality and economic exchange, and it enjoyed a monopoly position as supplier to neighboring countries of the cedar wood, a specialty of Lebanon.

introduce: Thyatira is a city in the region of Lydia in Asia Minor, corresponding to the Akhisar area of present-day Turkey. In the Roman period it flourished as a center of commerce and guilds, and in the Bible it is mentioned in connection with the apostle Paul's mission and as one of the seven churches of Revelation.
biblecontents: In Philippi, Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth who was from Thyatira, welcomed Paul and his companions (Acts 16:14). It is mentioned as one of the seven churches of Revelation and is a city to which the apostle John was told to send the revelation (Revelation 1:11). The church in Thyatira received a letter sent by the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze (Revelation 2:18). It was also stated that no other burden would be laid on those within the church who did not hold that teaching (Revelation 2:24).
geography: Thyatira lay in the valley of the Lycus River and was a strategic point on the major ancient road linking Pergamum and Sardis. It was set on a plain lacking natural defenses and so was vulnerable to outside invasion, but commerce developed there on the strength of its convenience for travel.
history: Around the third century BC it was rebuilt as a military colony by Seleucus I Nicator of the Seleucid dynasty. Afterward it came under Roman rule, and a strong system of guilds, powerful trade associations centered especially on dyeing, leatherwork, and metalcraft, developed. This guild culture served as the social background that caused conflict for the Christians of that time between economic activity and religious compromise.

introduce: Trachonitis (Trachonitis) is a name designating the northeastern region of Palestine in the ancient Roman period, meaning a rugged volcanic-rock terrain that includes part of the present-day Hauran region of southern Syria.
biblecontents: When Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, the word of God came to John the Baptist (Luke 3:1).
geography: This region is part of ancient Bashan, which was called Argob, and with wide stretches of rough basaltic rock it has the topographical character of being suited more to grazing or as a hiding place than to farming. To the east lies a lava field known as the Leja, forming an isolated environment advantageous for defense against outside invasion.
history: Herod the Great was granted and ruled this region by the emperor Augustus, and at that time it was famous as a base of bandits and rebels. After the death of Herod the Great, his son Philip II governed the region of Trachonitis together with Ituraea as tetrarch. Afterward it has a history in which jurisdiction changed several times in the course of Rome's reorganization of administrative districts.

introduce: Troas is an ancient port city located on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, also called Alexandria Troas. During the apostle Paul's second and third missionary journeys it served as a strategic base linking Europe and Asia.
biblecontents: Paul and his companions passed by Mysia and went down to Troas (Acts 16:8). Afterward, from Troas they set sail and ran a straight course to Samothrace and crossed over to Philippi in Europe (Acts 16:11). During his third missionary journey Paul waited at Troas for the companions who had gone ahead, and stayed there seven days (Acts 20:5, Acts 20:6). Paul came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, but because he did not find Titus there, he left for Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:12). In his letter to Timothy in the last period of his life, Paul asked him to bring the cloak and the books he had left at the house of Carpus in Troas (2 Timothy 4:13).
geography: Troas is located in the Troad region on the Aegean coast and lies on the coast near present-day Çanakkale in Türkiye. In ancient times, as a crossroads of sea trade, it served as a passage across the sea linking Macedonia and Asia Minor.
history: It was founded around the fourth century BC by Antigonus, a general of Alexander the Great, and was afterward named Alexandria Troas by Lysimachus. In the Roman period it flourished as a free city and functioned as an important port linking Rome and the eastern provinces.

introduce: Teman is a place name designating the northern or eastern region of the land of Edom in the ancient Near East, widely known in the Bible and in ancient Near Eastern literature as a place where wise men lived.
biblecontents: Teman is classified as territory of Edom and is mentioned in the context of prophesying the downfall of its mighty men (Obadiah 1:9).
geography: Teman was one of the principal cities of Edom; its specific location is uncertain, but it is presumed to have been located in the region north or east of Petra. In the ancient Near East this region had geographical importance as it lay adjacent to trade routes.
history: Teman had a high reputation in ancient society as a center of wisdom, and it was regarded as a region symbolizing the intellectual tradition of Edom. Historically, at or around the time of the Babylonian invasion, it lay under the political influence of the surrounding great powers together with the other cities of Edom.

introduce: Tahpanhes is an ancient Egyptian place name, mentioned in the Bible as one of the major towns of Egypt, and called Tahpanhes in the Hebrew Bible.
biblecontents: Tehaphnehes is mentioned in a prophetic context in which, when the power of Egypt is broken, the day will be dark there (Ezekiel 30:18).
geography: A city located on the eastern frontier of the Nile Delta, it is presumed to be the same area as present-day Tell Defenneh, and it served as a strategic defensive base on the northeastern border of Egypt.
history: Tahpanhes was developed in earnest, in the time of Psamtik I of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, as a garrison for foreign mercenaries, especially Greek-speaking Ionians. Afterward it is known as one of the major places where the Jewish refugees settled when they moved to Egypt following Johanan at the time of the fall of Jerusalem.

introduce: Telassar is a city-state of the ancient Near East, a region mentioned in the Bible as one of the objects of conquest during the period of expansion of the Assyrian Empire.
biblecontents: The servants of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, threatening Hezekiah, king of Judah, singled out Telassar as one of the nations that their ancestors had destroyed (2 Kings 19:12). Also in the book of Isaiah, in the same context, it records that the inhabitants of Telassar, together with Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, were conquered by the kings of Assyria (Isaiah 37:12).
geography: Archaeological and historical scholarship identifies Telassar with Teralla (Telassar) or Talassu (Talassu), located near the upper Euphrates River in present-day northern Syria. Its exact coordinates have not been specified, but it is presumed to be an area located on Assyria's western and northwestern campaign routes.
history: Telassar is one of the many small states occupied in the course of the expansion of the Assyrian Empire. Sennacherib mentioned it, intending to put psychological pressure on the kingdom of Judah through the example of having conquered this region. At that time Assyria carried out a policy of forcibly resettling the inhabitants of conquered lands, and Telassar too is understood to have been incorporated under this imperial system of rule.

introduce: Telaim is a place name that appears in 1 Samuel 15:4, a region mentioned as one of the places where King Saul mustered an army for the war with Amalek.
biblecontents: Saul summoned the people and counted them at Telaim, and there were two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah (1 Samuel 15:4).
geography: The exact location of Telaim has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but from the geographical context it is presumed to be a town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah. There is a view in scholarship that it is the same place as Rema, mentioned in Joshua 15:32, and in that case it is regarded as located in the Negev region of southern Judah.
history: In the time of King Saul, Telaim functioned as a military assembly point. This preserves the historical circumstance showing that the kingdom of Israel at that time systematically organized and counted the troops of all the tribes of Israel and of the tribe of Judah in order to campaign against Amalek.

introduce: Tirathites is a place name that appears in 1 Chronicles 2:55, a place recorded as the dwelling of the Tirathite clan, a clan of scribes.
biblecontents: The clans of scribes who lived at Jabez, namely the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites; these are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab (1 Chronicles 2:55)

remark: A town in Ephraim or Manasseh.
introduce: Tirzah was one of the towns of ancient Canaan; at first it was an area ruled by a Canaanite king, and afterward it was the place used as the early capital of the northern kingdom of Israel in the period of the divided kingdom of Israel.
biblecontents: Tirzah was originally a town ruled by a king of Canaan but was conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:24). Afterward the wife of King Jeroboam returned to Tirzah to inquire about her son's illness (1 Kings 14:17), and in order to block Ramah, which King Baasha had built, King Asa carried away the building materials of Ramah and used them to repair the town (1 Kings 15:21). Baasha reigned over Israel at Tirzah for twenty-four years (1 Kings 15:33) and, after he died, was buried at Tirzah (1 Kings 16:6). Baasha's son Elah became king at Tirzah (1 Kings 16:8), but was killed there by his servant Zimri (1 Kings 16:9). Zimri was king at Tirzah for seven days (1 Kings 16:15), and when Omri besieged the town, he set the palace on fire and took his own life (1 Kings 16:17). Afterward Omri reigned for six years with Tirzah as his capital and then moved the capital to Samaria (1 Kings 16:23).
geography: Tirzah is identified with the area of Tell el-Far'ah (North) in the present-day West Bank. It is located about 10 km northeast of Shechem, and is a strategic point with a fertile valley and abundant water sources.
history: Tirzah was known for its beautiful scenery and was even cited in ancient Israelite literature as a symbol of beauty. The reason the early kings of the northern kingdom of Israel made this their base was the topographical advantage of its closeness to a center such as Shechem and its ease of defense. However, as Samaria, which was broader and strategically more advantageous, was chosen as the new capital under the dynasty of Omri, the political influence of Tirzah gradually diminished.

introduce: Dimonah is one of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua 15 of the Bible.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the southern towns bordering Edom, at the end of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah received according to their families (Joshua 15:22).
geography: Dimonah is presumed to be located near the Negev desert in the southern region of Judah, but scholars disagree over whether it is the same place as the present-day Israeli city of Dimona, and a specific archaeological identification has not been completed.

remark: Son of Gomer, son of Japheth (1 Chronicles 1:6). In Genesis 10:3 the name is recorded as 'Riphath'.
introduce: Riphath is the name of a person or tribe appearing in the first chapter of Chronicles, recorded as a descendant of Gomer, the son of Japheth.
biblecontents: The sons of Gomer are Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah (1 Chronicles 1:6).

introduce: Tiberias is a city located on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, built in the Roman imperial period and serving as the administrative and political center of the Galilee region at that time. In the Bible it was also used as another name for the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: Jesus went to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias, and a great crowd followed him (John 6:1). Boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks (John 6:23). Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed Himself to the disciples. He made Himself known in this way: (John 21:1).
geography: It is set on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, in a lowland about 200 meters below sea level. It is an area where hot springs are well developed and a crossroads of traffic running north and south along the lake.
history: It is a city built by Herod Antipas to honor the Roman emperor Tiberius. Because it was said to have been built over graves, it was at the time regarded by the Jews as an unclean place, but it gradually grew into a major city of the Galilee region. It was an administrative base supporting the Roman system of rule, and afterward it also became a center of Jewish scholarship.

remark: 1. A town north of the Arnon River. It was rebuilt by the tribe of Gad and given to the tribe of Reuben, and then again came under Moab.
introduce: Dibon was an ancient town located between the Moabite plain east of the Jordan River and the region of Gilead, north of the Arnon River, and is identified with the area of present-day Dhiban in Jordan. According to the biblical record, it is mentioned as a strategic point in the settlement of the tribes of Israel and in the history of the kingdom of Moab.
biblecontents: When Israel struck Sihon king of Heshbon, even as far as Dibon was laid waste (Numbers 21:30). The descendants of Gad and the descendants of Reuben requested the region of Dibon, suited to raising livestock, as conquered territory (Numbers 32:3). Afterward the descendants of Gad built Dibon as a town (Numbers 32:34). In the time of Joshua it was a town on the edge of the Arnon valley and was included in the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:9, Joshua 13:17). The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah prophesied that Dibon would be judged and destroyed (Isaiah 15:2, Jeremiah 48:18, Jeremiah 48:22).
geography: It is located about 5 kilometers north of the Arnon River and adjoins the Madaba plateau. It is a plain region with fertile soil and abundant pasturage, and has geographical features favorable for grazing livestock and settlement.
history: Dibon is famous as the place where the Mesha Stele, known to have been built by Mesha king of Moab, was discovered. Various powers of the ancient Near East contended to take possession of this region, and before the settlement of Israel it was under the rule of Sihon king of the Amorites. Afterward, through the occupation by the tribes of Israel and the recapture by Moab, the town has a history in which its sovereignty changed repeatedly.

remark: 2. A town in Judah.
introduce: Dibon is a southern town of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Nehemiah 11 of the Old Testament, a settlement in the Negev of southern Judah distinct from the Dibon of Moab east of the Jordan.
biblecontents: Some of the descendants of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its villages, in Dibon and its villages, and in Jekabzeel and its villages (Nehemiah 11:25).
geography: It lies at the boundary between the southern end of the hill country of Judah and the Negev desert, and is identified with the same town as Dimonah (Dimonah) of Joshua 15:22. It is a dry plain area near Tel es-Seba, southeast of Beersheba.
history: It was a southern frontier settlement where residents of the tribe of Judah who returned to the land of Judah under the Persian Empire after the Babylonian exile resettled and rebuilt farming and herding.

introduce: Dibon-gad is one of the encampments where the Israelites stayed on their journey toward Canaan after the exodus. It is regarded as a place located near the Abarim mountains.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Iim and camped at Dibon-gad (Numbers 33:45). They left Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim (Numbers 33:46).
geography: Dibon-gad is identified as being located near Dhiban, south of the Madaba area of the present-day Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. This is a highland region north of the Arnon River and a strategic point connecting with the ancient Moabite plain.
history: Dibon-gad was territory of the ancient kingdom of Moab and in the Bible was also called Dibon. Afterward the tribes of Gad and Reuben of Israel occupied it and incorporated it into their own tribal territories. The Mesha inscription, recorded around the ninth century, preserves a record that Mesha, king of Dibon, ruled this region and carried out building projects.

introduce: Tibhath was one of the towns that David took from Hadadezer, king of Zobah, in the time of King David, a place name mentioned in 1 Chronicles of the Bible.
biblecontents: David took a great amount of bronze from Tibhath and Cun, towns of Hadadezer, and with it Solomon made the bronze basin, the pillars, and the bronze vessels (1 Chronicles 18:8).
geography: Tibhath is presumed to be a town located within the territory of the ancient Aramean kingdom of Zobah, and since 2 Samuel 8:8 refers to the same place as Betah, the linguistic relationship between the two place names is discussed in scholarship. Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but the possibility is raised that it was near the Beqaa Valley in the Syrian region or in the region east of the Anti-Lebanon mountains.
history: At the time of David's wars of conquest around the tenth century BC, the Aramean kingdom of Zobah was a great power that had extended its influence as far as the Euphrates River basin, and Tibhath appears to have been a major source of resources or a strategic point of this kingdom. After winning the battle with Hadadezer, David seized a large quantity of bronze here, and this was afterward used as building material within the kingdom of Israel.

introduce: Diblah is a place name mentioned in Ezekiel 6:14 as one of the boundaries of the region to which God's judgment would reach. It is generally presumed to be the same region as Diblathaim, located near the plain of Moab, or is regarded as a place name connected with it.
biblecontents: In judging Israel's idolatry, God proclaimed that he would lay waste their dwellings, saying that he would strike all their dwellings from the wilderness to Diblah (Ezekiel 6:14).
geography: Scholars disagree over the exact location of Diblah. From the context it is interpreted as a place name symbolizing a southern or eastern boundary, in contrast to the entrance of Hamath, the northern boundary of the territory of Israel mentioned by Ezekiel. If it is the same place as Diblathaim in the region of Moab, it lies on the highland east of the Dead Sea, east of the Jordan River.

introduce: Dizahab is one of the place names mentioned at the beginning of Deuteronomy to specify the place where Moses proclaimed the law to the people of Israel. It is presumed to be a location within the Arabah wilderness region east of the Jordan River, but scholars disagree over its specific present-day place-name location.
biblecontents: These are the words that Moses proclaimed to the assembly of Israel in the Arabah wilderness opposite the forest beyond the Jordan, that is, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab (Deuteronomy 1:1)
geography: From the geographical context, Dizahab is interpreted as located in the northern or northeastern part of the Arabah wilderness, east of the Jordan River. However, this is a place name that cannot be clearly identified in the major road networks of the ancient Near East or in general lists of place names. Some scholars hold that it should not be confused with Dahab near the Red Sea, and the exact coordinates the biblical text points to have not been clearly determined archaeologically at present.

introduce: Tishbe is a place name that appears in the Old Testament, known as the hometown of the prophet Elijah. It is presumed to have been located in the region of Gilead, and within the biblical record it appears mainly in the expression "the Tishbite," a designation applied to Elijah.
biblecontents: Elijah the Tishbite foretold a drought to King Ahab (1 Kings 17:1). The LORD told Elijah the Tishbite to go and meet Ahab over the matter of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21:17). Seeing that Ahab humbled himself, God said that he would not bring the disaster upon him in Elijah's time (1 Kings 21:28). The angel of the LORD told Elijah the Tishbite to intercept the messengers who were going to inquire about the illness of King Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:3). The messengers of King Ahaziah described Elijah's appearance as a man wearing a garment of hair with a leather belt around his waist (2 Kings 1:8). When God prophesied that Jehu would judge Jezebel, he referred to the word spoken through Elijah the Tishbite (2 Kings 9:36).
geography: The exact location of Tishbe has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but from the biblical context it is regarded as having been located within the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River. There is a view in scholarship that presumes it to be Tell el-Maqatam in present-day northern Jordan, or its vicinity.

introduce: Tizite is presumed to be a place name designating the origin of Jediael the Mahavite, a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles 11, or the family to which he belonged.
biblecontents: In the list of David's mighty men, it is specified as his background of origin when mentioning Jediael the Mahavite (1 Chronicles 11:45).

introduce: Dinhabah is a place name that appears in the biblical record, a town ruled by Bela, king of Edom.
biblecontents: Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah (Genesis 36:32). Bela son of Beor became king, and the name of his city was Dinhabah (1 Chronicles 1:43).
geography: It is presumed to be located within the region of Edom, but its exact archaeological location has not been specified. Scholars presume that it shared the topographical features of the area east of Moab or near the Arabah valley.
history: It is a place connected with Bela, the first king in the genealogy of the kings who ruled the land of Edom before there were kings of Israel. It has value as a historical source, showing one stage in the process by which a political organization in the form of a tribal confederation in the ancient Near East moved to a monarchical system.

introduce: Dilan is a town of the tribe of Judah recorded in Joshua 15 of the Old Testament, a place name presumed in biblical geography to have been located in the hill country of Judah or in the Shephelah region.
biblecontents: Dilan is mentioned as one of the list of towns that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained when Joshua distributed the land of Canaan to the tribes of Israel (Joshua 15:38).
geography: According to archaeological and geographical literature, the exact location of Dilan has not been definitively specified to date, but from the fact that it is listed together with towns belonging to the Shephelah region within the territory of the tribe of Judah, it is conjectured to have been located in the plains or hills nearby.

introduce: Timnath-serah was a town in the hill country of Ephraim that Joshua received as an inheritance from the people of Israel, a place also called Timnath-heres.
biblecontents: As the LORD commanded, Joshua received the town of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, which he had asked for, and he built the town and lived there (Joshua 19:50). After he died, the Israelites buried him in Timnath-serah, his own inheritance, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash (Joshua 24:30).
geography: It is located in the hill country of Ephraim and, in present-day terms, is presumed to be Khirbet Tibneh, within the Palestinian autonomous territories, or its vicinity. Topographically it belongs to the highlands and adjoins Mount Gaash.
history: It is the town that Joshua received as his own share in the course of distributing land to the tribes of Israel after the wars of conquest. Archaeologically, it is one of the areas where traces of habitation from the Late Bronze Age through the early Iron Age have been found.

introduce: Timnath-heres is a town in the hill country of Ephraim, known as the place that Joshua received as an inheritance after the wars of the conquest of Canaan and where he lived and was buried after his death.
biblecontents: The people of Israel buried Joshua in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash (Judges 2:9). Joshua asked for Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, built the town, and lived there; Timnath-heres is a name that refers to this same place (Joshua 19:50).
geography: It is located in the hill country of Ephraim; its present-day location has not been exactly identified, but it is generally presumed to be the area of Tell Tibneh. It lies north of Mount Gaash (Judges 2:9).
history: It carries historical significance as to the burial customs of Israel's leaders after Joshua's death and as a settlement. Within the Bible it is written as the same place as Timnath-serah, but the name Timnath-heres carries the meaning "portion of the sun" or "city of the sun."

remark: 1. A town west of the Euphrates River.
introduce: Tiphsah is a place name mentioned when describing the boundary of King Solomon's domain, denoting the western end point that defines the broad region west of the Euphrates River.
biblecontents: Solomon ruled over all the kings on this side of the Euphrates, and because he ruled everything on this side of the river from Tiphsah to Gaza, he had peace on all sides around him (1 Kings 4:24).
geography: Tiphsah is presumed to be a city located on the banks of the Euphrates River, a major river of the ancient Near East, and is identified with the present-day place name Tifsa or Tufsa. As an important strategic point and commercial base located along the Euphrates, it serves as a geographical coordinate symbolizing the northernmost or northeastern boundary of the territory of Solomon's kingdom.
history: Historical and archaeological scholarship regards this place as the same as Tipsak on the Euphrates, mentioned in the inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III and elsewhere. This city, which also appears in Aramaic-language literature and Assyrian records, was a strategic base linking Mesopotamia and Syria and a core passage of the ancient trade routes.

remark: 2. A town in Judah toward the Jordan River.
introduce: Tiphsah is a town of the northern kingdom of Israel recorded in 2 Kings 15, a town in the hill country of Samaria near Tirzah, to be distinguished from the Tiphsah on the bank of the Euphrates.
biblecontents: At that time Menahem came from Tirzah and struck Tiphsah and all who were in it and its territory, because they had not opened the gates; therefore he struck it, and ripped open all the pregnant women in it (2 Kings 15:16).
geography: It was located on a mountain valley road between Tirzah (northern Tell el-Far'ah), the former capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and the town of Samaria. It is identified with the ruins of present-day Khirbet Tafsah.
history: It is the historical site of a civil conflict in which, in the mid-eighth century BC, at the end of the northern kingdom of Israel, the town was utterly destroyed for resisting the military oppression of Menahem, who had killed Shallum and usurped the throne.

introduce: Racal is one of the towns located in the Negev region of southern Judah, a place mentioned when David distributed the spoils after pursuing the Amalekite raiders.
biblecontents: After David recovered the plunder taken by the Amalekites at Ziklag, when he sent the spoils to the elders of Judah and to his friends, he also delivered it to the people who lived in Racal (1 Samuel 30:29).
geography: It is presumed to be one of the towns belonging to the Negev desert region in the south of the territory of the tribe of Judah. Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it was distributed, together with neighboring towns such as Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa, in the southern border area of Judah (1 Samuel 30:26-29).

introduce: Lachish was a strategic point in southern ancient Canaan, a town located in the area of Tell ed-Duweir. It appears as one of the major towns that formed the southern coalition in the period of Joshua's wars of conquest of Canaan, and afterward it played an important role in the defensive line of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, sent word to Japhia, king of Lachish, asking him to attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:3). Thereupon five Amorite kings, including the king of Lachish, joined together and attacked Gibeon (Joshua 10:5). When the Israelite army led by Joshua won the victory, the five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah, but they were found and brought out (Joshua 10:23). Afterward Joshua advanced against Lachish, and in two days captured the town and destroyed everyone in it with the edge of the sword (Joshua 10:31, 32). Horam, king of Gezer, came up to help Lachish, but Joshua struck him and his people until no one was left (Joshua 10:33). Then Israel captured Lachish and utterly destroyed the town (Joshua 10:34, 35). The king of Lachish is recorded as one of the thirty-one kings of Canaan whom Joshua conquered (Joshua 12:11). Lachish is mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:39).
geography: Lachish is located on the plain of the Shephelah and has strategic value in controlling the passage linking the coastal plain with the hill country of Judah. It is identified with present-day Tell ed-Duweir, and has a structure suited to building strong walls by making use of natural topographical conditions.
history: From the Bronze Age it existed as a major city-state of Canaan, and in the New Kingdom period of Egypt it was under Egyptian influence. Afterward, when it was incorporated into the kingdom of Judah in the Iron Age, it was fortified as a key defensive stronghold blocking invasion toward Jerusalem. It drew attention as an important military stronghold also at the time of the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions, and through archaeological excavation the walls and gate system of that time have been confirmed.

introduce: Naioth in Ramah is a place name that appears in 1 Samuel of the Old Testament, the place in Ramah where Samuel lived, to which David fled to escape King Saul's pursuit. This place appears to have functioned as a base, or a lodging, where a company of prophets lived or was active.
biblecontents: Saul went to Naioth in Ramah to seize David, but there the Spirit of God came upon him and he prophesied (1 Samuel 19:22), and the messengers Saul sent likewise showed the same phenomenon of prophesying there (1 Samuel 19:23). David left Naioth in Ramah to escape Saul's pursuit and went to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:1).
geography: Naioth in Ramah is presumed to be a particular district within Ramah, in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but Ramah is sometimes identified with present-day er-Ram, located about 8 km north of Jerusalem. Since the name Naioth appears to derive from a Hebrew word meaning "dwelling" or "lodging," it is interpreted as designating an independent communal residential quarter within Ramah.

introduce: Ramathaim-zophim is a town located in the hill country of Ephraim, the hometown of Samuel and the center where he lived and worked.
biblecontents: In Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim there lived a man named Elkanah, an Ephraimite, who was a son of Jeroham and the father of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1). Samuel went on a circuit throughout his life and judged Israel, and he returned to Ramah, where his house was, and judged Israel there and built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 7:15-17). Even after Samuel died, he was buried in Ramah, where he had lived (1 Samuel 25:1).
geography: It is located within the hill country of Ephraim, and there are various theories about its present-day location, but the exact point has not been determined archaeologically. It is generally presumed to have been located on the highlands northwest of Bethel or north of Jerusalem.

introduce: Lahmas is one of the towns located within the territory distributed to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place that appears in the list of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah recorded in Joshua 15.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:40).
geography: Lahmas is included in the list of towns located in the Shephelah, the lowlands of Judah (Joshua 15:40). In modern archaeological surveys there are various theories about specifying the exact location of this area, and it is presumed to be geographically closely related to nearby Rehib, Eglon, and the like.

introduce: Ramath-lehi is a place name that appears in Judges 15:17, a name given to designate the place after the incident in which Samson defeated the Philistines using the jawbone of a donkey. The place name carries the meaning in Hebrew of "height of the jawbone" or "hill of the jawbone."
biblecontents: Samson threw the jawbone of the donkey out of his hand, and called that place Ramath-lehi (Judges 15:17).
geography: The exact location of Ramath-lehi has not been clearly specified archaeologically to date. It is presumed to be somewhere in the Shephelah, the lowlands of Judea, or in the surrounding area where the place name Lehi is mentioned, and it is regarded as the same place as the later place name Lehi.
history: At that time Israel was under the rule of the Philistines, and the record of Judges 15 is set against the background of the military tension between the Philistines and Samson. This place name was formed according to the custom of naming a place after an event, in order to commemorate Samson's victory.

introduce: Ramath-mizpeh is a place name located in the region east of the Jordan, a region mentioned in connection with the distribution of the tribes at the time of Joshua's conquest.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the regions in the area from Mahanaim to the border of Debir and from Mizpeh to Betonim, and is recorded as a region included within the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13:26).
geography: It is located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River and is presumed to be near the highlands of present-day northern Jordan. As the meaning of the place name "height" suggests, it was most likely situated on a ridge or on high ground easy to keep watch from.
history: After the people of Israel conquered the land of Canaan, it was set as one of the points on the northern boundary of the territory allotted to the tribe of Gad. It is one of the historical indicators showing the political boundaries of the division of the territories east of the Jordan in the Old Testament period.

remark: 1. A town of the Levites in Gilead, the same place as Ramoth-gilead and Ramath-mizpeh.
introduce: Ramoth is a town located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan; it was a strategic point where territorial disputes between Israel and the kingdom of Aram were frequent in the Old Testament period, and was one of the cities of refuge.
biblecontents: It was a town of the tribe of Reuben, one of the towns of the plain occupied by the tribe of Reuben, and was designated a city of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43). It is recorded as one of the towns given to the Levites who were descendants of Merari (1 Chronicles 6:80). It was the place that Joram king of Israel was guarding with his army in order to fight Hazael king of Aram, and it was also the base from which Jehu, after being anointed king of Israel, launched his rebellion (2 Kings 9:14).
geography: It is located on the Gilead highlands east of the Jordan River, presumed to be Tell ed-Duwe (Tell ed-Duwe) or Tell al-Husn in the area of present-day Jordan. Adjacent to the point where it intersects the King's Highway, it served as a key location for traffic and military movement.
history: By its geopolitical position, it was a vital battleground where the kingdom of Israel and the Aramean kingdom of Damascus contended for control of the area east of the Jordan. In particular it was a place where wars with Aram were frequent in the reigns of Ahab and Joram of the northern kingdom of Israel, and its strategic value was so high that military possession of it meant supremacy over the whole region.

remark: 2. A Levite town in Issachar.
introduce: Ramoth is a Levite town within the territory of the tribe of Issachar, recorded in 1 Chronicles 6 of the Old Testament, a place of residence of Levites in southern Galilee, to be distinguished from Ramoth-gilead east of the Jordan.
biblecontents: Out of the territory of the tribe of Issachar, Daberath with its pasturelands, Ramoth with its pasturelands, and Anem with its pasturelands were given to the Gershonites (1 Chronicles 6:73).
geography: It was located in the hill country on the northeast of the Jezreel Valley, which the tribe of Issachar occupied. It is presumed to be the same town as Remeth (Remeth) of Joshua 19:21 and Jarmuth (Jarmuth) of Joshua 21:29.
history: In the Iron Age it was a center around Jezreel, the farming plain of northern Israel, where Levites of the Gershonite line were in charge of farming and religious administration.

remark: 3. A town of Simeon in the Negev.
introduce: Ramoth is a region mentioned in the Old Testament as one of the places where David divided the spoils after the battle with the Amalekites. It is classified as one of the towns located in the Negev region, and is understood to have been under the influence of the tribe of Judah in the south.
biblecontents: When David sent the spoils he had taken from the Amalekites to the elders of Judah and to his friends, he also delivered a portion of the spoils to those in Ramoth (1 Samuel 30:27).
geography: Ramoth is presumed to be a town located in the Negev hill country or wilderness region south of Judah. Its exact archaeological location is disputed, but it is generally regarded as falling within the geographical range southeast of Beersheba or near Arad.

introduce: Rabbah was one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient times, included, through the record of the book of Joshua, in the list of the region distributed to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Kiriath-baal, that is, Kiriath-jearim, and Rabbah, these two cities with their villages, are mentioned as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:60).
geography: Rabbah belonged to the district of the hill country of Judah, and from the fact that it is listed together with nearby Kiriath-jearim, it is presumed to have been located on the central highlands of the hill country of Judah. Scholars disagree over its exact location, but on the basis of archaeological indicators it is regarded as somewhere in the mountainous region west of present-day Jerusalem.

introduce: Lasha is a place name related to the boundary of the descendants of Canaan recorded in Genesis 10, a place that appears in the course of explaining the geographical limits of ancient Canaan.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the border of Canaan ran from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha (Genesis 10:19).
geography: There is no agreed view among scholars on the exact location of Lasha. However, from the context of Genesis 10:19 it is presumed to be a boundary point in the eastern or southeastern region of Canaan. Some scholars raise the possibility that this area is Callirrhoe near the Dead Sea or a particular point in the east of Jordan, but there is a lack of archaeologically confirmed information.
history: Because Lasha is not a place name clearly identifiable in ancient literature outside the Bible, there are limits to establishing its historical identity. Biblical critics discuss the possibility that this place name was inserted in a later written edition, or that it was an idiomatic expression reflecting the geographical knowledge of Canaan at that time.

introduce: Lasea is a place name that appears in the Acts of the New Testament, a port city on the Mediterranean coast at that time. It is known as the place where the ship carrying the apostle Paul on his way to Rome stayed to avoid the wind.
biblecontents: The ship carrying the apostle Paul sailed with difficulty along the coast and came to a place called Fair Havens, which was near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:8).
geography: Lasea is an ancient port city located on the southeastern coast of the island of Crete. Geographically it lies about 8 km east of Fair Havens, and according to current archaeological surveys it is identified with the ruins of Lasea on the southern coast of Crete.

introduce: Rameses was a region located in the eastern Nile Delta of ancient Egypt, known as the place where Joseph settled his family and as the town where the Hebrews were later conscripted for forced labor.
biblecontents: At Pharaoh's command Joseph gave his father and brothers a possession in the best of the land of Egypt, the land of Rameses, and settled them there (Genesis 47:11). Afterward the people of Israel were conscripted in this region for the labor of building the store cities of Pithom and Rameses (Exodus 1:11).
geography: Rameses is located near Wadi Tumilat at the eastern end of the Nile Delta and is identified with the area of present-day Tell el-Daba. This region had fertile soil and a good supply of water, and had the topographical conditions suited to raising livestock and farming.
history: Rameses is closely connected with Pi-Ramesses, which Ramesses II, the pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt, made his capital. According to archaeological surveys, this area includes the Avaris area of the Hyksos period, and as large-scale building projects were carried out in the New Kingdom period, it flourished as a strategic point and economic center for the defense of northeastern Egypt.

introduce: Rameses was a town located in the eastern Nile Delta region of ancient Egypt, recorded in Exodus as one of the store cities that the Israelites built in Egypt through forced labor and as the starting point of the exodus.
biblecontents: The people of Israel built the store cities of Pithom and Rameses for Pharaoh (Exodus 1:11). When the Israelites left Rameses and came to Succoth, there were about six hundred thousand men on foot (Exodus 12:37). The Israelites left Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, that is, the day after the Passover (Numbers 33:3). The Israelites left Rameses and camped at Succoth (Numbers 33:5).
geography: Rameses is presumed to be located within the land of Goshen, the fertile region near Wadi Tumilat in the eastern Nile Delta. It is geographically connected with the area of present-day Tell el-Daba or Qantir, and served as a strategic point in northern ancient Egypt.
history: Rameses is known as a city built, or greatly expanded, by Ramesses II, pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty. As the capital of Egypt, this city was a military base for advancing into the region of Asia, and was one of the most prosperous royal cities in the history of Egypt.

introduce: Laodicea was a major city in the region of Phrygia in ancient Asia Minor, located in the Lycus Valley and serving as a crossroads of commerce, finance, and traffic. In the Bible it is mentioned as a region where an early Christian community formed and as the place where one of the seven churches of Revelation was located.
biblecontents: Paul mentioned that he was struggling for those in Laodicea (Colossians 2:1), and recorded that Epaphras was working hard for those in Laodicea (Colossians 4:13). He also sent greetings to the believers in Laodicea and urged that the letter sent to them be read together (Colossians 4:15, 4:16). In Revelation the church of this city is named as one of the seven churches in Asia (Revelation 1:11), and a specific message addressed to that church is delivered (Revelation 3:14).
geography: Laodicea is located near Denizli in present-day Türkiye, on the fertile plain of the upper Lycus River. Situated at the center of the triangle linking Hierapolis and Colossae, it had the geographical characteristic of receiving the hot spring water of Hierapolis and the cold water of Colossae, but because it was short of its own water sources it had to bring in water through aqueducts.
history: Around the third century BC it was founded by Antiochus II of the Seleucid dynasty, who named it after his wife Laodice. By the time of the Roman Empire it had become an economic center that accumulated great wealth from banking, the wool textile industry, and the manufacture of eye salve. A great earthquake around AD 60 destroyed the city, but it is a city that possessed such strong economic power that it rebuilt itself by its own means, even declining Roman financial aid.

introduce: Laishah is a place name mentioned in Isaiah 10:30, denoting a settlement near Jerusalem, to the north, located on the route of the Assyrian invasion.
biblecontents: The prophet Isaiah, describing the situation of the Assyrian army advancing toward Jerusalem, said, "Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth!" (Isaiah 10:30).
geography: Its present exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is presumed to be a point close to Anathoth, which lies north of Jerusalem. It is understood to be one of the villages on the approach road to Jerusalem along the route of the Assyrian invasion.
history: It appears to be one of the place names cited at the time of the invasion of Judah by the Assyrian king Sargon II or Sennacherib around the eighth century BC. It is interpreted as a place name reflecting the military pressure from the north that threatened the kingdom of Judah at that time and the situation of fear that resulted.

remark: A town of the Sidonian people at the northern end of Palestine.
introduce: Laish is a place name that appears in the book of Judges of the Old Testament, originally a peaceful and quiet town under the influence of the Sidonians. Afterward the tribe of Dan conquered it and renamed it Dan.
biblecontents: The people of Laish lived in peace, far from the Sidonians and without dealings with others (Judges 18:7). The spies confirmed that the land of Laish was very fertile and broad (Judges 18:14). The soldiers of the tribe of Dan went to Laish with the idols they had taken from Micah, struck the peaceful people with the edge of the sword, and burned the town (Judges 18:27). The tribe of Dan rebuilt the town and called it Dan after the name of their ancestor, but its former name was Laish (Judges 18:29).
geography: Laish is a region located at the northern end of the Huleh Basin, below the Lebanon mountain range, in the ancient Near East, and is identified with the area of present-day Tel el-Qadi. With abundant water resources and fertile soil, it has the topographical advantage of being suited to farming.
history: Laish was geographically within the sphere of influence of Sidon but was cut off from a centralized system of defense. The tribe of Dan, which had not obtained an inheritance and was looking for a place to migrate to, targeted Laish, which was poorly fortified and could hardly receive help from its neighbors, and carried out a war of conquest. This is one of the cases of the capture of a town that occurred in the course of the territorial expansion of the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Rakkath is one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Naphtali that appear in Joshua 19:35, a place presumed to have been located in the southwestern area of the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth (Joshua 19:35)
geography: It is classified as a town located on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, and is analyzed as having been situated on a plain adjacent to nearby Chinnereth.

introduce: Rakkon is one of the towns on the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Dan that appears in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament, a place name presumed to have been located near Joppa.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a region located opposite Joppa among the boundaries of the inheritance that the tribe of Dan obtained by lot (Joshua 19:46).
geography: Rakkon appears to have been located near Joppa, a plain region on the Mediterranean coast, and geographers presume that it is connected with the southern part of present-day Tel Aviv in Israel or the surrounding coastal plain area.

introduce: Lakkum is a place name that appears in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament, a location at a boundary point of the inheritance distributed by lot to the tribe of Naphtali.
biblecontents: Its boundary started from Heleph and the great tree of Zaanannim, passed Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, and reached Lakkum, and its end was the Jordan River (Joshua 19:33).
geography: Lakkum is presumed to be located in the northwestern or northern part of the Sea of Galilee, and is identified as a point connecting with the Jordan River along the eastern boundary of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but combined with the surrounding topography it was most likely situated in a valley or plain area flowing into the Jordan River.

introduce: Rabbah was the capital of the ancient Ammonites and a town that was the political and military center of the Ammonite kingdom in the biblical period. It is identified with the same area as Amman, the capital of the present-day Kingdom of Jordan.
biblecontents: The bed of Og, king of Bashan, was in Rabbah of the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 3:11). Rabbah was included in the boundary of the region occupied by the tribe of Gad among the tribes of Israel (Joshua 13:25). In the time of David the Israelite army led by Joab destroyed the land of the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah (2 Samuel 11:1). David attacked Rabbah and captured the royal city (2 Samuel 12:26), and Joab took the city of waters and brought Rabbah completely to its fall (2 Samuel 12:27, 29). When David attacked Rabbah, Joab led the army, struck Rabbah, and destroyed it (1 Chronicles 20:1). At the time of Absalom's rebellion, Shobi, from Rabbah of the Ammonites, supplied David's company with provisions and supplies (2 Samuel 17:27). The prophet Jeremiah prophesied that Rabbah of the Ammonites would become a ruin because of war (Jeremiah 49:2, 49:3).
geography: Rabbah is located on the Jordanian highlands and is flanked by a fertile valley through which a tributary of the Jabbok River flows. Topographically it was surrounded by several hills and was a strategic point favorable for defense, and, lying adjacent to the King's Highway, it was well placed to control the east-west trade routes.
history: From the Bronze Age it flourished as the dwelling place and capital of the Ammonites, and in the Iron Age it experienced continual territorial disputes with the kingdom of Israel. In the reign of David it became a vassal state of Israel, but afterward it underwent historical changes under the rule of the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian empires. In the Hellenistic period it was renamed Philadelphia after Ptolemy II Philadelphus.

introduce: Rabbith is a place mentioned as one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar at the time of the distribution of the land of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the list of towns distributed to the descendants of Issachar in Joshua 19 (Joshua 19:20).
geography: Rabbith is presumed to have been located near the Jezreel Valley, the plain region that the tribe of Issachar occupied in northern Israel, but its specific modern place name has not been determined in scholarship.

introduce: It is one of the towns ruled by the kings of Canaan who were conquered by Joshua at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: In the list of Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua, the king of Lasharon is mentioned together with the king of Aphek (Joshua 12:18).
geography: Scholars disagree over its exact location, but it is generally presumed to be a town near the Plain of Sharon or in the northern region of Canaan, and the exact archaeological site has not been specified.

introduce: Rhegium is the Latin-style rendering of Rhegium, a port city in southern Italy through which Paul passed on his way to being taken to Rome, mentioned in Acts 28:13.
biblecontents: Paul and his companions stayed at Syracuse, then set sail and arrived at Rhegium, and after spending one day there, they caught a south wind and the next day arrived at Puteoli (Acts 28:13).
geography: Rhegium corresponds to the area of present-day Reggio di Calabria in Italy and is a port city on the eastern shore of the Strait of Messina, facing Messina on the island of Sicily.
history: Founded as the ancient Greek colony of Rhegium, in the Roman period it served as the main gateway from the southernmost tip of the Italian peninsula over to Sicily and as a strategic maritime point.

introduce: Remeth is a place name of ancient Canaan that appears in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament; it was one of the inheritances allotted to the tribe of Issachar among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Remeth is mentioned among the towns of the inheritance that the descendants of the tribe of Issachar obtained by lot (Joshua 19:21).
geography: The exact location of Remeth is disputed in modern archaeology, but it is generally presumed to have been in the eastern part of the Jezreel Valley or in southern Galilee. Some scholars identify this area with Tel Yerma, but no definitive site has been established.

introduce: Lebanon is an ancient mountain range and forested region stretching long from north to south in the north of Palestine; in the Bible it is frequently mentioned as the northern boundary of the promised land and as a representative geographical marker known for its cedars and splendid scenery.
biblecontents: Moses instructed the people of Israel to go on to the hill country of the Amorites, the plain, the Negev, the seacoast, the land of Canaan, Lebanon, and as far as the great river, the Euphrates (Deuteronomy 1:7). Moses pleaded to be allowed to see the good land beyond the Jordan, the good hill country, and Lebanon (Deuteronomy 3:25). It was promised that the territory of Israel would extend from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River to the western sea (Deuteronomy 11:24). The LORD declared to Joshua that his territory would extend from the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the Euphrates River and to the Great Sea (Joshua 1:4). When they heard of Joshua's victories, the kings of the Canaanite peoples west of the Jordan, in the hill country, in the plain, and along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, formed an alliance (Joshua 9:1). Joshua struck down and conquered all the kings from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon (Joshua 11:17). A list was recorded of the kings of the land west of the Jordan whom he struck down and destroyed, from Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir (Joshua 12:7).
