The land of the Gebalites and all Lebanon toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath, were named as land not yet conquered (Joshua 13:5). It was announced that all the Sidonians who lived in the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim would be driven out before the people of Israel (Joshua 13:6). Among the nations left to test Israel were the Hivites who lived in the Lebanon mountains from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath (Judges 3:3).
geography: Lebanon consists of the Lebanon Mountains, which extend about 170 km along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean; the Anti-Lebanon Mountains to their east; and the fertile Beqaa Valley (the biblical valley of Lebanon) lying between the two ranges. The highest peak is Qurnat as Sawda, at 3,088 m above sea level; because its high summits are covered with perpetual snow and appear white, the name is derived from laban, which means "white" in the Semitic languages. Owing to abundant snowfall and rainfall, it serves as the source of major rivers such as the Litani and the Orontes.
history: In the Bronze and Iron Ages, Lebanon was the hinterland of the major Phoenician city-states that led Mediterranean trade, such as Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos (Gebal). Neighboring powers of the ancient Near East, such as Egypt, Mesopotamia (Assyria and Babylon), and Israel, imported the cedar and juniper timber of Lebanon, a high-quality building material, or collected it as tribute for the construction of large palaces and temples. It also had strategic importance as a military and commercial crossroads linking the Mediterranean sea-trade routes with the inland Syria-Mesopotamia routes, and as the northern limit of Canaan.

remark: 1. A town between Nineveh and Calah.
introduce: Resen is a city of the ancient Near East, a place name mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis as one of the towns built by Nimrod.
biblecontents: Resen is located between Nineveh and Calah and is recorded as a great city built by Nimrod (Genesis 10:12).
geography: Resen is presumed to have been located in the Tigris River valley, in the heartland of ancient Assyria, and is regarded as a base city lying on the geographical line between Nineveh and Calah.
history: Some scholars identify Resen with Resheph, one of the major cities of Assyria, or with a place of similar pronunciation, but opinions differ as to a location that has been clearly confirmed archaeologically. Some in academia raise the possibility that this town was a major settlement within the core capital region of Assyria.

remark: 2. A town west of Mount Hermon between Naphtali and Manasseh, called Laish or Dan.
introduce: Leshem is a place name in the Old Testament that denotes the name of a city before it was conquered by the descendants of Dan. Afterward, the descendants of Dan captured this city and renamed it Dan, after the name of their ancestor Dan.
biblecontents: The descendants of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, took possession of it, and lived in it; and they called Leshem Dan, after the name of their ancestor Dan (Joshua 19:47).
geography: Leshem was originally located in the northern part of Galilee, near the Huleh Basin, and is identified with the area of Tel el-Qadi, or Tel Dan. It is a strategic location with fertile soil and a water source that rises from Mount Hermon.
history: Historically, Leshem was also called by the name Laish, and it was a peaceful city under the sphere of influence of the Sidonians. When the tribe of Dan could not secure a dwelling place in the region allotted to it as an inheritance, it moved north, conquered this area, and made it a self-governing city; this is also treated in detail in Judges 18.

introduce: Rogelim is a place name in the Bible, located in the region of Gilead and known as the hometown of Barzillai.
biblecontents: The only record in which it appears says that Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim to help King David cross the Jordan (2 Samuel 19:31).
geography: It is presumed to be a region in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, but the location of a specific archaeological site has not yet been clearly determined.
history: It forms the setting of the place where Barzillai of Rogelim supported David and his company with provisions and acted as a political helper when David fled to the east of the Jordan to escape the rebellion of his son Absalom.

introduce: Rogelim is a town located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan, known as the residence of Barzillai, a helper of King David during the time of his flight.
biblecontents: When David came to Mahanaim, Barzillai of Rogelim brought and supplied beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, parched seeds, honey, curds, sheep, and cheese for him and the people who were with him (2 Samuel 17:27). Also, when David returned to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion had been put down, Barzillai came down from Rogelim and escorted him as far as the Jordan (2 Samuel 19:31).
geography: Rogelim is presumed to have been located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, but its exact location has not yet been determined archaeologically. It is regarded, however, as an area adjacent to Mahanaim, and it seems to have had terrain that made it easy to travel to the Jordan Valley.
history: Barzillai was a very wealthy man of Rogelim and a local leading figure loyal to David's kingship. When David fled to Mahanaim to escape Absalom's rebellion, Rogelim served as a strategic and economic rear base that supplied provisions to David's army.

introduce: Lotan is a name mentioned in the context of listing the chiefs of the Horite clans who lived in the land of Edom. Within the biblical text, it is interpreted as referring either to one of the heads of the Horite clans, who were inhabitants of the land of Seir, or to the territory he ruled.
biblecontents: These are the chiefs of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah (Genesis 36:29).
geography: It was located in the hill country of Seir in the region of Edom, and is presumed to be associated with the mountainous region of Seir where the Horites historically lived.

introduce: Lo-debar is a place name located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan in ancient Israel, known as the place where Machir son of Ammiel, a political figure of the era of David's monarchy, lived.
biblecontents: When David came to Mahanaim fleeing Absalom's rebellion, Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah of the Ammonites, together with Machir and Barzillai, brought beds, basins, earthenware, and other things and provided for David and his company; on this occasion it is mentioned that Machir was from Lo-debar (2 Samuel 17:27). There is also a record that Mephibosheth, the grandson of Saul and son of Jonathan, was staying in this place (2 Samuel 9:4-5).
geography: It is presumed to have been located on the Gilead plateau east of the Jordan River; its exact present-day location is disputed in archaeology, but it is generally identified with the northeastern region near Mahanaim.
history: Lo-debar was a strategic place of refuge where Mephibosheth, a survivor of the house of Saul, hid until David took him under his protection. Afterward, during David's reign, Machir, a leading man of the Gilead region, lived there, and it functioned as a base supporting the royal household with relief supplies.

introduce: Rhodes is an island located in the southeastern Aegean Sea, and also the name of the main city on that island. It functioned as a strategic crossroads on the ancient Mediterranean sea routes.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a place that the apostle Paul passed by ship on his journey back to Jerusalem after finishing his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1).
geography: Rhodes is an island located a short distance from the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. As a hub of ancient maritime trade, it had the geographical characteristic that ships sailing the Mediterranean, whether traveling from east to west or the reverse, had to pass through it or anchor there.
history: Rhodes flourished in the Hellenistic period as a center of commerce and naval power. It is especially famous for the Colossus of Rhodes, a huge bronze statue, and the Rhodians of that time possessed advanced seafaring skills and a legal system. In the Roman period, it maintained its status as an allied state with self-government and as a center of learning and the arts.

introduce: Lo-debar is a town located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and appears in 2 Samuel in the Old Testament as the place where Mephibosheth son of Jonathan lived in seclusion.
biblecontents: King David asked where Mephibosheth son of Jonathan was, and found out that he was in the house of Machir son of Ammiel (2 Samuel 9:4). Thereupon David sent and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar (2 Samuel 9:5).
geography: Lo-debar is presumed to have been located on the Gilead plateau east of the Jordan River; as to its exact location, there are views that place it near Debir or Mahanaim close to the Jordan Valley, but there is no archaeologically confirmed site.

introduce: Rome is a city located in central Italy; in New Testament times it was the capital of the Roman Empire, which ruled the Mediterranean world, and the center of its politics, administration, and culture. In the Bible, Rome is portrayed as a symbol of imperial authority and as the key destination to which the Christian gospel was to be carried.
biblecontents: When Jesus performed miracles, the Jewish leaders feared that the Romans would come and take away their land and nation (John 11:48). The charge against Jesus was written on the notice above the cross in Hebrew, Latin (the Roman language), and Greek (John 19:20). Among the crowd gathered in Jerusalem at Pentecost were visitors from Rome (Acts 2:10). Philippi was a Roman colony, a city that followed Roman customs (Acts 16:12). Those who accused Paul and Silas in Philippi claimed that they were proclaiming customs that they, being Romans, could neither accept nor practice (Acts 16:21). Paul pointed out that, although he was a Roman citizen, he had been beaten and thrown into prison without a trial (Acts 16:37). The magistrates were afraid when they heard that Paul and his companions were Roman citizens (Acts 16:38). Paul met Priscilla and Aquila because Emperor Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). In the Spirit, Paul made a plan: after passing through Jerusalem, he must also see Rome (Acts 19:21). Paul protested to the centurion about the situation in which he was being bound although he was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25).
geography: Rome is a city located on the lower course of the Tiber River in the west of the Italian peninsula. Beginning as a city-state formed around seven hills, it served as the center of the vast logistics and communications system of an empire centered on the Mediterranean. With its well-developed road system, it was a transportation hub connected to every part of the empire.
history: Rome, which began as a city-state around the 8th century BC, passed through the period of the Republic and entered the imperial age after Emperor Augustus took the throne in 27 BC. In the New Testament period, Rome maintained relatively stable rule and legal order throughout the empire through the Pax Romana. Governors and officials were dispatched to govern each province, and those who held Roman citizenship were granted various privileges, including judicial protection. This infrastructure and legal system of the empire became the background against which the missionary work of the apostle Paul spread throughout the empire.

introduce: Rosh is a place name or the name of a people that appears in the Book of Ezekiel in the Old Testament, mentioned together with Gog, the ruler of Magog. In ancient Near Eastern scholarship, there is a conflict between attempts to interpret it as the proper name of a particular region or tribe and the view that regards it as a common noun.
biblecontents: Ezekiel declares that God will set himself against Gog of the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, and will bring him out (Ezekiel 38:2). Ezekiel also emphasizes again that God will be against Gog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal (Ezekiel 38:3). Finally, the message of judgment is repeated concerning Gog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal (Ezekiel 39:1).
geography: The Hebrew word rosh is generally also interpreted as pointing in a northern direction, but there is insufficient evidence to establish a specific geographical location. Some scholars regard it as the name of a tribe of the ancient northern region, and the Septuagint translates it as a common noun rather than a proper name, so in many cases it does not define Rosh as a separate place.
history: Historically, there is a view that associates it with the Rashu, a northern people of Assyria who appear in Assyrian records around the 8th century BC. Some researchers also presume that this word is the etymology of the name for Russia, but this retroactively applies a linguistic interpretation from after the Middle Ages and is remote from the historical context of the ancient Near East. In academia, the tendency to understand it generally as an idiomatic expression referring to an unidentified ancient northern people prevails.

remark: A town of Benjamin, near Joppa.
introduce: Lod is a name denoting a town or region of ancient Israel where the descendants of the tribe of Benjamin lived.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the sons of Elpaal were Eber, Misham, and Shemed, and that he built Ono and Lod and the villages around them (1 Chronicles 8:12).
geography: Lod was located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin and, according to the biblical record, is described as an area adjacent to Ono. As for its present geographical location, work of specific archaeological identification is ongoing, but it is generally presumed to be an area near the Plain of Sharon.

introduce: Lycaonia is a region located on the Anatolian plateau in central Asia Minor, and was one of the main stages of activity during the apostle Paul's first missionary journey. This region was included in the Roman Empire's province of Galatia at that time.
biblecontents: Fleeing persecution in Iconium, Paul and Barnabas took refuge in the cities of the region of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding country, and preached the gospel there (Acts 14:6). When Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth in Lystra, the people there mistook Paul and Barnabas for the gods Hermes and Zeus, respectively, and tried to offer sacrifices to them (Acts 14:11).
geography: Lycaonia is a plateau region bordered by Galatia to the north, Cappadocia to the east, the Taurus Mountains to the south, and Phrygia to the west. Many of its plains are arid and short of water, so sheep herding developed as the main pastoral industry, and major cities such as Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe formed along the trade routes.
history: Lycaonia originally took the form of independent tribal states, but around the 1st century BC it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Galatia. When it became part of the Roman Empire under Emperor Augustus in 25 BC, it became a district of the province of Galatia. At that time the local Lycaonian dialect was spoken here, but Roman governance and Greek culture coexisted, centered on the urban areas.

introduce: Lycia is a region located on the southwestern coast of ancient Asia Minor, corresponding to the western part of present-day Antalya Province and the eastern part of Muğla Province in Türkiye. This region served as a major hub of Mediterranean trade and a crossroads of sea transport from ancient times.
biblecontents: There is a record that, in the course of Paul being taken to Rome as a prisoner, he crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and arrived at the city of Myra in Lycia (Acts 27:5).
geography: Lycia is a mountainous region where the Taurus Mountains stretch rugged to the north and the Mediterranean borders it to the south. Because the mountains run steeply down to the coast, the flat land is narrow, but some fertile valleys exist, such as the Xanthos River basin. Port cities such as Myra and Patara developed and were used as starting points for maritime trade.
history: Lycia formed a distinct culture from ancient times and maintained a powerful political system called the Lycian League. Around the 6th century BC it came under Persian rule, and afterward, through the conquests of Alexander the Great, it was incorporated into the Hellenistic cultural sphere. In the Roman period, Lycia and Pamphylia were administratively united and managed as a Roman province, and in the time of Paul, under direct Roman rule, it fulfilled the role of an important maritime supply route.

introduce: Rumah is a place name mentioned in 2 Kings 23:36 in the Old Testament, recorded as the hometown of Zebidah, the mother of Jehoiakim, king of Judah.
biblecontents: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother's name was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah (2 Kings 23:36).
geography: Its specific location within the ancient kingdom of Judah is disputed even among scholars, and no site has been definitively identified archaeologically to date. Some scholars conjecture it to be a place name in the southern region of Judah, but objective evidence is lacking.

introduce: Libya (Lubim) is a place name of the ancient Near East, meaning a region or people mentioned in the Book of Nahum as an ally of ancient Egypt.
biblecontents: It is recorded that Cush, Egypt, Put, and Libya helped their mighty strength and became their strength (Nahum 3:9).
history: Scholars presume the Lubim to be Libyans who lived in the region of Libya, and they were active as a core mercenary group of Egyptian military power during the 22nd and 23rd Dynasties of ancient Egypt. When the pharaohs of ancient Egypt formed a united front against great powers such as Assyria, the Libyans functioned as one of the main military partners.

remark: 1. A town of the Canaanites, later called Bethel.
introduce: Luz is an ancient city located in the land of Canaan, the place whose name Jacob changed to Bethel after he dreamed and met the angel of God. Throughout the biblical record, this place name is identified with Bethel or used to refer to its vicinity.
biblecontents: After Jacob dreamed, he named that place Bethel, but its former name was Luz (Genesis 28:19). Jacob came to Luz, that is, Bethel, and built an altar to God (Genesis 35:6). God appeared to Jacob at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed him (Genesis 48:3). The boundary of the descendants of Ephraim went from Bethel to Luz and passed along to the boundary of the Archites (Joshua 16:2). The boundary reached the south of Bethel and passed along by Luz (Joshua 18:13). The house of Joseph sent men to spy out Luz (Judges 1:23).
geography: Luz is identified with the same location as Bethel and is identified with the modern area of Beitin. It is a central hill country region about 18 km north of Jerusalem. It was a strategic crossroads connected to the major thoroughfares of central Canaan at that time, and being located in the Bethel hill country, its elevation is somewhat higher than the surroundings.
history: It was a place where a settlement had been formed since the Bronze Age, and a dwelling place of Canaanite tribes. In the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan, it was captured by the tribes of Israel, and afterward it settled in as one of the religious centers of Israel. At first it was called by the Canaanite place name Luz, but as the Israelite place name Bethel gradually became established, the former name gradually fell out of use.

remark: 2. A town of the Hittites.
introduce: A town located within the territory of the Hittite people in the land of Canaan; it is known as the same place name as the place later called Bethel, but the Luz mentioned in Judges 1:26 refers to a separate settlement built by the Hittites, a people of the Hittite line.
biblecontents: A man went to the land of the Hittites, built a city, and named it Luz, and that is its name to this day (Judges 1:26).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is presumed to be in either the northern region of Canaan or the region east of the Jordan, where the Hittites were active; it is analyzed as pointing to a geographical site different from Luz, the former name of the later Bethel.
history: This is a record that appears in the course of the Israelites capturing Bethel through spies of the house of Joseph, and it is the name of the new city that the man who fled after the capture of Bethel moved to the land of the Hittites and founded. It is an example that shows the political influence of the Hittites in the region of Canaan at that time and the process of settlement by the migrants.

introduce: Lystra was an ancient city located in the region of Lycaonia in southern Asia Minor, and was used as an important base during the apostle Paul's missionary journeys. Administratively, it was included in the Roman province of Galatia.
biblecontents: Paul and Barnabas fled from persecution in Iconium to Lystra and preached the gospel (Acts 14:6). Here Paul performed the miracle of healing a man who had been unable to walk from birth (Acts 14:8). Afterward, Paul and Barnabas returned to Lystra and strengthened the hearts of the disciples (Acts 14:21). On his second missionary journey, Paul visited Lystra and met Timothy, who was a man well spoken of by the believers there (Acts 16:1, Acts 16:2). In 2 Timothy, Paul mentioned the persecutions and sufferings he had endured in Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11).
geography: Lystra is presumed to be near Hatunsaray, southwest of the Konya region of modern Türkiye. This area lies on a fertile plain and, connected to the main Roman road network of the time, served as a crossroads of transportation and commerce.
history: In 6 BC, Lystra was designated a Roman colony (Colonia) by Emperor Augustus. This measure promoted the Romanization of the region and the spread of Latin, and aimed to strengthen the Roman Empire's control by settling retired soldiers. Accordingly, a unique social environment was formed in this city in which Greek culture and the Roman administrative system coexisted.

introduce: Luhith is a town that was located in the land of ancient Moab, a place name mentioned in the prophetic books of the Old Testament. Its exact location is currently a matter of archaeological dispute, but it is generally presumed to have been located on a hill or slope of the Moabite plateau.
biblecontents: In prophesying the judgment that would come upon Moab, the prophet Isaiah described the sound of weeping that would be heard on the ascent to Luhith (Isaiah 15:5). The prophet Jeremiah likewise mentioned, in his message of judgment against Moab, that weeping would continue on the ascent of Luhith, and recorded that Luhith was included in the path of destruction (Jeremiah 48:5).
geography: Luhith was located in the land of Moab and, judging from the biblical record, had the topographical feature of being adjacent to an ascending road or sloping hillside. As to its specific location, the theory that it was in the region south of the Arnon River or on the plateau east of the Dead Sea predominates, but there is insufficient evidence to connect it definitively with any present-day archaeological site.

introduce: Lub is a Hebrew place name referring to Libya, mentioned in the Book of Chronicles in the Old Testament. It means a tribe or nation that lived west of Egypt in the ancient Near East, and appears as a power that had political and military relations with the kingdom of Judah at that time.
biblecontents: When Zerah the Cushite attacked Judah with an enormous army, the people of Lub are mentioned as one of the forces included in that army (2 Chronicles 16:8).
geography: It refers to a people who lived centered on the northern coastal region of present-day Libya. It denotes the dwelling places of the Libyans who lived from the western border of ancient Egypt along the Mediterranean coast.
history: It is related to the historical situation of the period around the 9th century BC, when a dynasty of Libyan origin ruled Egypt or acted as the core mercenaries of the Egyptian army. At that time the kingdom of Cush had a close relationship with Egypt, and the people of Lub were mobilized as an important force of these armies.

introduce: Lydda was a settlement located in the ancient Palestinian plain, a city that in New Testament times served as a crossroads linking Judea and Samaria.
biblecontents: While Peter was visiting the believers, he met a man named Aeneas who lived in Lydda; he had been lying paralyzed for eight years, but Peter healed him (Acts 9:32, 9:33, 9:34). The people living in Lydda and Sharon saw this miracle and turned to the Lord (Acts 9:35). The disciples in Joppa heard that Peter was in Lydda and sent men to urge him to come quickly (Acts 9:38).
geography: Lydda is located on the plain of the Shephelah, about 40 kilometers northwest of Jerusalem and about 15 kilometers east of Joppa. Situated at a strategic point linking the fertile coastal plain with the hill country, it is an area where the road network has been well developed since ancient times.
history: In the Old Testament period, it is mentioned as a town of the tribe of Benjamin located in the Ono valley, and in the Hasmonean period and the time of Herod the Great it rose to prominence as a major administrative center. In the Roman period it was also called by the name Diospolis, and it prospered as an important commercial and transportation hub of the Judean region.

introduce: Letushites is the name of a tribe, or of the region where they lived, that appears in the Book of Genesis in the Old Testament, and is classified as a group connected with the descendants born to Abraham and his concubine Keturah.
biblecontents: The Letushites are mentioned as one of the sons of Jokshan, the son Abraham obtained through Keturah, and are recorded as the ancestor of the Dedan and Letushite clans (Genesis 25:3).
history: The Letushites are presumed to be related to the origins of nomadic tribes that settled in northern ancient Arabia or were active in that vicinity, and later archaeology and historical scholarship also interpret them as a Semitic tribal community that engaged in trade in the desert regions.

introduce: Lebaoth is a town recorded in Joshua 15 in the Old Testament, an ancient town allotted in the Negev plain, the southern border region of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Among the lists of towns near the Edomite border at the southern end of the tribe of Judah, Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon are recorded following Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah (Joshua 15:31).
geography: Lebaoth was located in the arid Negev region southeast of Beersheba and has the topographical features of being adjacent to the Edomite border and the wilderness of the Arabah. It is presumed to be the same place as Beth-lebaoth, which was reallotted to the tribe of Simeon in Joshua 19:6, and as Beth-biri in 1 Chronicles 4:31. Archaeologists identify it with Tel Masos (Khirbet el-Mishash), about 12 km southeast of Beersheba, or with a site near Wadi es-Seba.
history: During the transition from the Late Bronze Age to the early Iron Age, settled villages and networks of fortresses were formed around the oases and wadis of the southern Negev to protect the caravan trade routes and to defend against incursions by nomads. Lebaoth, adjacent to the trade route running from Arabia and Edom to the Mediterranean coast and the interior of Canaan, served as a southern line of defense and a border settlement for the tribes of Judah and Simeon.

remark: A valley southwest of Jerusalem, the boundary between Judah and Benjamin.
introduce: Rephaim is the name of an ancient tribe of the land of Canaan recorded in the Bible, and also refers to the specific place name where they lived or were active. According to ancient Near Eastern records and biblical descriptions, they were regarded as a tribe of giant stature, and they left traces in various regions on both the east and west sides of the Jordan River.
biblecontents: The Rephaim were regarded as a race of giants like the Anakites, and the Moabites called them Emites (Deuteronomy 2:11). Also, the Rephaim were known as the land where giants had lived in the past, and the Ammonites called them Zamzummites (Deuteronomy 2:20). Of the remnant of the Rephaim, only Og king of Bashan was left, and his bed was made of iron and was kept in Rabbah (Deuteronomy 3:11). Moses called all the region of Bashan the land of the Rephaim and gave it to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 3:13). The Valley of Rephaim lies on the boundary of Jerusalem and is situated on the west of the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Joshua 15:8). When Joshua urged the descendants of Ephraim and Manasseh to clear the forest region and live there, he mentioned the land of the Rephaim (Joshua 17:15). The boundary of the Valley of Rephaim has the topographical feature of continuing to the northern end of the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Joshua 18:16). The Philistines encamped in the Valley of Rephaim in order to attack David (2 Samuel 5:18). The Philistines again spread out and filled the Valley of Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:22). When the Philistine army encamped in the Valley of Rephaim, David was in the cave of Adullam (2 Samuel 23:13).
geography: The Valley of Rephaim is a fertile plain located southwest of Jerusalem. Topographically, it serves as a passage linking the hill country of Judah with the Philistine plain, and from ancient times it occupied an important position for agriculture and military movement. The land of the Rephaim east of the Jordan is described as a vast territory centered on the Bashan plateau.
history: The Rephaim refers to a group of ancient tribes whose reality has not been clearly established archaeologically. As the memory of the indigenous people who had lived in the land of Canaan since before the early Iron Age was passed down orally, their huge stature seems to have become fixed in the designation of a mythical or historical race of giants. In the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan, they are mentioned as objects of conquest or as a former place name, and afterward, in the time of David, the valley was used as a major battleground with the Philistines.

introduce: Lebonah is a place name appearing in the Old Testament, an ancient town located in the north of the territory of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a place north of Shiloh, east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem (Judges 21:19).
geography: It is identified with present-day Khirbet el-Lubban and is situated near the Patriarchs' Highway, the main road of the Samaria hill country. It has the character of an important point of passage on the north-south road network linking Jerusalem and Shechem.

introduce: Rephidim is a place name mentioned as the last place where the people of Israel encamped during the route of the exodus from Egypt before reaching the wilderness of Sinai.
biblecontents: The whole congregation of the people of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by stages and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink (Exodus 17:1). Then Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). The people of Israel set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai and camped in the wilderness, and there Israel camped before the mountain (Exodus 19:2). They set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink (Numbers 33:14). They set out from Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai (Numbers 33:15).
geography: Rephidim is presumed to be the area of Wadi Feiran near Jebel Musa, which is thought to be Mount Sinai, or a valley zone connected with it. This is a passage where an oasis is likely to form topographically, and it lies on a main approach to Mount Sinai.

introduce: Rehoboth-Ir was one of the cities located in the region of ancient Mesopotamia, a place included in the territory ruled by Nimrod mentioned in Genesis 10.
biblecontents: From that land he went out into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah (Genesis 10:11).
geography: The exact location of Rehoboth-Ir is difficult to pin down in modern archaeology, but the academic world presumes that this city was located in the vicinity of Nineveh in the Tigris River valley. Because the etymology of the name means, in Hebrew, the wide streets or squares of a city, it is also interpreted as a name referring to a part of the great metropolitan area centered on Nineveh.
history: According to the biblical record, this city is described as having been built by Nimrod. From the standpoint of ancient Near Eastern history, this reflects the process of city-state formation between the plain of Shinar and the region of Assyria in the early Mesopotamian civilization period. It is regarded as a satellite city adjacent to Nineveh, the center of Assyria, or as part of an administrative district.

remark: 1. A town of Assyria near Nineveh and Calah, built by Nimrod.
introduce: Rehoboth is a place name connected with a ruler of the Edomite dynasty, mentioned in the biblical record as a town of origin of a particular person or a town over which his authority extended. It carries the Hebrew etymological meaning of a broad place or square, but this place name is classified as a proper name of the region of Edom.
biblecontents: After Shaul king of Edom died, Hadad became king in his place, and his capital was Rehoboth (Genesis 36:37). Also in the record of Chronicles, it is described in the same way that after Shaul king of Edom died, Hadad became king and the name of his city was Rehoboth (1 Chronicles 1:48).
geography: It is presumed to be a town located within the region of Edom, but its exact location has not been determined in modern archaeology. However, it is recorded as one of the centers of the kingdom of Edom, distinguished from Rehoboth-Ir on the bank of the Euphrates.
history: Since it appears as the seat of Hadad's rule in the royal genealogy of Edom, it can be seen that it was a town with political and military influence in the Edomite region at that time. This name suggests that it served as an important administrative center in the period when the early monarchic system of Edom was being established.

remark: 2. The name of a well that Isaac dug.
introduce: A region to which Isaac moved to avoid a dispute with the Philistines over a well; he named it to commemorate that there was no longer any quarrel there.
biblecontents: He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” (Genesis 26:22)
geography: Its exact location is disputed among scholars, but it is generally thought to lie in the Negev desert region south or southwest of Beersheba. It is classified as a plain area near the Valley of Gerar, where Isaac was living at the time.
history: This was a place that reflects the migrations and the conflicts over securing water resources in the patriarchal period of the early Bronze Age. In nomadic society wells were essential to survival, and disputes over rights of possession among local tribes were a common historical phenomenon.

remark: A Levitical city in Asher, located on the upper Jordan River.
introduce: Rehob is a place name in the Old Testament: a city in the region of Aram and a historical site connected with King David's conquests. In the time of Nehemiah it also appears as the name of a person who took part in sealing the covenant.
biblecontents: When David went to strike Hadadezer king of Zobah, his power reached the bank of the Euphrates River; this is mentioned in the context of the struggle for supremacy over the region of Aram, which included Rehob (2 Samuel 8:3). It is implied that the region of Rehob in Aram came under David's rule in this process, since he dedicated to the LORD the things taken from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek, together with the plunder from Hadadezer king of Zobah (2 Samuel 8:12). In the time of Nehemiah it is recorded as the name of one of the leaders who took part in sealing the covenant (Nehemiah 10:11).
geography: Rehob is a region associated with Aram-zobah, and it is generally thought to have been near the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges. Its exact location is disputed archaeologically, but it is regarded as an important city north of Damascus, a strategic stronghold reaching to the entrance of Hamath on the north.
history: Around the tenth century BC, during David's wars of conquest in Aram, Rehob acted as part of the coalition of the kingdom of Zobah. After being conquered by David it was briefly brought within Israel's sphere of influence, but after the death of Solomon the Aramean kingdoms expanded their power again and Israel's control weakened. The Rehob mentioned in the time of Nehemiah is a case where the name is used not as a place name but as a personal name, referring to a particular family or individual within the community that returned from exile.

introduce: The Arameans of Rehob were one of the small Aramean kingdoms that existed in the ancient Near East, a political entity that came into military conflict with Israel in the time of David.
biblecontents: When the Ammonites realized that they had become odious to David, they hired Arameans, summoning foot soldiers from Rehob and men of Tob to fight against David's army (2 Samuel 10:6). Joab, commander of David's army, deployed his forces facing the Ammonites and the Aramean army, and the army of the Arameans of Rehob was confronted by Joab's brother Abishai (2 Samuel 10:8).
geography: Scholarly opinion is divided about the exact location of the Arameans of Rehob, but it is generally thought to have been south of Mount Hermon, in the northern part of Bashan, or near the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges.
history: Around the tenth century BC the Arameans were gradually expanding their power into the regions of Syria and Lebanon, and in this process a number of small kingdoms were formed. The Arameans of Rehob were one of the Aramean states that, in alliance with Ammon at that time, resisted the expansion of Israel; in the course of David's wars of conquest they appear to have gradually come under Israel's sphere of influence or to have been absorbed by other Aramean states.

introduce: Riblah was a strategic point in the ancient Near East, a city located in the valley of the Orontes River. In biblical geography it is mentioned mainly as a reference point on Israel's northern border and as a military base of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
biblecontents: In Numbers 34:11 Riblah is described as a point on the northern border of the promised land, recorded as a boundary line lying east of Ain (Numbers 34:11). It also appears in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 as the place where Zedekiah king of Judah was seized by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, interrogated, and had his eyes put out (2 Kings 25:6, Jeremiah 52:9).
geography: It is identified with the village of Ribleh in present-day Syria and lies on the fertile plain of the upper Orontes River. As the main route linking Hamath to the north and Damascus to the south, the area has topographical conditions favorable to military movement and supply.
history: From the late seventh century BC to the early sixth century BC it was used by the Neo-Babylonian Empire as a forward base for gaining control of the Levant. When Nebuchadnezzar II campaigned in Syria and Palestine, he set up his headquarters here and carried out administrative and military rule, using the place to pronounce political judgments on the surrounding vassal states.

introduce: Libya is a name that designates the ancient region of North Africa; in the Bible it is used mainly of the region lying to the west of Egypt and of the peoples who lived there.
biblecontents: It is recorded as a prophecy that the king of the North will gain power and take possession of the gold and silver and all the treasures of Egypt, and that the Libyans and the Cushites will be his attendants (Daniel 11:43).
geography: Ancient Libya meant the whole North African coast west of Egypt, including the territory of present-day Libya, and it comprised mainly the southern coast of the Mediterranean and the northern part of the Sahara Desert.
history: In the biblical period Libya had close diplomatic and military relations with ancient Egypt; historically it was brought into the Mediterranean world through Phoenician colonization and then through coming under the sphere of influence of the Hellenistic empires.

introduce: Libya is an ancient place name for present-day North African Libya and its surrounding region; in the Bible it is mentioned as one of the regions from which the Diaspora Jews who visited Jerusalem at the time of the event of Pentecost had come.
biblecontents: Among the Jews from many nations who gathered in Jerusalem after the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost were also people living in the parts of Libya near Cyrene (Acts 2:10).
geography: Libya is an ancient place name for the broad region of North Africa extending from the west of Egypt to the Atlantic coast, and Cyrene, mentioned in the Bible, corresponds to the Cyrenaica region of northeastern present-day Libya.
history: In the Hellenistic period and the time of the Roman Empire, many Greek and Roman colonial cities were built in the Libyan region, and it was a place where Jewish immigrants formed communities and lived; Cyrene in particular was a center with a high density of Jewish population and lively exchange with Jerusalem.

introduce: Rimmono refers to one of the cities allotted to the Merarite descendants of the tribe of Levi, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:77. In Joshua 19:13 and 21:34 it appears under the name Rimmon.
biblecontents: To the rest of the descendants of Merari, Rimmono with its pasturelands and Tabor with its pasturelands were given from the tribe of Zebulun (1 Chronicles 6:77).
geography: Rimmono was located within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun and is identified with Rummaneh in the Galilee region of present-day northern Israel, or with a nearby area. Topographically it lay in low hill country, with conditions suited to farming and grazing livestock.
history: After the tribes of Israel were allotted the land of Canaan, the tribe of Levi lived scattered throughout the territories of the tribes in order to carry out the duties of tending the sanctuary and teaching the law. Rimmono was designated as one of the strategic cities where the Merarites lived and carried out their duties.

remark: 1. A city in Simeon.
introduce: Rimmon was a city located within the territories of the ancient tribes of Judah and Simeon. In the biblical record this name is also mentioned in connection with En-rimmon, Rimmon-perez, and the like, and it was also used as a place name marking the boundary of a particular region.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities given as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah, and is listed together with Lebaoth and Eder (Joshua 15:32). It is recorded again as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Simeon (Joshua 19:7). In the prophecy of Zechariah it also appears in a description of the topographical features of Jerusalem, in the picture that the whole land, as far as Rimmon south of Geba, will become a plain (Zechariah 14:10).
geography: It is generally thought to have been located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah. Scholars link this place name with Tel Ain Rimmon or its vicinity, which is understood to be an area close to the present-day plain of Beersheba. The Rimmon mentioned in the book of Zechariah was used as a geographical reference point symbolizing the southern boundary of Jerusalem.

remark: 2. A city in Simeon, near Tochen.
introduce: Rimmon is a place name mentioned among the cities allotted as the inheritance of the tribes of Judah and Simeon. According to the biblical record, this place is recorded as one of the five cities where the descendants of Simeon lived.
biblecontents: The places where they lived were five cities: Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan (1 Chronicles 4:32).
geography: Rimmon is thought to have been located in the southern Negev region near Beersheba, and it is generally also identified as the same place as En-rimmon. This area lies in the border zone between the desert region and the plains and hill country of southern Judah.

introduce: Rimmon-perez was one of the stations at which the Israelites stayed as they moved through the wilderness after the Exodus from Egypt; it is the fifteenth encampment reached after setting out from Rithmah.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez (Numbers 33:19). They left Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah (Numbers 33:20).
geography: Its exact location is disputed among scholars, but it is thought to have been in the northern Sinai Peninsula or the Negev desert region. It is analyzed as one of the points formed along the ancient road network that served as the wilderness route of travel at that time.

remark: 1. The place where they stayed sixteenth after leaving Egypt, and fifth after setting out from Mount Sinai.
introduce: Libnah is a place designated as one of the main camps in the wilderness where the Israelites stayed during the journey of the Exodus.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah (Numbers 33:20), and they left Libnah and camped at Rissah (Numbers 33:21).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically up to the present, but it is thought to have been on the wilderness route in the northeastern Sinai Peninsula or in the vicinity of the Arabah valley.

remark: 2. A Levitical city in Judah, south of Jerusalem.
introduce: Libnah refers to a city that held a strategically important position in the period of the conquest of Canaan and in the period of the kingdom of Judah. It is recorded as lying mainly in the Shephelah region within the territory of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is one of the cities conquered by the Israelite army led by Joshua in the war of conquest of southern Canaan (Joshua 10:29). Israel left Makkedah, advanced on Libnah, and struck it (Joshua 10:31), and God gave Libnah and its king into the hand of Israel (Joshua 10:32). Joshua conquered Libnah and utterly destroyed its king (Joshua 10:39). The king of Libnah is included in the list of the Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:15). Libnah was classified as one of the cities of the inheritance that the tribe of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:42). It was also a city given to the descendants of the priest and assigned as a dwelling place together with Hebron, a city of refuge (Joshua 21:13). When Edom broke free of Judah's rule and became independent during the reign of Jehoram king of Judah, Libnah also revolted at the same time (2 Kings 8:22).
geography: Libnah is generally thought to have been located in the Shephelah, the hill country between the plain and the mountains of Judah. Archaeologically, Tel Burnat or Tel Safi (Tel Zayit) are mentioned as the leading candidates for the site. This area is a strategic stronghold, either for defending against the Philistine threat or, conversely, for controlling the route by which the kingdom of Judah advanced onto the plain.
history: In the late Bronze Age it was an independent Canaanite city-state, but after the Israelite conquest of Canaan it became the possession of the tribe of Judah. Afterward, in the early period of the kingdom of Judah, it was affected by the revolt of neighboring peoples such as Edom, and in the period of expansion of the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires it served as a line of defense for Judah and went through geopolitical upheaval.

introduce: Riblah was a city on the Orontes River in Syria, which Scripture calls "Riblah in the land of Hamath" (2 Kings 23:33, Jeremiah 39:5). It was the place where Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt confined Jehoahaz in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, and where Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon stayed when he attacked Jerusalem and passed judgment on Zedekiah and the nobles of Judah.
biblecontents: The Chaldean army captured King Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah; the king of Babylon interrogated him, slaughtered his sons before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him in chains, and took him away to Babylon (2 Kings 25:6-7). The captain of the guard, Nebuzaradan, brought Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, the three doorkeepers, and the men he had taken in the city to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath (2 Kings 25:18-21; Jeremiah 52:24-27).
geography: A city on the Orontes River in the land of Hamath, identified with the area of the village of Ribleh, south of Homs in western Syria, near the Lebanese border. Lying on the road leading north to Hamath through the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, it was a convenient place for armies traveling between Egypt and Mesopotamia to encamp. It is a different place from Libnah in the western plain of Judah (Joshua 10:29).
history: Around 609 BC, Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt confined Jehoahaz king of Judah here to keep him from reigning, and set Eliakim (Jehoiakim) on the throne in his place (2 Kings 23:33-34). When Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was staying here; he interrogated the captive Zedekiah and put to death his sons and all the nobles of Judah (Jeremiah 39:5-6; Jeremiah 52:9-10). Seraiah the chief priest and the others brought by Nebuzaradan were also executed here (Jeremiah 52:26-27). Scholars are divided over whether the "Riblah" that appears as the eastern border of Canaan in Numbers 34:11 is the same place.

introduce: Rithmah is one of the campsites where the Israelites stayed during the Exodus journey, and it lies on the route of travel after leaving Hazeroth.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah (Numbers 33:18). Afterward they left Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez (Numbers 33:19).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically up to the present, but it is thought to be a desolate wilderness area in the northeastern Sinai Peninsula or in the Arabah valley region. The Hebrew root ratam means a thicket or shrub, which suggests an environment in which there was vegetation that grew by retaining rainwater in that area.

introduce: Rissah is one of the camps where the Israelites stayed during the Exodus journey; it is a place located after leaving Libnah and before reaching Kehelathah.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Libnah and camped at Rissah (Numbers 33:21). They also left Rissah and camped at Kehelathah (Numbers 33:22).

introduce: Magadan is a place name appearing in the Gospel of Matthew in the New Testament, mentioned as the region where Jesus arrived by boat during his public ministry. Because Mark 8:10 records the place of the same event as Dalmanutha, the relationship between the two place names has become a subject of scholarly discussion.
biblecontents: After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. (Matthew 15:39)
geography: It is thought to be a region on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. The view that it is the same place as the ancient city of Magdala, or a region near it, is predominant. Because the Gospel of Mark calls this place Dalmanutha, archaeological exploration continues in order to identify its exact location.
history: At that time Magadan, or Magdala, was a commercial hub on the shore of the Sea of Galilee where fishing and the processing of fish products were developed. According to records from around the first century, it is known as one of the settlements where economic activity was lively within the region of Galilee under the rule of Herod Antipas.

introduce: Makaz is a place name mentioned in 1 Kings 4:9, which describes the administrative districts of Israel in the time of Solomon; it is a city included in the jurisdiction of Ben-deker, one of King Solomon's twelve district officers.
biblecontents: Makaz is recorded as one of the districts of Ben-deker, who had charge of Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kings 4:9).
geography: Makaz is thought to have been located in the Shephelah, the western lowland of the tribe of Judah, and together with nearby Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and others, it lies in a strategic zone linking the Philistine plain and the mountains of Judah.

introduce: Macedonia is a region located in the north of ancient Greece, a place name that appears in the Acts of the Apostles in the New Testament as a key base for Paul's mission in Europe.
biblecontents: In the night Paul saw a vision in which a man of Macedonia stood and urged him to come over to Macedonia and help us (Acts 16:9). After seeing this vision, Paul and his companions immediately endeavored to set out for Macedonia (Acts 16:10). They came to Philippi, the first city of the district of Macedonia, and stayed there for some days (Acts 16:12). Afterward Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia and joined Paul (Acts 18:5). Paul resolved to go to Jerusalem after passing through Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 19:21). Of those who helped him he sent two, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia (Acts 19:22). Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, were seized and rushed into the theater at Ephesus together with Paul (Acts 19:29). After the uproar ceased, Paul called the disciples, encouraged them, and left to go to Macedonia (Acts 20:1). Passing through the district of Macedonia, he encouraged the disciples with many words and came to Greece (Acts 20:3). When Paul boarded a ship of Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with him as well (Acts 27:2).
geography: It lies at the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula, bordered on the east by the Aegean Sea, on the west by Illyricum, and on the south by the region of Thessaly. Its major cities include Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, and a major Roman road, the Via Egnatia, ran through this region and served as a crossroads of east-west traffic.
history: In the fourth century BC, in the time of Alexander the Great, it formed a powerful empire, but afterward, in 146 BC, it was incorporated as a province of Rome. Under the Roman imperial system Macedonia was at times administered as an imperial province rather than a senatorial province, and at the time of the events recorded in Acts it was functioning as a strategically important region within the Roman administrative system.

introduce: Machir is the name in the Bible that refers to the firstborn of the tribe of Manasseh and to the clan and the particular region formed by his descendants. They lived on both the east and the west of the Jordan and formed an important military and political axis of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Machir is mentioned as the son of Manasseh and the father of Gilead (Numbers 26:29). In the book of Judges he appears, together with the tribe of Ephraim, as a military ally of Israel, and he performed the role of sending out military commanders in time of war (Judges 5:14).
geography: The descendants of Machir received as their inheritance the region of Gilead east of the Jordan, which included rugged mountain country and abundant pastureland. According to the record in Numbers, they were recognized for their merit in conquering Gilead and were allotted that territory.
history: The house of Machir is regarded as a group made up of warriors skilled in battle in the early settlement of Israel. At the time of the Judges, Machir's dwelling place functioned as an important strategic stronghold in the united front of the northern tribes of Israel, and it was deeply involved in military movements in central and northern Canaan.

introduce: Madon was a Canaanite city and kingdom in the north of ancient Canaan, a region that formed a coalition and opposed Joshua at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Jabin king of Hazor sent word to Jobab king of Madon so that they might together oppose Israel (Joshua 11:1), and the king of Madon is included in the list of the Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:19).
geography: It is thought to have been located west of the Sea of Galilee, in the vicinity of Hazor, but modern archaeology points to Tell Madon in Lower Galilee or the nearby Tell Qarnei Hittin as the leading candidates for the site.
history: In the late Bronze Age the small states of northern Canaan had formed a strong political and military alliance centered on Hazor, and Madon was a political entity that, as one of the powers in this Hazor-centered coalition, resisted Israel's activity of conquering Canaan.

remark: The first place where Israel stayed after crossing the Red Sea.
introduce: Marah is the place that the Israelites who left Egypt found after crossing the Red Sea, when for three days in the wilderness of Shur they could not find water; the place name was given because its water was bitter and could not be drunk.
biblecontents: The people of Israel entered the wilderness of Shur and walked for three days but found no water, and they came to Marah, but they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter (Exodus 15:23). The Israelites set out from the edge of Etham and camped at Marah (Numbers 33:8). When they left Marah and came to Elim, there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees there (Numbers 33:9).
geography: Present-day Marah is often identified with the spring of Ain Hawarah, south of the Ayun Musa area, on the route running south along the western coast of the Sinai Peninsula. Because of the limestone geology, this area has the topographical characteristic of springs whose groundwater has dissolved minerals such as magnesium sulfate and calcium sulfate, giving a bitter taste that makes it unsuitable for drinking.

introduce: Maralah is one of the border regions of the tribe of Zebulun recorded in Joshua 19:11.
biblecontents: It went up westward to Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and met the brook east of Jokneam. (Joshua 19:11)
geography: Maralah is thought to be a place name located on the western border of the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in southern Galilee. Its exact modern location has not been determined, but scholars generally conjecture that it was somewhere along the highland boundary between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea.

remark: A fortified city in the plain of Judea.
introduce: Mareshah was a strategic stronghold of the ancient kingdom of Judah and is the place identified with the archaeological site of Tel Maresha. It was a city located in the Shephelah of Judah that held great value from the standpoint of defense and economy.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:44). It was included among the cities built up as fortified cities for defense in the time of King Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:8). The battle between King Asa and Zerah the Cushite took place in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah (2 Chronicles 14:9). In this battle the army of King Asa drew up its battle line facing Mareshah (2 Chronicles 14:10). Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat and criticized his plan to build ships (2 Chronicles 20:37). The prophet Micah prophesied God's judgment against Mareshah and its destruction (Micah 1:15).
geography: Mareshah is identified with Tel Maresha, near Beit Guvrin in present-day Israel. Situated on a hill in the Shephelah linking the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain, it has topographical conditions advantageous for controlling the east-west routes of travel.
history: Mareshah served as the southwestern line of defense of the kingdom of Judah and had military importance; afterward, in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, Edomites flowed in and settled, and it was transformed into a main stronghold of Idumea. In the course of the Maccabean wars of the second century BC it was captured by the Hasmonean dynasty, and afterward, in the Roman period, as nearby Eleutheropolis prospered, it gradually declined.

introduce: Maroth is a place name appearing in the book of Micah in the Old Testament, thought to have been a city located in the Shephelah, the western plain of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the inhabitants of Maroth were grieved as they longed for good, because disaster had come from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem (Micah 1:12).
geography: Opinion is divided among scholars about its exact location, but it is generally understood to have been situated within the Shephelah (lowland) region, the territory of the tribe of Judah. This region lies near the main routes leading to Jerusalem.
history: Around the eighth century BC, when Sennacherib king of Assyria invaded Judah, Maroth is thought to have been one of the cities that lay in the path of the Assyrian army's advance and was directly threatened. It is mentioned against the confused background of the times, in which northern Israel had been destroyed and Judah was also being invaded.

introduce: The Horse Gate is one of the gates located in the wall of Jerusalem, a place whose name means a passage by which horses enter and leave.
biblecontents: Athaliah was dragged out of the temple and put to death, and the execution was carried out near the entrance of the Horse Gate, the place where she was killed (2 Chronicles 23:15). When Nehemiah rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, the priests each repaired the section above the Horse Gate in front of his own house (Nehemiah 3:28).
geography: It is thought to have been located near the southeastern corner of the wall of Jerusalem, and it was placed at a point close to the temple area, which connected to the Kidron Valley.

introduce: Mashal is a city mentioned in the Old Testament, a place recorded in connection with the allotment of territory to the tribes of Israel and the assignment of dwelling places to the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: Mashal, located within the territory of the tribe of Asher, is recorded as one of the cities allotted to the Gershonites, the descendants of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:74).
geography: The exact location of Mashal has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is generally thought to have been located in the Galilee region or near the northern boundary of the coastal plain occupied by the tribe of Asher.

introduce: Masrekah is a place name mentioned as the region of origin of Hadad, who was a king of Edom.
biblecontents: Hadad son of Bedad died, and Shaul of Masrekah, from Samlah, reigned in his place (Genesis 36:36). Hadad son of Bedad died, and Shaul of Masrekah, from Samlah, reigned in his place (1 Chronicles 1:47).

introduce: Maacah is a place name appearing in the Old Testament and refers to a region of Aram or to a person from that region. It is described mainly as a small Aramean kingdom located near Mount Hermon east of the Jordan, and it is mentioned in connection with people of the time of David and of the periods before and after the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: It was included in the border region, part of the territory of Og king of Bashan, that the half-tribe of Manasseh occupied (Joshua 12:5). The Ammonites, in order to wage war against David, hired foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, a thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men from Tob (2 Samuel 10:6). Among the troops the Ammonites had hired, the men of Maacah took up a separate formation and confronted David's army (2 Samuel 10:8, 1 Chronicles 19:7). Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, one of David's mighty men, was the son of a Maacathite (2 Samuel 23:34). Among those who came to Gedaliah, the governor of Judah who remained at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem, was Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite (2 Kings 25:23, Jeremiah 40:8). The expression "Maacathite" appears in the genealogical record concerning the wife of Naham (1 Chronicles 4:19).
geography: Maacah is thought to have been located southeast of Mount Hermon, in the northern or northeastern part of Bashan. It is one of the Aramean regions east of the Jordan River, and topographically it lies in a buffer zone between the northeast of the Sea of Galilee and the Hauran plateau.
history: Around the tenth century BC, when the kingdom of David was expanding its territory, Maacah, as an Aramean small kingdom together with the neighboring Zobah and Beth-rehob, allied itself with Ammon and opposed Israel. Afterward, as the Aram-Damascus kingdom expanded its power, these small Aramean kingdoms appear to have been absorbed or brought under its sphere of influence. Afterward, in the exilic period, it tends to be mentioned not as a place name but as an origin that distinguishes a particular family or person.

introduce: Maacath was a small Aramean kingdom located east of the Jordan River and northeast of the Sea of Galilee; in biblical geography it corresponds to the area north of Bashan and south of Mount Hermon.
biblecontents: Jair took the whole region of Argob as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and he called this region, after his own name, Bashan-havvoth-jair (Deuteronomy 3:14). Because the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites and the Maacathites, Geshur and Maacath lived among Israel to this day (Joshua 13:13). The Bible classifies all the cities of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, including Maacath, and all the kingdom of Bashan as the territory of Sihon king of Heshbon, and so establishes its geographical boundaries (Joshua 13:11).
geography: Maacath is a fertile hill country lying between the northern Golan Heights and the foot of Mount Hermon. On the west it borders the upper Jordan valley, and on the north it is connected to the rugged terrain of Mount Hermon, so that it had conditions that could serve as a natural fortress.
history: Maacath existed as an independent kingdom at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan, and because the tribes of Israel were unable to conquer this region completely, it coexisted with Israel for a long time and at times maintained a hostile relationship. Afterward, in the time of David, there appears a record that it allied with Ammon and fought a war against Israel, which shows the political position of Maacath as it tried to maintain its power among the surrounding great powers of the time.

introduce: Maarath is a place name mentioned as one of the cities of the hill country of Judah allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: In the book of Joshua it is listed, among the cities of the hill country distributed to the tribe of Judah, together with Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon (Joshua 15:59).
geography: It is thought to have been located in the southern region of the hill country of Judah or in the vicinity of Hebron, but its exact modern location has not been clearly identified archaeologically.

remark: A city in the hill country of Judah, near Ziph and Carmel.
introduce: Maon is a city located in the hill country of Judah, a place name identified with present-day Tell Ma'in. In Hebrew it means a dwelling or a place of residence, and it was a historical site connected with David's life as a fugitive and one of the important strongholds of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities in the list of those allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:55). In the book of Judges the Maonites are recorded as one of the peoples that oppressed Israel, but from the context this is interpreted as meaning a tribe or power connected with the place name Maon (Judges 10:12). When David was fleeing from King Saul he stayed in the wilderness of Maon (1 Samuel 23:24), and it is the place where Saul pursued David and surrounded him (1 Samuel 23:25). Also, Nabal, a wealthy man who lived in Carmel, is introduced as being from Maon (1 Samuel 25:2). According to the record of Chronicles, the Moabites and Ammonites allied themselves with the Maonites to strike Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:1), and it is also recorded that in the time of King Uzziah God helped Uzziah to strike the Philistines, the Arabs living in Gur-baal, and the Maonites (2 Chronicles 26:7).
geography: Maon is located about 13 kilometers south of Hebron and corresponds to the area of present-day Tell Ma'in. It lies at the southern edge of the hill country of Judah and is a strategic stronghold linking the surrounding wilderness with the hill country. Carmel and Ziph are located nearby, and because of its dry and rugged terrain it has conditions suited to grazing livestock or hiding.
history: From the early Iron Age Maon functioned as an administrative and defensive stronghold of the kingdom of Judah. The historical records in the Bible show that this region served as a buffer zone in the border area between the surrounding foreign peoples and the kingdom of Judah. In particular, the fact that Chronicles mentions the Maonites in association with Moab or Arabian powers suggests that the inhabitants of this region had complex relationships not only with the isolated tribes of Israel but also with the surrounding nomadic peoples. In the time of David it became a key stage of a period of political upheaval as David's hiding place, and in the later monarchy it is repeatedly recorded as a point of confrontation with invading forces.

introduce: Mahanaim is a strategic stronghold located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River, a place name recorded in biblical history in connection with Jacob's vision, a city of the tribe of Levi, and a refuge of the Davidic dynasty.
biblecontents: It is the place where Jacob, as he went on his way, met the angels of God, and he called that place Mahanaim (Genesis 32:2). After the conquest of Canaan, in the course of the allotment of the land east of the Jordan, it was incorporated into the territory of the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13:26), and it is also mentioned as a boundary of the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13:30). It was one of the cities of refuge and a dwelling city allotted to the Merarite descendants of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:38). It was the place where Ish-bosheth, son of King Saul, was enthroned as king of Israel after Saul's death (2 Samuel 2:8), and the place where Abner led the army and set up Ish-bosheth as king (2 Samuel 2:12). Afterward Abner's army crossed the Jordan River, passed Bithron, and arrived at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2:29). It is the place where David took refuge to escape Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 17:24), and when he arrived at Mahanaim, local notables including Barzillai provided supplies to David's party (2 Samuel 17:27, 2 Samuel 19:32).
geography: It is located east of the Jordan River, in the mountainous region of Gilead near the Jabbok River. In modern place names it is thought to be Tell edh-Dhahab or the nearby Tell Mahneh, but its exact location is under archaeological dispute. Having hilly terrain advantageous for defense that overlooks the Jordan Valley, it was used as a military fortress from ancient times.
history: It is a strategic stronghold where traces of human habitation have been found from the Bronze Age. In the time of David it was an administrative base reached by the influence of the central government, and during the reign of Ish-bosheth it was used as a political headquarters to assert legitimacy. This region served as a buffer zone between the nomadic peoples east of the Jordan and the tribes of Israel to the west.

introduce: Manahath is a proper noun in 1 Chronicles 2:54 that designates a place name or a tribal family. It is mentioned as a place connected with the lineage formed by the descendants of Salma.
biblecontents: The descendants of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, half of the Manahathites, the Zorites (1 Chronicles 2:54)

introduce: Mahaneh-dan is a place name that means "camp of Dan" in Hebrew, a place mentioned in the biblical record in connection with the activity of Samson and the movement of the tribe of Dan.
biblecontents: At Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol, the Spirit of the LORD began to stir Samson (Judges 13:25). Six hundred men of the Danites, armed with weapons, camped at Kiriath-jearim, and for this reason that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day (Judges 18:12).
geography: Mahaneh-dan is described as a region between Zorah and Eshtaol, which is thought to be the vicinity of the Valley of Sorek, the border zone between the tribes of Judah and Dan. Also, since it is located behind Kiriath-jearim, it corresponds to a buffer zone between the mountainous region west of Jerusalem and the coastal plain.
history: It was originally located within the territory allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Dan, but it was a place used as a military base or assembly point in the course of the tribe of Dan's migration north to Laish because of the pressure of the Philistines.

introduce: Mahavite is a place name mentioned as the place of origin of Eliel, one of David's mighty men.
biblecontents: Eliel the Mahavite is mentioned as included in the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:46).

introduce: Makkedah is an ancient Canaanite city appearing in the record of Joshua's conquest in the Bible, an area that belonged to the territory of the tribe of Judah. It is known as the place where a major military clash occurred between the southern Canaanite coalition forces and Israel, and where there was a cave in which the five Canaanite kings hid.
biblecontents: After winning the battle of Gibeon, Israel pursued the Canaanite coalition forces who had fled to Makkedah (Joshua 10:10). The five kings who fled hid in a cave at Makkedah but were discovered by Joshua and arrested (Joshua 10:16, 17, 21). Joshua executed the five kings here and blocked the mouth of the cave with stones (Joshua 10:28). Afterward the Israelite army captured the city of Makkedah and utterly destroyed its king (Joshua 10:28, 29), and this remains as one of the records of Joshua's conquest (Joshua 12:16). Afterward, following the period of the conquest of Canaan, Makkedah was included in the list of cities allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:41).
geography: Makkedah is generally identified as being located in the plain of Judah (the Shephelah). Modern scholars conjecture that this place is Tell el-Masediyeh or Khirbet el-Keiun, but opinion is divided in scholarship about its exact location. Topographically it is situated at a strategic stronghold linking the hill country of Canaan and the Philistine plain.

introduce: Magdala is an ancient city located on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, a place known as the hometown of Mary Magdalene. In Hebrew it is called Migdal, which means a watchtower.
biblecontents: Mary Magdalene stood by the cross of Jesus (Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40, John 19:25) and watched the tomb in which Jesus was laid (Matthew 27:61, Mark 15:47). Early on the first day of the week after the Sabbath she prepared spices and went to the tomb (Mark 16:1, Matthew 28:1), and she is recorded as one of the first persons to see the risen Jesus (Mark 16:9, Luke 24:10). She is also described as the one from whom seven demons had gone out through Jesus (Luke 8:2).
geography: It is located on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and corresponds to the area of Migdal in present-day Israel. It lies at the southern end of the plain of Gennesaret, and in ancient times it had conditions suited to the development of fishing and fish processing.
history: In the Roman period it was also called Tarichaeae, which in Greek means a fish-salting factory. At that time Magdala, as an economic hub of the Galilee region, prospered by exporting processed fish products to Rome and neighboring regions. Around the first century, during the Jewish War, it went through a turbulent history, including the destruction of the city by the Roman army.

introduce: Maktesh means "a place of wailing or crying out" in Hebrew, and it is known as a place name designating a particular district of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: The prophet Zephaniah warned the inhabitants of Maktesh that Jerusalem would be judged and that they would wail (Zephaniah 1:11).
geography: Opinion is divided about its specific location within Jerusalem, but it is thought to have been a low valley district within the city where merchants and traders mainly lived or carried on their activities.
history: It was the economic center of Jerusalem at the end of the kingdom of Judah, and it played the role of a commercial hub in which merchants who traded in silver were concentrated at that time.

introduce: Magdiel is mentioned as the name of one of the chiefs of Edom and as the name of the region he ruled.
biblecontents: In the genealogy of the descendants of Edom, Magdiel is the person listed last among the chiefs of Edom, and it is also the name of the place where he lived (Genesis 36:43). In Chronicles as well, Magdiel is likewise included in the list enumerating the chiefs of Edom (1 Chronicles 1:54).

introduce: Machpelah is a region located near Hebron in the land of Canaan; it refers to the field that Abraham bought from Ephron for the burial of Sarah, and the cave contained in it. Afterward it was used as a family burial place in which the principal figures of the patriarchal period were laid to rest.
biblecontents: In order to make the cave of Machpelah a burial place for Sarah, Abraham paid the price to Ephron the Hittite, the owner of the cave, and obtained ownership of it (Genesis 23:9). This transaction was carried out officially in the presence of the Hittites at the city gate, and the field, the cave in it, and all the trees around it were confirmed as Abraham's possession (Genesis 23:17). Abraham buried his wife Sarah in this cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:19). Afterward Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah were all laid to rest here (Genesis 25:9, Genesis 49:30, Genesis 50:13).
geography: Machpelah is located east of Hebron (Kiriath-arba) in southern Canaan. Archaeologically it is identified with the area of the Haram al-Ibrahimi in the city of Hebron in present-day Palestine, and it is a place that has been known from the past as the site of the tombs of the patriarchs.
history: In Bronze Age Canaan, land transactions were generally carried out by reaching an oral agreement in front of witnesses and following legal procedures. Abraham's purchase of Machpelah is interpreted as a historical event that went beyond merely obtaining a tomb and included the intention of securing for the patriarchal family a permanent claim to the land of Canaan.

introduce: Makheloth is one of the forty-two camps where the Israelites stayed in the course of the wilderness journey toward Canaan after the Exodus from Egypt.
