biblecontents: The Israelites left Haradah and camped at Makheloth (Numbers 33:25). The Israelites left Makheloth and camped at Tahath (Numbers 33:26).

introduce: Mattanah is one of the camps in the wilderness through which the people of Israel passed on their journey toward Canaan after the Exodus from Egypt.
biblecontents: The people of Israel went from Beer into the wilderness and came to Mattanah (Numbers 21:18). Afterward they moved from Mattanah by way of Nahaliel to Bamoth (Numbers 21:19).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is thought to be an area near the plain of Moab north of the Arnon valley.

introduce: Madmenah is a place name that existed in the time of the ancient kingdom of Judah, a village located on the route of advance of the Assyrian army.
biblecontents: The prophet Isaiah mentioned Madmenah as one of the points through which the Assyrian army passes as it moves south from the north toward Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:31).
geography: Madmenah is thought to be located north of Jerusalem, but its exact archaeological location has not been confirmed. However, considering the line of march listed in Isaiah 10:28-32, it is highly likely to have been one of the villages in the outskirts of Jerusalem near Nob or Anathoth.

introduce: Madmen is a city of Moab appearing in the book of Jeremiah in the Old Testament, a place mentioned as the object of a prophecy of judgment.
biblecontents: In Heshbon they plotted evil to harm him, saying, "Come, let us cut him off so that he can no longer form a nation." You also, O Madmen, will be silenced; the sword will pursue you (Jeremiah 48:2).
history: The region of Moab was traditionally a nation located to the east of Israel, and by the time of Jeremiah it had become one of the objects against which a message of judgment was proclaimed amid Babylon's invasion and political turmoil. Madmen is thought to be a city mentioned in the course of Moab's political destruction, together with the other cities of Moab.

remark: A country located on the Caspian Sea.
introduce: Media refers to an Iranian people who lived in the northwest of the Iranian plateau in the ancient Near East and to the kingdom they established. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly as a region to which Israel was exiled or as a political power allied with the Persian Empire.
biblecontents: After the king of Assyria captured Israel, he removed the people of Samaria and settled them in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6, 2 Kings 18:11). Media appears as the power that overthrows Babylon, and the Medes are described as a cruel people who have no regard for silver and take no delight in gold (Isaiah 13:17, Isaiah 13:18). In the time of Cyrus king of Persia, the decree of King Darius was found in the palace at Ecbatana in Media (Ezra 6:2). In the third year of his reign King Xerxes gave a banquet for all his officials and servants, and at this time the nobles of Persia and Media were present (Esther 1:3). The seven princes of Media and Persia were the king's counselors, who saw the king's face in his presence and sat in the first place in the kingdom (Esther 1:14). After the incident of Queen Vashti, it was foreseen that the noblewomen of Persia and Media would hear of the king's conduct and speak of it to the king's officials, and that contempt and anger would arise at that time (Esther 1:18, Esther 1:19). Media was included in the realm of King Xerxes, and it is recorded together with Persia as a core power of the empire (Esther 10:2).
geography: The region of Media is located centered on the Zagros Mountains in northwestern present-day Iran. It consists of mountainous country and plains bordering the Caspian Sea on the north, the Assyrian empire on the west, and the region of Elam on the south.
history: Around the seventh century BC Media grew into a powerful centralized state and played a decisive role in the fall of the Assyrian empire. Afterward, in the reign of King Cyaxares, it greatly expanded its territory, but around 550 BC it was annexed to Persia by Cyrus II (Cyrus). In the period of the Persian Empire, Media and Persia were run in union, and the biblical record reflects this historical state of political integration.

introduce: Metheg-ammah is a place name appearing in 2 Samuel 8:1 in the Old Testament, a place mentioned when David conquered the Philistines and took from their hands the place where they held power.
biblecontents: Afterward David struck the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines (2 Samuel 8:1).
geography: The exact location of Metheg-ammah has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but the dominant view interprets it as designating Gath, which was originally the capital of the Philistines, or as a name signifying control over the vicinity of Gath.
history: The event of taking Metheg-ammah signifies a military achievement that took place in the process by which David broke free of Philistine oppression and established supremacy over the surrounding nations. Considering the meaning of the Hebrew original, Metheg-ammah carries the sense of "the bridle of the mother," and so it is analyzed as symbolizing the center of the Philistines, or a stronghold from which Philistine suzerainty was exercised.

introduce: Medeba is an ancient city located on the Moabite plateau east of the Jordan River, a strategic stronghold that in biblical times became an object of territorial dispute between the tribes of Israel and Moab.
biblecontents: When Israel conquered Heshbon, even Medeba was destroyed (Numbers 21:30). In the time of Joshua this region was included in the boundary of the area allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:9, Joshua 13:16). In the time of King David the Ammonites hired Arameans and fought against the Israelite army in front of Medeba (1 Chronicles 19:7). The prophet Isaiah, in prophesying judgment against Moab, mentioned Medeba as a major city of Moab (Isaiah 15:2).
geography: Medeba corresponds to the area of Madaba in present-day Jordan and is located on the plateau about 10 km south of Heshbon. This area, lying beside a fertile plain, is favorable for agriculture, and, being adjacent to the King's Highway, it has the topographical conditions to serve as a center of transportation and trade.
history: Human habitation at Medeba began in the Bronze Age, and in the Iron Age it changed hands frequently between the domain of the kingdom of Moab and the sphere of power of the tribes of Israel. According to the Mesha Stele, the inscription of Mesha king of Moab from around the ninth century BC, there is a record that Moab recaptured Medeba from Israel and rebuilt it, which demonstrates the historical importance of this region. Afterward, in the Hellenistic and Roman periods, it prospered as a city famous for its mosaic art.

introduce: Meronoth is one of the place names of ancient Israel, a name used mainly to indicate the place of origin of particular persons or to identify the local community that took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: In the time of King David, Obil the Ishmaelite, who was in charge of the camels, is recorded as a Meronothite (1 Chronicles 27:30). Also, when the wall of Jerusalem was repaired, Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite rebuilt a part of that wall (Nehemiah 3:7).
geography: The exact location of Meronoth has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but from the geographical context it is thought to have been located within the territory of the tribe of Judah. Some scholars raise the possibility that this area was near Gibeon, close to the boundary with the tribe of Benjamin, or in the area north of Jerusalem.

introduce: Meroz is a place name mentioned only once in the book of Judges in the Hebrew Bible, recorded as a region that was cursed in the song of Deborah and Barak.
biblecontents: The angel of the LORD said, "Curse Meroz; again and again curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty" (Judges 5:23).
geography: Its exact location has not been pinpointed archaeologically up to the present. However, considering that the song of Deborah has as its background the battle near the Valley of Jezreel and Mount Tabor, the theory that it was a settlement near the Kishon River or around Mount Tabor is predominant.
history: The inhabitants of Meroz were cursed on the ground that they did not cooperate with the Israelite army at the time of the battle with the Canaanite army. It is interpreted as a community that refused military support when the allied forces of the tribes of Israel were waging war against the army of Sisera.

introduce: Merom is the place where the northern Canaanite coalition forces, headed by Jabin king of Hazor, clashed with the Israelite army during the wars of the conquest of Canaan, and it is an area thought to be located in the region north of the Sea of Galilee today.
biblecontents: The northern Canaanite coalition forces centered on Jabin king of Hazor camped at the waters of Merom in order to oppose Israel (Joshua 11:5). Joshua and the Israelite army made a surprise attack on them at the waters of Merom and defeated them (Joshua 11:7).
geography: Merom lies on the western edge of the Hula Basin, about 15 km north of the Sea of Galilee. In ancient times a Lake Merom or marshland existed here, giving it the topographical requirements suited to the stationing or ambushing of large armies.
history: At that time Hazor was the most powerful city-state of northern Canaan, and the battle at Merom became a decisive turning point in Joshua's wars of conquest in subduing the northern region. Through this victory Israel established a bridgehead from which it could extend its influence over the northern region of Canaan.

introduce: Mephaath is a city located on the plain of Moab mentioned in the Old Testament, known as one of the inheritances allotted to the tribe of Reuben.
biblecontents: Mephaath is included in the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:18). Afterward it appears again as a city allotted to the Merarite descendants of the tribe of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:79). In the prophecy of judgment against Moab by the prophet Jeremiah, it is mentioned as a city on the plain of the land of Moab (Jeremiah 48:21).
geography: Mephaath seems to have been located on the plain of Moab east of the Jordan River, but its exact archaeological location has not been determined. Together with Jahaz, Kedemoth, and others mentioned nearby, it is thought to have been in the northern plain region of Moab.
history: It was originally Moabite territory, but after the period of Israel's conquest of Canaan it became the portion of the tribe of Reuben, and afterward it became a dwelling place of the tribe of Levi. In records outside the Bible it is difficult to confirm specific historical facts about this place name.

introduce: Mesopotamia means "the land between two rivers" in Greek and generally refers to the fertile alluvial plain between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. It is the cradle of civilization in the ancient Near East, and in the Bible it is often mentioned in connection with Abraham's homeland.
biblecontents: Abraham commanded his servant to go to the city of Nahor in Aram-naharaim, his homeland, to seek a wife (Genesis 24:10). In writing the law, Moses stated that Balaam son of Beor of Aram-naharaim tried to curse Israel (Deuteronomy 23:4). When the people of Israel forgot the LORD and served the Baals, God sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and Israel served him for eight years (Judges 3:8). Afterward, when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up Othniel and saved them, and the Spirit of God came upon him and enabled him to defeat Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim (Judges 3:10). Among the devout Jews gathered in Jerusalem at Pentecost were also people from Mesopotamia (Acts 2:9). Stephen mentioned that the God of glory appeared to Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran (Acts 7:2).
geography: It is a terrain in the form of a vast basin that includes present-day Iraq and northeastern Syria. The north is mountainous, and the south consists of marshes and plains that lead to the Persian Gulf. It is a region where irrigation agriculture developed on the basis of the abundant water resources provided by the two rivers.
history: From around 3000 BC ancient civilizations and states such as Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia, and Assyria flourished. In the early biblical period it was the region where Abraham's ancestors lived, and afterward it was a politically strategic area where the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires and others contended for supremacy. Because of its geopolitical importance, it was a region that suffered repeated invasion and occupation by the surrounding great powers.

introduce: Me-jarkon is a place name mentioned as one of the cities included in the region allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Dan among the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: As one of the inheritances obtained by lot by the tribe of the descendants of Dan, Me-jarkon is recorded as a city located within the territorial boundary of the tribe of Dan, together with Rakkon (Joshua 19:46).
geography: Me-jarkon is thought to have been located on the coastal plain near Joppa, but its exact location has not been determined by modern archaeology. Scholars regard it as connected with the valley of the Yarkon River or the fertile lowlands around it (Joshua 19:46).

introduce: Malta is the island that appears in Acts 28:1, and it refers to the island of Malta located in the central Mediterranean. In ancient times it was a strategic stronghold used as a base for maritime trade.
biblecontents: This is the island on which Paul landed after being shipwrecked in a violent wind called the Northeaster while he was being taken to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 28:1). The native people of this place received Paul's party with special kindness, and while Paul was building a fire to keep off the cold, a viper bit him, but he suffered no harm at all (Acts 28:2-6). Paul also healed the sick, including the father of Publius, the chief official of the island, and when he departed, he was provided with the things he needed by the islanders (Acts 28:7-10).
geography: It is an island located in the central Mediterranean about 90 km south of the island of Sicily. With its complex coastline and well-developed natural harbors, it had conditions suitable for ships to anchor from ancient times.
history: In the first century Malta belonged to the administrative districts of the Roman Empire and was under the jurisdiction of the governor of Sicily. Linguistically, a dialect influenced by Phoenician was used, and it played an important role as a stopover on the maritime trade route linking Rome and Alexandria.

introduce: Moresheth is a settlement located in the Shephelah plain region in the south of the ancient kingdom of Judea, a place known as the hometown of the prophet Micah.
biblecontents: As the setting of the activity of the prophet Micah, it is mentioned as his place of origin through the designation Micah the Moreshite (Micah 1:1). Also, when Micah, who was active in the time of Hezekiah king of Judah, is singled out as the one who prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem, his hometown of Moresheth is mentioned once again (Jeremiah 26:18).
geography: Moresheth is located in the hill country of the Shephelah, thought to be near present-day Gath in Israel, and geographically it corresponds to a buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain.
history: Around the eighth century BC, at a time when the threat of Assyrian invasion was intensifying, it held influence as a strategic stronghold of the kingdom of Judah, and it was placed within a dynamic of relations in which Assyrian military pressure was frequent.

introduce: Moriah is a place name that in Hebrew has the meaning "chosen land" or "the place where God appears," and it is a proper noun designating a particular hill region in the Jerusalem area of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is first mentioned as the place to which Abraham went, having received a command from God to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering, and where he prepared the sacrifice (Genesis 22:2). Afterward King Solomon built the house of the LORD on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, and this was also the place where David had offered sacrifices to the LORD at the threshing floor of Ornan (2 Chronicles 3:1).
geography: Mount Moriah is a hill located in the northeast of ancient Jerusalem and is identified with the area of the present-day Temple Mount in Jerusalem. The Kidron Valley and the Tyropoeon Valley lie nearby, and topographically it forms an area higher than its surroundings, with a bedrock terrain suitable to be the foundation for building the temple.
history: Mount Moriah was part of Jerusalem, which was the dwelling place of the Jebusites, and it became the property of the Israelite royal house when King David bought the threshing floor from Ornan the Jebusite. Afterward, as King Solomon leveled this place and completed the temple, it was established as the religious center of Jerusalem and a space symbolizing the nation.

remark: A city of Benjamin.
introduce: Mozah is a place name mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the cities included in the inheritance of the descendants of Benjamin listed in Joshua 18:21-28 (Joshua 18:26).
geography: It is thought to be the Motza area west of present-day Jerusalem, a mountainous region on the route from Jerusalem to Joppa.

introduce: Moserah is one of the places through which the Israelites passed during their wilderness journey after the Exodus, a place name connected with the death of Aaron.
biblecontents: The Israelites set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan and came to Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and his son Eleazar served in his place in the office of priest (Deuteronomy 10:6).
geography: Its exact location is disputed among scholars, but it is generally thought to be a terrain in the southern part of the Arabah valley or near Petra. It is regarded as the same place as Moseroth mentioned in Numbers 33:30.

introduce: Moseroth is one of the camps where the Israelites stayed during the Exodus journey, a place name located on the route of travel after leaving Hazeroth.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Hazeroth and camped at Moseroth (Numbers 33:30). Then they left Moseroth again and camped at Bene-jaakan (Numbers 33:31).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly demonstrated archaeologically at present, but it is generally thought to be in the northern Sinai Peninsula or near the Arabah valley. Some scholars regard it as the same place as Moserah mentioned in Deuteronomy 10:6.

introduce: Mizpeh of Moab is a place name in the land of Moab that David visited in order to keep his parents safe as he fled the pursuit of King Saul. Within the Bible, the mention of Mizpeh of Moab appears limited to 1 Samuel 22:3.
biblecontents: David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab and said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me," and he brought them before the king of Moab, and they stayed with the king of Moab all the time that David was in the stronghold (1 Samuel 22:3).
geography: Mizpeh of Moab is thought to have been located on the Moabite plateau east of the Dead Sea, but its exact location has not been determined by modern archaeology. The name Mizpeh means a watchtower or lookout in Hebrew, and it was likely a city situated on a high place in the land of Moab that offered a strategic view.
history: By entrusting his parents to the king of Moab, who was hostile to Israel, David sought to protect his family from the threat of Saul. This is interpreted as a diplomatic decision that made use of the bond of kinship that David's great-grandmother was Ruth, a Moabite woman. At that time Moab was in a state of tension with Israel, but a temporary measure of protection appears to have been carried out in accordance with David's personal circumstances.

introduce: Meunim is a place name appearing in 1 Chronicles 4:41, recorded as a place that the descendants of Simeon in the tribe of Judah conquered and made their dwelling place.
biblecontents: According to the record, in the time of Hezekiah king of Judah the descendants of Simeon of the tribe of Judah struck and destroyed the Meunites who were living there and took possession of the place in their stead (1 Chronicles 4:41).
history: The Meunim mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:41 are generally identified with the Maonites, a people who lived in the region of Edom. They are thought to be a group near the hill country of Seir that appears in various historical records of the ancient Near East, and the event of their being conquered by the tribes of Israel in the time of King Hezekiah indicates the expansion of the power of the kingdom of Judah over this region.

introduce: Moladah is one of the cities located on the territorial boundary between the tribes of Judah and Simeon in ancient Israel, mentioned mainly as a dwelling place allotted in the southern Negev region.
biblecontents: Moladah is mentioned as one of the cities at the southern end of the inheritance that the tribe of Judah received (Joshua 15:26). Afterward it was included among the cities that the tribe of Simeon received out of the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 19:2). In 1 Chronicles as well, Moladah is recorded in the list of cities where the descendants of Simeon lived (1 Chronicles 4:28). After the return from exile it is mentioned as one of the settlements where the descendants of Judah lived again (Nehemiah 11:26).
geography: Moladah is thought to have been located east or southeast of Beersheba, and it lies in the Negev region, the dry highland of southern Judah. The prevailing view identifies it with Tell el-Milh in modern place names or an archaeological site near it.

introduce: Myra was one of the major cities of the ancient region of Lycia, a strategic port city located on the Mediterranean coast. In the Acts of the Apostles in the New Testament it is mentioned as a stopover in the course of Paul's being taken to Rome.
biblecontents: The ship carrying Paul crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to the city of Myra in Lycia, where the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put Paul on board (Acts 27:5).
geography: Myra lies in southwestern Asia Minor in the region of Lycia, near the mouth of the Andros River, and it connected to maritime traffic through the port of Andriake, about 5 kilometers from Mira, the center of the interior. It has the locational characteristic of being where rugged mountain terrain and the coastal plain intersect.
history: Throughout the Hellenistic period and the time of the Roman Empire it enjoyed prosperity as an important city of the Lycian League. In the Roman period in particular it was used as a port hub for grain transport, and it functioned as a stopover where the huge ships carrying grain from Egypt to Rome put in.

introduce: Mysia is a name designating the northwestern region of ancient Asia Minor, corresponding to the Marmara region of present-day Türkiye. It is one of the administrative districts of the Roman Empire through which Paul passed during his second missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul and his companions tried to go to Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them, and as a result they passed through Mysia and went down to Troas (Acts 16:7). Paul and his companions also passed by Mysia and came to Troas (Acts 16:8).
geography: It borders the Sea of Marmara on the north, the Aegean Sea on the west, Lydia on the south, and Bithynia and Phrygia on the east. Its major cities include Adramyttium and Pergamum, and topographically mountainous country and coastal plains are intermingled.
history: The name Mysia originally derived from the name of an ancient tribal state, but after the Hellenistic period it came within the sphere of influence of the kingdom of Pergamum. Afterward, in the time of the Roman Empire, it was incorporated as part of the province of Asia and received administrative management.

introduce: Mecherath is a term that can be interpreted as a personal name or a place name appearing in 1 Chronicles 11:36, but in scholarship it is generally regarded as the hometown of Hepher, one of David's mighty men from Ezbai, or it is conjectured to be a place name connected with a particular family.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the hometown of Hepher of Ezbai in the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:36).

introduce: Meconah (Mekonah) is a place name appearing in the book of Nehemiah in the Old Testament, recorded as one of the settlements where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile.
biblecontents: Meconah is one of the places mentioned when the descendants of Judah lived in Jerusalem and the surrounding cities (Nehemiah 11:28).
geography: Its exact location is disputed even in scholarship, but it is generally thought to have been located in the Negev region in southern Judah or near Ziklag, south of Jerusalem. Archaeologically, Tel Eitun or the surrounding area is also regarded as a leading candidate for the site.
history: It is one of the administrative districts mentioned as the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem and the resettlement of the population took place in the Persian Empire period after the Babylonian exile. Judging from its inclusion in the list of villages where the tribe of Judah resettled, it is a place name that shows the sphere of influence of the Judean community under the Persian administrative system.

introduce: Megiddo was a city-state located on the southwestern edge of the Jezreel plain, a strategic stronghold of great importance in the ancient Near East. Because it controlled the key passage of the Way of the Sea, an international trade route, it played the role of a military and economic center from ancient times.
biblecontents: Joshua conquered the king of Megiddo (Joshua 12:21). Megiddo was allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, but at first it remained a land that was not conquered because the native Canaanites were not driven out (Joshua 17:11, Judges 1:27, 1 Chronicles 7:29). The kings of Canaan fought against Israel at the waters of Megiddo (Judges 5:19). Solomon made Megiddo part of his administrative district and built a chariot city there (1 Kings 4:12, 1 Kings 9:15). King Ahaziah, fleeing from Jehu, was killed at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27). King Josiah died in battle against Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29, 2 Kings 23:30).
geography: It is situated in a position from which it could watch the passes of the Carmel range, and it is a crossroads connecting Galilee on the north with the plain of Sharon on the south. It has the characteristics of a tell formed on a high hill from which one can look down on the vast farmland of the Jezreel plain.
history: It is a place where a settlement was formed continuously from the Bronze Age, and it is known as the site of a large-scale battle in which Thutmose III of Egypt fought the Canaanite coalition forces. After the time of Solomon, fortifications, stable facilities, and the like have been excavated archaeologically as an important administrative and military base of the kingdom of Israel. Afterward, as it came under the sphere of influence of Assyria and Babylon, destruction and rebuilding were repeated along with changes in the ruling power.

introduce: Manahath is a name of a place or a family mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, and it designates a place or group closely connected with the region of Hebron.
biblecontents: Among the descendants of Shobal son of Judah are Haroeh and half of the Manahathites (1 Chronicles 2:52).
geography: Its exact location is a subject of scholarly debate, but it is strongly suggested from the context that it was a settlement near the region of Hebron.

introduce: Merathaim is a place name that has the meaning "double rebellion" in Hebrew, or it was used as a symbolic nickname designating Babylon.
biblecontents: The prophet Jeremiah, foretelling judgment against Babylon, commanded them to go up against the land of Merathaim and to strike down and utterly destroy the inhabitants of Pekod (Jeremiah 50:21).
geography: It is thought to be a geographical name designating the southern region of Sumer, the center of ancient Babylonia, or Babylon as a whole.
history: It carries the meaning of mocking the rebellious course of action by which Babylon refused the rule of the Assyrian empire, grew into an independent empire, and invaded Israel.

introduce: Meribah is the name that designates, in the biblical record, the place where the people of Israel quarreled with God and Moses because of a shortage of water. Etymologically in Hebrew it means quarrel or complaint, and as a place name Meribah either designates a particular area on the route of the Exodus or was used as a name commemorating the event itself.
biblecontents: Because the Israelites quarreled, this place was called Massah or Meribah (Exodus 17:7). When the Israelites quarreled with the LORD at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, He showed His holiness among them (Numbers 20:13). Because Aaron rebelled against God's command at the waters of Meribah, he was not allowed to enter there (Numbers 20:24). Because Moses and Aaron did not uphold God's holiness at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, they could not enter that land (Numbers 27:14, Deuteronomy 32:51). Concerning the tribe of Levi, it is recorded that they were tested at the waters of Meribah (Deuteronomy 33:8). God delivers those who call upon Him in distress, and He tested them at the waters of Meribah (Psalms 81:7). There is a warning that the people of Israel must not harden their hearts as at Meribah, as in the time of testing in the wilderness (Psalms 95:8). Because the people of Israel provoked the LORD to anger at the waters of Meribah, Moses suffered trouble on their account (Psalms 106:32).
geography: Geographically, Meribah is connected with Kadesh, which lies in the wilderness of Zin on the route of the Exodus. In the Bible the place near Kadesh-barnea where there was water is mainly the one called Meribah, and this region has the topographical characteristic of a dry environment, adjacent to the wilderness of the Arabah, in which the water supply is very limited.
history: It is an event that occurred in the course of the Exodus of the Hebrew people, and it is divided into the first event, which occurred near Rephidim, and the second event, which occurred later at Kadesh. In the case of the second event, because Moses and Aaron did not fully carry out God's instructions, it became the decisive historical occasion on which they, as leaders of Israel, were prevented from entering Canaan, the promised land.

introduce: Meribath-kadesh is a place name mentioned as one of the points on the restored southern boundary line of Israel that Ezekiel saw in a vision.
biblecontents: Next to the border of Gad, the southern boundary runs from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, and along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea; this is the land that you shall allot by lot to the tribes of Israel as an inheritance (Ezekiel 48:28).
geography: Meribath-kadesh as described in the book of Ezekiel is presented as a point on the southern boundary line of Israel. In other passages of the Old Testament the prevailing view regards this region as the same place as Kadesh or Kadesh-barnea, and it is thought to be near the area of present-day Ain el-Qudeirat.

introduce: Meribath-kadesh is a place mentioned as one point on the southern boundary among the boundary lines of the restoration of Israel that Ezekiel saw in a vision. This place name is interpreted as designating the same place as Kadesh-barnea, and it functions as one of the reference points that define the southern limit of the land Israel will possess.
biblecontents: On the south, from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, and along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea; this shall be your southern boundary (Ezekiel 47:19).
geography: Geographically, Meribath-kadesh refers to Kadesh-barnea, an oasis region in the southern Negev wilderness. It is thought to be the area of present-day Ain el-Qudeirat, and, lying west of the Arabah valley and on the northeastern border of the Sinai Peninsula, it is a strategic stronghold adjoining the Egyptian border.
history: This region is one of the principal bases where the people of Israel stayed in the route of the Exodus in the Old Testament, and the name Meribah was attached to it because of the incident in which Moses struck the rock and brought forth water. The book of Ezekiel used this region as the geographical coordinate that fixes the southern border at the time of Israel's restoration.

introduce: Mephaath is a place recorded as one of the Levitical cities that was located within the territory of the tribe of Reuben in the time of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Mephaath was one of the cities allotted to the tribe of the descendants of Reuben, and it is included in the list of cities given to the Merarites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:37).
geography: It is thought to have been among the cities of the tribe of Reuben located on the highland of Jordan east of the Jordan River, but no clear scholarly consensus has been reached on a specific archaeological excavation site or a modern place name.

introduce: Mezoba is a place name mentioned as the place of origin of Jaasiel, one of the mighty men of King David.
biblecontents: Jaasiel the Mezobaite is recorded as one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:47).

introduce: Mearah is a place name appearing in Joshua 13:4, mentioned as one of the remaining areas still to be conquered, not yet allotted to the tribes of Israel at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: All the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah, which belongs to the Sidonians, as far as Aphek, to the border of the Amorites, remained unconquered (Joshua 13:4).
geography: It is generally thought to be connected with the southern part of the Lebanon range or the coastal region near Sidon, and it is regarded as a point on the Mediterranean coast that was within the sphere of ancient Phoenicia.

introduce: Meonenim is a place name appearing in the text of the book of Judges in the Bible, interpreted as a proper noun designating a particular region or topographical feature located near Shechem.
biblecontents: Gaal came forward toward Shechem, and when he saw the people coming down from the mountain beside the road of Meonenim, he said that they were coming down from the mountaintop (Judges 9:37).
geography: Considering the meaning of the Hebrew original, it is thought to be a terrain connected with the oak of a diviner or sorcerer, and it appears to have been a place on the route leading from the highland near Shechem to the plain.

introduce: Meholah is a place name appearing in the Bible, a place thought to be the same as Abel-meholah. This region is mentioned in connection with the lineage of the house of Saul and was used as a name indicating the place of origin of a particular person.
biblecontents: Saul's daughter Merab was originally to have become David's wife, but she was given as a wife to Adriel of Meholah (1 Samuel 18:19). Also, Adriel of Meholah handed over to the Gibeonites the five sons he had by Saul's daughter Merab, and they put them to death (2 Samuel 21:8).
geography: It is identified with the same place as Abel-meholah, a region west of the Jordan Valley, south of Beth-shan. This area is located in the farmland of the Jordan Valley, which has fertile soil.

introduce: Migron is an ancient city or region located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin of Israel, a strategic stronghold mentioned in connection with military activity in the time of King Saul and on the route of the Assyrian invasion.
biblecontents: King Saul stayed under the pomegranate tree in Migron on the outskirts of Gibeah, and the people with him numbered about six hundred (1 Samuel 14:2). The Assyrian army came to Aiath, passed through Migron, and stored its equipment at Michmash (Isaiah 10:28).
geography: This area, thought to be present-day Tel Migron, corresponds to a key point in the hill country of Benjamin, and, being adjacent to Michmash, it has the topographical characteristics that allowed it to watch over the main passage linking north and south.
history: It served as a command post where forces were assembled and operations were planned during the war with the Philistines in the early reign of King Saul, and afterward, when Sennacherib of Assyria invaded southern Judah, it was recorded as a military stronghold lying on the line of advance toward Jerusalem.

introduce: Mithnite is a place name mentioned as the hometown of Adina, one of David's mighty men, the powerful military organization of King David.
biblecontents: It is recorded that Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite was chief of the descendants of Reuben, and that he had thirty followers with him (1 Chronicles 11:42-43). In this passage Adina is described as a Mithnite (1 Chronicles 11:43).

introduce: Mitylene is a major port city and center on the eastern coast of the island of Lesbos in the Aegean Sea of ancient Greece.
biblecontents: Paul met his companions at Assos, they took him aboard the ship and went to Mitylene, and passing through it, the next day they arrived opposite Chios (Acts 20:14).
geography: It lies on the eastern coast of the island of Lesbos, and since it has two natural harbors, it has been regarded from ancient times as a strategic point of Aegean navigation. It is regarded as the same location as present-day Mytilene.
history: In the Hellenistic and Roman periods it served as a base of maritime trade connecting Asia and mainland Greece. As a self-governing city of Rome at that time, it was guaranteed a certain administrative autonomy, and it was known as a city where learning and the arts flourished.

introduce: The Beautiful Gate is a particular entrance of the temple in Jerusalem that appears in the Acts of the Apostles in the New Testament, known as a place where beggars of that time gathered.
biblecontents: A man who was lame from birth was set every day at the temple gate called Beautiful in order to beg (Acts 3:2). He begged as he saw Peter and John entering the temple and was healed, and afterward the people who saw him walking and leaping and praising God in the temple recognized him as the one who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate, and they were amazed (Acts 3:10).
geography: The Beautiful Gate is thought to have been located on the passage leading from the Court of the Gentiles to the Court of the Women in the Jerusalem temple. According to ancient records, this gate was made of splendid Corinthian bronze and was said to be far more magnificent and beautiful than the other gates of the temple.
history: According to the record of the historian Josephus, this gate seems to have been erected when Herod the Great enlarged the temple, and it was made using an enormous quantity of Corinthian bronze. It is judged that it received the name "beautiful gate" because, when the sun rose, the whole gate shone dazzlingly and looked like gold.

introduce: Mizzah is a place name or person appearing in the list of the chiefs of Edom, one of the ruling families of Edom mentioned in Genesis 36:17.
biblecontents: Esau had a son Reuel, and the sons of Reuel, Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah, became chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:17).

introduce: Mishal is thought to be a place name located within the territory of ancient Israel, but there is a divided scholarly debate over whether the Mizar that appears in Psalm 42:6 is a proper noun designating a particular region or a common noun meaning a small mountain or a low place.
biblecontents: In Joshua 19:26, Mishal is mentioned as a region included in the territorial boundary allotted to the tribe of Asher. In Joshua 21:30 it is recorded again as one of the cities of the tribe of Asher. In Psalm 42:6, Mount Mizar is mentioned together with the Jordan and Mount Hermon, providing the geographical background of the place from which the psalmist remembers God (Joshua 19:26, Joshua 21:30, Psalms 42:6).
geography: The Mishal of the record of Joshua is thought to have been located near Mount Carmel or in the southern boundary area of the tribe of Asher, but the exact excavation site has not been confirmed. The prevailing view interprets Mount Mizar of Psalm 42:6 as designating a small peak near the upper Jordan River or at the foot of Mount Hermon.

introduce: Misgab is a place name mentioned among the cities of Moab in the book of Jeremiah in the Old Testament. It is classified as one of the place names whose exact location has not been confirmed archaeologically up to the present.
biblecontents: It appears in the context in which the prophet Jeremiah, proclaiming judgment against Moab, prophesied that Misgab, together with Nebo, would be put to shame and destroyed (Jeremiah 48:1).
geography: Misgab is thought to have been located on the plain or highland of Moab. Since the Hebrew etymology carries the meaning of a high place or a watchtower, the possibility is raised that it was a strategic stronghold or a city built on high ground. Because it is mentioned in the biblical text adjacent to Nebo, it is also identified with the northern region of Moab.
history: In biblical history Moab was in frequent conflict with Israel, and the major cities including Misgab served as political and military strongholds of Moab. At the time of Jeremiah's prophecy Moab was in an international situation in which it was threatened with invasion by the surrounding great powers in connection with the expansion of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

introduce: Mishraites is a place name or a group presumed to be connected with the clans of Kiriath-jearim, one of the families of the tribe of Judah, who settled there or entered into blood relationships with them.
biblecontents: The clans of Kiriath-jearim were the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these clans came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites (1 Chronicles 2:53).

introduce: Misrephoth-maim is a place name located in the northern region of ancient Israel, a place that appears in the records of victory as a major battlefield in Joshua's wars of conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: After the Israelite army led by Joshua defeated the northern coalition formed around Jabin king of Hazor, it pursued the fleeing enemy as far as Misrephoth-maim and annihilated them (Joshua 11:8).
geography: It is thought to be Khirbet al-Musheirifa, located in southern Lebanon or on the northern coastal zone of Israel today. This is a strategic stronghold where the Mediterranean coastal plain and the mountain region meet, and it is identified as an area between Acco and Tyre.
history: The city-states of northern Canaan in the late Bronze Age fought a decisive battle at the waters of Merom to stop the Israelite coalition but were defeated, and afterward the remnants fled north as far as Misrephoth-maim on the Phoenician coastal region, which contains the background of how the military influence of that region declined.

introduce: Misrephoth-maim is a place name recorded in the Bible, designating the northern border region of Canaan that had yet to be conquered in the time of Joshua.
biblecontents: At the time Israel was distributing the land of Canaan, one of the boundaries of the remaining land not yet taken is mentioned as all the land of the Sidonians from the hill country of Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim (Joshua 13:6).
geography: Misrephoth-maim is thought to be Ras al-Naqura on the coast of present-day Lebanon, or nearby Wadi al-Mushayrifa. This is a strategic stronghold with a narrow passage along the Mediterranean coast, and it lies in the coastal plain between Sidon and Acco.
history: Even after Joshua's wars of conquest, the northern coastal region of Canaan remained strongly dominated by Phoenician powers, including the Sidonians, and it continued to be a region in which it was difficult for the tribes of Israel to exercise actual authority.

remark: 1. A city of Gad in Gilead, another name for Galeed.
introduce: Mizpah is a place name that appears many times in the Old Testament, and in Hebrew it means a watchtower or lookout. In the Bible several places, including the region of Gilead east of the Jordan and the territory of the tribe of Benjamin west of the Jordan, are called by the same name, Mizpah.
biblecontents: It is the place where Jacob and Laban made a covenant not to cross each other's boundary (Genesis 31:49). When the Ammonites camped to invade, the Israelites also gathered and camped at Mizpah (Judges 10:17). Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah (Judges 11:11), and when Jephthah returned to his house at Mizpah, his daughter came out to welcome him, taking a tambourine and dancing (Judges 11:34).
geography: The Mizpah mentioned in Genesis and Judges is thought to have been located east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead. Its detailed location is identified archaeologically with Tel ed-Damiyeh or Tell Jal'ud and the like, but there is no clear consensus among scholars.

remark: 2. A valley in Manasseh, near Mount Hermon.
introduce: Mizpah is mentioned in the Bible as a place name located east of the Lebanon range, in the region below Mount Hermon. It appears as the assembly point of the northern coalition forces at the time of Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: In the war with the northern coalition forces led by Jabin king of Hazor, Joshua pursued them as far as the valley of Mizpah and won the victory (Joshua 11:3). In this process the Israelite army pursued them as far as the vicinity of Mizpah and annihilated the enemy (Joshua 11:8).
geography: Mizpah is generally thought to be a valley region at the foot of Mount Hermon. It appears to designate a fertile plain or valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, and it was a strategic stronghold suited to the assembling of the northern Canaanite coalition forces.
history: It shows the geopolitical situation of the period in the late Bronze Age when the city-states of northern Canaan were forming a united front to stop Israel's advance southward. At that time Mizpah was one of the main strongholds where the northern coalition forces gathered and confronted Israel.

remark: 3. A city in the plain of Judah.
introduce: Mizpah is a fortified city belonging to the plain (Shephelah) region of the tribe of Judah recorded in Joshua 15 in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Among the cities of the lowland of the tribe of Judah, Dilean, Mizpah, and Joktheel are recorded (Joshua 15:38).
geography: It is located in the second district of the Shephelah, the hill country at the western foot of the hill country of Judah, and it was situated on the plain between Lachish and Azekah. It is thought to be Khirbet Safiyeh near Tell es-Safi.
history: As part of the network of fortresses linking the Canaanite plain and the hill country in the late Bronze Age and Iron Age, it functioned as a western defensive stronghold of the kingdom of Judah to stop the eastward advance of the Philistines.

remark: 4. A city of Benjamin.
introduce: Mizpah means a watchtower or lookout in Hebrew, and it is a place name used as a strategic stronghold of ancient Israel and as a place for religious and political assemblies. There are several places with the same name in the Bible, and the Mizpah mentioned in Judges 20 and 21 is thought to be a place located near the territory of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: All the children of Israel came out from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead and gathered as one man before the LORD at Mizpah (Judges 20:1). The Benjamites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah (Judges 20:3). The men of Israel swore an oath at Mizpah before the LORD that anyone who did not come up to Mizpah before the LORD would surely be put to death (Judges 21:1). When the Israelites gathered at Mizpah, they asked who among them had not taken part in the assembly of the LORD (Judges 21:5).
geography: There is a scholarly dispute about the exact location of the Mizpah that appears in the book of Judges. Traditionally Tell en-Nasbeh northwest of Jerusalem or the area of Nebi Samwil is mentioned as a candidate, but when the results of archaeological excavation and the geographical descriptions of the Bible are taken together, it is highly likely that it was a central highland located within the boundary of the tribe of Benjamin.
history: Mizpah in the period of the Judges served as an administrative center where the tribes of Israel assembled in order to resolve the crime of the tribe of Benjamin and the resulting war with the allied forces of Israel. This suggests that in the early Israelite confederation Mizpah functioned as a central sanctuary or a political base for national decision-making.

remark: 5. The district governed by Shallun.
introduce: Mizpah was one of the administrative districts of the Persian-period governorate of Judah (Yehud), a strategic administrative center that Shallun governed as district ruler.
biblecontents: Shallun son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate, roofing it and hanging its doors, with its bolts and bars, and repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah by the king's garden as far as the stairs that go down from the City of David (Nehemiah 3:15).
geography: It is a fortified highland located at Tell en-Nasbeh, about 12 km northwest of Jerusalem, and it controlled the north-south main road linking Jerusalem and Samaria.
history: It is the place where the governor Gedaliah established his headquarters after the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, and under the Persian Empire as well it continued to exist as the center of an administrative district, dispatching large numbers of laborers and supplies to Nehemiah's project of rebuilding the wall.

remark: 6. The district governed by Ezer son of Jeshua.
introduce: Mizpah was one of the administrative districts that took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, a subdistrict of Mizpah that Ezer son of Jeshua governed as one of its divided rulers.
biblecontents: Next to him Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section, extending to the point opposite the armory at the angle of the wall (Nehemiah 3:19).
geography: It is an administrative district embracing the city of Mizpah in the highland of Benjamin and the satellite villages around it. It was responsible for rebuilding a stretch of the wall on the northeastern side of Jerusalem adjacent to the military armory.
history: It shows that, in the Yehud community of the return from exile, the Mizpah region was a core administrative unit in which population and economic strength were concentrated to such a degree that it was divided among several leaders.

introduce: Fair Havens is a small port located on the south coast of the island of Crete in the Mediterranean, a place mentioned in Acts 27 as a stopover when Paul was being taken to Rome.
biblecontents: The ship carrying Paul sailed with difficulty along the coast and came to a place called Fair Havens, which is recorded as being near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:8). Afterward Paul advised that it was not suitable for wintering, but it was decided to continue the voyage (Acts 27:9-12).
geography: Fair Havens is identified with the Kaloi Limenes area on the southern part of the island of Crete in present-day Greece. Topographically it has a somewhat imperfect structure for sheltering from the north wind, and it was an open harbor with many risk factors for sailors of that time to use as a winter anchorage.
history: In the Roman period the island of Crete lay on a main sea route, and Fair Havens served as an intermediate supply stop through which ships transporting grain from Egypt to Rome passed. With the navigational skills of that time, sailing the rough Mediterranean after October was dangerous, so coastal ports such as Fair Havens were used as places where ships waited or anchored during the season of seasonal bad weather.

introduce: Migdal-el is one of the cities of the tribe of Naphtali mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a name that means "watchtower" in terms of its Hebrew etymology.
biblecontents: It is stated as one of the cities in the list of those obtained by lot by the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali recorded in Joshua 19:38 (Joshua 19:38).
geography: It was located within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, and given the topographical characteristics of the Galilee region, it is thought to have been a fortress formed on high ground advantageous for defense.

introduce: Migdal-gad is a region mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah. In Hebrew the name is a combination of migdal, meaning "watchtower," and gad, meaning "fortune."
biblecontents: It is a city mentioned together with Segen and Ibneel among the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah received according to their families (Joshua 15:37).
geography: It is thought to have been located on the plain classified as the Shephelah region among the inheritance of the tribe of Judah. Its exact location has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it is regarded as being somewhere in the plain region of southern present-day Palestine.

remark: 1. West of the Red Sea.
introduce: Migdol is a general name designating a watchtower or fortress in the ancient Near East, and in the Bible it appears as a particular place name on the route of the Exodus. In Hebrew it means a watchtower, and it is thought to have been a defensive installation located in the eastern border region of Egypt.
biblecontents: The Israelites turned back from Etham and camped opposite Baal-zephon, between Migdol and the sea (Exodus 14:2). It is also recorded that the Israelites left Etham, turned back to Pi-hahiroth in front of Baal-zephon, and camped before Migdol (Numbers 33:7).
geography: Migdol appears to be located near the Isthmus of Suez, in the northeastern border region of Egypt, and its exact location is disputed archaeologically. Some scholars regard the area of Tell el-Heir as a leading candidate, and this place is adjacent to the Way of Horus, the eastern line of defense of ancient Egypt.
history: In ancient Egyptian records as well, Migdol often appears as a term designating a border garrison or a border city. In sources from after the time of Pharaoh Merneptah, its function as a fortress guarding the border is emphasized, which suggests that it was a strategic stronghold that Egypt built at that time to keep out invaders coming from Asia.

remark: 2. A city in the northeast of Egypt, as seen from Palestine.
introduce: Migdol is a place name designating a strategic stronghold located in the northeastern border region of ancient Egypt, and in Hebrew it means a watchtower. It is a place that served as Egypt's line of defense and that appears in biblical records and archaeological documents.
biblecontents: It is mentioned that the Jews living in the land of Egypt were living in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and the region of Pathros of Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1). There is also a passage warning Egypt to proclaim in Migdol and to proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes that they will be surrounded by the enemy (Jeremiah 46:14). God spoke of the desolation of Egypt and prophesied that it would be made desolate from Migdol to Syene (Ezekiel 29:10). It was further recorded that those who support Egypt will fall, and that from Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword within her (Ezekiel 30:6).
geography: Migdol is located in the northeast of the Nile Delta of Egypt, that is, on the route leading from Egypt to Palestine. It is thought to be a gateway to ancient Egypt and a military border point for defending against the invasion of outside forces. In modern geographical research, the vicinity of Pelusium and Tell el-Heir north of the Suez Canal are named as leading candidates.
history: Migdol is an important border garrison stronghold that is also mentioned in ancient Egyptian records. In particular, in the time of Egypt's Twenty-sixth Dynasty, as Jews came there as refugees or came to live there, it functioned as one of the main settlements of northern Egypt. It is a historical place that was an area where the Egyptian dynasty was building lines of defense under the threat of Neo-Babylonian invasion, and where political exiles stayed.

introduce: Michmash is an ancient city located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, northeast of Jerusalem. As a strategic stronghold it is mentioned as an important point in the military confrontation between Israel and the Philistines, and it is also recorded as a place where the returning community lived after the exile.
biblecontents: Saul chose three thousand Israelites, two thousand of whom stayed with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel (1 Samuel 13:2). The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel, with thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and they went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). When Samuel did not come, Saul had the burnt offering brought and offered it himself (1 Samuel 13:11). Saul and his son Jonathan and the people with them were in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash (1 Samuel 13:16). A garrison of the Philistines had gone out to the pass of Michmash (1 Samuel 13:23). One cliff stood on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba (1 Samuel 14:5). On that day the people struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon (1 Samuel 14:31). The descendants of Michmash numbered one hundred and twenty-two (Ezra 2:27). The descendants of Michmash numbered one hundred and twenty-two (Nehemiah 7:31). The descendants of Benjamin lived in Geba, Michmash, Aija, Bethel, and their villages (Nehemiah 11:31).
geography: Michmash is identified with the present-day Palestinian village of Mukhmas. It lies about 11 km north of Jerusalem and sits on the northern ridge of Wadi Suweinit, a narrow, deep wadi. Topographically it adjoins a rugged valley and is advantageous for defense, and it is a strategic stronghold from which the central mountain road could be controlled.
history: In the early Iron Age Michmash served as an important military bridgehead in the struggle for supremacy between the kingdom of Israel and the Philistines. In the time of King Saul the Philistines used Michmash as a base to put pressure on Israel, and there was an event in which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made use of the rugged terrain of this region to launch a surprise attack on the Philistine garrison and turned the tide of the battle. Afterward, in the period of the return from the Babylonian exile, it is recorded as one of the resettlement places of the community of Judah, showing that the Jews lived once again in the land of their ancestors.

introduce: Michmethath is one of the points on the northern boundary of the tribe of Ephraim mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a geographical landmark set when the land was distributed to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The boundary of the inheritance that the descendants of Ephraim received begins at Ataroth-addar on the east, continues north, and reaches Michmethath on the west (Joshua 16:6).
geography: In modern geography Michmethath is thought to be the same place as the Mikmetas area near Shechem, which lies in the border zone where the inheritance of the tribe of Ephraim and that of the tribe of Manasseh meet.

introduce: Michmethath is a place name mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Bible, a region that appears in connection with the western boundary of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the boundary of Manasseh runs from Asher to Michmethath, and from there goes to the right and reaches the boundary of the inhabitants of En-tappuah (Joshua 17:7).
geography: Michmethath is thought to be located near Shechem, and it marks the geographical starting point at which the territory of the tribe of Manasseh begins from the northern border of Asher and extends southward as far as the vicinity of Shechem.

introduce: Minni is a name designating a state or tribal confederation that existed in the ancient Near East, and in the book of Jeremiah in the Bible it is mentioned as a member of the coalition that attacks Babylon.
biblecontents: Minni is mentioned, together with Ararat and Ashkenaz, as one of the kingdoms summoned against Babylon, and they received the command to attack Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27).
geography: Minni is thought to have been located historically in the region between present-day eastern Türkiye and northwestern Iran, specifically in the vicinity of the Zagros Mountains southeast of Lake Van.
history: In Assyrian inscriptions this region is recorded as Mannai, and it appears as a people that formed a power between the kingdom of Urartu and Assyria between the eighth and seventh centuries BC. Afterward they were absorbed into the Median kingdom or came under its influence, and at the time the Bible was written they were regarded as one of the military agents that, allied with Media, pressed upon Babylon.

introduce: Minnith is a place name located in the ancient region east of the Jordan, mentioned through the biblical record in connection with the territory of the Ammonites and their economic product, wheat.
biblecontents: When Jephthah struck the Ammonites, he struck twenty cities from Aroer to Minnith and inflicted a great slaughter on them (Judges 11:33). Judah and Israel traded with Tyre, and they made wheat from Minnith, cakes, honey, oil, and balm their items of trade (Ezekiel 27:17).
geography: Minnith was located in the Ammonite region east of the Jordan River and is thought to have been a fertile plain between Heshbon and Rabbah. It is a region connected to the main road network of the ancient Near East in which the production of agricultural products was active.

introduce: Miletus was a major port city in the ancient region of Ionia, a place that appears as an important base in the course of the apostle Paul's third missionary journey and his later ministry. It is a city located on the western coast of present-day Türkiye.
biblecontents: On his third missionary journey Paul left Assos, passed Chios and Samos, and arrived at Miletus (Acts 20:15). Paul summoned the elders of the church at Ephesus to Miletus and delivered a farewell address (Acts 20:17). Paul also stated, at the time of writing 2 Timothy, that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).
geography: Because of the silting action at the mouth of the Meander River, Miletus was a coastal port in ancient times, but it now lies about 10 km inland from the coastline. At that time it was a strategic stronghold of Ionia with four harbors, and being adjacent to the Aegean Sea, maritime trade was active.
history: Around the sixth century BC Miletus was famous as the birthplace of Ionian philosophy and was a cultural center that produced scholars such as Thales and Anaximander. It was rebuilt after the Persian Wars, and through the Hellenistic period and the time of the Roman Empire it prospered greatly economically and architecturally. In the time of the apostle Paul it was a city belonging to the Roman province of Asia and was carrying out lively urban functions.

remark: 1. A fortress near Shechem.
introduce: In the Bible the place name Millo is generally used as a proper noun designating a defensive installation of Jerusalem or a particular fortified place in the region of Shechem. The Millo mentioned in Judges 9 means a strategic stronghold or political base located in the center of Shechem.
biblecontents: All the people of Shechem and all the houses of Millo gathered beside the oak of the pillar at Shechem and made Abimelech king (Judges 9:6). Jotham proclaimed to Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and to the houses of Millo, that fire would come out and consume one another, and so criticized their conspiracy (Judges 9:20).
geography: Millo is thought to be a name symbolizing a fortress, or supporting forces, joined to the topographical features of Shechem. Given the structure of the city-states of the ancient Near East, Millo is quite likely to have meant a part of the wall or a structure on high ground within the city that was in charge of defense and administration.
history: Shechem in the period of the Judges was a place where political conflict between the Canaanites and the tribes of Israel was frequent. The Millo here is interpreted as a term used to symbolize the influential families of Shechem, the core forces that supported Abimelech in the course of his usurping the kingship, or as signifying the defensive installation in which they lived.

remark: 2. An area near Jerusalem that David and Solomon expanded, and the palace where Joash was killed.
introduce: Millo is a name designating a particular structure or defensive installation that was located in the City of David area of ancient Jerusalem. From the Hebrew etymology it carries the meaning of filling or filling in, and it is understood as a structure built up to level the slope of the terrain or to reinforce the foundation of the wall.
biblecontents: David lived in the stronghold and called it the City of David, and he built the city around it from Millo inward (2 Samuel 5:9). The reason King Solomon raised up forced labor was to build the house of the LORD, his own house, Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem (1 Kings 9:15). When Pharaoh's daughter came up from the City of David to her house that Solomon had built for her, Solomon built Millo (1 Kings 9:24). Solomon built Millo and repaired the breach in the city of his father David, and this is how he came to build Millo (1 Kings 11:27). The servants of King Joash rose up in conspiracy and killed him at the house of Millo on the road down to Silla (2 Kings 12:20). Joab began to repair the city, and Millo repaired the rest, and David built the city around on every side (1 Chronicles 11:8). Hezekiah took courage and repaired all the broken sections of the wall, raising it as high as the towers, and built another outer wall, and strengthened Millo in the City of David (2 Chronicles 32:5).
geography: Millo is thought to have been located on the northern slope of the City of David in Jerusalem or at the point where a valley begins. Because Jerusalem at that time had many steep slopes owing to its topographical characteristics, earthworks that filled the slopes with earth or stone to make level ground were essential in order to put up walls or expand residential areas. Archaeologically it is judged to be closely related to the terrain-reinforcing structures near the Ophel hill.
history: After conquering Jerusalem, David built Millo as part of the fortification work and so raised the city's defensive strength. Afterward Solomon enlarged and repaired Millo as a core project of strengthening royal authority and constructing the national infrastructure, and this played an important role in Jerusalem taking on the aspect of a royal capital. In the time of King Hezekiah, in the course of reorganizing the wall in preparation for the Assyrian invasion, Millo is mentioned once again as a military stronghold. This structure functioned as one of the most essential civil engineering facilities in the defense system of the capital of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

introduce: Mibzar is recorded both as one of the chiefs of Edom and as the name of the territory they governed. It is a place name that appears in the course of setting out the genealogy of the chiefs who lived in the land of Edom.
biblecontents: Mibzar is mentioned as one of the chiefs of Edom, and the chiefs of Edom were recorded according to their dwelling places and names (Genesis 36:42). First Chronicles likewise lists the genealogy of the chiefs of Edom and includes Mibzar (1 Chronicles 1:53).
history: Mibzar is both the name of a leader who governed a particular district within the chieftain system of Edom and the name of the district he governed. The biblical record is part of a historical genealogy showing the early governing structure of the Edomite tribes founded by the descendants of Esau and the extent of their power.

introduce: Mithkah is one of the places the Israelites passed through on their wilderness journey after the exodus from Egypt, a place name located on the route from Hazeroth toward Ezion-geber.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Terah and camped at Mithkah (Numbers 33:28). They left Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah (Numbers 33:29).

introduce: Middin is one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the six towns belonging to the wilderness among the towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:61).
geography: It lies in the wilderness of Judah and, geographically, is thought to be a barren zone near En-gedi, adjacent to the northern part of the western shore of the Dead Sea.

introduce: Barnea is an area called Kadesh-barnea, a strategic stronghold that the people of Israel passed through after the exodus before entering the promised land in biblical history.
biblecontents: It was an eleven-day journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:2). At the command of the LORD, the people of Israel left Horeb and passed through the great and terrible wilderness and came to Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:19). It took thirty-eight years from leaving Kadesh-barnea until crossing the Brook of Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14). At Kadesh-barnea the people of Israel rebelled against the command of the LORD, did not believe Him, and did not listen to His word (Deuteronomy 9:23).
geography: Kadesh-barnea lies on the southern edge of the Negev desert and the northeastern border of the Sinai Peninsula, and with its abundant oases and springs it served as an essential base for settlement and travel in the arid zone of the ancient Near East.
history: From the Bronze Age this area played an important role as a trade route and a military route linking Canaan and Egypt, and it was the historical stage on which Israel, ahead of the wars of the conquest of Canaan, dispatched the spies or stayed for a long period and reorganized its tribal system.

introduce: Patara was a city located on the coast of the ancient region of Lycia, a port city mentioned in the book of Acts as a stopover on the journey of the apostle Paul returning to Jerusalem after completing his third missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul's party left the island of Cos, and the next day came to Rhodes, and from there to Patara (Acts 21:1). At Patara they found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, boarded it, and traveled toward Jerusalem (Acts 21:2).
geography: Patara is a major port city at the mouth of the Xanthos River in the region of Lycia in southwestern Asia Minor. It is adjacent to the Mediterranean Sea and served as a passage connecting with the inland city of Xanthos. The modern place name corresponds to the Gelemiş area of Türkiye.
history: In the Hellenistic period it flourished as one of the centers of the Lycian League, and in the time of the Roman Empire it developed into an administrative stronghold where the governor of the province of Lycia and Pamphylia resided and into a major maritime trade port. It was also known in the ancient world as a religious center with a temple of Apollo.

introduce: Parthia was a region in the northeast of the ancient Persian Empire, an ancient name designating the Khorasan province in the northeast of modern Iran and the surrounding area.
biblecontents: It is recorded that among the Jewish pilgrims who visited Jerusalem at Pentecost were Parthians (Acts 2:9).
geography: It is an inland plateau region lying southeast of the Caspian Sea, bordering Media on the west and Bactria on the east.
history: Parthia was originally one of the provinces of Achaemenid Persia, and later, after passing through the Seleucid Empire, it became the region where the Parthian Empire arose.

introduce: Pathros is the Hebrew name designating the region of Upper Egypt in ancient Egypt, and it derives from the Hebrew Patros. It means the territory that includes the upper Nile valley and its surroundings, and in the Bible it was used to indicate a particular administrative district or regional extent of Egypt.
biblecontents: It was prophesied that the LORD would again recover the remnant of Israel from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, and other places (Isaiah 11:11). The word came concerning all the Judeans living in the land of Egypt, in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and the region of Pathros (Jeremiah 44:1). Also, when Jeremiah proclaimed the judgment of God to all the people living in the region of Pathros, all the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, and the great assembly standing by, answered (Jeremiah 44:15). God said He would bring the captives of Egypt back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin, but that it would become a lowly kingdom there (Ezekiel 29:14). He warned that He would lay waste Pathros, send fire upon Zoan, and execute judgment on No (Ezekiel 30:14).
geography: Pathros means the region of Upper Egypt, which is distinguished from Lower Egypt, the delta region of the lower Nile. Geographically it refers to the highland valley stretching south along the Nile, including modern Luxor and Thebes, and it borders Nubia (Cush) to the south.
history: This region was one of the political centers in the period of the 25th Dynasty of ancient Egypt, and it is one of the places where Jews who fled the Babylonian invasion after the fall of the kingdom of Judah settled. In particular, the record of the book of Jeremiah shows that a Jewish community had formed in the Pathros region around the sixth century BC, which suggests that Egypt at that time was politically divided, or that the Jews were scattered and living throughout Egypt.

introduce: Parah is one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel, a place name mentioned in Joshua 18:23.
biblecontents: Parah is included in the list of towns of the inheritance that the descendants of Benjamin obtained by lot, listed in Joshua 18:21-28 (Joshua 18:23).
geography: Parah is thought to have been located in the hill country north of Jerusalem, the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, but its exact modern archaeological location has not been identified. Nearby places such as Avvim, Bethel, and Ophrah are mentioned together with it (Joshua 18:23).

introduce: Paran is a vast wilderness region lying across the northeast of the Sinai Peninsula and the south of the Negev desert, and it holds historical and geographical importance as a route of movement for the ancient people of Israel and as a dwelling place of the surrounding peoples.
biblecontents: Hagar lived in the wilderness of Paran with her son Ishmael, and there he took a wife (Genesis 21:21). The Israelites left Mount Sinai and stayed in the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 10:12). The people left Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 12:16). God sent men at the LORD's command from the wilderness of Paran to spy out the land of Canaan, through Moses (Numbers 13:3). The spies came to Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran and reported to Moses and Aaron (Numbers 13:26). Moses proclaimed the law to Israel beyond the Jordan, between Paran and Tophel (Deuteronomy 1:1). The LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir, and shone forth from Mount Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2). After Samuel died, David went down to the wilderness of Paran (1 Samuel 25:1). Hadad the Edomite left Midian, came to Paran, and from there took men with him and went to Egypt (1 Kings 11:18). God came from Mount Paran, and His glory covered the heavens (Habakkuk 3:3).
geography: Paran is an arid plateau region bordering the Arabah valley on the east, the mountain region of the Sinai Peninsula on the south, and the Negev desert on the north. By present-day geographical divisions it is understood as an area that includes the Tih mountain range in the northern Sinai Peninsula, and a water-scarce, barren wilderness environment predominates.
history: Paran played an important role as a major stopping place that the people of Israel passed through in the process of advancing toward Canaan at the time of the exodus. It was also used as a passage by which various tribes of the ancient Near East traveled or traded, and it is mentioned as a strategic stronghold that neighboring peoples such as Edom passed through at times of political exile or migration.

introduce: Bamoth-baal was an ancient place name located on the plains of Moab, thought to have been a place where there was a high place or an altar for the worship of the god Baal. It is mentioned as one of the areas distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben.
biblecontents: Heshbon and all its cities on the plateau, Dibon, Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon were allotted as the inheritance of the descendants of Reuben (Joshua 13:17). There is also a record that the people of Israel came to Bamoth during their journey in the wilderness (Numbers 21:19).
geography: It is thought to be located in the region of present-day Jordan, and is identified as a plateau region near Heshbon and Medeba. Because it carries the meaning of a high place for Baal, it was very likely a place of worship formed on high ground or on a hill.
history: Bamoth-baal is considered to be the same place as Bamoth, one of the places to which Balak, king of Moab, took Balaam and went up in order to curse Israel. Afterward this region was the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and after Israel's wars of conquest it was allotted to the tribe of Reuben.

introduce: Bashan and Gilead are regions located east of the Jordan River, and in 1 Chronicles 5:16 of the Bible the geographical connection of these regions and the extent of settlement of the descendants of Gad who lived there are mentioned.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad lived in Bashan and Gilead and their villages and in all the pasturelands of Sharon, and they lived throughout the neighborhood of those places (1 Chronicles 5:16).
geography: Bashan is a fertile volcanic plateau region corresponding to present-day southwestern Syria and northeastern Jordan, and it is a region suited to raising livestock. Gilead is a mountainous region stretching north and south centered on the Jabbok River, located south of Bashan, and it is a region where abundant forests and farmland developed.
history: Bashan and Gilead were originally the domains ruled by Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, but after Israel's wars of conquest east of the Jordan they were distributed as the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
