At the time of the writing of the Chronicles, the record shows that these regions had come to form clear boundaries and a governing structure at the level of villages as the dwelling places of the tribes.

introduce: Argob in Bashan was part of the kingdom of Bashan, located in the region east of the Jordan River, and it is a region mentioned in the Bible in connection with the expansion of Israel's territory and its administrative districts.
biblecontents: It was the region under the jurisdiction of Ben-geber, one of King Solomon's twelve administrative districts, and in the region of Argob in Bashan there were sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars (1 Kings 4:13). In the time of Moses, Israel distributed this region to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 3:13).
geography: It is thought to be the Leja region, a volcanic rock zone spanning present-day northern Jordan and southern Syria. This is rugged terrain made of black basalt, and it has geographical characteristics suited to serving as a natural fortress.
history: It was originally the domain ruled by Og, king of Bashan, but after Israel's victory in the battle of Edrei it was incorporated under Israelite rule. Afterward, in the time of Solomon, under a centralized administrative system, it was managed as a major base for collecting taxes.

introduce: Pas-dammim is a place name that appears in 1 Chronicles 11:13 of the Old Testament, and it is known as the place where David's mighty men fought the Philistines. In 2 Samuel 23:9 the same place name is recorded as Ephes-dammim.
biblecontents: When they gathered at Pas-dammim to fight the Philistines together with David, there was a small plot of ground there with a field of barley, and the people fled before the Philistines, but Eleazar, one of David's mighty men, stood in the midst of that field, struck down the Philistines, and won the victory (1 Chronicles 11:13).
geography: Pas-dammim is thought to have been located near the Valley of Elah in the territory of the tribe of Judah. The Valley of Elah is a strategic stronghold connecting the plains of the Philistines and the hill country of Judah, and topographically it contains fertile soil suited to growing grain.
history: Pas-dammim corresponds to a border region where territorial disputes between Israel and the Philistines were frequent. According to the biblical record, this region was a place where military confrontations occurred frequently, and it appears as a major battlefield especially in the process of defending against the invasion of Philistine forces in the early part of David's reign.

introduce: Baal is one of the towns of the tribe of Simeon mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:33 of the Bible, and it means a settlement located in the southern region.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns where the tribe of Simeon lived until the time of King David, and it is recorded as being called Baal and also as Baalath-beer (1 Chronicles 4:33).
geography: Baal is thought to be located in the Negev region, the southern area around Beersheba, and it lies near the southern boundary of the land allotted to the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:33).

introduce: Baal-hermon is an ancient place name located in the vicinity of the southern part of Mount Hermon, a name designating a mountain connected with the worship of Baal, the god of Canaan, or a dwelling place in that region.
biblecontents: The Hivites, one of the peoples that the Israelites left in the land of Canaan to test Israel, lived from Mount Baal-hermon as far as the entrance of Hamath (Judges 3:3).
geography: It refers to the area of the southern slopes of Mount Hermon and lies on an extension of the Anti-Lebanon range, in the border region of present-day Lebanon and Syria. Because of its high altitude this area forms abundant sources of water, and in ancient society it was regarded as a religious center or a border region.
history: Baal-hermon is presumed to be a place name derived from a religious center where Baal, the Canaanite god of storm and rain, was served. At the time of the conquest of Canaan this region was occupied by the Hivite clans, and because of its geographical character it was a strategic stronghold toward northern Canaan and Mesopotamia, where the movement and occupation of various peoples were frequent.

introduce: Baal-gad is an ancient place name located at the foot of Mount Hermon beneath the Lebanon range, a region mentioned as the northern boundary point at the time of Joshua's wars of conquest in Canaan.
biblecontents: The northern end of the region Joshua captured, the extent of the conquest was from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, to Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon (Joshua 11:17). It is confirmed again as the northern boundary point in the list of kings Joshua conquered west of the Jordan (Joshua 12:7). In describing the unconquered territory that Israel still had to conquer, Baal-gad below Mount Baal-hermon is also mentioned (Joshua 13:5).
geography: Baal-gad is thought to be the northern end of the Beqaa Valley, which lies between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, or the southwestern foot of Mount Hermon. It became the geographical reference point fixing the northern boundary of the land of Canaan, and it is a strategic stronghold connected with the major trade routes of the ancient Near East.
history: The word Baal included in the name suggests that it was a place where the Canaanite god Baal was worshiped. It appears to have been a place where the northern Canaanite coalition forces gathered or built a defensive line at the time of the wars of conquest, and afterward it came to carry the meaning of a boundary of the northern region over which Israel's actual rule did not extend.

introduce: Baal-tamar is a place name mentioned as the place where the Israelite army lay in ambush in order to surround Benjamin during the civil war between the tribes of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: All the men of Israel rose from their places and arrayed themselves at Baal-tamar, and the ambush of Israel charged out from its place, the meadow of Gibeah (Judges 20:33).
geography: It is thought to be located near Gibeah, a town of the tribe of Benjamin. Its specific archaeological location is not clear, but topographically it is interpreted as a place in the form of a meadow or level ground where an ambush was possible.
history: At the time of the civil war of Gibeah in Judges 20, it was used as a military assembly point and an ambush site when the allied forces of Israel set a strategic lure against the tribe of Benjamin.

remark: 1. A town of Judah, the same as Kiriath-jearim.
introduce: Baalah is an ancient Israelite place name, a region located on the northern boundary line of the tribe of Judah and known as the place where the ark of the covenant stayed for a time. This place is interpreted as being used interchangeably with the name Kiriath-jearim or as designating the same region.
biblecontents: The boundary ran from the spring of Nephtoah to the cities of Mount Ephron and reached Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim (Joshua 15:9). David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim of Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim, the ark that is called by that name (1 Chronicles 13:6).
geography: Baalah is a strategic stronghold located near the boundary of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin. Topographically it lies to the west or northwest of Jerusalem, and being situated at a passage where the hill country and the plain connect, it served as a center of traffic.
history: It was originally one of the towns of the Gibeonites, and it is the place where the ark of the covenant that had returned from the Philistines was kept for a considerable time before David moved it to Jerusalem. In the biblical record it appears as an important point in the setting of boundaries connected with fixing the territory of the tribe of Judah and in the process of moving the ark in the early part of David's reign.

remark: 2. A town on the southern boundary line of Judah.
introduce: Baalah is a place name located on the northern boundary of the ancient tribe of Judah, and it appears as an important geographical starting point in the process of fixing the boundary lines mentioned in Joshua 15. This place name is also identified with Mount Baalah or Kiriath-jearim.
biblecontents: Baalah lies on the boundary that turns west from Mount Seir, comes to the side of Mount Jearim, that is, Chesalon, goes down to Beth-shemesh, passes Timna, and proceeds north of Dan (Joshua 15:10). It also lies on the boundary line that goes out to the slope of Ekron on the north, passes Shikkeron, passes through Mount Baalah, and reaches Jabneel (Joshua 15:11).
geography: Baalah is located at the northern boundary point of the territory of the tribe of Judah and is thought to be connected with the area near present-day Tel el-Azar. It serves as a topographical buffer zone leading from the hill country to the Shephelah plain.

remark: 3. A town in the south of Judah.
introduce: Baalah is one of the towns of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua 15, a place name that, by geographical location, belongs to the group of towns in southern Judah.
biblecontents: Baalah is mentioned in the list of the southern towns distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:29).
geography: Baalah is thought to be a town located on the Negev plain, the southern border region of the tribe of Judah. Archaeologically it is analyzed as having been distributed, together with the surrounding towns listed in Joshua 15:29, near Beersheba or in the arid zone to its south.

introduce: Baalath-beer is a place name appearing in the record of Joshua in the Old Testament, one of the towns located on the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Simeon. This place, thought to be located in the southern Negev region, is mentioned as one of the bases around Beersheba.
biblecontents: The inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Simeon received by their clans consisted of their towns and the villages around them, and their towns were Beersheba, that is, Sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen towns and their villages—and also Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four towns—and all the villages around those towns, as far as Baalath-beer, that is, Ramah of the Negev; this was the inheritance the tribe of the descendants of Simeon received by their clans (Joshua 19:2-8).
geography: Baalath-beer is understood to lie in the area south of Beersheba. The name carries the meaning "spring of Baal," and it is interpreted as a point where securing water resources was easy in the arid Negev, or a strategic stronghold on an important traffic route. In the biblical text it is referred to as being the same place as Ramah, one of the southernmost boundary points or bases of the Negev region, or as its vicinity.

introduce: Baale of Judah is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, a place mentioned in the time of King David in connection with moving the ark of God to Jerusalem. In the Bible this place name is regarded as another name for Kiriath-jearim.
biblecontents: David arose and went with all the people who were with him to Baale of Judah to bring up from there the ark of God (2 Samuel 6:2).
geography: Baale of Judah was located within the territory of the tribe of Judah and is generally identified with present-day Kiriath-jearim. It is a plateau region west of Jerusalem, known as an area adjacent to Gibeah, the place where the ark of God stayed for a long time before it was moved to the house of Obed-edom.
history: In 2 Samuel 6 this region is called Baale of Judah, but in 1 Chronicles 13:6 the same place is called Kiriath-jearim or Baalah. This is an example showing that in ancient Near Eastern place names the word Baal was used in combination with the divinity of a region or its topographical characteristics. David's attempt to bring the ark from here was a move to secure religious legitimacy in the process of shifting the political center of Israel to Jerusalem.

introduce: Baal-perazim is a place name that in Hebrew carries the meaning "lord of breaking through" or "Baal of the breakthrough." It is an area that David named to commemorate the place after he won a victory over the Philistine army.
biblecontents: David came to Baal-perazim and struck them there, and David said, "The LORD has scattered my enemies before me like a breaking out of waters"; therefore he called the name of that place Baal-perazim (2 Samuel 5:20). The people went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them there, and David said, "God has scattered my enemies by my hand like a breaking out of waters"; therefore the people called the name of that place Baal-perazim (1 Chronicles 14:11).
geography: It is an area thought to be located in the Valley of Rephaim. The Valley of Rephaim lies southwest of Jerusalem and has the topographical feature of including a gentle slope between Bethlehem and Jerusalem.
history: This was the time when, after David was anointed king of Israel, the Philistines, wary of this, camped in the Valley of Rephaim in order to attack David. David repulsed the Philistines in this battle, and later, when the Philistines attacked again at the same place, he won again. This name is an example in which David's military victory was made a proper noun by embodying a topographical meaning.

introduce: Baal-peor is a place name located in the land of Moab, designating the place where there was a high place for serving Baal, the god of Canaan. In Hebrew it is called Baal Peor, which carries the meaning "the Baal of Peor."
biblecontents: When the people of Israel stayed at Shittim during their wilderness journey, they joined themselves to Baal-peor, and there occurred the incident of eating food sacrificed to foreign gods and worshiping idols (Numbers 25:3). The prophet Hosea said that when He found Israel in the wilderness, they went to Baal-peor and devoted themselves to the shameful idol (Hosea 9:10).
geography: Baal-peor means a mountain, or the area around it, located on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan, and it is thought to be a region connected with Mount Peor near Mount Nebo. Its exact location has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it appears to have been a major center of faith in Moab.
history: Baal-peor was a place where Baal, a god symbolizing fertility and fecundity in the ancient Near East, was worshiped. The worship rites in this area took a very licentious and morally corrupt form, and the Bible records the historical circumstances in which the people of Israel, before entering the land of Canaan, came to be connected with the religious culture of this region through contact with Moabite women.

introduce: Baal-shalishah is a place name appearing in 2 Kings 4:42 of the Bible, a place presumed to mean in Hebrew "the region of Baal" or "the lord of Shalishah."
biblecontents: A man from Baal-shalishah brought twenty loaves of barley bread and vegetables in a sack to Elisha the man of God (2 Kings 4:42).
geography: Baal-shalishah is presumed to be located near the plain of Sharon or in the area west of the hill country of Ephraim, and the prevailing theory identifies it with present-day Kafr Tilt or its vicinity.

introduce: Baal-zephon is a place name appearing in the records of Exodus and Numbers, one of the places where the Israelites camped just before they escaped from Egypt and crossed the Red Sea. The meaning of the name is interpreted as the manifestation of the god Baal, or a place under the protection of Baal.
biblecontents: The Israelites received God's instruction to camp by the sea opposite Migdol and Baal-zephon (Exodus 14:2). The Egyptian army pursued the Israelites and reached them at their camp by the sea opposite Baal-zephon (Exodus 14:9). The Israelites left Etham and turned back to Pi-hahiroth in front of Baal-zephon and camped in front of Migdol (Numbers 33:7).
geography: There are various theories about its exact location, but it is generally presumed to be near Pelusium north of the Suez Canal, or in the vicinity of the Isthmus of Suez, the northeastern border region of ancient Egypt. In ancient times it was a strategic stronghold bordering the sea and adjacent to Egypt's eastern boundary line of defense.
history: Baal-zephon is connected with Baal, the Canaanite god worshiped in the ancient Near East, which suggests that in the Egyptian border region at that time there was a temple or settlement where a god of West Asian origin was worshiped. In the period of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, this region very likely had military facilities connected with border guarding.

introduce: Baal-hamon is a place name mentioned as the place where Solomon entrusted his vineyard.
biblecontents: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon, and he entrusted the vineyard to those who kept it, so that each was to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit (Song of Solomon 8:11).
geography: There are many differing opinions about the specific location. Some scholars presume it to be Belameh near Samaria, or an area near En-gedi, but solid archaeological evidence is lacking.

introduce: Baal-hazor is a place located on the border of Ephraim, a place name recorded in biblical history as the place where Absalom held the sheepshearing festival.
biblecontents: After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons (2 Samuel 13:23).
geography: Baal-hazor lies in the hill country of Ephraim, and the prevailing view identifies it with the area of present-day Tell Asur. This area is about 18 km north of Jerusalem and corresponds to one of the highest points in the hill country of Ephraim.

introduce: Baal-hermon is a biblical place name designating a region located near Mount Hermon. It is mentioned as one of the northern boundary points of ancient Israelite territory, and it is understood as a place where traces of Baal faith connected with Mount Hermon remain.
biblecontents: The descendants of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived from Bashan as far as Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon, and their numbers increased (1 Chronicles 5:23).
geography: It is located on the southern foot of Mount Hermon, on the northeastern part of the present-day Golan Heights or on an extension of the Lebanon range. Because of the characteristics of its highland terrain, it has abundant dew and more rainfall than the surrounding areas, and it has climatic conditions favorable to farming and herding.
history: The place name Baal-hermon suggests that a high place or altar where Baal, the Canaanite god of storm and fertility, was worshiped existed in that region. After the period of Israel's conquest, the half-tribe of Manasseh took the northern region east of the Jordan and it came within Israel's sphere of influence, but originally it lay within the sphere of power of the Canaanite Amorite clans and the inhabitants of the Hermon mountain region.

introduce: Baharum is an ancient Israelite place name, mentioned as the region designating the hometown of Azmaveth, one of the mighty men of King David.
biblecontents: Azmaveth the Baharumite is included in the list of David's thirty mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:33).
geography: Baharum is presumed to be the same place as the region recorded as Bahurim in other passages of the Bible, and it is a town of the tribe of Benjamin located on the road east of Jerusalem, beyond the Mount of Olives, toward the wilderness of Judah.
history: Bahurim is the place where Shimei cursed David when David left Jerusalem to escape the rebellion of his son Absalom, and it is a strategic stronghold where David's servants, evading Absalom's scouts, hid in a well. Baharum is understood to be a geographical variant spelling of this region.

introduce: Paddan-aram is a place name designating the region of Upper Mesopotamia in the ancient Near East, and in Aramaic it was called Aram-naharaim or Padan-aram. This region was the main base where Abraham's family lived, and it forms an important spatial setting in biblical history for the marriages and settlement of the patriarchs.
biblecontents: At the age of forty Isaac took as his wife Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean (Genesis 25:20). Afterward it was the place to which Jacob fled to meet his maternal uncle Laban, and there he took wives, had children, and lived (Genesis 28:2, Genesis 31:18).
geography: Paddan-aram means the area of the plain of Haran, located in the border region of present-day northeastern Syria and southeastern Türkiye. It is a fertile semi-arid zone on the upper Euphrates, and in ancient times it was a grassland where herding and farming were possible, with a smooth supply of water around Haran and Nahor.
history: This region was the stage of activity of the Amorites and Arameans of ancient Mesopotamia. In the middle of the second millennium BC, Haran served as a commercial center as a strategic point on trade routes, and as the Aramean tribes gradually settled, it was incorporated into the Aramean cultural sphere. In particular, the figures of the patriarchal period maintained blood relations in this region and continued close exchange with the house of Abraham.

introduce: Paddan-aram is a name designating the plain region centered on Haran on the upper Euphrates in northern Mesopotamia, within the ancient Near East. In Aramaic it carries the meaning "field of Aram" or "plain."
biblecontents: Isaac instructed Jacob to go to Paddan-aram to seek a wife (Genesis 28:2). Jacob left for Paddan-aram at the command of Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 28:5, Genesis 28:6, Genesis 28:7). There he married the daughters of Laban, had children, gathered livestock, and returned to the land of Canaan (Genesis 31:18). Jacob returned from Paddan-aram and settled in the city of Shechem (Genesis 33:18), and God appeared again to Jacob, who had returned from Paddan-aram, and blessed him (Genesis 35:9). The sons of Jacob were born in Paddan-aram (Genesis 35:26, Genesis 46:15).
geography: Paddan-aram is regarded as the same region as Padan-aram, a fertile area on the upper Euphrates. From the standpoint of modern geography it indicates a region that includes the Haran area of present-day southeastern Türkiye. This area is a plain through which rivers flow, and it has an environment suited to farming and herding.
history: In the early and middle part of the second millennium BC, northern Mesopotamia and the Syrian region were an area of frequent movements of Hurrians and Arameans. This region was a strategic point on trade routes and had formed a social structure centered on city-states. The biblical record suggests that this region was the base of the Aramean people, who at that time had a close relationship, linguistic and kinship, with the region of Canaan.

introduce: Geba of Benjamin is a town located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel, a place used as a strategic stronghold and a military base.
biblecontents: Saul and his son Jonathan stayed in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash (1 Samuel 13:16).
geography: It is presumed to be near the present-day village of Jaba. It lies on high ground facing Michmash across the Michmash wadi, and it has the topographical feature of being able to control the route of entry into Jerusalem.
history: In the early period of the kingdom of Israel it became a center of military clashes in the conflict between King Saul and the Philistines, and because of its geographical importance it is a town that often appears afterward in border disputes between southern Judah and northern Israel and in the building of defensive lines.

introduce: Gibeah of Benjamin is a place name of ancient Israel appearing in the Old Testament, mentioned as a main stronghold and strategic point of the Israelite army in the time of King Saul. It was also Saul's hometown and served as the political center of the early kingdom of Israel.
biblecontents: Saul chose two thousand men to be with him and stay at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and his son Jonathan stayed in Gibeah of Benjamin (1 Samuel 13:2). Saul and Jonathan and the people with them stayed in Gibeah of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash (1 Samuel 13:15). Saul's watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin looked and saw the Philistines scattering here and there (1 Samuel 14:16).
geography: Gibeah of Benjamin is presumed to be present-day Tell el-Ful, a highland located about 5 km north of Jerusalem. As a military stronghold from which the surrounding plains and road network can be seen at a glance, this area has topographical features of high elevation that are advantageous for defense and observation.
history: It was the area Saul made his base after he took the throne as king, and in the course of the war with the Philistines it served as an assembly point and an outpost for the Israelite army. Afterward it functioned as a political center during Israel's process of centralization, but after the time of David, as the political center of gravity moved to Jerusalem, its importance gradually changed.

introduce: Bethlehem Ephrathah is an ancient town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah; in its early period it was called Ephrath or Ephrathah, and afterward it came to be identified with Bethlehem of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the residence where Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their two sons lived before they moved to the land of Moab (Ruth 1:2). Also, Jesse, the father of David, is recorded as an Ephrathite from this town (1 Samuel 17:12).
geography: It lies in the hill country of Judah about 8 km south of Jerusalem, and, being higher in elevation than the surrounding area, it is advantageous for defense and has abundant springs and fertile soil.
history: Traces of human habitation have been found from the Bronze Age, and after the conquest of Canaan it became settled as one of the main bases of the tribe of Judah. In the Hebrew Bible it was valued as the ancestral home of the house of David and as a place symbolizing the identity of the tribe of Judah.

introduce: Perez-uzzah is a name designating the place where Uzzah was struck down in the course of David's moving the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. In Hebrew this place name carries the meaning "the breach of Uzzah" or "the gap" (1 Chronicles 13:11).
biblecontents: When David was bringing up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim, the oxen stumbled near the threshing floor of Nacon, and Uzzah put out his hand and took hold of the ark. Then the LORD struck Uzzah, and he died there before God (1 Chronicles 13:11). Because of this incident, David called that place Perez-uzzah, since the LORD had struck Uzzah (1 Chronicles 13:11).
geography: Perez-uzzah is presumed to be near the threshing floor of Nacon, located between Kiriath-jearim and Jerusalem. Its exact modern place name is disputed archaeologically, but it is understood to have been a specific place along the route of travel in the hill country west of Jerusalem.
history: This was an incident that occurred during a national event in which David, in the early days of the Davidic kingdom, sought to establish his authority over Israel and to install the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem, the political center of the kingdom. The way the ark was transported at that time was not the way stipulated in the law of Moses, in which the Levites carry it on their shoulders, but a way using a cart pulled by oxen (1 Chronicles 13:7).

introduce: Perez-uzzah is the name David gave to the place after the incident in which Uzzah took hold of the ark of God and was struck down while David was moving the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, and in Hebrew it carries the meaning "He struck Uzzah" (2 Samuel 6:8).
biblecontents: Because the LORD tore Uzzah's body, David called that place Perez-uzzah, and that name remains to this day (2 Samuel 6:8).
geography: Perez-uzzah is presumed to be near the threshing floor of Nacon, located on the route from Kiriath-jearim toward Jerusalem, but the exact point has not been identified by modern archaeology (2 Samuel 6:6).
history: King David wished to move the ark of the covenant in order to establish Jerusalem as the religious center of Israel, and this is a place name connected with the accident that occurred in the process, when the ark was being carried on a new cart instead of following the manner stipulated in the law, in which the Levites carry it on their shoulders (2 Samuel 6:3-8).

introduce: Beth-tappuah was one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place mentioned in the biblical lists of place names.
biblecontents: In Joshua 15:53 it is recorded as part of the list of hill-country towns distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:53).
geography: It is presumed to have been located on the plateau of the hill country of Judah southwest of Hebron. It is classified as an independent town distinct from Tappuah, a nearby area of that time.

introduce: Beth-barah is a place name near the Jordan River mentioned in the book of Judges in the Old Testament, designating the Jordan crossing point and watercourse that the tribe of Ephraim seized in the operation of pursuing Midian.
biblecontents: Gideon sent messengers throughout the whole hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down and strike the Midianites, and get ahead of them to the Jordan River and seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan," and so all the men of Ephraim gathered and seized the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan (Judges 7:24).
geography: Beth-barah is presumed to be one of the main crossing points linking the east and west sides of the Jordan River, and it is a strategic stronghold adjacent to the watercourse that the Midianite army had to cross in its flight. Its exact location is disputed archaeologically, but it is regarded as a ford in the middle or lower reaches of the Jordan River.
history: After the judge Gideon's victory in the battle with Midian, in order to cut off the fleeing Midianite army he ordered the tribe of Ephraim to take control of Beth-barah, a strategic stronghold, and the waters of the Jordan River. This was a military measure to block the escape route and prevent the enemy from returning to its homeland.

introduce: Beth-baal-meon is an ancient town located near the plains of Moab east of the Jordan, a place name presumed to have been the site of a temple for Baal. Also called Meon or Baal-meon, it is one of the areas the tribe of Reuben captured and lived in.
biblecontents: Beth-baal-meon is mentioned in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Reuben after Israel conquered the region east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:17). Afterward this town often appears as an area of territorial dispute between Moab and Israel, and in the book of Jeremiah it is recorded as a town of Moab that became an object of judgment (Jeremiah 48:23).
geography: It is identified with the Main area near present-day Madaba in Jordan. This area lies south of Heshbon, and as a fertile plateau region it has an environment suited to grazing livestock or farming.
history: It was originally the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, but after Israel's conquest it became the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben. However, because of its geographical character, the kingdom of Moab often recaptured this region, and the inscription of Mesha, king of Moab, the Mesha Stele, also preserves a record that he rebuilt this town, proving that it was a strategic stronghold between Israel and Moab.

remark: 1. A village in the northern part of the boundary of the tribe of Judah.
introduce: Beth-shemesh is a place name meaning "house of the sun" in Hebrew, an ancient town located in the territory of the tribe of Judah. Archaeologically it is identified with the site of Tel er-Rumeilah near Tel es-Safi.
biblecontents: In Joshua's distribution it was mentioned as a point on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:10). Afterward it was designated as a town allotted to the descendants of Kohath of the tribe of Levi and as one of the towns where priests lived (Joshua 21:16).
geography: Located on the southern slope of the Sorek Valley, it is a strategic stronghold linking the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain. Bordering the Philistine plain on the west, it served geographically as a buffer zone.
history: It is a site where traces of continuous habitation are found from the Late Bronze Age to the Iron Age because of its strategic importance. This area was a border zone where struggles for power between the Philistines and Israel were frequent, and archaeological excavations confirm a pattern of cultural mixing among the Canaanites, Israelites, and Philistines of that time.

remark: 2. A town in the border region of the tribe of Issachar.
introduce: Beth-shemesh is a place name meaning "house of the sun" in Hebrew, and several places in the Bible share the same name. The Beth-shemesh mentioned in Joshua 19:22 is a town located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar.
biblecontents: Beth-shemesh is mentioned as one of the inheritances distributed to the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:22).
geography: It lies within the boundary of the tribe of Issachar and is described as the region reaching Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh (Joshua 19:22). It is presumed to be adjacent to the plain of the lower Galilee region.

remark: 3. A town of the tribe of Naphtali.
introduce: Beth-shemesh is a place name meaning "house of the sun" in Hebrew, a town that functioned as a strategic stronghold in the ancient Canaanite and Israelite periods.
biblecontents: In Joshua 19:38 it is mentioned as one of the list of towns distributed to the tribe of Naphtali (Joshua 19:38).
geography: It was located within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali and is presumed to be a town reflecting the topographical characteristics of the Galilee region. It is a place distinct from the other Beth-shemesh in the territory of the tribe of Judah.

remark: 4. An Egyptian temple, presumed to be the same place as On or Heliopolis.
introduce: Beth-shemesh is an ancient Egyptian religious city appearing in Jeremiah 43 in the Old Testament, the center of the temple of the sun god, called Heliopolis in Greek and On in Genesis in the Bible.
biblecontents: It was proclaimed that he would also break the stone pillars of Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt and burn the shrines of the Egyptian gods (Jeremiah 43:13).
geography: It is located in the El-Matariya and Ain Shams areas on the outskirts of northeastern Cairo, modern Egypt, on the east side of the southern end of the Nile Delta.
history: From the time of the Old Kingdom of ancient Egypt it was the headquarters of the worship of the sun god Ra, and huge obelisks and groups of temples were built there. In the sixth century BC it suffered thorough destruction at the time of the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon.

introduce: Beth-zur was a town located in the ancient hill country of Judah and served as a strategic stronghold.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:58).
geography: It lies about 7 kilometers north of Hebron, on high ground from which it could control the Way of the Patriarchs, the ancient main road linking Jerusalem and Hebron.
history: In the time of King Rehoboam it was rebuilt as one of the towns fortified to strengthen the southern defenses of the kingdom of Judah, and later, in the Maccabean period, it is recorded as a major battleground between the Seleucid Syrian forces and the Jewish independence fighters.

introduce: Beth-anoth was one of the towns allotted as an inheritance to the ancient tribe of Judah and is included in the list of towns located in the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned together with Maarath in the list of the towns of the tribe of Judah recorded in Joshua chapter 15, verse 59 (Joshua 15:59).
geography: Beth-anoth is identified with the modern Beit 'Anun, located about 8 km northwest of Hebron. It is a strategic stronghold within the ancient hill country of Judah and has an agricultural setting in the surrounding area.

introduce: Beth-arabah was a town located in the border region between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin in the time of Joshua; the name also refers to the plain of the Jordan Valley.
biblecontents: The northern boundary passed by Beth-hoglah and went up to the north of Beth-arabah (Joshua 15:6). Among the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, the towns belonging to the wilderness included Beth-arabah, Middin, and Secacah (Joshua 15:61). Beth-arabah is also mentioned in the list of towns given as the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:22).
geography: Beth-arabah lies in the low-lying area of the Jordan Valley (the Arabah) north of the Dead Sea, and denotes an extensive stretch of flat terrain that includes the region south of Jericho. It is situated at the point where the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah and the southern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin meet.

introduce: Beth-hoglah is a place name meaning "house of the partridge" in Hebrew, a town located in the border region between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin in ancient Israelite times.
biblecontents: Beth-hoglah is mentioned as one of the points on the northern boundary in the description of the boundaries of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:19). It is also included among the towns that the tribe of the children of Benjamin received according to their families (Joshua 18:21).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Ain Hajlah, located south of Jericho, west of the Jordan River, and in the low-lying land east of Jerusalem. The area is adjacent to the plain in the northwestern part of the Dead Sea and has geographical features formed around an abundant spring.

introduce: Beth-horon is a place regarded as a strategic stronghold in the ancient Palestinian region, and is divided into Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon. The region lies on a steep slope connecting the coastal plain with the central hill country, including Jerusalem, so its military and transportation value was very high.
biblecontents: Beth-horon is mentioned as a border area of the tribe of Ephraim, and the boundary is stated to go down westward to the border of Lower Beth-horon and on to the sea (Joshua 16:3). The border of Upper Beth-horon adjoins the border of the inheritance of the children of Ephraim (Joshua 16:5). The boundary is fixed as it reaches the south side of Luz, that is, Bethel, and goes down to the town beneath the mountain on the south of Beth-horon (Joshua 18:13). It then reaches Kiriath-baal, that is, Kiriath-jearim, at the sea in front of the mountain on the south of Beth-horon (Joshua 18:14). Afterward, Upper Beth-horon and its pasturelands are included among the towns obtained by the Kohathite families of the descendants of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:22).
geography: Beth-horon lies on the rugged mountain road that climbs from the Valley of Aijalon to the central mountain region of Jerusalem or the Benjamin plateau. Upper Beth-horon stands at about 500 meters above sea level and Lower Beth-horon at a lower point, so that there is a steep ascent between the two places. This passage is known as the ascent of Beth-horon and has been used since ancient times as a key route for troop movements.
history: Because of its terrain, this area was a gateway that outside forces had to pass through to enter the interior, or that interior forces had to pass through to reach the coast. Therefore, even after the wars of the conquest of Canaan, it became a strategic base where armies seeking to secure control frequently clashed. In particular, as a link connecting the Way of the Sea and the Way of the Patriarchs, the major road networks of the ancient Near East, it was treated as important in military campaigns.

introduce: Beth-gilgal is one of the names of areas that formed around Jerusalem after the period of the kingdom of Judah, and it is a place mentioned only very rarely in the Bible as a place name.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the areas where the singers who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile had been living (Nehemiah 12:29).
history: It is presumed to have been part of the settlement areas of those who returned to the province of Judah during the Persian Empire after the Babylonian exile. At that time the singers lived scattered in various villages around Jerusalem, and Beth-gilgal too is recorded as one of these dwelling places.

introduce: Beth-rehob of Aram is the name of a small town, or its surrounding territory, that existed in the Aramaic-speaking region in Old Testament times. This area is known as a place that, in the reign of David, allied with Aram-zobah and came into military conflict with Israel.
biblecontents: When the Ammonites saw that they had become odious to David, they hired Arameans with a thousand talents of silver, along with chariots and horsemen. The Aramean troops hired at that time were twenty thousand foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob (2 Samuel 10:6).
geography: Beth-rehob is generally presumed to be an area located north of the Huleh Valley, at the foot of Mount Hermon. Some regard it as the same place as Rehob in the upper Jordan region, and it lies at a geographical crossroads connecting northward with the interior of Syria.
history: Around the tenth century B.C., Aramean power was dispersed in the form of many small states, and Beth-rehob of Aram, one of them, had enough military influence in the region to take part as a mercenary in the war between Ammon and David. As Israel's power expanded in the early years of David's monarchy, conflict with the northern Aramean powers was an unavoidable political and military event.

introduce: Beth-maacah is a place name appearing in 2 Samuel in the Old Testament, and scholars interpret it as referring to Abel-beth-maacah. This area is one of the strategic points of northern Israel mentioned in connection with the political conflicts of the time of King David.
biblecontents: At the time of Sheba's rebellion, the army led by Joab pursued him and came to Abel-beth-maacah, where they besieged Sheba and attacked the wall (2 Samuel 20:14).
geography: It is identified with the present-day Tell Abel el-Qamh (Tell Abil el-Qameh) and is located in the Huleh Basin north of the Sea of Galilee. The area lies in the fertile plain of the upper Jordan River and at a crossroads of the routes leading toward the Lebanon mountain range.
history: In the Iron Age this area served as a buffer zone between the Aramean power of Damascus and the kingdom of Israel. Because of its high strategic value owing to its location, there are records that even after the time of King David it was captured or destroyed by Ben-hadad king of Aram and by Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria, among others.

introduce: Abel-beth-maacah was an ancient city appearing in the Old Testament, a strategic stronghold and one of the main bases of northern Israel. It is presumed to be the present-day archaeological site of Tell Abel Beth Maacah, and it is a place whose history is recorded from the era of the kingdom of David and through the later era of the divided kingdom.
biblecontents: David's army, led by Joab, besieged Abel-beth-maacah in order to put down Sheba's rebellion, and to capture the town they threw up an earthen siege ramp along the wall (2 Samuel 20:15). Afterward, a wise woman of the town negotiated with Joab and, by cutting off Sheba's head and throwing it out from the wall, spared the town from destruction (2 Samuel 20:22). There is also a record that it was attacked by Aramean forces in the time of Ben-hadad, a king contemporary with the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:20).
geography: It corresponds to the archaeological site of Tell Abel Beth Maacah, located near the present-day Lebanese border. The area lies at the northern end of the Huleh Valley and has topographical features of high strategic value, being able to control the ancient trade route linking Damascus and Tyre.
history: From the Iron Age this area, as a buffer zone between Israel and Aram, saw frequent military conflict. In the time of David it functioned as a city on the northern boundary of Israelite territory, but afterward, in the course of the expansion of the kingdom of Aram and the invasion of the Assyrian Empire, it suffered conquest and destruction several times, and its sphere of political influence changed.

introduce: Beth-merhak is presumed to be a place name meaning "the house at a distance" in Hebrew, a proper noun referring to a specific place in the vicinity of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the place where King David, when he left Jerusalem to flee from Absalom's rebellion, and all who followed him stopped and stayed (2 Samuel 15:17).
geography: It is presumed to be a place east of the city of Jerusalem, on the path leading across the Kidron Valley toward the Mount of Olives. Its exact location is difficult to pin down archaeologically, but it seems to have been an outlying area suited to being the first place at which the king, when leaving Jerusalem to flee, would set things in order or gather his people.
history: It appears in the urgent circumstances in which King David had to leave his palace in haste because of the coup of his son Absalom. This place has historical significance as the spot where the king's procession paused to inspect the troops and attendants and to reorganize the route of onward travel.

introduce: Beth-shemesh is a place name meaning "house of the sun" in Hebrew, a town that was located near the border between the tribes of Judah and Dan in biblical times. It is a place that played an important administrative and religious role from the period of the judges until the time of Solomon.
biblecontents: The tribes of Naphtali and Asher did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants but lived among them (Judges 1:33). The Philistines sent the ark of the covenant to Beth-shemesh, and it arrived by way of the road toward the border of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:9, 1 Samuel 6:12). The people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley, and they rejoiced when they saw the ark (1 Samuel 6:13). The cart carrying the ark came to a stop near the large stone in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:14). The Levites took down the ark and set it on the large stone, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrifices (1 Samuel 6:15). The number of the golden tumors was equal to the number of the cities of the five lords of the Philistines, as far as the large stone of the people of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:18). Because the people of Beth-shemesh looked into the ark of the LORD, many of the people died, and the people who remained were afraid, saying, "Who can stand before this holy God?" (1 Samuel 6:19, 1 Samuel 6:20). It is mentioned as one of the places in the second district under the administration of King Solomon (1 Kings 4:9).
geography: The site known today as Tel es-Safi or Tel Beth Shemesh is located in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah. It is a strategic stronghold overlooking the Sorek Valley and lies about 30 kilometers west of Jerusalem. Because the region has fertile soil, agriculture has been active there since ancient times.
history: A Canaanite town that flourished in the Late Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, where material evidence showing the influence of Egypt and the Mediterranean coast has been excavated. Located at the point where the sphere of influence of the Philistines and the territory of the Israelite tribes intersected, it was a place where contact and conflict between the two groups occurred frequently. In the time of Solomon it was incorporated into part of a centralized administrative district and used as a base for economic collection.

introduce: Beth-anath is one of the towns of ancient Canaan, a place mentioned as an area that the tribes of Israel were not able to take completely at the time of the conquest wars and where the native inhabitants continued to live.
biblecontents: The tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and the inhabitants of Beth-anath, but lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land (Judges 1:33).
geography: There is disagreement over its present-day location, but it is generally presumed to be Khirbet Ein Un or its vicinity in the northern Galilee region. Beth-anath is delimited geographically as having belonged to the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali.
history: This is a case showing that in the early Iron Age the native Canaanites continued to occupy strategic points in the northern Galilee region. It reflects the political situation of the time, in which the settlement of Israel was not accomplished all at once but continued over a long period in a state of coexistence or mixing with the native Canaanite powers.

introduce: Beth-azmaveth was a place name that existed in the time of the ancient kingdom of Judah, and is one of the settlements recorded in the list of those who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: In the list of returnees in the time of Nehemiah, a total of 42 descendants of Beth-azmaveth are mentioned (Nehemiah 7:28).
geography: The general view among scholars is that it is the present-day Hizma area, and it lies within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, northeast of Jerusalem.

introduce: Beth-aven is a place name mentioned from the time of the conquest of Canaan to the time of the kingdom of Israel, and refers to a town, or a nearby area, located in the border region of the tribe of Benjamin. Etymologically it carries the meaning "house of vanity," and because of its geographical proximity to Bethel it is often mentioned in historical literature in connection with Bethel.
biblecontents: Joshua sent men to spy out Ai, near Beth-aven to the east of Bethel (Joshua 7:2). The northern boundary of the land received by the children of Benjamin went across the Jordan River to the wilderness of Beth-aven (Joshua 18:12). When the Philistine army encamped at Michmash, Israel was at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). There is a record that the Israelite army fought a battle as it passed by Beth-aven (1 Samuel 14:23). The prophet Hosea warned them not to do evil at Gilgal and Beth-aven, criticizing the idolatry of Israel (Hosea 4:15). A warning appears to sound the trumpet in Gibeah and Ramah and cry out toward Beth-aven (Hosea 5:8). The inhabitants of Samaria were afraid because of the calf idol of Beth-aven (Hosea 10:5).
geography: Beth-aven is identified as lying east of present-day Bethel, in the vicinity of the area of Ai. Topographically it includes the rugged ridges and ravines of the central hill country, and it lies near the strategic pass leading to Michmash. This area is a complex hilly region forming the boundary between the tribe of Benjamin and the tribe of Ephraim.
history: From the early Iron Age it was used as a strategic point of Israelite military strategy, and in particular, in the time of King Saul, it was included in the main routes of military movement during the battle of Michmash against the Philistines. In later times it is mentioned as a place symbolizing the religious corruption of the northern kingdom of Israel, which reflects the historical circumstance that the worship of the golden calf set up at Bethel came to be called by the mocking name Beth-aven.

introduce: Beth-eden is an ancient city-state and kingdom of Aram (Syria) mentioned in Amos chapter 1, a place name that appears, together with Damascus, as one of the major centers of Aramean power.
biblecontents: It was proclaimed that the LORD would break the gate bars of Damascus, cut off the inhabitants from the Valley of Aven, and cut off the one who holds the scepter, the symbol of ruling authority, from Beth-eden, and that the people of Aram would go into exile to Kir (Amos 1:5).
geography: Beth-eden is identified with Bit Adini, an ancient small Aramean kingdom that stretched across both the east and west banks of the upper Euphrates River. Its capital was Tell Ahmar (ancient Til Barsip) in present-day northern Syria, located on the east bank of the Euphrates about 20 km south of Carchemish. It was situated at a river crossing connecting Mesopotamia, northern Syria, and Anatolia, and so formed a geographical stronghold.
history: Bit Adini (Beth-eden), an independent city-state founded by the Arameans around the tenth to ninth centuries B.C., exercised strong power by controlling the Euphrates trade route. However, in 856 B.C. it was conquered by Shalmaneser III of Assyria, its capital was renamed Kar-Shalmaneser, and it was incorporated as a province of Assyria. In proclaiming the destruction of the entire Aramean power in the middle of the eighth century B.C., the prophet Amos warned that the ruler of Beth-eden, which together with Damascus symbolized the former glory and supremacy of Aram, would be cut off.

introduce: Beth-ezel is a place name mentioned by the prophet Micah of the kingdom of Judah, presumed to be a name combined with a Hebrew word meaning "house" or "standing." Among the place names of the ancient Near East, it is regarded mainly as one of the cities of the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah.
biblecontents: The inhabitants of Zaanan do not come out; Beth-ezel is in mourning, and its support is taken from you (Micah 1:11)
geography: Its exact location is debated among scholars, but it is presumed to be a settlement on the Shephelah plain in southern Judah or near Mareshah. The exact present-day archaeological site has not been identified, and the possibility has even been raised that it is confused with nearby Bethel or other place names.
history: The background is the military blows and social disorder suffered by the cities of this region and its surroundings when Sennacherib king of Assyria invaded Judah around the eighth century B.C. Through this place name the prophet Micah expresses metaphorically the ruin and isolation that the cities of Judah would suffer.

introduce: Beth-haran was a town located in the ancient region east of the Jordan River, and was one of the administrative bases connected with the settlement of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad built Beth-haran, together with Beth-nimrah, as fortified cities (Numbers 32:36).
geography: It is presumed to be located east of the Jordan River, in the Jordan Valley area northeast of the Dead Sea. Tell Iktanu or its surrounding area is cited as the leading candidate site.
history: In the time of Moses, when the tribe of Gad requested this area, which was suitable for raising livestock, as their inheritance, it was rebuilt as an Israelite possession and defensive base. Later it is also mentioned under the name Beth-ramura in records of the Neo-Babylonian period and elsewhere.

introduce: Beth-haccherem is a place name meaning "house of the vineyard" in Hebrew, mentioned as a strategic stronghold in the time of the ancient kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: When the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt in the time of Nehemiah, Malchijah, ruler of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate (Nehemiah 3:14). The prophet Jeremiah also warned that disaster was coming from the north, and said to raise a beacon fire at Beth-haccherem and sound the trumpet to give notice of the danger (Jeremiah 6:1).
geography: It is generally presumed to be Ramat Rachel, located south of present-day Jerusalem. The place lies on high ground between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, so it is well suited for surveying the surrounding area, and it has topographical conditions favorable for sending signals by raising beacon fires.
history: In the Iron Age kingdom of Judah it was used as an important administrative and military base, and the archaeological discovery of the remains of a large royal building suggests that there were facilities connected with the rule of the central government. It is regarded as an area of high economic and military value around the time of King Josiah.

introduce: Beth-horon was a strategic stronghold linking the central hill country of Canaan with the coastal plain, and in the Bible it is mentioned as divided into Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon. This region holds historical importance as a route of military movement.
biblecontents: Joshua's army pursued the fleeing Amorite coalition at the Battle of Gibeon along the ascent of Beth-horon (Joshua 10:10), and the LORD struck them down by sending great hailstones from heaven (Joshua 10:11). One company of the Philistine army set out on the road of Beth-horon leading toward the land of Ophrah (1 Samuel 13:18). King Solomon built Upper Beth-horon (1 Kings 9:17, 2 Chronicles 8:5), and this town was assigned as a Levite city in the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 6:68). Also, it is recorded that Sheerah of the tribe of Ephraim built Lower Beth-horon and Upper Beth-horon (1 Chronicles 7:24). The Israelite soldiers dismissed by King Amaziah raided the cities of Judah from Samaria as far as Beth-horon (2 Chronicles 25:13).
geography: Beth-horon is located about 16 km northwest of Jerusalem, on a steep slope rising from the Valley of Aijalon to the central mountain range where Jerusalem stands. Lower Beth-horon lies at a lower elevation, and Upper Beth-horon is on higher ground, giving it topographical advantages. This road was a major passage connecting the coastal plain and the hill country from ancient times.
history: Beth-horon was recognized as a military stronghold from the time of the wars of the conquest of Canaan. In the time of Solomon it was fortified to strengthen the defense system of Jerusalem and to control trade routes. Afterward the area was frequently used as a route of movement in times of conflict between Judah and Israel or of foreign invasion. In particular, because of its terrain, it was regarded as an ideal place for blocking or defending the entrance to the hill country.

introduce: Beth-peor is an ancient place name that was located in the land of Moab east of the Jordan River, and is known as one of the places where the people of Israel last encamped just before entering the land of Canaan.
biblecontents: After defeating Sihon king of Heshbon, the people of Israel lived in the valley opposite Beth-peor, across the Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:46).
geography: Beth-peor is presumed to be the area at the foot of Mount Pisgah near Mount Nebo, east of the Jordan River, and it includes valley terrain adjacent to the plains of Moab.
history: It was part of the territory of Sihon, the Amorite king who lived in the Moab region, and it is a place that was used as a strategic base in the latter part of the Exodus journey before the Israelites crossed the Jordan River.

introduce: Bozez is a place name appearing in 1 Samuel in the Old Testament, and refers to one of the rugged features of terrain through which Jonathan passed in order to advance toward the Philistine camp at the time of the battle of Michmash.
biblecontents: On each side of the pass by which Jonathan intended to cross over to the Philistines there was a rugged crag; the name of one was Bozez and the name of the other was Seneh, and these crags stood facing Michmash from the north (1 Samuel 14:4).
geography: Bozez is a rocky formation guarding the southern entrance of the Michmash gorge, and together with Seneh, located opposite it, it forms a narrow passage. This area is topographically very rugged and consists of slopes and projecting rocks that limit military movement.

introduce: Bozkath is a town located in the Shephelah, the lowland of the kingdom of Judah, a place mentioned in the Old Testament as part of the territory of the tribe of Judah and as the hometown of a particular person.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns distributed as an inheritance of the tribe of Judah, located between Lachish and Eglon (Joshua 15:39). It is also recorded as the hometown of Jedidah, the mother of Josiah king of Judah (2 Kings 22:1).
geography: Bozkath is presumed to be located within the Shephelah plain of ancient Palestine, and the theory that identifies it with Tell el-Beida, an area near present-day Tell es-Safi, is dominant. This area corresponds to a buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain.

remark: 1. The city of Jobab, son of Zerah, an early king of Edom.
introduce: Bozrah was one of the major cities of the ancient region of Edom, and is mentioned in biblical records and archaeological documents as a stronghold of the kingdom of Edom and a commercial and strategic hub.
biblecontents: After Bela king of Edom died, Jobab from Bozrah became king (Genesis 36:33). The same record appears in 1 Chronicles 1:44, that Jobab from Bozrah became king (1 Chronicles 1:44). Isaiah prophesied that the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah and that there will be a great slaughter in the land of Edom (Isaiah 34:6). The figure of one coming from Bozrah of Edom in red garments is also described (Isaiah 63:1). Jeremiah proclaimed that Bozrah would become a horror and an object of scorn and be laid waste (Jeremiah 49:13). Jeremiah said that the enemy would fly like an eagle and strike Bozrah (Jeremiah 49:22). Amos delivered a message of judgment that he would burn the palaces of Teman and Bozrah (Amos 1:12). Micah used a figurative expression of gathering the flock together like the sheep of Bozrah (Micah 2:12).
geography: Bozrah is identified with the present-day Busayra in southern Jordan. It is located in the mountainous region north of Petra and southeast of the Dead Sea, and it served as a stronghold advantageous for defense by making use of the rugged terrain of ancient Edom.
history: Bozrah functioned as the political center of the kingdom of Edom from about the eighth century B.C. to about the sixth century B.C. Geopolitically it was located near the King's Highway and had economic value in controlling trade routes, but its influence gradually declined with the expansion of Babylonia and the influx of the Nabateans.

remark: 2. A place located on the plain of Moab.
introduce: Bozrah is an ancient town of Moab mentioned in Jeremiah chapter 48, a city located on the plateau of Moab (the Mishor), distinguished from Bozrah, the capital of Edom.
biblecontents: It is recorded that judgment came upon Kerioth and Bozrah and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near (Jeremiah 48:24).
geography: It is located in the plateau plain region of Moab east of the Dead Sea, and is presumed to be closely connected with Bezer, the city of refuge in Deuteronomy chapter 4, verse 43, or with Bosor on the border of Hauran (Deuteronomy 4:43).
history: It was a town built up as a defensive fortress as the kingdom of Moab expanded its northern border in the Iron Age, but it was destroyed along with all of Moab by the invasion of the Babylonian army in the early sixth century B.C.

introduce: Phoenix is a place name appearing in Acts chapter 27, a port city and the name of a harbor in the southwest of the island of Crete. In the Bible it is described as a harbor suitable for wintering.
biblecontents: Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to sail on, if somehow they could reach Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix was a harbor in Crete facing both southwest and northwest (Acts 27:12)
geography: Phoenix is presumed to be present-day Loutro or the nearby area of Phinikas. It is located on the southwest coast of the island of Crete, and topographically it is open toward the southwest and the northwest, giving it conditions favorable for ships to anchor.
history: In the Roman period Phoenix was used as a haven where ships sailing the Mediterranean stayed briefly to avoid rough winter seas. At that time it was the custom of sailors, when the winter season, dangerous for sailing, arrived, to look for a safe harbor and anchor there.

introduce: Penuel was a town located in the region east of the Jordan in the northern kingdom of ancient Israel, mentioned in the Bible as a place where Jeroboam I reinforced its defensive works in order to consolidate his kingship after he built Shechem.
biblecontents: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And from there he went out and built Penuel. (1 Kings 12:25)
geography: Located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River, it is regarded as a strategic stronghold controlling the valley of the Jabbok River. Because it lay at a point where ancient road networks intersected, it played an important role in defending the east-west routes of travel.
history: When Israel divided after the death of Solomon, Jeroboam I, who founded the northern kingdom, fortified major cities to strengthen national defense. Penuel was one of them, and it was rebuilt in order to defend the eastern border of the state against outside invasion and to strengthen control over the territory under his rule.

remark: The region of Buz and its inhabitants.
introduce: Buz is a place name located in the ancient Near East, referring to a people, or the land in which they lived, deriving from the name of one of the sons of Nahor, the brother of Abraham.
biblecontents: Elihu was the son of Barachel the Buzite (Job 32:2). Elihu, a figure in the book of Job, stated that he was a Buzite and intervened in the dialogue between Job and his three friends (Job 32:6). In the course of proclaiming God's judgment, the prophet Jeremiah mentioned Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who clip the hair at their temples (Jeremiah 25:23).
geography: Opinion is divided among scholars about its exact location, but it is generally presumed to be in northern Arabia or in the region between Edom and the Arabian desert. Considering that it is mentioned in the Bible together with Tema and Dedan, it is highly likely to have been located in northwestern Arabia.
history: Buz is the name of a descendant born to Nahor and Milcah, as recorded in Genesis chapter 22, verse 21, and it appears to have developed afterward into the name of a tribe. There is a view that identifies it with the region of Bazu mentioned in ancient Near Eastern texts, which is a place name in the Arabian region that also appears in ancient Assyrian records.

introduce: Pekod is a Hebrew place name referring to a region of ancient Babylonia, and in the Bible it is used as a term symbolizing or referring to the territory of the Babylonian Empire and the people living there.
biblecontents: The prophet Jeremiah, prophesying judgment on Babylon, commands that the inhabitants of Pekod be struck (Jeremiah 50:21). In a parable rebuking the apostasy of Israel, the prophet Ezekiel mentions that the men of Pekod would come together with the Babylonian army (Ezekiel 23:23).
geography: Pekod is presumed to be a place name historically indicating part of the heartland of Babylonia, that is, the southern region of Mesopotamia; its exact boundaries have not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is understood as a geographical name encompassing the area near Babylon.
history: It appears to be the name of a specific tribe or administrative district that lived near the center of Babylon at the time of the Babylonian Empire, and it reflects the regional identity of an area that was under the powerful military might and influence of the Neo-Babylonian Empire at that time.

introduce: Bene-berak is a place name mentioned as one of the towns of the inheritance allotted to the ancient tribe of Dan in Israel.
biblecontents: Bene-berak is recorded as one of the towns included within the border of the inheritance obtained by lot by the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:45).
geography: Bene-berak is presumed to be the area of Bnei Brak, located east of Tel Aviv in present-day Israel. It lies in the coastal plain region and corresponds to a fertile area adjacent to the Plain of Sharon and the basin of the Yarkon River.
history: Ancient Bene-berak was designated as part of the allotment of the tribe of Dan after the conquest of Canaan, but it was one of the areas where the tribe had difficulty expanding its territory because it was adjacent to the sphere of Philistine influence. Later, in the Roman period, it became known as the base and center of learning of the Jewish rabbi Akiva, and so rose to become a historically important city.

introduce: Bene-jaakan is one of the places that the Israelites who came out of Egypt passed through during their journey in the wilderness, and the place name carries the meaning "the place where the descendants of Achan live."
biblecontents: The Israelites set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan (Numbers 33:31). They set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad (Numbers 33:32). The Israelites set out from Bene-jaakan and came to Moserah, and there Aaron died and was buried (Deuteronomy 10:6).
geography: Bene-jaakan is presumed to be a hill region between the Arabah wilderness and the mountains of Edom, and modern geographers regard this place as an area located near the Wadi el-Arabah valley, north of the Gulf of Aqaba.

introduce: Peniel is a place name appearing in the book of Genesis in the Old Testament; it is the place where Jacob wrestled with the angel, and a region named by him in the sense that he had seen the face of God.
biblecontents: Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been preserved" (Genesis 32:30). The sun rose upon him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping because of his thigh (Genesis 32:31).
geography: Peniel is presumed to be an area located in the basin of the Jabbok River east of the Jordan River. There are various theories about its exact location, but it is generally regarded as a strategic stronghold near the hill country of Gilead.

introduce: Betonim is a place name mentioned in Joshua chapter 13, verse 26, in the description of the boundary of the land distributed to the tribe of Gad. It is recorded as one point in the area extending from Mahanaim to Lo-debar.
biblecontents: the territory from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir; (Joshua 13:26)
geography: It is presumed to be located in the region of Gilead east of the Jordan River. Its specific coordinates and exact archaeological site have not been clearly identified by modern archaeology, but topographically it is regarded as part of the highland plateau east of the Jordan.
history: It was used as a reference point for establishing geographical boundaries in the process by which the tribes of Israel received the land east of the Jordan after the conquest of Canaan. At that time this area was within the domain of Sihon, the Amorite king, but after it was conquered by Israel it was incorporated as the inheritance of the tribe of Gad.

introduce: Pethor is a place name located in the ancient Near East, known as the hometown of Balaam, and a place connected with the region of Aram in the Euphrates River basin.
biblecontents: Balak king of Moab tried to summon Balaam son of Beor, who lived in Pethor, to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5). Also, according to the record in Deuteronomy, it is mentioned that Balaam of Pethor was hired to curse Israel (Deuteronomy 23:4).
geography: In the Old Testament, Pethor is described as Aram-naharaim or as a region beyond the River, and modern scholars presume it to be the same place as Pitru in Hittite records, located in the middle Euphrates region.
history: The view that Pethor geographically coincides with Pitru, recorded as having been conquered by Shalmaneser III of Assyria around the ninth century B.C., is dominant, and as a major stronghold on the Euphrates at that time it was very likely a commercial or strategic hub.

remark: A town of the tribe of Simeon.
introduce: Bethuel is one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles chapter 4, verse 30.
biblecontents: Bethuel is mentioned as one of the towns given as the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:30).
geography: Bethuel is presumed to be a town located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah, adjacent to the area of Beersheba (1 Chronicles 4:30).

introduce: Bethul is a place name recorded as one of the towns located within the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Simeon among the ancient tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the list of towns that the tribe of the children of Simeon obtained by lot, and is recorded as located between Beersheba and Moladah (Joshua 19:4).
geography: It is located in the Negev desert region of southern Canaan and is included in the cluster of towns allotted to the tribe of Simeon. Its exact location has not been identified by modern geography, but it is presumed to be on the edge of the southern highlands or wilderness zone connected with the plain of Beersheba, a neighboring area.

introduce: Berothah, mentioned in Ezekiel chapter 47, verse 16, is a region recorded as one of the points on the northern boundary that Israel would obtain when it is restored.
biblecontents: Hamath and Berothah, and Sibraim, which is between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath, and Hazar-hatticon, which is beside the border of Hauran (Ezekiel 47:16).
geography: It is presumed to be a region located between the south of Hamath and the north of Damascus, but opinions among scholars differ on the specific location of the modern place name, and an exact identification is impossible.

introduce: Phrygia is an ancient region located in the central interior of Asia Minor, a place closely connected in biblical times with the administrative districts of the Roman Empire. As a center where the trade routes of East and West intersected, this region served as an important transit point in the course of the spread of early Christianity.
biblecontents: Among the devout Jews who visited Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost were people from Phrygia (Acts 2:10). Paul and his companions traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, because the Holy Spirit had forbidden them to speak the word in Asia (Acts 16:6). Paul traveled in order through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (Acts 18:23).
geography: It lies on the central plateau of the Asia Minor peninsula, bordering the province of Asia to the west and Galatia to the east. Mountainous terrain and fertile plains are mixed together, and the ancient main road network passed through this region, making it a key route connecting western coastal cities such as Ephesus with the eastern interior.
history: Phrygia, which had formed a powerful kingdom around the eighth century B.C., afterward passed under the rule of Lydia, Persia, and the Greek empire. In the Roman period it was divided and incorporated between the province of Asia and the province of Galatia and was administered accordingly. This region maintained a unique environment in which Greek culture and native culture were mixed, and under Roman rule commercial and cultural exchange flourished along with the improvement of major roads.

introduce: The Perizzites were one of the tribes living in the ancient land of Canaan, a people who frequently appear throughout the Bible in the lists of the native inhabitants of Canaan. They are mentioned as a people whom the children of Israel were to remove in the course of conquering the land of Canaan, and as a major rival group.
biblecontents: When there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock, the Perizzites also lived in that land (Genesis 13:7). The land of the Perizzite tribe was included within the boundary of the land that God promised to Abram (Genesis 15:20). After the incident in which Jacob's sons slaughtered the people of Shechem, Jacob feared that his situation would become difficult because of the Perizzite tribe (Genesis 34:30). In the book of Exodus, God promised that when He led Israel to the land of Canaan flowing with milk and honey, He would drive out the Perizzite tribe (Exodus 3:8, 3:17). They are listed as one of the seven nations that had to be exterminated when Israel entered Canaan (Exodus 23:23, 33:2, 34:11, Deuteronomy 7:1, 20:17).
geography: The exact dwelling place of the Perizzite tribe has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but according to the biblical record they are presumed to have lived scattered across the hill country and plains of Canaan. From the fact that they already lived in the land of Canaan when the herdsmen of Abraham and Lot quarreled in Genesis chapter 13, it can be seen that they were distributed over a wide area from the early period of settlement in Canaan.

introduce: Besor is a place name mentioned in the course of David's pursuit of the Amalekite army, and refers to a specific area called the Brook Besor.
biblecontents: David, leading the six hundred men who were with him, came to the Brook Besor, and left there those who were left behind (1 Samuel 30:9). David left two hundred men at the Brook Besor and pursued the Amalekites with four hundred men (1 Samuel 30:10). When David came back to the two hundred men whom he had left behind, they went out to greet David and the people who were with him (1 Samuel 30:21).
geography: The Brook Besor is presumed to be a wadi that begins in the southern part of the hill country of Judea and flows west to the Mediterranean coastal plain. It is an intermittent stream that flows only when it rains, and geographers judge it to lie somewhere between Ziklag, near the Philistine plain, and the Brook of Egypt.

introduce: Bealoth is one of the towns of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua chapter 15 in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Judah as an inheritance (Joshua 15:24).
geography: It is classified as a town located in the Negev region, the southern area of the tribe of Judah, but its exact archaeological location has not been confirmed at present.

introduce: Beeroth was a town where the Gibeonites lived in ancient Israelite times and an area included in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Etymologically in Hebrew it means "wells," and it is mentioned as the residence or hometown of various events and persons in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: The children of Israel came to Beeroth, one of the towns to which the inhabitants of Gibeon belonged (Joshua 9:17). Afterward it was allotted by Joshua as the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:25). After the death of King Saul, the incident occurred in which Baanah and Rechab from Beeroth assassinated Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 4:2, 4:3, 4:5, 4:9), and they were considered Benjamites (2 Samuel 4:2). Naharai, one of David's mighty men, is also recorded as a Beerothite (2 Samuel 23:37). In the list of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah after the Babylonian exile, the men of Beeroth are included (Nehemiah 7:29). Beeroth Bene-jaakan in Deuteronomy chapter 10, verse 6 is presumed by some scholars to be the same place as Beeroth, but there is controversy over the identification of the place name (Deuteronomy 10:6).
