geography: Beeroth is identified with the area of el-Bireh, located about 15 km north of Jerusalem. It was one of the main stations on the north-south road connecting Bethel and Jerusalem, and in the past it was a strategic stronghold in the central highlands of Canaan.
history: It was originally a town where the Gibeonites, who were Hivites, lived, but it was incorporated into the community of Israel through the peace treaty with Joshua. When the incident occurred in which King Saul slaughtered the Gibeonites, the inhabitants of Beeroth fled to Gibeon, and afterward it became the background for the appearance of men from this region as parties to political events in the time of the downfall of the house of Saul.

introduce: Beeshterah is a town allotted to the descendants of Gershon, of the tribe of Levi, mentioned in Joshua chapter 21, verse 27, of the Old Testament.
biblecontents: To the Levites of the descendants of Gershon were given, from the half-tribe of Manasseh, Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands, a city of refuge for the manslayer, and also Beeshterah with its pasturelands, two cities in all (Joshua 21:27)
geography: Because of differences between the Hebrew original place name and the versions, it is generally also presumed to be the same place as Ashtaroth, located within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, or its vicinity. Its specific coordinates have not been clearly determined archaeologically.
history: It is one of the towns designated for the dispersed residence of the tribe of Levi after the period of Israel's settlement, and at that time it was included in the holdings of the half-tribe of Manasseh. Beth-arath, which appears in Judges chapter 1, verse 31 and elsewhere, and Beeshterah of Joshua chapter 21, verse 27 are regarded as similar place names that arose in the course of the change of place names among the historical records.

remark: 1. The place where Israel, having come out of Egypt, stayed after the Arnon.
introduce: Beer means "well" in Hebrew and refers to a place where Israel settled during its journey in the wilderness, appearing in Numbers chapter 21.
biblecontents: This is the place where, as the people of Israel moved through the wilderness, the LORD told Moses to gather the people and promised to give them water (Numbers 21:16). Here Israel sang a song to the well, and the nobles, together with the commanders and the leaders of the people, dug the well with their staffs, according to the rule (Numbers 21:17-18).
geography: Its exact location is unclear, but it is presumed to lie somewhere to the north on the journey toward the plains of Moab. On Israel's route of travel at the time, it appears to be an arid zone either before or after passing through the Arnon valley.
history: This is a record from the time when Israel, after the Exodus, was passing through the region east of the Jordan on its way to Canaan. Beer is interpreted as the point where the people of Israel, in the wilderness environment short of water, dug wells in an organized way and strengthened their communal solidarity.

remark: 2. The place where Jotham, son of Gideon, fled because he was afraid of his brother Abimelech.
introduce: Beer is a place name recorded in the Bible as the place where Jotham fled to escape Abimelech's massacre.
biblecontents: Jotham fled from Abimelech, who had killed his brothers, and lived at Beer (Judges 9:21).
geography: Its exact location is debated among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be an area near Shechem. Given the topographical features of the ancient Palestinian region, it was very likely located in a mountainous area.

introduce: Beer-lahai-roi is a place name that means "the well of the Living One who sees me" in Hebrew. A place located in the Negev desert region of southern Canaan, it is mentioned in early biblical history as a principal dwelling place or route of movement of Hagar and Isaac.
biblecontents: When Isaac was living at Beer-lahai-roi, he was coming from the Negev region (Genesis 24:62). After Abraham died, God blessed his son Isaac, and Isaac lived near Beer-lahai-roi (Genesis 25:11).
geography: It is located in the Negev desert region of southern Canaan, and there are various theories about its specific location. Traditionally it is presumed to be an oasis area on the way to Kadesh-barnea and the wilderness of Shur. It is an important stronghold where a well, essential for survival in the desert environment, was secured.
history: It is a strategic stronghold where the patriarchs of the Bronze Age, living a nomadic life, were able to water their livestock and settle. At that time this area, as a border zone of Canaan, had the geographical character of a place where nomads and settled people intersected.

introduce: Beer-lahai-roi is a place name appearing in the book of Genesis in the Bible, meaning a well, or the area around it, located between Kadesh and Bered. Etymologically in Hebrew it carries the meaning "the well of the Living One who watches over me."
biblecontents: This is the place where the angel of the LORD appeared and met Hagar when she fled into the wilderness to escape Sarai's harsh treatment (Genesis 16:7). Afterward Hagar called the spring here Beer-lahai-roi, and it lies between Kadesh and Bered (Genesis 16:14). It is also mentioned as the place where Isaac later lived and meditated (Genesis 24:62, 25:11).
geography: It is presumed to be the northern part of the Negev desert or the area near Kadesh-barnea. The specific point is unclear, but it is analyzed to have taken the form of an oasis where a spring welled up in the wilderness region, where water is scarce.
history: It was an important water source stronghold on the route along which the nomads of the early Bronze Age patriarchal period moved to graze their livestock. The Kadesh region was the southern border zone of the ancient Near East, and the wells of this region had territorial value that determined the survival of tribes.

introduce: Beersheba is a major settlement located in the Negev desert of southern Canaan and an area with wells. In the biblical record, from the patriarchal period on, it frequently appears as a place name symbolizing the southern boundary of Israelite territory.
biblecontents: Hagar wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba and used up her water, but God caused her to discover a well (Genesis 21:14). It is the place where Abraham and Abimelech made a covenant, and it came to be called Beersheba, meaning "well of the oath" (Genesis 21:31). Abraham planted a tamarisk tree here and called on the name of the LORD (Genesis 21:33). After returning from Mount Moriah, Abraham lived at Beersheba (Genesis 22:19). Isaac went up there and experienced a manifestation of the LORD, and he dug the well again (Genesis 26:23). Isaac's servants discovered a new well and named it Shibah (Genesis 26:33). Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran (Genesis 28:10). Before going to Egypt, Jacob offered sacrifices at Beersheba and received an answer from God (Genesis 46:1, 46:5).
geography: Beersheba is located in the fertile plain in the northern part of the Negev desert. It lies about 45 km southwest of Hebron, and it is a strategic stronghold where, thanks to a well-developed groundwater layer, a stable supply of water could be secured even in an arid environment. It served as a gateway linking the hill country of Judah with the desert to the south.
history: It has been a base since the Bronze Age where nomads and settled people gathered around the wells. In the time of Abraham and Isaac it was a place where diplomatic negotiations took place over the use of water resources and territorial rights with Abimelech, of Philistine lineage, the ruling power of the region. Afterward, in the period of the kingdom of Israel, it functioned as a city on the southern boundary.

introduce: Beer-elim is a compound of Beer, meaning "wells" in Hebrew, and Elim, meaning "oak" or "terebinth tree," a proper noun referring to a specific place that was located in the ancient region of Moab.
biblecontents: In the prophecy of judgment against Moab, it is said that the cry of distress has gone around its border, and that its wailing reaches Eglaim and Beer-elim (Isaiah 15:8).
geography: The biblical text describes this place as near the border of Moab, but in modern archaeological surveys the place name Beer-elim has not been clearly identified. Some scholars raise the possibility that this place name is the same as Beer mentioned in Numbers chapter 21, verse 16, but no archaeological site has been found that is established geographically.

introduce: Beon is a place name located in the region east of the Jordan, and according to the biblical record it is one of the towns that the descendants of Gad and Reuben conquered and judged to be suitable for pasturing livestock.
biblecontents: “Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon, (Numbers 32:3)
geography: Beon is an area located near the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River; it corresponds to the present-day region of Jordan and, together with other surrounding towns, is known as a highland with abundant pastureland.
history: In the process of Israel's occupation of the region east of the Jordan after the Exodus, the tribes of Reuben and Gad took note of the economic value of this region and requested its occupation and rebuilding, and afterward they were allotted the region east of the Jordan, including this area, as their inheritance.

remark: Territory of Ephraim, a mountain in Moab.
introduce: Peor is a mountain located in the ancient region of Moab, and according to the biblical record it is one of the places where Balaam and Balak looked down on the people of Israel and attempted to curse them.
biblecontents: Balak took Balaam to the top of Mount Peor, which overlooks the wilderness, but even there Balaam blessed Israel (Numbers 23:28).
geography: Peor is presumed to be a mountain peak on the plateau of Moab east of the Jordan River, and it appears to be an area geographically closely related to nearby Mount Pisgah and Mount Nebo.

introduce: The Philistines means a people who lived in the coastal plain region of the ancient Near East, and also their dwelling place. In the early records of the Old Testament they appear in connection with the Gerar region in the time of Abraham and Isaac, and afterward in the book of Exodus they are depicted as a hostile power located on the road along which the people of Israel were heading to Canaan.
biblecontents: The Philistines are mentioned as a people who came from the Pathrusites and the Casluhites (Genesis 10:14). Abraham stayed in Gerar, the land of the Philistines, and made a covenant with Abimelech, the king there (Genesis 21:32). Abraham spent many days in the land of the Philistines (Genesis 21:34). Isaac too went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, who lived in Gerar (Genesis 26:1). While Isaac was staying there, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out through a window and saw Isaac playing with his wife Rebekah (Genesis 26:8). When the produce that Isaac harvested from his farming grew large, the Philistines envied him and stopped up the wells that he had dug (Genesis 26:14, 26:18). When Israel came out of Egypt, God did not lead the people by the road of the land of the Philistines, although it was near, for He said that if they met war they might change their minds and return to Egypt (Exodus 13:17). Together with the chiefs of Edom and the mighty men of Moab, the inhabitants of the Philistines too were seized with fear when they heard the news about Israel (Exodus 15:14). God set the borders of Israel from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines (Exodus 23:31).
geography: The Philistine region lies in the Shephelah, the plain on the Mediterranean coast of southwestern Canaan, and along the coast. This region has fertile farmland, and from ancient times it was a key stronghold of the Way of the Sea, the international trade route linking Egypt and Mesopotamia.
history: According to the biblical record, the early Philistines are associated with a settlement group centered on Gerar in southern Canaan in the middle of the second millennium B.C. Afterward, around the twelfth century B.C., the Philistines who arrived at the time of the great migration of the Sea Peoples of the Mediterranean formed five city-states, including Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath, and firmly established themselves as a political group possessing powerful military strength.

introduce: Pelonite is a person recorded in the Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles, and scholars interpret the term as another name for, or a variant in the record of, Helez, one of the mighty men of King David.
biblecontents: In 1 Chronicles chapter 11, verse 27, Helez the Pelonite is recorded as one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:27). Also, in 1 Chronicles chapter 11, verse 36, Ahijah the Pelonite is mentioned as one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:36).

introduce: Pinon is a name referring to a city or region of Edom that was ruled by Alvah, one of the chiefs of the Edom region.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the domain ruled by Alvah, chief of Edom (Genesis 36:41). In 1 Chronicles as well, it is recorded in the same way as the territory of Alvah, chief of Edom (1 Chronicles 1:52).
geography: The land of Edom is located centered on the Arabah valley southeast of the Dead Sea, and the exact location of Pinon has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is presumed to be a specific settlement within the territory of Edom.

introduce: Pithom was one of the store cities built in the period of the Nineteenth Dynasty of ancient Egypt, and refers to a city for whose construction the children of Israel were mobilized through forced labor.
biblecontents: A new king of Egypt set the children of Israel to forced labor in order to oppress them, and in this process the people of Israel built Pithom and Rameses, store cities for Pharaoh (Exodus 1:11).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Tell el-Maskhuta, which lies in the Wadi Tumilat region of eastern Egypt. This point is a strategic stronghold linking the Nile Delta and the Sinai Peninsula, and corresponds to the gateway of a trade route.
history: The dominant view among scholars associates this city with the building projects of the time of Ramesses II. At that time Pithom is analyzed to have served as a logistics base and military facility for managing the goods flowing in from western Asia and strengthening the defense of the border.

introduce: Bithynia refers to an ancient region located on the Black Sea coast in northwestern Asia Minor. In the time of the ancient Roman Empire it was administered as a single province combining Bithynia and Pontus, and in New Testament times it functioned as a strategic stronghold linking the Mediterranean world with the interior.
biblecontents: The apostle Paul and his companions, during the second missionary journey, tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them (Acts 16:7). Also, the first letter of Peter begins as a letter addressed to the sojourners scattered in various regions of Asia Minor, including Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1).
geography: Bithynia borders the Black Sea to the north and the Propontis (Sea of Marmara) to the west, and forms a boundary with Paphlagonia and Pontus to the east. Mountainous terrain and fertile plains are mixed together, and agriculture and herding developed around the basin of the Sakarya River. Major cities such as Nicaea and Nicomedia are included in this region.
history: Around the fourth century B.C., after the death of Alexander the Great, it developed into an independent kingdom, and afterward, in 74 B.C., when its last king, Nicomedes IV, bequeathed his territory to Rome, it became a Roman province. In the early Roman Empire it was classified as a senatorial province, but afterward it was also administered as an imperial province. There is a record that in the time of the emperor Trajan, Pliny was appointed governor of Bithynia and Pontus and carried out regional administration and an investigation of the Christians.

introduce: Bithron is a place name called Bithron in Hebrew, a region appearing in 2 Samuel along the route by which Abner's army crossed the Jordan River and moved.
biblecontents: Abner and his men marched all night through the Arabah, crossed the Jordan River, passed through the whole land of Bithron, and came to Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2:29).
geography: Bithron is presumed to be located in the region east of the Jordan River, and topographically it lies on the path connecting the Arabah valley with Mahanaim. Its exact archaeological location has not yet been clearly identified, but it is closely related to the approach roads to the highlands east of the Jordan Valley.
history: After the death of King Saul, it is mentioned as a stopping place on the way when Abner's army, which supported Ish-bosheth, after engaging David's army, crossed the Jordan River to escape pursuit and retreated to Mahanaim, a strategic stronghold.

introduce: Pi-beseth is an ancient Egyptian city, a major settlement located in the eastern part of the Nile Delta of Egypt. It is called Pi-beseth in Hebrew and is known in Egyptian as Bubastis.
biblecontents: In a message of judgment prophesying the destruction of Egypt, the prophet Ezekiel mentioned that the young men of Pi-beseth would fall by the sword and that the inhabitants of that city would be taken captive (Ezekiel 30:17).
geography: Pi-beseth was located on the bank of the Tanitic branch of the Nile and corresponds to the Tell Basta area near present-day Zagazig, Egypt. As a strategic stronghold in the eastern Nile Delta, it served as a hub of the trade route linking Memphis, the capital of Egypt, with the Sinai Peninsula.
history: As the capital of the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt, Pi-beseth held a politically and religiously important position in ancient Egyptian history. The city was famous as a center of worship of the cat-shaped goddess Bastet, and it was frequently mentioned in the course of wars and power struggles between Egypt and neighboring empires. It is presumed to have been destroyed or damaged in the invasion and conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylonia in the early sixth century B.C.

introduce: It is the river mentioned first among the four rivers that flowed out from the Garden of Eden and surrounded the whole land.
biblecontents: The name of the first river is Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there (Genesis 2:11)
geography: It is mentioned in connection with the region of Havilah, but scholarly opinion is divided over matching it archaeologically with a particular river. Some scholars interpret it in connection with Wadi al-Batin in the Arabian Peninsula or with an ancient dry-riverbed system.

introduce: Pisgah is a mountain, or part of a mountain range, located in the land of Moab east of the Jordan, with topographical features adjacent to Mount Nebo. In Hebrew it means "a cleft place" or "a cliff," and it is mentioned mainly as the place from which Moses viewed the land of Canaan, or as a major point through which the people of Israel passed.
biblecontents: The people of Israel passed through the land of Sihon, the Amorite king, went by way of the valley, and came to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah (Numbers 21:20). King Balak took Balaam to the top of Pisgah, the summit of the field of Zophim, and tried to curse Israel (Numbers 23:14). This place is mentioned as a boundary of the terrain near the Arabah and the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:17). God commanded Moses to go up to the top of Mount Pisgah, lift up his eyes, look to the west, north, south, and east, and see the land of Canaan (Deuteronomy 3:27). The domain of the Arabah beneath the slopes of Pisgah is also mentioned (Deuteronomy 4:49). Before his death Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Pisgah, saw the land of Canaan opposite Jericho, and ended his life there (Deuteronomy 34:1). The territory as far as the Sea of the Arabah beneath the slopes of Pisgah was included in the domain of Sihon (Joshua 12:3). Among the towns distributed to the tribe of Reuben was an area that included the slopes of Pisgah (Joshua 13:20).
geography: Pisgah is presumed to be part of the Abarim mountain range located near the Madaba region of the present-day Kingdom of Jordan. It lies on the Jordan Valley and the plateau northeast of the Dead Sea, and its high elevation allows one to look down on the whole of Canaan to the west, including Jericho. Topographically it forms steep slopes, and there are cliff-like stretches that make passage difficult.
history: In the late Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, this area was a strategic stronghold where border disputes between Moab and the Amorites were frequent. At that time the Amorite kingdom ruled by Sihon controlled the area, but in the course of Israel's war of conquest east of the Jordan it was occupied and incorporated as the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben. Historically, because of its geopolitical importance, even in the periods after the Bible it was the object of territorial disputes among various powers, together with the nearby regions of Heshbon and Medeba.

introduce: Biziothiah is a place name mentioned in Joshua chapter 15 of the Bible, presumed to have been located in the vicinity of the Beersheba region, as one of the towns allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns located at the southern extremity among the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:28).
geography: It is classified as a town located near the Negev desert, the southern region of the tribe of Judah, and its exact present-day archaeological location is difficult to pin down because of abnormality or confusion with other town names (Joshua 15:28).

introduce: Pisidia is a mountainous region located in the interior of southern Asia Minor. Administratively it was included in the Roman province of Galatia, and it became an important base on Paul's missionary journeys.
biblecontents: Paul and Barnabas passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia (Acts 14:24).
geography: A plateau region north of the Taurus Mountains, it is characterized by rugged mountain terrain. Its principal city is Pisidian Antioch, and because its elevation is higher than the surrounding areas, it has environmental features in which the climate and vegetation are distinct.
history: Around 25 B.C. Rome brought this region completely under its control and incorporated it as part of the province of Galatia. After Roman rule, military colonial cities were built to maintain public order, and these cities functioned as centers of administration that spread Roman culture and used Latin.

introduce: Pisidian Antioch is a city located in the region of Pisidia in ancient Asia Minor, and one of the key bases that the apostle Paul visited on his first missionary journey and where he proclaimed the gospel. It was a colony of the Roman Empire and a transportation hub located in the border zone between Pisidia and Phrygia.
biblecontents: Paul and Barnabas set out from Perga and arrived at Pisidian Antioch, and on the Sabbath day they entered the synagogue and sat down (Acts 13:14).
geography: It is located near present-day Yalvaç in Turkey, on the steep mountain slope of a plateau about 1,100 meters above sea level. In ancient times it was a strategic stronghold through which the Roman military road called the Via Sebaste passed, and it served as a passage linking the surrounding Pisidian mountain region with the plain region.
history: It was originally a city of the Phrygian region, but around 25 B.C. it was rebuilt by the emperor Augustus as a Roman colonial city (Colonia Caesarea). As retired soldiers settled there, it received a transplant of Roman administrative and military culture, and Latin was used as the official language. Because of this, even though it was in the interior of Asia Minor, it showed the characteristic of strongly maintaining a Roman-style urban structure and loyalty to the empire.

introduce: Pi-hahiroth is the third point at which the children of Israel pitched their tents in front of the Red Sea during the journey of the Exodus. This place name is presumed to have an Egyptian etymology, and it holds an important position in archaeological and geographical research tracing the route of the Exodus.
biblecontents: God commanded the children of Israel to turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exodus 14:2). Pharaoh of Egypt, thinking that Israel was shut in by the wilderness, led his army and pursued Israel, who were encamped by the sea beside Pi-hahiroth (Exodus 14:9). Israel set out from Etham and headed for Pi-hahiroth, which was in front of Baal-zephon (Numbers 33:7).
geography: Pi-hahiroth is described as a coastal area located between Migdol and Baal-zephon. There are various theories about its specific location, and the view that it is an area near Lake Timsah north of the Suez Canal stands opposed to the view that it is near the Bitter Lakes farther south. Topographically it is a shore close to the border fortresses of Egypt, with geographical conditions that allow it to be isolated by natural landmarks.
history: The name Pi-hahiroth quite possibly derives from the ancient Egyptian Pi-hahirot, which is interpreted as meaning a waterside where reeds or papyrus grow. It is being studied in connection with place names or administrative districts of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt at that time, but because this name is not directly recorded in Egyptian texts, its exact identification remains an archaeological task.

introduce: A city located in western Asia Minor, corresponding to the Alaşehir region of modern Turkey. It functioned as a strategic stronghold in the time of the Roman Empire and was the site of one of the seven churches mentioned in the book of Revelation in the Bible.
biblecontents: In Revelation, it is mentioned as the destination to which the apostle John sends a letter, as one of the seven churches (Revelation 1:11). Also, through the message sent to the angel of the church in Philadelphia, it is emphasized that the Lord is holy and true and holds the key of David (Revelation 3:7).
geography: It is located in the valley of the Cogamus River in the ancient region of Lydia, about 45 kilometers southeast of Sardis. It is a plain region with fertile soil, and as a crossroads linking the ancient east-west trade routes, it was geologically an area of frequent volcanic activity.
history: It was founded around the second century B.C. by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamum. The city name Philadelphia was given to commemorate his special brotherly love for his brother Eumenes II. Because of the regional characteristic of frequent earthquakes, it suffered great damage in the great earthquake of A.D. 17, and afterward the city was rebuilt with the financial support of the Roman emperor Tiberius. Against this background it was for a time also called Neocaesarea, after the name of the emperor.

introduce: Bileam is a place name mentioned in 1 Chronicles chapter 6, verse 70, one of the towns of the Levites allotted as an inheritance of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: To the rest of the families of the half-tribe of Manasseh were given Aner with its pasturelands, taken from the towns obtained by the clans of the descendants of Manasseh, and also Bileam with its pasturelands (1 Chronicles 6:70).
geography: Bileam was located within the territory of the tribe of western Manasseh, west of the Jordan, and another biblical passage, Joshua chapter 21, verse 25, records the same place as Ibleam. Geographically it is presumed to be the area of present-day Tel Bil'ame, which lies near Dothan, a strategic stronghold adjacent to the Jezreel Valley.
history: Bileam was a town distributed to the Kohathites among the descendants of Levi, and was a place where priests and Levites lived. It is also called Ibleam in the biblical record, and this area functioned as a crossroads of transportation and military affairs to the extent that it is mentioned historically on the route along which Ahaziah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, fled from the forces of Jehu.

remark: 1. The central city of Macedonia.
introduce: Philippi is a major city located on the Via Egnatia in eastern Macedonia, and one of the regions where the apostle Paul first proclaimed the gospel in Europe. As a Roman colony and a strategic stronghold, it occupies an important position in New Testament history.
biblecontents: Paul and his companions mentioned that Philippi was the first city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony (Acts 16:12). After the Days of Unleavened Bread, Paul and his companions sailed from Philippi and in five days met the other companions at Troas (Acts 20:6). Paul sent a letter to the saints in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons (Philippians 1:1). When Paul left Macedonia, the church at Philippi was mentioned as the only church that took part in giving and receiving at the beginning of the gospel (Philippians 4:15). Even though Paul had suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, he proclaimed the gospel of God (1 Thessalonians 2:2).
geography: Philippi was built near a marshland in the ancient region of Thrace and is located northwest of present-day Kavala in northeastern Greece. The city was a transportation hub through which the Via Egnatia, the key Roman road running east and west, passed, and it enjoyed economic prosperity thanks to the gold and silver mines produced on nearby Mount Pangaion.
history: This city, originally called Crenides, was taken in 356 B.C. by Philip II of Macedon, who renamed it Philippi after himself. It is also the site of the Battle of Philippi in 42 B.C., in which Octavian and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius. Afterward it was raised by the emperor Augustus to a Roman colony in which retired Roman soldiers settled, and its inhabitants enjoyed the privilege of holding Roman citizenship and being subject to Roman law.

remark: 2. Caesarea Philippi, a town near Mount Hermon in the north of Galilee
introduce: Caesarea Philippi is a city located at the foot of Mount Hermon in the north of ancient Palestine, and was one of the administrative and religious centers in the time of the Roman Empire.
biblecontents: As Jesus and His disciples were going out along the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked His disciples who people said He was (Mark 8:27).
geography: This area is where the Banias spring, one of the principal sources of the Jordan River, is found, and it has fertile soil and abundant water resources. Located on the southwestern slope of Mount Hermon, it forms highland terrain of strategic importance.
history: It was originally a place of worship of the god Pan and was called Paneas, but after Herod the Great came to rule it, he dedicated it to the emperor Augustus and named it Caesarea. Afterward Herod's son, the tetrarch Philip, added his own name and changed it to Caesarea Philippi, and this was a political act to express loyalty to the Roman emperor and to consolidate his own authority.

introduce: Put (or Phut), mentioned in Isaiah chapter 66, verse 19, is a name referring to an ancient country or people that was located in the ancient Near East and the African region.
biblecontents: It is one of the regions to which God said He would send survivors among the nations after setting a sign among them: Tarshish, Put, Lud, the archers of Lud, Tubal, and Javan (Isaiah 66:19).
geography: It is generally identified with the region west of ancient Egypt, that is, the area of present-day Libya or a particular coastal zone of North Africa.
history: In the ancient Hebrew Bible and the surrounding ancient literature, Put is also recorded as one of the sons of Ham, and it was used as a term for tribes or powers of Libyan lineage who served as mercenaries of ancient Egypt.

remark: 1. A town west of the plain of Judah.
introduce: Zanoah is a town that was located in the territory of the ancient tribe of Judah, a place name that appears in the records of conquest in the time of Joshua and in the records of rebuilding after the return from exile.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns that the tribe of Judah received as an allotment in the time of Joshua (Joshua 15:34). After the return from the Babylonian exile, when Nehemiah rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, the inhabitants of Zanoah took part, together with Hanun, in repairing the gate and building the wall (Nehemiah 3:13). It is recorded again as one of the villages where the descendants of Judah who had returned lived (Nehemiah 11:30).
geography: Zanoah is presumed to be present-day Khirbet Zanu'a, a point located in the hill country of Judah west of Bethlehem and near the Elah Valley. It is situated about 25 kilometers southwest of Jerusalem.
history: It is an area where traces of human habitation have been found from the early Iron Age. In the time of the kingdom of Judah it was used as part of the defense system, and after the Babylonian exile, under the rule of the Persian Empire, it functioned as an important base in the rebuilding and resettlement of the Judean community.

remark: 2. A town east of the hill country of Judah.
introduce: Zanoah is one of the towns that belonged to the territory of the tribe of Judah, a region located in the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in Joshua chapter 15, verse 56, as one of the list of towns of the inheritance that the tribe of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:56).
geography: A hill country area of Judah west of Hebron, it is identified with the present-day Khirbet Sanu'a area. Topographically it is situated in a mountainous region, giving it conditions favorable for defense.

introduce: Sardis was the capital of the ancient kingdom of Lydia and an important commercial and administrative center in western Asia Minor. In the New Testament it appears as the site of one of the seven churches mentioned in the book of Revelation.
biblecontents: Sardis is mentioned in Revelation as the destination of the letters sent to the seven churches (Revelation 1:11). The church here was judged to have a name that it was alive, yet in reality to be dead (Revelation 3:1). Even so, it is recorded that a few names who had not soiled their garments remained in Sardis (Revelation 3:4).
geography: Sardis is located in the Sart area of Manisa Province in present-day Turkey. It is situated on the northern foot of the Tmolus Mountains, and the surrounding Hermus River basin provided fertile soil, so that it had the topographical requirements suited for the development of agriculture and commerce.
history: Sardis flourished as the capital of the kingdom of Lydia around the seventh century B.C. In particular, because it lay along the gold-bearing Pactolus River, it is known as the city that issued the world's first metal coins. Afterward, passing through Persian rule, it functioned as a strategic stronghold through the Hellenistic period and the time of the Roman Empire. Topographically it was regarded as an impregnable fortress, but historically there is a precedent of its having been taken by surprise attack twice.

introduce: Zarephath was a coastal city of ancient Phoenicia, identified with the Sarafand area of present-day Lebanon. In the Old Testament period it was territory belonging to Sidon, and it is known as the stage of the activity of the prophet Elijah.
biblecontents: When a famine came, Elijah, following God's instruction, was sent to a widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon, and there he experienced the miracle in which the widow's jar of flour and jug of oil did not run out (Luke 4:26).
geography: Zarephath is located on the Mediterranean coast, between Sidon to the north and Tyre to the south. From ancient times this area was a fertile coastal plain region where maritime trade and agriculture were combined.
history: A city settled since the Bronze Age, where archaeological excavations have confirmed that Phoenician pottery production and dye-extraction industries flourished. In the Old Testament period it was under the influence of Phoenicia, and as a Gentile region it became a point of intersection with the activity of the prophets of Israel.

remark: 1. The plain extending from Joppa to Mount Carmel.
introduce: Sharon is a name referring to the northern and central parts of the Palestinian coastal plain, and it carries the meaning "fertile plain" in Hebrew. This region is located between the Mediterranean Sea and the central mountain region, and historically agriculture and herding developed there.
biblecontents: In the time of King David there was a separate overseer in charge of the herds of cattle grazing in Sharon (1 Chronicles 27:29). The Bible describes Sharon as a fertile region where flowers bloom (Song of Solomon 2:1), and it is also mentioned as a place that suffers the desolation of withering vegetation at the time of judgment (Isaiah 33:9). It was prophesied that the glory and beauty of God would appear in this region in the future (Isaiah 35:2), and it is described that in the future it would become a place where flocks lie down (Isaiah 65:10). In New Testament times, there is a record of the event in which the people living in Sharon saw Peter's miracle and turned to the Lord (Acts 9:35).
geography: The Plain of Sharon is a long, narrow plain region about 50-60 km in length, extending from Joppa in the south to the foot of Mount Carmel in the north. It borders the Mediterranean coast on the west and connects with the hill country of Samaria on the east. Because this region has abundant rainfall and fertile soil, its agricultural value was very high from early times, and it had the topographical feature of a mixture of poorly drained marshland and forest.
history: Sharon was a strategic stronghold through which the Way of the Sea, a major trade route of the ancient Near East, passed. Because this region was located on the border of the territories of the tribes of Israel, territorial disputes and struggles over spheres of economic influence between Israel and the surrounding nations were frequent there historically. In particular, population movement was active after the Babylonian exile and through the Persian and Greek periods, and in New Testament times, under Roman rule, major cities were formed and it developed as a commercial base.

remark: 2. A plain or town east of the Jordan River.
introduce: Sharon is a place name east of the Jordan appearing in 1 Chronicles chapter 5; it is pastureland in the regions of Gilead and Bashan, distinguished from the coastal Plain of Sharon on the Mediterranean coast.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad lived in Gilead and Bashan and its towns and in all the fields of Sharon, to the borders of them all (1 Chronicles 5:16).
geography: It is a fertile highland pasture region spread out between the Bashan plateau north of the Yarmuk River east of the Jordan and northern Gilead.
history: In the Iron Age it was a vast herding region where the tribe of Gad and the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh pastured their livestock, and it was recorded in the census documents of the time of Jeroboam II of the northern kingdom of Israel and Jotham king of Judah.

introduce: Sharuhen is a place name mentioned in the process of the distribution of the ancient tribes of Israel, one of the towns located in the southern region of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the thirteen towns allotted as the inheritance of the descendants of Simeon (Joshua 19:6).
geography: It is presumed to be the northwestern part of the present-day Negev, and although there is a tendency to identify it generally with the area south of Tell el-Far'ah, a connection with Tell el-'Ajjul is also under discussion in scholarship.

introduce: Zarethan is a town located in the Jordan Valley, a region mentioned in the biblical record as a geographical boundary and as a place of metal casting work.
biblecontents: When they crossed the Jordan River, the water rose up in a heap at the edge of the town of Adam, beside Zarethan (Joshua 3:16). Baana son of Ahilud administered Taanach, Megiddo, and all of Beth-shean, beside Zarethan below Jezreel (1 Kings 4:12). When Solomon made the temple utensils, they were cast in the earth in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kings 7:46).
geography: Zarethan is presumed to be located in the Jordan Valley (the Arabah), the plain on the east or west side of the lower Jordan River. As for its specific location, the view that regards Tell es-Saidiyeh, east of the Jordan River, as the leading candidate is dominant. This area has favorable topographical conditions for agricultural and industrial activity, since the channel of the Jordan River and the plain lie adjacent to each other.
history: Zarethan seems to have functioned in ancient Israelite times as one of the centers of Bronze Age and Iron Age civilization. In particular, from the fact that the casting of King Solomon's temple utensils was carried out in this area, it can be seen that Zarethan at that time was an industrial base closely connected with copper mines and casting technology. Geographically, this region was a strategic stronghold where the movement of goods and economic activity between Israel and the surrounding nations were active.

introduce: Zarephath is a coastal city located between Sidon and Tyre, the city-states of ancient Phoenicia. In the Bible it is mentioned as the stage of events connected with the prophet Elijah, and in Hebrew it is called Tsarephath.
biblecontents: God instructed Elijah to go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and obtain food from a widow (1 Kings 17:9). When Elijah came to the city gate, he met a widow gathering wood and asked her for water and bread (1 Kings 17:10). Also, in the book of Obadiah, Zarephath is mentioned as the land to be possessed by the children of Israel who had been taken captive (Obadiah 1:20).
geography: It corresponds to the Sarafand area of present-day Lebanon and is a port city formed along the Mediterranean coast. Located about 15 km from Sidon to the north and about 20 km from Tyre to the south, it lay on the main maritime trade routes of Phoenicia.
history: Zarephath was under the influence of Phoenicia around the ninth century B.C., and archaeological excavations have revealed that it was an industrial center at that time. In particular, this region enjoyed economic prosperity through glass manufacturing and the production of purple dye, and the time of Elijah was a period in which Phoenician religion and culture exerted a great influence on the Palestinian region.

introduce: Sarid is a place name mentioned as a border area of the tribe of Zebulun when land was distributed to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The third lot came up for the descendants of Zebulun according to their families, and the border of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid (Joshua 19:10); from Sarid it turned eastward toward the sunrise to the border of Chisloth-tabor, went out to Daberath, and went up to Japhia (Joshua 19:12)
geography: Sarid is presumed to be present-day Tel Shadud (Tel Shad) or its vicinity, and it lies on the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Plain, the lower plain of Galilee. This point was used as a geographical marker indicating the starting point at which the territory of the tribe of Zebulun extended eastward.

remark: 1. The capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, built by Omri, the sixth king of Israel.
introduce: Samaria is the name of a city built as the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel in the Old Testament period, and also of its surrounding region. It was chosen as a strategic stronghold by the dynasty of Omri, and afterward it served as the political center of Israelite history.
biblecontents: King Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there (1 Kings 16:24). Omri was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab succeeded to the throne (1 Kings 16:28). Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria and reigned for twenty-two years (1 Kings 16:29). Ahab built an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32). The famine in Samaria was severe (1 Kings 18:2), and Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his army, surrounded Samaria, and attacked it (1 Kings 20:1). Ben-hadad boasted that the dust of Samaria would not be enough to fill the hands of his people (1 Kings 20:10). When the king of Aram sent scouts, they reported that men were coming out from Samaria (1 Kings 20:17).
geography: Samaria is located in the central hill country of Israel, on a hill well suited to strategic fortification. It has the topographical advantage of overlooking the surrounding plain and the main trade routes, and so has a location with conditions favorable for military defense.
history: Samaria was established as the capital around the ninth century B.C. by Omri, the sixth king of the northern kingdom of Israel. Its geographical defensibility was far superior to that of Tirzah, the former capital, so it became a base for promoting the political stability and administrative integration of the northern kingdom. By the time of Ahab it was transformed into a center of Baal worship, becoming a symbolic place of religious and political conflict, and it appears as a major battlefield in the continuing wars with the kingdom of Aram.

remark: 2. The entire territory of the northern kingdom. In New Testament times, however, it meant only the region of Ephraim and Manasseh west of the Jordan River.
introduce: Samaria is the name of the capital of the ancient northern kingdom of Israel and also of its surrounding region. After being built by the dynasty of Omri, it served as the political and religious center of the northern kingdom.
biblecontents: In 1 Kings chapter 13, verse 32, Samaria is mentioned as the place concerning which it was prophesied that the LORD would surely fulfil His word against the altar at Bethel and against all the high places in the cities of Samaria (1 Kings 13:32).
geography: Samaria is located in the central hill country west of the Jordan River, between the hill country of Judah to the south and the region of Galilee to the north. Built on an isolated mountain peak, it has topographical conditions favorable for defense, and is adjacent to the main trade routes.
history: King Omri bought the hill from Shemer for two talents of silver, built a city, and named it Samaria after the name of its owner (1 Kings 16:24). Afterward, through the time of King Ahab, it became a city symbolizing the prosperity of the northern kingdom, with a magnificent ivory palace being built, but around 722 B.C. it fell to Shalmaneser and Sargon II of Assyria, and the kingdom of northern Israel perished.

introduce: Samos is an island located off the eastern coast of the Aegean Sea, a place that functioned as an important strategic stronghold and a center of maritime trade within the sphere of ancient Greek civilization.
biblecontents: When the apostle Paul was returning to Jerusalem after finishing his third missionary journey, he sailed and stopped opposite Chios, and arrived at Samos the next day (Acts 20:15).
geography: It is an island in the Aegean Sea off the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, specifically about 1.5 km from Cape Trogylium. Topographically it has much mountainous terrain, and in ancient times the strait between this island and the Asia Minor mainland was a major route of navigation.
history: Under the rule of Polycrates in the sixth century B.C. it enjoyed economic prosperity on the strength of powerful naval power, and it is also known as the birthplace of Pythagoras and as a religious center where the temple of Hera was located. In the Roman period it maintained its status as an autonomous or free city within the province of Asia and functioned as an important port of the Mediterranean world.

introduce: Samothrace is an island located in the northern Aegean Sea, a point on the route of sailing from Troas to Neapolis at the time of the apostle Paul's second missionary journey.
biblecontents: There is a record that Paul and his companions set sail from Troas, ran a straight course to Samothrace, and went on the next day to Neapolis (Acts 16:11).
geography: Samothrace refers to the present-day Greek island of Samothraki, located about 40 kilometers from the Thracian coast in the northeastern Aegean Sea. The island is rugged in terrain, and Mount Fengari in the center of the island, boasting a height of over 1,600 meters above sea level, served as an important landmark for ancient navigators.
history: Ancient Samothrace was famous for the mysteries of the Cabeiri, celebrated at the great sanctuary located on a mountain in the interior of the island. At that time these rites were recognized as authoritative throughout the Mediterranean, and many pilgrims visited the island. From the second century B.C. on it came under Roman influence, but its status as a religious center was maintained for some time.

introduce: Zaphon is a place name located in the region east of the Jordan in ancient Israelite times, one of the towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Gad.
biblecontents: Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon in the valley, the rest of the land of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, with the Jordan and the region along the Jordan up to the end of the Sea of Chinnereth, were given to the descendants of Gad (Joshua 13:27).
geography: Zaphon is located in the Jordan Valley east of the Jordan River, and geographically it is an area adjacent to Beth-haram and Beth-nimrah. Archaeologically it is sometimes presumed to be Tell Eiru in present-day Jordan or its vicinity, but scholars differ in their views on the exact identification.
history: It originally belonged to the domain of Sihon, the Amorite king, but after Israel's wars of conquest it was distributed to the tribe of Gad and incorporated into their territory.

introduce: Shaphir is a town of southern Judah appearing in Micah chapter 1 of the Old Testament, a city of the Shephelah region that was prophesied to suffer judgment and shame in the time of the Assyrian invasion.
biblecontents: It was proclaimed to the inhabitants of Shaphir to pass on in shame, in their nakedness (Micah 1:11).
geography: Shaphir is a town located in the southern part of the lowland of Judah (the Shephelah), identified with Khirbet es-Safira or es-Suafir near Tell es-Safi.
history: At the time of Sennacherib of Assyria's invasion of Judah in 701 B.C., it lay beside a military road of the Shephelah and, placed directly on the invasion route of the Assyrian army, suffered destruction.

introduce: Zaanan is a town of southern Judah appearing in Micah chapter 1 of the Old Testament; located in the Shephelah (the lowland), it is one of the representative towns of Judah that suffered from the invasion of the Assyrian army.
biblecontents: While warning the inhabitants of Shaphir to pass on in shame, in their nakedness, it was proclaimed that the inhabitants of Zaanan, because of siege and terror, would not come out of the city, and that through the wailing of Beth-ezel they would lose any place of support (Micah 1:11).
geography: Zaanan lies in the southern Shephelah, the hilly region at the western foot of the hill country of Judah, and is presumed to be the same place as Zenan, which appears in the list of towns in the lowland of Judah in Joshua chapter 15, verse 37. It is identified with Khirbet es-Sanat or the ruins of 'Arak el-Karab, located around Wadi el-Afranj near Lachish and Mareshah.
history: When Sennacherib king of Assyria invaded Judah in 701 B.C. in response to King Hezekiah's anti-Assyrian alliance, the fortress cities of the Shephelah, including Lachish, were destroyed on a large scale, and their inhabitants were taken away as captives. The prophet Micah described, through Hebrew wordplay, the tragedy suffered by the towns of the Shephelah near his hometown of Moresheth, and recorded as a historical scene the misery of the inhabitants of Zaanan, shut in by the invading army and unable to get out.

introduce: Zaananim is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, a place that appears mainly as a boundary of the tribe of Naphtali and as the dwelling of a particular person.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the border of the tribe of Naphtali begins at Heleph and the oak in Zaanannim and reaches Lakkum by way of Adami-nekeb and Jabneel (Joshua 19:33). Also, there is a mention that Heber the Kenite pitched his tent beside the oak near Zaanannim and lived there (Judges 4:11).
geography: It is presumed to be an area in the southwest of the Sea of Galilee or near the lower Jordan River, and is known as a point with an oak tree adjacent to ancient routes of travel. The exact archaeological location is disputed, but the view that it is a plain region near Kedesh is the general one.

introduce: Shaaraim is a town that was located in the territory of the ancient Israelite tribe of Judah, and it carries the meaning "two gates" in Hebrew.
biblecontents: Shaaraim is mentioned as one place in the Shephelah region in the list of towns distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:36). After David brought down Goliath, the Philistines were pursued, as they fled, as far as the road to Shaaraim (1 Samuel 17:52). Shaaraim is also recorded as one of the towns where the tribe of Simeon lived until the time of David (1 Chronicles 4:31).
geography: The location of Shaaraim is presumed to be the Shephelah region, the lowland of Judah. Archaeologists sometimes cite present-day Tell es-Safi or Khirbet el-Arayim as candidate sites, but scholarly views on a particular point remain divided.
history: Located in the border zone between the tribe of Judah and the Philistines in the early Iron Age, it had the character of a military stronghold. Being near the Elah Valley, it was used as a strategic passage when major engagements with the Philistines occurred.

introduce: Shaalabbin is a place name mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Dan at the time of the distribution of the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Shaalabbin is included among the list of towns allotted as the inheritance of the descendants of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:42).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Tell Selbit or its vicinity, and is understood to be located in the Shephelah region, the lowland near the Valley of Aijalon.

introduce: Shaalim is an ancient region mentioned in 1 Samuel chapter 9 of the Old Testament, a district of central Palestine located on the route along which Saul wandered in search of his father Kish's lost donkeys.
biblecontents: Saul went through the hill country of Ephraim and the land of Shalishah but did not find them; he went through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there either; and he went through the land of the Benjamites but did not find the donkeys (1 Samuel 9:4).
geography: Shaalim is presumed to be the area where the southern part of the hill country of Ephraim and the northwestern border of the tribe of Benjamin meet. The name appears to derive from shual, meaning "fox" or "jackal," and it is connected with Shaalbim (Joshua 19:42, Judges 1:35), a town of the tribe of Dan located northeast of the Valley of Aijalon, or with the hills and valley region near the Valley of Zeboim east of Michmash.
history: The Shaalim region, just before the formation of the united kingdom at the end of the eleventh century B.C., was a typical mountain farming and herding region where the tribes of Benjamin and Ephraim had settled and grew olives and grain. It was also a zone of military tension where the Philistine army had advanced deep into the interior, stationed garrisons, and pressed upon the hill country of Israel.

introduce: Shaalbonite is a place name referring to the hometown of Eliahba, one of David's mighty men, the elite military corps of King David.
biblecontents: Eliahba, one of David's mighty men, is recorded as a Shaalbonite (2 Samuel 23:32). In 1 Chronicles as well, Eliahba is likewise mentioned as a Shaalbonite (1 Chronicles 11:33).
geography: The exact location of Shaalbon has not been clearly identified archaeologically to this day, but there is a theory that presumes it to be related to Shaalbim on the basis of the etymology of the place name. Shaalbim was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Dan, and it is identified with the area of present-day Tel Shaalbim.

introduce: Shaalbim was a town located within the territory of an ancient Israelite tribe, a region that held strategic importance from the early settlement period until the time of Solomon's kingdom.
biblecontents: The Amorites were determined to live in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim, but when the power of the house of Joseph grew strong, they were put to forced labor (Judges 1:35). It is mentioned as an area included within the jurisdiction of the second district of King Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kings 4:9).
geography: It is presumed to be near present-day Selbit, and is located in a low hill country adjacent to the western boundary of the Valley of Aijalon. This area lay on the route connecting the coastal plain with the hill country of Judah, and so served as a topographically important passage.
history: It was originally a dwelling place of the Amorites, but conflict arose in the course of its incorporation into the territory of the tribes of Israel after the period of the judges. Afterward, as the Israelite monarchy was established, it was placed under Solomon's system of twelve administrative districts and became part of a systematic ruling district responsible for goods and taxes.

introduce: Gibeah of Saul is a town of the tribe of Benjamin, the place where Saul, the first king of Israel, was born, and the center where the royal residence was located during his reign.
biblecontents: After the war with the Amalekites, King Saul returned to his home base, Gibeah (1 Samuel 15:34). It is mentioned as the place where his house stood after Saul was chosen king, and it was used as Saul's residence from the early part of his reign (1 Samuel 10:26).
geography: It is presumed to be the present-day Tell el-Ful area, located on high ground about 5 km north of Jerusalem. It is a strategic stronghold from which the surrounding terrain can be seen at a glance, and it sits in the center of the hill country of Benjamin.
history: It is a town with a painful history in which, because of the incident of the wicked men of Gibeah that appears in the latter part of the book of Judges, the tribe of Benjamin faced the danger of near extermination. Afterward, with the rise of the dynasty of Saul, it again emerged as a political center, but when the dynasty of David made Jerusalem its capital, its importance gradually diminished.

introduce: Shaveh means "valley" or "plain" in Hebrew, and is a proper noun referring to a specific topographical feature called the King's Valley in the Bible.
biblecontents: When Abram returned after defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom met him in the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley (Genesis 14:17).
geography: The Valley of Shaveh is presumed to be located in the vicinity of Jerusalem, and is traditionally interpreted as a low-lying area near the point where the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley meet.

introduce: Shaveh-kiriathaim is a place name appearing in Genesis chapter 14, recorded as one of the places where military clashes occurred in the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and struck the Rephaites at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites at Ham, and the Emites at Shaveh-kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5)
geography: Shaveh-kiriathaim is presumed to have been located near the plains of Moab in the region east of the Jordan, and is also interpreted as the plain of Kiriathaim. Kiriathaim is generally identified with present-day Khirbet el-Qureiyat, located in the area south of Mount Nebo.
history: It is mentioned in the course of the eastern coalition forces, centered on Chedorlaomer king of Elam, conquering the main strongholds east of the Jordan as they moved southward in the Middle Bronze Age. The Emites who lived in this region at that time were known as a tall and powerful people, but were conquered by the coalition forces.

introduce: Zair, which appears in 2 Kings chapter 8, verse 21, is a place name mentioned as the site of a military clash that occurred during the reign of Joram king of Judah.
biblecontents: Joram king of Judah went to Zair with all his chariots, and rising by night he struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and the commanders of the chariots (2 Kings 8:21).
geography: The exact location of Zair has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it is presumed to be in the border zone between the kingdom of Judah and Edom, or a strategic stronghold within Edom.
history: At that time Edom had been under the influence of Judah since the time of Solomon, but during the reign of King Joram it declared independence and rebelled. The battle of Zair is interpreted as part of a military operation attempted by the kingdom of Judah to suppress Edom's rebellion.

introduce: Shahazumah is a place name mentioned in the process of the distribution of inheritances among the children of Israel, one of the areas located on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Issachar.
biblecontents: The border reached Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and ended at the Jordan. There were sixteen cities, along with their villages. (Joshua 19:22)
geography: Shahazumah was located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar and is presumed to be a geographical point linking the district between Mount Tabor and Beth-shemesh. Opinions among scholars are divided over its specific archaeological site, and no clear archaeological identification has been made.

introduce: Sansannah is one of the towns allotted to the ancient tribe of Judah, a place name whose existence is confirmed through the biblical record.
biblecontents: It is an area mentioned together with Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, and Hazar-susah in the list of towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:31).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly identified archaeologically to this day, but it is presumed to have been located in the Negev wilderness region of southern Judah.

introduce: Salamis is an ancient city located on the eastern coast of the island of Cyprus, a center of Mediterranean trade and the first port of call of the apostle Paul's first missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul and Barnabas came to Cyprus and arrived at Salamis, and there they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues (Acts 13:5).
geography: Salamis is a port city located at the mouth of the Pedieos River on the eastern coast of Cyprus. Situated in a fertile plain region, its agricultural productivity was high, and it served as a hub of maritime traffic linking the eastern Mediterranean.
history: Salamis, presumed to have been founded around the eleventh century B.C., flourished as the political and economic capital of Cyprus through the Hellenistic period and the time of the Roman Empire. At that time a Jewish community of considerable size had formed on Cyprus, and as a result Jewish synagogues were established in the city. In ancient times, as a center for exporting the resources produced in copper mines, it maintained an important position under Roman rule.

introduce: Shallecheth is a place identified as one of the gates of the temple of ancient Israel, and a name derived from the Hebrew shalleketh, carrying the meaning "the gate that is cast down" or "the gate of casting out."
biblecontents: Shuppim and Hosah were stationed beside the Shallecheth Gate on the ascending highway and carried out the duty of guarding the west gate of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:16).
geography: Shallecheth is presumed to be a gate located on the sloping road leading to the hill of Ophel on the west side of the temple, and it served as a main entrance of the city connected with the western wall of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:16).

remark: 1. The city of Melchizedek, who met Abraham.
introduce: Salem is a place name of the ancient Near East, mentioned in the biblical record as the place where Melchizedek ruled as king. Traditionally many scholars presume this region to be the same place as the later Jerusalem.
biblecontents: Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18). First, his name means "king of righteousness." Then also, "king of Salem" means "king of peace" (Hebrews 7:2). His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion (Psalms 76:2). This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Hebrews 7:1).
geography: It is regarded as a strategic stronghold located in the central hill country of ancient Palestine. In the Hebrew tradition and in biblical commentary, Salem and Zion in Psalm 76, verse 2 are taken as a parallel structure and interpreted as referring to the early form of Jerusalem or to that area.
history: It is presumed to have been one of the city-state systems of the Canaanite region in the Bronze Age. At that time Salem had a monarchical system exerting influence over the surrounding area, and it appears that a figure named Melchizedek held both kingship and the priesthood. Contemporary ancient Near Eastern documents, such as the Tell el-Amarna letters, support the existence at this time of a city-state named Urusalim in the Jerusalem area.

remark: 2. A town near Aenon, west of the Jordan River.
introduce: Salim is a place name mentioned in the Gospel of John in the New Testament as the place where John the Baptist was baptizing.
biblecontents: Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized. (John 3:23)
geography: It is presumed to be in the region west of the Jordan River and is adjacent to the place called Aenon. Scholars cite as candidate sites the vicinity of Scythopolis in the upper Jordan River or the region east of Shechem, but the exact location has not been established archaeologically.

introduce: Salecah is described in the Bible as a town located at the eastern end of the region of Bashan, a place name mentioned mainly as a boundary point connected with the domain of Og king of Bashan and the allotment of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Salecah is mentioned as one of all the cities of the kingdom that Og king of Bashan ruled (Deuteronomy 3:10). In the extent of the land conquered by Joshua, Salecah appears as the eastern boundary of the area under the rule of Og king of Bashan (Joshua 12:5). It also shows that the territorial boundary of the land of Bashan allotted to the half-tribe of Manasseh reached as far as Salecah (Joshua 13:11). The descendants of Gad lived in the land of Bashan and extended their pastureland as far as Salecah to raise livestock (1 Chronicles 5:11).
geography: Salecah is identified with the area of Salkhad in present-day Jordan, and it lies at the foot of the Jabal al-Druze range, the eastern edge of the Hauran plain. This point is a strategically important highland fortress, and it served as a gateway linking the plain of Bashan with the desert region to the east.
history: An area settled since the Bronze Age, in the time of the rule of Og king of Bashan it functioned as a key base defending the eastern border. After the Israelite conquest it was used as a border zone where the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh and the pastureland of the tribe of Gad met, and because of its geographical character it continued to be used in later times as a military stronghold for defending against outside invasion.

introduce: Zalmonah is one of the places where the children of Israel stayed during the journey of the Exodus, a place name located on the route of travel setting out from Mount Hor.
biblecontents: The children of Israel left Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah (Numbers 33:41). They left Zalmonah and camped again at Punon (Numbers 33:42).
geography: The exact location of Zalmonah has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be in the southern area between the mountain region of Edom and the Arabah valley. Considering the route of travel between Mount Hor and Punon in the biblical record, it is thought to have been located somewhere on the eastern border of Edom or west of the Arabah valley.

introduce: Salmone refers to a cape at the eastern tip of the island of Crete, located on the ancient Mediterranean sailing route.
biblecontents: After sailing slowly for many days, we arrived off Cnidus. When the wind impeded us, we sailed to the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone (Acts 27:7).
geography: Salmone is presumed to be the Cape Sidero area, located at the easternmost end of Greek Crete today. This is a major point where ships sailing the Mediterranean, when moving from east to west, must round the eastern end of Crete. With the sailing technology of the time, passing this cape was a key step in keeping to the sea route.
history: In the time of the Roman Empire the Mediterranean was actively used as a sea route linking Rome and its provinces. Salmone was a major maritime stronghold through which grain ships setting out from Alexandria in Egypt for Rome passed. At that time it was usual for ships, when affected by the northwest wind, to move along the southern coast of Crete, and only after passing Salmone could they enter the southern coastal waters of the island.

introduce: Three Taverns was a staging post and town on the Appian Way heading toward ancient Rome, known as the place where the apostle Paul, while being taken to Rome as a prisoner, met the Christians of Rome.
biblecontents: When the brothers in Rome heard about Paul, they came out as far as the Three Taverns to meet him, and when Paul saw them, he thanked God and was encouraged (Acts 28:15).
geography: Three Taverns is a stopping point on the Appian Way located about 50 km southeast of Rome. This area is located near the Pontine Marshes and served as the last major station before entering Rome.
history: In Latin, Tres Tabernae means "three inns." At that time this area was a place with a concentration of lodging and commercial facilities for travelers, a crossroads where officials and travelers entering Rome stayed and exchanged information.

introduce: Zamzummites is a name referring to a branch of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giants known to have lived in the region east of the Jordan River, east of the ancient land of Canaan.
biblecontents: This too was called the land of the Rephaim; the Rephaim formerly lived there, and the Ammonites called them Zamzummites (Deuteronomy 2:20).
geography: It is the region where the Ammonites lived, a highland east of the Jordan River, presumed to be the area near present-day Amman, Jordan.
history: The Zamzummites are classified as a branch of the Rephaim, a native race of giants who lived in the region east of the Jordan before the conquest of Canaan. They were driven out by the Ammonites and had their territory taken, and afterward the Ammonites became the masters of that land.

introduce: One of the gates mentioned at the time of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, a point located near the Pool of Siloam. It serves as a reference point dividing the major sections of the wall repair work and occupies a geographical position important for understanding the substructure of the city.
biblecontents: When Nehemiah inspected the wall of Jerusalem by night, he came to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, but there was no place for the animal to pass, so he turned back (Nehemiah 2:14). At the time of the wall repair, Shallun repaired the Fountain Gate; he roofed it and hung its doors, with its bolts and bars (Nehemiah 3:15). At the time of the dedication of the wall, Ezra went ahead, and the company that followed him came to the Fountain Gate, went up on the wall, and headed for the stairs of the City of David (Nehemiah 12:37).
geography: It is located at the southeastern end of the wall of Jerusalem, near the Pool of Siloam where the water flowing from the Gihon spring collects. It served as a gateway linking the City of David with the low-lying area to its south, and topographically it sits at the lower end where the Kidron Valley and the Central Valley meet.
history: This is a structure recorded in the time of Nehemiah, who carried out the project of rebuilding the wall under the Persian Empire after the Babylonian exile. The repair of the wall at that time was a process of restoring the defense system of ancient Jerusalem, and the Fountain Gate, as a point directly connected with securing water resources, was regarded as a key security zone in terms of the maintenance and management of the city.

introduce: The Fish Gate was one of the gates in the wall of ancient Jerusalem, a place presumed to have been the passage through which merchants brought fish caught mainly in the Sea of Galilee, the Mediterranean, and elsewhere into Jerusalem.
biblecontents: King Manasseh built an outer wall and raised it high, from the valley west of the City of David as far as the entrance of the Fish Gate (2 Chronicles 33:14).
geography: It seems to have been located toward the north or northwest of the wall of Jerusalem, and it is regarded as a strategic stronghold connected with the major road coming in from the north, through which commercial goods flowed in.

introduce: Smyrna was a major port city located on the western coast of ancient Asia Minor, corresponding to Izmir in modern Turkey, and is mentioned in the Bible as the site of one of the seven churches.
biblecontents: John, the author of Revelation, was instructed to send a letter to the church in Smyrna, among the seven churches in Asia (Revelation 1:11). The letter written to the angel of the church in Smyrna contains comfort for a church undergoing affliction and poverty and an exhortation to be faithful unto death (Revelation 2:8).
geography: A strategic stronghold on the Aegean coast of western Asia Minor, it possessed the geographical advantage of a natural harbor, with a deep gulf, and was a transportation center where the products of the surrounding interior region gathered.
history: After being rebuilt as a planned city by Alexander the Great, it developed as a center of Hellenistic culture, and in the time of the Roman Empire it is known as one of the centers of emperor worship. In its day learning and the economy flourished greatly, and with its high loyalty to Rome it enjoyed the status of a major allied city of Rome.

introduce: Spain is a place name of the period of the ancient Roman Empire, referring to the region of present-day Spain and Portugal located on the Iberian Peninsula. It was the region that the apostle Paul had in mind as the final destination of the mission to the West at the time he wrote the letter to the Romans.
biblecontents: The apostle Paul, who had not been able to go to Rome until then because there were many places he had to visit before, hoped, since there was now no more place for him to work in this region, to visit Rome on his way to Spain (Romans 15:23). Paul mentioned that after completing this task and confirming to them the fruit, he would set out for Spain and stop by Rome (Romans 15:28).
geography: Spain corresponds to the western extremity of the Roman world of the time and lies in the western Mediterranean. This was a very long distance as seen from Rome, and it was one of the major provinces of the Roman Empire accessible by the sea routes and land routes of the time.
history: Spain was under Roman rule under the name Hispania. After the Roman conquest campaigns that began in the second century B.C., it was a region where Romanization had progressed considerably, and with abundant mineral resources and as a core of Mediterranean trade, it served as an economic and political stronghold of the Roman Empire.

introduce: Secu is a place name that appears only once, in 1 Samuel chapter 19, verse 22, one of the places David passed through in the course of fleeing from King Saul.
biblecontents: This is the place that forms the setting of the incident in which Saul, who was pursuing David, came to the great well that is in Secu and asked where Samuel and David were, and the people answered that they were at Naioth in Ramah (1 Samuel 19:22).
geography: Secu is presumed to be a place located near Ramah, and the fact that there is a great well there is recorded as a geographical feature (1 Samuel 19:22).

introduce: Seneh is a place name appearing in 1 Samuel chapter 14 of the Old Testament, and refers to a rocky area of rugged terrain that had to be passed by the Israelite army confronting the Philistine army.
biblecontents: Between the places by which Jonathan intended to cross over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rugged crag on this side and a rugged crag on that side; the name of one was Bozez and the name of the other was Seneh (1 Samuel 14:4).
geography: Seneh refers to a sharp, rugged rock cliff on the northern slope across the Michmash gorge. Topographically it is very steep and difficult to traverse, and facing it on the opposite side is the rock called Bozez, together forming a line of defense like a natural fortress.
history: It was mentioned in the situation in which, in the time of King Saul, the Philistine army was encamped at Michmash and pressing upon Israel. This place name appears to explain a geographical difficulty, and it carries the meaning of a tactical obstacle that Jonathan and his armor-bearer had to cross in order to carry out a surprise attack on the Philistine camp.

introduce: Zereth-shahar is a place name mentioned in Joshua chapter 13, verse 19, as one of the towns included in the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the list of towns of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:19).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the Mishor region, the highland plateau east of the Jordan, but its exact present-day location has not been clearly identified archaeologically.

introduce: Zer is a place name mentioned in Joshua chapter 19, verse 35, one of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali, presumed to have been located in the vicinity west or northwest of the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, (Joshua 19:35)
geography: Zer appears to have been a town located on the plain or hills around the Sea of Galilee, and it was one of the strategic strongholds within the territory then allotted to the tribe of Naphtali. As to its specific archaeological location, the view that interprets it as an area adjacent to Hammath or Chinnereth is dominant, but the matching with a present-day place name is open to dispute among scholars.

remark: A town south of Judah, near Anam.
introduce: Shema is mentioned as one of the towns of the southern Negev region allotted to the ancient tribe of Judah in Israel.
