biblecontents: In Joshua chapter 15, verse 26, in listing the towns located at the southern extremity of the inheritance of the descendants of Judah, Shema is included and mentioned together with Amam and Shema (Joshua 15:26).
geography: It is located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah. Its detailed, exact location has not been clearly demonstrated archaeologically, but from the context of the passage it is presumed to be a settlement near Beersheba or farther south.

remark: 1. A town in Simeon, another name of Beersheba.
introduce: Sheba is one of the inheritance towns of the tribe of Judah recorded in Joshua chapter 19, verse 2, a place name mentioned together with Beersheba.
biblecontents: In the list of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah, it is mentioned together with Beersheba, Moladah, and Hazar-shual (Joshua 19:2).
geography: The exact location of Sheba is disputed archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah. Some scholars interpret it as another name for Beersheba or as indicating a particular area nearby.

remark: 2. The well dug by Isaac's servants near Beersheba.
introduce: Shibah is a place name appearing in Genesis chapter 26, a place closely connected with the Beersheba region. It is recorded as a name given after Isaac dug a well.
biblecontents: After Isaac dug the well, he called its name Shibah, and for that reason the name of that city has been Beersheba to this day (Genesis 26:33).
geography: Shibah is identified with Beersheba, which is located in the northern part of the present-day Negev desert. This region belongs to the arid climate zone of southern Canaan and has the topographical characteristic that makes it easy to secure groundwater.

introduce: Sheshach is a place name appearing in the book of Jeremiah, and in biblical commentary and historical scholarship it is interpreted as the product of the Atbash technique, a cryptic expression referring to Babylon.
biblecontents: In Jeremiah chapter 25, verse 26, after mentioning all the kings of the north and all the kingdoms of the earth on the face of the world, there is a record that finally the king of Sheshach will drink (Jeremiah 25:26). Also, Jeremiah chapter 51, verse 41, describes how Sheshach is captured and the city praised by the whole world is seized (Jeremiah 51:41).
history: When the Atbash method, which encrypts words by reversing the order of the Hebrew alphabet, is applied, Sheshach (Sh-sh-k) comes to have the same consonant structure as Babel (B-b-l). This is regarded as a highly literary and political metaphor pointing to Babylon, the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which led the destruction of Jerusalem at that time.

remark: The hill country south of the Dead Sea.
introduce: Seir is a place name for the mountainous region of the ancient Near East east of the Arabah valley, from south of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly as the dwelling place of the Edomite people, and it has at once rugged topographical features and the character of a strategic stronghold.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him struck the Horites in their hill country of Seir (Genesis 14:6). Jacob decided to send messengers to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom (Genesis 32:3). Jacob proposed sending Esau on ahead while he himself would go slowly to Seir, at the pace of the livestock and the children (Genesis 33:14). Esau returned that day to Seir (Genesis 33:16). Because Esau lived in the hill country of Seir, he was called Edom (Genesis 36:8). This is the genealogy of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:9). The chiefs of the Horites who lived in the land of Seir were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan (Genesis 36:30). A prophecy was recorded that Seir would become their possession and that Israel would grow strong (Numbers 24:18). It takes eleven days to go from Horeb by way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:2). The Amorites chased Israel from Seir and struck them as far as Hormah (Deuteronomy 1:44).
geography: The Seir mountain range is a mountainous region about 160 kilometers long, extending from the Valley of Zered in the north to the Gulf of Aqaba in the south. On the west it borders the Arabah valley and on the east it connects with the Arabian desert. It is rugged terrain rising from 1,000 meters to 1,500 meters above sea level, forming a natural fortress favorable for defense. Its principal cities include Petra and Bozrah, and because of its topographical character it served as a passage linking north and south.
history: In the early period it was a region where the Horites lived, but afterward the Edomites, descendants of Esau, the son of Isaac, pushed them out and settled there. The Edomites established a strong base by making use of the rugged terrain of this region, and through the period of the monarchy they had political and military conflicts with Israel and the surrounding nations. After the Neo-Babylonian period, the Nabateans migrated and settled, took control of the trade routes, and the history unfolded in which they brought a highly advanced civilization to flower.

introduce: Shen is a place name mentioned as the place where the prophet Samuel set up a memorial stone after defeating the Philistines.
biblecontents: Afterward, Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12)
geography: It is presumed to be a place located near Mizpah, but its exact location has not been identified archaeologically. Some scholars presume it to be near the area of present-day Tell en-Nasbeh.

remark: 1. Capital of Edom; Amaziah king of Judah renamed it Joktheel.
introduce: Sela is an ancient place name meaning "rock" in Hebrew; in the Bible it appears mainly as the name of a fortified town or a particular landform in the region of Edom.
biblecontents: Amaziah king of Judah went to war against Edom, struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, conquered Sela, and called its name Joktheel (2 Kings 14:7). In an oracle of judgment against Moab, there is a command to send tribute from Sela, by way of the wilderness, to the mount of the daughter of Zion (Isaiah 16:1). Elsewhere in Isaiah there is a passage urging the inhabitants of Sela to sing and shout for joy from the tops of the mountains (Isaiah 42:11).
geography: Sela is widely identified with Petra, located in present-day Jordan. It is surrounded by rugged mountains and narrow gorges, and so has terrain highly favorable for defense against outside invasion.
history: Sela was an important stronghold of the Kingdom of Edom in the Iron Age, and geopolitically it stood in a position controlling the trade routes linking the Red Sea and the Mediterranean. It was regarded as a strategic point during the period of frequent military clashes between the Kingdom of Judah and Edom, and later it developed into the capital of the Nabataean kingdom and established itself as a center of ancient Near Eastern trade.

remark: 2. A town of Benjamin; the place where Saul and his descendants were buried.
introduce: Zelah is a place name appearing in the Old Testament; it is mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, or described as the location of the burial place of the house of Saul. Scholars regard this name as a place distinct from Sela of Edom, and analyze it as a specific locality connected with the burial ground of the family of Saul.
biblecontents: According to Joshua 18:28, Zelah is recorded as one of the towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28). Also, 2 Samuel 21:14 records that the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan, together with the bones of the two sons of Rizpah and of the descendants of Mephibosheth, were buried in the tomb of Kish at Zelah in the land of Benjamin (2 Samuel 21:14).
geography: The exact location of Zelah is a matter of archaeological dispute, but it is generally presumed to lie north of Jerusalem or in the nearby hill country of Benjamin. Given the circumstances of the biblical text, it is highly likely to have been in an area adjacent to Gibeah, where the house of Saul was based.
history: It preserves a historical record: after the historical event involving the descendants of Saul who were handed over to the Gibeonites and executed, David gathered up their bones and laid them at Zelah, where the tomb of Kish was, thereby completing the funeral rites of the royal house.

remark: 3. A pool in the king's garden, located south of Jerusalem.
introduce: Shelah is a pool in the southern part of Jerusalem that appears in Nehemiah 3 in the Old Testament, and it is the same reservoir as the Pool of Siloam of the New Testament.
biblecontents: Shallun repaired the Fountain Gate, and repaired the wall by the Pool of Shelah near the king's garden, as far as the stairs that go down from the City of David (Nehemiah 3:15).
geography: It is a reservoir located near the king's garden, where the Central Valley (the Tyropoeon) and the Kidron Valley meet, at the southern end of the City of David in Jerusalem.
history: It was a key water facility that stored the water brought in from the Gihon Spring through Hezekiah's Tunnel, and after the Babylonian destruction it was restored by Nehemiah together with the wall.

introduce: Sela-hammahlekoth is a place name meaning "the rock of separation" in Hebrew; it is the place where King Saul, while pursuing David, heard the news of a Philistine invasion and stopped the chase.
biblecontents: While Saul was pursuing David, he heard the report that the Philistines had raided the land, so he gave up the pursuit of David and turned back; for this reason that place was called Sela-hammahlekoth (1 Samuel 23:28).
geography: It is presumed to be a rocky area near the wilderness of Maon in the Judean wilderness, but its exact archaeological location has not been determined to this day.
history: In the time of King Saul, Israel was in the process of strengthening its centralized system and was at the same time under the constant threat of an external power, the Philistines. The fact that the military operation to arrest David was broken off because of the urgent situation of the Philistine invasion shows that Israel at that time faced the double task of internal power struggles and external defense.

introduce: Zelzah is a place name presumed to have been located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It is one of the principal points along the route mentioned when Samuel delivers a prophecy to Saul in 1 Samuel 10:2.
biblecontents: Samuel prophesied to Saul that, after he finished the search for the donkeys, he would meet two men guarding Rachel's tomb beside Zelzah, at the border of Benjamin (1 Samuel 10:2).
geography: The exact location of Zelzah has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to lie within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, north or northwest of Jerusalem. The biblical text gives a geographical reference point: the neighborhood of Rachel's tomb (1 Samuel 10:2).

introduce: Sodom is an ancient city-state appearing in the book of Genesis, described as having been located in the fertile lowlands of the Jordan River valley. It is mentioned as one of the five cities of the plain, a league of cities of the ancient Near East, and is recorded as the setting for economic prosperity and the social conflict that accompanied it.
biblecontents: The border of Sodom became the reference point that marked the geographical limits of Canaan (Genesis 10:19). This was a region as prosperous as the garden of the LORD or the land of Egypt, since the whole plain of the Jordan was well watered (Genesis 13:10). Abram's nephew Lot moved toward Sodom and pitched his tent near it (Genesis 13:12). At that time the men of Sodom were wicked and great sinners against the LORD (Genesis 13:13). Bera, king of Sodom, formed an alliance with the kings of the other cities to oppose the coalition that included Amraphel king of Shinar and others (Genesis 14:2). In the battle fought in the Valley of Siddim the king of Sodom was defeated, and in the process all the goods and food of Sodom were carried off (Genesis 14:8, 14:10, 14:11). Lot, who was living in Sodom at the time, was also taken captive along with his possessions (Genesis 14:12). Afterward, when Abram returned from rescuing Lot, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (Genesis 14:17).
geography: The Bible emphasizes that Sodom was located in the lowlands of the Jordan (the Kikkar), suggesting that this region was farmland supported by abundant water resources at that time. In archaeological circles, research continues that proposes as candidate sites the Lisan Peninsula in the southeast of the Dead Sea or ancient sites nearby, but geological evidence and scholarly theories are divided on its precise geographical location.

introduce: Zorah was a town located in the border region between the tribes of Judah and Dan at the time of the distribution of the land among the tribes of ancient Israel. It is well known as the hometown of the judge Samson, and it corresponds to a strategic point in the Shephelah, a region of low hills.
biblecontents: Zorah is mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:33). Afterward it was included in the area assigned as the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:41). The household of Manoah, a man of the tribe of Dan, lived here (Judges 13:2), and it is also the place where Samson first experienced the stirring of the Spirit of the LORD (Judges 13:25). After his death, Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial place of his father Manoah (Judges 16:31). The five warriors whom the tribe of Dan sent to spy out new land were from Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 18:2), and it was also the region to which they returned to report to their kinsmen (Judges 18:8). Afterward 600 armed men of the tribe of Dan set out from Zorah and Eshtaol and moved on to Laish (Judges 18:11). In David's time, the clans of the people of Zorah are mentioned in connection with the genealogy of Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53, 1 Chronicles 2:54).
geography: Zorah is identified with Tel Zorah, northwest of Beth-shemesh in present-day Israel. It is set in the hill country called the Shephelah, and since it lies on a low hill overlooking the Sorek Valley, it has topographical features suited to controlling the surrounding routes of travel.
history: It was occupied from the Late Bronze Age through the Iron Age, and geographically it lay in a buffer zone between the Philistine plain and the hill country of Judah. For this reason it has the historical character of a border region in which territorial disputes between the tribes of Israel and the Philistine power were frequent. Later, in the time of Rehoboam, it was refortified as one of the towns fortified to strengthen the defense system of the Kingdom of Judah.

introduce: Sorek is one of the place names of ancient Israel, referring mainly to a valley, and the area around it, lying in the border zone between the tribe of Judah and the Philistine plain.
biblecontents: Samson loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah (Judges 16:4).
geography: The Valley of Sorek is a region formed along Wadi Sorek, which rises in the hill country of Judah, runs west across the Philistine plain, and flows into the Mediterranean. This region is known as a fertile vine-growing district, and it served both as a strategic passage linking the interior of Israel with the coastal plain and as a natural buffer zone.
history: In the early Iron Age, this region was a front line where the tribes of Israel and the Philistine power frequently clashed over territorial expansion. Because it lay on the border between Judah and the tribe of Dan, it is regarded as a place where cultural and military contact with outside powers was very frequent.

remark: The region between Hamath and Damascus.
introduce: Zobah was an Aramean kingdom that existed in the region of Syria between the 11th and 8th centuries BC, a powerful force that was drawn into close military conflict with Israel in the time of David.
biblecontents: When King Saul took the kingship over Israel and fought against his enemies on every side, he also fought against the kings of Zobah (1 Samuel 14:47). When David struck down Hadadezer king of Zobah, Zobah was extending its territory as far as the bank of the Euphrates River (2 Samuel 8:3). David defeated the Aramean army of Damascus that had come to help Zobah (2 Samuel 8:5), and he dedicated to the LORD the gold and silver he took from them (2 Samuel 8:12). The men of Zobah joined with the Ammonites and opposed David's army, but were defeated (2 Samuel 10:8, 1 Chronicles 18:5). Igal, the son of Nathan, one of David's mighty men, was a man of Zobah (2 Samuel 23:36). In Solomon's time Rezon fled from Hadadezer king of Zobah and became king of Damascus (1 Kings 11:23, 11:24). On his way to strike Hadadezer at the Euphrates River, David defeated him (1 Chronicles 18:3).
geography: The exact location of Zobah is difficult to pinpoint archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be the northern part of the Beqaa Valley, north of Damascus, between the upper Orontes River and the Euphrates River. At that time Zobah occupied a strategic point from which it could exert influence over the surrounding Aramean city-states, including Damascus.
history: Around the 11th century BC the Arameans gradually expanded their power in this region, and Zobah emerged as one of their central states. During the reign of Hadadezer, Zobah became a military great power by unifying the surrounding Aramean city-states or exerting influence over them. However, as David's Israel expanded it came into conflict with Zobah, and after Zobah was defeated by David its influence weakened. Afterward, as Damascus rose again as the center of Aram, the standing of Zobah was relatively diminished, and as a result it provided the spatial foundation for the growth of the Aramean kingdom of Damascus.

introduce: Aram-zobah refers to an Aramean tribal state that existed in the region of Syria from the 11th century BC to the early 10th century BC. It was one of the powerful political forces that frequently clashed militarily with Israel in the time of David.
biblecontents: When the Ammonites realized that they had become odious to David, they hired mercenaries, and at that time they hired twenty thousand foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah (2 Samuel 10:6). David defeated the kingdom of Zobah ruled by Hadadezer, and afterward, when Hadadezer king of Zobah tried to extend his power to the bank of the Euphrates River, David stopped him and won the victory (2 Samuel 8:3).
geography: The exact location of Zobah is disputed among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be the area near the Beqaa Valley, between the east of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains in present-day Syria and the north of Damascus. It stood on the route running north from Damascus, a major trade route of the ancient Near East, and served as a strategic point.
history: It was one of the several small kingdoms formed as Aramean tribes settled throughout Syria in the early Iron Age. During the reign of Hadadezer it expanded its power by unifying the neighboring Aramean tribes, and it contended for supremacy with David's kingdom of Israel. However, after it was defeated by David it gradually lost its influence, and it appears to have been absorbed into, or incorporated into the sphere of influence of, the Aramean kingdom that arose around Damascus.

introduce: It is the name of one of the chiefs of the Horite clans who appear in the early governing genealogy of the Edom region, and it also refers to a territorial unit presumed to be where he lived or which he administered.
biblecontents: The chiefs of the Horite clans were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these were the chiefs of the Horites, the descendants of Seir in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:29).
geography: The setting is the mountainous terrain of southern Edom, formed around the region of Mount Seir. It is regarded as one of the principal strongholds where the Horite clans settled.

introduce: It is an ancient Near Eastern place name mentioned as one of the military powers allied with Babylon.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the powers that accompanied the army of Babylon when it came to attack Jerusalem (Ezekiel 23:23).
history: It is presumed to refer to a tribe or region in Mesopotamia, or in its vicinity, that lay within the sphere of the Neo-Babylonian Empire at that time, but its specific location and records have not been clearly established historically.

introduce: Zoan was a major city in the northeastern Nile Delta of ancient Egypt, and in the Hebrew Bible it is mentioned as the center of events connected with the kings of Egypt. In the Egyptian language it was called Djanet, and in Greek it is known by the place name Tanis.
biblecontents: God led the people of Israel out by performing miracles in the fields of Zoan in Egypt (Psalms 78:12). The miracles performed at Zoan are recorded as signs proving the power of God (Psalms 78:43). The prophet Isaiah pointed out that the princes of Zoan were foolish and that their wisdom was of no use (Isaiah 19:11). He also mentioned that the princes of Zoan had been deluded and had led Egypt astray (Isaiah 19:13). The sending of envoys by the people of Judah to Zoan to seek help is recorded (Isaiah 30:4). A message of judgment was proclaimed that God would send fire upon Zoan (Ezekiel 30:14).
geography: It lies on the Tanitic branch of the Nile Delta and was a strategic point and an economic center. Situated in the delta region with its fertile soil, it was an area where agriculture and trade flourished.
history: During the Twenty-first and Twenty-second Dynasties it served as the capital of Egypt. Because it was close to the northeastern border, it served as a gateway for trade with Asia and for military movement. It was a politically very important city, where the royalty and officials of ancient Egypt lived and where diplomatic envoys were received.

introduce: Zoar is an ancient city that appears in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and the prophetic books of the Old Testament, and it is one of the five cities of the plain, originally called Bela. It is presumed to have been located near the southeast of the Dead Sea, and it is well known as the place to which Lot and his two daughters fled to escape the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.
biblecontents: When Lot lifted up his eyes and looked at the whole plain of the Jordan, the whole land as far as Zoar was well watered, like the garden of the LORD (Genesis 13:10). The king of Zoar took part in the war against the coalition that included the king of Shinar and others (Genesis 14:2, 14:8). It was the small town that Lot was permitted to stay in when Sodom was destroyed (Genesis 19:22), and the sun had risen when Lot entered Zoar (Genesis 19:23). Afterward Lot was afraid to live in Zoar, so he went up to the hills and lived in a cave with his two daughters (Genesis 19:30). Zoar is mentioned as one of the boundaries of the promised land that Moses viewed from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:3). Isaiah and Jeremiah, prophesying judgment against Moab, mentioned Zoar as a place name of Moab (Isaiah 15:5, Jeremiah 48:34).
geography: Zoar appears to have been located near the Valley of Siddim, the plain at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Geographically it lies at the southern end of the Jordan Valley, and it had an environment more fertile and better watered than the surrounding regions (Genesis 13:10). It was adjacent to the major trade routes of the ancient Near East, and topographically it lay below a mountainous area, so it had the spatial condition that allowed Lot to flee to the hills.
history: It is presumed to be one of the city-states that formed in the southern Dead Sea region in the Early Bronze Age. At that time the five cities, including Zoar, were under the rule of surrounding great powers or in a relationship of paying tribute to them. As time passed, it was included within the territory of Moab or became a city closely tied to Moab, which is confirmed by the fact that it is treated as a Moab-related place name in the records of the times of Isaiah and Jeremiah.

introduce: Zoheleth was a place near the walls of Jerusalem, a place name appearing in 1 Kings 1:9. It is known as the place where Adonijah, plotting to succeed to the throne, gathered his followers and offered sacrifices.
biblecontents: Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves by the stone of Zoheleth, near En-rogel, and invited all the princes, that is, all his brothers, and all the men of Judah who were the king's servants, but (1 Kings 1:9)
geography: Zoheleth is presumed to refer to a rock, or the area around it, near the Gihon Spring in Jerusalem. It is identified as lying near En-rogel, in the vicinity of the point where the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley, the valleys to the southeast of the City of David at that time, meet.
history: It is the place where, when the problem of succession arose in the last years of King David, Adonijah, David's fourth son, summoned his supporters and made a show of strength in order to make himself king. It is mentioned in a historical situation that stood opposed to the political moves of Nathan and Bathsheba, who sought to set Solomon on the throne after David.

introduce: Sychar is a town located in the region of Samaria, a place name mentioned in John chapter 4 as the place where Jesus and the Samaritan woman held their conversation.
biblecontents: While Jesus was passing through Samaria, He came to a town called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph (John 4:5). Jacob's well was there (John 4:6).
geography: From an archaeological and geographical standpoint, the view that identifies Sychar with the village of Askar, near the southeast of Shechem, is dominant. Jacob's well is located in the southeastern part of modern Shechem, and it lies on the gently sloping plain between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
history: Jacob's well, which is associated with Sychar, is linked with the movements of Jacob recorded in the book of Genesis in the Old Testament, and the region of Samaria acquired a mixed ethnic and religious background through the resettlement policy of Assyria after the fall of northern Israel. For this reason, a relationship of tension came to exist historically between the Jews and the Samaritans.

introduce: The Sucathites is a name connected with a clan or a particular region that appears in 1 Chronicles 2:55, and within the Bible it is mentioned as a place where scribes lived or as their place of origin.
biblecontents: The clans of scribes who lived at Jabez, namely the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites; these are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab (1 Chronicles 2:55)
history: The Sucathites are presumed to be the dwelling place of the scribal clans, a branch of the Kenites connected with the house of Rechab, or a name referring to them. The Kenites, as descendants of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, were assimilated into Israelite society and were active in it, and this verse shows that some of them performed the duties of scribes and were associated with the region called Jabez.

remark: A town of the tribe of Issachar, located on the slope of Mount Gilboa.
introduce: Shunem was a town located in the Jezreel Valley in northern ancient Israel, an area belonging to the allotment of the tribe of Issachar. In the biblical records this place is mentioned as a strategic military base and as the setting of episodes involving particular persons.
biblecontents: Shunem is recorded as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:18). It is also the place where the Philistine army camped in order to attack Israel (1 Samuel 28:4). It is mentioned as the hometown of Abishag, the Shunammite woman who served David in his last years (1 Kings 1:3), and she attended to him in David's bedchamber (1 Kings 1:15). Afterward, in connection with the incident in which Adonijah asked for Abishag to be given to him as his wife, it appears again that her place of residence was Shunem (1 Kings 2:17, 1 Kings 2:21, 1 Kings 2:22). Also, there is the episode of a prominent woman who received Elisha with great hospitality when he passed through Shunem (2 Kings 4:8); when her son fell ill and died, Gehazi was sent to look after him (2 Kings 4:12), and afterward Shunem is mentioned in the course of the woman going to Elisha on Mount Carmel to seek help (2 Kings 4:25).
geography: Shunem, identified with present-day Tell Sunam, is set on a plain at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley. Lying on the southwestern slope of Mount Moreh, it can strategically survey the Jezreel plain, and as a crossroads it has an environment favorable to military movement and agriculture.
history: Shunem faces Mount Gilboa across the Jezreel Valley, so it was a region where military clashes between the Philistines and Israel were frequent. In the early Old Testament period it was the territory of the tribe of Issachar, but the fate of the town alternated with the invasions of surrounding great powers and the political circumstances of the Davidic dynasty. In particular, the appearance of Abishag from Shunem in the events connected with the royal succession at the end of David's reign contains a historical situation that shows an aspect of the internal power dynamics of the royal house at that time and of the concubinage system.

introduce: Syracuse was a major port city on the southeast coast of the ancient island of Sicily, and it is recorded in the book of Acts as a port of call where Paul stayed briefly while being taken to Rome as a prisoner.
biblecontents: The ship of Alexandria on which the apostle Paul was sailing came to Syracuse and stayed there three days (Acts 28:12).
geography: A strategic point on the eastern coast of the island of Sicily, it had a natural harbor and served as a major base on the Mediterranean sea lanes.
history: A Greek colonial city founded around the 8th century BC by the Corinthians, it was one of the most prosperous city-states of the ancient western Mediterranean world. After coming under Roman rule, it carried out administrative and economic functions as the center of the province of Sicily.

introduce: Syrophoenician is a place name mentioned in Mark chapter 7, verse 26 of the New Testament; it is a designation that combines the regional identity of ancient Phoenicia with the administrative division of Syria.
biblecontents: When Jesus went to the region of Tyre and Sidon, a woman who had a daughter possessed by a demon came to Jesus and begged Him, and the Bible records that this woman was a Greek, of Syrophoenician origin (Mark 7:26).
geography: It means the region of Phoenicia, which was included in the province of Syria in the administrative divisions of the Roman Empire at that time. Geographically it refers to a broad western coastal zone that includes Tyre and Sidon, the coastal area of present-day Lebanon.
history: The name Syrophoenician is a compound of ancient Syria and Phoenicia. For the sake of distinguishing it within the adjacent province of Libya, the Roman Empire incorporated that region as part of the province of Syria, and in this process the inhabitants of Phoenician descent were classified and called Syrophoenicians, a Roman administrative designation.

remark: A country north of Palestine, extending to the Euphrates River in the northeast and to the Taurus Mountains in southern Turkey in the northwest, and bordering the Mediterranean on the west; the same as the Aramean kingdom of the Old Testament.
introduce: Syria is the Greek name for the region called Aram in Hebrew, and it means a broad territory in the ancient Near East that includes the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. Throughout the Bible this region maintained close political and military relations with Israel, and in the New Testament period it functioned as one of the principal administrative districts of the Roman Empire.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the region ruled by Rezon, the adversary of Solomon (1 Kings 11:25), and it appears as the place to which people fled to Jerusalem to escape the army of the Chaldeans when King Nebuchadnezzar invaded Judah (Jeremiah 35:11). The report about Jesus spread throughout all Syria, and the sick came to Him (Matthew 4:24), and when Quirinius was governor of Syria, a registration was carried out by the decree of Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:2). The commander Naaman was a Syrian who was healed in Israel (Luke 4:27), and after the Jerusalem council a letter was delivered to the Gentile brothers in Antioch, Syria, and elsewhere (Acts 15:23). During his missionary journey Paul traveled through Syria to Cilicia (Acts 15:41), after completing a vow at Cenchreae he left for Syria (Acts 18:18), and he made a plan to go to Syria again (Acts 20:3). The latter part of the book of Acts describes a voyage by ship toward Syria (Acts 21:3).
geography: Its boundaries are the Taurus Mountains to the north, Galilee and the upper Jordan River region to the south, the Mediterranean to the west, and the Euphrates River and the Syrian Desert to the east. Its principal centers were Antioch in the Orontes River valley and Damascus, and it served as a geopolitical crossroads where trade routes intersected.
history: In the first millennium BC it was the center of the Aramean kingdoms, but afterward it passed under the rule of the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian empires. After the death of Alexander the Great it became the core territory of the Seleucid dynasty, and in 63 BC it was conquered by Pompey for the Roman Empire and became a Roman province. In the New Testament period, Syria, with Antioch as its capital, held an important position as a military and administrative control base of the Roman East.

introduce: Shumathites is a place name or a family name mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:53 as one of the clans of Kiriath-jearim.
biblecontents: The clans of Kiriath-jearim were the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites (1 Chronicles 2:53)

introduce: Suphah is a place name mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, a place presumed to be a region located near the Valley of the Arnon.
biblecontents: The place name Suphah is mentioned in a document called the Book of the Wars of the LORD, which explains the origin of the name, and it indicates that this region was near the Valley of the Arnon (Numbers 21:14).
geography: It is identified with an area near the Arnon River in the western part of the present-day Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, and is thought to be a place with topographical features adjacent to the ancient plain of Moab.

introduce: Susa was the capital of the ancient Persian Empire and a major administrative center of the Achaemenid dynasty, a city that appears in the books of Esther and Nehemiah as the setting for the royal residence and important political events.
biblecontents: Xerxes, king of the Persian Empire, took his throne and reigned in the palace at Susa (Esther 1:2). Nehemiah, staying in the palace at Susa, heard the news of the ruin of Jerusalem and grieved (Nehemiah 1:1). In a vision, Daniel found himself at the Ulai Canal in the citadel of Susa in the province of Elam (Daniel 8:2).
geography: It is the area of Shush in the Khuzestan Province of southwestern present-day Iran, a strategic point between the Zagros Mountains and the Mesopotamian plain. Located in a fertile zone through which the Shaur and Dez rivers flow, it had an environment suited to the development of a city from ancient times.
history: Susa, which had been the capital of the Elamite kingdom, rose to become a major administrative city of the Persian Empire after it was conquered by Cyrus II around the 6th century BC. Darius I designated it the winter capital of the empire and built splendid palaces there. The Persian kings used Susa as the core site of administration, diplomacy, and residence, and it served as the center of imperial power until the Achaemenid dynasty was conquered by Alexander the Great.

introduce: The Zuzites is an ancient place name mentioned in Genesis 14, a region that lay on the route along which the eastern coalition led by Chedorlaomer moved in its campaign of conquest.
biblecontents: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came out and defeated the Rephaites in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, and the Emites in Shaveh-kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5)
geography: The Zuzites are presumed to have been east of the Jordan, and because material from inside and outside the Bible is lacking, it is difficult to pinpoint their specific location by modern geography. However, in context it is highly likely to have been near an ancient trade route of the Transjordan region.
history: The Zuzite clan living in the region of the Zuzites is classified as a group of indigenous inhabitants from before the Canaanite settlement. Historically, it is recorded as one of those conquered when the coalition led by Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, subdued the peoples east of the Jordan and moved south.

remark: A town of Benjamin.
introduce: Shual is a region mentioned in 1 Samuel 13:17, recorded as one of the place names along the route taken by the Philistine army when it moved to attack Israel.
biblecontents: From the Philistine camp raiders went out in three companies, and one of the companies turned toward Ophrah by the road leading to the land of Shual (1 Samuel 13:17).
geography: Geographically, Shual is presumed to have been located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, and is regarded as an adjacent area connected with the region of Ophrah near Mizpah.

introduce: Syene was the southernmost border city of ancient Egypt, corresponding to the area of present-day Aswan. In the Bible it is used as a place name symbolizing the southern end of Egypt, in contrast to Migdol, the northern boundary of Egypt.
biblecontents: God prophesied that Egypt would become a wasteland, and that from Migdol to Syene neither man nor beast would pass through (Ezekiel 29:10). It is also recorded that those who help Egypt will fall, and that from Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword there (Ezekiel 30:6).
geography: Syene is a strategic point near the First Cataract of the Nile, and it faces Elephantine Island, an island in the upper Nile. Topographically it was the limit of navigation on the Nile, and it served as a gateway linking ancient Egypt and the region of Nubia.
history: During the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt and the Persian period that followed, Syene prospered as a military fortress and a commercial center. In particular, records have been found of Jewish mercenaries stationed there during the Persian occupation, who formed a community, and it was also an economic base that supplied major building materials as a quarry of ancient Egyptian granite.

remark: 1. East of the Jordan; the place where Jacob made shelters for his livestock.
introduce: Succoth is an ancient place name located in the region east of the Jordan River; it is the place where Jacob, on his way back from Paddan-aram, settled and built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock.
biblecontents: Jacob came to Succoth and built a house for himself and made shelters for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Succoth (Genesis 33:17).
geography: It is located in a fertile plain area near the point where the Jabbok River joins the Jordan, east of the Jordan River. It is presumed to be Tell Deir Alla in the region of present-day Jordan.

remark: 2. The first place where Israel stayed after leaving Rameses in Egypt.
introduce: Succoth is a place name recorded in the route of the ancient exodus from Egypt as the first place where the Israelites camped after leaving Rameses.
biblecontents: The people of Israel left Rameses and came to Succoth (Exodus 12:37). Leaving Rameses, they camped at Succoth at the edge of the wilderness (Exodus 13:20). The people of Israel left Rameses and camped at Succoth (Numbers 33:5). Leaving Succoth, they camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness (Numbers 33:6).
geography: There are several theories about the location of Succoth. The dominant view regards it as the same region as Tjeku, the ancient Egyptian place name, and this is presumed to be near Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat region.
history: In the New Kingdom period of Egypt, the Wadi Tumilat was a strategic point that protected the eastern border of the Nile Delta and managed trade with the region of Asia. Succoth is regarded as a place that served as a border garrison or a supply base within the Egyptian administrative system.

remark: 3. Located in the tribe of Gad, near Beth-haram. Presumed to be the same place as 1.
introduce: Succoth is an ancient city located east of the Jordan River; it is the place where Jacob, on his way back from Paddan-aram, settled and built shelters for his animals, and it is the region allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Gad after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon in the valley of the Jordan were assigned as the inheritance of the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13:27). While Gideon was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, he asked the men of Succoth for bread, but was refused (Judges 8:5). The princes of Succoth refused to give bread, on the grounds that Gideon's army had not yet won the victory (Judges 8:6). Gideon asked the men of Succoth for bread in the same way as he had the men of Penuel, but was refused again (Judges 8:8). Gideon seized a young man of Succoth and obtained the list of the princes and elders of that place, and he judged their disobedience (Judges 8:14).
geography: Succoth is a fertile plain area east of the Jordan River, near the confluence where the Jabbok River flows out into the Jordan Valley. In modern archaeological surveys, the area of Tell Deir Alla is identified as the likely site of Succoth. This region is rich in water resources and has conditions suited to farming and herding.
history: From the Bronze Age through the Iron Age it was used as a major stronghold east of the Jordan, and in particular in the time of Solomon it was a region where metalworking was so developed that the bronze casting work to make the vessels of the temple was carried out between Succoth and Zarethan on the plain of the Jordan.

remark: 4. A city in Ephraim, near Zarethan.
introduce: Succoth was a foundry district in the Jordan Valley where the bronze vessels of the temple were cast in the days of King Solomon.
biblecontents: The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the thick clay between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kings 7:46). The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay between Succoth and Zeredah (2 Chronicles 4:17).
geography: It is a plain in the middle of the Jordan Valley, near the point where the Jabbok River joins the Jordan, opposite Zarethan and in the vicinity of Tell Deir Alla. The abundant clay made it well suited for making molds.
history: In the tenth century BC, during the large-scale state building projects of Solomon in the united kingdom, it was a center of the metal industry where bronze objects were cast in great quantities.

introduce: Shulammite is interpreted as a designation connected with a person or a particular region appearing in the Song of Solomon in the Old Testament. In the biblical text it is used in the expression "the Shulammite woman," which carries the sense of an adjective derived from the place name Shunem.
biblecontents: Return, return, O Shulammite woman; return, return, that we may look at you. Why do you want to gaze at the Shulammite woman, as one watches the dancing at Mahanaim? (Song of Solomon 6:13)
geography: Shulammite is identified with the region of Shunem (present-day Sulam, Solam), located in the Jezreel Valley. Shunem lies in the plain between southern Galilee and northern Samaria, and is a strategic crossroads between Mount Tabor and Mount Gilboa.
history: In ancient Israelite times Shunem was a fertile region with well-developed agriculture. In biblical history, Shunem is close to the area where King Saul encamped before the battle of Gilboa, and it is well known for the story of the prophet Elisha and the Shunammite woman. The name Shulammite became fixed as a designation for a woman from this region.

introduce: Secacah is one of the towns located in the Judean wilderness among the areas allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: In Joshua 15:61, it is mentioned as one of the six towns in the wilderness in the list of towns apportioned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:61).
geography: Secacah was located in the northeastern part of the Judean wilderness, and is presumed to have stood in the rugged, arid terrain west of the Dead Sea. The area is classified as adjoining the highland that runs from Jerusalem to En-gedi.

introduce: Scythia refers to the region where the Scythians, a nomadic people who lived in the steppe lands north of the Black Sea and in Central Asia, dwelt according to ancient Greek and Roman literature. In ancient society they were sometimes regarded as a byword for uncivilized barbarians.
biblecontents: There cannot be Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all, and is in all (Colossians 3:11)
geography: Scythia covers the vast Eurasian steppe region, beginning in the steppe lands of Ukraine north of the Black Sea, passing through the Caspian Sea, and reaching the Altai Mountains of Central Asia. It is the dwelling place of nomadic communities without fixed borders, and its geographical character is that migration routes were determined by climate and pasture.
history: The Scythians were a people who built a powerful nomadic empire in the steppe lands of Central Asia from the seventh century BC to the third century BC. They were famous for their excellent horsemanship and metalworking skills, and appeared in ancient history by trading with, or clashing with, the Persian Empire and the Greek city-states. By the time the New Testament was written, Scythia was already past the decline of the early Scythian kingdom, but the term was commonly used in a general sense for the uncivilized northern foreign peoples who lived beyond the borders of the Roman Empire.

introduce: Zenan is one of the towns of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a settlement that was located in the lowland region of southern Judah.
biblecontents: Zenan is included in the list enumerating the towns that the tribe of Judah received as an inheritance in Joshua 15:37 (Joshua 15:37).
geography: Zenan is classified as a town located in the western lowland region called the Shephelah, within the portion of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:37). Scholars are divided over its exact location, and some identify it with modern Khirbet es-Sanah.

introduce: Senir is an Amorite name for Mount Hermon in the biblical record, a place name denoting the highlands in the eastern part of the Lebanon range. From the perspective of ancient Near Eastern geography, it is regarded as a strategic crossroads connected with the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges.
biblecontents: The Sidonians call Mount Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir (Deuteronomy 3:9). The half-tribe of Manasseh lived from Baal-hermon to Senir and Mount Hermon, and they became numerous (1 Chronicles 5:23). In a figurative expression the bride is invited to come down from the peak of Senir and Hermon (Song of Solomon 4:8). There is a record that the fir trees needed for building the ships of Tyre were taken from Senir (Ezekiel 27:5).
geography: Senir is the region of present-day Mount Hermon, including the highest peak, located on the border between Lebanon and Syria. This region has perpetual snow and is a key water-source area that forms the headwaters of the Jordan River. To the north it is joined to the Lebanon range, and by blocking the moisture blowing in from the Mediterranean it exerts a great influence on the climate and vegetation of the Galilee region.
history: In the Bronze Age and Iron Age, the Senir region was famous as a major source of building timber such as cedar and fir. Tyre of ancient Phoenicia established political and economic relations in order to secure the high-quality timber of this region, which is clearly seen in the description of the merchants of Tyre in Ezekiel 27. In addition, this region serves as an indicator of the historical process of territorial boundaries and the expansion of settlement between the Amorite peoples and the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Zedad is a place name mentioned in the Bible as one of the points on the northern boundary of the inheritance the people of Israel were to receive.
biblecontents: It stipulates that the northern boundary of the land of Canaan that the people of Israel were to possess would run from Mount Hor to the entrance of Zedad and extend to Hamath (Numbers 34:8). It is also recorded that the northern boundary of Israel that the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision likewise passes by the entrance of Zedad and continues to Hamath (Ezekiel 47:15).
geography: In ancient geography and biblical archaeology, the prevailing view identifies Zedad with the area of Sadad, located in the north of the Beqaa Valley, the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges. It lies to the southeast of present-day Homs in Syria, and is traditionally regarded as the northernmost boundary line that Israel was to occupy.

introduce: Zeredah, as mentioned in the biblical text, is a place name indicating the hometown of Jeroboam, a servant of Solomon who became the first king of northern Israel.
biblecontents: Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon, was an Ephraimite from Zeredah (1 Kings 11:26). In connection with the record of the return to Tirzah, where Jeroboam's house was, in order to report the child's illness to Jeroboam's wife, Zeredah appears in Chronicles as an important setting (2 Chronicles 4:17).
geography: Zeredah is presumed to be a region located near the Jordan Valley. If it is interpreted as the same place name as Zarethan, where the metal-casting work of Solomon's royal household was carried out, it is a strategic location west of the Jordan River with the regional characteristic of abundant clay soil.

introduce: Zererah is a place name appearing in Judges 7:22, a place mentioned in the course of the battle between Gideon's army and the Midianite coalition forces.
biblecontents: When Gideon's three hundred men blew their trumpets, the LORD caused the enemy troops to strike one another with the sword, and the multitude fled as far as Beth-shittah in Zererah (Judges 7:22).
geography: Zererah is presumed to be a place name located near the Jordan Valley, and is known as a point along the route by which the Midianite army retreated toward the Jordan River in the east. Scholars analyze that this name may be related to a plain near Beth-shan or a specific area west of the Jordan River, but at present its exact archaeological location is difficult to pinpoint.

remark: 1. A town near Bethel, to the north of Benjamin.
introduce: Zemaraim is a place name mentioned in the course of describing the boundaries of the tribe of Benjamin in the time of Joshua, and in the Bible it appears as one of the towns included within the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: Zemaraim is listed among the towns of the inheritance that the descendants of Benjamin received for their clans (Joshua 18:22).
geography: The exact location of Zemaraim has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but from the context of the biblical text it is presumed to have been near Jericho or in the eastern boundary region of the tribe of Benjamin.

remark: 2. A part of Ephraim.
introduce: Zemaraim is a place name located in the hill country of Ephraim, mentioned in the Book of Chronicles, and it is recorded as the place where King Abijah gave a speech before the war with Jeroboam.
biblecontents: Abijah, king of Judah, went up on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and addressed Jeroboam and all Israel (2 Chronicles 13:4).
geography: It is located in the hill country of Ephraim, and archaeologically it is also presumed to be the same area as Tell el-Marajim, located near present-day Ramallah, but the exact identification is still under discussion among scholars.

remark: 1. Near the northern part of Ethiopia.
introduce: Seba refers to an ancient kingdom, or the people of that region, regarded in the Hebrew Bible mainly as located in the southwestern part of Arabia. In the biblical record they are described as wealthy traders, a people who dealt in spices, gold, and precious stones.
biblecontents: After the flood of Noah, Seba is mentioned as a descendant of Shem and as a son of Cush, a descendant of Ham, respectively (Genesis 10:7, Genesis 10:28). There is a record that the queen of Sheba visited Jerusalem to test Solomon's wisdom, bringing gold, precious stones, and spices (1 Kings 10:1-2). In the prophetic books the people of Seba are described as a people who amassed great wealth through trade, and they are also mentioned as those who would present gifts to God (Isaiah 45:14, Psalms 72:10). They are also mentioned in connection with Ethiopia (Isaiah 43:3).
geography: According to archaeological and historical research, Seba is presumed to correspond to the Kingdom of Saba in the southwestern Arabian Peninsula, the region of present-day Yemen. This region was a key point on the spice trade route passing through the Red Sea, and was a center of maritime and overland trade connecting Arabia and the African continent.
history: Throughout the first half of the first millennium BC, the Kingdom of Saba, located in southern Arabia, built a powerful economic base through the production of and trade in frankincense and myrrh. They built the Marib Dam to maximize agricultural productivity, and used their own Sabaean script and language. In various records of the ancient Near East as well, Seba or Saba is confirmed as a powerful force that held a monopoly position in the spice trade.

remark: 2. The southwestern region of Arabia.
introduce: Sheba was a nation or region located in the ancient Near East, mentioned in the biblical record mainly as a distant land possessing immense wealth, spices, and precious stones in the time of King Solomon. In modern archaeological research, the prevailing view identifies it with the Kingdom of Saba, which was located in the region of present-day Yemen.
biblecontents: The queen of Sheba, having heard of Solomon's fame, visited Jerusalem with a large retinue, carrying spices, gold, and precious stones, in order to test him with hard questions (1 Kings 10:1, 2 Chronicles 9:1). The queen was greatly amazed when she saw Solomon's wisdom and his buildings (1 Kings 10:4, 2 Chronicles 9:3), and she gave him 120 talents of gold and an enormous quantity of spices and precious stones as gifts (1 Kings 10:10, 2 Chronicles 9:9). Afterward Solomon in turn gave the queen everything she desired, and she returned to her own land with her servants (1 Kings 10:13, 2 Chronicles 9:12). Meanwhile, the Book of Job records that the Sabeans plundered Job's cattle and killed his servants (Job 1:15), and Sheba is also described as a station on the trade route where the caravans of Tema and the travelers of Sheba sought water (Job 6:19).
geography: Sheba is presumed to be the territory of the ancient Kingdom of Saba, that is, the region of present-day Yemen, in the southwestern Arabian Peninsula. Because it is located at the gateway of the Red Sea connecting Asia and Africa, it had a very advantageous position for controlling the spice trade routes.
history: From about 1000 BC, the Kingdom of Saba prospered as a trade center producing and exporting valuable spices such as frankincense and myrrh. According to ancient records and archaeological excavations, they built advanced irrigation facilities such as the Marib Dam and developed agriculture, and on this basis accumulated economic wealth and maintained active trade with neighboring countries.

introduce: Zephathah is a place mentioned in the Book of Chronicles as the battlefield of a war fought in the time of Asa, king of Judah. It is known as a valley located near Mareshah.
biblecontents: Asa went out to fight, and they drew up their battle lines in the Valley of Zephathah before Mareshah (2 Chronicles 14:10)
geography: Zephathah is a valley near Mareshah located in the border zone between the hill country of the tribe of Judah and the Shephelah plain. It lies about 40 km southwest of Jerusalem, and served as a strategically important passage at that time.
history: It is the place where Asa, king of Judah, set up a defensive line when Zerah the Cushite invaded Judah with a great army. Because of its topography, the site was used as a space suitable for large armies to maneuver or to confront one another.

introduce: Sepharad is a place name mentioned in the Book of Obadiah in the Old Testament, signifying a specific region where the Israelites were prophesied to return and settle after the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: It is recorded that many of the captives of Israel will again possess the land of Canaan, and that the people of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will possess the cities of the south (Obadiah 1:20).
geography: Opinions in scholarship are divided over the exact location of Sepharad. Some regard it as referring to Sardis in Asia Minor, while other views hold it to be a place in the Persian region or to be Spain, but there is no geographically established conclusion.
history: Sepharad is mentioned as a place symbolizing the restoration of the Jewish community and the expansion of its geographical range after the Babylonian exile. It appears in a prophetic context in which, amid the political circumstances at the time the Book of Obadiah was written, the Jews who had been scattered in foreign lands would return and recover their territory.

introduce: Shebarim is a place name mentioned in the course of the Israelite army's retreat after its defeat at the city of Ai in the time of Joshua.
biblecontents: The men of Ai struck down the men of Israel before the gate of the city and chased them as far as Shebarim, striking them on the descent, so that the hearts of the people melted and became like water (Joshua 7:5).
geography: It is presumed to be a slope or valley area running down to the east from the city of Ai in the direction of Jericho. Its specific archaeological location has not been confirmed, but it appears to be a landmark in the nearby area not far from the town.

introduce: Sephar is an ancient place name mentioned in the genealogical record of Genesis to explain the extent of the territory where the Joktan clan lived, and it is presented as a boundary line referring to the eastern mountain region.
biblecontents: The place where they lived was the hill country of the east, from Mesha as far as the road to Sephar (Genesis 10:30)
geography: In ancient Near Eastern scholarship, the prevailing view interprets this place name in connection with the Kingdom of Saba in the Yemen region of the southwestern Arabian Peninsula, or with the Zafar region near Oman. However, scholars still disagree about its exact location.

introduce: Sepharvaim was a city of the ancient Near East, to which, after it was conquered under the expansion policy of the Assyrian Empire, its inhabitants were transferred to Samaria as part of a policy of forced relocation. In the biblical record this city is mentioned together with the cities of other countries conquered by the kings of Assyria, and is described as a place where a group with its own religious belief system lived.
biblecontents: The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the people of Israel (2 Kings 17:24). The people of Sepharvaim served gods called Adrammelech and Anammelech, and burned their children in the fire as sacrifices to these gods (2 Kings 17:31). The Rabshakeh of Assyria retorted by asking where the gods were that had conquered Samaria, mentioning that the gods of Hamath and Arpad, and the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah, had not saved Samaria (2 Kings 18:34, Isaiah 36:19). In the prayer of King Hezekiah, too, the fact that the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, and the kings of Hena and Ivvah had been destroyed was brought up (2 Kings 19:13, Isaiah 37:13).
geography: Sepharvaim is generally regarded as the same place as Sippar, which was located in northern Babylonia. It lay along the Euphrates River and was a strategic location adjacent to the major trade routes of ancient Mesopotamia.
history: From the time of ancient Babylonia, Sepharvaim was famous as a temple city that worshiped the sun god Shamash. In the late eighth century BC, in the course of the Assyrian Empire's powerful wars of conquest, it was incorporated under Assyrian rule. Assyria carried out a policy of forcibly relocating populations in order to prevent rebellions in conquered lands and to maintain productivity, and the inhabitants of Sepharvaim were likewise moved to the Samaria region in this process.

remark: 1. A town of Moab captured by the tribe of Reuben, also called Sibmah.
introduce: Sebam is a town located in the region east of the Jordan, rebuilt after being captured by the tribe of Gad. It appears in the biblical record in connection with grape cultivation.
biblecontents: Sebam is mentioned as one of the towns rebuilt after being captured by the tribe of Gad (Numbers 32:3). In addition, in the time of David it was treated as important as a grape-producing area, to the extent that separate officials were appointed over the vineyards and the wine cellars (1 Chronicles 27:27).
geography: Sebam is presumed to be in the Gilead region east of the Jordan River or a fertile plain nearby. Although there are differing views on its detailed location, it is generally assessed as an area close to Heshbon, with a climate and soil suited to farming and grape cultivation.
history: During the Israelite conquest of Canaan, the tribe of Gad valued the economic worth of this region highly and requested the land as its inheritance. Later, in the period of the Davidic monarchy, we can see that the vineyards and wine cellars here were systematically managed as part of the royal economy.

remark: 2. The eastern shore of Chinnereth, in the north, between Hazar-enan, and Riblah and Ain.
introduce: Shepham is a place mentioned in the Bible as one of the points on the eastern boundary set when the people of Israel were to receive the land of Canaan as their inheritance.
biblecontents: According to Numbers 34:10 and 11, when the eastern boundary of Canaan was fixed, the boundary was set from Hazar-enan to Shepham, and it is recorded that the boundary goes down from Shepham to Riblah and reaches the east side of Ain (Numbers 34:10, Numbers 34:11).
geography: The exact location of Shepham has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be southeast of Mount Hermon or in the area near Damascus. In the context of the biblical text, it serves the geographical function of a starting point or waypoint on the northeastern boundary line of Canaan.

remark: A town of Simeon south of the border between Judah and Edom, also called Hormah.
introduce: Zephath was a town located in the southern region of ancient Canaan, a place named Hormah after it was conquered by the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Simeon.
biblecontents: The tribe of Judah went with their brother, the tribe of Simeon, and struck the Canaanites who lived in Zephath and utterly destroyed it, so the name of the city was called Hormah (Judges 1:17).
geography: Zephath is presumed to be located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah, and although its specific archaeological site has not been identified, there are theories placing it in the vicinity of Tell el-Milh or Tel Arad.
history: It is an example of a name that was changed in the course of the allied tribes of Judah and Simeon conquering the native Canaanites of the area and formalizing their occupation during the Israelite conquest of Canaan.

introduce: Zepho is a name that refers to a tribe of the Edom region or the chieftain of that tribe, a name that appears among the descendants of Esau, the ancestor of Edom.
biblecontents: Esau listed the chiefs among the sons of his son Eliphaz, and the chief Zepho is included in that list (Genesis 36:15).
geography: The land of Edom is a region centered on the Seir mountain country southeast of the Dead Sea, and the specific place name or location ruled by the chief Zepho is not recorded in detail in the Bible.

remark: 1. One of the five cities of the Valley of Siddim, destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah.
introduce: Zeboiim is one of the five city-states, mentioned along with Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Bela, that were located in the Valley of Siddim in the ancient Near East. These cities are often cited together as a byword for destruction and judgment.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the boundary of Canaan reached as far as Zeboiim (Genesis 10:19). Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, made an alliance with Sodom, Gomorrah, and the others and took part in the war to resist the coalition forces, including Chedorlaomer, king of Elam (Genesis 14:2). At the time of the war, Zeboiim allied with the other kings in the Valley of Siddim and fought against the enemies (Genesis 14:8). Moses, warning the people of Israel of the consequences of disobedience, mentioned that Zeboiim had been destroyed by the LORD (Deuteronomy 29:23). The prophet Hosea cited Zeboiim as a destroyed city in the course of expressing God's compassionate heart (Hosea 11:8).
geography: Zeboiim is presumed to have been located in the Valley of Siddim, an area of the Jordan lowlands in or near the southern Dead Sea. Its exact location has not been pinpointed archaeologically, but scholars discuss the possibility that, together with the surrounding cities, it was buried or submerged by geological upheaval or disaster.
history: In the early Bronze Age the city-states of this region prospered by occupying key points on the trade routes, but in the early second millennium BC they became caught up in political and military conflicts. Zeboiim is reported to have been destroyed amid the struggle for supremacy between the Mesopotamian powers centered on Elam and the city-states of southern Canaan.

remark: 2. A valley in Benjamin on the eastern slope of the Jordan plain.
introduce: Zeboim is a place name that existed within the territory of ancient Israel; in the Bible it is mentioned as a strategic crossroads in the Old Testament period and as one of the dwelling places of the tribe of Benjamin after the return from exile.
biblecontents: There is a record that, when the Philistine army invaded Israel, one company of the army went along the road toward the Valley of Zeboim (1 Samuel 13:18). In addition, Zeboim is included in the list of places where the descendants of Benjamin who had returned from the Babylonian exile lived (Nehemiah 11:34).
geography: Zeboim is presumed to be located in the hill country of the tribe of Benjamin, and the Valley of Zeboim includes rugged terrain heading toward the Dead Sea. The prevailing view interprets it in connection with the area near the present-day Wadi Fara.
history: In the time of King Saul it was a strategic crossroads of high value as a military route, but afterward, in the post-exilic period, it changed into a place with administrative or residential significance as a resettlement area of the tribe of Benjamin.

introduce: Zebulun refers to the region where the tribe of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes of Israel and descended from the tenth son born to Jacob and Leah, settled. The inheritance of this tribe, allotted after the conquest of Canaan, was located in the southern part of Galilee, and in Israelite history it served as a key point for economic activity and military defense.
biblecontents: In the census, Eliab son of Helon was appointed as commander of the tribe of Zebulun (Numbers 1:9), and its population was counted as 57,400 (Numbers 1:31). In the arrangement of the camps it marched as part of the camp of Judah (Numbers 2:7). When the spies were sent out, Gaddiel son of Sodi was chosen as the tribe's representative (Numbers 13:10). In the later census on the plains of Moab it was recorded as 60,500 (Numbers 26:27). After entering Canaan it was included among the tribes that pronounced the curses on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 27:13), and in the blessing of Moses it received the prophecy that it would gain the abundance of the seas and the treasures of the mountains (Deuteronomy 33:18). Its geographical boundary touched the boundaries of Asher and Naphtali (Joshua 19:27), and included the region reaching to the east side of the Jordan (Joshua 19:34). In addition, four of the towns given to the tribe of Levi were within the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 21:7).
geography: The inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun was located between the southwest of the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean coastal plain. It bordered the tribe of Asher on the north, the tribe of Naphtali on the east, and the tribe of Issachar on the south. This region had a mixture of highlands, including Mount Tabor, and flat valleys, so it had terrain suited to farming and herding.
history: During the wars of conquest, Zebulun settled by securing strongholds in the interior of Canaan. Because of its geographical advantage of being connected to the major trade routes of Israel, the territory of this tribe was also a place frequently invaded by outside powers. Historically, throughout the period of the judges and the early monarchy, it served as a core member of the administrative and military defense network of the northern Galilee region.

introduce: Seirah is a place mentioned in Judges 3:26, a point that Ehud passed through while fleeing after he killed Eglon, king of Moab.
biblecontents: While they were hesitating, Ehud fled, passed the stone quarries, and escaped to Seirah (Judges 3:26)
geography: The specific location of Seirah has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be near the hill country of Ephraim or near the highlands west of the Jordan Valley. It appears to be located on the route from the Gilgal area, described as the place where stone was quarried, toward the hill country of Ephraim.

introduce: Shelishiyah was a place name located in the ancient Moab region, a place mentioned in the judgment prophecy of the Book of Isaiah as one of the refuges or landmarks of Moab.
biblecontents: The prophet Isaiah, prophesying the destruction of Moab, described a situation in which their cries are heard as far as Zoar and the refugees go up toward Shelishiyah (Isaiah 15:5).
geography: It was located within the territory of Moab, and judging from the name Eglath-shelishiyah, it is presumed to have been a place with the topographical features of the northern or central Moab region. Although no specific archaeological site has been clearly identified, it is understood to be an area lying along a travel route on the Moabite plain or in the mountainous region.
history: Moab, as a country adjacent to Israel, historically experienced frequent territorial disputes and changes of regime. Around the eighth century BC, during the expansion of Assyria, Moab and the neighboring countries were exposed to the threat of invasion by the surrounding powers, and the prophecy of Isaiah 15 is interpreted as having been written in the context of this political instability and national collapse through foreign invasion.

introduce: Ziklag was a town located on the boundary of the territories of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Simeon in ancient Israelite times. It is known as the place that David was given as a residence when he took refuge with Achish, king of Philistine Gath, to escape the pursuit of King Saul, and afterward it functioned as a strategic point of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: Ziklag was first mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:31). It was later reassigned as the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon (Joshua 19:5), and when David fled to Philistine territory to escape Saul, it was given to him by King Achish as his own possession (1 Samuel 27:6). The Amalekites invaded Ziklag, seized David's family and goods, and burned the town (1 Samuel 30:1), but David, after pursuing them, defeated them and recovered the spoil (1 Samuel 30:14, 30:26). After conquering the Amalekites and returning, David stayed here (2 Samuel 1:1), and it was also the place where he received the news of Saul's death (2 Samuel 4:10). In addition, in the Chronicles it appears as a dwelling place of the tribe of Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:30), and as the gathering place of the mighty men who came to help David when he was hiding from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:1).
geography: Ziklag is located at the northern boundary of the Negev desert in southern Judah. Although there are differing views on its exact location, archaeologically Tell Halif or Tell esh-Sharia are mentioned as the leading candidate sites. This region is a buffer zone between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country of Judah, and in ancient times it was a strategic point for controlling trade routes and military movement routes.
history: In the early Iron Age Ziklag was within the sphere of influence of the Philistines, but when David came to administer this town as a Philistine mercenary, it was in effect incorporated into Israel's sphere of rule. Using this as a base, David subdued nomadic tribes such as the neighboring Amalekites and consolidated his political and military foundation. After Saul's death, Ziklag served as the front-line defensive position protecting the southern border of the kingdom of Judah and defending against Philistine invasion.

introduce: Shinar is a place name of the ancient Near East, a term used in the Bible and ancient historical records to refer to the southern region of Mesopotamia. It mainly means the Babylonian plain, and is recorded as the early cradle of human civilization and the setting of the incident of the Tower of Babel.
biblecontents: Shinar is mentioned as one of the places where Nimrod's kingdom began, a region that includes Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh (Genesis 10:10). It is the place where people, migrating from the east, came upon a plain in Shinar, settled there, and built the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). In the time of Abraham there is a record that Amraphel, king of Shinar, joined with Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and others to wage war (Genesis 14:1, Genesis 14:9). Among the things Achan took from Jericho was a cloak from Shinar (Joshua 7:21). Isaiah prophesied that the LORD would recover His people from Shinar and other places (Isaiah 11:11). The place to which Daniel was taken captive was the temple of a god in the land of Shinar, and King Nebuchadnezzar carried the vessels of the temple there (Daniel 1:2). In the vision of Zechariah, the land of Shinar is mentioned as the place to which wickedness is carried (Zechariah 5:11).
geography: Shinar refers to the fertile alluvial plain in the lower reaches of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers. It corresponds to the southern part of present-day Iraq, and in ancient times it was terrain in which marshes and farmland were intermingled, where the Sumerian and Babylonian civilizations flourished.
history: Scholars understand Shinar to be the ancient Hebrew name referring to the Sumerian Engi or the region of Sumer. This reflects the city-state system of southern Mesopotamia that began around 3000 BC, and it became established as a customary expression for referring to that region when describing the history of the early period of the Babylonian Empire.

introduce: Sinai is mentioned in the Bible as the mountain, and the name of the wilderness, where the people of Israel arrived after the exodus and received the law.
biblecontents: The people of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Wilderness of Sinai (Exodus 16:1). In the third month after the exodus they arrived at the Wilderness of Sinai (Exodus 19:1). They left the wilderness and camped in front of Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:2). The LORD said that on the third day He would come down on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:11). Because the LORD descended on Mount Sinai in fire, the whole mountain was thick with smoke (Exodus 19:18). The LORD descended on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain, and called Moses up to it (Exodus 19:20). Moses replied that boundaries must be set so that the people would not go up Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:23). The glory of the LORD rested on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered the mountain for six days (Exodus 24:16). When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony (Exodus 31:18). The LORD commanded Moses to come up to Mount Sinai in the morning and wait there (Exodus 34:2).
geography: The exact location of Mount Sinai is still a controversial topic in ancient Near Eastern geography, but Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula and its surrounding area are generally regarded as the leading candidate. The wilderness means the rugged terrain surrounding this mountain.
history: In the late Bronze Age, the Sinai Peninsula, which was under Egyptian influence, is presumed to have been a region where the operation of mines for extracting copper and turquoise was active. This region was a point where the migration routes of nomads and the major trade routes intersected.

introduce: Aswan is a place name appearing in Isaiah 49:12, the only place in the whole Bible where it is mentioned. Various hypotheses have been raised among ancient Near Eastern scholars and biblical geographers to determine the exact location of this region, and it is mainly interpreted as referring to a distant region.
biblecontents: Some from far away, some from the north and the west, some from the land of Aswan will come (Isaiah 49:12)
geography: There are several theories about the location of Aswan. There is the view that it is a Semitic name referring to the city of Aswan in southern ancient Egypt, and some scholars interpret it as meaning China. In addition, there is the view that it is the Sina region of Phoenicia or a place name on the Mediterranean coast, but no archaeologically established location has been confirmed.
history: Taking the time when the Book of Isaiah was written as the reference point, it is possible that Aswan was used with the meaning of a pronoun for the end of the world as the people of Israel of that time could perceive it, or for a very distant foreign region. There is a lack of archaeological evidence to prove a connection with any particular nation.
