introduce: Sirah is a Hebrew place name, mentioned as the place where Joab lured Abner and killed him. This area is presumed to be a place near Hebron where there was a well or reservoir.
biblecontents: Joab's messengers called Abner back from the well of Sirah in order to bring him, and David did not know of this (2 Samuel 3:26).
geography: It is identified with the Ain Sarah area near Wadi el-Kaf, located about 3 km north of Hebron. Located on the approach into Hebron from ancient times, it served as an important water source where travelers obtained water and rested.
history: In the early period of the establishment of the Davidic dynasty, when Abner, the military commander of the house of Saul, was about to defect to David, Joab used a ruse at this spot to assassinate Abner in order to avenge the death of his brother Asahel. This was an incident of a time when the strengthening of David's rule and power struggles within the military were intricately entangled.

introduce: Sirion is a biblical place name, the name by which the Sidonians call Mount Hermon.
biblecontents: The Sidonians call Mount Hermon Sirion, and the Amorite tribe called it Senir (Deuteronomy 3:9). It is also recorded that God makes Lebanon skip like a calf and Sirion like a young wild ox (Psalms 29:6).
geography: It refers to Mount Hermon, the highest peak, located at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range. It has the topographical characteristic of being high in elevation and covered with snow all year round, so that it serves as the source of water resources.
history: It was a region called by different names according to the peoples who lived there at the time; the Sidonians named it Sirion, and the Amorite tribe called it Senir. This shows that in the ancient Near East, various peoples assigned names to the same geographical object according to their own differing linguistic customs.

introduce: Shimron-meron was an ancient city-state located in the northern region of Canaan, mentioned as a member of the coalition that opposed the Israelite army at the time of Joshua's conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The king of Shimron-meron is recorded as one of the thirty-one kings of Canaan whom Joshua conquered (Joshua 12:20).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Tel Shimron, and is located between the southwest of the Sea of Galilee and the northern end of the Jezreel Valley, giving it the character of a strategic crossroads.
history: As a city-state that flourished in the late Bronze Age, it took part in the northern Canaanite coalition led by Jabin, king of Hazor, and confronted Israel, but was defeated.

introduce: Sheba refers to an ancient kingdom located in the southwest of Arabia in the ancient Near East, in the region of present-day Yemen. This region is known as a center of the spice trade, and in the biblical record it is described as a wealthy and distant place.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the kings of Sheba will present gifts and bring tribute (Psalms 72:10). It is also said that frankincense coming from Sheba and sweet cane brought from a distant land are not suitable as offerings to the LORD (Jeremiah 6:20).
geography: Located southeast of the Red Sea, at the southern end of the Arabian Peninsula, its terrain combines highlands and coastal plains. In particular, it has a climate optimal for producing spices such as frankincense and myrrh, so it served as a key point on the ancient spice trade routes.
history: As a power that prospered in southern Arabia from about 1000 BC to several centuries BC, it accumulated wealth by monopolizing maritime trade through the Red Sea and caravan trade across the desert. In particular, it built an economic system exporting spices to the Mediterranean world, and records remain of its exchanges with various states of the ancient Near East.

introduce: Sibraim is a place name mentioned as one of the points on the restored northern boundary of Israel that Ezekiel saw in a vision.
biblecontents: Sibraim is described as lying between Hamath and Berothah, an area between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath (Ezekiel 47:16).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the region of present-day Syria, but no specific modern place name or exact archaeological site has been identified. According to the description in the Bible, it is one of the principal points that fix the northern border line of Israel (Ezekiel 47:16).

introduce: Ziphron is one of the points on the northern boundary of Israel that was indicated to Moses before the people of Israel entered the land of Canaan.
biblecontents: God specified that the northern boundary of the land of Canaan would go out from Hazar-enan, reach Ziphron, and that its end would extend to Hazar-enan (Numbers 34:9).
geography: In ancient Near Eastern geography Ziphron is generally regarded as a place name on the northern boundary line of Canaan, but to date there is no agreed conclusion in scholarship about its exact physical location. However, some scholars presume Ziphron to be Zibron, an area near Damascus in Syria, or a particular settlement with a similar sound.

introduce: Zior refers to a town near Hebron that was allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot, an area near Hebron (Joshua 15:54).
geography: It is presumed to have been one of the towns located in the hill country of Judah, situated in the hills southeast or south of Hebron. Archaeologically it is also identified with the site of Khirbet Si'air.

introduce: Shihor is a geographical name of the ancient Near East, used mainly to refer to a branch of the lower Nile in Egypt or to the border region between Egypt and Canaan. Etymologically in Hebrew it means dark-colored water, and depending on the context it is sometimes identified with the Brook of Egypt, meaning the Nile or its tributary.
biblecontents: In describing the unconquered territories that Israel was to conquer, Joshua defined Shihor as the stream before Egypt and presented it as the western end of the boundary of Canaan (Joshua 13:3). When David assembled all Israel in order to bring up the ark of the covenant, he defined its extent as from Shihor to the entrance of Hamath (1 Chronicles 13:5). Isaiah described the grain of Shihor as growing by the waters of the Nile and becoming the merchant of the nations (Isaiah 23:3). Jeremiah figuratively referred to Israel drinking the waters of Shihor in Egypt and drinking the waters of the Nile of Shihor, warning against pagan dependence (Jeremiah 2:18).
geography: Shihor generally means the Nile Delta region, and is regarded as a watercourse located on the southwestern boundary line of Canaan. Geographically it is also explained in connection with Wadi el-Arish or the Pelusiac branch of the Nile. It was a geographical turning point on the way from the southern end of Canaan into Egypt, and a key point for trade using the waterway.
history: Historically, Shihor was a buffer zone where the spheres of influence of the Egyptian empire and the Canaan region intersected. Ancient Egypt secured fertile farmland through the flooding of the Nile, and Shihor was regarded as a symbol of the granary region that was the economic foundation of Egypt. In Israelite history, Shihor was often used as a geographical marker symbolizing the powerful influence of Egypt, and it appears as a major boundary region mentioned when Israel sought to rely on the strength of the surrounding great powers.

introduce: Shihor-libnath is a place name mentioned in Joshua 19:26 as one of the boundaries of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher. The Hebrew place name Shihor-libnath, literally translated, carries the meaning of a stream or river and white, so it is presumed to be a place related to a specific watercourse that can be identified geographically.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the boundaries of the land allotted to the tribe of Asher, passing through Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal, and reaching Shihor-libnath in the west (Joshua 19:26).
geography: It is presumed to be a river flowing near Mount Carmel or a feature of the Mediterranean coast. Biblical commentators and archaeologists also associate this area with the Nahal Kishon (Kishon River) in present-day northern Israel, or with a sandy beach nearby or a specific area where river sediments appear light-colored.

introduce: Shikkeron is a place name mentioned in Joshua 15 as a point on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah. Its exact location has not at present been clearly established archaeologically, but in biblical geography it is regarded as one of the main points that set the territorial boundary line between the tribes of Judah and Dan.
biblecontents: The northern boundary reaches the northern slope of Ekron, goes on to Shikkeron, passes Mount Baalah, and extends to Jabneel, and its end is the sea (Joshua 15:11).
geography: Shikkeron lies on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah and is a point connected with the northern area of Ekron. According to the biblical record, this area lies on the route heading west toward the Mediterranean coast, and signifies a topographical key point between Ekron and Mount Baalah.

remark: 1. The wilderness south of Judah.
introduce: The Wilderness of Zin is a geographical boundary located in the southern region of the ancient Near East, and is a region mentioned as one of the important travel routes during the Israelites' wilderness journey.
biblecontents: The spies explored the land of Canaan from the Wilderness of Zin as far as the entrance of Hamath (Numbers 13:21). In the first month the people of Israel came to the Wilderness of Zin and stayed at Kadesh, and there Miriam died and was buried (Numbers 20:1). Because Moses and Aaron did not uphold God's holiness at the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, they were denied entry into Canaan (Numbers 27:14). The people of Israel left Ezion-geber and camped in the Wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh (Numbers 33:36). The southern boundary of the land of Canaan was set to run along the Wilderness of Zin, passing by Edom (Numbers 34:3).
geography: The Wilderness of Zin includes the southern Arabah and Kadesh-barnea, and broadly it is an arid zone spanning the lower part of the Negev desert and the northeastern boundary of the Sinai Peninsula. To the west it connects with the Wilderness of Shur, and to the southeast it borders the mountainous region of Edom.
history: From the Bronze Age this region was used as a passage connecting Egypt and Canaan and as a migration route for neighboring peoples such as Edom and Amalek. Archaeologically, it has a strong character as a route of movement for nomads or for military movement rather than for settled habitation, and it was often used as a geographical reference point for designating the southern boundary of Canaan.

remark: 2. The wilderness between Elim and Mount Sinai.
introduce: The Wilderness of Sin is a geographical area located between Elim and Mount Sinai, and was a major stopping point that the people of Israel passed through on their journey toward Canaan after the exodus.
biblecontents: The people of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai (Exodus 16:1). The people of Israel left the Wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah (Numbers 33:12). In the Wilderness of Sin the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron because they lacked food (Exodus 16:2-3). Also, the journey in the Wilderness of Sin before moving on to Rephidim is mentioned (Exodus 17:1). The people of Israel camped by the Red Sea and then camped again in the Wilderness of Sin (Numbers 33:11).
geography: The Wilderness of Sin is generally presumed to be a plain area near the west or southwest coast of the Sinai Peninsula. Although there are several theories about its specific location, it is regarded as a vast desert region where highlands and lowlands intersect. It is understood as a place passed through while traveling in a southeasterly direction from Elim, and lies on the route leading to Rephidim and Mount Sinai.
history: It has also been suggested that this region may overlap with the routes of ancient Egyptian mining operations. Considering the travel routes and supplies of the time, the people of Israel appear to have entered this region by way of the Wilderness of Shur. Historically, it is understood to be one of the major passages used by the nomads of the ancient Near East as they moved about.

remark: 3. A border region in the northeast of Egypt, called Belsummot.
introduce: Pelusium is a fortress city in northeastern ancient Egypt that appears in the Book of Ezekiel in the Old Testament, a gateway town of Egypt known in Greek as Pelusium.
biblecontents: It was proclaimed that I will pour out My wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the crowds of Thebes (Ezekiel 30:15). It was warned that I will set fire to Egypt, and Pelusium will be in great anguish (Ezekiel 30:16).
geography: It is located in the Mediterranean coastal marshland at the mouth of the Pelusiac branch at the northeastern end of the Nile, and is identified with present-day Tell el-Farama.
history: As a gateway and fortress on the military road entering Egypt from Asia, it was the scene of major international wars, such as the invasion of Egypt by the Persian Cambyses II in 525 BC.

remark: A region in or near Jerusalem.
introduce: Silla is a place name appearing in 2 Kings 12:20, mentioned as the place where Joash, king of Judah, was assassinated by his servants. Because detailed descriptions of this place name or additional mentions of it in other contexts are limited in the Old Testament, it is a place whose exact location is difficult to pinpoint.
biblecontents: The servants of Joash, king of Judah, rebelled and struck Joash down at the house of Millo, on the road that goes down to Silla (2 Kings 12:20).
geography: Silla is presumed to be located near the Millo in Jerusalem, but archaeological evidence to prove its specific topographical features or its exact relationship to the city wall is lacking. Some scholars interpret it as a passage located inside the city of Jerusalem or on an adjacent slope.

introduce: Shiloah refers to a watercourse and pool located in the Kidron Valley southeast of Jerusalem, a key water-supply facility that drew water from the Gihon spring and supplied it to the city of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: Because this people has rejected the slowly flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoices over Rezin and the son of Remaliah (Isaiah 8:6)
geography: It is situated in the Kidron Valley at the southern end of the wall of Jerusalem, and is the point where water flows in through a tunnel connected underneath the City of David from the Gihon spring.
history: Representative is the waterworks construction by which Hezekiah, king of Judah, around the eighth century BC, in preparation for an Assyrian attack, blocked the Gihon spring outside the city and cut an underground tunnel to bring water into the Pool of Shiloah inside the city. As the lifeline of Jerusalem, Shiloah was a strategic point that enabled the city to withstand a long time even under siege by foreign powers.

introduce: Siloam refers to a reservoir or pool located at the end of the channel connected from the Gihon spring, southeast of the wall of Jerusalem, and in Hebrew it has the meaning "sent."
biblecontents: There is a mention asking whether the eighteen who died when the tower in Siloam in Jerusalem fell and crushed them were more guilty than all the others who lived in Jerusalem (Luke 13:4). Jesus commanded a man blind from birth to go and wash in the Pool of Siloam, and he went and washed and came back seeing (John 9:7). Also, the man who had been blind testified that when Jesus put mud on his eyes and told him to go to Siloam and wash, he went and washed and could see (John 9:11).
geography: Siloam is located south of the City of David in Jerusalem, near the point where the Kidron Valley and the Tyropoeon Valley meet. It is the terminus of Hezekiah's Tunnel, the underground channel built in the time of King Hezekiah to bring the water coming from the Gihon spring into the city.
history: Around the eighth century BC, in preparation for an Assyrian invasion, King Hezekiah carried out the underground channel project that diverted the stream of the Gihon spring outside the city to the Pool of Siloam inside the city. According to Jewish tradition, during the Feast of Tabernacles the priests also performed an official rite in which they drew water from this pool and poured it out on the altar of the temple.

introduce: Seleucia is a port city built as the outer harbor for Antioch in ancient Syria, and was an important maritime transport hub on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
biblecontents: It is recorded that Barnabas and Saul, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and from there sailed by ship to Cyprus (Acts 13:4).
geography: Seleucia was located on the Mediterranean coast, north of the mouth of the Orontes River. It was about 20 kilometers from Antioch, the large inland city, and was the essential port through which all the maritime freight and travelers entering and leaving Antioch passed.
history: It was built around 300 BC by Seleucus I Nicator, the founder of the Seleucid dynasty. As a strategic point of the Seleucid dynasty, this city served as the maritime gateway of Antioch through to the Roman period. Because it was situated in rugged mountainous terrain it was advantageous for defense, and during Roman rule it also enjoyed the status of a free city.

introduce: Shilhim is one of the towns in the southern region allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, appearing in the record of Joshua in the Bible.
biblecontents: Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon; in all twenty-nine towns with their villages (Joshua 15:32)
geography: Shilhim is presumed to be a town located in the Negev desert, the southern region of the tribe of Judah. Its detailed geographical coordinates and the exact present-day location of its remains have not been clearly confirmed archaeologically, but together with the surrounding towns it was situated in the southern border region of Judah.

introduce: Sibmah was a town located on the plain of Moab east of the Jordan; it was originally the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, but was afterward allotted to a tribe of Israel and in later times was an area captured by Moab.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns built by the descendants of Reuben (Numbers 32:38). It is included in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:19). The prophet Isaiah recorded that the vines of Sibmah languish, that their branches reached to Jazer and extended to the sea (Isaiah 16:8). Isaiah also proclaimed that he will weep for the vines of Sibmah as Jazer weeps, and that the sound of the harvest of its fruit has ceased (Isaiah 16:9). Jeremiah lamented that the vines of Sibmah spread across the desert as far as the sea, but that a plunderer has carried off its summer fruit and grape harvest (Jeremiah 48:32).
geography: Sibmah is presumed to have been located near Heshbon in present-day Jordan. Topographically, it has fertile soil suited to grape cultivation, and is known as an important agricultural zone in the northern Moabite plateau.
history: It was originally the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, but after the conquest by Israel it was allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben. Historically, however, this region was a place of frequent territorial disputes between Israel and Moab, and in the latter part of the Old Testament period it came again under the rule of Moab. The prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah describe the destruction of Sibmah's once-flourishing grape farming within the context of judgment against Moab.

introduce: Siphmoth is a town in southern Judah appearing in 1 Samuel 30 in the Old Testament, one of the places mentioned when David distributed the spoil that had been plundered by the Amalekites.
biblecontents: David sent the spoil he had taken from the Amalekites to the elders of Judah and to his friends, and at this time the spoil was also delivered to the elders of Siphmoth (1 Samuel 30:28).
geography: Siphmoth is presumed to be located in the southern Negev region of the tribe of Judah, but its exact location has not been pinpointed archaeologically. Geographically it is understood as one of the towns that, together with Arad, Beersheba, Aroer, and others, formed the defensive line or dwelling places of southern Judah.

introduce: It is a place name mentioned in the ancient Near East as the name of a well dug by the servants of Isaac. In Hebrew it means hostility or an adversary, and it was one of the places where Isaac quarreled with the people of Gerar over ownership of a well.
biblecontents: Isaac's servants dug another well, but they quarreled over that well also, so he called its name Sitnah (Genesis 26:21).

remark: 1. Located in Moab, east of the Dead Sea.
introduce: Shittim is a place name that means acacia trees in Hebrew, and in the Bible it refers to a specific area on the plain of Moab east of the Jordan River. It is recorded as one of the last camps where the people of Israel stayed after the exodus, on the eve of entering Canaan.
biblecontents: While Israel was staying at Shittim, the people began to commit sexual immorality with Moabite women and took part in sacrificing to their gods (Numbers 25:1). Joshua secretly sent two spies from Shittim to Jericho (Joshua 2:1). The people of Israel rose early in the morning at Shittim, moved to the bank of the Jordan, and prepared to cross (Joshua 3:1). The prophet Joel prophesied that in the future a spring would flow out from the house of the LORD and water the Valley of Shittim (Joel 3:18). The prophet Micah urged the people to remember what God did from Shittim to Gilgal, so that they might know the righteousness of God (Micah 6:5).
geography: Shittim lies east of the Jordan River, within the plain of Moab in the northeastern part of the Dead Sea region. In modern geography it is regarded as the same area as Abel-shittim, and is presumed to be Tell el-Hammam in present-day Jordan or its vicinity. This area is an arid plain where many acacia trees grow, a strategic point from which one can look down on the Jordan Valley and the place that became the starting point of the conquest of Canaan.
history: Immediately before the people of Israel entered Canaan, this Shittim holds historical importance as Israel's last major encampment. Here Moses carried out the military and religious preparations for the conquest of Canaan. Historically, Shittim was also a border region where conflict between Moab and Israel was frequent, and according to archaeological investigation, traces have been found that a settlement was formed here across the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.

remark: 2. A fortified town in Naphtali.
introduce: Ziddim is a place mentioned among the ancient Israelite place names, whose name means a place with many acacia trees in Hebrew. In Joshua 19:35 it appears as one of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali.
biblecontents: The fortified cities are Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth (Joshua 19:35).
geography: It is presumed to be a town located in the zone west or northwest of the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, but its specific site has not been clearly established archaeologically. It is regarded as a namesake of, or a different place from, Shittim, which was on the plain of Moab east of the Jordan.

remark: 3. An area on the shore of the Dead Sea, where Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim were.
introduce: Siddim is a place name of the ancient Near East meaning a place with many acacia trees in Hebrew. The Valley of Siddim that appears in Genesis 14 refers to a topographical location adjacent to the region where Sodom and Gomorrah were located.
biblecontents:
All these came together in the Valley of Siddim, that is, the present Salt Sea (Genesis 14:3)
The king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar, came out and set up their battle lines against them in the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:8)
The Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and when the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, they fell into them, and the rest fled to the hills (Genesis 14:10)
geography: The Valley of Siddim is generally presumed to be located at the southern end of the Dead Sea. At that time this region was marshland or lowland richly deposited with bitumen, and topographically, being adjacent to the Salt Sea, it showed the characteristic that natural resources such as petroleum and bitumen erupted to the surface.
history: In the early Bronze Age this region was a strategic point and a battlefield of the confederation of five city-states including Sodom. At that time this region was a place troubled by invasions and demands for tribute from neighboring powers, and in particular the topographical element of the bitumen pits was used as the spatial setting influencing military movements and the outcome of battles.

introduce: The Valley of Achor is a place name located near Jericho; in the biblical record it is a place connected with an incident of wrongdoing in the time of Joshua, and afterward it is mentioned as a symbolic point of Israel's restoration.
biblecontents: Joshua took Achan to the Valley of Achor in order to find the things he had hidden (Joshua 7:24). There all Israel stoned Achan and burned him, and because of that incident the place is called the Valley of Achor to this day (Joshua 7:26). Joshua 15:7 records that the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah runs from Debir through the Valley of Achor to the slope of Adummim opposite Gilgal on the north (Joshua 15:7). Isaiah prophesied that when Israel is restored in the future, the Valley of Achor will become a place for herds to lie down (Isaiah 65:10). Hosea used a figure of speech saying that when God loves Israel again, He will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (Hosea 2:15).
geography: The Valley of Achor is a topographical feature located west of the Jordan Valley near Jericho, situated on the route going down from the hill country of Judah to the plain of Jericho. Topographically, it is a strategic point forming the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah, and an area lying on the route along which Israel advanced at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
history: In the early conquest of Canaan, immediately after the battle of Jericho, the incident occurred in which Achan took plunder for himself. When Israel was therefore defeated in the battle of the city of Ai, the Valley of Achor was chosen as the place for carrying out the sentence, in order to punish the wrongdoer and turn away God's wrath. Afterward this valley became a symbolic place of discipline and suffering for the people of Israel, but was reinterpreted by later prophets as a space symbolizing future hope and restoration.

introduce: Imperial is a name appearing in the Acts of the Apostles in the New Testament, a term referring to the unit to which belonged the ship carrying Paul's party, who were being taken to Rome to appeal to the Roman emperor. It is interpreted as a proper name connected with the organizational system of the Roman army of that time.
biblecontents: When it was decided that Paul should be sent to Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius of the Imperial Cohort (Acts 27:1).
history: Imperial is a name derived from the Latin Augusta, and means a unit named after Emperor Augustus. In the Roman army of that time there were independent units named in honor of the emperor, and the Imperial Cohort was very likely a special unit representing the emperor's authority, or a high-ranking escort unit working closely with the Roman governor's office. Such a name suggests that the unit in question was directly connected to the administrative or military center of the Roman Empire.

introduce: Akrabbim is a place name called Akrabim in Hebrew, with the meaning "hill of scorpions." It is a place mentioned as a major landmark of the southern boundary of Canaan.
biblecontents: The southern boundary of Canaan begins at the stony slope of Akrabbim, passes on to Zin, and reaches south of Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 34:4). The boundary of the inheritance of the descendants of Judah is described as going up from the slope of Akrabbim, passing on to Zin, and reaching south of Kadesh-barnea (Joshua 15:3). The boundary of the Amorite tribe extended upward from the rock at the slope of Akrabbim (Judges 1:36).
geography: It is presumed to be the Akrabim Pass, located southwest of the present Dead Sea. This is a steeply sloping zone connecting the Arabah wilderness with the Negev highlands, and topographically it includes steep and rugged slopes.

introduce: Anaharath is one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Issachar in ancient Israel, a place mentioned only once as a place name in the Bible.
biblecontents: The lot was cast for the inheritance of the tribe of the descendants of Issachar according to their families, and the boundary of their inheritance is Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Joshua 19:19)
geography: The exact location of Anaharath has not been clearly established archaeologically, but a view exists in scholarship that generally presumes it to be Tell el-Mukarkh near present-day Afula, an area in the northeast of the Jezreel plain.
history: In the record of the Battle of Megiddo of the Egyptian New Kingdom pharaoh Thutmose III (Thutmose III Annals), Anaharath appears under the name Anaharat, and this proves that this region existed as a major place name in the Canaan region from about the fifteenth century BC.

introduce: The Anakites were a people who inhabited the region of Canaan, as recorded in the Bible, and are described as a race of giants with outstanding physical stature. They were one of the most threatening presences to the people of Israel at the time of the wars of the conquest of Canaan, and lived mainly in the hill country of southern Canaan, centered on Hebron.
biblecontents: In the past the Emites lived there, a people as great and strong and numerous as the Anakites (Deuteronomy 2:10). Like the Rephaim, they were also called Anakites, but the Moabites called them Emites (Deuteronomy 2:11). That land too was considered a land of the Rephaim; formerly the Rephaim lived there, but the Ammonites called them Zamzummites (Deuteronomy 2:21). Joshua came at that time and destroyed the Anakites from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel, and utterly destroyed their cities (Joshua 11:21). No Anakites were left in the land of the people of Israel; they remained only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22). "Now give me this hill country about which the LORD spoke on that day. You also heard on that day that the Anakites were there, and that the cities were great and fortified. If the LORD is with me, I will drive them out as the LORD said" (Joshua 14:12). The former name of Hebron was Kiriath-arba; Arba was the greatest man among the Anakites. And the land had rest from war (Joshua 14:15).
geography: The Anakites had their base mainly in the southern hill country of Canaan, in the areas of Hebron, Debir, and Anab. Afterward, as they were driven out by Joshua's campaigns of conquest, they are recorded as having moved to and remained in the coastal plain of Gaza and in Philistine town areas such as Gath and Ashdod.
history: They are presumed to have been a particular social group that existed in the Canaan region in the late Bronze Age. The biblical record shows that they were regarded as of the same kind as great peoples such as the Rephaim, the Emites, and the Zamzummites. They were one of the strongest forces of military resistance that Israel faced during the conquest of Canaan, and through Joshua's wars of conquest they were expelled from places such as Hebron, which had been their main stronghold.

introduce: Anab was one of the towns located in the hill country of Judah at the time of the conquest of Canaan, a place name that is mentioned in the biblical record both as an object of conquest and as the inheritance of a particular tribe.
biblecontents: Joshua destroyed the Anakites from the hill country of Judah and captured Anab, where they had lived (Joshua 11:21). Afterward Anab appears in the list of the hill-country towns among the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:50).
geography: Anab is classified as a town located within the hill country of Judah, and is presumed to have been situated in an area geographically adjacent to the neighboring towns of Debir and Hebron.
history: Anab was a stronghold inhabited by the Anakites, known as a people of giant stature in the ancient Canaanite period, and it became a major strategic objective in the course of expelling them during the wars of Israel's conquest of Canaan.

remark: A Levitical town of Manasseh west of the Jordan River.
introduce: Aner is a place name mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:70, one of the towns for the Levites located within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: Within the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner and its pasturelands and Bileam and its pasturelands were allotted from the tribe of Manasseh and distributed to the remaining clans of the Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:70).
geography: Its exact location is difficult to pinpoint archaeologically at present, but it is presumed to be in the western Jezreel Valley, the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh, or in the area near the Plain of Sharon. In Joshua 21:25, the parallel passage to 1 Chronicles 6, the same town is recorded as Taanach, so Aner and Taanach are interpreted either as the same place name or as nearby geographical names.

introduce: Anem is a place mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the descendants of Gershon, of the tribe of Levi, in the process of distributing the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: It was located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar, and is recorded as a town given to the descendants of Gershon to live in (1 Chronicles 6:73).
geography: Although there are differing views about its present-day location, it is generally presumed to be the same place as En-gannim near the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel. Because archaeological excavation data are lacking, it is difficult to determine clearly the exact physical boundaries of the ancient town.

introduce: Anim was one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place that appears in the list of allotments in the southern part of the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: Anim is mentioned as included in the list of towns of the hill country of Judah among the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:50).
geography: It is presumed to have been located in the area near Hebron in the southern hill country of Judah, but its exact present-day location has not been clearly identified archaeologically.

introduce: Adadah is a town appearing in Joshua 15 in the Old Testament, a border town in the Negev region at the far south of Canaan that was allotted to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Adadah is mentioned following Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, and Dimonah, among the towns located near the Edomite border at the southern end of the descendants of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:22).
geography: Adadah was located in the southeastern Negev, where the wilderness south of the hill country of Judah meets the western boundary of Edom. It is identified with Khirbet Adadah (present-day Horvat Adadah), located near Wadi Adadah southeast of Beersheba and south of Arad, and is surrounded by arid wadi terrain and desert hills.
history: In the Iron Age the kingdom of Judah built fortresses and garrisons at key points in the Negev in order to guard its southern border and to control the southern trade routes leading toward the Arabah wilderness and the Red Sea (Elath). Adadah functioned as an outpost defensive stronghold protecting the farmland and pastures of southern Judah from raids by the Edomites and nomads.

remark: 1. A town east of the Jordan River.
introduce: Ataroth is mentioned in the Bible as a town located in the region east of the Jordan, and is described as a place with the topographical advantage of being suited to raising livestock.
biblecontents: Ataroth, together with Jazer, is the area designated as land suitable for raising livestock (Numbers 32:3). Afterward the tribe of Gad rebuilt this area and made it a town (Numbers 32:34).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the southern Gilead highland east of the Jordan River or in the area near Heshbon. It has the geographical character of a grassland easy for raising sheep and cattle within the pastoral culture sphere of the ancient Near East.
history: After the Israelites defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, east of the Jordan in the course of the conquest of Canaan, this is the region that the tribes of Reuben and Gad requested and were allotted as land for their herds of livestock. Afterward, through the settlement and defensive fortification by the tribe of Gad, territorial rights over the region were established.

remark: 2. A town in Ephraim.
introduce: Ataroth is a town located in the border region of the tribe of Ephraim in the time of Joshua, mentioned in the Old Testament as a major place name distinguishing the territory of Ephraim.
biblecontents: Ataroth: the boundary goes from Bethel to Luz, passes along the border of the Archites, and reaches Ataroth (Joshua 16:2). Also, to the east it passes Janoah, reaches Ataroth and Naarah, meets Jericho, and goes out to the Jordan (Joshua 16:7).
geography: Ataroth lies on the southern boundary line of the tribe of Ephraim, and is presumed to have been situated in the hill country or gently rolling hills between Bethel and Jericho. Although there are several theories about its detailed location when compared with modern place names, no exact archaeological identification has been confirmed.

introduce: Ataroth-addar is a town or place name that was located in the border region of the tribe of Ephraim and the tribe of Benjamin in the age of the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned in the record of Joshua as a point distinguishing topographical boundaries, and its exact present-day location is the subject of archaeological debate.
biblecontents: The eastern end of the boundary of the inheritance of the descendants of Ephraim begins at Ataroth-addar and reaches Upper Beth-horon (Joshua 16:5). In addition, it is recorded that the boundary of the descendants of Benjamin goes to Luz beside the southern side of Bethel, goes down to Ataroth-addar, and reaches the hill beside the lower side of Beth-horon (Joshua 18:13).
geography: Geographically, Ataroth-addar is presumed to be located near the Beth-horon area, a mountainous zone northwest of Jerusalem. It served as a key branching point distinguishing the territories among the tribes of Israel at that time, and appears to have been located on a major passage formed along the mountain terrain.

introduce: A place name mentioned in connection with the descendants of Salma in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, referring to the name of a clan established by the sons of Salma or of the region where they settled.
biblecontents: The sons of Salma were Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, half of the Manahathites, and the clans of the Zorites, and Atroth-beth-joab is recorded as connected with the descendants of Salma (1 Chronicles 2:54).

introduce: Atroth-shophan is a place name east of the Jordan mentioned in the Book of Numbers in the Old Testament, recorded as one of the towns that the tribe of Gad rebuilt and fortified.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth-nimrah, and Beth-haran, and made them fortified cities (Numbers 32:34-35).
geography: It is presumed to be located on the Gilead highland east of the Jordan River or on its southern plain, but scholars debate whether it corresponds exactly to a modern place name. It is generally regarded as a point distinct from the Ataroth near Heshbon.
history: It reflects the historical circumstances in which, after the Israelites defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, east of the Jordan in the course of the conquest of Canaan, the tribe of Gad requested this region, suited to raising livestock, as its inheritance, and settled and built defensive installations.

introduce: Atharim is a place name located in the Negev region of southern Canaan, a place mentioned in the course of the Israelites who came out of Egypt entering Canaan.
biblecontents: When the Canaanite who lived in the Negev, that is, the king of Arad, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he attacked Israel and took some of them captive (Numbers 21:1).
geography: The way of Atharim is presumed to be one of the main passages going up from the Arabah wilderness to the hill country of Judea. Its exact location is disputed archaeologically, but it is generally understood as part of the ancient road network connecting Arad and the region of Edom.
history: In the late Bronze Age, the city-states of southern Canaan controlled the main approaches and built defensive lines to prevent the entry of outside forces. Arad, as a strategic point, served as a military stronghold for stopping Israel's advance northward.

introduce: Adamah is one of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali mentioned in Joshua 19 in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Among the inheritance that the descendants of Naphtali received by lot are included Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, Adamah, Ramah, and Hazor (Joshua 19:35-36).
geography: The exact location of Adamah has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to have been a town located northwest or north of the Sea of Galilee, within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. The Talmud, a rabbinic text, also mentions Adamah as a place near the Sea of Galilee.

introduce: Adami-nekeb is an ancient place name appearing in Joshua 19:33, a town located on the boundary of the land allotted to the tribe of Naphtali.
biblecontents: Their boundary began at Heleph and the oak of Zaanannim, passed Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, and reached as far as Lakkum, and its end is the Jordan River (Joshua 19:33).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the area west or northwest of the present Sea of Galilee, and scholars hold differing opinions about linking it to a specific modern place name. As a general theory, Khirbet Damiyeh, southwest of the Sea of Galilee, is also proposed as a candidate site.

introduce: Athach was one of the towns located in the Negev region of southern Judah, a place name mentioned when David distributed the spoil plundered by the Amalekites.
biblecontents: When David, after his victory in the battle with the Amalekites, sent the spoil he had taken to the elders of Judah and to his friends, he also delivered gifts to those who lived in Athach (1 Samuel 30:30).
geography: It is presumed to be a town located in the southern Negev desert region of the tribe of Judah, but its specific modern location has not been identified. However, since it is mentioned together with the major strongholds of southern Judah, it appears to have been a strategic point or a settlement of nomads.

introduce: Addar is a place name located in the southern border region of the tribe of Judah appearing in Joshua 15, a point mentioned in the Bible in the course of describing the boundary of Judah's inheritance.
biblecontents: Its southern boundary runs from the south of the slope of Akrabbim to Zin, goes up to the south of Judah and reaches the south of Kadesh-barnea, passes Hezron and goes up to Addar, then turns around and reaches Karka (Joshua 15:3)
geography: Addar is a point presumed to be located between Kadesh-barnea and Karka, but its exact present-day archaeological location is unclear. Scholars interpret this area as the northern part of the Negev desert or the northeastern border zone of Kadesh-barnea.

introduce: Atad was a place east of the Jordan River, the site of a threshing floor where Jacob's funeral procession stopped on its way from Egypt to Canaan after his death.
biblecontents: When Jacob's funeral procession reached the threshing floor of Atad across the Jordan River, they wept loudly and mourned there, and mourned for seven days (Genesis 50:10). The Canaanite inhabitants of the land, seeing the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, said it was a great mourning by the Egyptians, and so they called the name of that place Abel-mizraim (Genesis 50:11).
geography: It is specified as a region located east of the Jordan River, but its exact location has not been revealed by modern archaeology. However, it is presumed to be a point adjacent to the mainland of Canaan, with the Jordan River as the boundary.

introduce: Athens was a city-state of ancient Greece and the center of the Attica peninsula, recorded in the Acts of the Apostles in the Bible as the place Paul visited on his missionary journey, where he debated with philosophers and preached the gospel.
biblecontents: Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and they left after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to Paul as quickly as possible (Acts 17:15). While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was provoked in his spirit when he saw that the city was full of idols (Acts 17:16). All the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there spent their time on nothing else but telling or hearing something new (Acts 17:21). Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and preached to the Athenians, remarking that they were very religious (Acts 17:22). After that Paul left Athens and went to Corinth (Acts 18:1). Unable to bear it any longer, Paul thought it good to be left behind alone at Athens, and sent Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:1).
geography: Athens is a port city located on the Attica peninsula in the southeast of mainland Greece, bordering the Saronic Gulf. The urban area developed around a high hill called the Acropolis, and the Areopagus hill and the Agora square were located in the center of the city, serving as the main stage of the citizens' activities.
history: Athens is known as the birthplace of ancient Greek philosophy, art, and democracy. In the Roman imperial period its political influence declined compared with before, but it still maintained its reputation as a center of learning and philosophy. At that time the city had numerous temples and idols set up, and it was an intellectual center in which various philosophical currents, including the Epicurean and Stoic schools, coexisted.

introduce: Adoraim was one of the fortress cities used as defensive strongholds of the ancient kingdom of Judah, and is presumed to be the Dura region near present-day Hebron in Palestine.
biblecontents: King Rehoboam rebuilt Adoraim as one of the fortified towns, in order to defend the southern border and strategic points of the kingdom of Judah (2 Chronicles 11:9).
geography: It is located about 8 km southwest of Hebron, situated on the terrain of the western slope of the hill country of Judah, and is a strategic point advantageous for watching over and defending the Shephelah, the plain region along the Mediterranean coast.
history: After being fortified in the process of building the defensive line of the kingdom of Judah in the time of Rehoboam, it reappears in historical records in the Hellenistic period as Adora, an important administrative center of the Idumea region. It was conquered by John Hyrcanus I of the Hasmonean dynasty, and afterward functioned as a political stronghold in the region until the Roman period.

introduce: Adullam was an ancient Canaanite city-state and a strategic point belonging to the territory of the tribe of Judah. It is mentioned mainly in the Old Testament as the setting of particular events or as a military stronghold, and geographically it is an area located between the hill country of Judah and the Shephelah plain.
biblecontents: Hirah, the friend of Judah, was an Adullamite, and Judah visited Hirah the Adullamite (Genesis 38:1, Genesis 38:12, Genesis 38:20). At the time of Joshua's wars of conquest, the king of Adullam was one of the kings conquered by Israel (Joshua 12:15). Afterward Adullam became one of the towns of the Shephelah allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:35). David fled from Saul to the cave of Adullam and joined with a company of men there (1 Samuel 22:1). When David fought the Philistines, the cave of Adullam became his military stronghold (2 Samuel 23:13, 1 Chronicles 11:15). King Rehoboam built up the town of Adullam strongly for the defense of Israel (2 Chronicles 11:7). It is also recorded as one of the places where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:30).
geography: Adullam is presumed to be present-day Tel Adullam, which is located on a hill south of the Valley of Elah. Because it lies at the entrance of the Shephelah region connecting the highlands of the hill country of Judah with the coastal plain to the west, it has terrain highly advantageous for transportation and defense. This area has many natural caves characteristic of limestone terrain.
history: From the Bronze Age, Adullam was an independent Canaanite city-state with its own ruler. After being destroyed in the time of Joshua, it became a settlement of the Israelite tribe of Judah, and because of its geographical advantages it was used as a military refuge in the time of David. During the reign of Rehoboam it became the center of the fortification work to defend the western border of the southern kingdom of Judah, and its military importance was highlighted anew.

introduce: Adummim means "red ones" in Hebrew, and is a place name located on the route connecting Jerusalem and Jericho. It is a place mentioned for setting the boundaries of ancient Israelite territory and as a strategic crossroads.
biblecontents: Adummim appears in the course of describing the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, and is recorded as a boundary point on the ascent of the valley east of Jericho (Joshua 15:7, Joshua 18:17).
geography: It is located in the eastern part of the Judean wilderness and includes the steeply sloping terrain going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. It is characterized by a ravine where reddish soil appears between limestone strata, and it has the terrain conditions of having been used as a main transportation route since ancient times.
history: Because this region was one of the only passages connecting Jerusalem and the Jordan Valley, it was in a position of great military and commercial importance. Owing to the ruggedness of the terrain and its isolated environment, it has also been well known since ancient times as a dangerous area where robbers lying in wait for travelers appeared.

introduce: Adramyttian refers to a port city located in the Mysia region of ancient Asia Minor, a place name mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles in the Bible as the port of departure of the ship used when Paul was taken to Rome.
biblecontents: We boarded an Adramyttian ship that was about to sail for the ports along the coast of Asia, and put to sea; and Aristarchus, a Thessalonian of Macedonia, was with us (Acts 27:2)
geography: It corresponds to the Edremit area in Balikesir Province, present-day Turkey, and is situated on the northeastern coast of the Gulf of Edremit. In ancient times it was located at the southern foot of Mount Ida, and functioned as a strategic port overlooking the Adramyttian Gulf.
history: It is known to have been founded around the fourth century BC by Adramys, an Athenian general, and flourished as an important commercial port throughout the Hellenistic and Roman imperial periods. In Paul's time, the ships of this city were serving as hubs of maritime transport, sailing along the coast of Asia Minor and carrying cargo and passengers.

introduce: Adriatic is an ancient place name that refers to the present Adriatic Sea. In ancient times this name was used as a concept including not only the sea between the Italian peninsula and the Balkan peninsula, but also a wider body of water between Sicily and Crete.
biblecontents: While Paul was being taken to Rome, he met a violent wind called the Northeaster and drifted, and on the fourteenth night he was driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea (Acts 27:27).
geography: In ancient geography the Adriatic Sea meant a much wider area than the present Adriatic Sea. This was a concept including the Ionian Sea and part of the Mediterranean, and the sailors of the time called even the waters between south of Crete and north of Libya by this name.
history: In the Roman period the Adriatic Sea was one of the main maritime routes of the Roman Empire, and navigators of the time entered the Italian port cities of Puteoli or Ostia through these waters. According to the records of the geographers Strabo and Ptolemy, the Adriatic of that time was a term referring to an area extending much farther to the west and south than the modern definition.

introduce: Admah is an ancient city-state appearing in the Bible, a place classified, together with Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboiim, and Bela, as one of the so-called five cities.
biblecontents: It is mentioned that the boundary of Canaan began at Sidon and extended to Gaza, passing Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha (Genesis 10:19). Shinab, king of Admah, together with Bera, king of Sodom, Birsha, king of Gomorrah, Shemeber, king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, fought a war against the coalition forces, including Chedorlaomer, king of Elam (Genesis 14:2). They fought against the coalition forces in the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:8). Moses warned of a situation in which this land would be set aflame with sulfur and salt and become unable to be cultivated, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in His wrath (Deuteronomy 29:23). The prophet Hosea, expressing God's will of judgment toward Israel, figuratively mentioned that He would destroy Admah as He did Sodom (Hosea 11:8).
geography: Admah is presumed to have been located near the Valley of Siddim in the lower Jordan River, and is known as a lowland plain area near the Dead Sea. The exact excavation site has not yet been archaeologically determined.

introduce: Adithaim was one of the towns of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place mentioned in the geographical lists of the Bible.
biblecontents: Adithaim was recorded as included in the list of towns located on the Shephelah plain among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:36).
geography: Adithaim is presumed to be located in the Shephelah region, the buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain, but its exact site has not been archaeologically identified in modern times (Joshua 15:36).

remark: 1. The mountain on which Noah's ark rested.
introduce: Ararat is a place name of the ancient Near East, and in the Bible it is the region mentioned as the place where Noah's ark came to rest after the great flood. It is called Ararat in Hebrew, and this shares a linguistic origin with the kingdom of Urartu in Assyrian records.
biblecontents: In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat (Genesis 8:4)
geography: Ararat is a highland region that includes eastern present-day Turkey, Armenia, and northwestern Iran. Mount Ararat, which rises more than 5,000 meters above sea level, is the symbolic high peak representing the volcanic terrain of this region, and corresponds to the core territory of the former kingdom of Urartu.
history: Ararat is the Hebrew name referring to the kingdom of Urartu, which existed from about the ninth century BC to the sixth century BC. In the cuneiform records of the Assyrian Empire Urartu appears as a powerful northern rival state, and afterward this name was taken into the biblical record and became fixed as a term referring to a particular mountainous region.

remark: 2. The place where the descendants of Togarmah and Japheth lived.
introduce: Ararat is a regional name of the ancient Near East, a term that refers to the kingdom of Urartu in the Hebrew Bible. This region is distributed mainly around the present Armenian highland, and the name was used to include the mountainous region of northern ancient Mesopotamia.
biblecontents: Adrammelech and Sharezer, the sons of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, killed him with the sword and then fled to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19:37, Isaiah 37:38). Also Jeremiah prophesied that the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz should be summoned against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27).
geography: Ararat refers to the Armenian highland between Lake Van and Lake Urmia. It consists of a high mountain region bordering the Caspian Sea to the east, the Anatolian plateau to the west, and the Caucasus Mountains to the north. Its terrain is extremely rugged, so it served as a fortress advantageous for defense, and it occupied a barren but strategic position.
history: Ararat refers to the kingdom of Urartu, which flourished on the Armenian highland from about the ninth century BC to the early sixth century BC. This kingdom expanded its power for a long time in opposition to Assyria on the northern border of the Assyrian Empire. From the late seventh century BC, with the decline of Assyria, it gradually weakened under pressure from the Medes and the Scythians, and was afterward absorbed into the sphere of influence of Achaemenid Persia.

introduce: Arabah means a wasteland or dry land in Hebrew, and is a proper noun that geographically refers to the immense rift zone running from the Gulf of Aqaba south of the Jordan Valley, through the Dead Sea, to the southern end of the Sea of Galilee.
biblecontents: Moses proclaimed the law to the people of Israel in the region east of the Jordan River, including the Arabah, Bashan, and Gilead (Deuteronomy 1:1). The hill country of the Amorites and the neighboring Arabah, the plain, the Negev, the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon were mentioned as the boundaries of the territory that Israel was to conquer (Deuteronomy 1:7). The people of Israel moved along the Arabah plain, passing by Elath and Ezion-geber (Deuteronomy 2:8). The boundary where the Jordan River flows into the sea of the Arabah, that is, the Salt Sea, was used as a topographical reference (Deuteronomy 3:17). All the Arabah east of the Jordan extended to the foot of Mount Pisgah (Deuteronomy 4:49). The Canaanites who lived in the Arabah were beside the oaks of Moreh opposite Gilgal (Deuteronomy 11:30). The waters of the Jordan River flowed down toward the sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, and were completely cut off (Joshua 3:16). The king of Ai prepared for battle with Israel at a set place in front of the Arabah (Joshua 8:14). The northern Canaanite coalition forces encamped in the Arabah south of Chinnereth, on the plain, and in the heights of Dor on the west (Joshua 11:2). Joshua conquered this hill country, the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the plain, the Arabah, and the hill country and plain of Israel (Joshua 11:16).
geography: The Arabah is a geological fault zone about 180 km long that begins at the Sea of Galilee in the north, runs along the Jordan River valley through the Dead Sea, and continues to the Gulf of Aqaba of the Red Sea in the south. This region has high mountain ranges rising on both sides, and the southern Arabah in particular maintains a desert environment with very little annual rainfall and sparse vegetation. Because it includes the area around the Dead Sea, which is below sea level, the differences in elevation are extreme, and to the east and west it borders the highlands of Moab and Edom.
history: The Arabah was a main north-south passage in the ancient Near East and an economic key point where mineral resources such as copper and iron were mined and smelted. According to the biblical record, it was an important travel route in the wilderness journey of the people of Israel, and it was also a buffer zone where territorial disputes between Edom and Israel were frequent. In addition, because the terrain is rugged and dry, it is a region where ambush and frontal breakthrough were strategically considered in ancient military operations.

introduce: Arabah-chinneroth is a name combining, in Hebrew, Arabah (valley or plain) and Chinneroth (the area around the Lake of Gennesaret), a geographical term referring to the lowland of the northern Jordan Valley.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in the list of the Canaanite kings whom Joshua conquered, when describing the boundary of the eastern Jordan Valley, and includes the Arabah region as far as the Sea of Chinneroth, that is, the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 12:3).
geography: As part of the Jordan fault block, it means the northern zone of the Jordan Valley, from the Sea of Galilee (the Sea of Chinneroth) in the north to the Dead Sea (the Sea of the Arabah) in the south. This region is a lowland below sea level, and has the characteristic of forming abundant water resources and fertile soil.

remark: The Arabian Peninsula.
introduce: In the Bible, Arabia is the name for the vast desert zone located south and east of Palestine and the nomadic peoples who live there. It means the region that is adjacent to the trade routes of the ancient Near East and had economic and military relations with the kingdom of Israel.
biblecontents: In the time of King Solomon, the kings of Arabia and the governors brought gold and silver (1 Kings 10:15). The kings and merchants of Arabia also brought gold and silver to Solomon (2 Chronicles 9:14). In the time of King Jehoshaphat the Arabians presented him with animals as gifts (2 Chronicles 17:11). In the time of King Jehoram the Philistines and the Arabians invaded Judah (2 Chronicles 21:16). The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king because the army had been killed by the Arabians (2 Chronicles 22:1). In the time of King Uzziah God helped him against the Arabians who lived in Arabia (2 Chronicles 26:7). When Nehemiah rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, Geshem the Arabian mocked it (Nehemiah 2:19). At the news that Nehemiah was building the wall, the Arabians became angry (Nehemiah 4:7). Sanballat and Geshem opposed Nehemiah and slandered him (Nehemiah 6:1). In the prophecy of judgment on Babylon, it is mentioned that the Arabian will not pitch his tent there (Isaiah 13:20).
geography: Arabia generally includes the vast desert and steppe zones of eastern Jordan and northern Saudi Arabia. The Arabia of biblical times was a main passage of ancient trade routes, and was used as a term referring to a wide area stretching from the present Syrian desert to the Gulf of Aqaba and the coast of the Red Sea.
history: In the Iron Age, Arabia took the form of various tribal confederations. They accumulated economic wealth by transporting spices, gold, and other goods to Palestine and the Mediterranean coast through caravan trade using camels. They sometimes entered into a tribute-paying relationship with the kingdom of Israel, but at other times they maintained political and military tension by raiding the kingdom of Judah as a force in border disputes. In particular, in the time of Nehemiah they appear as one of the local forces obstructing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.

introduce: Hararite is a place name designating the hometown of Shammah, a figure appearing in 2 Samuel 23:33 in the Old Testament. In the original Hebrew it is written Harari (Hararite), which means a person from the Harar region.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the hometown of Shammah the Hararite, one of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:33).

introduce: Geshur of Aram was an independent small kingdom that existed within the Aramaic-speaking world of the ancient Near East, a political entity located in the upper Jordan River region of the northeast in the days of David's kingdom.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the place where David's son Absalom fled to Aram in Geshur and stayed for three years (2 Samuel 15:8).
geography: It lay north of the eastern Sea of Galilee and the region of Bashan, and is presumed to correspond to the southern part of the present Golan Heights. Because it bordered the upper Jordan River valley, it was a strategic crossroads and had an environment suited to herding.
history: Geshur of Aram had maintained an independent system of government since before the time of David, and David, in order to strengthen a political alliance, took Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, as his wife, and she bore Absalom. Afterward, as the power of the Davidic dynasty expanded, it entered into complex diplomatic and military relations with the various small kingdoms of the Aramean lineage, but later it was gradually absorbed under the influence of Aram of Damascus.

introduce: Aram-naharaim means "Aram between two rivers" in Hebrew, and is a place name that generally refers to northern Mesopotamia, the upper region between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers.
biblecontents: When the Ammonites realized that they had become odious to David, they sent men to Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah to hire chariots and horsemen to oppose him (1 Chronicles 19:6). A record exists that in the superscription of Psalm 60, the psalm was composed by David while he was fighting Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah (Psalms 60:1).
geography: This region corresponds to the area of northeastern present-day Syria and southeastern Turkey, and is a fertile plain centered on the basins of the Balikh and Khabur rivers, including Haran.
history: It is a region where Arameans began to migrate and settle from the second millennium BC, and in the Neo-Assyrian period the various small states of the Aram-naharaim region maintained relations of either clashing with Assyrian expansion or paying tribute.

introduce: Aram-maacah refers to one of the several small kingdoms of Aram that were part of the territory inhabited by the Arameans of the ancient Near East and came into military conflict with Israel in the time of David's reign.
biblecontents: When the Ammonites realized that they had become odious to David, they spent a thousand talents of silver and sent men to Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah to hire chariots and horsemen (1 Chronicles 19:6).
geography: Aram-maacah is a region adjacent to Aram-naharaim, and is presumed to have been located in the northern part of the Fertile Crescent in the upper Euphrates or in northeastern Syria.
history: The various small kingdoms of Aram at that time maintained independent political systems, and, at the request of Hanun, king of the Ammonites, they formed a coalition against David's kingdom of Israel in the form of supplying mercenaries.

introduce: Aram-zobah was a powerful kingdom of the Arameans that existed in the Syrian region from the eleventh century BC to the early tenth century BC, a region that was in relations of political and military conflict with the surrounding states at the time.
biblecontents: On his way back after conquering Edom, David defeated Hadadezer, king of Aram-zobah, and afterward also conquered the Arameans of Damascus who came to help the army of Hadadezer (2 Samuel 8:3-5). There is a record that in the time of Solomon he conquered Hamath-zobah and ruled it (2 Chronicles 8:3). In the superscription of Psalm 60 there is a reference to the time when David was fighting Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah (Psalm 60, superscription).
geography: Aram-zobah is presumed to have been a state formed around the northern part of the Beqaa Valley between the east of the Lebanon range and the west of the Euphrates River. Its specific center appears to have been near the Anti-Lebanon range in the region of present-day Syria, but its exact archaeological location has not yet been clearly established.
history: Aram-zobah was one of the most influential powers in Syria in the early Iron Age, and under King Hadadezer it extended its influence over the surrounding states. However, it suffered military defeat in clashing with the expansion policy of David of the kingdom of Israel, and afterward its power gradually weakened as the Aramean states centered on Damascus grew.

introduce: Arab, as mentioned in the Bible, refers either to one of the towns located in the hill country of Judah, or appears as a place name indicating the origin of one of David's mighty men.
biblecontents: In Joshua 15:52 Arab is recorded as one of the towns in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:52). In 2 Samuel 23:35, Baara the Arbite, one of David's thirty-seven mighty men, is mentioned (2 Samuel 23:35).
geography: Arab is presumed to be a town located in the southern part of the hill country of Judah, and in the list of Joshua 15 it has a geographical position classified together with Beth-tappuah and Eshtemoh.

remark: A region located south of Judah.
introduce: Arad was an ancient town located in the Negev region of southern Canaan, a place mentioned as a strategic crossroads and the site of a major conflict in the course of the people of Israel entering Canaan.
biblecontents: When the Canaanite who lived in the Negev, that is, the king of Arad, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he struck Israel and took some of them captive (Numbers 21:1). The Canaanite who lived in the Negev, the king of Arad, heard the news that the people of Israel were coming (Numbers 33:40). There was one king of Arad (Joshua 12:14), and the Kenites, descendants of Moses' father-in-law, went up with the descendants of Judah from the City of Palms to the wilderness of Judah south of Arad and settled among the people (Judges 1:16).
geography: Arad is located on the northern boundary of the Negev desert, about 30 kilometers southeast of Beersheba. As a highland of southern Canaan it serves as a crossing point connecting Edom and the hill country of Judea, and has the geographical characteristics of low rainfall and a dry climate.
history: Archaeologically, the Tel Arad area was settled from the Early Bronze Age, and afterward during the period of Israelite settlement it was used as a strategic fortress. At the time Israel entered Canaan, the kingdom of Arad was one of the powers holding supremacy in the southern Negev, and is recorded as an actual political group that came into military conflict with Israel.

introduce: The Areopagus is a rocky hill located west of the Acropolis in ancient Greek Athens, and also the name referring to the supreme judicial and deliberative body that met there.
biblecontents: The Athenians seized Paul and took him to the Areopagus and asked what this new teaching was that he was proclaiming (Acts 17:19). Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and began his speech, remarking that the Athenians were very religious (Acts 17:22). As a result, some people, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, and a woman named Damaris, followed Paul and believed (Acts 17:34).
geography: The Areopagus is a limestone hill located near the western entrance of the Acropolis of Athens. The meaning of its name is the Hill of Ares, and topographically it rises somewhat higher than the flat ground, forming a space suited to public speaking or holding assemblies.
history: Originally, the Council of the Areopagus was the supreme governing body of Athens and a judicial institution that tried murder cases, and was the core of the aristocratic government that exercised powerful authority. However, as time passed its political standing gradually diminished, and in the Roman imperial period when Paul visited, it had mainly the character of an advisory body and court dealing with moral questions and religious matters.

remark: 1. A town on the border of Ephraim, between Luz and Ataroth.
introduce: Archites is mentioned in the Bible as a place name associated with Hushai the Archite, and is presumed to have been a place located in the border region of the tribe of Ephraim.
biblecontents: The Archites are mentioned as an area passing between Bethel and Luz on the boundary of the descendants of Ephraim (Joshua 16:2). Hushai the Archite, David's friend and counselor, came from Archi to help David at the time of Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:32). Absalom received Hushai, mistakenly thinking that he had betrayed David (2 Samuel 16:16). In Absalom's camp, Hushai refuted the strategy of Ahithophel and presented a strategy that helped David escape (2 Samuel 17:5). Absalom and the men of Israel judged Hushai's counsel to be better than Ahithophel's counsel and adopted it (2 Samuel 17:14). Hushai, who was David's close associate and the king's friend, is recorded as an Archite (1 Chronicles 27:33).
geography: The Archites area is presumed to be near Bethel, the border region of the tribe of Benjamin and the tribe of Ephraim, but its exact location has not been determined by modern archaeology. Geographically it is interpreted as being near a strategic point between north of Jerusalem and the hill country of Ephraim.

remark: 2. A town of the kingdom of Nimrod on the plain of Shinar, whose inhabitants were forcibly relocated to Samaria by Ashurbanipal.
introduce: Erech is one of the cities of the ancient Near East, a region mentioned in Ezra 4:9 as one of the places of origin of the officials who sent a petition to Artaxerxes, king of Persia.
biblecontents: Erech appears in the list of recipients of the petition sent to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple by Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates, the people of Dinah, the Apharsathchites, the people of Tripolis, the Apharsites, the people of Erech, the Babylonians, the people of Susa, the Dehavites, and the Elamites (Ezra 4:9).
geography: Erech is presumed to be the same place as Uruk, a city located in the Babylonian region of southern Mesopotamia. As a major city of ancient Sumer, it stood in the fertile alluvial plain of the lower Euphrates River.
history: Erech, known as Uruk, was an ancient city-state that existed from the fourth millennium BC, and was also the setting of the Epic of Gilgamesh. In the Persian imperial period, it was a part of the Babylonian administrative district, and it shows that officials from that region were active within the imperial system of government.

remark: 1. An Ammonite town near Rabbah.
introduce: Aroer is an ancient town located in Transjordan, the region east of the Jordan River, a place name situated mainly on the northern edge of the Arnon valley. There are several Aroers in the Bible, but these passages refer to the Aroer before Rabbah and to the town in the Arnon valley.
biblecontents: Aroer before Rabbah is mentioned as one of the territories that the people of Israel allotted to the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13:25). There is also a record that when Jephthah struck the Ammonites, he attacked them from Aroer as far as Minnith and won the victory (Judges 11:33).
geography: It is identified with the Ara'ir area on the northern bank of the Arnon River (Wadi Mujib) in the present Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. This area is located on a highland overlooking the valley, and has terrain features advantageous as a military crossroads and a defensive stronghold.
history: It was originally the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, but after Israel conquered it, it was incorporated as a border area of the tribes of Reuben and Gad. Afterward this region was a border zone where disputes over territorial possession between Moab and Israel were frequent, and archaeological materials such as the Mesha Stele confirm that Mesha, king of Moab, reconquered and fortified this area.

remark: 2. An Amorite town on the bank of the Arnon River.
introduce: Aroer is a strategic crossroads located on the edge of the Arnon valley east of the Jordan, a major town that appears in the biblical record on the boundaries of the inheritance of the tribe of Gad and the tribe of Reuben.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad built Aroer (Numbers 32:34), and Aroer on the edge of the Arnon valley is mentioned as the southern boundary of the conquered territory (Deuteronomy 2:36). Israel occupied the land from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon valley as far as Gilead (Deuteronomy 3:12, Deuteronomy 4:48). Aroer was located on the boundary of the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites (Joshua 12:2), and was recorded as a town on the edge of the Arnon valley, part of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:9, Joshua 13:16). There is also a record that the Ammonites had occupied the area from Aroer to the Arnon for 300 years (Judges 11:26).
geography: Aroer is identified with the Aroer (Ara'ir) area of present-day Jordan, and, located on the cliff north of the Arnon River (present-day Wadi Mujib), it has a naturally strong defensive terrain overlooking the valley. It has the geographical advantage of being able to watch over the main north-south passage on the highland east of the Jordan.
history: At the time Israel conquered the region east of the Jordan in the time of Moses, it was the domain ruled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and afterward it was allotted to the tribes of Israel. This area was a buffer zone and strategic border region where not only the tribes of Israel but also neighboring states such as Ammon and Moab were in conflict over territorial rights for a long time.

remark: 3. A town in the south of Judah.
introduce: Aroer is an ancient town in the southern Negev of the tribe of Judah appearing in 1 Samuel 30, a town of Judah distinguished from the Moabite Aroer on the bank of the Arnon.
biblecontents: David sent the spoil he took from the Amalekites to those who were in Aroer (1 Samuel 30:28).
geography: It is identified with the ruins of Tel Aroer (Horvat Aroer) located in the Wadi Aroer valley, about 19 km southeast of Beersheba.
history: In the Iron Age II period it was a key fortress of the southern defense network of the kingdom of Judah, and prospered as a trade and military stronghold that controlled the Arabian trade routes.

remark: A hill near Asher.
introduce: Aloth is a proper name that appears in the Hebrew Bible when mentioning genealogies and the administrative districts of Solomon's kingdom. It refers to a clan of the tribe of Asher, and at the same time appears as a member of the Asher and Aloth region, one of Solomon's administrative districts.
biblecontents: Numbers 26:17 mentions the genealogy of the Arodites among the descendants of Gad and specifies the clan that is the ancestor of Aloth (Numbers 26:17). 1 Kings 4:16 records that Baana son of Baana lived in Asher and Aloth and exercised administrative jurisdiction on behalf of King Solomon (1 Kings 4:16).
