geography: It is presumed to be an area located within the territory of the tribe of Asher, and from the standpoint of modern geography the view that it is connected with the coastal plain zone of the northwestern Galilee is dominant. Its specific boundaries are not clear, but it is analyzed as having been a stronghold geographically adjacent to the Asher district as an administrative unit.

introduce: Arumah is a place that was adjacent to Shechem in the period of the judges, a place name used as the residence of Abimelech during his reign.
biblecontents: Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers so that they could not live in Shechem (Judges 9:41).
geography: It is known to have been located in the vicinity of Shechem, but its exact archaeological location has not been clearly determined to this day. Some scholars also presume it to be the same site as al-Urma, southeast of Shechem.

introduce: Arubboth was a region that administered the third of the twelve administrative districts of King Solomon, and was one of the economic and administrative centers, including Socoh and all the land of Hepher.
biblecontents: Ben-hesed, the son of Hesed, administered Arubboth, and he was the official who governed Socoh and all the land of Hepher (1 Kings 4:10).
geography: The exact location of Arubboth is disputed archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be near the eastern boundary of the Plain of Sharon or the hill country of Ephraim west of the Jordan River, and is assessed as a strategic crossroads geographically adjacent to Socoh.
history: The reorganization of administrative districts in the time of Solomon was carried out across the boundaries of the tribes for the purposes of efficient tax collection and military administration for the royal house, and the region including Arubboth played an important role in supplying food to the royal house on the basis of its fertile land.

remark: A city of Og, king of Bashan.
introduce: Argob is part of the region of Bashan recorded in the Bible, and refers to the towns located within the territory conquered by the half-tribe of Manasseh and their surrounding area. As an ancient Near Eastern place name, it is closely connected with the domain ruled by Og, king of Bashan.
biblecontents: The whole region of Argob that the half-tribe of Manasseh occupied at that time was the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan, and there were sixty towns there (Deuteronomy 3:4). Moses gave the half-tribe of Manasseh the rest of Gilead and the whole region of Argob, which had been the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan (Deuteronomy 3:13). Jair, a son of Manasseh, took the whole region of Argob and the land of Bashan as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and named it after himself, calling it Havvoth-jair to this day (Deuteronomy 3:14).
geography: Argob is located on the Bashan plateau east of the Jordan River, and includes rugged terrain covered with basalt, known as the Lejah region. This area is described as a place where strong towns advantageous for defense were densely clustered.
history: At the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan it was the region ruled by Og, king of the Amorites, but it was conquered by Israel's invasion. Afterward this region was distributed to the tribe of Manasseh and incorporated as Israelite territory, and there is a historical record that a man named Jair occupied a major part of this region and renamed it with the place name Havvoth-jair.

introduce: The Arnon is a major river and valley located in the land of Moab east of the Jordan River, an important geographical landmark that the people of Israel passed through, or took as their boundary, on their journey toward Canaan in the early biblical period.
biblecontents: The people of Israel came to the Arnon, the boundary of the Amorites, and camped there (Numbers 21:13). The Arnon is the boundary region between Moab and the Amorites (Numbers 21:13). In the Book of the Wars of the LORD, Waheb in Suphah and the valley of the Arnon are mentioned (Numbers 21:14). Israel took the land of Sihon, king of the Amorites, from the Arnon to the Jabbok (Numbers 21:24). Heshbon was the capital city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and was located north of the Arnon valley (Numbers 21:26). The expression appears that a fire from the Arnon consumed Ar of Moab (Numbers 21:28). Balak, king of Moab, heard the news that Balaam was coming and went as far as the city on the Arnon, at the extreme border of Moab, to meet him (Numbers 22:36). God commanded them to pass by Moab, cross the Arnon valley, and take the land of Sihon, king of the Amorites (Deuteronomy 2:24). Israel occupied the land from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon valley, with the town in the middle of the valley, as far as half of Gilead (Deuteronomy 2:36). They took the land of the Amorite kings east of the Jordan, from the Arnon valley to Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:8). From Aroer on the edge of the Arnon valley, half of the hill country of Gilead and its towns were given to the descendants of Reuben and the descendants of Gad (Deuteronomy 3:12).
geography: The Arnon is known today as the Wadi Mujib in Jordan. This river rises in the eastern desert and flows west into the Dead Sea, forming a deep and rugged gorge. This gorge functions geographically as a natural fortress, and in the past it was the natural boundary line dividing Moab from the land of the Amorites to its north.
history: In the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, the Arnon was a disputed area between the kingdom of Moab and the powers to the north. According to the biblical record, at the time Israel was advancing toward Canaan this region was ruled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and through the war with Sihon Israel conquered the area north of the Arnon and distributed it to the tribes of Reuben and Gad. Afterward as well, the Arnon continued to serve as the border between Israel and Moab.

introduce: Arbathite is a place name mentioned as the hometown of Abi-albon the Arbathite, one of David's mighty men. Through the Hebrew Bible record, it is confirmed as a name indicating the places of origin of the members of David's military organization.
biblecontents: Abi-albon the Arbathite is included in the list of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:31). Also in the record of Chronicles, Abiel the Arbathite is mentioned as one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:32).
geography: Its exact geographical location has not been clearly identified with any present-day site. It is only presumed, on the basis of the biblical record, to be a particular area within the territory of the tribe of Judah or within Israel, which David ruled.

introduce: Arpad was a city-state in northern Syria that was destroyed during the expansion of the ancient Assyrian Empire. In the biblical record it is mentioned together with the kingdom of Aram and Hamath as an object of Assyrian conquest, or as an example of conquest, and appears in the context of displaying Assyria's military power.
biblecontents: The Rabshakeh of Assyria threatened Jerusalem, asking where the gods of Hamath and Arpad were, and threatened that just as they had not saved Samaria, they would not be able to save Jerusalem either (2 Kings 18:34, Isaiah 36:19). The king of Assyria, mentioning that he had destroyed Arpad along with other conquered lands, displayed the power by which he had destroyed nations (2 Kings 19:13, Isaiah 37:13). It was suggested that in the conquests of King Sargon, Arpad had been conquered like Calno and Hamath (Isaiah 10:9). In the book of Jeremiah, Hamath and Arpad are described as being distressed on hearing the news of destruction, their hearts melting like the sea, with no peace (Jeremiah 49:23).
geography: Arpad is identified with the Tell Rifaat area, located near Aleppo in northern Syria. Situated north of Aleppo, it had high strategic value as a trade route and military crossroads of the ancient Near East.
history: Arpad was around the 8th century BC the capital of Bit Agusi, an Aramean kingdom. It resisted Assyria's expansion policy and joined an anti-Assyrian alliance, but it was conquered by Tiglath-pileser III in 740 BC, and was finally and completely incorporated into the Assyrian Empire by Sargon II around 720 BC.

remark: An island near Sidon.
introduce: Arvad was a major port city-state of ancient Phoenicia, corresponding in modern place names to Ruad Island in Syria. It is a strategic crossroads famed for maritime trade and shipbuilding in the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: He is mentioned as the ancestor of the Arvadites, one of the sons of Canaan (Genesis 10:18, 1 Chronicles 1:16). In the prophet Ezekiel's lament concerning Tyre, the men of Arvad are described as serving as soldiers in Tyre's army, guarding its walls and acting as mighty warriors (Ezekiel 27:8, Ezekiel 27:11).
geography: Arvad was located on a small rocky island about 3 kilometers off the northern Syrian coast of the Mediterranean. It had a close relationship with the nearby mainland port of Antaradus, and thanks to the geographical character of being an island, it had conditions advantageous for defense against outside attack and suitable for controlling maritime traffic.
history: Existing since the second millennium BC, Arvad led maritime trade as one of the core powers of Phoenician civilization. During the expansion of the Assyrian Empire it became a state paying tribute to them, and afterward, in the period of the Persian Empire, it played an active role as an important member of the Phoenician fleet. While maintaining an independent monarchy, this city sought survival on the foundation of its sea power under the political influence of the surrounding great powers.

introduce: Arimathea is a place name mentioned in the New Testament as the hometown of Joseph of Arimathea, who is known as the man who buried the body of Jesus. In ancient literature outside the Bible, it is difficult to pinpoint its location.
biblecontents: Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man and a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57). As a respected member of the council, he was a man waiting for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43). He had not consented to the council of the Jews and their actions (Luke 23:51), and he is described as one who was a disciple of Jesus but had kept it hidden for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).
geography: The exact location of Arimathea has not been clearly established archaeologically. Scholars raise the possibility that it is the same region as Ramathaim-zophim, which appears in 1 Samuel 1:1, and some presume it to be Rantis in the hill country of Ephraim or the Ramla area northwest of Jerusalem, but nothing has been confirmed.

introduce: Armageddon is a place name derived from the Hebrew Har Megiddo, and refers to the ancient city of Megiddo, which the book of Revelation describes as the place where the eschatological final battle takes place.
biblecontents: The three spirits gather the kings to the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).
geography: Megiddo is located at the western end of the Jezreel Valley, and is a strategic crossroads that crosses the Carmel range and connects the coastal plain with the Jordan Valley. It corresponds to the present-day Tel Megiddo area in Israel.
history: Megiddo was a key stronghold on the Way of the Sea, a major trade route of the ancient Near East, and was the site of numerous military clashes, including the battle between Thutmose III of Egypt and the Canaanite coalition, and the place where King Josiah was killed in battle fighting Neco of Egypt.

introduce: Abanah is a place name known as a part of the Lebanon mountain range, and is mentioned as a place related to the northern boundary of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: When Naaman, commander of Aram, was told at Elisha's instruction to wash in the Jordan River, the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, were presented as the grounds for refusing, on the argument that they were better than all the rivers of Israel (2 Kings 5:12). It also appears in the Song of Solomon as an expression of invitation to the bride to come down from the top of Abanah (Song of Solomon 4:8).
geography: Abanah is presumed to refer to the Abana River located in the present-day Anti-Lebanon mountain range, and this river is a major source of water flowing through the Damascus plain. The top of the mountainous terrain, or the area around its source, seems to have been called the Abanah mountain region, and this connects to the northern part of the Lebanon mountain range.
history: Abanah is frequently mentioned in ancient Assyrian records as the Abanah mountain range, and this was a strategic crossroads and boundary region through which the Assyrian Empire passed when it set out on campaigns to the west. It was used as a place name symbolizing the rivers and mountains that formed the major economic and ecological foundation of the Damascus region in biblical times.

introduce: Amalek refers to a people who lived a nomadic life in the ancient Near East and to the particular region where they lived or were active. They were active mainly in the Negev region and the northern Sinai Peninsula, and had historical conflicts with the people of Israel in areas overlapping Israel's routes of travel.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings with him came to En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh, and struck all the country of the Amalekites and also the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar (Genesis 14:7). The sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Edom, the chiefs Korah, the chief Gatam, and the chief Amalek, these are the chiefs who came from Eliphaz in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:16). Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Moses said to Joshua, "Choose men for us, and go out and fight with Amalek" (Exodus 17:9). Joshua did as Moses had instructed him and fought against the Amalekites, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. (Exodus 17:10) As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. (Exodus 17:11) Joshua mowed down Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword (Exodus 17:13). The LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua: I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven" (Exodus 17:14). He said, "The LORD has sworn: the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation" (Exodus 17:16). The Amalekites live in the land of the Negev. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites live in the hill country, and the Canaanites live by the sea and along the Jordan (Numbers 13:29).
geography: The dwelling place of Amalek was not a settlement with clear borders, but covered a broad region centered on the Negev desert and the Arabah valley. The Old Testament records that they lived around Kadesh (Genesis 14:7) and in the Negev region (Numbers 13:29), and geographically they encompassed the rugged wilderness zone south of Canaan and the northeastern part of the Sinai Peninsula. Place names such as Rephidim show that they penetrated or moved even into the interior of the Sinai Peninsula, which was Israel's route of travel.
history: The Amalekites are regarded as descendants of Amalek, a chief of Edom (Genesis 36:16), and appear as a political force with the character of nomads of the ancient Near East. Judging from the fact that they were already living near Kadesh in Genesis 14, it can be seen that they were a people who had settled and been active in that region even before the exodus of the people of Israel. They came into military conflict with Israel, who had come out of Egypt, at Rephidim, and this became the starting point of the hostile relationship between Israel and Amalek that runs through the entire Old Testament thereafter.

introduce: Amam is one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Amam is recorded as one of the towns at the southern end of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot, close to the border of Edom (Joshua 15:26).
geography: It is classified as a town in the Negev region south of Judah, and its exact archaeological location has not been identified today, but it is generally presumed to be an arid zone south of Beersheba or near Arad.

introduce: Amad is a town or place name mentioned as one of the border areas allotted to the tribe of Asher at the time of the ancient distribution of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: In the course of describing the boundary of the tribe of Asher, it is recorded as a place located along the way, passing through Allammelech and Mishal and going west to Shihor-libnath (Joshua 19:26).
geography: It is presumed to be a coastal area between the north of Mount Carmel and the plain of Acre, but its exact archaeological location has not been identified at present.

introduce: Amon refers to a major god of ancient Egypt and the patron god of the Thebes region, and in the Bible it appears as a name symbolizing the authority of No (Thebes), the capital of Egypt, and of the Egyptian dynasties centered on it.
biblecontents: The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, says: Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, and the gods of Egypt and its kings, that is, Pharaoh and those who rely on him (Jeremiah 46:25)
geography: The center of the worship of Amon was the Thebes region (No in the Bible) on the upper Nile River in Egypt, where the huge Karnak temple complex stood and served as a core stronghold of ancient Egyptian religion and politics.
history: Amon was elevated to the supreme god of Egypt after the Middle Kingdom period, and exercised enormous political influence in the periods of the 18th and 25th Dynasties based in Thebes. In the period when Jeremiah was active, Amon was perceived as an idol representing Egypt's military power and imperial pride.

introduce: Abarim is a mountainous region adjoining the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River, and the last major stopping point that the people of Israel passed through before entering the land of Canaan. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly in connection with the place where Moses looked out over the land of Canaan and met his death.
biblecontents: The LORD commanded Moses to go up Mount Abarim and look at the land of Canaan that he had given to the children of Israel (Numbers 27:12). The children of Israel left Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim (Numbers 33:47). They left the mountains of Abarim and camped on the plains of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 33:48). The LORD told Moses to go up Mount Abarim, that is, Mount Nebo, and see the land of Canaan (Deuteronomy 32:49). The prophet Jeremiah wrote, warning of the destruction of Judah, that one should cry out in Lebanon and Bashan and cry out from Abarim (Jeremiah 22:20).
geography: Abarim refers to a mountain range located on the highland east of the Dead Sea, and includes Mount Nebo to the north. This area consists of steep cliffs and high ground, and has a strategic view from which one can look down on the Jordan Valley to the west and the Dead Sea at a glance.
history: In ancient times the Abarim mountain range functioned as a territorial boundary or buffer zone between the kingdom of Moab and the tribes of Israel. Historically, this mountain range was recognized as a geographical crossroads, a route of movement for nomads and one of the gateways for entering Canaan.

introduce: Apharsachites is a term for the title of the governor who administered the region beyond the Euphrates River, one of the provinces of the Persian Empire, or for that region itself.
biblecontents: This name is mentioned in the report submitted to King Darius, opposing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, by Tattenai the governor beyond the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their colleagues (Ezra 5:6). After confirming this report, King Darius issued a decree to the governors beyond the Euphrates not to hinder the work on the Jerusalem temple (Ezra 6:6).
geography: It means an administrative district of the Persian Empire that, in the ancient Near East, included the Levant and Palestine regions west of the Euphrates River.
history: It is interpreted as a term referring to the governor of the Eber-Nari district, which administered the territory west of the Euphrates River under the satrapy system, the administrative district system of Achaemenid Persia.

introduce: Apharsites refers to a group, or the region they came from, appearing in the petition that officials living in Samaria submitted to the king in the time of King Artaxerxes of the Persian Empire.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in the petition that Rehum and Shimshai, officials of Samaria at that time, together with their colleagues, sent to officials of various regions, including the Apharsites (Ezra 4:9).
geography: According to ancient Near Eastern literature and the research of biblical scholarship, the Apharsites are presumed to be one of the peoples whom King Ashurbanipal of Assyria resettled in the Samaria region through his policy of deportation, and their specific geographical location is identified as the northern Mesopotamian region, which was the center of the Assyrian Empire (Ezra 4:9).
history: After the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel in the late 8th century BC, the Assyrian Empire carried out a policy of forcibly relocating the peoples of conquered lands, and the Apharsites are understood to be one of the groups of immigrants who flowed into Samaria at this time. They grew into an official class exercising administrative influence in the Samaria region, and acted as part of the political forces that hindered the Judeans' rebuilding of the temple in the early Persian Empire (Ezra 4:9).

introduce: Aphekah was one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Canaan, and is included in the list of towns enumerated in Joshua 15.
biblecontents: Aphekah is mentioned as one of the hill-country towns of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:53).
geography: Aphekah is presumed to have been located within a district that includes the northern hill country of Judah and the area near Hebron, but no specific archaeological site has been clearly identified, so it is difficult to determine its exact geographical coordinates. Scholars consider that this area would have been adjacent to other major towns in the hill country of Judah.

remark: 1. A place in the region of Canaan where there was a royal palace, which Joshua seized and gave to the tribe of Issachar.
introduce: Aphek is a place name mentioned as a strategic crossroads in the ancient Levant, and is interpreted as referring to at least three different places within the Bible. It mainly refers to towns located at gateways between the coastal plain and the hill country, or in military border zones.
biblecontents: Joshua defeated the king of Aphek at the time of the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 12:18). Aphek is included within the boundary allotted to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:30). Aphek is also mentioned as a northern border region adjoining the land of the Sidonians (Joshua 13:4). It appears as a place where wars between Israel and the Philistines took place, and is also where Israel camped before the ark of the covenant was captured (1 Samuel 4:1). It is also recorded as the area where the Philistine army camped before its final battle with Israel (1 Samuel 29:1).
geography: The Aphek that appears in the Bible is presumed to be at three main points. The first is Tel Aphek, located at the eastern end of the Plain of Sharon, which lies on the route linking Joppa and Samaria. The second is presumed to be Tel Afqa, located within the territory of the tribe of Asher in the north of Galilee. The third is the Aphek of the Bashan region, which is identified with the Fiq area, a military crossroads east of the Sea of Galilee.
history: Aphek was located at a point where the major trade routes and military roads of the ancient Near East intersect, and so it always became a center of foreign invasion or the expansion of power. In particular, it frequently appears as a strategic crossroads in records of Thutmose III of Egypt and in inscriptions of Sargon II of Assyria. Because, by its geopolitical position, it served as a passage between the Egyptian and Mesopotamian civilizations, it was a point where territorial disputes between Israel and neighboring states frequently occurred historically.

remark: 2. A town east of Chinnereth, where Ben-hadad was defeated by King Ahab.
introduce: Aphek is an ancient fortress town located on the Golan Heights east of the Sea of Galilee (Chinnereth), a strategic military battleground where fierce struggles over the border between the northern kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Aram took place.
biblecontents: When the year turned, Ben-hadad, king of Aram, mustered his army and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel (1 Kings 20:26). After the Aramean army was defeated, the survivors fled to the town of Aphek, but the wall collapsed and crushed twenty-seven thousand men to death, and Ben-hadad hid in an inner room in the town (1 Kings 20:30). The prophet Elisha, nearing his death, had Joash, king of Israel, open the east window and shoot an arrow, and prophesied that this was the LORD's arrow of salvation to annihilate Aram, and that the king would strike and destroy the Arameans at Aphek (2 Kings 13:17).
geography: This Aphek is located about 5 km east of the Sea of Galilee, at the entrance of the Golan Heights north of the Yarmuk Valley. It is identified with the village of Fiq (also Afik) on the highland east of present-day Ein Gev and with the archaeological site of Tell Soreg. It lies at a major passage of the international highway that enters the Galilee basin and the Jezreel Valley from Damascus.
history: During the 9th and 8th centuries BC, the northern kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Aram of Damascus clashed continually over territory in northern Transjordan, including Bashan and Gilead. In the time of King Ahab, a large invading Aramean army was repelled on the plain of Aphek and a treaty was made (1 Kings 20:26, 1 Kings 20:30), and in the time of King Joash as well, the recapture of Aphek, a border stronghold, became a decisive watershed for gauging the recovery of the national strength of the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 13:17).

introduce: Abel-keramim is a place name mentioned in the book of Judges, a region that Jephthah passed through while subduing the Ammonites. In Hebrew it carries the meaning of a field of vineyards.
biblecontents: Jephthah struck the Ammonites from Aroer as far as Minnith, took twenty towns, and defeated them with a great slaughter as far as Abel-keramim, and the Ammonites surrendered before the people of Israel (Judges 11:33).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the Ammonite region east of the Jordan, and though its present exact location is disputed archaeologically, scholars have raised the possibility that it is near Amman in Jordan or in the area southeast of Heshbon.

introduce: Abel-maim is a place name recorded in the Old Testament, a town located in the northern region of ancient Israel. It is presumed to be the same place as Abel-beth-maacah, and appears in biblical history as a strategic crossroads.
biblecontents: There is a record that when King Asa sent a gift to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, asking him to stop the invasion of Baasha of the northern kingdom of Israel, the army that Ben-hadad sent struck Ijon, Dan, and Abel-maim (2 Chronicles 16:4).
geography: Abel-maim is known to be located in the fertile area near the upper valley of the Jordan River and the Huleh basin. Geographically it is adjacent to the northern boundary of Galilee, and lies at a point serving as a passage linking the road coming down from the north with the Israelite towns to the south.
history: It has a historical background showing how the kingdom of Aram came to intervene in the course of the dispute between the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah around the 9th century BC. At that time Ben-hadad, king of Aram, at the request of Judah for help, attacked this place on the northern border of the northern kingdom of Israel, carrying out a strategic military action that caused the army of Baasha to withdraw.

introduce: Abel-meholah is an area located east of the Jordan Valley in ancient Israel, known mainly as a place with farmland and abundant water. This area is recorded as Elisha's hometown and as a place name connected with the battle between the judge Gideon and the Midianite coalition.
biblecontents: When Gideon's 300 men pursued the Midianite army, the boundary of the pursuit reached Beth-shittah, at the border of Abel-meholah (Judges 7:22). It also belonged to the district of Baana, the fifth province among King Solomon's administrative districts, and its location is described as Abel-meholah below Zarethan (1 Kings 4:12). It is also the place where Elisha was plowing the field when he received God's call (1 Kings 19:16).
geography: It is located inside the Jordan Valley on the west bank of the Jordan River, and in modern place names it is presumed to be Tell Abu Sus or nearby Tell el-Hilu. This is a fertile plain zone of the lower Jordan River, with geographical characteristics suited to farming because of its abundant water. It was located on the road leading south from Beth-shean and served as a transportation crossroads.
history: Traces of human habitation have been found from the early Iron Age, and in the period of the kingdom of Israel it functioned as a strategically important agricultural production area. In particular, during the period of the northern kingdom of Israel it was classified as a region of high administrative and economic value and was included in Solomon's provincial districts. Historically it carried great weight as a hub of exchange between the east and west of the Jordan River and as a military route of movement.

introduce: Abel-meholah is a place name appearing in the Old Testament, a region located near the Jordan Valley. It is known as the place where Elisha was driving oxen and plowing the field when the prophet Elijah designated Elisha as his successor.
biblecontents: God commanded Elijah to anoint Elisha son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah and appoint him as a prophet (1 Kings 19:16). Afterward Elijah went to Elisha, who was plowing the field at Abel-meholah with twelve yoke of oxen before him, threw his cloak over him, called him, and made him his successor (1 Kings 19:19). Also, in the book of Judges there is a record that Gideon, who stood against the Midianite army, carried on a pursuit as far as Abel-meholah (Judges 7:22). In the time of Solomon, Abel-meholah was included as one of the administrative districts, and it is described as located beside Zarethan, east of the Jordan (1 Kings 4:12).
geography: Abel-meholah is generally identified with a point west of the Jordan Valley, some distance south of Beth-shean. Modern scholars mainly regard Tell Abu Sus or Tell el-Hilu as the leading candidate sites. Situated in the fertile plain zone near the Jordan River, it has an environment suited to farming, and it served as a strategic base connected to the major road network.
history: Abel-meholah was a place of military and economic importance from the period of the judges through the period of the northern kingdom of Israel. It was mentioned as a strategic passage at the time of Gideon's campaign against the Midianites, and under Solomon's system of rule it served as an administrative center that collected taxes and supplied food. Judging from the biblical record, this area is understood as a place where the economic activity of the tribes of Israel and the ministry of the prophetic community coexisted.

introduce: Abel-mizraim is the name referring to the place where Jacob's funeral procession stopped and mourned greatly, and in Hebrew it carries the meaning of the mourning of the Egyptians.
biblecontents: When the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw the great mourning at the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan River, they called that place the mourning of the Egyptians (Genesis 50:11).
geography: It is located in the region east of the Jordan River, and is presumed to be a place on the route that Jacob's funeral procession, coming up from Egypt, passed through just before entering Canaan.

introduce: Abel-beth-maacah was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in northern ancient Israel, a strategic crossroads and an area where disputes between Aram and Israel were frequent.
biblecontents: The commanders of the armies that King Ben-hadad sent against Baasha, king of Israel, invaded Abel-beth-maacah, and struck and captured Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, all of Chinnereth, and all the land of Naphtali (1 Kings 15:20).
geography: It is identified with Tell Abil, near the present-day border of Lebanon. Located on the northwestern edge of the Huleh basin, it lies in a fertile plain zone able to control the road entering Israel from the north.
history: Around the 9th century BC it became a target of military attack amid the border disputes between the northern kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Aram centered on Damascus. By its geographical character this area served as a front line defending against invasion from the north, but it went through a history in which its sovereignty was often threatened or it was occupied according to the political interests of the great powers.

introduce: Abel-beth-maacah was a town located in the northern border region of ancient Israel, a place mentioned in the Old Testament as a strategic crossroads of the northern kingdom of Israel. In modern place names it is known as Tel Abel Beth Maacah.
biblecontents: In the time of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, invaded and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and took the people captive and carried them to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29).
geography: Abel-beth-maacah is located northwest of the Huleh Valley, near the present-day border between Israel and Lebanon. This area lies on the road connecting the hill country of Galilee and the Huleh basin, and has locational conditions very advantageous for controlling the military route of movement coming down from north to south.
history: In the late 8th century BC, in the course of the Assyrian Empire's expansion policy, the northern kingdom of Israel lost its strategic crossroads one after another. In particular, the large-scale campaign of Tiglath-pileser III resulted in incorporating the northern territory of Israel as Assyrian crown land, and in that process Abel-beth-maacah was conquered by the Assyrian army and suffered the harm of its inhabitants being forcibly relocated.

introduce: Abel-shittim is a place name that was located on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River, and was one of the last campsites where the people of Israel camped before the war of conquest of Canaan. It carries the meaning of a valley thick with acacia trees.
biblecontents: The children of Israel camped by the Jordan on the plains of Moab, from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim (Numbers 33:49). Also Joshua sent two men as spies from Shittim to view Jericho (Joshua 2:1).
geography: It is located on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River in the northeastern area of the Dead Sea. In modern place names it is presumed to be Tell el-Hammam in western Jordan or its vicinity, and it has the topographical features of being dry and flat, suited to the growth of acacia trees.
history: It was a strategic crossroads where the people of Israel assembled in great numbers just before entering Canaan, after finishing their wilderness life following the Exodus. Being in a position from which one could look out over nearby Jericho and the Jordan River, it served as a bridgehead for the conquest of Canaan.

introduce: Apollonia is a city located in the ancient region of Macedonia, a major stopping place on the route along which the apostle Paul traveled via Amphipolis to Thessalonica during his second missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul and Silas passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews (Acts 17:1)
geography: Apollonia is a city located on the Via Egnatia, situated between Amphipolis and Thessalonica of the kingdom of Macedonia. It corresponds to the present-day region of northern Greece, and was a transportation crossroads connecting the Mediterranean coast with the interior.
history: Apollonia was a city of the province of Macedonia under the rule of the Roman Empire, and its strategic importance was high, especially because the Via Egnatia, a Roman military and commercial road, passed through it. The name of the city derives from the ancient Greek god Apollo, and it was one of the cities that made up the administrative and commercial network of Macedonia at that time.

introduce: Abronah is one of the campsites of the children of Israel that appears in the itinerary of the Exodus, a place name located in the stage before Ezion-geber.
biblecontents: The children of Israel left Jotbathah and camped at Abronah (Numbers 33:34). They left Abronah again and camped at Ezion-geber (Numbers 33:35).
geography: The exact location of Abronah has not been clearly established archaeologically at present, but it is generally presumed to lie on the route running from north to south in the Arabah Valley. It is regarded as an area that existed on the way to Ezion-geber at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba.

remark: The descendants of Manasseh, the eldest son of Joseph, and their dwelling place.
introduce: Abiezer is a place name appearing in the book of Judges of the Old Testament, or a name referring to a family within a tribe of Israel, and is closely connected with the place of origin of the judge Gideon.
biblecontents: When the angel of the LORD sat down under the oak at Ophrah, that place belonged to Joash the Abiezrite (Judges 6:11). Gideon built an altar there for the LORD and called it The LORD Is Peace, and that altar is still at Ophrah of the Abiezrites to this day (Judges 6:24). When the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon and Gideon blew the trumpet, the Abiezrites were summoned to follow him (Judges 6:34). Gideon asked the men of Ephraim whether the late grapes of Ephraim were not better than the first grapes of Abiezer (Judges 8:2). Gideon was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah, the town of the Abiezrites (Judges 8:32).
geography: Abiezer is an area located within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, and is presumed to be, more specifically, an area west of the Jordan River adjoining the hill country of Ephraim. The center of this place was Ophrah, and the record of Judges shows that it had topographical features related to farming.
history: Abiezer was a family or clan unit belonging to the tribe of Manasseh, and is known as the home base of Gideon, who saved Israel from the Midianite invasion in the time of the judges. They were under the oppression of an outside power at that time, and judging from the record of Judges, the political and military influence of the region expanded greatly during the period of Gideon's activity as judge.

introduce: Aphik is an ancient place name mentioned in Judges 1:31, recorded as one of the Canaanite settlements that the tribe of Asher could not take. Modern archaeological investigations presume it to be a particular site in the plain of Acre, but the grounds are insufficient to specify a definitive matching point within scholarship.
biblecontents: The tribe of Asher could not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, the inhabitants of Sidon, and of Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob, so they lived among the Canaanite people, the inhabitants of the land (Judges 1:31-32).
geography: Aphik is presumed to be an area adjoining the western coastal plain of Galilee. It is located within the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Asher, and topographically belongs to a strategic zone linking the coast with the inland hills. Archaeologically it is sometimes discussed in connection with Tel Aphek in the plain of Acre, but because the Aphik in the Bible could be confused with the Aphek of other regions, it is difficult to determine its exact geographical location.
history: In the late Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, the Canaanite city-states possessed strong walls and chariot forces. At that time the tribe of Asher did not completely subdue the main strongholds of the coastal plain, and as a result it continued in a state of coexisting with the native Canaanites or being pressured under them. The neighboring cities, including Aphik, both symbolized Canaanite dominance and served as a line of physical resistance to the territorial expansion of the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Abilene refers to a small territory located on the eastern foothills of the Lebanon mountain range in northern Palestine in the New Testament period, and was one of the districts of a tetrarch under the Roman imperial system of rule of that time.
biblecontents: According to the record between Luke 3:1 and 3:2, it is mentioned that when John the Baptist began his ministry, Abilene was being ruled by Lysanias as tetrarch (Luke 3:1).
geography: Abilene was situated on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range, and is located about 30 kilometers northwest of Damascus. The center of this region was Abila, and since it included the valley of the Barada River, it was geographically a strategic crossroads linking the Damascus plain with the Lebanese hill country.
history: Abilene at first maintained the form of an independent kingdom, but it became a client state of Rome as Roman influence expanded. Around 40 BC it was ruled by Ptolemy of Chalcis, and afterward Lysanias governed it. During the reign of the Roman emperor Tiberius it was incorporated under the tetrarchy system as a Roman administrative district, and afterward it went through complicated political changes, being incorporated into the territory of Herod Agrippa I and II or managed as Roman direct territory.

remark: A town of Ephraim.
introduce: Ayyah is an area included within the inheritance boundary of the tribe of Ephraim, a place name mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:28 of the Bible. It is presumed to be a stronghold in the western border zone in the process of the distribution of land by tribe in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Their inheritance and dwelling places were Bethel and its surrounding villages, with Naaran to the east, and Gezer and its surrounding villages to the west, and also Shechem and its surrounding villages, as far as Ayyah and its surrounding villages (1 Chronicles 7:28)
geography: It is located in the western boundary area of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. Judging from its being mentioned together with nearby Gezer and Shechem, it is understood as a strategic crossroads linking the Plain of Sharon and the hill country of Ephraim, or as a settlement in that vicinity. However, scholars differ in their views on its present exact archaeological identification.

introduce: Ashan was a town located within the territory of the ancient tribe of Judah and tribe of Simeon. According to the records of Joshua and Chronicles, this area was mentioned as one of the towns of the tribe of Judah and was afterward incorporated into the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon.
biblecontents: Ashan was mentioned as one of the towns within the territory of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:42). Afterward it appears in the list of towns allotted as the inheritance of the descendants of Simeon (Joshua 19:7). Also in Chronicles it is recorded as one of the villages where the descendants of Simeon lived (1 Chronicles 4:32), and it is also mentioned as one of the towns distributed to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:59).
geography: Ashan is presumed to be located in the Shephelah region, the lowlands of Judah. Opinions differ about its exact location, but the view that identifies it with Tell Asha near Beit Jibrin, or its vicinity, is the one mainly raised in scholarship.

introduce: Azekah is a strategic crossroads located in the Shephelah plain region, which was the territory of the tribe of Judah, and is an ancient town mentioned in the biblical record mainly as a point of military standoff between Israel and neighboring states.
biblecontents: The LORD defeated them before Israel as far as Azekah (Joshua 10:10). Large hailstones fell from the sky as far as Azekah (Joshua 10:11). Azekah is included in the list of towns that the tribe of Judah received as an inheritance (Joshua 15:35). The Philistines pitched camp between Socoh and Azekah to fight against Israel (1 Samuel 17:1). King Rehoboam built Azekah as a fortified city for the defense of Judah (2 Chronicles 11:9). It was mentioned as one of the villages where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:30). It was mentioned when the Babylonian army attacked Jerusalem and Lachish and Azekah, the remaining towns of Judah (Jeremiah 34:7).
geography: Azekah is identified with present-day Tell Zakariya, and is located in the Shephelah region, the buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain. As a strategic fortress overlooking the Elah Valley, it stands about 25 km southwest of Jerusalem, in a position able to control the road entering the hill country of Judah from the coastal plain.
history: Azekah was used as a military crossroads from the time of the conquest of Canaan to the late period of the kingdom of Judah. In the early period it functioned as a front line in the wars with the Philistines, and in the time of Rehoboam it became a key base for building a defensive line to block invasion from the west. Archaeologically, from the Lachish Letters and others written at the time of the Babylonian invasion in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, it is confirmed that Azekah, together with Lachish, was one of the last strongholds of resistance of Judah.

introduce: Azotus is the Greek name that refers to Ashdod, one of the major cities of the ancient Philistines located on the Palestinian coastal plain. In the biblical record it is mentioned as one of the routes of travel connected with the spread of the gospel.
biblecontents: Philip appeared at Azotus, passed through various towns preaching the gospel, and came to Caesarea (Acts 8:40).
geography: It is located in the plain zone on the Mediterranean coast, north of Gaza and south of Joppa. In ancient times it was an important stronghold on the Way of the Sea, the international highway that linked Egypt and the Levant along the coast.
history: In the Old Testament period it was a region that often came into conflict with Israel as one of the five major cities of the Philistines. In the intertestamental period and the New Testament period it was called by the name Azotus under Greek influence, and even through the administrative changes of the Hasmonean dynasty and the Roman period it still functioned as a strategic crossroads.

introduce: Asher is a place name mentioned in 2 Samuel 2:9 of the Bible, a region that appears in the context of explaining the domain ruled by Ish-bosheth.
biblecontents: Ish-bosheth was made king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel (2 Samuel 2:9).
geography: Opinions in scholarship are divided about the exact location of Asher. Some scholars interpret this place name in connection with Gilead, located east of the Jordan, but there is insufficient basis, from archaeological excavations or from geographical literature outside the Bible, to identify this place name definitively.

introduce: Ashkenaz is a people or place name appearing in ancient Near Eastern literature and the Bible, a name regarded as connected mainly with the Scythians who lived north of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
biblecontents: In the scene of summoning a coalition against Babylon, the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz are mentioned, and it appears in the context of the command to them to attack Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27).
geography: It is presumed to be the Ishkuza region of the ancient Assyrian records, which means a territory including the steppe zone in the northeast of the Black Sea and north of the Caucasus Mountains (Jeremiah 51:27).
history: It appears under the name Ishkuza in records from the period of Esar-haddon, king of Assyria, around the 7th century BC, and they are known as a nomadic people who drove out the Cimmerians, settled in the northwestern part of the Iranian plateau, and entered into relations with the Medes (Jeremiah 51:27).

remark: One of the five major cities of the Philistines.
introduce: Ashkelon was a major port city located on the ancient Palestinian coastal plain and one of the five towns of the Philistine confederation, a strategic crossroads in the southwest of the region of Canaan.
biblecontents: It was mentioned as one of the five Philistine towns not conquered in the time of Joshua (Joshua 13:3), and the tribe of Judah once occupied it, but afterward it remained Philistine territory (Judges 1:18). It appears as the place where Samson killed thirty men of Ashkelon and took their clothes to pay the price of the riddle (Judges 14:19). It was one of the towns for which the Philistines sent a guilt offering when they returned the ark of the covenant they had taken from Israel (1 Samuel 6:17). David, mourning the deaths of Saul and Jonathan, sang a lament hoping that this news would not be told in the streets of Ashkelon (2 Samuel 1:20). The prophet Jeremiah mentioned Ashkelon in his messages of judgment against Egypt and the peoples around the Philistines (Jeremiah 25:20, Jeremiah 47:5, Jeremiah 47:7), and the prophets Amos and Zephaniah likewise singled out Ashkelon as a place where God's judgment would come (Amos 1:8, Zephaniah 2:4).
geography: Ashkelon, located on the Mediterranean coast, is a port city lying north of Gaza and south of Joppa. Situated in the fertile coastal plain zone, it had an environment favorable for agriculture and trade, and served as a transportation node connecting the inland and the sea.
history: Ashkelon, where settlement began in the Bronze Age, became a main stronghold of the Philistines when they, a Sea People, settled there around the 12th century BC. Because of its strategic importance among the great powers of the ancient Near East such as Assyria and Egypt, it was frequently the object of conquest and recapture, and it was a core coastal city-state of Philistine civilization that enjoyed prosperity as a center of international trade routes.

remark: 1. A town west of Judah.
introduce: Ashnah is one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament.
biblecontents: In the list enumerating the towns of the land the tribe of Judah obtained by lot, it is recorded as a town of the lowland region (Joshua 15:33).
geography: It belongs to the lowland (Shephelah) region among the four districts dividing the territory of the tribe of Judah, and geographically it is located in the buffer zone between the coastal plain and the hill country of Judah.

remark: 2. Another town in the plain of Judah.
introduce: Ashnah is one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place located in the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: Ashnah was mentioned in the course of listing the towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:43).
geography: It is located in the third district of the lowland of Judah (the Shephelah), and is a hilly area adjoining Nezib, Keilah, Achzib, and others between Libnah and Mareshah. It is presumed to be near present-day Idhna.

introduce: Aznoth-tabor is a place name mentioned in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament, recorded as a place located on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Its west reaches to Aznoth-tabor, and from there it goes out to Hukkok, reaching Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west, and on the east it reaches Judah at the Jordan (Joshua 19:34)
geography: Aznoth-tabor is presumed to be located near Mount Tabor in the region of Galilee, but its exact archaeological point has not been specified. The meaning of the name may be interpreted as the peaks of Tabor or the flank of Tabor, and topographically it appears to be a stronghold in the border area where the Galilean hill country meets the plain.

introduce: Ashtaroth is an ancient town located in the Bashan region east of the Jordan, the seat of rule of the Rephaim people and a major city where the royal palace of Og, king of Bashan, stood. In the biblical record it is mentioned mainly in connection with the domain ruled by Og, king of Bashan, and afterward appears as a boundary point of the region allotted to the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Moses conquered Og, king of Bashan, who lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei (Deuteronomy 1:4). The inhabitants of Gibeon deceived the Israelites, saying that they had come from a far country, where Og, king of Bashan, who ruled at Ashtaroth and elsewhere, had lived (Joshua 9:10). Ashtaroth was in the territory of Og, king of Bashan, where the remnant of the Rephaim lived (Joshua 12:4). God gave the region including Ashtaroth, which had been the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan, as an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13:12). Ashtaroth was the kingdom of Og in Bashan, and is a region confirmed as the inheritance of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:31). The tribe of Manasseh gave Ashtaroth in Bashan and its surrounding villages to the descendants of Gershon (1 Chronicles 6:71).
geography: Ashtaroth is presumed to be Tell Ashtara, located in southwestern Syria today. It lies in the fertile area of the Bashan plain, east of the Jordan River and southeast of the Sea of Galilee. As a strategic crossroads where the major trade routes of the ancient Near East intersect, this point has abundant water sources and an environment suited to farming.
history: Ashtaroth was a long-established town settled from the Bronze Age, known as a dwelling place of the Rephaim people. In the time of the rule of Og, king of Bashan, it served as the political and military center of the region. Afterward, through Israel's wars of conquest, it was incorporated into the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, and as it was allotted as a town of the Gershonites, descendants of the tribe of Levi, it was recorded as a region performing religious and administrative functions.

introduce: Ashdod is one of the five city-states of the ancient Philistines, a strategic crossroads located on the Mediterranean coastal plain, and an area where military and religious clashes between Israel and the Philistines frequently occurred in the biblical record.
biblecontents: It is recorded as a place where some of the descendants of Anak remained at the time of the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 11:22). In the time of Joshua it was regarded as one of the territories of the five rulers of the Philistines, but was not completely conquered (Joshua 13:3). It was included among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:46, 15:47), but afterward appears as a stronghold of the Philistines opposed to Israel. The Philistines took the ark of the covenant of Israel and placed it in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod, but the idol of Dagon fell down, and an incident occurred in which a plague of tumors came upon the people of Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:1, 5:3, 5:5, 5:6, 5:7). Ashdod was afterward mentioned as one of the places that offered golden tumors to the LORD as a guilt offering by way of compensation (1 Samuel 6:17).
geography: Ashdod is located near present-day Ashdod in Israel, and is a transportation hub linking the coastal plain with the inland hill country. Because it lay on the route of the Via Maris, the ancient coastal road, it was of very high military and commercial value.
history: From the late Bronze Age through the Iron Age it developed as the center of Philistine culture. The Philistines are presumed to have been a Sea People who migrated from the vicinity of the Aegean Sea, and Ashdod, as a core city of their iron-making technology and of the confederation of five city-states, a political association, underwent incessant territorial disputes among the surrounding powers of Israel and Judah, and between Egypt and Assyria.

introduce: Ashterathite is a place name mentioned as the place of origin of Uzzia the Ashterathite, a companion of Asahel, the younger brother of Joab, one of David's mighty men, and one of the Thirty, David's powerful military organization.
biblecontents: Uzzia the Ashterathite is mentioned as a man from Ashterathite (1 Chronicles 11:44).
geography: It appears to refer to the same place name as Ashtaroth, located in the Bashan region east of the Jordan, and is presumed to be a strategic crossroads situated near the King's Highway, a major road network of the ancient Near East.

introduce: Ashteroth-karnaim is a place name of the ancient Near East, a place known as the dwelling place of the Rephaim people who appear in Genesis 14.
biblecontents: In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings with him came out and struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites at Ham, and the Emites at Shaveh-kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5)
geography: It is presumed to be the same region as Ashtara, in northern Jordan today, and is located at a strategic crossroads in the Bashan region. In the place name, Ashteroth means a place of worship of the goddess Astarte, and Karnaim means two horns, which seems to reflect the topographical feature of the two hills located in this area.
history: As an ancient city inhabited from the Bronze Age, it was a center closely connected with the polytheistic culture of Canaan. Located along the major trade routes of the ancient Near East, it became an object of political and military contention, and apart from the Old Testament it is recorded as a major stronghold of the Bashan region in ancient documents such as the Amarna letters of Egypt.

remark: The boundary between Judah and Benjamin; also called Beth-azmaveth.
introduce: Azmaveth is a place name appearing in the Old Testament, used chiefly to refer to a settlement of the tribe of Benjamin or to persons who came from there.
biblecontents: In the Book of Nehemiah it is mentioned as one of the villages where the singers who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem lived (Nehemiah 12:29). It is also interpreted as being connected with the home region of Azmaveth the Barhumite, one of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:31).
geography: It is presumed to be the area of present-day Al Hizmeh, a town of the tribe of Benjamin located about 6 km northeast of Jerusalem. The area lies near a strategic point for entering Jerusalem.
history: In the course of the Jews who returned after the Babylonian exile rebuilding and resettling the old towns around Jerusalem, the Azmaveth area also came to be inhabited again. From the record of the dedication of the wall, it can be seen that at that time this place was one of the residences of Levites or temple servants who had close ties with the religious community centered on the Jerusalem temple.

introduce: Azmon is one of the principal points of the southern boundary line set in the period of the settlement of Canaan by ancient Israel. Located on the route connecting Kadesh-barnea and the Brook of Egypt, this area became a geographical reference point dividing the territories of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: When God designated the southern boundary of Canaan to Moses, He specified that the southern boundary would go down along Edom, pass Azmon, reach the Brook of Egypt, and extend to the sea (Numbers 34:4). Also, the course that turns from Azmon, passes the Brook of Egypt, and reaches the sea was mentioned as the southern end of the boundary (Numbers 34:5). In describing the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah as well, it is recorded that the southern boundary passes Azmon, reaches the Brook of Egypt, and ends at the sea (Joshua 15:4).
geography: The exact location of Azmon is open to dispute in modern archaeology, but it is generally presumed to be the southern Negev Desert or the upper reaches of Wadi al-Arish near Kadesh-barnea. This is an arid desert region, and in ancient times it was part of the trade routes and travel routes connecting southern Palestine and the Sinai Peninsula. Topographically it lies at the meeting point of the southern plain and the hill country, and so it possessed geographical features that made it easy to fix a boundary line.

introduce: The Asia mentioned in the Bible is not the name of a modern continent but means the province of Asia, an administrative district of the Roman Empire. It refers to a district centered on the western coastal region of present-day Asia Minor.
biblecontents: Among the people who visited Jerusalem at Pentecost were Jews from Asia (Acts 2:9). There was a synagogue of the people from the Freedmen, the Cyrenians, the Alexandrians, and Cilicia and Asia (Acts 6:9). The Holy Spirit prevented them from speaking the word in Asia (Acts 16:6). All who lived in Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord (Acts 19:10). Paul sent two of those who helped him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed in Asia for a time (Acts 19:22). Paul's influence spread through nearly all of Asia (Acts 19:26). The majesty of the temple of Artemis, which all Asia worshiped, was in danger of being diminished (Acts 19:27). Some of the officials of Asia who were friends of Paul urged him not to enter the amphitheater (Acts 19:31). Sopater of Berea, Aristarchus of Thessalonica, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus, and Trophimus went as far as Asia (Acts 20:4). Paul decided to sail past Ephesus so as not to spend time in Asia (Acts 20:16).
geography: The ancient Roman province of Asia refers to the western end of the Anatolian peninsula. Its major cities included Ephesus, Smyrna, and Pergamum; it bordered the Aegean Sea on the west, and its geographical extent took in inland regions such as Phrygia, Mysia, Lydia, and Caria.
history: It became a Roman province in 133 BC when Attalus III, king of Pergamum, bequeathed his territory to Rome. Under the Roman imperial system, the province of Asia was an economically very wealthy region, and on the basis of a highly developed urban culture it was a region where Hellenistic culture and emperor worship were strongly present. At the time the events of the Book of Acts were recorded, Ephesus served as the administrative center of this province.

introduce: Achaia is the name of an administrative district of the Roman Empire that included the Peloponnese peninsula in southern ancient Greece and the surrounding area. It was one of the base regions where the missionary activity of the apostle Paul was carried out vigorously in the New Testament period.
biblecontents: When Gallio became proconsul of Achaia, the Jews opposed Paul and brought him to court (Acts 18:12). When Paul wished to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him (Acts 18:27). Paul resolved to go to Jerusalem after passing through Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 19:21). The people of Macedonia and Achaia gladly made a contribution for the poor saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). The household of Stephanas, the firstfruits of Achaia, is a household that has resolved to serve the saints (1 Corinthians 16:15). Paul sent a letter to all the saints who were in Achaia (2 Corinthians 1:1). The people of Achaia had been preparing the relief work for Jerusalem since a year before (2 Corinthians 9:2). The intention that Paul's boasting in the region of Achaia should not be stopped is mentioned (2 Corinthians 11:10). The report of the gospel spread to the believers in Achaia (1 Thessalonians 1:7). The word of the Lord sounded forth not only in Achaia but spread to every place (1 Thessalonians 1:8).
geography: Achaia was a principal region of ancient Greece that bordered Macedonia on the north, and its major cities included Corinth and Cenchrea. Port cities on the Mediterranean coast were located there, and it served as a hub of maritime trade.
history: After Rome destroyed and conquered Corinth in 146 BC, Achaia was administered as part of the province of Macedonia, and in 27 BC, during the reign of Emperor Augustus, it was separated as a distinct senatorial province. In the middle of the first century AD, Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia and the center of administration and economy where the governor resided.

remark: A town of Canaan southeast of Bethel; another name for Ai.
introduce: Aija is a place mentioned as one of the villages where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile in the time of Nehemiah.
biblecontents: From Geba they lived in Michmash, Aija, Bethel, and their villages (Nehemiah 11:31).
geography: Its exact present location has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it is presumed to be an area in the north of Jerusalem adjacent to the other towns of the tribe of Benjamin listed in Nehemiah 11.

remark: 1. The name of a valley in Dan.
introduce: Aijalon is a town located in the Shephelah, the lowland region of Canaan, and is a strategic crossroads connecting the Mediterranean coastal plain with the hill country leading to Jerusalem.
biblecontents: It is the place where Joshua, while fighting the Amorites in the battle of Gibeon, asked that the sun and the moon be made to stand still, and afterward he pursued the enemies in the Valley of Aijalon and won the victory (Joshua 10:12).
geography: Aijalon is known as the present-day Aijalon Valley, and it lies at the western entrance connected to the Beth-horon ascent that links the coastal plain with the hill country of Judah. This valley has the topographical feature of running between the hill country of Ephraim in the north and the hill country of Judah in the south.
history: This region was treated as important as a military route from the Canaanite period, and during the period of Israel's settlement it was even included in the boundary of the land allotted to the tribe of Dan. Aijalon is also recorded as one of the towns that Rehoboam fortified for the defense of the kingdom of Judah in the divided kingdom period after the death of Solomon.

remark: 2. A Levitical city of Dan.
introduce: Aijalon refers to a place located in the Valley of Aijalon, a strategic point, which was both a town allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Dan in ancient Israel and one of the towns allotted to the Levites.
biblecontents: Aijalon is mentioned as one of the towns that the tribe of Dan received as an inheritance (Joshua 19:42). Afterward it became a town allotted to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:24, 1 Chronicles 6:69), and because the Amorites held out stubbornly, living in Mount Heres and Aijalon, the tribe of Dan was unable to drive them out completely (Judges 1:35). It is also recorded as one of the places where the Israelite army, pursuing the Philistine army in the time of Saul and Jonathan, stayed (1 Samuel 14:31).
geography: Aijalon lies in the Valley of Aijalon, a strategic passage located between the hill country of Judea and the Shephelah plain. This valley serves as a key route linking the coastal plain with the entrance to the hill country leading to Jerusalem, and it occupies a militarily very important position. As a modern place name it is presumed to be Yalo.
history: From the Bronze Age it was an important city-state, to the extent that it appears in the Egyptian Amarna letters, and after the war of the conquest of Canaan it was used as a border area and military base for Israel's territorial expansion. Because of its topography, it was a region where clashes frequently occurred between forces trying to enter the mountainous region and forces defending against them.

remark: 3. A town in Zebulun, the place where the judge Elon was buried.
introduce: Aijalon is a town recorded in the Book of Judges within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee, a northern town where the judge Elon ruled and was buried.
biblecontents: When Elon the Zebulunite, a judge, died, he was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun (Judges 12:12).
geography: It is identified with Khirbet el-Lon or the ruins of Tell el-Wawiyat, near the Beit Netofa plain in lower Galilee.
history: It was a mountain settlement that served as the political and judicial center of the tribe of Zebulun in the Iron Age I.

remark: 4. A town in Benjamin or Judah.
introduce: Aijalon is a strategic point within the territory of ancient Israel, a town and plain mentioned chiefly in the border area between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Dan.
biblecontents: Beriah and Shema, as the heads of the inhabitants of Aijalon, drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chronicles 8:13). King Rehoboam fortified Aijalon to strengthen the defenses of Judah and Benjamin (2 Chronicles 11:10). The Philistines invaded the lowland and southern towns of Judah and captured Aijalon (2 Chronicles 28:18).
geography: Aijalon lies in the Valley of Aijalon, which connects the Shephelah region with the central hill country. Because this region lies on the main route going up from the Mediterranean coastal plain to Jerusalem, it has important geographical value as a military and commercial passage.
history: Aijalon was a border zone where territorial disputes between Israel and neighboring nations frequently occurred from the time of the conquest of Canaan. During the period of the kingdom of Judah it was used as a key base for building a defensive line against invasions by hostile forces such as northern Israel or the Philistines.

introduce: Aiath is a place name appearing in the Book of Isaiah in the Old Testament, a town presumed to have been located north of Jerusalem in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the routes along which the Assyrian army advanced toward Jerusalem, and it is recorded that they came to Aiath, stored their baggage there, and passed on (Isaiah 10:28).
geography: Aiath appears to be located near Michmash and is analyzed to be one of the major strategic points for entering Jerusalem (Isaiah 10:28). Its exact present location is sometimes identified archaeologically with Ai, but there is no clear consensus.
history: It appears in a context describing the military route, whether hypothetical or actual, along which the Assyrian army marched south from northern Israel toward Jerusalem at the time of the campaign of the Assyrian king Sennacherib against southern Judah around the 8th century BC (Isaiah 10:28).

introduce: Avva is a place name of the ancient Near East, a locality mentioned in the process by which the Assyrian Empire forcibly resettled the conquered peoples of Israel and the surrounding nations.
biblecontents: The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and placed them in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites (2 Kings 17:24). The people of Avva made Nibhaz and Tartak and served them (2 Kings 17:31). Rabshakeh of Assyria threatened Judah, asking in return where the gods of Hamath and Arpad were, and where the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Avva were (2 Kings 18:34). The king of Assyria stated that he had destroyed the kings of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, and the kings of Hena and Avva (2 Kings 19:13).
geography: Scholars are divided over its exact location, but it is presumed to be a town that lay somewhere in the middle Euphrates region or in northern Mesopotamia. Judging from the fact that it is mentioned together with Hamath, Arpad, and Sepharvaim, which were the main target areas of Assyria's resettlement policy, it appears to have been one of the administrative districts within the Assyrian Empire.
history: The Assyrian Empire carried out a policy of forced resettlement in order to weaken the nationalist feeling of conquered lands and to prevent rebellion. Avva is one of the towns whose inhabitants, after it was conquered by Assyria under this policy, were forcibly resettled in the region of Samaria. This is a typical example of the population movements that appeared in the course of Assyria's territorial expansion.

introduce: Avvim is a name referring to an ancient people who lived in the coastal plain region near Gaza in the period before the conquest of Canaan, or to their settlement. They are known to have been driven out or conquered by the Caphtorites in the southwestern region of Canaan.
biblecontents: The Avvim lived in the villages as far as Gaza, but they were destroyed by the Caphtorites, who came to live in their place (Deuteronomy 2:23). Also, in the time of Joshua, in describing the boundary of the remaining land that Joshua had not taken, the land of the Avvim, from Gaza to Ekron, is mentioned (Joshua 13:3).
geography: Geographically it lies in the southwestern coastal plain region on the Mediterranean coast. Specifically, it encompasses the coastal zone reaching the Ekron area, the northern boundary of the Philistine plain, including the present-day Gaza Strip.
history: It is analyzed that in the Late Bronze Age the Caphtorite group, presumed to have migrated from the Minoan cultural sphere or the Aegean coast, drove out the Avvim, the earlier native inhabitants, and settled there. Afterward this region became the base of the major city-states of the Philistine people.

introduce: Avvim is one of the towns allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Avvim is included in the list of towns that the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin obtained by lot, and it is mentioned together with Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba (Joshua 18:23).
geography: The exact location of Avvim has not been clearly identified archaeologically at present, but it is presumed to have been located in the hill country of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:23).

introduce: Avith is a place name in the land of Edom, mentioned as the hometown of Hadad, an early ruler of the Edomite dynasty.
biblecontents: After Hadad son of Bedad defeated the Midianites in the fields of Moab, he called his city Avith (Genesis 36:35). The record in Chronicles likewise states that when Hadad son of Bedad died, Samlah of Masrekah became king in his place, and after him Shaul became king, and that the name of Hadad's city was Avith (1 Chronicles 1:46-48).

introduce: Ai was a town located in the central region of Canaan, a strategic point that the Israelite army led by Joshua attempted to conquer after the capture of Jericho. Located near the east of Bethel, it appears in the travel route of Abraham and in the records of Israel's war of conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: When Abram moved to the mountain east of Bethel and pitched his tent, Ai was on its west (Genesis 12:8). Abram set out from the Negev and came to the place where he had pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 13:3). Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai to spy it out, and Ai was beside Beth-aven, east of Bethel (Joshua 7:2). The spies reported that since Ai was a small town, it would be enough for only a few men to go up (Joshua 7:3). Israel was defeated by the men of Ai, and about 36 men died and they were driven back (Joshua 7:4-5). Afterward the LORD commanded Joshua to take all the soldiers, go up, and strike Ai (Joshua 8:1). God permitted him to take the king of Ai, his people, and the town as he had done to Jericho, but to plunder the goods and the livestock (Joshua 8:2). Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men and sent them to Ai by night (Joshua 8:3). They lay in ambush between Bethel and Ai, and Joshua spent the night among the people (Joshua 8:9).
geography: Ai sits on high ground about 3 km east of Bethel. It occupies a strategic position near Beth-aven, and because it lay where it could control the pass of the central mountain range leading from Jericho to Jerusalem, it was a gateway that had to be passed in the war of the conquest of Canaan.
history: Scholars usually identify the location of Ai with the ruins of et-Tell, but the possibility has also been raised, on the basis of archaeological excavations, that at the end of the Bronze Age the Ai area was an uninhabited ruin. In this connection scholars discuss various hypotheses, such as that the Ai recorded in the Bible refers to another nearby city, or that it reflects a place-name tradition of a particular period.

remark: 1. Located between Riblah in the northeast of Canaan and the Sea of Chinnereth.
introduce: Ain is a place name mentioned in the process of determining the northern boundary line of the land of Canaan, a place located in biblical geography near the northernmost point of the territory of Israel.
biblecontents: When God described the boundary of the land of Canaan to Moses, it is recorded that the northern boundary continues from Ain as far as Hazar-enan (Numbers 34:11).
geography: Ain lies east of Riblah, and as to its specific location, the theory that presumes it to be the region of the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges, northeast of Dan, the source of the Jordan River, is the dominant one.

remark: 2. A Levitical city in Simeon, originally the possession of the tribe of Judah.
introduce: Ain is a town recorded as having been located within the territories of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Simeon in the process of the distribution of land among the tribes of ancient Israel. This name derives from a Hebrew word meaning spring or source.
biblecontents: Ain is mentioned as one of the list of towns that the tribe of Judah received (Joshua 15:32). Afterward it appears again as one of the towns that the tribe of Simeon received as their allotment from the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 19:7). It is also recorded as one of the towns given to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:16). In the passage listing the dwelling places of the descendants of Simeon in the time of King David, Ain is mentioned as one of the five towns that included Rimmon (1 Chronicles 4:32).
geography: Ain is presumed to have been located in the Negev region of southern Judah, and because of its geographical proximity to Rimmon, many scholars also interpret it as the compound place name Ain-Rimmon. Archaeologically, Tel Eiter, Tel Horaf, and others are cited as candidate sites, but discussion continues in scholarship about the exact location.

introduce: Ahava refers to the name of a riverside place where the group led by Ezra gathered for the last time and stayed before departing for Jerusalem at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: To find the returning Levites, Ezra gathered the group by the river that flows to Ahava and camped there for three days (Ezra 8:15). There Ezra proclaimed to the people a fast, so that they would seek from God a smooth journey (Ezra 8:21). Afterward the returning company left the Ahava River and set out for Jerusalem (Ezra 8:31).
