geography: Ahava is presumed to have been located on the route leading from Babylon to the upper Euphrates. Although its exact location has not been clearly identified archaeologically, it is regarded as a settlement located on a canal northwest of Babylon or on a tributary of the Euphrates.
history: Ahava was the place where, during the reign of the Persian emperor Artaxerxes I, the Jews were preparing for the second return from Babylon to Jerusalem. At that time the returning company needed a strategic assembly point in order to be protected from hostile forces, and Ahava was used as a major base where a large number of people could procure supplies and make preparations.

introduce: Ahoah is a place name referring to the home district of the mighty men, the elite troops of King David of ancient Israel. People from this place are recorded as having played key roles in David's military organization.
biblecontents: Eleazar son of Dodo, an Ahohite, fought together with David against the Philistines, and when the people withdrew, he alone remained and struck down the Philistines (2 Samuel 23:9). Zalmon the Ahohite is included in the list of David's thirty mighty men (2 Samuel 23:28). Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite is mentioned as David's first mighty man (1 Chronicles 11:12). Ilai the Ahohite is recorded as one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:29). Eleazar son of Dodo, as the commander of the army for the second month, was in charge of 24,000 men (1 Chronicles 27:4).
geography: The exact location of Ahoah has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but it is presumed to have been located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This is because Ahoah, the ancestor of the Ahohites, is connected with a family of the tribe of Benjamin.
history: Ahoah appears to be a place name derived from Ahoah, a person mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. It can be seen that by the time of David, persons from this place were active as key members of the group of mighty men who solidified David's military base.

introduce: Accad was a city located in the region of ancient Mesopotamia and the center of the Akkadian Empire founded by Sargon the Great. In the Bible it is mentioned as one of the cities included in the dominion of Nimrod.
biblecontents: His kingdom began in Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:10).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the northern or central part of Mesopotamia, the alluvial plain between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Its exact location has not yet been confirmed archaeologically, but it is generally identified with the area near Kish, north of Babylon.
history: Built around the 24th century BC by Sargon the Great, it became the capital of the Akkadian Empire, the world's first centralized empire. This city played a role as a political and economic center that fused Sumerian civilization with Semitic culture, but after the fall of the empire it declined, and its specific location disappeared from history.

introduce: Acco was a town located within the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher during the period of the conquest of Canaan by ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns where the tribe of Asher, having been unable to drive out the native inhabitants of Canaan, came to live together with them (Judges 1:31).
geography: Acco is a port city located in the plain region of the Mediterranean coast, corresponding to the present-day Acre (Akko) area of Israel, and as a strategic point it served as a nodal point of Mediterranean maritime trade and overland traffic.
history: It is a city so old that it appears in Egyptian records from the Bronze Age, and even after the period of the conquest of Canaan, without being fully brought under the control of the tribes of Israel, it remained for a long time within the sphere of influence of Phoenicia and the powers of the Mediterranean coast.

introduce: Ecbatana was one of the major cities of the Persian Empire, the capital of the Median kingdom, and the place where the summer palace of the Persian kings stood.
biblecontents: It is the place where the officials of King Darius found a scroll in the palace at Ecbatana in the province of Media, while searching for the record of King Cyrus's decree permitting the building of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:2).
geography: It is presumed to be the Hamadan area in the Zagros Mountains in northwestern present-day Iran. Because it lay in the highlands and had a cool climate, it had an environment suitable as a summer retreat for the Persian royal family.
history: It was built around the 7th century BC as Ecbatana, the capital of the Median kingdom. After Cyrus II conquered Media around 550 BC, it was used as an important administrative base of the Persian Empire and as a place where treasures were kept. It performed the function of an archive in which royal documents and records were kept.

introduce: Achshaph is one of the towns of northern Canaan recorded in the Bible, a place mentioned in connection with the northern coalition during Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: Jabin king of Hazor sent word to the king of Achshaph and formed the northern coalition (Joshua 11:1). The king of Achshaph is included in the list of the Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:20). Afterward this area is recorded as one of the towns located on the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:25).
geography: Achshaph is generally identified with Tel Keisan, near the Achzib valley in the Galilee region. It belongs to the territory of the tribe of Asher and is situated at a strategic point between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country of Galilee.
history: From the Late Bronze Age through the Iron Age it was an area under the cultural influence of Canaan and Phoenicia. At that time it was included in the sphere of Hazor, the coalition of Canaanite city-states, and it has a political history of having confronted the Israelite army as a core member of the northern coalition in the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan.

remark: 1. A town in the west of Judah.
introduce: Achzib was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah, a place name of the ancient Palestinian region mentioned in the Book of Joshua and the Book of Micah in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: When listing the towns of the land that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot, Joshua included Achzib in that list (Joshua 15:44). Afterward the prophet Micah, in the course of prophesying the judgment of Israel, mentioned that the houses of Achzib would be a deception to the kings of Israel (Micah 1:14).
geography: Achzib is generally presumed to have been located in the Shephelah, the lowland region of Judah, and there is a view in scholarship that identifies it with present-day Tell el-Hesi or its vicinity.
history: In the early Iron Age it had a strong character as a place of political conflict and an economic base between the kingdom of Judah and its neighboring nations, and in particular it reflects the geopolitical situation around the kingdom of Judah during the period when the prophet Micah was active.

remark: 2. A town of the tribe of Asher on the coast of Galilee.
introduce: Achzib is an ancient city-state and port city located on the northern coastal plain of Canaan, mentioned in the Bible in connection with the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Asher.
biblecontents: Joshua cast lots for the tribe of the descendants of Asher, and its boundary reached Tyre and Achzib (Joshua 19:29). Afterward the tribe of Asher was unable to drive out the inhabitants of Achzib, and they came to live among the Canaanites (Judges 1:31).
geography: Achzib is known as present-day Tel Akhziv, and is located about 14 km north of Acco on the Mediterranean coast. This area is a strategic point on the coastal road connecting Beirut and Acco, and is adjacent to the fertile coastal plain.
history: From the Bronze Age it prospered as a major port city under Phoenician influence. Even after the period of the conquest of Canaan, the tribe of Israel was unable to capture it completely, so an independent Phoenician cultural sphere was maintained, and it was an economic base whose existence frequently appears in ancient Near Eastern documents such as Assyrian records.

introduce: Antipatris is a city located in the ancient Palestinian region, a base that appears on the route of the Roman military escort from Jerusalem to Caesarea, as recorded in Acts 23.
biblecontents: The Roman soldiers, as they had been ordered, took Paul by night and brought him to Antipatris (Acts 23:31).
geography: Antipatris lies at the eastern edge of the Plain of Sharon and sits on the main highway from Jerusalem to Caesarea. This city is a place identified with present-day Tel Aphek, and it is a strategic point where one passes from the mountainous region to the coastal plain.
history: Originally called Gebar, this city was rebuilt by Herod the Great, who gave it the name Antipatris in honor of his father Antipater II. In the Herodian period it was developed for military and administrative purposes, and during the period of Roman rule as well it served as an important military stopover between Caesarea and Jerusalem.

introduce: The Arkites refers to a person mentioned as one of the sons of Canaan, and to the tribe or city-state formed by his descendants.
biblecontents: The Arkites are recorded in the genealogy as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17). Chronicles likewise specifies them as one of the sons of Canaan (1 Chronicles 1:15).
geography: The Arkites are identified with the city of Arqa in the ancient Phoenician region. This region is located at Tell Arqa in northern present-day Lebanon, between the Mediterranean coast and the Lebanon mountain range.
history: Arqa is an ancient city that also appears in the Egyptian Amarna letters of the second millennium BC and in Assyrian records. As a trade route and strategic point of the ancient Near East, this region lay under the influence of various civilizations.

introduce: Allammelech is one of the towns included in the territorial boundary of the tribe of Asher recorded in Joshua 19.
biblecontents: Allammelech is included in the list of the boundaries of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:26).
geography: Allammelech is presumed to have been located north of Mount Carmel, in the southern border area of the tribe of Asher, but its exact modern location has not been clearly identified archaeologically. Some propose Tell el-Melik as a candidate site, but geographical confirmation is lacking.

introduce: Ahlab was one of the towns located within the boundary of the land distributed to the tribe of Asher during the period of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, the inhabitants of Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land (Judges 1:31).
geography: It is presumed to have been located in the Mediterranean coastal plain, the territory of the ancient tribe of Asher, but the exact archaeological site has not been definitively identified to date.

introduce: Alvah is the name of one of the chiefs who ruled in the land of Edom, and is one of the chiefs of Edom recorded in the genealogy of Chronicles.
biblecontents: The chiefs of Edom are chief Timna, chief Alvah, and chief Jetheth (1 Chronicles 1:51).
geography: Edom is a region formed around the southeast of the Dead Sea and the Arabah valley, and there is no record concerning the specific town or the boundaries of the territory that Alvah ruled.

introduce: Alexandria is a port city located west of the mouth of the Nile in Egypt, and from the Hellenistic period through the Roman imperial period it served as a core center of commerce, culture, and learning on the Mediterranean coast.
biblecontents: In the synagogue of those called Freedmen, people from Alexandria disputed with Stephen (Acts 6:9). A Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus; he was learned and well versed in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). In the course of Paul being sent as a prisoner to Rome, the centurion found an Alexandrian ship about to sail for Italy (Acts 27:6). Also, when Paul left after staying three months on the island of Malta, he traveled in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at that island (Acts 28:11).
geography: It is a natural port city located on the western edge of the Nile Delta, situated between the Mediterranean Sea and Lake Mareotis. It had an eastern harbor and a western harbor, where large ships could anchor, with the island of Pharos connected by a breakwater.
history: After it was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC, it prospered as the capital of the Ptolemaic dynasty. It was a center of knowledge in which the greatest library of its time was located, and a large Jewish community had formed there. After the Roman Empire took possession of it, its economic importance increased still further as the key grain-shipping base supplying food to Rome.

introduce: Allon-bachuth is the place where Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, was buried, and its name carries the meaning in Hebrew of the oak of weeping.
biblecontents: When Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, she was buried under the oak below Bethel, and therefore that tree was named Allon-bachuth (Genesis 35:8).
geography: It is recorded as being located in the area near Bethel, but its exact site has not been identified by modern archaeology.

introduce: Alush is one of the stages among the places where the children of Israel stayed during the journey of the Exodus, a place passed through after setting out from Dophkah and before going to Rephidim.
biblecontents: The children of Israel set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush, and set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim (Numbers 33:13-14).
geography: The exact location of Alush has not been clearly identified archaeologically, but the dominant theory presumes it to be the Wadi Feiran area in the southern Sinai Peninsula or a plain area nearby.

introduce: Almon is a place name recorded in Joshua 21, a Levitical town that was located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: Almon is a town given as an inheritance to the descendants of Merari, descendants of Levi, within the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18).
geography: Almon is presumed to be the same place name as Alemeth mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:60, and the view that regards it as the present-day Almit area northeast of Jerusalem is dominant.
history: When, after Israel's conquest of the land of Canaan, the land was distributed tribe by tribe, the priests and Levites were allotted towns in which to live within the territories of specific tribes, and Almon was one of them, serving as an administrative and religious base.

introduce: Almon-diblathaim is one of the camping places where the children of Israel stayed during the journey of the Exodus, and is part of the wilderness itinerary recorded in the Book of Numbers.
biblecontents: The children of Israel set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim (Numbers 33:46). Afterward they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim before Nebo (Numbers 33:47).
geography: Almon-diblathaim is presumed to have been located in the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River, and modern geographers identify it as a point northeast of Dibon or near the Arnon valley, but its exact location has not been confirmed archaeologically.

introduce: Alvah is a place name or tribal name mentioned as the name of chief Timna, one of the chiefs of Edom.
biblecontents: These are the names of the chiefs of Edom, according to their clans, their dwelling places, and their names: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth (Genesis 36:40).
geography: It is presumed to have been located in the hill country of Seir in the region of Edom, but its exact archaeological location has not been specified.

introduce: Amphipolis is one of the major cities of the region of Macedonia, a strategic point through which the apostle Paul passed on the route from Philippi toward Thessalonica during his second missionary journey.
biblecontents: The apostle Paul and his companions passed through Philippi, Amphipolis, and Apollonia and arrived at Thessalonica (Acts 17:1).
geography: Amphipolis is located near the mouth where the Strymon River flows into the Aegean Sea, and it sits on the Via Egnatia, the major Roman military and commercial road linking eastern and western Macedonia. The city was formed on a hilly area advantageous for defense, being surrounded on three sides by the river.
history: It was founded as a colony by the Athenians in 437 BC, and afterward developed into an important administrative and military base under the rule of the kingdom of Macedonia and the Roman Empire. In the Roman period it served as the capital of the first district of the four administrative districts into which the region of Macedonia was divided, and as a junction of the Via Egnatia it occupied a key position in transportation.

introduce: Appius was a city of ancient Italy, one of the stopovers located on the Appian Way leading to Rome.
biblecontents: When the apostle Paul, being taken as a prisoner to Rome, passed through that place, the brothers in Rome heard the news of Paul and came out to meet him as far as the Forum of Appius (Acts 28:15).
geography: Appius is a place located at the forty-third mile of the Appian Way, southeast of Rome. This place lay near the Pontine Marshes and served as an important stopover and resting place for ancient travelers.
history: This place was named after Appius Claudius Caecus, the Roman censor who built the Appian Way. At that time it was a market town where commercial transactions were brisk, and it was an important transportation hub where travelers changed carts or made repairs before entering Rome.

introduce: Addan is a place name mentioned as the area where people who could not prove their families or genealogies lived during the return from the Babylonian exile.
biblecontents: There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not show whether their fathers' houses and genealogies belonged to Israel (Ezra 2:59).
geography: It is presumed to have been located within the region of Babylonia, but its specific geographical coordinates or exact present location have not been identified archaeologically.
history: Within the Jewish community returning to Jerusalem under the decree of Cyrus of Persia after the Babylonian exile, it is recorded as one of the settlements where groups who could not clearly establish their places of origin were staying.

introduce: Attalia was a port city located in the Pamphylia region of southern ancient Asia Minor, a place mentioned as the last port of call of the missionary journey during the apostle Paul's first missionary journey.
biblecontents: After the apostle Paul and Barnabas spoke the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, and from there they took a ship and returned to Antioch (Acts 14:25).
geography: It lies in the Antalya region of present-day Turkey, at the mouth of the Cataractes River at the western end of the Pamphylian plain, and so it served as a strategic port for Mediterranean trade.
history: It was founded around the 2nd century BC by King Attalus II Philadelphus of the kingdom of Pergamum, and afterward, under the administrative system of the Roman Empire, it prospered as a major trade center and naval base.

introduce: Addon is a place name appearing in the list of those who returned from the Babylonian exile, or a name referring to the people from that place.
biblecontents: There were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not show whether their fathers' houses or genealogies belonged to Israel (Nehemiah 7:61).
history: It is presumed to be one of the regions or communities included in the list of returnees at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile, but no archaeological evidence for its detailed location or size can be confirmed.

introduce: Assos is an ancient port city located on the western coast of Asia Minor, a place that the apostle Paul passed through during his third missionary journey.
biblecontents: Paul's party set out by ship for Assos, and Paul traveled by land, met them at Assos, took them on board, and left for Mitylene (Acts 20:13-14).
geography: It is located about 30 km south of Troas, and is a port city built on a high, steep hill overlooking the Aegean Sea. Topographically it is divided into a low harbor district on the coast and an upper town on the high ground.
history: It was founded around the 4th century BC by the Aeolians, and developed as a strategic point in the Hellenistic period. It is also known as the place where Aristotle stayed for about three years and ran a school of philosophy. In the Roman period it was one of the major cities of the province of Asia, with active economic and cultural exchange.

remark: The land of Assyria and its inhabitants.
introduce: Assyria was an empire formed around the northern region of ancient Mesopotamia; located in the upper Tigris River region, it was a nation that seized supremacy over the ancient Near East on the strength of its powerful military.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the Hiddekel River, one of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, flows east of Assyria (Genesis 2:14). Nimrod went out from that land into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen (Genesis 10:11). Among the descendants of Dedan, the Asshurites and the Leummites are mentioned (Genesis 25:3). The descendants of Ishmael lived from Havilah to Shur, which leads toward Assyria (Genesis 25:18). It was prophesied that the Kenites would be destroyed and taken captive to Assyria (Numbers 24:22). It is recorded that ships would come from the coast of Kittim and afflict Assyria (Numbers 24:24). When Pul king of Assyria came against Israel, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver, wishing to establish his kingdom firmly (2 Kings 15:19). Menahem exacted that silver from the wealthy men of Israel in order to give it to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 15:20). Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria attacked Israel and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and took the people captive (2 Kings 15:29). Ahaz king of Judah sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, calling himself his servant and asking for deliverance (2 Kings 16:7).
geography: It is a hill country in the middle and upper Tigris River basin, corresponding to the region of present-day northern Iraq. It borders the Anatolian plateau on the north and the Zagros Mountains on the east, and agriculture and trade developed on the basis of its fertile soil and abundant water resources.
history: Beginning in the form of city-states from the third millennium BC, it grew into a great empire through the Middle Assyrian period and the Neo-Assyrian period. In particular, during the 8th and 7th centuries BC it conquered all of Western Asia and carried out strong centralized rule and resettlement policies, and afterward, when Nineveh fell to the allied forces of Babylon and Media in 612 BC, it was destroyed.

remark: The cradle of a civilization centered on the Nile River basin, or a nation
introduce: A nation located in the Nile River basin of the ancient Near East, depicted in the Bible as a major region that the ancestors of Israel chose as a dwelling place or went to in order to escape famine.
biblecontents: When the famine in the land of Canaan became severe, it was the place where Abram went down to live (Genesis 12:10). Abram was concerned that danger would arise for him in Egypt because of the beauty of his wife Sarai (Genesis 12:11, Genesis 12:12). When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw how beautiful Sarai was (Genesis 12:14). Abram went up again from Egypt to Canaan (Genesis 13:1). Abram perceived the region of Egypt as a fertile place like a garden (Genesis 13:10). God promised the boundary of the land to be given to Abram's descendants as extending from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18). Hagar, the maidservant of Sarai, was an Egyptian (Genesis 16:1, Genesis 16:3, Genesis 21:9).
geography: It is a fertile plain region formed around the delta zone and the riverbanks of the lower Nile. Thanks to its abundant water resources, which contrast with the surrounding desert zones, it served as a major granary of the ancient Near East.
history: Egypt in the Bronze Age maintained strong royal authority under the centralized system of the Pharaoh, and it was an international center that offered economic opportunities to immigrants and merchants arriving from outside. At that time it was frequent for nomads from the Asian region to flow into the Nile Delta region to escape drought.

introduce: Zoan is a major city of ancient Egypt and a strategic point, located in the eastern region of the Nile Delta. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly as the center of rule of the Egyptian dynasties or as the setting of historical events connected with ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Through the record that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt, it appears as a reference for comparing the construction times of the two cities (Numbers 13:22).
geography: It is located in the Tanis area in the eastern Nile Delta, and in ancient times it was connected to the Mediterranean Sea through the Pelusiac branch and was used as a base for trade and military affairs. It had the geographical advantage of being able to produce abundant agricultural products on the strength of its fertile soil.
history: It flourished as the capital of the kingdom during the 21st and 22nd Dynasties of Egypt, and in the period of the Hyksos dynasty it was linked to Avaris and served as a center of power in northern Egypt. As a diplomatic center of the ancient Near East, it maintained a close geopolitical relationship with the history of the Hebrew people.

introduce: Aenon is a place name mentioned in the Bible as the place where John the Baptist baptized, and it is a place located near Salim.
biblecontents: John the Baptist baptized at Aenon near Salim because there was much water there, and people kept coming there and were baptized (John 3:23).
geography: Scholars are divided over the view that Aenon was in the region of Samaria west of the Jordan River or in the Decapolis region east of the Jordan River, and it is presumed to have been a terrain with a spring or reservoir rich in water.

introduce: Jagur is a place name mentioned in Joshua 15 in the Old Testament, a town in the border zone with Edom at the southernmost point of the Negev allotted to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Kabzeel, Eder, and Jagur are recorded as towns that approached the Edomite border at the southern end of the tribe of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:21).
geography: Jagur is presumed to have been located in a buffer zone between the southern end of the Dead Sea and the Negev Desert, north of the Wilderness of Zin. It appears to be a desert valley area east of Beersheba or south of Arad, and ancient sites in the vicinity of Tell el-Ghurra or Al-Qusaymah are cited as candidate sites, but the exact location has not yet been specified.
history: It is a town recorded in the process by which the tribe of Judah fixed its southern boundary in the early Iron Age, and it formed the border zone with the people of Edom. It was a settlement that, in a semi-arid zone with little rainfall, was formed around oases and wells and took on the function of herding and of monitoring trade routes.

remark: 1. A town north of Naphtali.
introduce: Janoah was a town located in the northern region of ancient Israel, recorded as one of the places conquered at the time of the Assyrian invasion.
biblecontents: In the time of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria invaded and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and took the people captive and moved them to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29).
geography: Janoah is traditionally presumed to be in the northern Galilee region or adjacent to the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, and in later times it has also been identified with the Yanouh area of southern present-day Lebanon.
history: It is one of the towns that were destroyed or conquered during the military campaign of Tiglath-pileser III, who invaded the northern kingdom of Israel in accordance with the expansion policy of the Assyrian Empire in the mid-8th century BC.

remark: 2. A town between Ephraim and Manasseh.
introduce: Janoah is a place name mentioned in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament as the northern boundary of the tribe of Ephraim, a town that was located in the region of the present-day West Bank of the Jordan River.
biblecontents: The boundary turns from the west to the north around Janoah, reaches Ataroth and Naarah, meets Jericho, and goes out to the Jordan (Joshua 16:6-7).
geography: Janoah is presumed to be located near the eastern slope of the hill country of Ephraim, and it is often identified with the area of Khirbet Yanun, southeast of Nablus, in the present-day area under the jurisdiction of the Palestinian Authority. It lies on a topographical passage by which the territory of the tribe of Ephraim leads to the Jordan Valley.
history: Janoah is also interpreted as the same place name as Yanuamu, which appears in the inscription of Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria, a record outside the Bible. Since it is included in the list of towns that fell during the Assyrian invasion of northern Israel in the mid-8th century BC, it suggests that this region was a military strategic point at that time.

introduce: Janim is one of the towns allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah, a place name included in the list of the towns located in the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: Janim is mentioned as one of the towns of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:53).
geography: Janim is presumed to be a town located in the southern part of the hill country of Judah, and judging from the fact that it is mentioned together with the neighboring towns of Jadim and Dabuvil, it appears to have been situated southwest of Hebron or in the southern hill country. Several theories exist about its present exact location, but it has not been clearly identified archaeologically.

introduce: Jareb is a name appearing in the prophetic book of Hosea in the Bible, portrayed as the one on whom northern Israel relied to seek help in a time of crisis and as an entity that provided the cause of their being judged. In Hebrew etymology it carries the meaning of a contender or an enemy, and it is interpreted as an epithet referring to the king of Assyria, a great power of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to King Jareb, but he cannot cure you or heal your wound (Hosea 5:13). That calf will be carried to Assyria and presented as a gift to King Jareb; Ephraim will be put to shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its own plans (Hosea 10:6).
history: Around the 8th century BC, northern Israel came under political and military pressure because of Assyria's expansionist policy. At that time the kings of northern Israel sought to survive by paying enormous tribute to Assyria, and the prophet Hosea warned that such diplomatic dependence was an act of apostasy that did not trust God and a vain scheme that would lead in the end to destruction. Here Jareb is used as a historical title referring to the ruler of Assyria to whom Israel, mobilizing its economic wealth, sent envoys to ask for aid.

remark: 1. A town of Judah, at first the possession of the Amorites.
introduce: Jarmuth is one of the towns of ancient Canaan, a locality that belonged to the allied forces of the king of Jerusalem at the time of Joshua's wars of conquest. It was allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah, and it is recorded as a town in which the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile.
biblecontents: Piram, king of Jarmuth, on hearing the news that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, formed an alliance with the king of Jerusalem to attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:3). Five kings of the Amorites, including the king of Jarmuth, went up to attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:5). Afterward they hid in a cave, were captured by Joshua, and were put to death (Joshua 10:23). The king of Jarmuth is included in the list of the kings of Canaan conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:10). Jarmuth is mentioned in the Shephelah region in the list of towns distributed to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:35). After the Babylonian exile it appears again as one of the dwelling places of the descendants of Judah who settled in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:29).
geography: Jarmuth is identified with the present-day Tel Yarmuth. It is located southwest of Beth-shemesh and lies in the Shephelah region, the plain zone of Judah. Being located on strategically important high ground, it had the topographical feature of making it easy to survey the surrounding area.
history: It took the form of a city-state that flourished in the Bronze Age and was at that time one of the powerful towns of Canaan. Through the Egyptian Amarna letters and other ancient Near Eastern records, it reflects the picture of the time in which the city-states within the region of Canaan formed political alliances and expanded their power. After the war of conquest it was incorporated into the administrative district of the tribe of Judah and administered, and from the records after the exile it can be seen that it continued to be maintained as a town in which Jews lived.

remark: 2. A Levitical city within Issachar.
introduce: Jarmuth is a town mentioned in the period of the conquest of Canaan and in the subsequent process of the distribution of land among the tribes of Israel, a town of the Levites located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar.
biblecontents: Jarmuth belonged to the territory of the tribe of Issachar, and is recorded as one of the towns allotted to the Gershonites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:29).
geography: Jarmuth is presumed to be located in a plain area near the Valley of Jezreel, and its exact present location is disputed archaeologically, but it is also identified with Tell er-Rameh and the like.

remark: 1. (Place) Short for Jabesh-gilead.
introduce: Jabesh (Jabesh-gilead) was a town of ancient Israel located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, mentioned in 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles as the setting of major events.
biblecontents: Nahash the Ammonite came up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead, and for this reason the elders of Jabesh wished to make a covenant with Nahash (1 Samuel 11:1). The elders of Jabesh asked Saul for rescue by sending messengers, and had messengers sent throughout all the territory of Israel to seek help (1 Samuel 11:3). Saul, coming from the field behind his oxen, heard the news about the men of Jabesh and summoned Israel (1 Samuel 11:5). After the victory won with Saul's help, the men of Jabesh heard the news that they would be delivered tomorrow when the sun was hot (1 Samuel 11:9). The men of Jabesh gave the Ammonites the false message that they would surrender tomorrow, but the Ammonite army was wiped out by Saul's forces (1 Samuel 11:10). After Saul died, all the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead heard at the battle of Gilboa that the bodies of Saul and his sons were hung on the wall, and set out (1 Samuel 31:12). The valiant men of Jabesh took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, burned them, and buried their bones under a tree (1 Samuel 31:13). This is described in the same way in the Chronicles account as well (1 Chronicles 10:12).
geography: Jabesh-gilead was a locality east of the Jordan River, near the Wadi Yabis valley, and a strategic point commanding a view over the Jordan Valley. It is presumed to be Tell el-Muqdeh (Tell el-Muqde) or its vicinity, and it was an area where agriculture was carried on, based on fertile soil and abundant water resources.
history: Jabesh-gilead is the place where, by delivering this town from the Ammonite invasion in the early part of his reign, King Saul had his leadership recognized by the early Israelite coalition, which became a decisive turning point. Moreover, when Saul fell in battle against the Philistines, the inhabitants of Jabesh recovered his body and performed the burial, proving their loyalty to the king who had saved them; this is regarded as a historical example showing an exceptionally strong bond in the tribal confederation society of that time.

remark: 2. (Place) A town of Judah.
introduce: Jabez is a place name appearing in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, known as a village where scribes lived.
biblecontents: The families of scribes who lived at Jabez were the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab (1 Chronicles 2:55)
geography: The exact location of Jabez has not been identified archaeologically at present. It is, however, presumed to have been a village in the hill country of Judah or within the sphere of influence of the tribe of Judah, and is mentioned as a center of activity of later scribes.
history: Jabez was originally a place where scribes with blood or social ties to the Kenite clan settled. This is an example showing that, within the social structure of the tribe of Judah at that time, particular occupational groups or outside tribes were incorporated while forming their own local communities.

introduce: Jabesh-gilead was a town located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, and it appears as a major setting in events connected with the tribe of Benjamin at the end of the period of the Judges.
biblecontents: When the children of Israel assembled at Mizpah in the general assembly of Israel to punish the tribe of Benjamin, it was found that the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead had not taken part (Judges 21:8). So the congregation of Israel ordered twelve thousand warriors to go to Jabesh-gilead and destroy its inhabitants (Judges 21:9). When they came to Jabesh-gilead, they struck the inhabitants with the edge of the sword and conquered the town (Judges 21:10). From there they took four hundred young virgins captive and brought them to Shiloh (Judges 21:12), and afterward gave them as wives to the remaining men of the tribe of Benjamin (Judges 21:14).
geography: Jabesh-gilead was a town located near the Wadi Yabis valley east of the Jordan River, and topographically it served as a crossroads connecting the Gilead highlands with the Jordan Valley.

introduce: Jabneh is a place name, a strategic point located on the coastal plain of ancient Palestine, whose importance is confirmed through its biblical background and archaeological remains. In Hebrew it is also called Jabneel, and it lies adjacent to the territory of the Philistines and the border of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: Uzziah king of Judah went out and waged war against the Philistines, and broke down the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod, and built towns in the territory of Ashdod and among the Philistines (2 Chronicles 26:6).
geography: Jabneh is located in the Shephelah plain region along the Mediterranean coast, and is identified with the present-day Tel Yavne area in Israel. Situated south of the Yarkon River, it has the topographical advantage of serving as a nodal point of transportation linking the coastal road with the interior.
history: In the early Iron Age it was one of the principal strongholds of the Philistines, but it is recorded that it was brought under the sphere of influence of Judah through the military campaign of King Uzziah. Afterward, through the Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman periods, it was a city continuously inhabited as an important administrative and religious center.

remark: An unidentified place, presumed to be the same as Beth-bethlet.
introduce: Japhlet is a place name mentioned in the Book of Joshua, a place connected with the western boundary of the tribe of Ephraim. Its exact present location has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it appears in the course of describing the geographical divisions at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Japhlet is mentioned in describing the boundary of the descendants of Ephraim, and it is recorded that the boundary goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites and reaches as far as lower Beth-horon and Gezer (Joshua 16:3).
geography: The specific location of Japhlet is not known, but from the context it is presumed to be the area between Beth-horon and Gezer. This signifies the southwestern boundary area of the tribe of Ephraim and a buffer zone between the coastal plain and the hill country.

introduce: Jahzah is a place name in the land of Moab appearing in the biblical record, a place connected with the allotment of territory to the tribes of ancient Israel and with the prophecy of judgment against Moab.
biblecontents: Jahzah is recorded as one of the towns distributed as territory to the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan, and as a town given to the descendants of Merari, who were Levites (1 Chronicles 6:78). Also, the prophet Jeremiah, in proclaiming judgment against Moab, prophesied that judgment would come upon Jahzah, a town in the plain (Jeremiah 48:21).
geography: Jahzah is presumed to be located in the Moabite plateau region east of the Jordan River, and is generally classified as a town belonging to the plain region north of the Arnon valley. The view that it was near the plain of Medeba is predominant regarding its specific location, but it has not been clearly established archaeologically.
history: Jahzah was historically located in an area where territorial disputes between Israel and Moab were frequent. It was mentioned at first as a town of the tribe of Reuben, but in later times it is confirmed through the inscription of Mesha king of Moab and the prophecy of Jeremiah that it was under Moabite control, which shows the political instability of this region at that time and the frequent changes of territory.

remark: A town of Gilead, taken from the Amorites and allotted to the tribe of Gad.
introduce: Jazer was a town located in the region east of the Jordan; it was at first the territory of the Amorites, but afterward it was conquered by the tribes of Israel and became a dwelling place of the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: Moses had Jazer spied out and captured its villages (Numbers 21:32). Jazer is mentioned as one of the inheritances of the descendants of Gad and is described as land suitable for raising livestock (Numbers 32:1, 32:3). The tribe of Gad built Jazer (Numbers 32:35), and it later became a town allotted to the Levites, the descendants of Merari (Joshua 21:39, 1 Chronicles 6:81). At the time of Joshua's conquest, Jazer was classified as part of the territory reaching to half of the land of the Ammonites (Joshua 13:25). In the time of David, Joab and the commanders of the army, who were carrying out the census, came to Jazer and encamped (2 Samuel 24:5). The prophet Isaiah lamented the withering of the vines of Jazer and mentioned this area in connection with the destruction of Moab (Isaiah 16:8).
geography: Jazer is generally presumed to be in the southern part of the Gilead region east of the Jordan River, and appears to have been located north or northwest of Heshbon. As for its specific location, the view that it is Khirbet Sar (Khirbet Sar) in the territory of present-day Jordan or its vicinity has been raised in scholarship.
history: It originally belonged to the domain ruled by Sihon king of the Amorites, but after Israel's war of conquest it was incorporated as the inheritance of the tribe of Gad. Because of its geographical character it was adjacent to the border zone between Ammon and Moab, and it was a strategic point continually exposed to territorial disputes and changes in spheres of influence with the surrounding nations.

introduce: In the Bible, Jair is used chiefly as a name referring to a descendant of the tribe of Manasseh, or to the towns of the Gilead region that he conquered and ruled. In 2 Samuel 20:26, Ira the Jairite is mentioned as a minister of David.
biblecontents: Ira the Jairite became a minister of David (2 Samuel 20:26). According to other records of the Old Testament, Jair was a man of the tribe of Manasseh who captured the towns of Gilead and called them Havvoth-jair (Numbers 32:41, Deuteronomy 3:14).
geography: The region of Jair is located in the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River. According to biblical geographical information, this region is adjacent to the district of Argob, which had been the territory of Og king of Bashan, and is described as an area encompassing a wide range of towns east of the Jordan.
history: In the course of Israel's conquest east of the Jordan, after Jair son of Manasseh conquered the towns of the Amorites, the name of that place came to be given in connection with Jair. Ira the Jairite, mentioned in 2 Samuel 20:26, is presumed to have been a person from the region having this geographical origin, and signifies an official who played an important role in the administrative organization of the early Davidic dynasty.

introduce: Jahaz was a town located north of the Arnon River in the region east of the Jordan, and it is the place where Sihon king of the Amorites fought a battle against the Israelites on their way to Canaan.
biblecontents: Israel tried to pass through the territory of Sihon king of the Amorites, but Sihon refused and came out as far as Jahaz and made war against Israel (Numbers 21:23). Deuteronomy likewise records that Sihon fought against Israel at Jahaz (Deuteronomy 2:32). Afterward this land was conquered and distributed to the tribe of Reuben as one of its towns (Joshua 13:18), and it was designated as one of the Levite towns given to the descendants of Merari, of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:36). In Judges, it is mentioned as the region where Israel defeated Sihon, when Jephthah confronted the Ammonites (Judges 11:20). In the prophetic books of Isaiah and Jeremiah, this town is described as belonging to Moab, and in connection with the destruction of Moab the sound of crying at Jahaz is mentioned (Isaiah 15:4, Jeremiah 48:34).
geography: Jahaz is located on the highland north of the Arnon River. There are several views on its exact location, but archaeologically the predominant opinion presumes it to be Khirbet el-Mudeiyine (Khirbet el-Mudei), southeast of Madaba, or a site in its vicinity. This area, as a strategic point of the highlands east of the Jordan, served as a passage connecting with the plain.
history: Jahaz was historically a place that became the object of territorial disputes among Israel, the Amorites, and Moab. At first it was under the rule of Sihon king of the Amorites, but after Israel's conquest it became the territory of the tribe of Reuben. Afterward, whenever the influence of the kingdom of Israel weakened or fluctuated, Moab appears to have occupied it again or exercised influence over it, and the Mesha Stele records that Mesha king of Moab conquered Jahaz and incorporated it into his own territory.

introduce: Jalam is a person recorded in Genesis 36 as one of the chiefs of Edom, and his name was also used as a particular place name.
biblecontents: Jalam was a son born to Esau's wife Oholibamah, a person included in the list of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:18).

remark: 1. A town southwest of Judah.
introduce: Jabneel is a place name in the region of ancient Palestine, a town located on the boundary line forming the northern boundary point of the tribe of Judah in the time of Joshua.
biblecontents: In the description of the northern boundary of the inheritance of the descendants of Judah, it is said that from the northern slope of Ekron the boundary passes Shikkeron, reaches Mount Baalah, extends to Jabneel, and ends at the sea (Joshua 15:11).
geography: Jabneel is presumed to be Tel Yavne, located in the coastal plain region of the Mediterranean in present-day Israel, which is northwest of Ekron and an important strategic point of the coastal plain.
history: In later history it was called Jabneh (Jabne), and there is a record that around the 8th century BC Uzziah king of Judah broke down its wall in the war against the Philistines (2 Chronicles 26:6).

remark: 2. A town in the border region of Naphtali.
introduce: Jabneel is a town located in the border region allotted to the tribe of Naphtali among the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the points of the boundary of the inheritance of the descendants of Naphtali, and the boundary passes from Heleph and the great tree of Zaanannim through Adami-nekeb and Jabneel to Lakkum (Joshua 19:33).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the southwest or northwest region of the Sea of Galilee, but the specific archaeological site and place name are unclear.

introduce: The Jabbok River is a major stream flowing through the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan River, a wadi landform well known in biblical history as a geographical boundary and as the place where Jacob wrestled with an angel.
biblecontents: Jacob sent his family ahead and had them cross the ford of the Jabbok, and then, left alone, wrestled with a man (Genesis 32:22). Israel struck Sihon king of the Amorites and occupied his land, and the boundary of that territory was from the Arnon to the Jabbok (Numbers 21:24). The land of the Ammonites could not be approached because of its strong border, but they did not draw near the land along the banks of the Jabbok (Deuteronomy 2:37). The land distributed to the tribe of Reuben and the tribe of Gad was the region extending from the valley of the Arnon to the Jabbok River (Deuteronomy 3:16). The conquered territory east of the Jordan reached from the valley of the Arnon to the Jabbok River (Joshua 12:2). The king of the Ammonites claimed that when Israel came up out of Egypt, they had taken his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan (Judges 11:13). The Ammonite king also accused Israel of having seized the territory from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan (Judges 11:22).
geography: The Jabbok River is known as the Wadi Zarqa, located in present-day Jordan, and it rises in the hill country of Gilead, flows westward, and joins the Jordan River. The volume of water in this river varies greatly with the season, and in ancient times it served as a natural boundary line dividing Gilead into north and south.
history: In the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, the Jabbok basin was a buffer zone where territorial disputes among the Amorite kingdom, Ammon, and the tribes of Israel frequently occurred. This region was adjacent to a major trade route passing through the highlands east of the Jordan and so was highly valued economically and militarily, and the biblical record reflects the historical conflict over holding this geographical strategic point.

introduce: Jattir was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, and later one of the dwelling places allotted to the Levites.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the towns located in the hill country of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:48). Afterward it was allotted as a dwelling place to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:14), and 1 Chronicles 6:57 likewise mentions it as a town of the Kohathites. After David recovered what the Amalekites had plundered, when he sent spoils to the elders of Judah, Jattir was also included among the beneficiary localities (1 Samuel 30:27).
geography: It is presumed to be Tel es-Sera (Khirbet Attir), about 19 km southwest of Hebron. Situated in the border zone between the hill country of Judah and the Negev Desert, topographically it corresponds to hilly terrain, and has the character of a buffer zone where farming and grazing are possible.
history: It was a place where Israelite settlers lived from the early Iron Age, and in the period of the kingdom of Judah it served as a base for border defense and administration. In the time of David, it can be confirmed through 1 Samuel 30:27 that it functioned as a point where the central authority and the network of local administration were connected.

introduce: The Sheep Gate was a gate located in the northern section of the wall of Jerusalem, known as the entrance used to bring into the city the sheep that were to be used for temple sacrifices. It is the first gate mentioned in the project of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah.
biblecontents: Eliashib the high priest and his brothers the priests built the Sheep Gate, consecrated it, and set up its doors (Nehemiah 3:1). From the upper chamber of the corner to the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and the merchants each built separate sections (Nehemiah 3:32). Passing the Gate of Ephraim, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred, they reached the Sheep Gate and stopped at the Gate of the Guard (Nehemiah 12:39).
geography: The Sheep Gate is presumed to have been located near the northeast corner of the wall of Jerusalem. Being close to the temple area, it had the topographical advantage of being suitable for moving the livestock to be used as offerings quickly to the temple. Modern archaeological research holds that this gate was probably located near the Pool of Bethesda.
history: After the Babylonian exile, in the time of Artaxerxes king of Persia, when Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem and rebuilt the fallen wall, it was one of the gates repaired first. From the fact that the high priest himself took part in the construction and the consecration ceremony, we can see that its symbolism and practical importance as the entrance toward the temple, the religious center, were very great.

introduce: The Fish Gate was the name of a gate located in the northern section of the wall of ancient Jerusalem, and it was one of the main commercial and logistics centers of Jerusalem at that time.
biblecontents: The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate, laid its beams, set up its doors, and fitted its bolts and bars (Nehemiah 3:3). Over the Gate of Ephraim, past the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate, and they stopped at the Gate of the Guard (Nehemiah 12:39). On that day a cry will go up from the Fish Gate, a wail from the Second District, and a loud crashing from the hills (Zephaniah 1:10).
geography: The Fish Gate stood on the northern boundary of the wall of Jerusalem, and by its geographical position it was a passage through which merchants carrying fish caught on the Mediterranean coast or at the Sea of Galilee transported them to the market of Jerusalem.
history: In the project of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah after the Babylonian exile, it was rebuilt as one of the important defensive strongholds, and according to the biblical record the vicinity of this gate reflects the character of a commercial district where the fish trade was brisk.

introduce: En-gannim was a town located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar at the time of the allotment among the tribes of ancient Israel. It is a place recorded as one of the dwelling places for the Levites.
biblecontents: As one of the towns located within the territory of the tribe of Issachar, it is mentioned as one of the four towns given to the Levites, the descendants of Gershon (Joshua 21:29).
geography: The exact location continues to be debated among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be near the Valley of Jezreel, the territory of the tribe of Issachar, or in the southern Galilee region.

introduce: En-gannim is one of the towns of the tribe of Issachar in Israel appearing in the Book of Joshua of the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Lots were cast for the tribe of the descendants of Issachar according to their families, and the boundary of their inheritance was Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Joshua 19:19-21)
geography: Scholarship presumes that it has come down to the present through irregular changes of the place name, to the area of present-day Jenin. Located on the southeastern edge of the Valley of Jezreel, it is topographically a strategic point where the plain and the hill country meet.

remark: The northernmost of the five major cities of the Philistines.
introduce: Ekron was a strategic point located at the northernmost of the five city-states of the ancient Philistines, and it is a place name where Israel frequently clashed or had dealings from the time of the conquest of Canaan to the early monarchy.
biblecontents: Ekron was originally one of the five cities ruled by the rulers of the Philistines (Joshua 13:3). In the process of the conquest of Canaan it was allotted as part of the boundary of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:11), but at first it was also mentioned as one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:43). The tribe of Judah tried to conquer Ekron (Joshua 15:45, 15:46), but in fact until the early period of the Judges it was not completely taken and remained under the sphere of Philistine power (Judges 1:18). Later, when the Philistines seized the ark of the covenant, it was moved to Ekron, and the inhabitants there, fearing disaster, sent the ark back to Israel (1 Samuel 5:10, 6:16, 6:17). By the time of Samuel, the towns of Israel that the Philistines had seized were recovered between Ekron and Gath (1 Samuel 7:14).
geography: Ekron is identified with Tel Miqne in present-day Israel. Geographically it was located at the boundary point where the Shephelah plain and the Philistine coastal plain meet, and it served as a crossroads linking the hill country of Judah with the coastal plain. This region had fertile soil favorable to agriculture.
history: A city formed from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age; in the Iron Age in particular, large-scale olive oil production facilities have been discovered, showing that it was an economic center at the time. Like the other cities of the Philistines, records of invasion by the neighboring great power Assyria are confirmed in inscriptions and elsewhere, and geopolitically it was both a buffer zone between Israel and the Philistines and a major area of conflict.

introduce: Eglaim is one of the place names of Moab appearing in the book of Isaiah in the Old Testament, a region mentioned in connection with the destruction of Moab.
biblecontents: The cry of Moab has gone around the boundary of its territory, its wailing reaches Eglaim, and its crying reaches Beer-elim (Isaiah 15:8)
geography: The exact location of Eglaim has not been established archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be a settlement in the plain of Moab in the region east of the Dead Sea or in its vicinity. In the biblical text, Eglaim appears together with Beer-elim as a region designating the southern boundary of Moab or its vicinity.
history: In Isaiah 15, Eglaim is described as a major point to which the news of the judgment coming upon Moab spreads. This is interpreted as a literary and historical expression for emphasizing, by listing geographical names, the political and military crisis that Moab was experiencing at that time.

introduce: Eglath is a place name located in the ancient land of Moab, a place appearing in the context of describing the judgment coming upon Moab in the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah.
biblecontents: In describing the suffering of Moab, the prophet Isaiah likened Eglath to a third heifer and mentioned that the fugitives of Moab would flee as far as this place (Isaiah 15:5).
geography: The exact location of Eglath has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is presumed to have been located in the southern or south-central region of Moab. The Hebrew place name Eglath-shelishiyah contains the meaning "third heifer," and it appears to express figuratively a topographical feature or regional scale.
history: Moab was a nation located to the southeast of Israel, and throughout the Old Testament period it experienced frequent conflicts and wars with Israel. The prophecy of Isaiah 15 declares judgment on Moab, and it is set against the background of the struggles for supremacy among the surrounding great powers of that time and the political instability of Moab.

introduce: Eglath-shelishiyah is a place name mentioned when the book of Jeremiah prophesies judgment against Moab, an ancient town about whose exact location and character various views exist among scholars.
biblecontents: The cry of Heshbon and Elealeh is heard as far as Jahaz; from Zoar to Eglath-shelishiyah and Horonaim they have raised their voice, for the waters of Nimrim too have become desolate (Jeremiah 48:34)
geography: It is presumed to be located within the region of Moab, but it cannot be clearly connected with a modern place name. There is a view that interprets the meaning of the name in connection with a young heifer, but archaeological grounds for specifying geographical coordinates are lacking.

introduce: Enaim is a place name located in the region of Canaan, appearing in Genesis 38 as the place where Tamar set out to meet her father-in-law Judah. This place name carries the Hebrew meaning "springs."
biblecontents: Tamar took off her widow's garments, covered herself with a veil, and sat at the gate of Enaim, because Shelah had grown up and she had not been given to him as a wife (Genesis 38:14). Afterward, Judah asked the men of Enaim, in order to look for a prostitute, where the prostitute who had been there was, but they answered that there had been no prostitute in that place (Genesis 38:21).
geography: Enaim is presumed to be a town located within the territory of the tribe of Judah, and its specific location is mentioned as a roadside spot near Timnah. Scholars identify it as a place on the road between Timnah and Adullam.

introduce: Enam was a town included in the territory of the tribe of Judah in the region of ancient Palestine, a place name listed and mentioned in Joshua 15:34 as an inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is recorded in Joshua 15:34 as one of the list of towns distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:34).
geography: Enam is presumed to be located in the hill country of Judah or in the nearby Shephelah plain region, but its specific modern location has not been clearly established archaeologically. Some also identify its location in connection with neighboring towns such as Tappuah or Jarmuth, but there is no confirmed site.

introduce: En-eglaim is a place name appearing in the book of Ezekiel in the Old Testament, a region mentioned as one of the places where fishermen will spread their nets in the restored land of Israel.
biblecontents: It is recorded that when the water flowing out of the temple that Ezekiel saw in a vision flows into the Dead Sea and makes the sea water fresh, there will be places for spreading nets along its shore from En-gedi to En-eglaim (Ezekiel 47:10).
geography: The exact location of En-eglaim is presumed to be on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and it is regarded as an area adjacent to and north of En-gedi. Modern archaeological surveys point to Ain Feshkha on the western shore of the Dead Sea or its vicinity as a strong candidate.

remark: A city built by Cain, named after his son.
introduce: Enoch is, according to the biblical record, the name of the first city built in the history of humankind. This place name, given by Cain, is mentioned in the Bible as an early settlement without a description of its specific location.
biblecontents: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he built a city, and called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch (Genesis 4:17).
history: Seen in the early process of urban formation in the Mesopotamian civilizational sphere, this is interpreted as an early form of dwelling place symbolizing the archaeological change from nomadic life to settled life. However, within the biblical text there is no additional record of specific geographical information or historical dating regarding this place.

introduce: En-rogel is known as an ancient spring located southeast of the wall of Jerusalem, at the point where the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley meet. This place appears in the biblical record as a strategic point and as the setting of political events.
biblecontents: It is the place where Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited, at the time of Absalom's rebellion, to convey secretly to David the situation inside the city of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 17:17). It is also mentioned as the place where Adonijah, in order to make himself king, invited David's other sons and all the men of Judah, and slaughtered oxen, sheep, and fattened calves and offered sacrifices (1 Kings 1:9).
geography: En-rogel is presumed to be Bir Ayyub (Bir Eyyub) of today, southeast of ancient Jerusalem. It is the confluence point where the Kidron Valley, the Hinnom Valley, and the Valley of Rephaim meet, a place located on topographically low ground and having abundant water sources.
history: En-rogel was used as one of the reference points in fixing the boundaries of ancient Jerusalem. From the fact that this place is mentioned in Joshua 15:7 and 18:16 when explaining the boundary between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, we can see that it played an important role as a geographical reference point and boundary marker of the area around Jerusalem at that time.

introduce: En-rimmon was a town located in the southern region of the ancient kingdom of Judah, and one of the places where the returned exiles lived in the time of Nehemiah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:29).
geography: It is presumed to be a region north of Beersheba, and is generally regarded as the same place as Ain-Rimmon. It is situated in the hilly country of the southern Negev, near the border area between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Simeon.
history: Originally, in the time of Joshua, it was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah, but afterward it was included in the territory of the tribe of Simeon. Historically it was one of the main strongholds of southern Judah, and after the exile, as the community was rebuilt, Jews settled there again and kept its name alive.

remark: 1. A town of the tribe of Simeon.
introduce: Etam is a person or place name appearing in 1 Chronicles 4:3, a name mentioned in connection with the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: The sons of Etam were Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, and the name of their brother-in-law was Hazzelelponi (1 Chronicles 4:3)

remark: 2. A town of Judah rebuilt by King Rehoboam.
introduce: Etam is a fortress town in the hill country of the tribe of Judah recorded in 2 Chronicles 11, a city that Rehoboam son of Solomon built for the defense of southern Judah.
biblecontents: Rehoboam built fortified cities in Judah, namely Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa (2 Chronicles 11:6).
geography: It is identified with Khirbet el-Khokh and Ein Atan, located about 10 km south of Jerusalem and southwest of Bethlehem, near Solomon's Pools.
history: It was one of the core fortress networks that King Rehoboam constructed at the end of the 10th century BC, just after the division of the united kingdom, in preparation for the invasion of Shishak of Egypt and the attack of northern Israel.

remark: 3. The rocky region west of Judah.
introduce: Etam is a rugged zone of rocky cliffs within the territory of the tribe of Judah appearing in Judges 15, the place where the judge Samson hid after defeating the Philistines.
biblecontents: Samson struck the Philistines with a great slaughter, then went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam (Judges 15:8). Three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, wishing to bind Samson and hand him over to the Philistines (Judges 15:11).
geography: It is a rugged limestone gorge zone in the upper part of the Sorek Valley where the hill country of Judah meets the Shephelah, and it is presumed to be the cave of Araq Ismain, near present-day Beit Atab.
history: It was a base for the guerrilla activity of Samson, of the tribe of Dan, who resisted the Philistine oppression in the early Iron Age at the beginning of the period of the Judges, and it is a site showing the military tension between the tribe of Judah and the Philistines at that time.

remark: 4. The second place where the Israelites stayed after the Exodus.
introduce: Etham is the border zone at the entrance of the wilderness where the children of Israel encamped after setting out from Rameses in Egypt and passing through Succoth.
biblecontents: They left Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness (Exodus 13:20). They left Succoth and encamped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness (Numbers 33:6).
geography: It is identified with the border zone of the wilderness around Lake Timsah (the Crocodile Lake) near Ismailia, at the eastern end of the Wadi Tumilat, east of the Nile Delta.
history: It was a gateway zone facing the border defense line (the Shur fortress wall) built to defend the northeastern frontier in the period of the New Kingdom of ancient Egypt.

remark: 1. A large fortified town of Og king of Bashan.
introduce: Edrei was a core town of the region of Bashan and a strategic point of the ancient Near East, a place mentioned in the biblical record as the capital of Og king of Bashan.
biblecontents: The Israelites advanced to Edrei to wage war with Og king of Bashan, and there they defeated Og and his people and took possession of their land (Numbers 21:33). Og king of Bashan was a king who lived and ruled in Ashtaroth and Edrei (Deuteronomy 1:4, Joshua 13:12). Moses recorded Edrei as one of the towns of Bashan conquered by Israel (Deuteronomy 3:1), and it was included as part of the territory distributed to the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 3:10, Joshua 13:31). The Bible also describes Edrei as part of the domain of Og, who, as a remnant of the Rephaim, lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei (Joshua 12:4).
geography: Edrei, presumed to be in the area of Daraa in present-day Jordan, is located on a hilly zone called Tell Edhra. This region sits on the fertile Hauran plateau and served as a crossroads of traffic and logistics connecting the surrounding plain with Damascus to the north. Topographically it occupies higher ground than its surroundings, and so has an environment favorable for defense against external attack.
history: Edrei is known as a place where a settled community existed from the Bronze Age. During the reign of Og king of Bashan it functioned as one of the political centers of the kingdom of Bashan. After Israel's conquest it was incorporated into the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh, and afterward it also became an area of territorial dispute between the kingdom of Aram and Israel. In the New Testament period, under the Roman provincial system, it was called by the name Adraa and maintained its urban function continuously.

remark: 2. A town of the tribe of Naphtali.
introduce: Edrei is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, a place recorded as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Naphtali at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Lots were cast for the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali according to their families, and their inheritance was Adamah, Ramah, Hazor, Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor, Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh, nineteen towns with their villages (Joshua 19:37)
geography: Edrei is presumed to have been located north of the Sea of Galilee within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, but the specific archaeological site is at present not clearly identified. It is geographically distinct from the other Edrei, which was the capital of Og king of Bashan.

introduce: Ethiopia as mentioned in the Bible refers to the ancient kingdom of Kush, distinct from the present-day East African nation, and means a political entity formed chiefly around the upper Nile region.
biblecontents: An Ethiopian eunuch, an official in charge of the entire treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning, met Philip, heard the gospel, and was baptized (Acts 8:27).
geography: The Ethiopia that the Bible refers to is a region south of Egypt, including Nubia and the area of the kingdom of Kush in what is now northern Sudan, and it has the geographical character of having formed along the Nile.
history: Ethiopia at that time is known as the kingdom of Kush, which had Meroe as its capital, and the name Candace was used not as a proper noun but as a title for the queens who ruled this kingdom.

introduce: Erech was a major city-state located in the southern region of ancient Mesopotamia, a place mentioned in Genesis as one of the domains ruled by Nimrod.
biblecontents: The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:10).
geography: Erech corresponds to the Warka area in southern present-day Iraq, and is located on the alluvial plain of the lower Euphrates River.
history: Erech is one of the centers of Sumerian civilization, and is also well known by the name Uruk; from the Early Dynastic period it played an important role as a political, economic, and religious center of Mesopotamian civilization.

introduce: Emek-keziz is a place name mentioned in the Hebrew Bible as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. In the Korean Revised Version it is written without a space, as Emek-keziz, and it is a region included within the inheritance boundary of the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: The inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin received according to their families was Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, and so on (Joshua 18:21).
geography: Emek-keziz was located within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, but its specific modern geographical location has not been clearly established archaeologically. By etymology, "emek" means a valley, and "keziz" is presumed to indicate a particular place name or a topographical feature, but there is as yet no agreed view in archaeological circles.

introduce: Emim is the name of an ancient race of giants recorded as having lived in the land of Moab, and it also refers to the region where they lived. They are described as a great, numerous, and strong people like the descendants of Anak.
biblecontents: Like the Anakites, they were called Rephaim, but the Moabites called them Emites (Deuteronomy 2:11).
geography: The region of Moab is a highland east of the Dead Sea, extending from the valley of the Arnon in the north to the valley of the Zered in the south. The Emites are presumed to have lived on the eastern and central highlands of this land.
history: The Emites were a branch of the Rephaim, the indigenous group that had lived in the Transjordan region before the Israelites entered Canaan. Afterward the Moabites, descendants of Lot, drove them out and took possession of the land and settled there.

introduce: Ephah is a name referring to a tribe, or its region, that existed in the ancient Near East, and in the Bible it is mentioned chiefly as a people connected with Midian.
biblecontents: In the book of Isaiah, the people of Ephah appear in a prophetic description in which they come bringing gold and frankincense and proclaim the praises of the LORD (Isaiah 60:6). Also, in Genesis, Ephah is recorded as a son of Midian, born to Abraham and his concubine Keturah, which explains the origin of the people (Genesis 25:4).
geography: Ephah is generally presumed to have lived in the northwestern region of the Arabian Peninsula. Judging from ancient Assyrian records, it is known as the dwelling place of a nomadic people who moved along the caravan routes located in the desert zone and carried on trade.
history: Historically, Ephah was a tribe responsible for trade in northern Arabia, and its name is found in the inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III and Sargon II of Assyria around the 8th century BC. They were major participants in the spice trade by camel at that time, and appear to have held an important position in the major commercial networks of the Middle East.

remark: A rocky mountain in Ephraim.
introduce: Ebal is a mountain located in the Samaria region of central Canaan, a place name defined in the Bible as the place for proclaiming curses.
biblecontents: After the people of Israel crossed the Jordan River, a command was given to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 11:29). Moses commanded the people of Israel to set up large stones on Mount Ebal, plaster them with lime, write on them the words of the law, and build an altar (Deuteronomy 27:4). The tribes designated to stand on Mount Ebal and proclaim the curse were Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali (Deuteronomy 27:13). In accordance with the command of Moses, Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel (Joshua 8:30). The elders, officers, and judges of Israel stood on both sides of the ark of the covenant, on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and read aloud the blessings and curses of the law (Joshua 8:33).
geography: Mount Ebal is a limestone mountain about 940 meters above sea level, located on the north side of the Shechem valley. Its terrain is somewhat higher and more barren than that of Mount Gerizim, which faces it to the south, and with sparse vegetation it shows an arid climatic character.
history: Mount Ebal was used in the early period of the conquest of Canaan as a ritual place for establishing the identity of the Israelite community and accepting the law. According to archaeological surveys, near the summit of Mount Ebal the remains of an early Iron Age altar, which have been suggested as possibly connected with the time of Joshua, have also been found.

introduce: Ephesus was a major port city on the western coast of ancient Asia Minor and the administrative and economic center of the Roman province of Asia. In the book of Acts in the New Testament it appears as the setting of events connected with Paul's missionary activity and the worship of the goddess Artemis.
biblecontents: Paul arrived at Ephesus with Priscilla and Aquila and reasoned with the Jews in the synagogue (Acts 18:19). Paul left Ephesus, promising to return if it was God's will (Acts 18:21). A Jew named Apollos, who came from Alexandria, arrived at Ephesus and taught the way concerning Jesus (Acts 18:24). Paul passed through the upper regions, arrived at Ephesus, and met some disciples (Acts 19:1). The Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus learned of this, were afraid, and exalted the name of Jesus (Acts 19:17). Paul persuaded and taught many people not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia (Acts 19:26).
