When Demetrius the silversmith stirred up a riot, the people cried out "Great is Artemis" and the city of Ephesus was thrown into confusion (Acts 19:28). The people shouted for about two hours, crying out for the goddess Artemis (Acts 19:34). The town clerk quieted the crowd by declaring that the people of Ephesus were the keepers of the temple of Artemis (Acts 19:35). Paul decided to sail past Ephesus so as not to spend time in Asia (Acts 20:16).
geography: Ephesus was a port city at the mouth of the Cayster River on the western coast of Asia Minor, and it was a trade crossroads linking the Mediterranean with the interior. At that time maritime traffic was well developed through the harbor connected to the sea, but because of silt deposition it is now located several kilometers inland from the coastline.
history: In the Roman imperial period, Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia and one of its most prosperous metropolises. The city was famous for the huge temple dedicated to the goddess Artemis, which functioned not only as the religious center of the city but also as a repository of economic assets and a core base of commercial activity. At that time Ephesus was under Roman administrative jurisdiction, and there existed a system of various offices, such as the town clerk, where the governor resided or public administration was carried out.

introduce: Ebez is a place name mentioned as one of the towns of the tribe of Issachar recorded in the Book of Joshua of the Old Testament.
biblecontents: Lots were cast for the tribe of the descendants of Issachar according to their families, and the boundary of their inheritance was Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Abez, Remeth, Engannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Joshua 19:20)
geography: Ebez is presumed to be located in the eastern part of the Valley of Jezreel or within the territory of the tribe of Issachar, but the specific archaeological site has not been clearly identified.

introduce: Ephes-dammim is a place name located within the territory of the tribe of Judah, a place where a military clash between ancient Israel and the Philistines occurred.
biblecontents: The Philistines gathered their armies for battle, assembled at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped at Ephes-dammim, between Socoh and Azekah (1 Samuel 17:1).
geography: Ephes-dammim is located in the Shephelah region of Judah, in a valley zone between Socoh and Azekah. As a strategic point linking the coastal plain with the hill country of Judah, this area forms part of the Valley of Elah.
history: In the early Iron Age, it was a point where frequent territorial disputes with Israel arose in the course of the Philistine forces advancing inland. Topographically it is recorded as a place where plain and hill country intersect, making troop movement and tactical maneuver easy.

introduce: Ebenezer is a place name carrying the Hebrew meaning "stone of help," a strategic point where military clashes between Israel and the Philistines were frequent. It is recorded as the place where the army of Israel encamped in the time of Samuel and as the place where Samuel set up a victory monument to commemorate God's help.
biblecontents: The Israelites encamped at Ebenezer to fight against the Philistines, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek (1 Samuel 4:1). Israel, defeated by the Philistines, saw the ark of God, which had been seized at Ebenezer, taken by the Philistines to Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:1). Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, "Thus far the LORD has helped us" (1 Samuel 7:12).
geography: Ebenezer is generally identified with Izbet Sartah, on the eastern border of the Sharon plain in present-day central Israel, or its vicinity. Located near Aphek, a buffer zone between the Ephraim hill country, the central mountain region, and the Philistine plain, it is a military strategic point linking the coastal plain with the inland hill country.
history: At the end of the period of the Judges, Israel was confronted with the expansionist threat of the Philistines. The battle in the Ebenezer area lies within the historical current in which Israel, after settling in Canaan, sought to secure the initiative against the iron civilization and military power of the Philistines. The defeat in the early battle brought about a political and religious crisis for Israel, but the victory won afterward at Ebenezer under Samuel's leadership is regarded as one of the turning points by which Israel escaped from Philistine domination and advanced toward becoming a monarchic state.

remark: The old name of Bethlehem.
introduce: Ephrathah means "fertile land" in Hebrew and is a place name located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel. In the Bible it is used mainly as a proper name identified with Bethlehem or referring to its surrounding area.
biblecontents: The psalmist says that he heard of the ark at Ephrathah, recalling historical memory connected with the ark of the covenant (Psalms 132:6). The prophet Micah singled out Bethlehem Ephrathah as the place from which the one who would rule Israel in time to come would come forth, and prophesied that his origins are of old (Micah 5:2).
geography: Geographically, Ephrathah refers to the Bethlehem area south of Jerusalem and belongs to the hill country of Judah. This area, with its hilly terrain, has fertile soil where grain can be grown, and it has long been known as a place with conditions suitable for agriculture.
history: Ephrathah was recognized as an important stronghold in the process of the early settlement of the tribe of Judah. According to the biblical record, this place name was also called Ephrath in connection with the event in which Jacob's wife Rachel died on the road to Bethlehem and was buried, and afterward it acquired political and religious symbolism as the birthplace of the house of David.

remark: A town of Judah.
introduce: Ephrath is a place name located in the region of ancient Canaan, a name that is either the same place as Bethlehem or refers to its vicinity. In the biblical record it appears chiefly in connection with the death and burial place of Rachel.
biblecontents: On the way as Jacob's party left Bethel for Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth and died there after labor (Genesis 35:16). Rachel was buried on the way to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). Jacob recalled that when he came back from Paddan, Rachel died in the land of Canaan, and that he buried her not far from the way to Ephrath (Genesis 48:7). The people blessing the marriage of Boaz and Ruth wished that Boaz would be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem (Ruth 4:11).
geography: Ephrath is situated on the highland of the hill country of Judea, south of Jerusalem. From the archaeological context and the biblical circumstances, this place name is interpreted as an archaic name pointing to Bethlehem, or as a general term for the fertile area around it.
history: The name Ephrath was used from the early period of the settlement of Canaan, and it reflects the system of geographical names from before the formation of the tribes of Israel. When the name Bethlehem became established in later times, Ephrath was listed alongside it as an ancient place name qualifying Bethlehem or specifying the area.

introduce: Eshan is one of the towns distributed to the tribe of Judah in ancient times, a locality appearing in the geographical lists of the Bible.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the towns included in the hill country region among the land that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:52).
geography: Eshan is presumed to be located in the southern hilly zone of the hill country of Judah, and this region falls within a range that includes the highland between present-day south of Hebron and Beersheba.

introduce: The region of Esau was located in the Seir hill country of the ancient Near East, and means the territory where the Edomites, descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother, lived. Historically, it was a kinsman nation geographically adjacent to Israel, but as a strategic point it was a region where military conflicts between them occurred frequently.
biblecontents: The house of Jacob will be a fire and the house of Joseph a flame, but the house of Esau will be stubble; they will set them ablaze and consume them, and there will be no survivor of the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken (Obadiah 1:18). The people of the Negev will possess the mountain of Esau, the people of the lowland will possess the land of the Philistines, and they will also possess the fields of Ephraim and the fields of Samaria, and Benjamin will possess Gilead (Obadiah 1:19). The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD. (Obadiah 1:21).
geography: The region of Esau is located in the Seir mountain range from the southeast of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. It borders the Arabian Desert on the east, and on the west faces the hill country of Judah across the Arabah valley. Its rugged mountain terrain is advantageous for defense, and the King's Highway, the ancient Arabian trade route, passes through this region, giving it the character of an economic crossroads.
history: Historically, Edom, as a nation on the southern border of Israel, experienced territorial disputes with the kingdom of Israel. In the time of Solomon and in the period of the kingdom of Judah, it repeatedly became subject or became independent, and in particular the act of Edom's hostility toward Judah at the time of the fall of Jerusalem was cited in the later prophetic books as the main ground for judgment. Around the 6th century BC, because of the expansion of Babylonia and the migration of Arab tribes, it was gradually pushed out of its former dwelling places and moved into the region of southern Judah.

remark: The well in the valley of Gerar dug by Isaac's servants.
introduce: Esek is a name meaning "contention" or "dispute" in Hebrew, and it refers to the place connected with a well where Isaac, while staying in the valley of Gerar, came into conflict with the herdsmen of Gerar.
biblecontents: The herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen and claimed that the well Isaac had dug was theirs, and for this reason Isaac called the name of that well Esek (Genesis 26:20).
geography: Esek is presumed to be located near the valley of Gerar, which belongs to the region of the Philistines, and it has the topographical condition in which, because of the dry climate of the ancient Near East, securing water resources was a key factor for survival.
history: In the patriarchal society of that time, a well was an essential economic asset for sustaining vast herds of livestock, and it reflects a historical custom symbolizing ownership and possession of a particular region.

introduce: Eznite is a name appearing in 2 Samuel 23:8 of the Old Testament, a name mentioned as the home of a man known as Adino, one of David's mighty men, or as a military stronghold connected with him.
biblecontents: These are the names of David's mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite, also called Adino the Eznite, who killed eight hundred men at one time (2 Samuel 23:8)
geography: Among scholars there is a dispute over whether Eznite in the Hebrew text is a personal name or a place name, and since the specific location of that region has not been clearly confirmed archaeologically, it is difficult to determine precise geographical coordinates or topographical features.

remark: A memorial rock near Saul's residence.
introduce: Ezel is a name appearing in Genesis 36 and 1 Samuel 20, a place name and common noun analyzed as referring, in the Hebrew original, to different meanings and objects respectively.
biblecontents: Genesis 36:30 mentions Ezer, one of the chiefs of the Horite clan living in the land of Seir (Genesis 36:30). In 1 Samuel 20:19, in connection with the place where David was hiding, the name "the stone Ezel" appears, which is interpreted as referring to a place name Ezel or to a tree (1 Samuel 20:19).
geography: The Ezer of Genesis 36:30 is presumed to be a personal name or a dwelling place of a tribe connected with the Seir hill country of the Edom region. The stone Ezel of 1 Samuel 20:19 is a landmark from the time when David was fleeing from King Saul, and is understood as a strategic point in the wilderness of Judea or near Gibeah.

introduce: Ezem is a southern town of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the Old Testament, a place name recorded as one of the inheritances distributed to the tribe of Simeon.
biblecontents: Ezem was mentioned as one of the towns located at the southern end of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:29). Afterward it is also included in the list of towns that the tribe of Simeon received out of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 19:3). It is also stated once again as a town that belonged to the tribe of Simeon down to the time of David (1 Chronicles 4:29).
geography: Ezem is presumed to be located in the Negev Desert region around Beersheba, and as for the exact site, scholars propose Tel es-Sei or a neighboring area as a candidate, but there is no archaeologically confirmed conclusion.

remark: A valley near Hebron.
introduce: Eshcol is a valley located in the southern region of Canaan, a place name mentioned in the Bible as an important stopover when the spies explored the land of Canaan.
biblecontents: The Israelite spies came to the Valley of Eshcol, cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and carried it on a pole between two men, and they also gathered pomegranates and figs there (Numbers 13:23). Because of this, that valley came to be called the Valley of Eshcol (Numbers 13:24). Afterward the children of Israel went up to the Valley of Eshcol, saw the land, and returned and discouraged the children of Israel from going into the land the LORD had given them (Numbers 32:9). Moreover, according to the record of Moses, the fact that the spies came to the Valley of Eshcol, spied out the land, and returned bringing a cluster of grapes is confirmed again (Deuteronomy 1:24).
geography: The Valley of Eshcol is presumed to be in the vicinity of Hebron, and is known as a fertile zone where viticulture and agricultural activity were flourishing from ancient times.

remark: A town in the plain of Judah.
introduce: Eshtaol is a place name mentioned in the Bible as a village located near the boundary between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Dan, appearing as an important point especially in the life of the judge Samson and in the migration of the tribe of Dan.
biblecontents: Eshtaol was allotted as one of the towns located in the plain region of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:33). Afterward it was included in the area allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:41). The place where Samson was first stirred by the Spirit of the LORD was Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 13:25), and after his death Samson was laid to rest between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial place of his father Manoah (Judges 16:31). When the tribe of Dan sent spies to seek an inheritance, they chose five valiant men from Zorah and Eshtaol and sent them (Judges 18:2), and the spies returned and proposed to their companions that they capture the region of Laish (Judges 18:8). Afterward six hundred men of the family of the tribe of Dan set out armed from Zorah and Eshtaol and carried out the migration (Judges 18:11). Meanwhile, 1 Chronicles records that the clans of Kiriath-jearim gave rise to the people of Eshtaol (1 Chronicles 2:53).
geography: Eshtaol is presumed to be present-day Tell Eshtaol and is located in the Shephelah region, the plain of Judah. This area lies about 2 km east of Zorah, and, adjacent to the hill where Zorah stands, shares the valley or plain region called Mahaneh-dan (the camp of Dan).
history: From the Late Bronze Age through the early Iron Age, this region served as a buffer zone among the tribes of Judah and Dan and the Philistine forces. When the territory first allotted to the tribe of Dan became difficult to live in because of Philistine pressure, the tribe of Dan took Zorah and Eshtaol as its base and carried out a historic movement of migration to Laish in the north. Eshtaol served as the early settlement and military stronghold of this tribe of Dan.

introduce: Eshtemoh is one of the towns located in the hill country of Judah, an ancient settlement found in the biblical lists of place names.
biblecontents: It was mentioned as a town located in the hill country among the list of the inheritance that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Judah after conquering the land of Canaan (Joshua 15:50).
geography: It is identified with present-day Es-Semu'a, and is located about 15 km southwest of Hebron. Situated in the rugged terrain of the southern hill country of Judah, it has conditions favorable for defense.

introduce: Eshtemoa is a town of the tribe of Judah appearing in the Old Testament, identified by a modern place name as Tel es-Semia. This town is mentioned chiefly as a town of the Levites and as a place connected with the deeds of David.
biblecontents: Eshtemoa is recorded as one of the towns allotted to the descendants of Aaron, descendants of the tribe of Levi (Joshua 21:14). David sent the spoils he had taken from the Amalekites to the elders of Eshtemoa, repaying them for their cooperation (1 Samuel 30:28). Also the Chronicles once again states Eshtemoa as a town given to the descendants of Aaron (1 Chronicles 6:57).
geography: Eshtemoa is located in the hill country of Judah, about 15 km southwest of Hebron. It is identified with the modern place name As-Samu', which was one of the main strongholds on the ancient highway linking Beersheba and Hebron.
history: Since remains of the Iron Age have been found, we can see that it was a town continuously inhabited during the period of ancient Israel. In the time of David, as a strategic point, it played an important role in securing the security and control of the southern region of Judah.

introduce: This place name, known as Ezion-geber, appears in the Bible as a strategic point on the route of the Israelites' exodus and as a base of maritime trade in the time of Solomon.
biblecontents: The children of Israel traveled along the way of the Arabah past Elath and Ezion-geber (Deuteronomy 2:8). King Solomon also built ships at Ezion-geber on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom (1 Kings 9:26).
geography: It is located on the northeastern coast of the Gulf of Aqaba, the northern end of the Red Sea, and is presumed to be present-day Aqaba in Jordan or the area of Tell el-Kheleifeh nearby. With the desert zone and the harbor adjacent to each other, it is a point where Red Sea trade and overland traffic intersect.
history: It is confirmed to have been used as a major copper smelting and trading site from the early to the middle Iron Age. In the time of Solomon it was used as a base of maritime trade for carrying gold from Ophir, and afterward it became the object of a dispute over possession between the kingdom of Judah and Edom.

introduce: Ezion-geber was a port city located at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea in ancient Israel, a strategic point that played the role of a center of maritime trade and shipbuilding after the time of Solomon.
biblecontents: It is one of the places where the children of Israel stayed during the course of the exodus (Numbers 33:35). Also, they left Ezion-geber and came to the wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh (Numbers 33:36). King Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom (1 Kings 9:26). The servants of Hiram sailed with Solomon and brought gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:26). Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber (1 Kings 22:48). Solomon came to Ezion-geber and the coast of the land of Edom (2 Chronicles 8:17). Jehoshaphat joined with Ahaziah to make ships and built them at Ezion-geber (2 Chronicles 20:36).
geography: Ezion-geber is located deep in the Gulf of Aqaba on the north of the Red Sea, presumed to be near present-day Aqaba in Jordan or Eilat in Israel. This region lies at the southern end of the Arabah valley and served as a gateway through which one could advance via the Red Sea to the Arabian Peninsula and the eastern coast of Africa.
history: In the reign of King Solomon, Ezion-geber was developed as a base of maritime trade symbolizing Israel's economic prosperity, and through it gold and rare resources were imported from Ophir. Afterward, in the period of the kingdom of southern Judah, King Jehoshaphat tried once again to rebuild maritime trade, but because of the shipwreck he did not achieve great results. On the basis of traces of ancient smelting facilities found in this area, scholars raise the possibility that it was not merely a port but a center of the copper smelting and metalworking industry.

introduce: En-gedi is an oasis region located on the western shore of the Dead Sea, a place of high strategic value from ancient times because of its abundant fresh water and unique terrain. Its Hebrew name carries the meaning "spring of the young goat."
biblecontents: En-gedi was included in the list of the wilderness towns of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:62). David hid in the strongholds and the wasteland of En-gedi to escape Saul's pursuit (1 Samuel 23:29, 1 Samuel 24:1). Saul set out with three thousand men to look for David at the Rocks of the Wild Goats of En-gedi (1 Samuel 24:2). In Solomon's Song of Songs, the beloved is compared to a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi (Song of Solomon 1:14).
geography: Located beneath the cliffs of the wilderness of Judea on the western shore of the Dead Sea, it is an oasis zone formed by hot spring water and waterfalls gushing forth from below. Owing to the topographical character of the Dead Sea shore, which lies lower than sea level, a unique microclimate has formed, in which tropical plants and rare animals live.
history: Traces of habitation have been confirmed from the Iron Age, and in ancient times it had economic importance as a major production site for perfume and balsam cultivation. There is archaeological record that fortresses and agricultural facilities were also operated in the periods of the Hasmonean dynasty and the Herodian dynasty, and that the settlement was maintained until the Byzantine period.

introduce: En-rogel is a spring located on the outskirts of Jerusalem, a place mentioned in the Old Testament period as a major landmark marking the boundary between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the boundary line of the tribe of Benjamin passes the area at the foot of the valley of the son of Hinnom and goes down to En-rogel (Joshua 18:16). It is also the place where Adonijah, David's son, offered sacrifices beside this spring when he tried to make himself king (1 Kings 1:9).
geography: Located southeast of the wall of Jerusalem, at the point where the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley merge, it is presumed to be present-day Bir Ayyub. This place corresponds topographically to the low ground of Jerusalem and serves as a water source rich in water.
history: It appears as the site of political conflict over the succession to the throne in the last years of King David, and it is a symbolic place that Adonijah, the opposing party in the process of Solomon's accession, chose in order to rally his supporters and secure legitimacy. It is regarded as a point of strategic value connected with control of the water resources of Jerusalem at that time.

introduce: En-shemesh is a place name carrying the meaning "spring of the sun," a place located on the boundary line between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin at the time of Joshua's conquest.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah goes up from the valley of Achor, turns toward Debir in the north, faces Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim on the south side of the river, passes the waters of En-shemesh, and comes to En-rogel (Joshua 15:7). Also the boundary of the tribe of Benjamin likewise has its location fixed by a route passing En-shemesh and going toward En-rogel (Joshua 18:17).
geography: By present-day place name, it is presumed to be Ain el-Haud, near En-rogel in the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, or a spring in that vicinity, and it lies at a strategic point dividing the territory of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin.

introduce: En-hazor is a fortified town in northern Galilee recorded in Joshua 19 of the Old Testament, a place name belonging to the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Naphtali.
biblecontents: Among the fortified cities obtained by the tribe of the descendants of Naphtali, Kedesh, Edrei, and En-hazor were mentioned side by side (Joshua 19:37).
geography: En-hazor was located northwest of the Sea of Galilee, in the mountainous zone of Upper Galilee. The place name means "spring of Hazor," and it is identified with the vicinity of Hazor or with Ain Hazur (Ain Hazur, Khirbet Hazur) in Upper Galilee, or with the valley northeast of present-day Maghar. Settlements developed on the basis of the abundant spring water gushing out of the limestone hills.
history: Adjacent to Hazor, the great city-state of the Bronze Age, it was either a dependent settlement under its economic and military sphere of influence or an independent water-resource fortress. After the Israelite settlement, it was reorganized as a defensive stronghold of the tribe of Naphtali, and it played the role of watching the northern mountain road and defending the surrounding farmland.

introduce: En-gannim is a locality mentioned as one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah at the time of the allotment among the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is listed among the towns of the lowland plain region in the list of the towns of the inheritance that the tribe of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:34).
geography: It is recorded as being located in the Shephelah region of the tribe of Judah, but its exact location has not been identified in modern archaeology. The place name itself contains the meaning "spring" or "source of the eye," but it is classified as a region different from En-gannim of the tribe of Issachar, a place of the same name.

introduce: En-gedi is an oasis zone located on the western shore of the Dead Sea, a region possessing abundant spring water. Because of its topographical features like a natural fortress, it was often used as a hiding place from ancient times, and it was a place famous in the ancient Near East for palm trees and vineyards.
biblecontents: David went down to the stronghold of En-gedi and stayed there (1 Samuel 23:29). When Saul returned from pursuing the Philistines, someone brought word that David was in the wilderness of En-gedi (1 Samuel 24:1). The Moabites and Ammonites joined together and came against Jehoshaphat at Hazazon-tamar, that is, En-gedi (2 Chronicles 20:2). My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi. (Song of Solomon 1:14). From En-gedi to En-eglaim will be a place for spreading nets, and it will be full of fish of every kind (Ezekiel 47:10).
geography: It lies on the Dead Sea shore at the eastern end of the wilderness of Judea and is located in a lowland below sea level. Because of the freshwater springs gushing out among the limestone cliffs, it forms a unique ecosystem in a desert environment. The Dead Sea lies to the east, and because of the rugged terrain it has the conditions of a natural fortress that is difficult to approach.
history: In the Old Testament period it is recorded chiefly as the refuge to which David fled to escape Saul. Afterward, in the time of King Jehoshaphat, it was also included in the invasion route of neighboring nations. Historically, En-gedi was known as a region producing precious resources such as spices and balsam, on the basis of the abundant minerals and unique climate of the Dead Sea, and its economic value was high.

introduce: En-tappuah is a place name mentioned in the Book of Joshua in the Bible, a place connected with the boundary of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblecontents: The boundary of Manasseh goes from Asher to Michmethath, and from there goes to the right and reaches the boundary of the inhabitants of En-tappuah (Joshua 17:7).
geography: En-tappuah is presumed to be located on the northern boundary line of the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, and is interpreted as the area near a spring named Tappuah. As for its specific archaeological location, there is a theory identifying it with present-day Tell es-Safina or Khirbet Abu in its vicinity, but it has not been clearly determined.

introduce: Endor is a settlement located in the northern region of Canaan, known in ancient Israel as a strategic stronghold and as the place where a woman who was a medium lived.
biblecontents: It was mentioned as one of the towns that the tribe of Manasseh received within the territories of the tribes of Issachar and Asher (Joshua 17:11). It is the place where lived the woman who was a medium whom King Saul visited to seek counsel before the battle with the Philistines (1 Samuel 28:7). In the Psalms, it is mentioned figuratively as the place where Sisera and Jabin perished (Psalms 83:10).
geography: Endor is located on the northern slope of the Hill of Moreh in lower Galilee, and, adjacent to the Valley of Jezreel, has a topographical character that makes it easy for traffic and military movement.
history: It is a place where traces of human habitation have been found from the Bronze and Iron Ages, and in the early period of the occupation of Canaan it was included in the territory of the tribes of Israel, but actual occupation proceeded slowly. In the time of King Saul, it was located at the point where the sphere of influence of the neighboring great power the Philistines and the power of Israel intersected, and a politically unstable situation continued.

introduce: En-rogel is an ancient well or spring located near Jerusalem, a place that served as a geographical marker defining the boundary point between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin.
biblecontents: En-rogel is mentioned as one of the points setting the northern boundary line of the tribe of Judah, and it is located on the boundary that goes up along the valley from Debir and heads north (Joshua 15:7). In the time of David, it was a strategic place where Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed hidden and relayed information in order to help David, who was fleeing from Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 17:17). It is also recorded as the place where Adonijah offered sacrifices himself in order to become king (1 Kings 1:9).
geography: En-rogel is identified with Bir Ayyub, located at the southeastern point where the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley of Jerusalem meet. It is located at the lower southern part of the City of David, the ancient dwelling place of Jerusalem, and because of the regional characteristic that water sources are scarce, it functioned as an important water supply.
history: This place was a politically sensitive site that became the stage of a succession dispute during David's reign. Geographically it lies on the boundary line of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and so was used as an administrative and military reference point such as for territorial division, and it is regarded as a point closely connected with the major waterways and irrigation system of ancient Jerusalem.

introduce: En-mishpat is an ancient place name presumed to be the same place as the region called Kadesh.
biblecontents: They turned back and came to En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh, and struck all the country of the Amalekites and the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar (Genesis 14:7)
geography: It is regarded as the same region as present-day Kadesh-barnea, an oasis region located on the boundary between the northeastern Sinai Peninsula and the Negev Desert.
history: It is mentioned as a major stopping point on the route along which the allied army of four kings, led by Chedorlaomer, passed, conquering the dwelling places of the Amalekites and the Amorites before invading Sodom and Gomorrah.

introduce: En-hakkore is a place name carrying the Hebrew meaning "spring of the one who cries out," and refers to the place where God caused water to come forth for Samson to drink when he suffered severe thirst after slaughtering the Philistines.
biblecontents: After Samson struck the Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, he felt severe thirst and cried out to God, and God split open a hollow place in Lehi so that water came out, and Samson drank it and his spirit was restored (Judges 15:19).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the region of Lehi, and its exact site is at present not clearly established archaeologically, but it is regarded as a lowland region belonging to the territory of the tribe of Judah.

introduce: En-haddah is a locality mentioned as one of the towns of the inheritance distributed to the tribe of Issachar among the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: In Joshua 19:21 it is recorded as one of the towns of the inheritance for which lots were cast for the tribe of the descendants of Issachar (Joshua 19:21).

introduce: Elkosh is a place name appearing in Nahum 1 of the Old Testament, the hometown of the prophet Nahum, who proclaimed the destruction of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria.
biblecontents: The book opens with the oracle concerning Nineveh, namely the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite (Nahum 1:1).
geography: Several traditions and theories exist about the exact location of Elkosh. The most plausible view is that it was a village in the Shephelah (lowland) of southern Judah, the ruins of Helkesei (Elcesi) near Beth Gubrin (Eleutheropolis), to which the ancient church father Jerome (Hieronymus) bore witness. Other traditions point to the vicinity of Capernaum in Galilee (meaning "village of Nahum") or to Alqosh, north of Mosul in Iraq, within Assyrian territory, but the critical-historical scholarly community judges the region of southern Judah, the stage of Nahum's activity, to be the most credible.
history: In the middle and late 7th century BC, as the Neo-Assyrian Empire, which then dominated all of western Asia, declined and its capital Nineveh was about to fall in 612 BC to the allied forces of Media and Babylon, Nahum, from the small town of Elkosh in the kingdom of Judah, carried out a prophetic ministry announcing the empire's destruction and judgment to a people crushed under the empire's oppression.

introduce: Eltolad is a town located in the southern inheritance boundary region of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place name appearing in the record of Joshua.
biblecontents: Eltolad is mentioned as one of the towns located at the southern end of the inheritance distributed to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:30). Also Eltolad is recorded in the list of towns that the tribe of Simeon was allotted out of the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 19:4).
geography: It is presumed to be the area around Beersheba near the Negev Desert, but its exact present location has not been specified archaeologically. From the geographical circumstances it can be understood that it was situated in the southern plain zone adjacent to Beersheba.

introduce: Eltekeh is one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Dan when land was distributed to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Eltekeh is mentioned as one of the towns of the inheritance obtained by lot by the tribe of the descendants of Dan (Joshua 19:44). Afterward this town was designated again as a town given to the Kohathites, descendants of Levi, located within the territory of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 21:23).
geography: The exact location is still being debated among scholars, but it is generally presumed to be Tel esh-Shallaf, in the area near the Sharon plain in present-day Israel, or its surrounding area. This corresponds to the Mediterranean coastal plain zone, the early holding of the tribe of Dan.

introduce: Eltekon is one of the towns of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua 15:59, a place name appearing in the text of the Septuagint (LXX).
biblecontents: In the list enumerating the towns distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, it is mentioned together with Maarath and Beth-anoth (Joshua 15:59).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the hill country of Judah, but its exact present-day archaeological location has not been identified.

remark: The valley of Judah where David killed Goliath.
introduce: Elah is used in the Bible in two different senses. The first is a proper noun referring to a chief of the Edom region or the territory he ruled, and the second means the Valley of Elah, a strategic point where the armies of the Philistines and Israel confronted each other.
biblecontents: Elah is mentioned as the name of one of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:41). It also refers to the region where the chiefs of Edom lived (1 Chronicles 1:52). As a geographical name, Elah appears in the time of King Saul as the place where the Philistines encamped (1 Samuel 17:2). The army of Israel and the army of the Philistines confronted each other in the Valley of Elah and prepared for war (1 Samuel 17:19). It also appears as the setting connected with the place where David took Goliath's sword after killing him (1 Samuel 21:9).
geography: The Valley of Elah lies south of the Valley of Sorek, one of the five major valleys linking the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain. This region has a topographical character in which steep hills and fertile plains intersect, and in ancient times it served as a strategic passage linking the interior and the coast.
history: In the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, the Valley of Elah was a buffer zone between the tribes of Israel and the Philistines and a place of frequent border disputes. Because it was the main passage by which Israel, living in the mountain region, and the Philistines, living in the plains, entered each other's domains, it is recorded as a historic place where many military clashes occurred.

introduce: A region ruled by the ruler of Ellasar, a city-state of the ancient Near East that appears in Genesis 14, which made an alliance with Amraphel king of Shinar and fought a war with the allied forces of Sodom and Gomorrah.
biblecontents: Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim made war with Bera king of Sodom and others (Genesis 14:1). These four kings formed an allied army against the five kings of the Canaan region (Genesis 14:9).
geography: The exact location of Ellasar is disputed archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be Larsa, located in the southern Mesopotamian region. Larsa was a city on the lower Euphrates River and one of the important political centers of the Sumerian and Akkadian regions at that time.
history: Ellasar is discussed in scholarship as being deeply connected with the Larsa dynasty before the ancient Babylonian period. In the early 2000s BC, Larsa exercised strong regional hegemony, and in particular a linguistic similarity has been pointed out between the name Arioch and the Elamite-lineage name Arriyuk of the time. This reflects the historical situation in which the small kingdoms of Mesopotamia at that time launched expeditions to extend their power as far as the western Canaan region and to collect tribute.

remark: The region where the descendants of Elam lived.
introduce: Elam means an ancient civilization and state located east of ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now southwestern Iran. In the Bible it appears chiefly as a power that allied with or invaded neighboring great powers, and in the flow of Old Testament history it formed close political relations with surrounding nations.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer king of Elam, who invaded Sodom and Gomorrah together with Amraphel king of Shinar, appears (Genesis 14:1, Genesis 14:9). In the time of Ezra, the Elamites are mentioned as one of the peoples who had migrated to Samaria (Ezra 4:9). Isaiah, in a prophecy of God's judgment, mentions that Elam will attack Babylon (Isaiah 21:2), and describes Elam mobilizing an army and, together with Kir, attacking the walls riding in chariots (Isaiah 22:6). Isaiah singles out Elam as one of the regions from which the people scattered in Assyria and Egypt and elsewhere will return (Isaiah 11:11). Jeremiah prophesies the judgment that Elam will suffer (Jeremiah 25:25, Jeremiah 49:34), and warns that their bow will be broken and the people scattered by the winds blowing from every direction (Jeremiah 49:35, Jeremiah 49:36).
geography: Elam includes the plains and plateaus of the western Zagros Mountains, corresponding to the area of present-day Khuzestan and Fars provinces in Iran. On the west it borders the Tigris River and the Mesopotamian plain, and on the east it connects with the interior of the Iranian plateau. Its main base city was Susa, and in this region an early agricultural society developed on the basis of fertile river basins.
history: Elam is an ancient civilization existing from the third millennium BC, and the kingdom of Elam constantly interacted or fought wars with the Sumerian, Akkadian, and Babylonian powers of Mesopotamia. Around the 12th century BC it conquered Babylon and even carried the stele of the Code of Hammurabi to Susa. Afterward it was conquered by Ashurbanipal of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and its national strength declined, and in the end around the 6th century BC it was absorbed into Achaemenid Persia. The references to Elam recorded in the Bible reflect this geopolitical standing and the complex political relations among neighboring great powers.

introduce: Elath is an important port city of the ancient Near East, identified with the Aqaba area located at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba today. This region was a strategic point linking maritime trade through the Red Sea with the overland routes of the wilderness of the Arabah.
biblecontents: When the people of Israel passed through the wilderness, they traveled past Elath and Ezion-geber (Deuteronomy 2:8). Azariah king of Judah built Elath and restored it to Judah (2 Kings 14:22). Afterward Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath, drove out the men of Judah, and the Edomites came to live there (2 Kings 16:6).
geography: Elath is located at the northernmost end of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea, bordering the Edomite mountains on the east and the Negev Desert on the west. Topographically situated at the lower end of the Arabah rift, it has the geographical environment to serve as a gateway linking the Red Sea, a maritime trade route, with the interior of Asia.
history: In the Iron Age this region was a place of frequent military conflict among the kingdom of Judah and neighboring nations such as Edom and Aram over the securing of copper smelting and the maritime trade sphere. In particular after the time of Solomon, control of the port was directly tied to national economic power, and for this reason, according to its geopolitical importance, it showed a history in which dominion was exchanged among various powers.

introduce: Haeleph is one of the towns allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel appearing in the Book of Joshua of the Bible.
biblecontents: Haeleph is mentioned in the last verses of the list of the towns of the inheritance for the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin enumerated between Joshua 18:21 and 28. It is recorded together with Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath as towns of the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28).
geography: The exact location of Haeleph has not been clearly established archaeologically. However, since it lies within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin according to the biblical record and is mentioned together with towns near Jerusalem, it is presumed to have been located in the mountainous region north or west of Jerusalem.

introduce: Elon-beth-hanan is a locality mentioned as one of the centers of the second district of King Solomon's administrative districts.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a place included in the jurisdiction of Ben-deker, the second of the twelve district governors whom Solomon appointed over Israel (1 Kings 4:9).
geography: Its present location is difficult to specify exactly, but it is generally presumed to be near Beth-shemesh, in the plain zone around the Valley of Aijalon. This is a strategic point close to the border region between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Dan.
history: The reorganization of the twelve administrative districts in the time of Solomon meant a shift from the earlier tribe-centered system to a centralized system of taxation and military mobilization. In this administrative division, Elon-beth-hanan played the role of a base region responsible for supplying food to the royal house and collecting taxes.

introduce: Eloth is an ancient port city located at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea, a region that Israel and the kingdom of Judah strategically valued after the time of Solomon for maritime trade and the securing of resources.
biblecontents: King Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber, near Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom (1 Kings 9:26). When Solomon came to Ezion-geber and Eloth, he carried on maritime trade there (2 Chronicles 8:17). King Uzziah built Eloth and restored it to Judah (2 Chronicles 26:2).
geography: Eloth is located at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba, near the present-day border between Jordan and Israel. As the southern end of the Arabah valley and the gateway to the Red Sea, it is situated as a crossroads of maritime traffic through the Red Sea and on the route linking with the Sinai Peninsula and the Arabian Peninsula.
history: Eloth was adjacent to the Arabah region, where copper mines are concentrated, and was used as a base for exporting mineral resources. This region belonged to the territory of Edom, but after the time of David it came under the sphere of influence of Israel. Afterward, as the kingdom of Judah declined, ownership changed frequently according to the political situation, as it returned again to Edomite rule or became the object of war with neighboring countries.

introduce: Elealeh was a town located near the plain of Moab east of the Jordan River, a place name mentioned in connection with the tribe of Reuben of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: The descendants of Reuben built Elealeh together with Heshbon (Numbers 32:3, Numbers 32:37). Afterward the prophet Isaiah, prophesying judgment against Moab, recorded that the cry of Elealeh is heard as far as Jahaz (Isaiah 15:4), and prophesied that with the disappearance of Moab's wine and harvest, Elealeh would be drenched with tears (Isaiah 16:9). Jeremiah likewise, proclaiming the destruction of Moab, described a crying out heard from Heshbon to Elealeh (Jeremiah 48:34).
geography: It is identified with the El-Al area northeast of present-day Madaba in Jordan. About 3 km northeast of Heshbon, it lies on the highland of Jordan, a fertile land favorable to the cultivation of grain and grapes.
history: It was originally the territory of Sihon king of the Amorites, but after Israel's conquest it was allotted to the tribe of Reuben. In the later part of the biblical period it passed again into the sphere of influence of Moab and was recognized as a town of Moab, and it is a region where archaeological remains of the Iron Age have been found.

introduce: Elim is one of the places the children of Israel reached in the course of passing through the wilderness after the exodus, recorded as an oasis region with abundant water resources and vegetation.
biblecontents: It is the place they arrived at after the incident of the bitter waters of Marah, and there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees (Exodus 15:27). The children of Israel encamped and stayed at Elim (Numbers 33:9), and leaving Elim they encamped by the Red Sea (Numbers 33:10). Afterward they left Elim and moved on to the wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16:1).
geography: This region, presumed to be today's Wadi Gharandel, is located on the western coastal plain of the Sinai Peninsula. This point is a lowland close to the Red Sea, and because it has a spring from which groundwater wells up, it has an environment favorable for the formation of a plant community even in an arid desert environment.

introduce: El-paran is a place name that existed in the ancient Near East, mentioned in Genesis 14 of the Bible as a place the eastern allied forces centered on Chedorlaomer passed through on their journey of conquest.
biblecontents: El-paran is recorded as the point the allied forces passed when, having conquered the Horites living in the hill country of Seir, they reached the vicinity of the wilderness (Genesis 14:6).
geography: El-paran is generally regarded as a region connected with the wilderness of Paran, and is presumed to be a wilderness zone south of the hill country of Seir or near the Arabah valley. In Hebrew etymology it is also interpreted as the oak of Paran or the plain of Paran, and its specific archaeological location is disputed.
history: In the early or middle Bronze Age this region was a main route along which nomads and ancient tribes moved. The record of military conquest in the Canaan region appearing in Genesis 14 has as its historical background the westward advance of the Mesopotamian powers of that time and the regional conflict that followed.

introduce: El-bethel is a place name given by Jacob when he built an altar again at Bethel, the place where he had met God, on his way back from Paddan-aram.
biblecontents: Jacob built an altar there and called the place El-bethel, because there God had appeared to him when he fled from the face of his brother (Genesis 35:7)
geography: It is presumed to be near the Beitin area in the present-day West Bank, a highland about 18 km north of Jerusalem.
history: From before the patriarchal period it was regarded as one of the religious centers of Canaan, and it is recorded as the same point as the place where Jacob, while fleeing to Haran, saw the vision of the ladder.

introduce: El-Elohe-Israel is the name of the altar that Jacob built while staying near Shechem after returning from Paddan-aram, and it is a proper noun that also refers to that region. Its meaning carries the sense "God, the God of Israel."
biblecontents: Jacob, having returned from Paddan-aram, came before the city of Shechem and pitched his tent, and bought the field where he pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitahs. There he built an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:19-20).
geography: El-Elohe-Israel is located near the east side of Shechem in the central region of Canaan. Shechem lies in the fertile valley between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and is a strategic crossroads where the Patriarchs' Road, the main route linking north and south at that time, and the ancient road connecting east and west intersect.
history: At that time Shechem was the dwelling place of the Hivite people ruled by Hamor. Jacob, after returning from Paddan-aram, purchased land in order to settle as an outsider, which was one of the ways by which immigrants secured social and religious rights in the region. This altar suggests that Jacob proclaimed his identity as Israel and established a center of faith for his family within that region.

introduce: Emites is the name that refers to the dwelling place of the Emites, a branch of the race of giants who lived near the Jordan River east of the ancient region of Canaan.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings with him came out and struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites at Ham, and the Emites at Shaveh-kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5). The Emites formerly lived there, strong and many and tall like the Anakites, so they were called Rephaim like the Anakites, but the Moabites called them Emites (Deuteronomy 2:10-11).
geography: The region where the Emites lived is presumed to be the area of the plain of Moab east of the Jordan, and is understood topographically as a wide range including the highland near the valley of the Arnon.
history: The Emites are classified as ancient indigenous people who lived east of the Jordan from the early Bronze Age. Because of their characteristic of being physically huge, they were regarded as members of the Rephaim, and when the Moabites later occupied this region, they were recorded under the name Emites.

introduce: Emmaus is a village near Jerusalem mentioned in the Gospel of Luke in the New Testament, known as the place where the risen Jesus walked and talked with two disciples.
biblecontents: At a distance of about twenty-five li from Jerusalem to the village called Emmaus, the risen Jesus walked with two disciples and took part in their conversation (Luke 24:13).
geography: The exact location of Emmaus is disputed archaeologically, and as strong candidate sites, El-Qubeibeh, about 11 km northwest of Jerusalem, Amwas, about 30 km away, or Nicopolis are mentioned. Since the distance of twenty-five li stated in the Bible means roughly 10 to 12 km, modern scholars presume the area of El-Qubeibeh or Motza to be the main candidates.
history: There is a record that during the First Jewish–Roman War the Roman army was stationed in this region or built a settlement there, and afterward in the Byzantine period a church was also built here. At that time Emmaus is judged to have functioned as one of the crossroads linking Jerusalem and the neighboring regions.

introduce: Eth-kazin is a place name recorded in the Book of Joshua in the Old Testament, one of the boundary points of the towns distributed to the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Passing Gath-hepher, it goes through Eth-kazin to Rimmon and extends to Neah, turns on the north side to Hannathon, and ends at the valley (Joshua 19:13).
geography: Eth-kazin is presumed to be located in the lower Galilee region, but it is difficult to specify the exact archaeological site. It is commonly regarded as one of the northern boundary points within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun.

introduce: Jegar-sahadutha is an Aramaic place name referring to the heap of stones that Jacob and Laban set up to confirm their covenant relationship with each other.
biblecontents: Laban called it by the Aramaic name Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed in Hebrew (Genesis 31:47). This heap of stones functioned as a boundary between the two men and as evidence of their promise of mutual non-aggression (Genesis 31:48).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the hill country of Gilead, and lies on the route of Jacob's return from Paddan-aram to Canaan.
history: It reflects a culture in which, according to the custom of the Mesopotamian region at that time, a monument was set up when a covenant was concluded and a name was given to it in each party's own language. Jegar-sahadutha means "heap of witness," and shows the cultural background of Laban, who spoke a language of the Aramaic family.

introduce: Jekabzeel is one of the villages where the descendants of Judah lived after the return from captivity, a place name recorded in the book of Nehemiah in the Bible.
biblecontents: Among the villages where the descendants of Judah lived, Jekabzeel and its surrounding area are mentioned (Nehemiah 11:25).
geography: Jekabzeel is presumed to be the same place as Kabzeel mentioned in Joshua 15:21 of the Old Testament, a village located near the Negev Desert in the southern border region of the tribe of Judah.
history: It is one of the regions included in the list as the descendants of Judah restored their dwelling places in the process of resettling in Jerusalem and the surrounding towns after the Babylonian exile.

introduce: Jetheth appears as the name of one of the chiefs of the land of Edom and as a name referring to the region he ruled.
biblecontents: The name of Chief Jetheth is mentioned in the list of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:40). Also in the process of enumerating the chiefs of Edom in 1 Chronicles 1:51, Jetheth is included (1 Chronicles 1:51).
geography: It is presumed to be located within the Edom region, but the exact archaeological site has not been specified. Edom means the geographical area formed around the Seir hill country southeast of the Dead Sea.

introduce: Jerahmeel is a name referring to a family within the tribe of Judah and to the region where they lived, and in the Bible it is mentioned chiefly in connection with the Negev region south of Judah.
biblecontents: It appears as a place name in the incident in which David, while staying in the land of the Philistines to escape Saul, falsely reported to King Achish that he had raided the south of Judah and the south of the Jerahmeelites (1 Samuel 27:10).
geography: It is located in the Negev Desert zone south of the hill country of Judah, and although its specific boundaries are not clear, it is presumed to be a dry grassland and wilderness zone adjacent to the southern border region of the tribe of Judah.
history: Jerahmeel is a collective dwelling place formed by a family that originated with Jerahmeel, the eldest son of Hezron among the descendants of Perez, son of Judah, and in the time of David it was a strategic point that was both the southern defense line of the kingdom of Judah and a place where the spheres of influence of neighboring powers such as the Philistines and the Amalekites intersected.

introduce: Jeruel is a particular region mentioned in the period of the kingdom of Judah, meaning a field located on the way up to En-gedi.
biblecontents: In the time of King Jehoshaphat, when the allied forces of Moab and Ammon came up by way of En-gedi, it was prophesied that they would be found in the fields of Jeruel (2 Chronicles 20:16).
geography: It is presumed to be a part of the wilderness of Judea, and refers to a strategic point heading from En-gedi on the western shore of the Dead Sea toward Jerusalem, or a rugged highland in its vicinity.

introduce: Jebus refers to the region occupied by the Jebusites, one of the ancient peoples who lived in the land of Canaan. This region is known as the point that was later conquered by King David and became Jerusalem, the capital of Israel.
biblecontents: The Jebusites are mentioned as one of the seven peoples living in the land of Canaan (Genesis 10:16). God promised Abraham that He would give the land of Canaan, including the Jebusites, to his descendants (Genesis 15:21). In the course of the exodus they appear repeatedly as a people living in the land flowing with milk and honey that was promised to the people of Israel (Exodus 3:8, Exodus 3:17, Exodus 13:5). God announced that He would drive them out when Israel entered Canaan (Exodus 23:23, Exodus 33:2, Exodus 34:11). According to the report of the spies, the Jebusites were living in the hill country (Numbers 13:29). Moses described them as a people stronger than Israel and mentioned the confrontation with them (Deuteronomy 7:1).
geography: Jebus is a strategic point located on a highland about 700 meters above sea level in the central part of the hill country of Judah. Surrounded by the Kidron Valley and the Hinnom Valley as natural lines of defense, and having secured a stable water source in the Gihon Spring, it had very favorable topographical conditions as an ancient city.
history: It is considered a town settled from the Bronze Age, and the Jebusites held it as a strong fortress until David captured Jerusalem. According to the biblical record, this region went through the process of being incorporated as the political and religious center of Israel when David bought the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and built an altar.

introduce: Jebus refers to the town occupied by the Jebusites, a tribe of Canaan that had lived in the Jerusalem region from before the period of the conquest of Canaan. Until it was conquered by King David, they were active with Jerusalem, a strategic point, as their base.
biblecontents: David and all Israel came to Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, but the Jebusites, the inhabitants of that land, said to David, "You will not come in here"; yet David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the City of David (1 Chronicles 11:4, 11:5). David said, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander," and Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, and so he became chief (1 Chronicles 11:6).
geography: Jebus refers to the Jerusalem area in the central part of the mountains of Judah. It is flanked by the abundant water source of the Gihon Spring, and, surrounded on all sides by valleys, it has the terrain of a natural fortress that is very advantageous for defense.
history: The Jebusites remained a town that the tribes of Israel were unable to drive out completely from the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan, through the period of the Judges, until the time of David. After unifying Israel, David conquered this fortress as a strategic center and for the integration of the northern and southern tribes, and afterward he called it the City of David and made it the political and religious capital of Israel.

introduce: Jeshanah is one of the towns of the kingdom of Judah that Abijah king of Judah captured after winning the war against Jeroboam king of Israel.
biblecontents: Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took his towns, namely Bethel and its villages, Jeshanah and its villages, and Ephron and its villages (2 Chronicles 13:19)
geography: Since Jeshanah is mentioned in the biblical text together with Bethel and Ephron, it is presumed to be a town located near the hill country of Ephraim, and its exact present location has not been clearly identified archaeologically.
history: It is a town temporarily incorporated into the territory of Judah as a result of the military victory that Abijah king of Judah won against Jeroboam of northern Israel in the early period of the divided kingdom.

introduce: Jeush refers to a clan, or the region where they lived, named after the chief Jeush, one of the descendants of Esau, who were chiefs in the region of Edom.
biblecontents: Jeush, a son of Oholibamah, the wife of Esau, became a chief and ruled in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:18).
history: Jeush was a descendant born through Esau's wife Oholibamah, and served as the head of a particular tribe under the system of chiefs that governed Edom. This shows that the descendants of Edom divided the territory around Mount Seir and formed a tribal structure of government.

introduce: The LORD Is There is the new name of the future temple and the rebuilt Jerusalem that Ezekiel saw in a vision; it is a symbolic name, meaning that from that day on the city will be called The LORD Is There.
biblecontents: The perimeter on all sides totals eighteen thousand cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be The LORD Is There (Ezekiel 48:35)
geography: The exact location of the city described in Ezekiel 48 is not based on actual physical terrain; it lies within the boundaries of an ideal city that, in the vision, includes the temple precinct and the territories of the twelve tribes of Israel as they are divided.

introduce: The LORD Will Provide is a name meaning "the LORD will prepare" in Hebrew; it refers to a mountain in the land of Moriah, the place where Abraham found a ram to offer as a sacrifice in place of his son Isaac.
biblecontents: Because Abraham named that place The LORD Will Provide, people say to this day, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided" (Genesis 22:14)
geography: It is recorded as a mountain located in the land of Moriah, and according to ancient literature and the common view of biblical scholarship, it is identified with the area of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.

introduce: Jehud is a city mentioned as one of the inheritances allotted to the tribe of Dan in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Joshua 19:45 names it explicitly as one of the cities in the inheritance that the tribe of Dan obtained by lot (Joshua 19:45).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically to this day. It is presumed, however, to have been near the Philistine border region adjoining the Mediterranean coastal plain, which was the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan at that time.

introduce: The Valley of Salt, called Ge Hamelach in Hebrew, is a valley named in the biblical record as the place where significant victories over Edom were won in the days of David and of King Amaziah.
biblecontents: When David returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites, he won a victory in the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13). David's son Abishai also struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt (1 Chronicles 18:12). Amaziah, king of Judah, killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, took Sela, and called it Joktheel (2 Kings 14:7). The incident in which Amaziah killed ten thousand sons of Edom in the Valley of Salt is also recorded in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 25:11). The Valley of Salt mentioned in the superscription of Psalm 59 is set against the background of David's military achievement in defeating Edom (Psalms 59:17).
geography: The Valley of Salt is thought to refer to the valley of the Arabah near the southern end of the Dead Sea, or to the lowlands adjoining it. It reflects the terrain of the salty region around the Dead Sea, which lay on the route leading to ancient Edom.
history: The Valley of Salt was a strategic military site where Israel conquered Edom and made it a vassal state in the time of David; later, in the time of Amaziah, it was again used as a major battlefield as Judah reasserted its influence over Edom and secured its southern territory.

introduce: The City of Salt is one of the cities located within the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, a place name mentioned in Joshua 15.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the six cities of the wilderness in the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:62).
geography: It is thought to have been in the wilderness of Judea or in the lowland region along the western shore of the Dead Sea, but its exact location has not been clearly determined archaeologically. Since it is mentioned together with coastal cities such as En-gedi, it was probably located in the arid region near the Dead Sea.

introduce: The Salt Sea is the biblical name for what is today called the Dead Sea, a highly saline inland lake at the southernmost end of the Jordan Valley. Called Yam HaMelach in Hebrew, it has an environment in which living creatures can hardly survive because of its distinctive high salinity.
biblecontents: The Valley of Siddim is the Salt Sea (Genesis 14:3). The southern border begins at the end of the Salt Sea (Numbers 34:3). The border goes down to the Jordan and ends at the Salt Sea (Numbers 34:12). The Sea of the Arabah, that is, the Salt Sea, into which the Arabah flows (Deuteronomy 3:17). The waters that flowed down from above stopped and rose up in a heap at a very great distance, at the edge of the city of Adam, near Zarethan, and the waters flowing toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off (Joshua 3:16). It extends eastward to the Sea of the Arabah, and eastward by way of Beth-jeshimoth to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea (Joshua 12:3). Their southern border begins at the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces south (Joshua 15:2). The eastern border is as far as the end of the Salt Sea, the mouth of the Jordan (Joshua 15:5). The northern border passes north of Beth-hoglah and reaches the northern end of the Salt Sea (Joshua 18:19).
geography: The Salt Sea lies at the lowest point of the Jordan Rift Valley, more than about 400 meters below sea level, the lowest point on earth. Much water flows in from the Jordan, but there is no outlet, so evaporation is very high, and in this process large amounts of minerals and salt become concentrated, making it one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world. Topographically, it serves as the boundary connecting the Jordan Valley in the north with the Arabah desert in the south.
history: In the ancient Near East, the Salt Sea was used as a major landmark marking the western and eastern boundaries of the territories of the tribes of Israel. In biblical times salt was actively harvested, and the surrounding area was regarded as a strategic stronghold and as barren wilderness. In ancient society it was also a geographical reference point that had to be consulted when defining the locations of neighboring city-states or when setting military routes.

introduce: Jerusalem is a city of strategic importance in ancient Canaan, mentioned as a major area of conflict during Joshua's wars of conquest. It was first inhabited by the Jebusites, and later became an object of conquest and allotment for the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard of Israel's victories and formed an alliance with the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon to attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:1, Joshua 10:3, Joshua 10:5). Joshua subdued these five kings, brought them out of the cave at Makkedah, and put them to death (Joshua 10:23). This city is recorded as one of the thirty-one kings whom Joshua conquered (Joshua 12:10). Geographically, it lies beside the Valley of the Son of Hinnom and forms the border of the Jebusites (Joshua 15:8). Because the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusite inhabitants of Jerusalem, the Jebusites lived with the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:63). It is mentioned as one of the cities allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:28). Adoni-bezek was brought to Jerusalem and died there (Judges 1:7), and the descendants of Judah struck Jerusalem with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire (Judges 1:8).
geography: Jerusalem lies in the central part of the hill country of Judah, and has natural defensive terrain, situated between the Valley of Hinnom and the Kidron Valley. The area commands the main road of the central mountain range running north and south, and thus occupies a position of great military importance.
history: From the Late Bronze Age onward, Jerusalem was a city inhabited by the Jebusites, and was one of the major city-states of the Canaanite region at that time. It became an object of Israel's conquest in the time of Joshua, but because of the city's strong defenses it took considerable time before the tribes of Judah and Benjamin completely captured it and settled there.

remark: A city of Benjamin, near Moladah.
introduce: Jeshua is a place name recorded as one of the cities in which the descendants of Judah lived after the return from exile, and as one of the administrative districts of Jerusalem and its surroundings in the time of Nehemiah.
biblecontents: Some of the descendants of Judah lived in Jeshua and the villages around it (Nehemiah 11:26).
geography: The exact location of Jeshua has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but judging from the list of other cities mentioned in Nehemiah 11, such as Moladah, Beth-pelet, and Hazar-shual, it is presumed to have been in the Negev region of southern Judah, centered on Beersheba.
history: It is one of the cities that were reorganized as administrative units as the descendants of the tribe of Judah, after the return from the Babylonian exile, recovered and resettled the territory where their ancestors had once lived. This is part of the historical record that shows the reconstruction of the province of Judah and its population distribution under Persian rule.

introduce: This is a region mentioned in 1 Kings 4:31 as the place of origin, or one of the clans, of the men whose wisdom was compared with that of Solomon.
biblecontents: Because Solomon's wisdom was greater than that of Ethan the Ezrahite and of Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, his fame spread to all the surrounding nations (1 Kings 4:31)

introduce: Ono is a city that was located in ancient Palestine; it is closely associated with the dwellings of the tribe of Benjamin and is situated near the plain of Sharon.
biblecontents: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, sons of Elpaal, built Ono and Lod and the villages around them (1 Chronicles 8:12). When Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall, Sanballat and Geshem proposed meeting him on the plain of Ono with the aim of harming him, but Nehemiah refused (Nehemiah 6:2). The descendants of Benjamin who returned after the Babylonian exile lived in Ono and Lod and made them their base (Nehemiah 11:35).
geography: Ono is thought to be Khirbet el-Ona, east of present-day Tel Aviv, Israel. It lies in the plain of Sharon, a strategic crossroads between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country of Judea, and was on the route connecting Joppa and Jerusalem.
history: Ono was incorporated into the territory of the tribe of Benjamin after the conquest of Canaan, but because it bordered the plain of Sharon geographically, it came under the sphere of influence of various political powers. In particular, the fact that after the exile, during the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, the Samaritans and the Arabs tried to use the plain of Ono as a meeting place in order to threaten the community of Judah suggests that Ono was then a border region reached by Judah's influence. Afterward, down to the Roman period, the area continued to be maintained as a center of agriculture and commerce.

introduce: Ophel is a name for a part of the wall of ancient Jerusalem or the district around it; it mainly means the high ground on the eastern slope of the City of David, where the royal palace and the temple were located.
biblecontents: King Jotham built the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD and built extensively on the wall of Ophel (2 Chronicles 27:3). King Manasseh built a wall outside the City of David, on the west side, from the Gihon in the valley to the entrance of the Fish Gate, and he brought it around Ophel and raised it very high (2 Chronicles 33:14). When Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall, the Nethinim lived on Ophel and made repairs as far as in front of the Water Gate on the east (Nehemiah 3:26). After them the men of Tekoa repaired from the great tower that juts out as far as the wall of Ophel (Nehemiah 3:27). The Nethinim lived on Ophel, and Ziha and Gishpa were in charge of them (Nehemiah 11:21).
geography: Ophel lies on the eastern hill of Jerusalem, a slightly projecting hilly area at the point connecting the Temple Mount and the City of David. The Kidron Valley adjoins it on the east, so it is a strategic stronghold favorable for defense, and because of its easy access to the Gihon spring it has great geographical advantages as an early settlement of Jerusalem.
history: From the early Iron Age, Ophel occupied a key position in Jerusalem's defensive system. In particular, when its wall was greatly reinforced by the kings Jotham and Manasseh during the period of the kingdom of Judah, it functioned as the main line of defense protecting the royal palace and the temple precinct. In the time of Nehemiah after the exile, it was used as the area where the Nethinim, who were responsible for temple service, lived, which is an important clue for understanding the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem and its social structure at that time.

introduce: Oboth is one of the encampments where the Israelites stayed during the journey of the Exodus, a place presumed to be in the border region northeast of Edom.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Oboth and camped (Numbers 21:10), and moving on from Oboth they camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness east of Moab (Numbers 21:11). Also, Israel left Punon and camped at Oboth (Numbers 33:43), and left Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, on the border of Moab (Numbers 33:44).
geography: Oboth is thought to lie southeast of the Dead Sea, within the territory of present-day Jordan. Although a precise archaeological identification is difficult, the prevailing view generally places it near Wadi el-Hasa, close to the border between ancient Edom and Moab, or on the plateau to the east of it.
history: It is one of the major points through which Israel passed as it moved east of the Jordan, bypassing the territory of Edom. This region lay on a route connected to the trade routes of the ancient Near East, and had an environment well suited to nomads who moved through it and used it as a temporary dwelling place.

introduce: Ophni is a place name mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: The inheritance received by the tribe of the descendants of Benjamin, according to their families, was Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, Avvim, Parah, Zemaraim, Ophni, Gebani, and Gebaini, twelve cities with their villages (Joshua 18:21-24)

remark: Located south of Arabia; the place from which the products of India were carried to the West.
introduce: Ophir is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament as a region that produced valuable resources such as high-quality gold, gems, and sandalwood. It was regarded as a major source of gold in the ancient Near Eastern trade network, and appears as a place central to the economic prosperity of Solomon's time.
biblecontents: Solomon went by ship with the servants of Hiram to Ophir and brought back 420 talents of gold (1 Kings 9:28). When the ships of Hiram brought gold from Ophir, they also carried almug wood (sandalwood) and precious stones (1 Kings 10:11). King Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to send to Ophir for gold, but the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber (1 Kings 22:48). For the building of the temple, David gave three thousand talents of the gold of Ophir from his own private property (1 Chronicles 29:4). The servants of Solomon, together with the servants of Hiram, went to Ophir and brought back 450 talents of gold (2 Chronicles 8:18). With the almug wood (sandalwood) brought from Ophir, steps were made for the house of the LORD and for the royal palace (2 Chronicles 9:10). In Job there appears the figure of counting dust as the gold of Ophir (Job 22:24), and the value of wisdom is compared with the gold of Ophir (Job 28:16). The queen is described standing before the king adorned with the gold of Ophir (Psalms 45:9). There is a prophetic expression that a man will count pure gold more precious than the gold of Ophir (Isaiah 13:12).
geography: The exact location of Ophir has not been determined archaeologically. According to the biblical record, it is a region that can be reached by a sea route departing from Ezion-geber, which is connected with the Red Sea. Scholars have variously proposed that it was the southern part of the present-day Arabian Peninsula, the region of Ethiopia or Somalia in Africa, or southern India and Sri Lanka. In particular, as a source of gold it is regarded as a strategic point on the ancient trade routes.
history: In the time of Solomon, Israel jointly operated maritime trade with Hiram, king of Tyre in Phoenicia, and imported the resources of Ophir. This shows that Solomon's kingdom had secured a maritime trade route through the Red Sea.
