Afterward, an attempt was also made to use this route in the time of Jehoshaphat, king of southern Judah, but it seems that, because of geographical and technical limits, it was difficult to maintain a lasting trade network. In ancient Near Eastern society, the gold of Ophir was used as a byword for the finest quality.

introduce: Oholibamah is the name of a chief of ancient Edom and also the name of the region that chief ruled. It is one of the place names mentioned in the process of listing the genealogy of Edom in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.
biblecontents: The chief Oholibamah is recorded as one of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:41). He also appears in 1 Chronicles, included in the list of the chiefs of Edom (1 Chronicles 1:52).
geography: Edom is located around Mount Seir, a mountainous region extending from the southeast of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. The place name Oholibamah is presumed to refer to the settlement of a particular tribe within this Edomite highland, but its exact location has not been determined by modern archaeology.

remark: A city of Lower Egypt, east of the Nile.
introduce: On is one of the major cities of ancient Egypt, mentioned in the Bible as a place associated with the family of Asenath, the wife of Joseph. Called On in Hebrew, it is well known by its Greek name, Heliopolis.
biblecontents: Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as his wife (Genesis 41:45). Before the years of famine came, Joseph had two sons by Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Genesis 41:50). In the land of Egypt Joseph fathered Manasseh and Ephraim, who were born to him by Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Genesis 46:20).
geography: On lay at the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, in the area near present-day Heliopolis, northeast of modern Cairo. Situated on a fertile plain close to a branch of the Nile, it functioned from ancient times as a hub of transportation and agriculture.
history: From before the New Kingdom of Egypt it was a major religious center for the worship of the sun god Ra. At that time On was a place where advanced learning and theology flourished, and its priestly class exercised influence at the national level. As a political and religious center of Egypt, it was a city closely connected with the authority of Pharaoh.

introduce: Waheb is a place name found in the Hebrew Bible, a location cited from an ancient document called "the Book of the Wars of the LORD," which appears in Numbers 21:14. This place name is generally understood to refer to a particular area near the Arnon River.
biblecontents: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD: "Waheb in Suphah, and the Valley of the Arnon, and the slopes of all the valleys incline toward the towns of the Arnon and reach the border of Moab" (Numbers 21:14)
geography: Waheb is presumed to be a point located near the Valley of the Arnon, east of the Jordan. Its exact location has not been determined archaeologically, but in the context of the text it is regarded as an area related to the topographical features around the Arnon River or the distribution of its towns.

introduce: The King's Valley is the place, in Genesis 14, to which the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram as he returned after defeating Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and his allies.
biblecontents: When Abram returned after crushing Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom came out to meet him at the King's Valley, that is, the Valley of Shaveh (Genesis 14:17)
geography: The King's Valley is described as the same place as the Valley of Shaveh. According to the traditional view, it is sometimes identified with the Kidron Valley near Jerusalem or its surrounding area, but its exact location is difficult to determine scholarly.

remark: The great river of Palestine.
introduce: Jordan is a geographical term referring to the Jordan River, which runs north and south through the region of Palestine, together with the lowland plains and valleys around it. In the biblical context, Jordan frequently means the eastern boundary of the land of Canaan, or is used to indicate the fertile region near the Jordan River.
biblecontents: Lot lifted up his eyes and looked at the whole region of the Jordan, and the whole land as far as Zoar was well watered, like the garden of the LORD and like the land of Egypt (Genesis 13:10). Lot chose the whole region of the Jordan and moved east, and so they separated from each other (Genesis 13:11). When Jacob crossed the Jordan he had only a staff, but afterward he became two companies (Genesis 32:10). The funeral procession of Jacob came to the threshing floor of Atad beyond the Jordan, and they wept and lamented greatly there (Genesis 50:10). When the inhabitants of the land saw this, they said, "This is a grievous mourning for the Egyptians beyond the Jordan," and named the place Abel-mizraim (Genesis 50:11). The Amalekites live in the land of the Negev, the Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites live in the hill country, and the Canaanites live by the sea and along the Jordan (Numbers 13:29). The Israelites set out and camped in the plains of Moab, which was beyond the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 22:1). Moses and Eleazar the priest took a census of the people in the plains of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 26:3). These were those numbered by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who numbered the Israelites in the plains of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 26:63). Moses brought the captives and the plunder to the camp in the plains of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 31:12).
geography: The Jordan region is formed around the Jordan Rift Valley, which begins at Mount Hermon in the north, passes through the Sea of Galilee, and reaches the Dead Sea. The plains along the Jordan mentioned in the Bible were abundant in water and had fertile soil favorable to farming and herding. In particular, the plains of Moab lie on the east side of the lower Jordan and are a strategic location geographically close to Jericho.
history: The Jordan region was the main gathering place where the people of Israel assembled before crossing the Jordan River in the course of the conquest of Canaan. The plains of Moab by the Jordan, which appear in Numbers, were the place where Israel conducted a census and made its military preparations before entering Canaan, and are a turning point in biblical history. It also served as an important geographical setting from the patriarchal period, including the separation of Abraham and Lot and Jacob's return, down to the period of Israel's settlement.

remark: 1. A Levitical city of Zebulun.
introduce: Jokneam is a place recorded as one of the cities of the Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua at the time of the conquest of Canaan, and afterward, in the distribution among the tribes of Israel, as a city located in the border region of the tribe of Zebulun and allotted to the Levites.
biblecontents: The list of the Canaanite kings conquered by Joshua includes the king of Jokneam in Carmel (Joshua 12:22). When the land of Canaan was divided, the border of the tribe of Zebulun extended eastward past Jokneam (Joshua 19:11). Afterward it was designated as a city for the Levites, the descendants of Merari (Joshua 21:34).
geography: It is identified with Tel Yokneam in present-day northern Israel, which lies at the eastern foot of Mount Carmel and is a strategic gateway into the Jezreel Valley. Because of its geographical advantage of being close to Megiddo and the spring of Harod, it was a key base for transportation and military defense from ancient times.
history: Traces of human habitation have been found from the Bronze Age, and before the Israelite settlement it was under the rule of Canaanite city-states. After Joshua's conquest it became territory of the tribes of Israel, and it is judged to have played an important role as a northern line of defense of the kingdom of Israel in the Iron Age.

remark: 2. A city of Ephraim.
introduce: Jokmeam is a city belonging to Solomon's fifth administrative district, recorded in 1 Kings 4, and is identified with Jokmeam in the central Jordan Valley.
biblecontents: Baana the son of Ahilud had Taanach and Megiddo and all of Beth-shean beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as beyond Jokmeam (1 Kings 4:12).
geography: It is presumed to be the site of Tell el-Mazar, near Zarethan and Abel-meholah, west of the mouth of the Jabbok River in the central Jordan Valley.
history: In the 10th century BC it was a major administrative base of Solomon's kingdom, and a jurisdictional center that oversaw the transport of grain and supplies from the granary region running through the Jordan Valley.

introduce: Jokdeam is an ancient city mentioned as part of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah. It is one of the places appearing in the place-name lists of the ancient Near East, and is included in the list of cities located in the hill country of Judah.
biblecontents: Jokdeam is recorded in the list of the cities of the inheritance obtained by the tribe of the descendants of Judah when the Israelites were allotted the land of Canaan (Joshua 15:56).
geography: Jokdeam is presumed to be one of the cities located in the Hebron highlands in the southern part of the hill country of Judah. Scholars differ on its detailed geographic coordinates and on the exact site of its ruins today, and together with nearby cities such as Ziph, Gattah, and Bozkath, it is classified as part of the southeastern area of the hill country of Judah.

remark: 1. A city in the west of the lowland of Judah.
introduce: One of the cities allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah, a place name located in the Shephelah plain of southern Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities that Joshua apportioned by lot to the tribe of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 15:38).
geography: It is included in the list of the southern cities of the tribe of Judah, and geographically it is presumed to belong to the Shephelah, a buffer zone between the hill country of Judah and the Philistine plain.

remark: 2. The name given by Amaziah after he conquered Sela of Edom.
introduce: Joktheel is a city of Edom that was conquered in the time of Amaziah, king of Judah, and temporarily incorporated into the territory of Judah.
biblecontents: Amaziah, king of Judah, killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, took Sela in battle, and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this day (2 Kings 14:7).
geography: Scholarly opinion is divided over the exact location of Joktheel, but it is generally presumed to be the same place as Sela (Petra), the capital of Edom. It is a strategic stronghold in the rugged mountain region south of the Arabah valley.
history: Around the 8th century BC the kingdom of Judah launched a military expedition against Edom to the south and temporarily controlled the area. At that time King Amaziah renamed the conquered Sela as Joktheel, seeking to display Judah's authority. However, this rule of Judah was not maintained for long, and the region afterward returned to the influence of Edom.

introduce: Jokmeam is a strategic location in the northern plain of Canaan, and was one of the cities allotted to the descendants of the tribe of Levi in Old Testament times.
biblecontents: Jokmeam is recorded as a Levitical city located within the territory of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the dwellings distributed to the clan of Gemu, a descendant of Kohath (1 Chronicles 6:68).
geography: It corresponds to Tel Yokneam at the eastern foot of Mount Carmel in present-day northern Israel, and has the geographical advantage of watching over the route linking the Jezreel plain and the coastal plain.
history: It was originally a region ruled by Canaanite kings, but it was captured in the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan, and afterward was managed as an important base defending the northern border and main transportation routes of Israelite territory.

introduce: Jogbehah is one of the cities located east of the Jordan in ancient Israel, an area captured and rebuilt by the Gadites.
biblecontents: The descendants of Gad built Atroth-shophan, Jazer, and Jogbehah (Numbers 32:35). When Gideon went up by the way of those who lived in tents on the east and surprised the Midianites, he passed near Jogbehah (Judges 8:11).
geography: It is identified with the area of Jai, about 10 km northwest of Amman, Jordan, today. This area lies on the route going up from the Jordan Valley to the plateau, and so has the character of a strategic stronghold.
history: In the process by which the tribes of Israel were allotted the land east of the Jordan before the conquest of Canaan, it was incorporated into the inheritance of the tribe of Gad. Afterward, in the time of the judges, its geographical position is mentioned as a military route when Gideon pursued the Midianite army.

introduce: Joppa is an ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast that served as the closest sea gateway to Jerusalem. It corresponds to the Tel Aviv-Yafo area of present-day Israel, and throughout the Bible is described as a center of maritime transport and trade.
biblecontents: Joppa is mentioned as one of the cities located on the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:46). For the building of the temple, Solomon floated the cedars cut in Lebanon on the sea to Joppa, and had them carried from there to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 2:16). Later, when the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, cedars brought from Lebanon were likewise delivered through the port of Joppa (Ezra 3:7). In order to avoid God's command to go to Nineveh, Jonah boarded a ship at Joppa bound for Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). In the New Testament era, there was a woman disciple in Joppa named Tabitha, and when Peter performed the miracle of raising her, many people learned of it and believed in the Lord (Acts 9:36, 38, 42). While staying in Joppa, Peter saw a vision, and he went to Caesarea to meet the men sent by Cornelius (Acts 9:43, 10:5, 8).
geography: Joppa lies in the central part of the coastal plain of Palestine and is a natural harbor on the Mediterranean coast. It had conditions suitable for anchoring ships, and served as the main passage from inland Jerusalem to the sea. However, unlike Caesarea to the north, it had many reefs, so there were geographical limits on the docking of large ships.
history: Joppa served as an international trading port from ancient times, so much so that it appears even in Egyptian records of the second millennium BC. Because of its geopolitically important position, it often came under the rule of the surrounding great powers, such as Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, and Greece. In particular, it was closely connected with the maritime activities of the Phoenicians and was used as a logistics base for carrying materials for the building of the temple.

introduce: Jotbah is a place name recorded in the Bible as the hometown of Meshullemeth, the mother of Amon, king of the kingdom of Judah.
biblecontents: Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for two years. His mother's name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah (2 Kings 21:19)

introduce: Jotbathah is one of the places the Israelites passed through on the route of the Exodus, a region located between Hadad and Abronah.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah (Numbers 33:33), and left Jotbathah and camped at Abronah (Numbers 33:34). Later, in Deuteronomy, it is said that Israel left Budera and came to Jotbathah, which is mentioned as a region where streams flow (Deuteronomy 10:7).
geography: Jotbathah is presumed to be located in the Arabah valley region of southern present-day Jordan, and is known as a place with the topographical feature of abundant flowing water (Deuteronomy 10:7).

introduce: The Well of the Serpent is the name of a gate that Nehemiah scouted at night while assessing the condition of the wall in order to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: When Nehemiah rose by night with a few men to inspect the wall of Jerusalem, he went out by the Valley Gate and headed toward the Well of the Serpent, and came to the Dung Gate (Nehemiah 2:13).
geography: The Well of the Serpent is presumed to have been in the southwestern section of the wall of Jerusalem, and appears to have stood between the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate. Whether this place was topographically connected with water sources such as the Gihon spring or En-rogel is under archaeological discussion.
history: After the Babylonian exile, with the wall of Jerusalem in ruins, this was a strategic point through which Nehemiah passed to gather basic information for rebuilding the wall. The name Well of the Serpent is understood to refer to a particular well or spring that existed near the wall at that time.

introduce: Uphaz is a place name appearing in the biblical text, referring to a region known in the ancient Near East as a source of gold. Some ancient translations suppose it to be the same place as Ophir.
biblecontents: Craftsmen made ornaments with silver brought from Tarshish and gold brought from Uphaz (Jeremiah 10:9). In a vision Daniel saw a man dressed in linen, with a belt of pure gold from Uphaz around his waist (Daniel 10:5).
geography: Its exact geographical location has not been confirmed. However, on the basis of its characteristic, mentioned in the text, as a source of gold, scholars conjecture that it was a particular region in the southern Arabian Peninsula, in Ethiopia, or near India.

introduce: Uzzen-sheerah is an ancient place name that appears in 1 Chronicles 7:24, a place related to the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim.
biblecontents: Sheerah, a daughter of Ephraim, built Lower Beth-horon, Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah (1 Chronicles 7:24).
geography: Uzzen-sheerah is presumed to have been located near Beth-horon, but no specific archaeological site or modern place-name location has been clearly confirmed. It is generally classified as a neighboring village or settlement of the Beth-horon area.

introduce: Ummah is a place name that is thought to have been located in the northern Galilee region, one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Asher mentioned in the book of Joshua.
biblecontents: Ummah is recorded as one of the cities included within the boundaries of the inheritance that the tribe of Asher obtained by lot (Joshua 19:30).
geography: Opinions differ among scholars about its exact location, but it is generally presumed to have been in the Galilean coastal plain or the area near the Acre River. Archaeologically, several candidate sites, such as Tell ed-Duweir in the Acre area, have been proposed, but there is no clearly identified point.

introduce: Izal is a place name mentioned in Ezekiel 27:19 as one of the regions that traded with Tyre. In the Hebrew original it is read as Udal or Vedan, and it is presumed to have been a place that supplied spices and finely made goods within the trade network of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: Izal and Javan traded with Tyre in goods produced at Uzal, and among the goods they sold were bright iron, cassia, and spices (Ezekiel 27:19).
geography: There is debate among scholars about its exact location, but there are broadly two views. The first regards it as a region in the northwest of the Arabian Peninsula; the second identifies it with the area of Waddan, near Yemen in southwestern Saudi Arabia. In both cases it has the character of a major hub on the spice trade route passing through the Arabian Peninsula.
history: Around the 6th century BC, the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula supplied spices, ironware, and precious metals, by camel caravan trade, to commercial states such as Tyre on the Mediterranean coast. At that time Izal functioned as one of the trade hubs where goods produced in the Arabian interior or imported from places such as India were gathered. This passage is a historical source showing that the international trade network of the ancient world extended widely as far as the southern and interior parts of the Arabian Peninsula.

remark: 1. The descendants of Judah and the territory they possessed.
introduce: Judah is the name of a major tribe of Israel that began with Jacob's fourth son, and also of a particular region of southern Canaan. This tribe was regarded as a line symbolizing ruling authority and spiritual authority in the history of Israel, and played a central role in the census and in military marches.
biblecontents: Jacob prophesied to Judah that the scepter would not depart from Judah, and that the ruler's staff would not depart from between his feet (Genesis 49:10). Bezalel, a grandson of Hur of the tribe of Judah and a son of Uri, was appointed to be in charge of making the tabernacle (Exodus 31:2, Exodus 35:30, Exodus 38:22). In the census the tribe of Judah was recorded as having Nahshon as its commander, and a total of 74,600 was reported (Numbers 1:7, Numbers 1:27). When marching in the wilderness, the tribe of Judah led the camp, marching at the front with its standard (Numbers 2:3, Numbers 2:9, Numbers 10:14). At the dedication of the tabernacle, Nahshon, the commander of the tribe of Judah, brought his offering (Numbers 7:12).
geography: The region of Judah is terrain that includes the mountainous country of southern Canaan and the wilderness around it. On the north it borders the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, and on the west it adjoins the Shephelah, the coastal plain. On the south it continues into the Negev desert, and on the east it connects to the Dead Sea and the wilderness of Judah, forming a natural line of defense.
history: Judah established itself as the tribe that exercised leadership among the sons of Jacob, and after the Exodus, in the course of the movement through the wilderness, it showed organized military strength and administrative standing. Afterward, in the period of the conquest of Canaan, it settled mainly in the southern region and laid the political foundation that became the basis of the Davidic dynasty, and throughout the history of Israel it played the role of a center of legitimacy and government.

remark: 2. The region ruled by Rehoboam after the rebellion of the ten tribes.
introduce: Judah refers to the territory of the southern kingdom of Judah, ruled by Rehoboam and his descendants, who succeeded the Davidic dynasty when the kingdom of Israel was divided after the death of Solomon.
biblecontents: Rehoboam became king over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah (1 Kings 12:17). No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah (1 Kings 12:20). When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, and there were 180,000 warriors (2 Chronicles 11:1).
geography: This is the territory of southern Palestine, including the central hill country of Judah, the Shephelah, the Negev desert, and the western shore of the Dead Sea. On the north it touches the border of the tribe of Benjamin, and on the south it borders Edom.
history: From the division of the united kingdom of Israel around 930 BC until its destruction by Babylon in 586 BC, for about 340 years, it was an ancient state that maintained the legitimacy of the Davidic dynasty and continued to exist centered on the temple in Jerusalem.

introduce: Judea is a place name referring to the highland of southern Palestine; historically it signifies the main settlement area of the people of Israel and a political and religious center that includes Jerusalem.
biblecontents: It was prophesied that Bethlehem in the land of Judea is by no means the least among the towns of Judea, and that a ruler would come out of the land called Judea (Matthew 2:5-6). The Magi came to Judea to seek the one who was born king of the Jews (Matthew 2:2). Hearing that Archelaus had succeeded his father Herod as king of Judea, he was afraid to go there (Matthew 2:22). John the Baptist began to preach in the wilderness of Judea (Matthew 3:1), and people came out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region around the Jordan (Matthew 3:5). The news about Jesus spread throughout all Syria, and great crowds followed him from Judea, the Decapolis, and beyond the Jordan (Matthew 4:25). When Jesus had finished his teaching, he left Galilee and came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan (Matthew 19:1). There is a warning that those who are in Judea should flee to the mountains (Matthew 24:16), and Pilate asked Jesus, "Are you the king of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11).
geography: Judea is a mountainous region bordered on the south by the Negev desert, on the north by Samaria, on the west by the coastal plain, and on the east by the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea. The highland centered on Jerusalem has terrain favorable for defense.
history: After the Babylonian exile, through the Persian and Hellenistic periods, the Hasmonean dynasty maintained independence. Afterward, through Roman intervention, the Herodian dynasty came to rule, and in the New Testament period it was a province of the Roman Empire, a system in which it was either directly administered by a Roman governor or ruled by tetrarchs of the house of Herod.

introduce: Bethlehem in Judea is an ancient city located in the territory of the tribe of Judah, in the central mountain region of Palestine, about 8 km south of Jerusalem. This area is known as the hometown of David, and in the New Testament period it is recorded as the place to which Joseph and Mary, who were from Nazareth, traveled for the birth of Jesus.
biblecontents: In the time of King Herod, Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, and Magi from the east came to Jerusalem and said (Matthew 2:1). "And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judea, are by no means the least among the rulers of Judea; for from you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel" (Matthew 2:6).
geography: It lies on high ground at about 770 m above sea level, and is a hilly region composed of limestone geology. The surroundings consist of terraced fields, with conditions suitable for cultivating grain, grapes, olives, and the like. It is a stopping point on the north-south road network linking Jerusalem and Hebron, and has the topographical feature of adjoining the wilderness.
history: In the Old Testament period it was also called Ephrath, and appears as a center related to the period of the judges and the origin of the Davidic dynasty. Around the 1st century, under Roman imperial rule, it was under the Roman governorship of Judea and functioned as an administrative base for the census. In the political turmoil of Judean society at that time, it was often mentioned as a region onto which messianic expectations connected with a figure from David's lineage were projected.

introduce: The Euphrates is the longest river with the greatest flow in western Asia, the cradle of ancient Near Eastern civilization, and, in the biblical setting, a geographical crossroads mentioned as the boundary of the promised land and as a reference point for the spheres of influence of major political powers.
biblecontents: It is described as the fourth of the four rivers that flowed out of the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:14). In the covenant God made with Abram, it was set as the northern boundary of the land to be given to the descendants of Israel (Genesis 15:18). It is mentioned as the home of Saul of Rehoboth on the River (Genesis 36:37). It is repeatedly stated as the limit of the territory Israel was to occupy (Deuteronomy 1:7, Deuteronomy 11:24, Joshua 1:4). King David went as far as the Euphrates to restore his rule (2 Samuel 8:3). King Josiah marched toward the Euphrates to stop Neco, king of Egypt (2 Kings 23:29). The king of Egypt lost the territory as far as the Euphrates to the king of Babylon (2 Kings 24:7). The descendants of Reuben raised livestock and lived from the Euphrates to the entrance of the wilderness (1 Chronicles 5:9).
geography: It rises in the Armenian Highlands of eastern Turkey, passes through the plains of Syria and Iraq, and then joins the Tigris and flows into the Persian Gulf. It forms the western side of the ancient Mesopotamian plain, and served as the water source essential to agriculture and irrigation systems in the surrounding region.
history: It was the central stage on which the major empires of Mesopotamia, such as Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, and Assyria, rose and fell. In biblical history it functioned as a strategic crossing that the great powers north of Israel had to cross when marching toward Egypt or the southern Near East, and as a major point in the struggles for supremacy that decided the balance of power between empires.

introduce: Juttah was a city located within the territory of the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel, one of the inheritances distributed to the descendants of Judah after Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: Among the cities of the land that the tribe of Judah obtained by lot, Juttah is mentioned together with Maon, Carmel, and Ziph (Joshua 15:55). It is also recorded as one of the cities given to the descendants of Aaron, a descendant of Levi (Joshua 21:16).
geography: It is presumed to have been located near Hebron in the southern part of the hill country of Judah, and the prevailing theory identifies it with the same place as the modern site Khirbet et-Tarr.
history: After the conquest it was included in the hill-country district of Judah in Israel's administrative divisions, and was designated a priestly city, a dwelling place of the tribe of Levi, where it performed religious and administrative functions.

introduce: Ulai is a place name appearing in the book of Daniel in the Old Testament, the name of a river or canal located in the region of Elam. It is recorded as the place where Daniel saw a vision.
biblecontents: Daniel records that when he was in the citadel of Susa in the province of Elam, he saw a vision by the Ulai canal (Daniel 8:2). There also appears a scene in which a man's voice from between the banks of the Ulai commands Gabriel to make Daniel understand the vision (Daniel 8:16).
geography: The Ulai is presumed to be a landform in the Khuzestan plain, in the southwestern part of present-day Iran. It appears to refer to a stream or part of the canal network that flowed near the ancient city of Susa, and scholars analyze it as having been within the system of waterways associated with the present-day Karun or Karkheh rivers.
history: In the period of the Babylonian Empire and later the Persian Empire, Susa was used as a major administrative center and a residence of the king. The Ulai, as a major waterway flowing around Susa, played an important role in the city's economic activity and water transport. Ancient records identify this waterway as a canal or river near Susa.

introduce: Iconium was a city in the region of Lycaonia in ancient Asia Minor, a place that served as a major base during the apostle Paul's first and second missionary journeys. It corresponds to the area of Konya in present-day Turkey.
biblecontents: After Paul and Barnabas were driven out of Pisidian Antioch, they went to Iconium and preached the gospel in the Jewish synagogue there (Acts 13:51, Acts 14:1). Many Jews and Greeks believed in Iconium, but when the Jews who rejected the gospel stirred up the Gentiles and tried to stone Paul and his companions, they fled to Lystra and Derbe (Acts 14:19). Afterward Paul visited Iconium again in order to encourage the disciples (Acts 14:21). Timothy is mentioned as a man well spoken of by the brothers in Iconium (Acts 16:2), and in 2 Timothy Paul recalls that he endured the persecution he suffered at Iconium (2 Timothy 3:11).
geography: Iconium lies in a fertile plain at an altitude of about 1,000 meters on the Anatolian plateau. It is a strategic crossroads where major routes of travel such as the Royal Road intersect, connecting with Pisidian Antioch to the west and Derbe to the east. Thanks to its topographical characteristic of securing abundant water resources in contrast to the surrounding mountainous regions, the city developed early.
history: Iconium was originally part of the kingdom of Phrygia, but in the Roman period it was incorporated into the province of Galatia. During the reign of the Roman emperor Claudius it was also called by the name Claudia, and it had a Roman-style system of city administration. It was a place where Greek culture and the Roman administrative system coexisted, and it had a multicultural environment in which Roman citizens and the Jewish community lived mixed together.

introduce: Idalah is a city of ancient Palestine mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a place recorded as one of the inheritances distributed to the tribe of Zebulun.
biblecontents: Idalah is included among the cities chosen as an inheritance for the tribe of the descendants of Zebulun according to their families (Joshua 19:15).
geography: Opinions are divided among scholars about its exact location, but it is generally presumed to have been within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in the southern part of the Galilee region.

introduce: Italy is a place name that refers to Italia in Latin, a name covering the whole Italian peninsula, the center of the ancient Roman Empire. In the biblical record it is mentioned as a base for administrative, military, and travel purposes connected with the Roman Empire.
biblecontents: At Caesarea appears Cornelius, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment (Acts 10:1). Aquila and Priscilla, a married couple, left Italy at the command of the emperor Claudius and settled in Corinth (Acts 18:2). When the apostle Paul was being taken to Rome as a prisoner, he boarded a ship bound for Italy (Acts 27:1). The centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put Paul on board (Acts 27:6). The writer of Hebrews notes that those from Italy also send greetings to the recipients (Hebrews 13:24).
geography: Italy refers to the boot-shaped Italian peninsula in the middle of the Mediterranean. As the core homeland of the ancient Roman Empire, it was joined to the European continent along the Alps, and played the role of a strategic hub of Mediterranean maritime trade. The major port city of Puteoli and the city of Rome were the centers of this region.
history: In the 1st century, Italy was the political, economic, and judicial center of the Roman Empire. The Italian Regiment is presumed to have been a unit of the Roman legions composed of citizens from Italy. The Roman emperor Claudius issued an edict expelling the Jews from Rome on account of disturbances among the Jews, and as a result Jewish diaspora movement occurred throughout the Mediterranean. Italy was also the final destination to which prisoners who had appealed to the Roman emperor were taken to be tried.

introduce: Ithrite is a place name mentioned in the biblical record as the place of origin of Ira, one of David's mighty men, and is reported to be a region related to the origin of the family of Ira.
biblecontents: Ira, one of David's mighty men, is recorded as an Ithrite (2 Samuel 23:38). According to the record in 1 Chronicles, the Ithrites appear as a family or region where one of the clans of Kiriath-jearim settled, and it is stated that the clans of Kiriath-jearim consisted of four clans, including the Ithrites (1 Chronicles 2:53). Also in the list of David's mighty men, it is confirmed again that Ira was an Ithrite (1 Chronicles 11:40).
geography: The exact location of the Ithrites has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is presumed to be an area with a close kinship or geographical connection to Kiriath-jearim. Kiriath-jearim is located in the hill-country region of the tribe of Judah.

introduce: Ituraea is the name of an administrative district that referred to the northeastern part of Palestine in the New Testament period, one of the territories of the tetrarchs who were then under Roman rule.
biblecontents: In Luke, when explaining the time at which John the Baptist began his ministry, Ituraea appears in the mention that Philip was tetrarch of the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1).
geography: Ituraea is a region lying east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, and includes the mountainous country between the western slopes of Mount Hermon and the southwest of Damascus. It corresponds to the border area between southeastern Lebanon and southwestern Syria today.
history: It was originally a region inhabited by the Itureans, a nomadic people of Arab stock, and around the 2nd century BC it was conquered by Aristobulus I of the Hasmonean house and forcibly converted to Judaism. Afterward, after Pompey of Rome occupied the region, upon the death of Herod the Great his son Philip was entrusted by the Roman emperor, as tetrarch, with authority over the territory including the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and governed it.

introduce: Idumea is a Greek place name derived from the Hebrew Edom, a name referring to the southern region of ancient Palestine and the descendants of the Edomite people who lived there.
biblecontents: When Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, a great crowd followed from Galilee, and from Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and around Tyre and Sidon, many people who heard of the great things he was doing came to him (Mark 3:8)
geography: Idumea refers to the region that includes Hebron, south of the hill country of Judah, and extends in the south as far as the Negev desert and the Arabah valley. On the east it adjoins the east side of the Jordan, and this region generally has the topographical features of being dry and barren.
history: During the Babylonian exile the Edomites migrated to the southern region of Judah and settled there. Later they were forcibly converted to Judaism by John Hyrcanus I of the Hasmonean house and annexed to the Jewish state. In the late 1st century BC, when Herod the Great, who was from Idumea, became king of the Jews, it came to occupy a politically important position.

introduce: Ithlah is one of the cities included in the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Dan, recorded in Joshua 19 in the Bible.
biblecontents: Ithlah is included in the list of cities of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Dan obtained by lot (Joshua 19:42).
geography: Ithlah is presumed to have been located in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judea, but no specific archaeological site has been clearly identified. Rabbinic literature and the like classify it as geographically adjacent to the neighboring places Aijalon and Shaalabbin.

introduce: Iram is a name referring to the chiefs of the Edomite clans, or to the region of the tribal unit they ruled. It is mentioned together with the list of the rulers of Edom in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, and is used as a proper noun that shows the social structure and settlements of Edom.
biblecontents: The chiefs of Edom were called after their dwelling places and names, and among them Iram is included in the list that continues: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth, chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon, chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar, chief Magdiel, and chief Iram (Genesis 36:43). In 1 Chronicles as well, chief Iram is mentioned in the course of listing the chiefs of Edom in the same way (1 Chronicles 1:54).
geography: The region of Edom, where Iram was located, is a mountainous area centered on the Arabah valley southeast of the Dead Sea, and in ancient times it was also called the hill country of Seir. It is difficult to determine archaeologically the specific boundaries or exact point of Iram, but as the base of the Edomite chiefs it is presumed to have been distributed on the eastern plateau of the Arabah valley.

introduce: Iron is a place name mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, one of the tribes of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: According to Joshua 19:38, Iron is included in the list of cities of the inheritance that the descendants of Naphtali obtained by lot. This city is recorded as one of nineteen cities, together with Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh (Joshua 19:38).
geography: The exact location of Iron has not been clearly identified archaeologically at present. However, from the context of the Bible, it is presumed to have been within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, in the northern Galilee region or near the Hula basin.

introduce: Irpeel is one of the cities allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Benjamin, appearing in Joshua 18:27.
biblecontents: It is recorded as one of the twelve cities distributed to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18:27).
geography: Irpeel is a city within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, but its exact modern location has not been clearly identified archaeologically. Since the cities of the tribe of Benjamin were mostly distributed between the north of Jerusalem and the Jordan Valley, this place too is presumed to have been located in that vicinity.

introduce: Ir-shemesh is a place name mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, one of the cities included in the inheritance border of the tribe of Dan, one of the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: The border of the inheritance of the descendants of Dan was Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Shaalabbin, Aijalon, and Ithlah (Joshua 19:41)
geography: It is described as a region adjoining Zorah and Eshtaol, and is presumed to have been located in the plain or hill country near the Valley of Sorek. Archaeologically, the prevailing view is that it refers to the same area as Beth-shemesh.

introduce: Ibleam is a city in northern Canaan mentioned in the Old Testament, a strategic stronghold that was located within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh but where the native Canaanites lived.
biblecontents: The descendants of Manasseh were allotted Ibleam and its surrounding villages within the territory of the tribes of Issachar and Asher, but did not capture them (Joshua 17:11). Because the tribe of Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants of Ibleam, the Canaanites continued to live in this land (Judges 1:27). Ahaziah, king of northern Israel, fleeing from Jehu's rebellion, was wounded on the ascent of Gur near Ibleam, fled as far as Megiddo, and died there (2 Kings 9:27).
geography: It lies at the southern end of the Jezreel Valley, and is identified with the area of Tel Bil'ameh today. Situated at the entrance of the Dothan valley, it was in a position controlling an important military passage linking Jezreel in the north with the hill country of Samaria in the south.
history: From the Bronze Age to the Iron Age it was an important stronghold, so much so that it even appears in the records of the Egyptian Thutmose III. In the early period of Israel's settlement, although it had been allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, its capture was delayed for a long time because of the strong defenses of the native Canaanites, and afterward its importance as a military route continued down to the period of the northern kingdom of Israel.

introduce: Izrahite appears as the place of origin of Shamhuth, a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles 27:8, or as the name of the division to which he belonged; it is a place name for which no geographic reality or historical event is specified in the biblical record.
biblecontents: Shamhuth the Izrahite, commander of the fifth month in the organization of King David's army, led his division (1 Chronicles 27:8).

remark: 1. The nation established by the descendants of Jacob, the territory in which they lived, and the house of Israel.
introduce: Israel is the name Jacob received after wrestling with an angel at the ford of the Jabbok, and afterward became a proper noun referring to the nation made up of his descendants and the region in which they lived.
biblecontents: The name Israel was given as Jacob's new name after the incident of his wrestling with the angel (Genesis 32:32). In the incident at Shechem, it is mentioned that Jacob's sons did a disgraceful thing in Israel (Genesis 34:7). The descendants of Jacob lived in the land of Goshen and were fruitful and multiplied (Genesis 47:27). In blessing the sons of Joseph, Jacob wished that the name Israel would be invoked through them (Genesis 48:20). Jacob remarked that the anger of Simeon and Levi was cruel, and prophesied that he would divide them in Israel (Genesis 49:7). The tribe of Dan, as one of the tribes of Israel, is said to carry out judgment (Genesis 49:16). Jacob confesses that Joseph's strength came by the hands of the Mighty One of Israel (Genesis 49:24). These are the ones who make up the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 49:28). Moses was instructed to gather the elders of Israel and convey the commission he had received from God (Exodus 3:16). Afterward Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and told him that the LORD, the God of Israel, said to let the people go (Exodus 5:1).
geography: Located in the Levant region of the ancient Near East, it is a strategic crossroads linking the Fertile Crescent in the north with the Sinai Peninsula in the south and the Goshen region of Egypt.
history: It was formed along the migration routes of the early patriarchal period, and contains a national identity that combines the historical experience of migrating to and living in Egypt with the settled will to return to the land of Canaan.

remark: 2. The nation established by the ten tribes that rebelled.
introduce: Israel refers to the northern kingdom of Israel, established by the ten northern tribes centered on Jeroboam I, who rebelled against Rehoboam's oppressive rule after Solomon's death.
biblecontents: When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel (1 Kings 12:20). The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he reigned, are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel (1 Kings 14:19).
geography: It is a fertile and vast territory encompassing the hill country of Samaria west of the Jordan River, all of Galilee, and Gilead and the plateau of Bashan east of the Jordan. The capital was settled finally in Samaria, after Shechem and Tirzah.
history: Founded around 930 BC, it enjoyed prosperity during the reigns of Omri, Ahab, Jeroboam II, and others, but after frequent coups it was destroyed in 722 BC by the Assyrian empire, under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II.

remark: 1. A city in the hill country of Judah, near Jokdeam and Zanoah.
introduce: Jezreel is one of the cities in the southern hill country of Judah, the hometown of Ahinoam, David's early wife, and a homonymous place name within the territory of the tribe of Judah, distinct from the Jezreel Valley in northern Galilee.
biblecontents: Jezreel was included in the list of cities of the southern hill country distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, together with Jokdeam and Zanoah (Joshua 15:56). David took Ahinoam the Jezreelite as his wife (1 Samuel 25:43). When David went into exile to Achish, king of Gath of the Philistines, he accompanied Ahinoam (1 Samuel 27:3). When the Amalekites raided Ziklag, Ahinoam was taken captive and rescued by David (1 Samuel 30:5). When David went up to Hebron at God's direction, he took Ahinoam the Jezreelite with him (2 Samuel 2:2).
geography: It is located in the southern mountainous region of the tribe of Judah, and was situated in the hilly country near Maon, southeast of Hebron, and the wilderness of Ziph. It is a barren mountain settlement completely separated geographically from the plain of Jezreel in northern Galilee.
history: It was a dwelling place of a family of the tribe of Judah, formed in the course of the tribe of Judah's settlement of the hill country in the early Iron Age. By forming a marriage alliance with a leading family of Jezreel at the time when David, escaping Saul's oppression, was gathering a base of support in the southern mountain region of Judah, he strengthened his political standing.

remark: 2. A city of the tribe of Issachar, near Megiddo and Beth-shean; later the possession of the tribe of Manasseh.
introduce: Jezreel is a city located in the Jezreel Valley, a fertile plain in northern Israel; it was a strategic stronghold and one of the centers of political and military conflict in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Jezreel is mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Issachar (Joshua 19:18). In the time of King Saul, the Philistine army camped at Jezreel (1 Samuel 29:1), and the Philistines went up to Jezreel (1 Samuel 29:11).
geography: A vast plain lying between the Galilee region and the hill country of Samaria, it serves as an east-west crossroads connecting Megiddo and Beth-shan. It has fertile soil, favorable for farming, and because its elevation is lower than the surrounding terrain it was often used as a military route.
history: In the Bronze and Iron Ages it was connected to the Way of the Sea, the international road linking Egypt and Mesopotamia, and so was of very high political and economic value. For this reason it was a strategic stronghold where military clashes frequently occurred among Egypt, the Canaanite city-states, and the kingdom of Israel.

remark: 3. A valley or plain facing Jezreel.
introduce: Jezreel refers to the fertile plain region lying between southern Galilee and the hill country of Samaria in northern Palestine, and to the city of the same name that formed around it. It has important significance as a strategic place linking the major trade routes and military strongholds of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: At the time of the conquest of Canaan, the descendants of Joseph complained that the hill country was too narrow, but the Canaanites living in the Valley of Jezreel had iron chariots, so they had difficulty conquering them (Joshua 17:16). Afterward, when the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the people of the east joined together, camped in the Valley of Jezreel, and invaded, Gideon, receiving the Spirit of the LORD, blew the trumpet and fought against them (Judges 6:33).
geography: The plain of Jezreel is a triangular landform stretching long from east to west; on the west it connects with the plain of Asher on the Mediterranean coast, and on the east it continues to the Jordan Valley. This region is composed of volcanic soil and alluvium, and has been known since ancient times as a fertile granary optimized for agriculture. Lying at the boundary with the surrounding hill country, it is encircled like a folding screen by highlands such as Mount Tabor, Mount Moreh, and Mount Gilboa.
history: From the Bronze Age it was the connecting point between the Way of the Sea and the King's Highway, international routes, and became a point of military confrontation between the civilizations of Egypt and Mesopotamia. As it entered the Iron Age, the Canaanite tribes that operated iron chariots built a strong defensive system by making use of the flat terrain of the plain, and this acted as a considerable military threat to the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Ishmael was a person born to Abraham and Hagar, but in the biblical record the descendants of Ishmael are used mainly as an ethnic concept referring to nomadic groups living in northern Arabia and the regions near it. They frequently appear as merchant groups connected with the caravan trade of the ancient Near East.
biblecontents: Joseph's brothers sold Joseph to the Midianites, but these were caravans of Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:25). Those who bought Joseph were a caravan of Ishmaelites, and his brothers agreed to this (Genesis 37:27). When the merchants of the Ishmaelites passed by, they drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him for twenty pieces of silver, and they took Joseph to Egypt (Genesis 37:28). Joseph, who had been sold into Egypt, was purchased by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, and Potiphar was the one who had bought him from the Ishmaelites who brought him there (Genesis 39:1). The gold earrings that Gideon obtained as plunder after defeating the Midianites were collected because the Ishmaelites had the custom of wearing gold earrings (Judges 8:24). Amasa, one of the commanders of David's army, was born to Jether the Ishmaelite and David's sister Abigail (1 Chronicles 2:17). Among the officials who managed King David's livestock was Obil the Ishmaelite, who was in charge of the camels (1 Chronicles 27:30). Among the list of allies against Israel are the tents of the Ishmaelites (Psalms 83:6).
geography: The descendants of Ishmael lived mainly in the broad region of the northern Arabian Peninsula, from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt. This region was a strategic center of the overland caravan trade carrying ancient spices and precious metals, and they were active mainly in dry steppe-climate regions, adopting a mobile form of dwelling that relied on camels.
history: Between the 2nd millennium BC and the 1st millennium BC, the Ishmaelites are recognized as an Arab nomadic people who carried on economic activity along the trade routes of the ancient Near East. Through their commercial networks they served as an intermediary linking Egypt and the Levant, and rather than forming a particular state, they maintained a tribal confederation and entered into political and economic relations, or into conflict, with neighboring countries.

introduce: Iye-abarim is a place name on the border of Moab through which the people of ancient Israel passed on their journey toward Canaan after the Exodus.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, the open country east of Moab, toward the sunrise (Numbers 21:11). It is also recorded that the Israelites broke camp at Iye-abarim and camped at Dibon-gad (Numbers 33:44).
geography: Iye-abarim is located in the Moabite border region, and the name is interpreted as meaning the ruins or heaps of the hill country of Abarim. Its exact location is difficult to pin down archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be a boundary point of Moab north of the Arnon River or adjoining the region east of the Dead Sea.

introduce: Ijon is a city that was located on the border of the tribe of Naphtali in northern ancient Israel, a place name that, as a strategic stronghold, frequently appears in the disputes between Israel and the kingdom of Aram.
biblecontents: King Ben-hadad, ordered to attack the cities of Israel, struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, all of Chinnereth, and all the land of Naphtali (1 Kings 15:20). In the time of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, and took the people captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Ben-hadad sent to Baasha, king of Israel, and had Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali struck (2 Chronicles 16:4).
geography: Ijon is presumed to be the Marj Ayyun plain in present-day southern Lebanon. It lies in a fertile basin between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges, and has the topographical characteristic of serving as a major gateway into the northern Galilee region.
history: Around the 9th century BC, when Baasha, king of Israel, was in conflict with Asa, king of southern Judah, Ben-hadad I, king of Aram, at the instigation of Judah, invaded northern Israel, and Ijon was destroyed for the first time. Afterward, in the late 8th century BC, under the expansionist policy of the Assyrian empire, it was invaded by Tiglath-pileser III, and met the fate of being completely excluded from the administrative districts of Israel and of having its inhabitants forcibly deported.

introduce: Iim is a place mentioned as one of the cities of the southern Negev region distributed to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: There is a record that the Israelites left Iim and camped at Oboth (Numbers 33:45). Iim is also listed, together with Baalah and Ezem, among the cities distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:29).
geography: It is presumed to be a city located in the southern Negev region of Judah, but its specific modern location has not been clearly determined archaeologically. Some have raised the possibility that this name is a shortened form of Iye-abarim.

introduce: In the Bible, India is a place name appearing in the book of Esther in the Old Testament, signifying the far eastern limit of the range of the Persian Empire ruled by King Xerxes.
biblecontents: King Xerxes ruled over 127 provinces from India to Cush (Esther 1:1). The king's edict was written in the script of each province and in the language of each people, and was delivered to all the provinces from India to Cush (Esther 8:9).
geography: In the Hebrew Bible text it is written with the name Hoddu, which is presumed to refer to the Indus River valley in the east of the Persian Empire. It symbolizes the geographical limit connected with the territorial expansion of the Persian Empire at that time.
history: In the late 6th century BC, during the reign of Darius I, the Persian Empire extended its territory to the Indus Valley and incorporated the Hindush region as a province. The India that appears in the book of Esther refers, on the basis of historical fact, to the eastern end of the empire that Persia actually ruled or over which it exercised influence at that time.

introduce: Illyricum is one of the provinces of the ancient Roman Empire, referring to a region on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea. It is the western limit mentioned by the apostle Paul when he explained the extent of his missionary work.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the apostle Paul traveled all around from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and fully preached the gospel of Christ (Romans 15:19).
geography: It corresponds to the western part of the present-day Balkan Peninsula, and faces the Italian peninsula across the Adriatic Sea. It is a region dominated by mountainous terrain, bordering Pannonia on the north and Epirus and Macedonia on the south.
history: Around the 2nd century BC the Roman Republic began to conquer this region, and in 27 BC it was officially incorporated as a Roman province by the emperor Augustus. In the early Roman Empire it played an important role as a military stronghold, and was a strategic base for advancing to the Danube.

introduce: Iphtah-el is a place name recorded in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a region mentioned as one of the boundaries of the land distributed to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: In the course of describing the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, this place is cited as one of the points on the northern boundary (Joshua 19:27).
geography: It lies in the northern part of the territory of the tribe of Asher, and is presumed to be somewhere northeast of the Plain of Kabul, near the border of southern Lebanon or northern Israel today. Scholars are divided over its detailed location, and archaeological confirmation of a specific site is lacking.

introduce: Iphtah-el refers to a city or region mentioned in connection with the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun at the time of the distribution among the tribes of Israel.
biblecontents: Iphtah-el was mentioned as a point in the inheritance divided to the descendants of Zebulun, where the boundary turned north to Hannathon and ended at the Valley of Iphtah-el (Joshua 19:14).
geography: Its exact location today has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to have been in the lower Galilee region, on the northern boundary of the tribe of Zebulun. The Valley of Iphtah-el is regarded as a point where, by its topographical character, the hill country and the plain meet (Joshua 19:14).

introduce: Ithnan is one of the cities located on the southern boundary of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah in ancient Israel.
biblecontents: It is mentioned together with Kedesh and Jagur in the list of the southern cities of the tribe of Judah enumerated in Joshua 15:21 through 32 (Joshua 15:23).
geography: It is presumed to be located in the Negev region of southern Judah, but its exact location today has not been clearly determined archaeologically. It is classified as part of the southern border region that the tribe of Judah was allotted at that time (Joshua 15:23).

remark: The descendants of Issachar and the land allotted to them.
introduce: Issachar was Jacob's ninth son and Leah's fifth son, the ancestor of the tribe of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel; the name also means the region in which that tribe lived.
biblecontents: Nethanel son of Zuar was the commander of the descendants of Issachar (Numbers 1:8). In the census, the descendants of Issachar who were twenty years old or more and able to go to war numbered fifty-four thousand four hundred (Numbers 1:29). The descendants of Issachar camped beside the camp of Judah, and their commander was Nethanel son of Zuar (Numbers 2:5). On the second day Nethanel son of Zuar, the commander of Issachar, presented his offering (Numbers 7:18). Among the spies, Igal son of Joseph was sent from the tribe of Issachar (Numbers 13:7). The descendants of Issachar were counted by their clans, and their number was sixty-four thousand three hundred (Numbers 26:25). They are mentioned as one of the tribes that were to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people (Deuteronomy 27:12). Moses blessed Issachar, saying, "Rejoice in your tents" (Deuteronomy 33:18). The boundary of Issachar adjoined Asher and Manasseh (Joshua 17:10). The tribe of Issachar had, within the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, Beth-shean and its villages, Ibleam and its villages, the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, the inhabitants of Endor and its villages, the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, the three heights region (Joshua 17:11).
geography: The territory of the tribe of Issachar was located centered on the Jezreel Valley and Mount Tabor in southern Galilee. It adjoined the tribe of Asher on the west, the tribe of Manasseh on the south, and the tribe of Naphtali and the Jordan River on the north and east. Because it included the Jezreel Valley, a fertile plain, its agricultural productivity was high, and it was a strategic stronghold where major trade routes crossed.
history: The territory allotted after the conquest of Canaan was fertile, but because of the topographical feature that major international roads passed through it, it was often exposed to conflict with neighboring powers or native Canaanite forces and to wars of conquest. In the early settlement period it took the form of an agricultural society based on its geographical advantages, and afterward, as it was incorporated into the system of the kingdom of Israel, it played a political and military role as one of the main tribes of northern Israel.

introduce: The name Straight is a proper noun referring to a particular street or district of Damascus that appears in Acts 9:11.
biblecontents: The Lord appeared to Ananias in a vision and instructed him to go to the street called Straight in Damascus and to look in the house of Judas for a man called Saul (Acts 9:11).
geography: Straight refers to the main arterial road that ran east and west across the city of ancient Damascus. In Latin it was called Via Recta, which means a straight road. It is presumed that the central road running east and west in the Old City of present-day Damascus lies along the same route.
history: It is one of the grid-like road networks created when Damascus reorganized its city plan in the Hellenistic period. In the period of Roman rule it functioned as the city's core commercial route and thoroughfare, and was widened into a large road about 25 meters wide, serving as the central axis of the city.

introduce: Hachilah is a place name located in the wilderness of Judah, a strategic stronghold where David hid while escaping the pursuit of King Saul.
biblecontents: The men of Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah and denounced David, saying that he was hiding in the strongholds in the wooded hill of Hachilah, south of the wilderness (1 Samuel 23:19). The men of Ziph again informed Saul of David hiding on the hill of Hachilah facing the wilderness (1 Samuel 26:1), and Saul camped beside the road on the hill of Hachilah while David stayed in the wilderness (1 Samuel 26:3).
geography: Hachilah is a mountainous area located near the wilderness of Ziph, in the territory of the tribe of Judah; with its rugged terrain and dense forest, it is presumed to have been a place favorable for hiding and defense.
history: At that time David was moving about the wilderness of Judah to escape King Saul's political purge, and Hachilah, adjacent to the wilderness of Ziph, where the Ziphites' denunciations were frequent, was a region of high military tension between Saul's army and David's followers.

introduce: The Tower of Hananel was one of the major defensive structures on the northern boundary of the wall of Jerusalem, and, through the biblical record and its archaeologically presumed location, is regarded as an important point for understanding the structure of the wall of Jerusalem.
biblecontents: The high priest Eliashib and his fellow priests built the Sheep Gate and consecrated the wall, and built the wall as far as the Tower of Hananel (Nehemiah 3:1). Passing the Gate of Ephraim, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred, they came to the Sheep Gate and performed the ceremony of dedication (Nehemiah 12:39). "Behold, the days are coming when this city will be rebuilt for the LORD, from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate" (Jeremiah 31:38). "From the first month to the place of the Gate of Benjamin, from the Tower of Hananel to the king's winepresses, the wall will be set up again" (Zechariah 14:10).
geography: The Tower of Hananel was located near the northeastern corner of the wall of Jerusalem, and was a key stronghold defending the northern wall between the Gate of Ephraim and the Sheep Gate. Archaeologically, it is presumed to have stood on high ground connected with the terrain of the northwestern or northeastern corner of the Temple Mount within the northern wall section of present-day Jerusalem.
history: The Tower of Hananel is mentioned as one of the main reference points of the wall at the time of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah in the Persian period. In the prophetic books this tower was used as a geographical coordinate to define the boundary of Jerusalem or to describe the extent of the eschatological rebuilding of the city. Because the north was the topographically weakest section in the defense system of ancient Jerusalem, the Tower of Hananel performed a defensive function to secure the safety of the city.

introduce: Hanes is an ancient Egyptian place name, mentioned in the book of Isaiah as one of the places where the kingdom of Judah sought to ask for diplomatic help in order to resist the threat of Assyria.
biblecontents: The prophet Isaiah recorded that, when the people of Judah, not relying on God, went down to Egypt to rely on it and to seek its protection, their officials were at Zoan and their envoys had arrived at Hanes (Isaiah 30:4).
geography: Hanes is presumed to be located in the eastern part of the Nile Delta in Egypt, and there is a view in scholarship that identifies it with the same area as Tahpanhes or Heracleopolis, major cities of ancient Egypt.
history: In the late 8th century BC, the kingdom of Judah was undergoing a security crisis caused by the expansionist policy of Assyria, and at that time the rulers of Egypt's 25th Dynasty were forming an anti-Assyrian alliance against Assyria and drawing out the support of Judah and other neighboring small states. Hanes was one of the strategic cities of Egypt where such diplomatic negotiations were carried on.

introduce: Hadad-rimmon is a place name mentioned in the book of Zechariah in the Old Testament, known to refer to a location in the northern plain region of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: Prophesying that there will be great mourning in Jerusalem, it compares the degree of that mourning to the mourning that took place at Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (Zechariah 12:11).
geography: It is presumed to be a region located near the Megiddo plain in northern Israel today, and traditionally it is interpreted as referring to the area near Tel Megiddo.
history: It is also understood as a place closely associated with the event in 609 BC in which Josiah, king of Judah, was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco of Egypt in the battle of Megiddo, and there is a theory that the name is a combination of the names of the ancient Near Eastern deities Hadad and Rimmon.

introduce: It is one of the cities located in the plain region of Judah allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as included in the list of the cities of the land that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:37).
geography: It is classified as a city located in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah. Its specific archaeological location is presumed to be the southern part of the plain of Judah, but opinions differ among scholars about its exact identification today.

introduce: Hadrach is a place name appearing in Zechariah 9:1 in the Bible, a term referring to a country or city of the ancient Near East. In modern scholarship this name is regarded as the same region as Aramaic Hadrach or Hatarikka in Assyrian documents.
biblecontents: It is recorded that the word of the LORD comes upon the land of Hadrach and will rest upon Damascus (Zechariah 9:1). This is mentioned in the context of prophesying that God's judgment will fall on neighboring countries, including Hadrach and Damascus (Zechariah 9:1).
geography: Hadrach is presumed to be a city in the region of ancient Syria or an administrative district around it. Specifically, it is understood as a strategic stronghold located between Hamath and Aleppo in the Orontes River valley, and it was situated on a major trade route of the ancient Near East.
history: Hadrach often appears in Assyrian inscriptions under the name Hatarikka, and is a place name mentioned in the records of the conquests of Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria, in the 8th century BC. At that time this region was either territory of the kingdom of Hamath or the center of an independent city-state closely connected with it, and in the course of Assyria's expansionist policy it was treated as an important military base.

introduce: Hara (Halah) is a region mentioned in Chronicles as one of the places to which the tribes of Israel were forcibly deported by the kings of Assyria.
biblecontents: Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, took captive the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and carried them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan (1 Chronicles 5:26).
geography: It is presumed to be in northern Mesopotamia, territory of the ancient Assyrian empire, and occupies a geographical position adjacent to the valley of the Habor River.
history: It is one of the settlements to which the inhabitants of the conquered territories of northern Israel were forcibly moved, as part of the large-scale population transfer policy carried out by the Assyrian empire around the 8th century BC.

introduce: Haradah is a place name recorded in Numbers 33, one of the places the Israelites passed through on their journey through the wilderness after the Exodus.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Rithmah and camped at Haradah (Numbers 33:24). They left Haradah again and camped at Makheloth (Numbers 33:25).

remark: A city in northern Mesopotamia, where Abraham moved after coming from Ur.
introduce: Haran is a city located in northern ancient Mesopotamia, in the southeastern part of present-day Turkey. According to the biblical record, it was the place where Abraham's family settled for a time on their way from Ur of the Chaldeans toward Canaan, and it is an important base deeply connected also with the family history of Isaac and Jacob.
biblecontents: Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot the son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, Abram's wife, and set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan, and when they came to Haran they settled there (Genesis 11:31). Terah died in Haran at the age of two hundred and five (Genesis 11:32). Abram went as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him, and Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4). Abram took his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, and all the possessions they had gathered in Haran and the people they had acquired, and set out to go to the land of Canaan, and they entered the land of Canaan (Genesis 12:5). Jacob fled to Haran, where his uncle Laban was (Genesis 27:43). Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran (Genesis 28:10). Jacob said to them, "Do you know Laban, the grandson of Nahor?" They said, "We know him." He said to them, "Is he well?" They said, "He is well, and see, his daughter Rachel is coming with the sheep" (Genesis 29:4). "Did the gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed deliver them, Gozan and Haran and Resheph and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?" (2 Kings 19:12). "Did the gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed deliver them, Gozan and Haran and Resheph and the sons of Eden in Telassar?" (Isaiah 37:12). "Haran, Canneh, Eden, Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad traded with you" (Ezekiel 27:23).
geography: Haran is located in the valley of the Balikh River, at the crossroads of the major trade routes connecting ancient Mesopotamia with Syria and Anatolia. The surroundings are a dry plain, but thanks to its key position in the trade network its strategic value was very high.
history: Haran is recorded as a center of trade from the 2nd millennium BC, and is especially well known as a religious center for the worship of the moon god Sin. In the period of the Assyrian empire it was one of the main cities of the empire, and after Assyria lost Nineveh in the 7th century BC, it also served as the last capital of the remnants of Assyria. Through the Babylonian and Persian periods it maintained for a long time its standing as an economic and military stronghold of the ancient Near East.

introduce: Hararite appears in the Hebrew Bible as a name referring to a person, or a region, connected with David's mighty men. It is a word interpreted mainly as the place of origin of a particular person in David's military organization, or as having an adjectival sense describing that person.
biblecontents: 2 Samuel 23:11 mentions Shammah son of Agee the Hararite, who fought in a field of grain gathered at Lehi during the battle with the Philistines, and the context suggests that the place was near Hararite territory (2 Samuel 23:11). Shammah the Hararite, one of David's mighty men, is also mentioned (2 Samuel 23:33), and in the record of 1 Chronicles the place name is used in the information about the sons of Hashem of Kishon and about Jonathan and Ahiam the Hararites (1 Chronicles 11:34, 1 Chronicles 11:35).
geography: The exact location of the Hararites has not been determined archaeologically. Scholars presume that within the biblical text this place name most likely refers to a small village or hill region in the hill country of Judah or within the sphere of David's activity, but no clear archaeological site has been excavated.

introduce: Harosheth-hagoyim means the military stronghold city governed by Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin, king of Canaan, in the time of the judges. The Hebrew place name Harosheth-hagoyim means "Harosheth of the Gentiles," and it is recorded as a core military base of the Canaanite forces at that time.
biblecontents: Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor, lived in Harosheth-hagoyim (Judges 4:2). Sisera gathered nine hundred iron chariots and all the people who were in Harosheth-hagoyim, and assembled them at the river Kishon (Judges 4:13). Pursued by Barak, Sisera's army fell by the edge of the sword as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and not a man was left (Judges 4:16).
geography: There is disagreement archaeologically about the exact location of Harosheth-hagoyim, but it is generally presumed to be Tell el-Amr, at the western entrance of the plain of Jezreel. This is a strategic stronghold able to control the gorge through which the Kishon River flows, and it lies on the route connecting the plain of Jezreel and the coastal plain.
history: At that time Jabin, king of Canaan, had his base at Hazor, but Harosheth-hagoyim served as a military supply base. In particular, the fact that Sisera, who operated iron chariots, took this region as his base was in order to oppress the tribes of Israel efficiently by making use of the flat terrain. This region is historical evidence showing that the remnants of the Canaanites maintained strong military power in the early stage of Israel's settlement.

introduce: Harorite is the hometown of Hel the Harorite, one of David's mighty men, and the place of origin used to refer to him.
biblecontents: Hel, one of David's mighty men, is recorded as a Harorite (1 Chronicles 11:27).

remark: A spring in the plain of Jezreel, west of the Jordan River, in Manasseh and Gilboa.
introduce: Harod is a spring located in the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel, and the name also refers to the area around it. Through the biblical record it is known as the site of Gideon's military operation and as the place of origin of one of David's mighty men.
biblecontents: The spring of Harod, where Gideon and the people who followed him camped, is recorded as the place where they confronted the Midianite army (Judges 7:1). Elika the Harodite, one of David's mighty men, is also mentioned (2 Samuel 23:25).
geography: It is presumed to be present-day Ain Harod, a strong gushing spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa on the east side of the Jezreel Valley. The surrounding terrain takes the form of a flat valley, with conditions suitable for a large army to be stationed or to move.
history: In the early Iron Age this region was a strategic stronghold where clashes between the tribes of Israel and the surrounding nomadic peoples occurred frequently. As a water-resource center able to control the main passages of the northern Canaan region, the spring of Harod served as a military base.

introduce: Haruphite is a place name mentioned as the hometown of Bealiah, one of the mighty men of the tribe of Benjamin who joined David when he stayed at Ziklag, or as the region to which he belonged.
biblecontents: Among the mighty men who came to help David when he was hiding at Ziklag to escape Saul, Bealiah, a Benjamite, is recorded as a Haruphite (1 Chronicles 12:5).

introduce: This is a place name appearing in Amos 4:3, a special place mentioned only within the biblical text. It is written Harmon in the Hebrew original, and is generally interpreted as a place name located on the route by which the women of Samaria were taken into exile.
biblecontents: Each of you will go straight out ahead of you and be cast into Harmon, declares the LORD (Amos 4:3)
geography: Its exact location has not been established by scholars.
