Some regard it as referring to Mount Hermon, and the possibility has been raised that it was a particular fortress in the region of Samaria or a city included on the route by which people were led off to Assyria. To date there is no site that has been identified through archaeological excavation.
history: It appears in a context that prophesies that around the 8th century BC the upper-class women of Samaria in northern Israel would be taken captive because of the Assyrian invasion. It was mentioned as part of a warning against the luxury and corruption of Samaria at that time, and Harmon symbolizes the destination, or the point of passage, to which they would be forcibly led away.

remark: A city in the upper Syria region, in the valley of the Orontes River.
introduce: Hamath refers to an important city-state that was located in the valley of the Orontes River in ancient Syria and to its surrounding territory. In the Bible it is frequently mentioned as the northern boundary of Israel and as a geopolitical stronghold where exchanges with neighboring powers took place.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the base of the Hamathites, a branch of the Canaanite peoples (Genesis 10:18). It is the point where the Israelite spies who came out of Egypt checked the northern boundary (Numbers 13:21). It was set as the northern boundary of Canaan that Israel was to occupy (Numbers 34:8, Joshua 13:5). It is recorded as one of the lands that Israel did not conquer (Judges 3:3). In the time of David, Tou, king of Hamath, sent envoys to express friendship (2 Samuel 8:9). It is specified as the northern end of the territory ruled by Solomon (1 Kings 8:65). Jeroboam II restored the boundary of Israel as far as the entrance of Hamath (2 Kings 14:25, 2 Kings 14:28). After Sargon II of Assyria conquered Israel, he also resettled people from the region of Hamath in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24).
geography: It is identified with the area of Hama in present-day Syria. It lies on a fertile plain in the middle course of the Orontes River, and occupies a strategic position controlling the northern entrance of the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges.
history: An ancient city-state that existed from the 2nd millennium BC, in the Iron Age it was one of the centers of the Neo-Hittite kingdoms. Together with Damascus it formed a powerful force of the Aramean line, and around the 8th century BC it was conquered and made a province under the expansionist policy of the Assyrian empire. Afterward, through the Neo-Babylonian and Persian periods, it continued to serve as an administrative center of the region.

introduce: Hamath-zobah is the name of an Aramean state that was located in the ancient Near East, referring to a region that was under the influence of Israel in the time of King Solomon.
biblecontents: Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and captured it (2 Chronicles 8:3).
geography: Hamath-zobah is presumed to be a region including Hamath in the valley of the Orontes River in present-day northern Syria and the surrounding area of Zobah, and is a strategic stronghold between the north of Damascus and the west of the Euphrates River.
history: The kingdom of Zobah existed between the 11th and 10th centuries BC as one of the main states of Aram, and in the time of kings David and Solomon it experienced military clashes with Israel, in which its supremacy was replaced or a relationship of paying tribute was formed.

introduce: Hamonah is a place name appearing in the book of Ezekiel, the name of the city designated for burying Gog and his horde after their defeat. This name is derived from a Hebrew word meaning a multitude or a horde.
biblecontents: "The name of the city will also be Hamonah. Thus they will cleanse the land," he said (Ezekiel 39:16)
geography: Hamonah is described as lying beside the road of those who travel east of the sea, and is a symbolic or prophetic place whose specific modern place name has not been identified (Ezekiel 39:11).

introduce: A place name appearing in Ezekiel 39, it means the place designated for burying them after the army of Gog was defeated. The name Hamon-gog carries the meaning "the horde of Gog."
biblecontents: "On that day, declares the LORD, I will give to Gog a burial place in Israel, the valley of those who travel east of the sea, and it will block the travelers. There they will bury Gog and all his horde, and they will call it the Valley of Hamon-gog" (Ezekiel 39:11). "When those who pass through the land see a human bone, they will set up a marker beside it until the buriers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog" (Ezekiel 39:15).
geography: According to the record of the book of Ezekiel, it is described as the valley of those who travel east of the sea, which is interpreted as meaning the region east of the Dead Sea. A specific archaeological site or topographical location is difficult to establish today.

introduce: Hapharaim is a region mentioned as one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Issachar in the time of ancient Israel.
biblecontents: The inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Issachar received according to their families was Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez (Joshua 19:18-21).
geography: The exact location of Hapharaim has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to have been within the territory of the tribe of Issachar, near the Jezreel Valley, the plain of southern Galilee.

introduce: Havvoth-jair is a place name in the region east of the Jordan recorded in the Bible, meaning the collection of villages that Jair of the tribe of Manasseh conquered and named after himself.
biblecontents: Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured those villages and called them Havvoth-jair (Numbers 32:41). Jair the son of Manasseh captured all the region of Argob as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called this Bashan region by his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day (Deuteronomy 3:14). He had thirty sons who rode thirty young donkeys and had thirty cities, which are in the land of Gilead to this day and are called Havvoth-jair (Judges 10:4).
geography: It lies in the Bashan region east of the Jordan River and on the northern border of Gilead. Specifically, it includes the region of Argob and is described as an area adjoining the borders of the Geshurites and the Maacathites (Deuteronomy 3:14).
history: It was formed when, in the course of Israel's wars of conquest of Canaan, after Og, king of Bashan east of the Jordan, was defeated, Jair of the tribe of Manasseh captured the cities of the Bashan region. It can be seen that afterward, down to the period of the judges, the house of Jair kept control of the cities of this region and maintained its dominance (Judges 10:4).

introduce: Hazazon-tamar is a place name of the ancient Near East, a place identified, according to the biblical record, with En-gedi on the west side of the Dead Sea. This place name appears as the setting of a historical event connected with the Amorites, and geographically it means an oasis region along the shore of the Dead Sea.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings with him returned and came to En-mishpat, that is, Kadesh, and struck all the land of the Amalekites and the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar (Genesis 14:7). Afterward the Moabites and the Ammonites, together with the Meunites, came to make war against Jehoshaphat; and some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A great multitude is coming against you from beyond the sea, from Aram; and now they are in Hazazon-tamar, that is, En-gedi" (2 Chronicles 20:1-2).
geography: Hazazon-tamar is regarded as the same as the En-gedi area in the central part of the western shore of the Dead Sea. This is an oasis region formed beneath the rugged cliffs of the wilderness of Judah, and thanks to its abundant freshwater sources it was a strategic stronghold where settlement and farming were possible from ancient times. Topographically, it is a place greatly affected by changes in the water level of the Dead Sea and by the neighboring wadis.
history: It is recorded as a region where the Amorites lived from the Bronze Age, and later, in the period of the kingdom of Judah, it was used as an avenue of advance when the combined armies of Moab and Ammon invaded Judah. The name Hazazon-tamar was later fixed as the name En-gedi, and it functioned as an important landmark on the military routes of the ancient Near East.

introduce: Hazar-shual is a compound of hazar, which in Hebrew means a court or village, and shual, which means a fox; it is a city that was located in the Negev region of southern ancient Palestine.
biblecontents: It is included in the list of cities of the southern inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:28). It is also mentioned as one of the cities that the tribe of Simeon received from the inheritance of the descendants of Judah (Joshua 19:3).
geography: It lies in the northern part of the Negev desert, centered on Beersheba. Together with neighboring places such as Beersheba and Moladah, it is classified as one of the cities forming the defensive line or residential district of southern Judah. Scholars differ on its specific archaeological identification, but Tel al-Mishashi and others are generally cited as candidate sites.

introduce: Hazar-gaddah is one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah, meaning a settlement located in the Negev region of southern Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained when Joshua distributed the land of Canaan (Joshua 15:27).
geography: It is presumed to be a city located near the Negev desert in southern Judah, and its exact archaeological location is still disputed among scholars.

introduce: Hazar-susah is one of the southern cities allotted as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the cities listed as the inheritance of the descendants of Simeon (Joshua 19:5).
geography: Its exact location has not been clearly identified by current archaeological investigation, but it is presumed to be one of the group of cities located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah.

introduce: Hazar-susim is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, one of the villages included in the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: Hazar-susim is recorded as a city that belonged to the descendants of Simeon until the time of David (1 Chronicles 4:31).
geography: Hazar-susim is presumed to be located in the southern Negev region around Beersheba, but its exact location has not been determined by modern archaeology.

introduce: Hazar-shual is one of the settlements that were located in southern ancient Israel, a place name mentioned mainly in lists of cities connected with the territories of the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Simeon.
biblecontents: Hazar-shual, together with Beersheba and Moladah, is recorded as one of the cities that the tribe of Simeon received (1 Chronicles 4:28). It is also mentioned as one of the villages where the descendants of Judah lived after returning from the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:27).
geography: Scholarship holds various views on the exact location of Hazar-shual, but it is generally presumed to be Tell el-Mashash, northeast or southeast of Beersheba, or the area near Tel Arad. This area corresponds to the northern border zone of the Negev desert, and has the characteristics of an arid zone more favorable to herding or to securing a stronghold than to irrigation and agriculture.

introduce: Hazar-addar is one of the major points on the southern boundary that was set when the Israelites were to receive the land of Canaan as an inheritance, in the book of Numbers in the Old Testament.
biblecontents: The boundary turns south of the Ascent of Akrabbim and goes to Zin, and its south reaches south of Kadesh-barnea, and it goes on past Hazar-addar to Azmon (Numbers 34:4)
geography: It is presumed to be a point between Kadesh-barnea and Azmon, a stronghold lying on the boundary line of the Negev desert region in southern Canaan. Its exact modern location has not been clearly determined archaeologically, but it is judged to be terrain formed along the western side of the Arabah valley or along the highland route of the Negev region.

introduce: Hazar-enan is a place name mentioned as a point on the northern boundary of the land of Canaan. It is written Hatsar Enan in Hebrew, and carries the meaning of a village near a spring.
biblecontents: It was designated as the point forming the northern boundary when the Israelites were to receive the land of Canaan as an inheritance (Numbers 34:9). Also, in the process of fixing the eastern boundary line of the land of Canaan, the boundary going down from Hazar-enan to Shepham was mentioned (Numbers 34:10).
geography: As for its exact present location, the view that identifies it with the Qaryatayn area northeast of Damascus is influential in scholarship. As a strategic stronghold determining the northeastern boundary of Canaan, it lies in a vast plain region linking the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges.

introduce: Hazar-enan is a city mentioned in Ezekiel 47 and 48 of the Old Testament, a strategic boundary reference point forming the northeastern border of the land of Israel that is to be restored.
biblecontents: The northern boundary line of the new land was prescribed as running from the shore of the Mediterranean Sea to Hazar-enan on the border of Damascus, with its northern end reaching the border of Hamath (Ezekiel 47:17). When the territories of the tribes were divided, the whole northern boundary line, from the northern end by way of the road of Hethlon, past the entrance of Hamath, to Hazar-enan on the border line of Damascus, was allotted as the portion of the tribe of Dan (Ezekiel 48:1).
geography: In Hebrew, Hazar-enan means "court of springs," and it is located in an oasis region leading into the Syrian desert northeast of Damascus. It also appears as a marker of the northern border in Numbers 34:9-10, and is identified with Qaryatein or Hawwarin, an oasis town with abundant natural springs about 110 km northeast of Damascus in present-day Syria.
history: From ancient times Hazar-enan was an essential water supply point and a trading base on the desert-crossing caravan route linking Damascus and Hamath with Palmyra (Tadmor) and the direction of the Euphrates. It was a border control point of the Aramean kingdoms and the Assyrian empire, and the prophet Ezekiel in the Babylonian exile, inheriting the tradition of the ideal northern boundary of the ancient time of David and Solomon, presented Hazar-enan as the terminal point of the northeastern territory of the future Israel.

introduce: Hazeroth is one of the places where the people of Israel stayed during the journey of the Exodus, and is where the Israelites settled after leaving Kibroth-hattaavah (Numbers 11:35). The origin of the name is, in Hebrew, a word meaning a court or village, and it is regarded as an important stopping point in studies that trace the route of the Exodus.
biblecontents: The people of Israel left Kibroth-hattaavah and came to Hazeroth and stayed (Numbers 11:35). Here an incident occurred in which Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and Miriam was struck with leprosy (Numbers 12:1). Afterward the people left Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 12:16). According to the record of the stages of the Exodus, they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth (Numbers 33:17), and left Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah (Numbers 33:18). In Deuteronomy, the words that Moses proclaimed to the assembly of Israel in the wilderness of the Arabah east of the Jordan, between Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab, are mentioned, with Hazeroth taken as a geographical reference point (Deuteronomy 1:1).
geography: The exact location of Hazeroth is under archaeological debate, but the view that generally identifies it with the Ain Hudra area in the eastern Sinai Peninsula is influential in scholarship. This is a point about 40 km northeast of Jebel Musa, the presumed Mount Sinai, and has springs and flat land suitable for a large number of people to stay.

introduce: Hazer-hatticon is one of the place names included in the ideal northern boundary line of Israel recorded in the book of Ezekiel, a place presumed to be located near the region of Hamath.
biblecontents: The northern boundary of Israel is described as including Hamath, Berothah, and Sibraim, which is between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath, as well as Hazer-hatticon, which is on the border of Hauran (Ezekiel 47:16).
geography: It appears to be located in the northern Syrian region between Hamath and Damascus, but its exact present location has not been determined archaeologically. From the geographical description of being near the border of Hauran, it is presumed to be a border zone east of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range or around it (Ezekiel 47:16).

remark: 1. A fortified city between Ramah and Kedesh, allotted to the tribe of Naphtali.
introduce: Hazor was the largest and most influential city-state in the northern region of Canaan. At the time of Joshua's wars of conquest it was the center of the northern Canaanite coalition, and as a strategic stronghold it is a city continually mentioned throughout the biblical record.
biblecontents: Jabin, king of Hazor, summoned the northern Canaanite coalition to oppose Israel (Joshua 11:1). In the course of the wars of conquest Joshua captured Hazor and struck the king of Hazor with the edge of the sword and killed him (Joshua 11:10). The city of Hazor and all its inhabitants were utterly destroyed, and the city was burned (Joshua 11:11). Unlike the other cities built on mounds, Joshua burned only Hazor, which was built on level ground (Joshua 11:13). After the conquest of Canaan, Hazor was recorded as one of the thirty-one kings conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:19). Afterward Hazor became one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Naphtali (Joshua 19:36). In the time of the judges Hazor was again under the rule of Jabin, king of Hazor, and his army commander Sisera oppressed Israel (Judges 4:2). Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, after killing Sisera, maintained peaceful relations with Jabin, king of Hazor (Judges 4:17).
geography: Hazor lies about 15 km north of the Sea of Galilee, and is identified with the area of Tel el-Qedah today. Situated at a strategic point overlooking the Huleh basin, it was a strategic stronghold able to control the Way of the Sea, the main trade route running from north to south. Hazor was divided into an upper city and a lower city, and in the Canaanite period it formed a city of very large scale.
history: In the Middle and Late Bronze Age Hazor was the city-state that exercised the strongest influence in the Canaanite region. Archaeological excavation has confirmed Hazor as a center of trade with Egypt and Mesopotamia, and it occupied a diplomatically important position, so much so that its existence is even mentioned in the Amarna documents. In the early Iron Age fortification work was carried out after Israel's occupation, and afterward, in the time of Solomon, a large-scale rebuilding project is understood to have been carried out because of its strategic importance.

remark: 2. A city at the southern end of Judah.
introduce: Hazor was a major city-state in the northern region of Canaan and a strategic stronghold of the ancient Near East, and it is one of several places in the Bible with the same place name. The Hazor mentioned in Joshua 15:23 refers to a city located on the southern boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as a place located at the southern end of the list of cities allotted to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:23).
geography: The Hazor shown in Joshua 15:23 is presumed to be located in the border region between the hill country of Judah and the Negev desert. This is geographically a completely different region from Hazor, the large city of northern Canaan.
history: This Hazor appears to have been a military stronghold or settlement on the southern boundary of Judah, but apart from the biblical record there is no activity recorded that has been clearly established archaeologically.

remark: 3. Hazor-hadattah, that is, "New Hazor," another city in the south of Judah.
introduce: Hazor was a strategic stronghold and major city-state in northern Canaan, mentioned in the Old Testament as a region of strategic importance. In Joshua 15:25 it is mentioned as one of the southern cities of the tribe of Judah, which is presumed to be a separate place from the great city of Hazor in the north.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the list of southern cities of the tribe of Judah, together with Hazor-hadattah (Joshua 15:25).
geography: The Hazor mentioned in Joshua 15:25 is presumed to be located in the southern part of the hill country of Judah or in the Negev region, and is generally distinguished from Hazor, the large city near the Sea of Galilee in the north.

remark: 4. Where the Benjamites who returned from exile lived, located north of Jerusalem.
introduce: Hazor is a city of the tribe of Benjamin recorded in Nehemiah 11 in the Old Testament, a settlement north of Jerusalem that is distinguished from the Hazor of Galilee.
biblecontents: The descendants of Benjamin lived in Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, and Neballat (Nehemiah 11:33).
geography: It is identified with present-day Khirbet Hazzur, located about 7 km northwest of Jerusalem, between Gibeon and Gibeah.
history: It is a city that the descendants of the tribe of Benjamin, who returned to their homeland in the Persian period after the Babylonian exile, rebuilt as a northern defensive line of Jerusalem and as an agricultural settlement.

remark: 5. A nation east of Arabia.
introduce: Hazor is a confederation of nomadic tribes and settlements in the Arabian desert appearing in Jeremiah 49, referring to the Arabian kingdoms that were invaded by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon.
biblecontents: A word of judgment was proclaimed against the nations of Kedar and Hazor, conquered by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (Jeremiah 49:28). The inhabitants of Hazor were warned to flee, to go far away and dwell in the depths (Jeremiah 49:30). It was proclaimed that Hazor would become the dwelling place of great serpents and be desolate forever, and that no one would live there (Jeremiah 49:33).
geography: It is an oasis region in the interior of the Syro-Arabian desert east of the Jordan, the dwelling place of Arabian tribes who lived in unwalled villages and in tents.
history: It reflects the historical background in which, during the eastern desert campaign of the Neo-Babylonian empire in the early 6th century BC, the wealthy nomadic confederations of Arabia that carried on caravan trade were conquered on a large scale and plundered.

introduce: Hazor-hadattah is a city included in the list of the inheritance of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Joshua 15 in the Bible, a place name presumed to have been located in the Negev region of southern Judah.
biblecontents: Joshua 15:25 records it as one of the southern cities that the tribe of Judah received (Joshua 15:25).
geography: It is classified as a city located in the Negev desert zone near the southern border of the tribe of Judah. Its exact archaeological location is disputed, but it is generally regarded as a place name combining Hazor (Hazor) and Hadattah (Hadattah), and there is a view in scholarship that identifies it with the area of Tell el-Karyatein today.

introduce: Hashmonah is one of the encampments where the Israelites stayed on the wilderness route as they left Egypt and headed for Canaan.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah (Numbers 33:29). They left Hashmonah again and camped at Moseroth (Numbers 33:30).
geography: The exact location of Hashmonah has not been clearly identified archaeologically at present, but it is generally presumed to have been in the northeastern Sinai Peninsula or the southern region of the Negev desert.

introduce: Harsith is a place name appearing in Jeremiah 19:2 in the Bible, known as a particular gate located on the south side of the wall of Jerusalem. It is written Harsith or the Gate of Harsith in the Hebrew original, and is generally interpreted as the passage leading to the Valley of Hinnom.
biblecontents: God commanded Jeremiah to buy a potter's earthen flask, take the elders and priests of Jerusalem, go out to the entrance of the Harsith Gate, and proclaim a message of judgment there (Jeremiah 19:2).
geography: This area is presumed to be located at the southern or southeastern end of the wall of Jerusalem, and is traditionally regarded as the same place as the Potter's Gate, which adjoins the Valley of Hinnom. Because the nature of the soil is rich in clay suitable for pottery making, it is very likely that the name Harsith Gate was attached to it.
history: Harsith is closely connected with the pottery market, a space of the social and economic activity of ancient Jerusalem. In Jerusalem at that time pottery making was done mainly on the low ground outside the wall, and this place was recognized as a place where religious rites and social gatherings were frequent. Jeremiah chose this place as the site for proclaiming judgment because it was a symbolic place that could best show the destruction of Jerusalem.

introduce: Hauran is a place name of the ancient Near East, meaning the Hauran plateau region, a volcanic-rock zone spanning southwestern present-day Syria and northern Jordan. In the Bible it appears as one of the points on the northern boundary of the restored Israel that Ezekiel described in a vision.
biblecontents: Hauran is mentioned in the book of Ezekiel in the course of setting the northeastern boundary line of the ideal land of Israel. Ezekiel records that the boundary passing between Damascus and Hamath will connect with the region of Hauran (Ezekiel 47:16). Its position is also specified once more as a marker explaining the boundary line between Gilead and the land of Israel, with the Jordan River in between (Ezekiel 47:18).
geography: Hauran includes a broad volcanic-rock plateau known as the Leja and a plain of fertile basalt soil. On the west it adjoins the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan Valley, and on the east it continues into the Syrian desert. Thanks to the soil formed by volcanic activity, it has been well known since ancient times as fertile farmland with a high yield of grain.
history: Historically Hauran was the core of the region of Bashan. In the Old Testament period it was a region where territorial disputes between the kingdom of Aram and the kingdom of Israel were frequent, and afterward it came under the rule of Assyria and Babylonia. In the Greco-Roman period it was called Auranitis, and it played the role of a strategic stronghold, becoming part of the Decapolis or being included in the domain ruled by the house of Herod.

introduce: Hahiroth, called Pi-hahiroth in Hebrew, is one of the places where the Israelites camped just before crossing the Red Sea at the time of the Exodus.
biblecontents: The people of Israel camped before Hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon (Numbers 33:8). This is mentioned as the last place where they stayed before crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 14:2).
geography: It is presumed to be located at the northern end of the Red Sea or near the Isthmus of Suez, but the exact archaeological point has not been determined. As a feature of the place name, it was located between Migdol and Baal-zephon and was used as a reference point forming a geographical coordinate (Exodus 14:2).

introduce: Hachmoni is a name appearing in 1 Chronicles 11, a place name referring to the family of Jashobeam, the highest-ranking mighty man who assisted King David, and to their base.
biblecontents: Among the chiefs of the mighty men who followed David was Jashobeam the son of a Hachmonite, who is recorded as a man who raised his spear and killed three hundred at one time (1 Chronicles 11:11).
geography: Hachmoni is presumed to be an ancient settlement that was located in the hill country of Judah or in the border region with the tribe of Benjamin. It appears to have been a clan settlement in the hills of Judah near bases from the time of David's exile, such as the cave of Adullam and Ziklag, but no clear archaeological site has been identified by modern archaeological indicators.
history: Around the 10th century BC, in the founding period of the united kingdom of Israel, when David lived in exile escaping Saul's pursuit, influential mighty men of southern Judah and the tribe of Benjamin joined him. Jashobeam, from the house of Hachmoni, was active in David's military organization as the chief of the Three, the elite corps, and Jehiel, the royal counselor who looked after the sons of David in 1 Chronicles 27:32, also appears as a son of Hachmoni, so that they formed the core force of military and administration in the early monarchy.

introduce: Hannathon is a place name mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a city cited as a border area of the tribe of Zebulun in the process of distributing the land to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The boundary of the tribe of Zebulun reached Hannathon on the north and ended at the Valley of Reda, and that became the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 19:14).
geography: Hannathon is identified archaeologically with Tel Amun in the Galilee region of present-day Israel. It lies at the point forming the northern boundary of the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, and is situated near the Netofa Valley, a strategic crossroads between north of Nazareth and the plain of Acco.

introduce: Halah is a place name mentioned as one of the places to which the people of northern Israel, conquered by the ancient Assyrian empire, were forcibly relocated.
biblecontents: Shalmaneser V, king of Assyria, after capturing Samaria, took the Israelites captive and placed them in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6). In the time of King Hezekiah as well, these regions are mentioned in the same way as the places to which the descendants of Israel were taken captive (2 Kings 18:11). It is also recorded that Pul and Tiglath-pileser, kings of Assyria, who carried off the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh as captives, moved them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan (1 Chronicles 5:26).
geography: Halah is presumed to have been located in northern ancient Mesopotamia, in the northern part of present-day Iraq. Scholars regard the valley of the Khabur River, near the heartland of Assyria, as the leading candidate site, and identify it as a point closely related geographically to the region of Gozan or Habor.
history: Around the 8th century BC, the Assyrian empire carried out a policy of forcibly relocating conquered peoples throughout the empire in order to strengthen control over the conquered lands and suppress rebellions. Halah was one of the bases to which Israelite exiles were assigned as settlements, as part of this large-scale Assyrian population-movement policy. This was the result of an administrative strategy by which Assyria sought to dismantle the national identity of conquered peoples and use them as labor for the empire.

introduce: Mount Halak is a mountain mentioned in biblical geography as the southern boundary point to which the Israelite army advanced at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: In the extent of the land that Joshua conquered, the southern boundary was Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir (Joshua 11:17). Mount Halak is also specified as a boundary when recording the list of kings whom Joshua and the Israelites conquered west of the Jordan (Joshua 12:7).
geography: Mount Halak is generally presumed to be a hill country west of the Arabah valley, about 30 km southwest of the southern end of the Dead Sea. In Hebrew, halak has the meaning "smooth" or "bald," and this is interpreted as a name reflecting the bare-hill terrain of the area. Lying on the approach to the hill country of Edom, it serves as a strategic stronghold.

remark: The place where Chedorlaomer struck the Zuzites.
introduce: Ham is a place name referring to the ancient Near East and the region of Egypt, used in the Bible mainly as another name for the land of Egypt. It is analyzed as meaning the place where the descendants of Ham, the son of Noah, settled, and as having a linguistic connection with Kemet, the ancient Egyptian name for the land.
biblecontents: Chedorlaomer and the kings with him struck the Rephaites at Ashteroth-karnaim, which was something that took place in the region of Ham (Genesis 14:5). Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham (Psalms 105:23). God showed signs and wonders in the land of Ham (Psalms 105:27). They performed wonders in the land of Ham and awesome deeds in the land of Canaan (Psalms 106:22).
geography: The geographical extent of Ham refers to the whole of Egypt, including the fertile delta of the lower Nile and the Nile Valley. It has the topographical characteristics of adjoining the Sinai Peninsula on the east, the Libyan desert on the west, and the region of Nubia on the south.
history: Historically, this region, as the cradle of ancient Egyptian civilization, maintained a powerful centralized pharaonic system. The biblical record reflects the anthropological tradition that the descendants of Ham settled this region and formed a civilization, and it expresses the history of the Israelite people's stay in Egypt, before the book of Exodus, with the term "the land of Ham."

remark: 1. A fortified city of Naphtali, one mile from Tiberias.
introduce: Hammath was a city that existed within the territory of ancient Israel, one of the inheritances allotted to the tribe of Naphtali after Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: The fortified cities Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth were distributed as the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali (Joshua 19:35).
geography: It is a region located on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, presumed to be the hot-spring district south of present-day Tiberias. In its Hebrew etymology it is connected with a name meaning hot water, reflecting the hot-spring resources of the area.

remark: 2. A person or place mentioned in the genealogy of Judah, as the ancestor of the Kenites and chief of the Rechabites.
introduce: Hammath is a name recorded in 1 Chronicles 2, the ancestor of the Kenite scribal families and of the house of Rechab who lived within the tribe of Judah, or their place of origin.
biblecontents: The clans of scribes who lived at Jabez, namely the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites, were all Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab (1 Chronicles 2:55).
geography: It is presumed to be a settlement near Hebron and Jabez in the south of the hill country of Judah, and is the southern mountain region of the tribe of Judah where the nomadic Kenites were settling down.
history: The Kenites, descendants of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, joined with the tribe of Judah and formed the class of scribes who were in charge of law and written administration in ancient Israelite society, and became the matrix of the house of Rechab, which kept a tradition of piety.

introduce: Hammeah is a name designating a specific point on the wall, or a tower, mentioned at the time of the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the days of Nehemiah. In Hebrew it is called Hammeah (Hammeah), and this can also mean the number one hundred.
biblecontents: Eliashib the high priest and his brothers the priests built the Sheep Gate and consecrated it and set up its doors, and they built the wall and consecrated it as far as the Tower of the Hundred, and as far as the Tower of Hananel (Nehemiah 3:1); and above the Gate of Ephraim, and by the Old Gate, and by the Fish Gate, and the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they stopped at the Gate of the Guard (Nehemiah 12:39).
geography: The Tower of the Hundred was located in the northern section of the wall of Jerusalem and was adjacent to the Tower of Hananel. This point is presumed to be a defensive structure near the northeast corner of the wall of Jerusalem or at the northern boundary of the temple area.

remark: 1. A city of the tribe of Asher.
introduce: Hammon is one of the place names located on the boundary of the land distributed to the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan, a city included on the boundary of the inheritance of the tribe of Asher.
biblecontents: The boundary of the tribe of Asher reaches Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, as far as Great Sidon (Joshua 19:28).
geography: Hammon is located in the northern border region of the tribe of Asher, and is presumed to be the area of Wadi Hamul in southern present-day Lebanon, or Tell ed-Diba in its vicinity. It lies in the northern zone adjoining the Mediterranean coast, on the approach to the Sidon region.

remark: 2. A city distributed to the Levites from the territory of Naphtali
introduce: Hammon is a Levitical city of the tribe of Naphtali in Galilee recorded in 1 Chronicles 6 in the Old Testament, a place name identified with Hammoth-dor and Hammath in the book of Joshua.
biblecontents: They gave to the descendants of Gershom Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, Hammon with its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim with its pasturelands, from the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chronicles 6:76).
geography: It is identified with Hammath-Tiberias, the hot-spring district on the southern part of the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, south of present-day Tiberias.
history: It was an ancient Canaanite hot-spring resort city famous for its natural hot spring water, and a major settlement of Galilee that prospered through the Bronze Age and Iron Age down to the Roman period.

introduce: Hammoth-dor is a city in the region of Galilee mentioned in the book of Joshua in the Old Testament, a city of refuge and a residential city for the Levites allotted to the descendants of Gershon of the tribe of Levi.
biblecontents: A city located within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, it was given as a dwelling place to the clans of the house of Gershon, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:32).
geography: It is presumed to be a city in the hill country of Naphtali, and 1 Chronicles 6:76, a later record, writes the same place as Hammon. Beyond its being in the northern Galilee region, there is no archaeologically confirmed site for its exact ruins.

introduce: The Inspection Gate is a place name mentioned in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, a term designating a particular section of the wall. This name derives from the Hebrew Miphkad Gate, and carries the meaning of a place of review or inspection.
biblecontents: Nehemiah oversaw the work of repairing the wall past Malchijah the goldsmith, as far as opposite the Inspection Gate (Nehemiah 3:31).
geography: The Inspection Gate is presumed to have been located in the northeastern part of the wall of Jerusalem, and is regarded as one of the main points adjoining the Sheep Gate and leading into the temple area. Its exact archaeological location is disputed, but it is generally specified as a district near a tower or gate.
history: When the Jews rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem in the Persian period after the Babylonian exile, this place seems to have been used as a space where administrative or military inspection took place. Since the name Inspection Gate itself means an official assembly point or a place of inspection, it suggests that it was used as an important stronghold at the time of the repair of the wall.

introduce: Kibroth-hattaavah was a place where the Israelite people who left Egypt stayed during the wilderness journey, and it is where an incident occurred in which, through craving, they ate a great quantity of quail and many people died.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as the place where the Israelites, by indulging their craving in the wilderness, provoked the anger of the LORD and incurred His wrath (Deuteronomy 9:22). It was also the place where the people craved meat, complained, and suffered a plague (Numbers 11:34).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is presumed to lie on the route from the wilderness of Sinai to the wilderness of Paran, and it is recorded as a stage of the journey before Hazeroth.

introduce: Mount Hermon is a mountain about 2,814 meters above sea level at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range, situated in the border zone between northern Israel, Lebanon, and Syria. In the Bible it is often mentioned as a symbol of abundant water resources, compared to the dew that falls on Mount Zion, and as the northern boundary of Canaan.
biblecontents: The dew of Hermon is described as falling on the mountains of Zion, and this is portrayed as the place where the LORD commanded the blessing (Psalms 133:3). It is recorded that the boundary of the region the Israelites conquered extended as far as Mount Hermon on the east side of the Jordan (Joshua 12:1). Also, in the love song of Solomon, the view looking down from the top of Hermon is mentioned (Song of Solomon 4:8).
geography: Mount Hermon is covered with snow all year round and becomes the main source of water for the upper Jordan River. As the moist winds blowing from the Mediterranean meet the cold air of this mountain, they form thick fog and a large amount of dew. This area is composed of limestone terrain, and thanks to its altitude, markedly higher than the surrounding plains, its influence extends as far as the area north of the Sea of Galilee.
history: In biblical times this mountain was called Baal-hermon by the Canaanites and became an object of worship. In the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan, this region was regarded as the limit line of the northern territory. Historically it was included in the territory of Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites, and afterward it was treated as a strategic stronghold of the region distributed to the tribes of Israel.

introduce: Hena is a place mentioned in the Old Testament as one of the cities conquered during the period of expansion of the Assyrian empire. In the Hebrew Bible this name appears mainly alongside Ivvah (Iva) or Avva (Ava), and it is cited as an example of the nations that the kings of Assyria destroyed through their conquests.
biblecontents: The Rabshakeh, an official of the king of Assyria, boasted to Hezekiah king of Judah of Assyria's military victories and, asking in return where the kings of Hamath and Arpad were, and the kings of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah, threatened that Jerusalem too could not escape from the hand of Assyria (2 Kings 18:34). Afterward also, in the letter sent by Sennacherib king of Assyria, he urged Hezekiah to surrender by mentioning the destruction of the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, and the kings of Hena and Ivvah (2 Kings 19:13). The same content is described in the book of Isaiah as well, stating that the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, and the kings of Hena and Ivvah had been conquered by Assyria (Isaiah 37:13).
geography: The exact location of Hena has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to have been in northern Mesopotamia or the region of Syria. Considering that Hamath and Arpad, which appear together in the list of cities Assyria conquered at that time, were major cities of the Syrian region, it is suggested to be highly likely that Hena too was a strategic stronghold on the upper Euphrates River or in its vicinity.
history: Between the 8th and 7th centuries BC, Assyria expanded its empire and subjugated the surrounding small states one after another. Hena appears to be one of the city-states conquered in the course of this Assyrian westward policy. The quotation recorded in the Bible contains the historical circumstances showing that the Assyrian empire subdued the surrounding nations as part of a coercive diplomatic policy. In scholarship Hena is sometimes identified with the region of Ana (Ana) appearing in Akkadian records, but clear archaeological proof still requires further research.

introduce: Hethlon is a place name appearing in the book of Ezekiel in the Old Testament, one of the reference points defining the future northern boundary of Israel when it is restored.
biblecontents: In describing the boundary of this land, Ezekiel recorded that the northern boundary would be from the road to Hethlon to the entrance of Zedad (Ezekiel 47:15). Also, Ezekiel 48:1 mentions that the region from the northern end by way of the road of Hethlon to the entrance of Hamath is the northern boundary of the territory that will be the portion of the tribe of Dan (Ezekiel 48:1).
geography: Hethlon is presumed to be located near the Beqaa Valley, the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges, and is a strategic point lying on the way to the entrance of Hamath. It corresponds to the area of present-day Lebanon or the northern Syrian border region.

remark: A mountain near Aijalon on the boundary between Judah and Dan.
introduce: Heres is a place name mentioned in the book of Judges, referring both to a place located in the region of the Valley of Aijalon and to a place that Gideon passed through on his way back after the battle with Midian.
biblecontents: The Amorites continued to live in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but as the power of the house of Joseph grew strong, they were put to forced labor (Judges 1:35). After Gideon pursued Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, he returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres (Judges 8:13).
geography: Heres is presumed to refer to a mountainous region or a sloping road around the Valley of Aijalon. The Valley of Aijalon is a strategic stronghold linking the hill country of Judah with the coastal plain, and is adjacent to the areas near Beth-shemesh.
history: It shows the political situation in which, in the course of the early Israelite tribes settling in the land of Canaan, the native Amorites, relying on powerful weapons, occupied the plains and valley regions and checked the expansion of the Israelite tribes. It can be seen that in the time of Gideon this region was used as a military route of movement running from east to west.

introduce: Hereth is a forested district of Judah known as the place where David hid while escaping the pursuit of King Saul.
biblecontents: On the advice of the prophet Gad to David to go into the land of Judah, David departed and came to the forest of Hereth (1 Samuel 22:5).
geography: Its exact location has not been confirmed, but it is presumed to be a densely wooded area within the territory of the tribe of Judah, and it had topographical features that made it easy to hide from Saul's army.

introduce: Hermon is a high mountain region at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range, a geographical stronghold that is the source of the headwaters of the Jordan River. In the Bible it is mentioned mainly as the northern boundary of Israel and as a geographical reference point of the wars of conquest.
biblecontents: Israel took the land east of the Jordan from the Valley of the Arnon as far as Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:8). The Sidonians call Mount Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir (Deuteronomy 3:9). The land Israel took was from Aroer as far as Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 4:48). The coalition of northern Canaan encamped in the land of Mizpah below Mount Hermon and resisted (Joshua 11:3). Joshua conquered the region from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, to Baal-gad below Mount Hermon (Joshua 11:17). The land east of the Jordan that Israel conquered extends as far as Mount Hermon (Joshua 12:1). The region ruled by the half-tribe of Manasseh was Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all of Bashan (Joshua 12:5). The territory of Mount Hermon includes the region extending from Baal-gad to the entrance of Hamath (Joshua 13:5). Israel conquered Mount Hermon and all of Bashan, the land of the Geshurites and the Maacathites (Joshua 13:11). The descendants of the half-tribe of Manasseh spread out and lived from Bashan as far as Mount Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon (1 Chronicles 5:23).
geography: Mount Hermon boasts a height of about 2,814 meters above sea level and is covered with snow all year round, so it becomes an important source of water for the Jordan River. Geographically it lies at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range, at the point where the borders of present-day Lebanon, Syria, and Israel meet. This mountain served as the northern boundary of Canaan and as a strategic military barrier.
history: Mount Hermon was a region with religious and strategic significance for the various peoples of the ancient Near East. According to the biblical record, the name by which this mountain was called differed from people to people, which shows that various cultures crossed and occupied this region. In the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan, Hermon functioned as the limit line and symbolic stronghold of the northern conquest. The region of Bashan and Hermon was distributed as the inheritance of the half-tribe of Manasseh, and it has the historical background of forming the northeastern line of defense of Israel.

introduce: Hezron is a proper noun used in the Bible both as a personal name and as a place name. As personal names there are Hezron son of Reuben (Numbers 26:6) and Hezron son of Perez (Numbers 26:21), and as a place name it is a place on the southern boundary of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:3).
biblecontents: Hezron, as the son of Perez, became the ancestor of the clan of the Hezronites (Numbers 26:21). Also, among the descendants of Jacob, Hezron, the son of Perez, is recorded as being of the generation of the grandsons of Judah (Numbers 26:6). Geographically, Hezron is located on the boundary line of the tribe of Judah in southern Canaan, and is mentioned at the point where, passing Addar, it reaches Azmon and arrives at the Brook of Egypt (Joshua 15:3).
geography: Hezron is presumed to be a place located in the Negev desert region of southern Canaan. The southern boundary of the tribe of Judah described in Joshua 15 begins at the Ascent of Akrabbim and passes Zin and continues south of Kadesh-barnea, and Hezron appears as a major stronghold within this boundary line. In modern geographical terms it is difficult to pinpoint its exact location, but it is generally regarded as a strategic stronghold near the east or south of Kadesh-barnea.
history: Hezron functioned as one of the reference points dividing territory in the early process of setting the boundaries for the settlement of the tribe of Judah. Given the character of the Negev region, where herding and farming were mixed, this area served as a passage linking Egypt and Canaan, and became a reference for administrative and military boundaries in the process by which the tribe of Judah secured its influence over the southern region.

introduce: Heshmon is one of the southern cities of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the book of Joshua, a place name located on the boundary of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: Heshmon is included in the list of cities at the southern end of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:27).
geography: Heshmon is presumed to be located in the Negev desert region of southern Judah, and although its exact location has not been clearly established archaeologically, it is generally interpreted as the southern boundary region southeast of Beersheba or near Arad.

introduce: Heshbon was an ancient city located in the Amorite land east of the Jordan, a strategic stronghold that the Israelites conquered on their journey to Canaan.
biblecontents: Israel asked to pass through the territory of Sihon king of the Amorites but was refused, and after a battle at Jahaz they captured that territory, including Heshbon (Numbers 21:25). Heshbon was originally the royal city of the king of Moab, but Sihon took it and made it his own capital (Numbers 21:26). The fall of Heshbon was sung by the poets as an event symbolizing the defeat of Sihon and the victory of Israel (Numbers 21:27, Numbers 21:28, Numbers 21:30). God commanded Moses to conquer Sihon and his land (Numbers 21:34), and afterward the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked to rebuild this region as cities for their livestock (Numbers 32:3, Numbers 32:37). Moses recalled that he had destroyed Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth, and Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon (Deuteronomy 1:4). God delivered Sihon the king of Heshbon and his land into the hand of Israel and had them begin the conquest (Deuteronomy 2:24).
geography: Heshbon is presumed to be Tell Hesban, near Madaba in present-day Jordan. This is a plateau east of the Jordan, and with fertile farmland flowing with milk and honey and broad pastures suitable for raising livestock, it has an economically important location.
history: It appears to have been inhabited from the Bronze Age, and in the early Iron Age it held regional supremacy as the center of the Amorite kingdom. After the Israelite conquest, it lay in the border region of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and at times became an object of territorial dispute, and in later times it was a city that went through continual political change in its relations with neighboring states such as Ammon and Moab.

introduce: Heshbon Bath-rabbim is a figurative place name appearing in Song of Solomon 7:4, meaning the large pool (pond) near the gate of ancient Heshbon.
biblecontents: It is mentioned in the passage of Song of Solomon where the bridegroom compares the eyes of the bride to the pools in Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim, describing her beauty (Song of Solomon 7:4).
geography: Heshbon is a city located in the border region of Moab and Ammon east of the Jordan, presumed to be Tell Hesban near Madaba in present-day Jordan. Bath-rabbim is a name designating a reservoir or large pond that is known to have been near the gate of Heshbon (Song of Solomon 7:4).
history: Heshbon was originally the capital of Sihon king of the Amorites, and it became an important stronghold in the course of Israel's conquest of Canaan. The name Bath-rabbim carries the meaning in Hebrew of daughter of many or a place where many gather, which suggests that the water facility of the city of Heshbon at that time was a center of commercial or social exchange (Song of Solomon 7:4).

introduce: Helkath is a place name mentioned in the Old Testament, a place that appears in the process of the allotment of the tribes of Israel and in the list of cities of the Levites.
biblecontents: Helkath is recorded as one of the cities included in the boundary of the inheritance that the tribe of Asher obtained by lot (Joshua 19:25). Afterward it was assigned as one of the cities of the descendants of Gershon, the Levites, within the territory of the tribe of Asher (Joshua 21:31).
geography: Its exact location is debated among scholars, but it is generally presumed to have been within the territory of the tribe of Asher in the region of Galilee. Some scholars explain it by associating it with a modern site such as Tell al-Khar, but this has not been clearly established archaeologically.

introduce: Helkath-hazzurim is a place name that in Hebrew carries the meaning "field of flints" or "field of sharp swords." It is a place appearing in 2 Samuel 2:16, recorded as having been named in the course of the clash between the army of David and the army of Ish-bosheth in the early period of the Davidic dynasty.
biblecontents: When David's men and the men of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul met by the pool of Gibeon, each seized his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his side, so that they fell down together; after this incident occurred, that place was called Helkath-hazzurim (2 Samuel 2:16).
geography: It is presumed to be located near Gibeon, but its exact location has not been determined archaeologically. Gibeon is presumed to be the area of present-day el-Jib, and the place is understood as a point in the hill country that was either where the boundaries of the tribe of Benjamin and the tribe of Judah crossed or a strategic military stronghold at that time.
history: It is an event that occurred at the time when the dispute over succession to the throne between David and Ish-bosheth was intensifying after the death of King Saul. It reflects the historical situation in which this battle began as a contest of strength between elite troops, or a ritual duel, before leading to a large-scale war between the two armies, but ended in a tragic slaughter.

remark: A country of southern Europe, located west of Central Asia and east of Italy.
introduce: Greece is a term used in the Bible mainly to refer to the region of ancient Greece and its cultural sphere, or to the people who came from there. In the Old Testament it is mostly translated as Javan and signifies a future great power or a trading partner, while in the New Testament it is used as a term for the Hellenistic cultural sphere, in contrast to the Jewish tradition, or for Gentiles who spoke the Greek language.
biblecontents: Daniel 8:21 says that the shaggy male goat is the king of Greece, and prophesies an empire that will arise in the future (Daniel 8:21). Daniel 10:20 and 11:2 appear in a context implying that after the Persian empire, the rulers of Greece will arise (Daniel 10:20, Daniel 11:2). Joel 3:6 describes a situation in which the people of Judah and Jerusalem are sold to the Greeks (Joel 3:6). Zechariah 9:13 shows a military confrontation in which the sons of Zion are stirred up against the sons of Greece (Zechariah 9:13). In the New Testament the Syrophoenician woman is called a Greek (Mark 7:26), and there appears the concern that the Jews who were dispersed might go to the Greeks among them and teach (John 7:35). Among those who wished to see Jesus at the Passover were Greeks (John 12:20), and when Jesus was hung on the cross, one of the languages recorded on the inscription was Greek (John 19:20). There is also a record of conflict within the early church over the matter of relief between the Hellenistic Jews and the Hebrew Jews (Acts 6:1).
geography: Ancient Greece means a broad cultural and geographic sphere that includes the southern tip of the Balkan Peninsula, the islands around the Aegean Sea, and Asia Minor and the eastern Mediterranean coastal region, which expanded afterward through the conquests of Alexander the Great. The region of Greece in the Bible, seen from Palestine, embraces not only mainland Greece to the northwest but all the Hellenized cities where Hellenistic culture had taken root.
history: In the Old Testament period Greece was regarded as a relatively rising power compared with Babylon or Persia, but after the wars of conquest of Alexander the Great it took hegemony over the Mediterranean world. Afterward, as the Hellenistic empires were formed, the Greek language and culture spread throughout the Near East. In the New Testament period the Roman empire ruled Palestine, but the common language of the Mediterranean world was Greek, and Greek ways of thinking and philosophy had deeply permeated society as a whole.

introduce: Helam is a region mentioned in 2 Samuel 10 as the site of a decisive battle that took place between David's army and the Aramean coalition.
biblecontents: Hadadezer sent and brought out the Arameans who were beyond the Euphrates River, and they came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer leading them (2 Samuel 10:16). David gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam; and the Arameans arrayed themselves against David and fought with him (2 Samuel 10:17).
geography: The exact location of Helam has not been clearly established archaeologically. However, according to the biblical record, it was the place where the Aramean coalition that came from beyond the Euphrates River assembled, and since it is the point David reached after crossing the Jordan River in pursuit, it is presumed to be somewhere in the region east of the Jordan. Some regard it as northern Syria or the vicinity of Hauran.
history: It is the site of a battle that took place in the course of the war that the Ammonites waged against Israel by hiring the Arameans, in the reign of King David. In this battle David killed Shobach, the commander of the Arameans, and defeated the Aramean coalition, so that the Davidic kingdom gained military superiority over the Aramean power, then a neighboring great power, and laid the foundation for territorial expansion.

introduce: Helbah is one of the cities located in the land distributed to the tribe of Asher in ancient Israelite times, recorded as a place from which the Israelites, in the course of the conquest, failed to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants.
biblecontents: Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon, or of Ahlab, or of Achzib, or of Helbah, or of Aphik, or of Rehob (Judges 1:31)
geography: Its exact location is a matter of dispute among scholars, but it is generally presumed to have been in ancient Phoenicia or near the plain of Acco in the region of northern Galilee.

introduce: Helbon was a city famed for its wine production in the ancient Near East, a region that supplied an important commodity in the trade network of Tyre.
biblecontents: Damascus traded with Tyre in the wine of Helbon and white wool (Ezekiel 27:18).
geography: It is identified with the Aleppo region of present-day Syria. Aleppo, lying on a fertile plain, has been a center of agriculture and transportation since ancient times, and in particular had climate and soil conditions suited to the cultivation of grapes.
history: Helbon was one of the major cities of the Aramean kingdom, and it is mentioned as an important production center in Assyrian and Babylonian records as well. In the period of the ancient Persian empire it was famous as a region supplying fine wine to the Persian royal court, and it was evaluated as a trading base of very high economic value.

introduce: Horem is an ancient city recorded in Joshua 19 in the Old Testament, one of the nineteen fortified cities distributed to the tribe of Naphtali in northern Galilee.
biblecontents: As fortified cities belonging to the inheritance of the descendants of Naphtali, Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, Beth-shemesh, and others are mentioned, nineteen cities in all with their villages (Joshua 19:38).
geography: Horem was located in the rugged mountain plateau region of Upper Galilee. The place name means a devoted place or a sacred sanctuary, and it is identified with Khirbet Harah (Khirbet Harah, present-day Horvat Harim), the ruins of a high ridge overlooking the Huleh basin just south of the present-day Lebanese border. Situated on a strategic height southwest of Kedesh, it has topographical conditions that allowed it to watch over the mountain routes of northern Galilee.
history: It developed into a fortified defensive city from the Late Bronze Age of Canaan, and in the Iron Age, in the period of Israelite settlement, it was incorporated as a key defensive stronghold guarding the northern border of the tribe of Naphtali. Together with the neighboring Migdal-el and Beth-anath, it performed the function of a military stronghold protecting the agricultural settlements of Upper Galilee against invasion by northern foreign powers.

introduce: Horeb is mentioned in the Bible as a place identified with the mountain of God or Mount Sinai, and is depicted as the place where Moses first met God and a symbolic point where the Israelites received the law.
biblecontents: Moses, who was tending sheep in the wilderness of Midian, met God, who appeared in the flame of the burning bush at Horeb, the mountain of God (Exodus 3:1). When the Israelites quarreled at Rephidim because there was no water, God instructed Moses to strike the rock at Mount Horeb (Exodus 17:6). The Israelites repented at Mount Horeb by stripping off their ornaments (Exodus 33:6). Horeb appears as a point eleven days' journey from Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:2). God commanded the Israelites to depart from Mount Horeb and march on (Deuteronomy 1:6). The Israelites passed through the wilderness and arrived at Mount Horeb (Deuteronomy 1:19). At Mount Horeb God gathered the people and let them hear the law (Deuteronomy 4:10). God gave the Ten Commandments out of the midst of the fire (Deuteronomy 4:15). God made a covenant with Israel at Horeb (Deuteronomy 5:2). At Mount Horeb the Israelites made a golden calf and incurred the wrath of God (Deuteronomy 9:8).
geography: There are differences of opinion in scholarship about the exact location of Horeb; traditionally the Jebel Musa area in the southern Sinai Peninsula is cited as the leading site, but some scholars propose the northern Arabian Peninsula or other regions as candidates. It is generally regarded as an isolated mountainous terrain or a part of a massive rock mountain range.
history: It is an important historical place connected with the route of the Exodus of the Israelite people from the end of the Bronze Age to the early Iron Age. It is possible that this region lay near a point where the nomads of the ancient Near East and trade routes crossed, and according to archaeological investigation, traces of religious rites performed in a particular period have also been found.

introduce: Horonaim was a city located in the territory of the ancient kingdom of Moab, a place mentioned as one of the main place names when judgment against Moab is pronounced in the prophetic books of the Bible.
biblecontents: Isaiah, prophesying the destruction of Moab, described that a cry of anguish would be heard on the road to Horonaim (Isaiah 15:5). Jeremiah spoke of the cry of ruin and great destruction coming from Horonaim (Jeremiah 48:3), and prophesied that there would be wailing on the descent of the slope to Horonaim as well (Jeremiah 48:5). Horonaim also appears as a region where the cry from there spreads so widely that it is heard as far as Jahaz (Jeremiah 48:34).
geography: The exact location of Horonaim has not been confirmed archaeologically, but it is generally presumed to be a city located on the Moabite plateau, the region southeast of the Dead Sea, or on a slope in its vicinity. The etymology of the name carries the meaning of two caves, so it seems to be related to its topographical features.
history: Horonaim also appears in the record of Mesha king of Moab, known as the Mesha Stele, in which Mesha mentioned the Horonites who lived in this region. This suggests that this city was a region that played an important role in the governing power and economic situation of the kingdom of Moab.

introduce: Horonite is a place name appearing in the book of Nehemiah in the Bible, mentioned mainly in connection with the origin of the person Sanballat. This place name is presumed to refer to Beth-horon or a region adjacent to it.
biblecontents: When Sanballat the Horonite heard that a man had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel, he was greatly disturbed (Nehemiah 2:10). When Tobiah the Ammonite, Geshem the Arab, and Sanballat the Horonite heard this news, they mocked and despised Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:19). Because one of the grandsons of Eliashib the high priest had become the son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, Nehemiah drove him away (Nehemiah 13:28).
geography: Scholars regard Horon as referring to the regions of Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon in the hill country of Ephraim. It lies about 16 km northwest of Jerusalem, on a slope near the Valley of Aijalon, a strategic stronghold linking the coastal plain and Jerusalem.
history: It is deeply connected with the region of Samaria under Persian imperial rule. Sanballat is presumed to be the governor of Samaria at that time, and his being called a Horonite suggests that he was an influential regional official within the Persian administrative district. This region was one of the centers of political and religious opposition while the Jewish community was rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem.

remark: 1. A mountain on the Edomite border region, where Aaron died.
introduce: Mount Hor is a place name located on the border of the land of Edom, known as an important turning point in the Exodus journey of the Israelite people and as the place where Aaron the high priest died.
biblecontents: The Israelites left Kadesh and came to Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22). The LORD told Moses and Aaron that Aaron would be gathered to his fathers at Mount Hor (Numbers 20:23). Moses took Aaron and his son Eleazar and went up Mount Hor (Numbers 20:25). Aaron died on the top of the mountain in the sight of the congregation (Numbers 20:27). Israel set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea to go around the land of Edom (Numbers 21:4). The Israelites left Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor (Numbers 33:37). When Aaron went up Mount Hor at the command of God and died there, he was one hundred and twenty-three years old (Numbers 33:38, 33:39). The Israelites left Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah (Numbers 33:41).
geography: Mount Hor is traditionally identified with Jebel Harun near Petra in Jordan. It is adjacent to the border of the land of Edom, and its surrounding terrain is formed of rugged, high rock mountains, giving it the geographic character of a strategic stronghold and a boundary marker.
history: In the Bronze Age and early Iron Age, the Edomite region was within the sphere of influence of states neighboring Israel. Mount Hor is mentioned as an important stronghold in the course of the movement along the border with the kingdom of Edom during Israel's wilderness journey, and it reflects the political and geographic tension between Israel and Edom, who were trying to pass through this region at that time.

remark: 2. A hill on the northern boundary of Israel.
introduce: Hor means mountain in Hebrew, and in Numbers 34:7 it is a place name mentioned as a reference point fixing the northern boundary of the land of Canaan that the Israelites were to take.
biblecontents: When God explained to Moses the boundary of the land of Canaan that the Israelites would obtain as an inheritance, it was specified that the northern boundary should run from the Great Sea to Mount Hor (Numbers 34:7).
geography: The Mount Hor mentioned in Numbers 34:7 is presumed to be a different place from the mountain in the Edomite region where Aaron died. Scholars regard this point as referring to the Lebanon mountain range, the northern boundary of Canaan, or a high mountainous region in its vicinity.
history: In the geographical perspective of the ancient Near East, this region has meaning as a political and administrative marker setting the northern limit of the territory where the tribes of Israel were to settle. Because it is difficult to find a case in which this name became fixed as a specific place name in literature outside the Bible, it is interpreted as a geographical indicator representing the ideal territorial extent of Israel at that time.

introduce: Hormah is an ancient city located in the Negev region of southern Canaan, a place that appears as an important military and administrative stronghold in the Israelites' conquest of Canaan and in the period of the allotment of the tribes.
biblecontents: Hormah is the place to which the Israelites fled when, trying to enter Canaan, they were defeated by the Amalekites and the Canaanites (Numbers 14:45). Afterward Israel utterly destroyed the cities of the Canaanites and named that place Hormah (Numbers 21:3). Deuteronomy also records that Israel was defeated by the Amorites in Mount Seir and was chased as far as Hormah (Deuteronomy 1:44). The king of Hormah is included in the list of the Canaanite kings that Joshua conquered (Joshua 12:14). It is also mentioned as one of the cities that the tribe of Simeon received as an inheritance (Joshua 19:4), and Judah and Simeon together captured the city called Zephath and changed its name to Hormah (Judges 1:17). In the time of David it is recorded as one of the cities to which David sent the spoil he had taken from the Amalekites (1 Chronicles 4:30).
geography: Hormah is presumed to be located in the wilderness region of the Negev, east or southeast of Beersheba. As for its specific location, Tell el-Milh and Tell Masos are cited as candidates, but there is no single archaeologically established point.
history: Hormah was originally the area called Zephath, a defensive stronghold of southern Canaan. According to the biblical record, it has significance both as the place of Israel's early failed entry and as the spoil of the subsequent successful conquest. After it was conquered jointly by the tribes of Judah and Simeon, it was incorporated into the territory of the tribe of Simeon, and it functioned as a southern strategic stronghold down to the era of the Davidic monarchy.

introduce: According to the biblical record, the Horites were one of the ancient tribes who lived in the hill country of Seir, and are regarded as a native group of early southern Canaan and the Edomite region.
biblecontents: The coalition led by Chedorlaomer struck the Horites in their hill country of Seir, as far as El-paran (Genesis 14:6). The names of Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan, the chiefs of the Horite clans, descendants of Seir, are recorded (Genesis 36:20-21). The list of the chiefs of the Horite clans from the land of Seir is mentioned once more, and it is stated that they became chiefs according to their clans in the land of Seir (Genesis 36:29-30). There is a record that in the past the Horites lived in Seir, but the descendants of Esau destroyed them and lived in their place (Deuteronomy 2:12, Deuteronomy 2:22).
geography: The main dwelling place of the Horites was the hill country of Seir, a rugged mountainous region east of the Arabah valley in present-day southern Jordan. This area has the topographical character of extending from the south of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba, and with its many caves and rocky terrain favorable to defense, it had conditions suitable for the early inhabitants to live.
history: From the viewpoint of biblical archaeology, a hypothesis has been raised that the Horite tribes are etymologically connected with the Hurrians of the ancient Near East, but within the biblical text they are described as the original inhabitants of Edom. They appear to have been conquered or absorbed by the Edomites, the descendants of Esau, and afterward integrated as members of Edomite tribal society. This process shows one aspect of the history of the movements and replacements of peoples that the people of Israel encountered on their way to Canaan.

remark: 1. A Levitical city in Judah.
introduce: Holon was a city located within the territory of the ancient tribe of Judah, and it was one of the cities distributed to the tribe of Levi after Joshua's wars of conquest.
biblecontents: It is mentioned among the cities in the hill country of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:51), and it was afterward assigned, as a city for the Levites belonging to the descendants of Kohath, in which to carry out the priestly office (Joshua 21:15).
geography: Holon is thought to have been located in the hill country of Judah, specifically in the region near Hebron. Judging from the order of the biblical list, its exact location is classed as the southern hill country adjoining Debir, Anab, and Eshtemoa.

remark: 2. A city of Moab.
introduce: Holon was one of the cities located in the ancient land of Moab, a place name mentioned when the book of Jeremiah declares judgment upon Moab.
biblecontents: Judgment has come upon the plain, that is, upon Dibon, Nebo, Beth-diblathaim, Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon, Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near (Jeremiah 48:21-24). Holon is listed among the principal cities of Moab that were the object of this judgment (Jeremiah 48:21).
geography: Holon is thought to have been located on the plain of Moab, the plateau east of the Dead Sea, on the east side of the Jordan River. Its exact location has not been clearly established archaeologically, but together with nearby Dibon and Jahaz, it appears to have been included within the core administrative and defensive districts of the kingdom of Moab.
history: Holon originally belonged to the territory of the Moabites, but it is possible that its ownership changed hands as a result of territorial disputes with neighboring powers and shifting political dynamics. In the time of Jeremiah it was part of the territory of Moab and stood in the midst of the expansion of the Babylonian empire and the resulting danger of regional destruction.

introduce: Hormah was one of the cities located in the southern part of the ancient Wilderness of Judea; in the geographical records of the Bible, it is a place mentioned in connection with the distribution of territory to the tribe of Judah and with the movements of David.
biblecontents: In Joshua 15 it is listed among the cities of the inheritance that the tribe of the descendants of Judah obtained by lot (Joshua 15:30). Also, in 1 Samuel 30, it is one of the places mentioned when David, after his victory in the battle with the Amalekites, divided the spoil and sent it to the elders of Judah who were with him and to various localities (1 Samuel 30:30).
geography: It is thought to have been located in the Negev desert region in the south of Judea, and scholars consider that it lay geographically close to towns such as nearby Beersheba and Moladah.

introduce: Hor-haggidgad is one of the places where the Israelites camped during the journey of the exodus; it is a place they passed through after setting out from Bene-jaakan, before moving on to the next destination, Jotbathah.
biblecontents: The Israelites set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad (Numbers 33:32). They set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah (Numbers 33:33).
geography: Its exact location has not been pinpointed archaeologically to this day; it is thought to have been somewhere near the Arabah valley, or in the northern or eastern part of the Negev desert.

introduce: The Hebrew Yam Suph, translated in the Bible as the Red Sea, literally means "Sea of Reeds," and it appears as an important boundary and geographical setting in the route of the exodus and in Israel's journey through the wilderness.
biblecontents: God raised a strong west wind and drove the swarm of locusts into the Red Sea (Exodus 10:19). God did not lead the people by way of the land of the Philistines, but led them around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea (Exodus 13:18). Pharaoh's chariots and his army were cast into the Red Sea (Exodus 15:4). Moses led Israel on from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur (Exodus 15:22). It was promised that the boundary of Israel's territory would extend to the Red Sea (Exodus 23:31).
