Because the Amalekites and the Canaanites lived in the valley, the people were told to set out toward the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea (Numbers 14:25). Israel set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea to go around the land of Edom (Numbers 21:4). Israel camped by the Red Sea and then moved on to the Desert of Sin (Numbers 33:10, 11). God commanded Israel to set out once more into the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea (Deuteronomy 1:40).
geography: Yam Suph is understood not as a term for the whole of the modern Red Sea but as a geographical term covering the reed-filled marshlands east of the Nile Delta, the Gulf of Suez, or the region of the Gulf of Aqaba. Given the topographical features of the ancient Near East, it is likely that it included coastal areas where fresh water and sea water meet.
history: Research continues to compare the geographical names of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the late Bronze Age with the biblical record. At that time the eastern frontier of Egypt was an environment suited to the growth of papyrus and other reeds, and, in connection with Egypt's defense system, it served as an important route of travel.

introduce: Hukok is one of the cities allotted to the descendants of the tribe of Levi, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6 of the Old Testament, and it was a place located within the territory of the tribe of Asher.
biblecontents: Hukok, located within the territory of the tribe of Asher, is recorded as a city allotted to the Levites who were descendants of Merari (1 Chronicles 6:75).
geography: Its specific location has not been clearly established archaeologically, but it is generally thought to have been in the inland region of northern Galilee, which was the territory of the tribe of Asher.

introduce: Hukkok is a place name mentioned in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament, specified as one of the boundary points of the inheritance allotted to the tribe of Naphtali at the time of the conquest of Canaan.
biblecontents: The boundary reaches Aznoth-tabor on the west, and from there goes out to Hukkok; it reaches Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west, and on the east it reaches Judah at the Jordan (Joshua 19:34).
geography: Its exact present-day location has not been established archaeologically, but scholars suggest that it may be connected with the village of Yaquq near the inland region west of the Sea of Galilee, or near the Arbel valley.

introduce: Humtah is one of the cities included in the inheritance of the tribe of Judah recorded in the book of Joshua of the Old Testament. It is classified as a place located near Hebron.
biblecontents: It is mentioned as one of the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the Israelites as the inheritance of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:54).
geography: It belongs to the hill country of Judah and is thought to be a city located close to Hebron. Its exact modern location has not been clearly established archaeologically, but scholars generally conjecture that it lay somewhere in the hilly country southeast or south of Hebron.

introduce: The Sukkites are a name that appears in 2 Chronicles 12:3, a people or place mentioned as one of the military groups that Shishak king of Egypt mobilized with him when he invaded Judah.
biblecontents: The background is mentioned of how, in the text of 1 Samuel 14:21, the Hebrews who had formerly been with the Philistines and had gone up with them into the camp from all around turned to the side of Israel, and how in a particular version the name came to be rendered as Sukkites (1 Samuel 14:21).
geography: According to research by ancient Near Eastern sources and historians, the Sukkites are thought to refer to a people or a dwelling place in the region of Libya. Ancient Egyptian records mention Lub or Rebu, tribes who lived in the western part of Libya, and this name is considered to be linguistically related to the biblical name.
history: When Shishak, of Libyan origin and of the Twenty-second Dynasty, invaded Judah around the tenth century BC, he included Libyan mercenaries in his army. They were the main military resource mobilized for Shishak's policy of military expansion, and through the origins of these troops the Bible depicts the formidable military coalition of Shishak.

introduce: Hierapolis was an ancient city located in the region of Phrygia in Asia Minor, situated near Pamukkale in present-day Denizli Province, Türkiye. In antiquity it gained renown as a city of healing because of its hot spring waters and limestone terrain, and it was one of the regions where an early Christian community formed.
biblecontents: I testify that Epaphras labors much for those in Colossae and Laodicea and for those in Hierapolis (Colossians 4:13).
geography: Hierapolis lies on the high plateau on the north side of the Lycus Valley, facing Laodicea and Colossae. It has the topographical feature of enormous limestone terraces formed by hot spring waters rich in lime that well up from underground.
history: It is known to have been founded around the second century BC by Eumenes II of the kingdom of Pergamum. Afterward, under Roman rule, it flourished greatly as a hot spring resort, and after the great earthquake that occurred around AD 80 it was rebuilt, and public facilities typical of a Roman-era city, such as a theater, a gymnasium, and baths, were expanded. In the early Christian period, tradition also holds that it was the place where the apostle Philip was martyred, and it served as an important religious center up to the Byzantine period.

introduce: The Hivites are a people recorded as one of the sons of Canaan, and throughout the Bible they are mentioned as one of the seven principal peoples who lived in the land of Canaan. Spread over many cities of the Palestinian region, they appear as a group that interacted with the Israelites in their process of settlement in the Old Testament period.
biblecontents: The Hivites are mentioned as one of the descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17). Hamor, the father of Shechem, who violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, is recorded as a Hivite (Genesis 34:2). Oholibamah, the daughter of Esau's wife Anah, appears as the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite (Genesis 36:2). God promised to deliver the Israelites from the suffering of Egypt and to bring them to a good and broad land where the Hivites dwell (Exodus 3:8, Exodus 3:17, Exodus 13:5). When Israel entered Canaan, God declared that He would drive out the Hivites (Exodus 23:23, Exodus 33:2, Exodus 34:11). He also said that He would send the hornet ahead to drive them out (Exodus 23:28).
geography: The biblical text describes the dwelling place of the Hivites as the whole land of Canaan, and in particular records that they lived in the area of Shechem and in the land of Mizpah below Mount Hermon. Specifically, it implies that they were spread over a wide area, from the hill country of southern Canaan to the vicinity of the Lebanon range in the north.
history: From the viewpoint of history and archaeology, it has continued to be suggested that the Hivites may have been related to the Hurrians. On the basis of the migration routes of the Hurrian people that appear in ancient Near Eastern cuneiform records and the linguistic similarity of the name Hivite, there is a theory that they were one of the migrant groups of Indo-Aryan or Hurrian stock who entered the land of Canaan in the latter half of the second millennium BC.
